items: Science is both a body of knowledge and a process for building it. It explains the natural world using evidence gathered by observation and experiment, and that evidence requirement is what separates scientific claims from opinions.

A scientific claim must be testable against evidence from the natural world. Questions of value or morals, such as “should we clone animals?”, can be informed by science but cannot be answered by it, because no experiment can measure what is right or wrong.

Scientific knowledge is evidence-based (empirical): ideas are accepted because they agree with observations and experimental results, not because of who proposed them. A famous name does not make an idea correct.

An observation is what is directly detected with the senses or instruments, such as “the broth went cloudy”. An inference is an explanation drawn from an observation, such as “microorganisms grew in the broth”. Scientists keep them separate, as an inference can be wrong when the observation is right.
Scientific ideas are never declared final, yet the best of them last for generations. Two ideas explain why: ideas are open to revision, and they must be capable of being shown wrong.

Scientific knowledge is tentative but durable: any idea can be revised if new evidence contradicts it, yet well-tested ideas survive for a long time. The cell theory (the idea that all living things are made of cells) has survived more than 150 years of testing.
Tentative does not mean weak or a guess. It means the idea is held open to revision, while still being backed by a large amount of evidence.

An idea must be falsifiable: it must be possible, in principle, to imagine an observation that would show the idea is wrong. The philosopher Karl Popper made falsifiability his test of whether an idea is scientific.
Evidence can support an idea or refute it, but it can never prove an idea true for all time, because a later observation might contradict it. One reliable contrary result can disprove an idea.
Textbooks sometimes present “the scientific method” as a fixed recipe, but real science is messier. The first half of the usual cycle takes a scientist from noticing something to having data.
There is no single fixed scientific method. The process is often complex and iterative (it loops back on itself), following many different paths, but it usually involves the stages below.
1. Observation: the scientist notices something in the natural world.
2. Question: the scientist asks why or how it happens.
3. Hypothesis: a proposed, testable explanation is put forward.
4. Prediction: the scientist works out what should be found if the hypothesis is correct.
5. Experiment or further observation: the prediction is tested.
6. Collection and analysis of data: results are gathered and worked on to see what they show.
Once the data is in, the work is not finished. The second half of the cycle checks the result and shares it, so that other scientists can judge it.
7. Conclusion: the hypothesis is judged to be supported or rejected by the data.
8. Repetition and checking: the work is repeated, so that one odd result is not relied on.
9. Comparison with existing knowledge: the result is set against what is already known.
10. Publication in a scientific journal after peer review, which means other experts check the work before it is published.
11. Testing of the findings by other scientists, who try to confirm or challenge them.
12. Over time, well-supported findings are developed into a theory or law.
A rejected hypothesis leads to a new or modified hypothesis, so the cycle starts again. This is why the process is a loop and not a straight line.

Diagram: the cycle drawn as a loop with arrows. Labels: observation, question, hypothesis, prediction, experiment, data analysis, conclusion, repeat and check. Arrow from “hypothesis rejected” back to “new hypothesis”; “publish and peer review” leading out to “theory or law”.
The cycle suggests that every investigation is a laboratory experiment, but that is only one way of testing ideas. Science also needs imagination.
Not all science is experimental. Some fields test ideas by observation and comparison, for example fossil records and comparative anatomy as evidence for evolution, or field surveys of ecosystems.

Science is creative: imagining hypotheses and designing ways to test them takes imagination, and chance observations can start new lines of work, such as the discovery of penicillin, the standard example. There is more on this in Science, scientists and society.
No scientist works alone for long. Science is a shared activity in which claims are expected to face challenge.
Scientists work in teams, build on others’ published work and expect their claims to be checked and challenged, because a claim that survives checking is more reliable.
Scepticism means doubting a claim until the evidence for it is good. It is a norm of science, not a personal attack on the scientist. There is more on this in Science as a global enterprise.
Scientists are human, so the way science is done reflects the world they live in.
Science is influenced by the society, culture, funding and technology of its time, which affect what questions get investigated and what can be measured.
Individual scientists can be biased. There is more on the types of bias in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
The scientific method is powerful, but it has limits. Knowing them helps you judge how far a result can be trusted.

Limited by current knowledge and technology: some questions cannot yet be investigated. Cells could not be observed until microscopes were invented, and the internal structure of organelles could not be observed until electron microscopes were available.
The basis of the investigation may be wrong: if the theory or assumption a hypothesis rests on is false, the conclusions may be false too.
Human error and interpretation: data can be misread, and scientists can interpret the same results in different ways.
Experimental design: a poorly designed experiment can give results that seem to support a hypothesis when they do not. There is more on this in Designing and conducting investigations.

Applying results to nature: conditions in a laboratory are simpler and more controlled than in a living organism or an ecosystem, so results may not apply outside the laboratory. A drug that works on cells in a dish may not work in a person.
Science cannot answer questions of value, ethics or the supernatural, and it cannot prove a hypothesis absolutely, because evidence can only support or refute an idea.
A hypothesis is the first step from an observation towards an explanation. It is the lowest-status kind of scientific idea, since it has yet to be tested.
A hypothesis is a proposed, testable explanation for an observation. It makes predictions that can be checked by experiment or observation.
A hypothesis may be supported or rejected; it is never proved.

Example: in the early 1980s Robin Warren and Barry Marshall proposed that stomach ulcers are caused by infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, not by stress and excess acid as was then believed. There is more on writing a testable hypothesis in Questioning and predicting.
In everyday speech “theory” means a hunch. In science it means the opposite: the most thoroughly tested kind of explanation.
A theory is a broad, well-tested explanation of a wide range of observations, supported by many confirmed hypotheses and by evidence from many independent sources.
A theory explains why something happens and makes predictions. It is the highest status an explanation reaches in science.
A theory is not a guess, so the everyday phrase “just a theory” misuses the word.
The cell theory states that all living things are made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life, and that all cells come from pre-existing cells.

Matthias Schleiden proposed in 1838 that plants are made of cells. Theodor Schwann extended this to animals in 1839. Rudolf Virchow added in 1855 that all cells arise from existing cells (“omnis cellula e cellula”).

Other biological theories include the theory of evolution by natural selection, proposed by Darwin and Wallace, and the germ theory of disease, which holds that many diseases are caused by microorganisms. There is more on the first in The theory of evolution by natural selection.
A law is a different kind of knowledge from a theory. Where a theory explains, a law describes a pattern.
A law, or principle, is a statement, often mathematical, that describes a pattern that always occurs under stated conditions. It describes what happens but does not explain why.
Biology has few laws because living systems are variable, so patterns rarely hold without exception.

Mendel’s laws of segregation and independent assortment describe how alleles (versions of a gene) pass to offspring. They have known exceptions, for example linked genes. There is more on this in Mendel's Laws.
The laws of thermodynamics apply to living things. Energy is not created or destroyed, only converted, as when light energy is converted to chemical energy in photosynthesis.
Examiners now ask you to tell these three apart. They differ in scope, purpose and the evidence behind them, and none is a stage on the way to another.
Scope: a hypothesis concerns one observation, a theory covers a wide range of observations, and a law covers one pattern.
Purpose: a hypothesis proposes an explanation, a theory gives a tested explanation, and a law describes a pattern.
Evidence: a hypothesis has little or none yet, a theory rests on a large body of evidence from many independent sources, and a law is repeated observation without exception under stated conditions.
All three can be revised or rejected if the evidence demands it.

A theory does not grow up into a law: they are different kinds of knowledge. A law describes a pattern and a theory explains it. A theory can explain a law; for example, Mendel’s laws are explained by the behaviour of chromosomes in meiosis.

A scientific fact is a repeatable observation, for example “DNA is found in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells”. A model is a simplified representation used to explain or predict. There is more on this in Models.
Because scientific knowledge is tentative, it changes over time. The cases that follow show this in action.

Ideas change because of new evidence that the old idea cannot explain, new technology that allows new observations (for example microscopes and DNA sequencing), reinterpretation of existing evidence, and replication (repeating of the work) by other scientists.
Change is usually gradual refinement. Occasionally a whole framework is replaced; the historian Thomas Kuhn called this a paradigm shift, in his book The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962).
For a long time people believed that small creatures could appear from non-living matter. Two careful experiments, a couple of centuries apart, showed otherwise.
Old idea (spontaneous generation): living things such as maggots and microorganisms arise from non-living matter.
In 1668 Francesco Redi put meat in jars that were open, sealed or covered with gauze. Maggots appeared only on the meat in the open jars, which flies could reach.
In the gauze-covered jars, flies laid their eggs on the gauze, not on the meat, so no maggots appeared.
In the early 1860s Louis Pasteur boiled broth in swan-neck flasks, which have an S-shaped neck. Air could enter, but dust and microorganisms were trapped in the bend, and the broth stayed clear.
When the neck was broken off, or the broth was tipped into the bend, microorganisms grew in it. This showed the microorganisms came from the dust and not from the broth itself.
New idea: living things come only from other living things (biogenesis), which supported the germ theory.
The cell theory was not announced in one go. It grew as better microscopes let scientists observe more.

The cell theory (all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from pre-existing cells) was built up by several scientists over decades as microscopes improved.
It is still being extended. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have been found to contain their own DNA.
This case shows how a well-established belief was overturned by a bacterium that doctors thought could not exist in the stomach.
Old idea: ulcers are caused by stress, spicy food and excess acid, and no bacterium could survive stomach acid.
Warren observed curved bacteria in biopsies (small samples of tissue) of inflamed stomach linings. Marshall and Warren cultured (grew in the laboratory) Helicobacter pylori in 1982.
In 1984 Marshall drank a culture of the bacteria, developed gastritis (an inflamed stomach lining) and treated it with antibiotics.
Other scientists repeated the findings, and trials showed that antibiotics cured most ulcers.
New idea: most stomach ulcers are caused by H. pylori infection and are treated with antibiotics.
Marshall and Warren received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2005.
The case shows that a new idea is often resisted at first and is accepted when the evidence is reproduced.
In this case the evidence was clear, yet the idea was ignored for years because nobody could say why it worked.
In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis, at Vienna General Hospital, noticed that far more mothers died of childbed (puerperal) fever on the ward run by doctors than on the ward run by midwives.
The doctors who ran that ward came from dissecting corpses, while the midwives did not.
He made staff wash their hands in chlorinated lime solution, and deaths fell sharply.
Many doctors rejected his idea because it lacked an explanation. It was accepted only after the germ theory of disease explained it.
The case shows that evidence without an explanatory theory can be ignored.
The same pattern of old idea, new evidence and refined idea appears again in other topics in this course.
The five-kingdom system of classifying living things was replaced by three domains and six kingdoms.

The lock-and-key model of enzyme action was refined to the induced-fit model, and the membrane “sandwich” model was replaced by the fluid mosaic model. There is more on these in Domains of life, Classification and Models.

Science is not done by one person or one country working alone. Scientists everywhere work on shared problems and build on each other’s published results, and that is what makes it a global enterprise.
Scientists in many countries work on the same problems, share data and build on each other’s published results. Knowledge is not owned by one country or person.
Because claims are tested by people with different backgrounds and assumptions, mistakes and hidden bias are more likely to be spotted than if one group checked its own work.

Large problems need international teams, shared funding and shared equipment. The Human Genome Project (1990–2003) sequenced the human genome (read out all of a person’s DNA) through an international consortium of 20 research groups in six countries: the USA, the UK, Japan, France, Germany and China.
Under the Bermuda Principles (1996), the Human Genome Project released its sequence data publicly within 24 hours, free for anyone to use, so other researchers could start work straight away.

Speed through sharing: in January 2020 Chinese scientists published the genome sequence of the new coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) online. Research groups around the world used it within days to design tests and begin developing vaccines.

Funding is international too. Irish researchers are funded by Research Ireland, the state agency formed in 2024 from Science Foundation Ireland and the Irish Research Council, and by the EU research programme Horizon Europe (2021–2027), which funds teams that include several countries.

Science needs four things to work across borders: clear communication, international conventions, peer review and reproducibility. Each gets its own block below. There is more on funding as a source of bias in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
A discovery only helps science once other scientists can read it, understand it and use it. So scientists publish in a standard form and use precise language that anyone in the field can follow.

Scientists communicate mainly through papers in scientific journals. They also use conferences, review articles (summaries of many studies on one topic) and shared online databases such as genome databases (stores of DNA sequences). There is more on genome databases in Bioinformatics: genome databases.

A research paper has a standard structure: title and authors; abstract (a short summary); introduction (background and the aim or hypothesis); methods (exactly what was done, with materials and conditions).
The paper then gives results (data in tables and graphs); discussion (what the results mean, the limitations, and comparison with other work); and references to other work.
The methods section must be detailed enough for another scientist to repeat the work, which makes reproducibility (others getting the same result) possible.

Scientific language must be precise and unambiguous. Terms have one agreed meaning (e.g. “theory” in science is not “a guess”), quantities are given with units, and uncertainty is stated rather than hidden. English is the main shared language of international science.
Open access journals make papers free to read for everyone, not only subscribers, so more people can use the findings.

Preprints are papers posted online before peer review (checking by independent experts), e.g. on bioRxiv, launched 2013, and medRxiv, launched 2019, for medical research. They speed up sharing, as in the COVID-19 pandemic, but readers must remember that they have not yet been checked.

Poor communication slows science. Gregor Mendel published his results on inheritance in pea plants in 1866, in the journal of the Natural History Society of Brünn (now Brno, Czech Republic). They were little read, and their importance was recognised only when other scientists reached the same conclusions independently in 1900.

Communicating with the public (news, policy and outreach) is also part of a scientist’s work. There is more on evaluating media reports in Evaluating evidence, and on presenting your own findings in Communicating results.
For scientists in different countries to compare and repeat each other’s work, they must use the same units, names and rules. These shared agreements are called international conventions.

An international convention is a set of rules or standards agreed by scientists or governments across countries, so that results mean the same everywhere and can be compared and repeated. Standards also cover laboratory safety signs (hazard symbols) and depositing data in public databases.

SI units (Système International) are the agreed units of measurement: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), mole (amount of substance) and kelvin (temperature), with degrees Celsius also widely used.
Prefixes such as milli- and micro- are used with SI units, e.g. mm, and µm, the unit for cell sizes. The unit nm is used for organelles and molecules, which are smaller still.

Binomial nomenclature gives each species a two-part Latin name, genus then species, e.g. Homo sapiens. The genus starts with a capital letter, the species name is lower case, and the name is printed in italics or underlined when handwritten.

Carl Linnaeus established the system; the starting point for plant names is his Species Plantarum (1753). One scientific name avoids confusion between common names, which differ between languages and regions. There is more on this in Classification.

Other naming conventions: human genes have agreed symbols, written in italics, e.g. the CFTR gene, whose faulty alleles (versions of a gene) cause cystic fibrosis. The protein is written without italics. Chemical names and formulas follow agreed rules, e.g. CO₂ and C₆H₁₂O₆.

Ethical conventions set rules for research. The Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 1964) sets out ethical principles for research on people, including informed consent and independent ethical review. It followed the Nuremberg Code (1947), which was written after the trials of Nazi doctors.

The Convention on Biological Diversity (1992, agreed at the Rio Earth Summit) commits countries to conserving biodiversity, using it sustainably and sharing fairly the benefits of genetic resources. CITES (1973) controls international trade in endangered species.
Before a paper is published, other experts check it. This is peer review, a quality check that follows a set sequence of steps.
Peer review is the evaluation of a scientific paper by independent experts in the same field, the author’s “peers”, before it is published.

Steps 1 to 3: the scientists submit the paper to a journal; the editor checks that it suits the journal and is of reasonable quality, and may reject it straight away; if it passes, the editor sends it to usually two or three independent experts, called reviewers or referees.

Step 4: the reviewers check whether the methods are suitable, the data support the conclusions, the analysis is sound, the work is original and important, ethical rules were followed and other work is properly referenced.
Step 5: they recommend accept, accept with minor revisions, revise and resubmit (major revisions), or reject.
Steps 6 and 7: the authors revise the paper and reply to each comment, and the editor makes the final decision before the paper is published.
Single-blind review: the reviewers know who the authors are, but the authors do not know the reviewers. This lets reviewers judge freely, but they may be swayed by the authors’ reputation.
Double-blind review: neither side knows the other, which reduces bias from the authors’ reputation, gender or country. Open review: names, and sometimes reports, are published.
Diagram: a flowchart of the seven steps, with a loop from “revise” back to “reviewers”.
Peer review is valuable, but it is not a guarantee of truth. Knowing what it can and cannot do explains why scientists keep checking work after it is published.

Peer review filters out poor-quality or unsupported work, improves papers before publication, and gives readers some confidence in published work. A peer-reviewed paper is a more reliable source than one that is not. There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
Reviewers do not normally repeat the experiments, so they cannot detect well-hidden fraud or errors in raw data. Peer review does not guarantee that a paper is correct.
Reviewers can be biased, e.g. against ideas that challenge their own, or towards famous laboratories. The process is slow, and reviewers are usually unpaid volunteers.
Some low-quality “predatory” journals charge authors to publish while doing little or no real review, so a paper in such a journal has not really been checked.

Checking continues after publication. Other scientists read, cite and try to repeat the work; errors lead to published corrections, and serious errors or misconduct lead to retraction, when the journal withdraws the paper.

Hwang Woo-suk’s team published papers in the journal Science in 2004 and 2005 claiming to have made stem cells from cloned human embryos. The data were found to be fabricated, and the papers were retracted in 2006. Peer review had not caught the fraud; scrutiny after publication did.
One result on its own is not enough to count as knowledge. Science accepts a finding only when others can get the same result, which is why reproducibility matters.

A result is reproducible if other scientists, working independently in other laboratories, get the same result when they repeat the work, using the same or different methods. There is more on repeatability and reproducibility in Objectivity and data quality.

Science relies on reproducibility because a single result may be due to chance, error, an unusual sample, bias or fraud. Agreement between independent groups shows that the result is a real feature of nature.

Only reproduced findings become accepted knowledge and can support theories. For example, the H. pylori explanation of stomach ulcers (that a bacterium causes them) was accepted once others reproduced the findings. There is more on this in The nature of scientific knowledge.
Reproducibility depends on clear communication: full methods, raw data and materials must be shared so that others can repeat the work.

Not all published results reproduce. Scientists at the company Amgen reported in 2012 that they could confirm the findings of only 6 of 53 “landmark” preclinical cancer studies (early studies done before testing in patients).
Causes of failure include small samples, selective reporting of positive results, pressure to publish, poorly described methods and, rarely, fraud.
Responses include sharing data openly, registering study plans in advance and publishing replication studies (repeats of earlier work), so that results are checked and not hidden if they disagree.
Before you can judge information, you need words for where it comes from and how it can go wrong. The terms below are easy to mix up, so learn each one precisely.
A source is anything that provides information: a journal article, a textbook, a website, a news report, a government or agency report, a company leaflet, a video or a social media post.
A primary source is the original report of research by the people who did it, e.g. a research paper in a peer-reviewed journal (one checked by independent experts before publication).
A secondary source summarises or interprets primary sources, e.g. a review article, a textbook, a news report or a documentary. A tertiary source compiles secondary sources, e.g. an encyclopaedia.
Primary data are data collected by yourself; secondary data are data collected by somebody else, e.g. a table of national vaccination rates, a population survey, or the results in a published paper.

A research paper is a primary source, but its data are secondary data to a student who uses them, because the student did not collect them. So primary and secondary sources are not the same as primary and secondary data.

Bias is a one-sided influence that pushes information or its interpretation away from the truth in a consistent direction. A biased source is not necessarily false, but it selects, presents or interprets information to favour one view.
Good research is a planned process, not a quick search. This is the research that the Biology in Practice Investigation requires, and each step below makes the next one more reliable.

1. Define the issue and a focused research question, e.g. “Does eating ultra-processed food raise the risk of type 2 diabetes?” rather than “Is food bad for you?”. A narrow question is easier to search for and to answer.

2. Choose keywords, including scientific terms and synonyms, and search suitable places: the school or public library; scientific search engines and databases, e.g. Google Scholar, and PubMed for medical research; the websites of scientific and public bodies; and textbooks.
3. Gather several different types of source, including some primary sources and some secondary data, and sources that take different views, so that you do not see only one side.
4. Record each source as you use it, so that it can be referenced (credited in a standard written form) and checked later. There is more on this in Communicating results.
5. Evaluate each source with the criteria for evaluating a source, noting what it lacks and any bias.

6. Cross-check, or corroborate, important claims in independent sources. A claim found in several independent reliable sources is more trustworthy than one found in a single source, because one source could be mistaken or biased.
7. Separate facts, evidence and opinions, and summarise in your own words. Reference every source: copying another’s words or ideas without acknowledgement is plagiarism.
To decide how far to trust a source, ask the same set of questions of every one. Each criterion below has a question to ask and a sign that tells you whether the answer is good or poor.

Authority: who wrote it, and are they qualified and named? Good sign: named scientists at a university, research institute or public health body. Poor sign: an anonymous author, or a celebrity or influencer with no expertise.

Peer review and publisher: has it been checked by experts before publication? A peer-reviewed journal article is more reliable than a blog or press release, because errors are more likely to have been caught. There is more on this in Science as a global enterprise.

Currency: when was it published or updated? Biology moves quickly, so older sources may be out of date, e.g. a source describing a five-kingdom classification. Older sources are still useful for historical background.

Purpose: why was it written, to inform, to teach, to persuade, to sell or to entertain? A source written to sell or persuade is more likely to be biased, because it has a reason to present only one view.

Evidence and references: does it give data, describe how they were collected, and reference its sources so that they can be checked? Claims such as “studies show” or “scientists say” with no reference are a warning sign, because you cannot check them.
Relevance: does it address the research question, for the right organism, population or place? A study on mice, for example, may not apply to humans.
Accuracy and consistency: does it agree with other reliable sources and with established science? Are there factual errors, or emotive (feeling-driven) or exaggerated language?
A memory aid used in schools and libraries is the CRAAP test: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

Even a source that looks professional may leave out the information you need to judge it. Missing detail matters because without it you cannot tell whether a result is valid or can be compared with other work.
Missing method: without knowing how data were collected, a reader cannot judge whether they are valid or repeat the work.
Missing sample size, or a very small sample: a result from a handful of people or plants may be due to chance rather than a real effect.
Missing units, dates, location or definitions, e.g. what counts as “obese” or “a heavy drinker”, so data cannot be compared with other data.

Averages or percentages alone, without the range or the raw data (the original unprocessed measurements), can hide great variation or very small numbers. For example, “50% improved” could mean 1 of 2 patients.
No control or comparison group, which means you cannot tell whether the result was caused by the treatment. A source may also give no information on who funded the work, and state no limitations.
Simplified summaries, such as news reports, infographics and social media posts, often leave out the uncertainty, the limitations and the conditions under which a result applies.
Secondary data are data someone else collected, and students often rely on them in research. They are powerful but come with limits, so you need to weigh both sides and know what to ask.
Advantages: secondary data can cover far larger samples, longer periods and more places than a student could collect, e.g. national health statistics, long-term climate records and genome databases.
They are also quick and cheap to obtain, and they allow results to be compared with others.
Limitations: they were collected for someone else’s purpose, so they may not exactly fit your question. You do not control how they were collected or how carefully.

Methods, definitions or units may be unclear or may change over time, which makes comparison unreliable. The data may be out of date, incomplete, or already processed by averaging or selection, and the collector may be biased.

Questions to ask of secondary data: who collected them and why; how, when and where they were collected; how big the sample was; whether the method is described; whether the data are raw or processed; and whether other sources give similar data.
Bias can enter a source in several ways, from who paid for it to which data were chosen. Knowing the named types lets you spot them in a real advert or article.

Funding or commercial bias: a source paid for by a company or individual that gains from a particular conclusion may favour that conclusion, e.g. research on sugary drinks funded by a drinks manufacturer, or a supplement company’s website reporting only its own favourable trials.

A conflict of interest is a situation in which a person’s financial or personal interests could influence their judgement. Reliable journals require authors to declare them, so readers can take them into account.
Selection bias, or cherry-picking: choosing only the data or studies that support a view and ignoring the rest, e.g. quoting one cold winter as evidence against climate warming.
Publication bias: studies with positive or exciting results are more likely to be published than those finding no effect, so the published literature can overstate how well a treatment works.
Confirmation bias: the tendency of authors, and of readers, to look for, interpret and remember information that confirms what they already believe.
Sampling bias: a sample that is not representative of the population, e.g. a diet survey carried out only among gym members, or a drug trialled only on young men and then recommended for everyone.

Political, ideological or cultural bias: a source from a campaign group, political party or lobby group presents the evidence that suits its cause. This can apply to groups on either side of an issue, e.g. both for and against genetically modified crops.
Sensationalism means exaggerating a result to attract readers or clicks.

Recognising bias: check who produced and who paid for the source; look for one-sided presentation, emotive language, no mention of limitations or opposing evidence, and claims not supported by references. A biased source can still contain accurate facts, so check them against independent sources rather than simply dismissing the source.
Some kinds of source are checked more carefully than others, so type is a useful first guide to reliability. It is only a guide, though, because each individual source still has to be judged.

Usually most reliable: peer-reviewed research papers and systematic reviews; reports of national and international scientific and public health bodies, e.g. the World Health Organization (WHO), the Health Service Executive (HSE, Ireland’s public health service) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA, Ireland); and up-to-date textbooks.
Usually least reliable: anonymous websites, social media posts, advertisements and personal blogs, because they are rarely checked by experts and may aim to sell or persuade.
Each source must still be judged on the criteria, not just on its type. A reliable body can make mistakes, and a blog can be accurate.

A scientific investigation starts with a question that evidence can answer. Questions of value, taste, morality or belief cannot be settled by investigation alone, so the first skill is telling the two kinds apart.
A question is appropriate for scientific investigation when it can be answered by collecting evidence through observation or measurement of the natural world.

It must refer to things that can be observed, measured or counted, and the answer must be capable of being tested against data. This is why a question about numbers, rates or changes in organisms qualifies.

Questions science cannot answer by investigation include questions of value, taste, morality or belief, e.g. “Is it wrong to keep animals in zoos?” or “Which flower is the most beautiful?”. No measurement can settle them, because people can weigh the same evidence differently.

Science can supply evidence that informs a question of value, e.g. how captivity affects an animal’s stress hormones (chemical signals released when an animal is under strain), but evidence alone cannot settle it. The ethical side of scientific work is dealt with in Designing and conducting investigations.

A broad question must be narrowed by naming the factor to be changed and the effect to be measured. “Does temperature affect enzymes?” becomes “How does temperature affect the rate at which catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide?”

“Does salt affect plants?” becomes “How does the concentration of a salt solution affect the change in mass of potato cylinders?” Notice that both versions now name something you can change and something you can measure.

A good investigable question is specific, names one independent variable (the factor you change) and one dependent variable (the factor you measure), can be carried out with available equipment in the time available, and is safe and ethical to carry out.

Scientific investigation moves in a sequence from a question to a hypothesis, from the hypothesis to a prediction, and then to a test of the prediction. Hypothesis and prediction sound alike but are different things, and telling them apart is the key distinction.

Investigation usually begins with an observation or with existing knowledge that raises a question. The question leads to a hypothesis, the hypothesis leads to a prediction, and the prediction is tested by experiment or further observation.

A hypothesis is a proposed, testable explanation for an observation, or a proposed relationship between two variables (factors that can change), based on existing scientific knowledge. It explains why something might happen.

Example of a hypothesis: “Increasing the temperature increases the rate of catalase activity, because molecules move faster and collide more often with the active site, up to the temperature at which the enzyme denatures.” Catalase is an enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
A prediction is a specific statement of the result that will be observed if the hypothesis is correct, often written “If … then …”. It says what will happen in this particular experiment, not why.

Example of a prediction: “If potato cylinders are placed in sucrose solutions of increasing concentration, then their percentage change in mass will decrease, becoming negative in the more concentrated solutions.” It names a measurable result and gives no reason.

The hypothesis is the explanation: general, and it gives a reason. The prediction is the expected observation: specific, and a measurable outcome of the planned test. One hypothesis can generate several predictions, one for each test you could run.

A null hypothesis states that the independent variable has no effect on the dependent variable, e.g. “The concentration of sucrose has no effect on the change in mass of potato cylinders.” An experiment tests whether the data give reason to reject it.

Diagram: flow diagram of observation, question, hypothesis, prediction, test, data and conclusion, with an arrow from the conclusion back to a new question, showing that a hypothesis is supported or rejected and the cycle continues.
Not every explanation can be put to the test. A hypothesis is only useful to science if an investigation could show it to be wrong, and if it is built on real biology rather than a hunch.
A testable hypothesis is falsifiable: it is possible to imagine a result that would show it to be wrong. If no possible result could count against it, it cannot be tested.

“Plants grow better when people talk to them because they enjoy it” is not testable as stated, because enjoyment cannot be measured. “Plants exposed to sound grow taller than plants kept in silence” is testable.

A testable hypothesis names variables that can be measured or controlled (kept the same), and it states the direction of the expected effect: an increase or a decrease, not just “will have an effect”.
A hypothesis is developed from scientific theories and explanations, not from a guess, so the reasoning comes from known biology.

Collision theory (a reaction needs the reacting molecules to collide, so more collisions mean a faster rate) and denaturation (the enzyme’s active site losing its shape at high temperature) support an enzyme-rate hypothesis.

Osmosis supports a hypothesis about potato cylinders: water moves from a dilute solution (higher water concentration) to a more concentrated one across a partially permeable membrane. Cylinders therefore gain mass in distilled water and lose mass in concentrated sucrose solution.
Light as the energy source for photosynthesis supports a hypothesis about a light-intensity investigation, for example that more light gives a faster rate of photosynthesis.
A hypothesis is supported or not supported by data; a single investigation never proves it. This judgement is made at the conclusion stage. There is more on this in Producing and analysing data.

Scientists can test the same hypothesis in several ways, and each gives different evidence. To evaluate and compare strategies, judge them against the same set of criteria, starting with the controlled laboratory experiment.

Criteria for comparing strategies: whether it can show cause and effect or only correlation (a link between two things); how many variables can be controlled; how realistic the conditions are; the sample size achievable; time, cost and equipment; safety; and ethics.

Controlled laboratory experiment: the investigator changes one variable and controls the others. Strength: the strongest evidence that a change in one variable causes a change in another, because nothing else is changing.
Laboratory limitation: artificial conditions may not match the real world, e.g. an enzyme in a test tube compared with an enzyme in a living cell.
Laboratory limitation: some variables cannot be changed in a lab for ethical or practical reasons.
Some questions cannot be answered by changing things in a lab. A field study works in the organisms’ own habitat, while secondary data lets you use evidence somebody else has already gathered.
Field study or survey (observational study): the investigator observes and measures organisms where they live without changing anything, e.g. comparing the number of a plant species in sun and shade.
Field strengths: the conditions are real, and large areas and many organisms can be studied.
Field limitations: many variables cannot be controlled, so they must be measured and recorded. A survey can show a correlation but not prove a cause, because other factors may be responsible.
Analysis of secondary data (data collected by somebody else), e.g. published datasets, databases of genetic information and government health statistics.
Secondary data strengths: large data sets, long time periods, or data the student could never collect, and the analysis is cheap and quick.

Secondary data limitations: the user did not control how the data were collected and may not know their quality, and the source may lack detail or show bias (a one-sided slant). There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
Some questions are too slow, dangerous or unethical to test directly. Models and human trials handle these in different ways, and the best investigations often combine strategies.

Modelling and simulation use a physical model or computer simulation to test how a system behaves, e.g. a simulation of population growth. Strength: fast, safe, and able to test conditions impossible in reality.
A model is only as good as its assumptions (the simplifications built into it), so its predictions must be checked against real data. There is more on this in Models.
Trials with human participants, e.g. testing a treatment, are needed for questions about human health. Strength: direct evidence about people.

Human trials are limited by ethical restrictions, the need for informed consent (participants agree after being told the risks), high cost and large natural variation between people. This is why large samples and blinding (participants not knowing which treatment they get) are needed.
Often the best answer uses more than one strategy: a field survey suggests a hypothesis and a laboratory experiment tests it.
Every investigation has factors that are deliberately changed, measured or kept the same. Sorting them into the right type is the first step in designing a fair investigation.
A variable is any factor that can change or be changed in an investigation.

The independent variable is the one variable the investigator deliberately changes, for example the temperature of the water bath in an enzyme investigation, or the concentration of sucrose solution in an osmosis investigation.

The dependent variable is the variable that is measured, because it is expected to change as a result; it depends on the independent variable. Examples: the volume of oxygen released per minute by catalase, or the percentage change in mass of potato cylinders.

Controlled variables are all other variables that could affect the dependent variable, so they are kept the same. For enzyme rate these are pH (kept constant with a buffer), substrate concentration and volume, the amount of enzyme, and the time of measurement.

For osmosis the controlled variables are the size and surface area of the cylinders, the potato they are cut from, the volume of solution, the time in solution and the temperature. Any of these could change the result if allowed to vary.
Name variables precisely, with their unit and how each is measured: “temperature” is an independent variable, but “the enzyme” is not, because it is not a factor you change by amount.
Saying a variable is controlled is not enough; the plan must say how it is held constant, and which values of the independent variable will be tested.

Variables are kept constant with equipment and technique: a thermostatically controlled water bath or incubator for temperature, because these hold a set temperature over time; a buffer solution for pH, because a buffer resists changes in pH.
Use a graduated pipette, syringe or graduated cylinder for volumes, so each set-up gets the same amount, and a stopwatch for timing.
For tissue, use the same cork borer and trim every piece to the same length, so that size and surface area are the same in every set-up.

Choose a range of at least five values of the independent variable, spread across the range in which a change is expected, for example 0 °C to 60 °C in 10 °C steps for an enzyme. This gives enough points to show a pattern.
Add closer intervals around a key point such as an apparent optimum (the value that gives the highest rate), so that the key point is located more exactly.
A preliminary (pilot) trial is a quick practice run. It helps choose the range and checks that the method works before the full investigation.
To show that the factor you changed caused the result, you need a fair test and a control. These two ideas are linked but are not the same thing.

A fair test is an investigation in which only the independent variable is changed and all other variables are controlled, so any change in the dependent variable can be put down to the independent variable.

A control (control experiment) is a set-up identical to the experiment in every way except that the factor being tested is absent or not applied. It is a standard for comparison, showing that the result is due to the factor being investigated and not something else.

Example of a control: boiled (denatured) enzyme used in place of active enzyme. Boiling denatures enzymes, so this shows that the enzyme, rather than the substrate breaking down on its own, causes the reaction.
A negative control is a set-up expected to give no response, for example boiled enzyme, or distilled water in place of the test solution.

A positive control is a set-up known to give a response, which shows that the method can detect one. For example, glucose is a reducing sugar and gives a positive Benedict’s test, so a known glucose solution shows the food test works.
Controlled variables and the control are different: controlled variables are the factors kept the same in every set-up, while the control is a separate set-up used for comparison.
A fair test is not much use unless it also measures the right thing. Validity is about whether the investigation really answers the question asked.
An investigation is valid if it actually measures what it sets out to measure and answers the question asked. This needs a fair test and a suitable dependent variable.

Example of an invalid investigation: if a lamp is moved closer to pondweed to increase light intensity and also warms the water, temperature has changed as well as light, so the investigation cannot show the effect of light alone.
A heat shield, such as a beaker of water between the lamp and the plant, restores validity because the water absorbs heat and so reduces the heating.
A conclusion is valid only if it is supported by data from a valid investigation. In other words, a flawed method cannot give a trustworthy conclusion, however neat the results look.
Students often use these words interchangeably, but each one describes something different about a measurement.

Error in measurement is the difference between a measured value and the true value. Every measurement has some error, and error is not the same as a mistake. There is more on this in Objectivity and data quality, which covers the types of error.
Accuracy is how close a measurement or a mean is to the true value. It is improved by calibrated equipment (checked against a known standard) and a method that measures the right thing.
Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other, meaning there is little spread around the mean.

The precision of an instrument is its resolution: the smallest change it can show. A balance reading to 0.01 g is more precise than one reading to 1 g, and a graduated pipette is more precise than a beaker for measuring 5 cm³.
Precise results need not be accurate: a balance that reads 0.5 g too high gives readings close to each other (precise) but all wrong (inaccurate).
Diagram: four targets showing accurate and precise; precise but not accurate; accurate on average but not precise; neither.
One measurement can be a fluke. Reliability is about whether results can be trusted because they come out the same when the investigation is repeated.

Reliability is how far results can be trusted because they are consistent when the investigation is repeated. It is improved by replicates, repeats and a large sample size. There is more on judging reliability in Objectivity and data quality.
Replicates are several identical set-ups at each value of the independent variable, run at the same time, for example three potato cylinders in each sucrose concentration.
Repeats are carrying out the whole measurement again. Both replicates and repeats allow a mean to be calculated and an anomalous result (one that does not fit the pattern) to be spotted.
Sample size is the number of organisms, samples or measurements in each group. Living things vary naturally: two potato cylinders, two leaves or two people are never identical.
A larger sample, chosen at random, reduces the effect of individual variation and gives a more representative and reliable result.
Sample size is limited by time, cost, materials and the ethics of using organisms, so a plan has to balance these against the need for reliable results.
The equipment you choose decides how good your data can be. A plan should pick each item for a reason, not just name it.

Choose equipment whose resolution suits the size of the change: a syringe, graduated pipette or burette for small volumes rather than a beaker; a balance reading to at least 0.01 g for small masses; a stopwatch for time; a thermometer or temperature probe for temperature.
Choose equipment that measures objectively where possible, meaning the reading does not depend on opinion. A colorimeter measures colour or cloudiness as a number instead of judging by eye.
A gas syringe or an inverted graduated cylinder over water measures the volume of gas, instead of counting bubbles, which vary in size.
Data loggers with sensors (temperature, pH, oxygen, light) record readings automatically at set intervals, so no readings are missed and there is no human timing error.
Justify each choice in the plan: say what it measures, why its resolution or range is suitable, and how it reduces error.
Practical work can cause harm, so risks are thought through before starting. A risk assessment is the written record of that thinking.

A risk assessment is carried out before practical work. It identifies each hazard (anything that could cause harm), judges the risk (how likely and how serious the harm is) and states a control measure that reduces it.

General control measures: wear safety glasses and a lab coat; tie back long hair; heat with a water bath rather than a direct flame where possible; clean up spills at once; wash hands after practical work; never eat or drink in the laboratory.
Hot water baths and boiling tubes can scald or burn, so use tongs or a test-tube holder.
Corrosive or irritant reagents such as hydrogen peroxide or Benedict’s reagent can harm skin and eyes, so wear glasses and gloves and avoid skin contact.
Sharp scalpels and cork borers can cut, so cut downwards onto a tile, away from the body.

Microorganisms can cause infection, so use aseptic technique (methods that keep unwanted microbes out), sealed plates and disinfected benches, and dispose of cultures by sterilising them. There is more on this in Microorganisms.
Electrical equipment must be kept away from water, because water conducts electricity and risks shock.
Safety also covers the organisms used: living material should be treated with care and returned to its habitat where possible.
Science only works if people can trust what is reported. Scientific integrity means being honest in how investigations are carried out and reported.
Record all results as they were measured, including unexpected and anomalous ones, because a result you did not expect may still be real.
Never invent results (fabrication) or change them to fit the hypothesis (falsification).
Never present others’ work or data as your own (plagiarism), so acknowledge every source.
Integrity also means reporting limitations and errors openly, and not leaving out data because they do not support the hypothesis.
Investigations involve living things, so the investigator must weigh the harm they might cause. Ethics sets the rules for how animals, people and habitats are treated.
Ethics with animals: use animals only where there is no alternative, and cause the minimum harm or stress.

The 3Rs: Replace (use non-animal alternatives such as cell cultures or computer models), Reduce (use the fewest animals that give reliable results), and Refine (improve methods to minimise suffering).
Return organisms collected from the wild to where they were found.

Ethics with human participants covers informed consent (participants know what is involved and agree freely), the right to withdraw at any time, confidentiality of personal data, and no physical or psychological harm.
Investigations on people, for example measuring reaction time after a caffeinated drink, must take account of health conditions and exclude anyone at risk, because caffeine could harm them.
Ethics also covers the environment: avoid damaging habitats when collecting. There is more on the wider ethical, social and economic consequences of research in Science, scientists and society.

A plan must be detailed enough that someone else could repeat the investigation exactly. A worked outline for the effect of temperature on catalase (the enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen) shows the structure. There is more on the full method in Enzymes.
A plan states, in order: the question and hypothesis; the independent, dependent and controlled variables; the control; and the equipment and reagents with reasons for choice.
It then gives a numbered method with amounts, concentrations, times and temperatures; the number of replicates or repeats; how data will be recorded; a risk assessment; and ethical considerations.
Worked outline, catalase: the independent variable is temperature, with five or more values set with water baths.

Worked outline, catalase: the dependent variable is the volume of oxygen collected in a fixed time, and the controlled variables are pH (kept with a buffer), the volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide, and the mass or volume of the enzyme source.
Worked outline, catalase: the control is boiled enzyme; there are three replicates at each temperature; and safety glasses are worn for hydrogen peroxide.

Results and conclusions should depend on the evidence, not on the investigator's opinions, expectations or wishes. A subjective judgement depends on the person making it, so two people can judge the same thing differently.

Investigators can unconsciously influence results, for example by reading a scale generously, deciding later which results “count”, or judging a colour change sooner when they expect it. This is experimenter (observer) bias.

Measure with instruments and record numbers rather than judging by eye. For example, use a colorimeter (an instrument that measures how much light a solution absorbs) instead of deciding when a blue-black starch–iodine colour has gone.

Iodine turns blue-black with starch, and the colour disappears as amylase (the enzyme that digests starch) breaks the starch down, so the end-point can be recorded as a number instead of a personal judgement.

Decide the method, the end-point (the point at which you stop and record) and how results will be analysed before collecting data, and record all results. This stops you choosing, after the event, the results that suit what you hoped to find.

Allocate samples or participants to groups at random, and sample at random, for example using random coordinates for quadrats (square frames placed on the ground to sample an area). There is more on this in Investigating an Ecosystem.
Random allocation and random sampling mean every individual has an equal chance of being chosen or placed in a group, so the investigator's choices cannot make one group different from another.
Use blinding, which keeps people from knowing which group is which, so that their expectations cannot affect what they report or record.
Expectations can change what people report and what researchers record. Blinding and placebos in trials on people remove those expectations from the results.
A single-blind trial hides the group from the participants: they do not know whether they are in the treatment group (given the real treatment) or the control group (not given it).

A double-blind trial hides the group from both the participants and the researchers who give the treatment and record the results, until the results are analysed. Double-blinding removes bias from the expectations of both.

A placebo is a dummy treatment with no active ingredient that looks the same as the real one, for example a sugar pill. It is given to the control group in a trial on people, so participants cannot tell which group they are in.
People given a placebo sometimes improve because they expect to (the placebo effect). So the real treatment must do better than the placebo to show that it works.
A placebo is a form of the control: a comparison group treated in the same way except for the factor being tested. There is more on controls in Designing and conducting investigations.
Every measurement in an investigation has some error. Random error is unpredictable variation in measurements. It cannot be removed completely, but its effect can be reduced.
Random error makes repeated measurements scatter on both sides of the true value, by different amounts each time, because the cause changes unpredictably from one reading to the next.
Sources in biology investigations include human reaction time when starting and stopping a stopwatch, judging an end-point colour by eye, and reading a scale between divisions.

Other sources include small fluctuations in water-bath temperature, and natural variation between biological samples: cylinders cut from different parts of a potato, leaves of different ages, or individuals of different fitness.
Random error reduces precision (how close repeat readings are to each other), so repeat readings spread out.
Random error is reduced by taking repeats and replicates and calculating a mean, because random errors partly cancel out: readings that are too high are balanced by readings that are too low.

Random error is also reduced by increasing the sample size, using more precise instruments or automatic measurement such as a data logger (a device that records readings automatically) or colorimeter, and controlling the variables more tightly.
Systematic error is a consistent error that affects every measurement in the same way, so it cannot be seen by repeating the measurement.
Systematic error shifts every measurement in the same direction by the same amount or proportion, so results are all too high or all too low.

An instrument that is not calibrated (checked against a known standard), or has a zero error (reads something when it should read zero), causes systematic error: for example a balance that reads 0.05 g with nothing on it, or a thermometer that reads 2 °C too high.
Reading a scale from the same wrong angle every time causes a parallax error, because the reading shifts the same way each time.

A flaw in the method that is repeated every time also causes systematic error: for example never blotting potato cylinders dry, so every mass includes surface solution, or a leaking delivery tube, so some gas is never collected.
Systematic error reduces accuracy (closeness to the true value) but not precision: repeats can agree closely and still all be wrong.
Repeating the measurement does not reduce systematic error, because the same error occurs every time.
Systematic error is reduced by calibrating instruments against a known standard, zeroing (taring) the balance before use, reading scales at eye level, and improving the method.
Comparing results with another method or with published values can reveal systematic error, because the two sets of results will disagree.
Exams often ask you to tell the two types of error apart. Mistakes are a third thing and must not be confused with either.
Random error is unpredictable, occurs in both directions, affects precision, and is reduced by repeats and means.
Systematic error is consistent, occurs in one direction, affects accuracy, is not reduced by repeats, and is reduced by calibration and a better method.
Mistakes, such as spilling a sample, misreading a number or using the wrong solution, are neither random nor systematic error. The result is discarded and the measurement repeated.
Avoid the vague phrase “human error” in answers: name the specific source and its effect, such as reaction time when timing, which is a random error.
Diagram: a number line or target showing a true value, with (a) readings scattered on both sides (random error) and (b) readings clustered together but all displaced to one side (systematic error).
Repeatability and reproducibility are two tests of whether data can be trusted, and they differ in who repeats the investigation and how.
Repeatable: the same investigator, using the same method and equipment under the same conditions, repeats the investigation and gets the same or very similar results.
Reproducible: a different person or group repeats the investigation, or uses different equipment or a different method, and obtains similar results.

To evaluate data for repeatability, compare the repeats or replicates for each value of the independent variable (the factor you change). A small range (spread) means the data are repeatable and precise; a large range shows high random error or an uncontrolled variable.

To evaluate data for reproducibility, compare the class's results with other groups' results, or with secondary data (data collected by someone else) from a textbook or published source. Agreement increases confidence that the results are reliable and not due to one person's error or equipment.

Results that are repeatable but not reproducible point to a systematic error or a feature of one set-up, for example one group's balance or one batch of potatoes, because the same fault was present each time that set-up was used.
Repeatable and reproducible data increase confidence in a conclusion but do not make it certain.
Every investigation produces data, and the type of data decides how you can record, process and graph it. Biologists sort data by what it describes, how it behaves and who collected it.

Qualitative data are descriptions or categories that are not numerical, e.g. a positive Benedict’s test for a reducing sugar, which turns from blue to brick-red through green, yellow and orange; the presence or absence of a species; or “cloudy” or “clear”.

Quantitative data are numerical measurements or counts with units, e.g. volume of oxygen in cm³, mass in g, or number of daisies per quadrat (a square frame laid on the ground to sample a small area).

Quantitative data are more objective (less dependent on the observer’s judgement) and can be analysed mathematically, so they are preferred where possible. A qualitative result can often be made quantitative, e.g. a colorimeter (an instrument that measures how much light a solution absorbs) reading instead of a colour.
Continuous data can take any value in a range, including decimals, e.g. mass, temperature or time.
Discrete data are whole-number counts, because you cannot have half a seed, e.g. number of seeds or number of stomata (the pores in a leaf).
Categoric data are named groups, e.g. eye colour or type of habitat.
Primary data are collected by the investigator. Secondary data are collected by somebody else, e.g. published results, databases or other groups’ results.

Selecting data means choosing the data that are relevant to the question and of good enough quality. Secondary data can extend or check primary data, for example by adding values you could not measure yourself. There is more on judging a secondary source in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
A results table is where raw data first go, so a clear layout makes the later calculations and graph easy. A few fixed conventions apply every time.

The independent variable (the factor you change) goes in the first column. The dependent variable (the factor you measure) goes in the following columns, with a column for each repeat and a column for the mean.
Each column heading gives the quantity and its unit, e.g. “Temperature (°C)” or “Volume of oxygen (cm³)”. Units go in the heading, not after every number, which keeps the table uncluttered.
Record every reading to the same number of decimal places, matching the resolution of the instrument (the smallest change it can show). A balance reading to 0.01 g gives 2.45 g, not 2.4 g or 2.453 g.
List the values of the independent variable in order, so the pattern can be seen down the column.

Record raw results straight into the table during the investigation, including any that look wrong. Writing them down later from memory risks errors, and a result that looks wrong may turn out to matter.

Raw readings are processed into a few summary numbers before they are graphed. The mean gives the typical value of repeats, and the range shows how closely the repeats agree. The worked numbers here are checked and illustrative.
Mean: add the values and divide by the number of values. Anomalous values (ones that do not fit the pattern) are left out of the mean, and the fact is stated.
Worked example for the mean: the final masses of four replicate (repeat) potato cylinders are 2.45 g, 2.44 g, 2.46 g and 2.10 g.
The value 2.10 g is anomalous, so the mean of the other three is (2.45 + 2.44 + 2.46) ÷ 3 = 7.35 ÷ 3 = 2.45 g.
Range: the largest value minus the smallest. It shows the spread of repeat readings, and a small range means the readings are precise (close to each other).
Worked example for the range: 2.46 − 2.44 = 0.02 g, a small spread, so the readings are precise.
The range of the independent variable is the lowest to highest value tested, e.g. 0 °C to 60 °C. It tells the reader which conditions the results cover.
Two further calculations let you compare results fairly. Percentage change deals with samples that started at different sizes, and rate deals with changes that took different times.

Percentage change = (final value − initial value) ÷ initial value × 100. It allows samples that started with different masses to be compared, because each change is expressed relative to its own starting value.
Worked example for percentage change: a cylinder with an initial mass of 2.50 g and a final mass of 2.45 g has a percentage change of (2.45 − 2.50) ÷ 2.50 × 100 = −2.0%.
A negative percentage change is a loss, and a positive value is a gain.
Rate = amount of change ÷ time. For example, 24 cm³ of oxygen in 4 minutes is a rate of 6 cm³ per minute.
When the time taken for something to happen is measured, e.g. the time for starch to disappear, the rate can be calculated as 1 ÷ time. A time of 50 s gives 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02 s⁻¹.
A shorter time means a faster rate, because 1 ÷ time gets larger as the time gets smaller.
Different data suit different graphs. The choice depends on whether the variables are continuous, discrete or categoric (see the previous block’s data types) and on what you want to show.
Line graph: used when both variables are continuous, e.g. rate of enzyme activity against temperature.

Bar chart: used when the independent variable is categoric or discrete, e.g. the number of a species in three habitats. Bars are separate and of equal width, because the categories are distinct groups.
Histogram: shows the frequency (how many) of a continuous variable divided into classes, e.g. the number of students in each height range. Bars touch, because the classes run on from one to the next.
Scatter graph: used to look for a correlation (a link) between two measured variables, e.g. light intensity and the number of a plant species in quadrats.
Pie chart: shows proportions of a whole, e.g. the percentage of each blood group in a class.
Once the graph type is chosen, marks come from drawing it carefully. Axes, scales, plotting and the line each follow a rule.
The independent variable goes on the horizontal (x) axis and the dependent variable on the vertical (y) axis. Label both with the quantity and unit.

Use even, linear scales that use more than half of the grid in each direction, so the graph is large enough to read. The scale need not start at zero if the data do not come near zero, but this must be shown clearly.
Plot points accurately as small crosses or circled dots, and plot the means rather than every repeat.
Draw a line or smooth curve of best fit that shows the trend, with points balanced on either side. Where no trend line can be assumed, join the points with straight ruled lines.
Do not force the line through an anomalous point, because one unreliable reading would distort the trend.
Give the graph a title in the form “the effect of [independent variable] on [dependent variable]”.

Diagram: a line graph of rate of enzyme activity against temperature. Labels: axes with units, plotted points, smooth curve rising to a peak (optimum) then falling, one circled anomalous point off the curve.
A graph is only useful once you can say what it shows. Describing a trend, naming its key features and classifying the relationship between the variables are the first steps in analysing data.

Describe the trend in words and quote data, e.g. “the rate increased from 2 to 8 cm³ per minute as temperature rose from 10 °C to 40 °C, then fell to zero by 60 °C”. Using figures makes the description specific.
Name key features of a graph: a peak or optimum (the value giving the highest result), a plateau (levelling off), and the point where a line crosses zero.
A positive correlation means that as one variable increases, the other increases. A negative correlation means that as one increases, the other decreases. No correlation means there is no pattern.
A straight line through the origin shows that the variables are directly proportional, so doubling one doubles the other.
Diagram: three small scatter graphs side by side. Labels: positive correlation (points rise), negative correlation (points fall), no correlation (points scattered), with both axes marked.
A graph also lets you find values that were not measured and work out how fast something is changing. Each use has its own limits.
Interpolation is reading a value from the graph between plotted points. It is fairly reliable, because the line is supported by data on both sides.
Extrapolation is extending the line beyond the data range to predict a value. It is less reliable, because the pattern may not continue, e.g. an enzyme’s rate does not keep rising with temperature.
The gradient (steepness) of a line graph of amount against time is the rate. A steeper line means a faster rate.
A line levelling off means the reaction is slowing, e.g. as substrate (the substance the enzyme acts on) is used up.
Finding a pattern between two variables is not the same as finding out why. A correlation is a starting point, and several different explanations can lie behind it.
A correlation shows that two variables change together. It does not show that one causes the other.
Other explanations of a correlation are chance, especially with a small sample; a third variable (a confounding variable) that affects both; or a cause that runs the other way.

Illustrative example: people who carry cigarette lighters are more likely to develop lung cancer, but the lighter does not cause cancer. Smoking, the third variable, causes both, because smokers carry lighters and smoking causes lung cancer.

Evidence that one variable causes a change in another comes from a controlled experiment (a fair test with a control, where only the factor being tested changes), together with a biological mechanism that explains it.
Surveys and secondary data alone usually show correlation, because they cannot control other variables. There is more on the strategies in Questioning and predicting.
Real data rarely come out perfectly, and sometimes one result sits well away from the rest. You need to recognise these results and know exactly how to treat them.
An anomalous result (outlier) does not fit the pattern of the other results. It is far from the other repeats at the same value, or off the line of best fit on a graph.
Possible causes are a mistake in measuring or recording, an uncontrolled variable, faulty equipment, or an unusual biological sample.
Check the reading and the calculation, and repeat that measurement if possible. This shows whether it was a simple mistake.

Leave the anomalous result out of the mean and the line of best fit, but keep it in the results table and report it with a possible reason. Hiding it would be dishonest. There is more on this integrity in Designing and conducting investigations.
A result is not anomalous just because it disagrees with the hypothesis. If repeats confirm it, it may show the hypothesis is wrong or reveal something new.
The conclusion is where the data answer the question the investigation set out to test. A good conclusion states the finding, backs it with evidence, explains it and admits its limits.
A conclusion states the relationship found between the independent and dependent variables, e.g. “As sucrose concentration increased, the percentage change in mass of the potato cylinders decreased.”
A conclusion is justified with evidence: quote values or describe the trend in the graph, and say whether the data support or do not support the hypothesis. Never say that the data prove it.
A conclusion explains the result using biological knowledge, e.g. water left the cells by osmosis (the movement of water across a membrane) into the more concentrated solutions.
A conclusion is limited to what was tested: the range of the independent variable, the organism or tissue used, and the conditions. It does not claim more than the data show.

Confidence in a conclusion depends on whether the test was fair and valid, the sample size, the number of repeats, the spread of the data, the number of anomalies, and whether the results are repeatable and reproducible. There is more on this in Objectivity and data quality.
A conclusion is valid when it is supported by valid, reliable data.

Once the results are in, a scientist asks two questions: did the method really answer the question, and can the data be trusted? Evaluating means judging both, then saying what should change. It is a separate step from the conclusion, which only states what was found.

Strengths: say what worked and why. For example, variables were well controlled with a water bath (keeps temperature steady) and a buffer (keeps pH steady), there were enough replicates (repeat runs), the repeat readings had a small range, and results agreed with other groups.

Limitations: identify specific weaknesses and say how each affected the results. Examples are a variable that could not be controlled, too few values of the independent variable (the thing you change) to locate an optimum (the best value), or a small sample.
Other limitations include an end-point judged by eye, which is subjective, and an anomaly (a result that does not fit the pattern) that could not be repeated, so its cause stays unknown.
Name each source of error as random or systematic. There is more on this in Objectivity and data quality.

Confidence: state how confident you are in the conclusion and why, linking to the evidence, such as the spread of the data, the repeats and whether the test was fair. Close, repeated values and a fair test justify more confidence.
Further work: an evaluation can suggest a new question or an extension, such as testing the same enzyme at different pH values, or testing a different tissue.
Investigation is iterative, meaning it goes round in cycles: results lead to a revised hypothesis or method, which is then tested again.
Saying a method was weak is only half the job. A good improvement names the change and says how it makes the data better, which is what earns the marks.

Improvements must be specific and say how each one improves the data. “Use a colorimeter (an instrument that measures colour) instead of judging the colour by eye, to remove a subjective judgement and reduce random error” is specific.
“Test at 2 °C intervals between 30 °C and 50 °C to locate the optimum more precisely.” Smaller steps near the peak show where the best value lies, which a few widely spaced values cannot.
“Use five replicates instead of two, to reduce the effect of natural variation.” More repeats mean one odd result matters less to the average.
“Calibrate the balance against a known mass, to remove a systematic error.” Calibrating means checking an instrument against a known value, so a balance that always reads too high is corrected.
“Be more careful” or “do it again” earns nothing, because neither says what changes or how the data improves.
Reflection looks back at the investigator’s own decisions as well as at the data. It asks what you did, why, and what you would do differently.
Reflection covers why the question and hypothesis were chosen, how the method was planned, what problems arose and how they were solved, and what changed during the work and why.
An investigative log is a dated lab notebook that records plans, decisions, changes, raw data (the readings as first recorded), problems and ideas as the work happens.
