A log makes reflection honest and specific, because it shows how the work actually unfolded rather than how it was meant to go.

Good reflection identifies the skills used, such as planning, measuring, handling equipment, recording, analysing, working in a team and finding and using sources, and says which went well and which to improve next time.
An investigation that does not support its hypothesis, or gives unexpected results, is still valuable, because explaining why is good scientific thinking.
Exam questions describe investigations you have not done before, with new organisms, equipment or data. The same seven steps work every time, so a new setting is never a new problem.
2. Identify the independent variable (what was changed) and the dependent variable (what was measured).
3. List the variables that should be controlled (kept the same) and how.
4. Suggest a suitable control, a comparison set-up where the factor being tested is absent.
5. State a prediction using biological knowledge.
6. Read the data or graph for the trend and any anomaly.
7. Draw a conclusion, and give a limitation and an improvement.

Transferable checks for any unfamiliar context: Is it a fair test? Is the sample big enough and random? Was there a control? Could a correlation have another cause? Are there ethical issues with the organisms or people used?
Here the seven steps are applied to the question “Does the length of time spent exercising affect pulse rate?”. Follow each step and see what it produces.
Step 2, variables: the independent variable is exercise time (e.g. 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 minutes of stepping). The dependent variable is pulse rate in beats per minute, measured straight after exercise.

Step 3, controlled variables: the type and pace of exercise, rest before starting, the way pulse is measured (same site, counted for the same time), and the time of day. Each could change pulse rate by itself.
Step 4, control: the resting pulse of participants with no exercise, which shows what pulse rate is without the factor being tested.
Sample: a larger group chosen at random gives more reliable results, because fitness, age and health vary between people.
Ethics: participants give informed consent and may withdraw at any time, and anyone with a health condition is excluded.
Step 5, prediction: pulse rate increases with exercise time. Respiring muscles need more oxygen and glucose, so the heart beats faster to deliver them, and the increase may level off.

A report is organised in standard sections so that a reader can follow the investigation and repeat it. Each section answers one question a reader would ask, from why you did it to what you found and how far it can be trusted.

Sections in order: title; aim or question; hypothesis and prediction; background (the biological theory behind the hypothesis, with sources); equipment and materials; method; risk assessment and ethical considerations.

The sections after that, in order: results (tables and graphs); analysis (calculations, patterns and anomalies, meaning results that do not fit the pattern); conclusion; evaluation (limitations, sources of error and improvements); and references.

The method is written as numbered steps with exact quantities, concentrations, times and temperatures, so that someone else can reproduce it. It is usually in the past tense and impersonal style, e.g. “10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide was added”.

A scientific paper written for other scientists begins with an abstract: a short summary of the aim, method, main results and conclusion. This lets readers decide quickly whether the paper is relevant to them.
Results sections present data and do not explain them, so the reader can judge the evidence before being told what it means. Explanation belongs in the analysis and the conclusion.

The same findings are communicated differently depending on who will read them and why: the audience's background knowledge, what they need to know, and what they will do with it. A format that suits scientists can confuse the public, so you choose the format and the level of detail to match the reader.
Scientists and examiners need a full report or paper. Technical terms are used precisely, and full data, methods, limitations and references are included, so the reader can check and repeat the work.

The general public needs plain language, with technical terms explained or avoided. The main finding and why it matters come first, because these readers will not work through the detail. Use simple graphs or infographics (pictures that present data at a glance).
The general public also needs uncertainty stated honestly, without exaggeration. Suitable formats include a poster, article, presentation, video, infographic and social media post.

Decision-makers, e.g. a school board, a council or a health service, need a short summary of the evidence, its reliability and its implications, with recommendations, because they must decide what to do rather than check the method.

A poster or presentation is selective: a clear title, the question, a brief method, one or two key graphs and the conclusion, with little text. A full report includes everything, which is why it suits readers who need to check the work.
Science only works as communication if every term means the same thing to every reader. Using exact words, symbols and units removes ambiguity and makes your results reproducible.

Use precise scientific terms with their correct meanings, e.g. “independent variable” (the factor you change), “control” (the comparison set-up), “precise” (close repeat values), “accurate” (close to the true value), “reliable” (repeatable) and “anomalous” (not fitting the pattern). There is more on these in the other notes on this chapter.

Use biological terms precisely: write “denatured” (its shape changed so it no longer works) rather than “killed” for an enzyme, since enzymes are not alive. Write “osmosis” rather than “soaking up water”.

Use SI units (the international standard units) and their symbols consistently: g and kg, cm³ and dm³, °C, s and min, and mm and µm. Write a unit with every quantity, because a number without a unit cannot be interpreted.

Write scientific names of organisms in binomial form (two-part names). The genus takes a capital letter and the species a lower-case letter, in italics in print or underlined by hand, e.g. Homo sapiens: genus Homo, species sapiens.
Avoid vague words such as “a lot”, “it worked” or “the results were good”, because they give the reader nothing to check. State what changed, by how much and in which direction.

A representation is the form in which results or ideas are shown, such as a table, graph, diagram or photograph. Each form shows something different well, so the best one depends on the point you want the audience to take away.
A table gives exact values, whereas a graph shows a trend or comparison at a glance. There is more on graph types in Producing and analysing data.

A labelled diagram shows apparatus or a structure. A flow chart shows the steps of a method or process in order. A photograph records a result, e.g. a colour change or colonies on an agar plate (the jelly on which microbes are grown).

A diagram of apparatus is drawn in two dimensions as a cross-section (as if the apparatus were cut through), in pencil. Ruled label lines touch the part labelled and do not cross, so each label is clearly linked to one part.
Biological drawings use clear single lines with no shading, labels to the side, and a title with magnification or scale where relevant, so that the size of the real structure can be worked out.
Every table, graph and figure has a title or caption and is referred to in the text, so the reader knows what it shows and when to look at it.

Readers trust a report only if it is honest and its sources can be traced. Integrity means reporting what you actually found, giving credit for other people's work, and claiming no more than your evidence supports.
Report all results honestly, including anomalies and results that do not support the hypothesis, and state the limitations. Leaving them out would mislead the reader.
Acknowledge every source by citing it in the text and giving a reference list. A reference gives at least the author or organisation, the year, the title and where it was published.
For a website, the reference gives the web address and the date it was accessed, because web pages can change or be removed.
Do not exaggerate findings. A small school investigation cannot show that something is true in general, and communication to the public should not overstate certainty.

Digital tools support communication: spreadsheets record, process and graph data; presentation and word-processing software produce reports and posters; and data loggers (devices that measure and store readings automatically) collect and display data.

The specification's digital technology section names using digital technology to collect, record, analyse and display data, and to develop investigative research, communication and report-writing skills.

Leaving Certificate Biology is not assessed by a single exam. Alongside the written paper there is a second component in which you do your own scientific investigation, so it is worth knowing how the two fit together.

Leaving Certificate Biology has two assessment components: a written examination worth 60%, taken at Higher and Ordinary level, and an additional assessment component, the Biology in Practice Investigation, worth 40%.

The investigation is based on one common brief (the same task for all students) and is worth 200 marks. It is assessed at the level at which you take the written paper, so only the written examination has two levels.
Both components are set and examined by the State Examinations Commission (SEC), the body that runs the state exams. The investigation is not coursework marked by your own teacher.

You complete the work during the course and, in Year 2 (sixth year), submit to the SEC evidence of your ability to conduct scientific research on a particular issue and to use appropriate primary data (data you collect yourself) to investigate aspects of that issue.
The specification envisages that the investigation will take up to 20 hours to complete. Further details are given in the Guidelines for the Biology in Practice Investigation.
The investigation is there to let you show what you have learned across the whole course, not to test one topic. It also builds the habits of a working scientist.

It gives you an opportunity to display evidence of your learning throughout the course, in particular the learning in the Unifying Strand (Nature of Science): the outcomes in this chapter and in Scientific Knowledge, Science in Society and Biological Reasoning.

It is designed to be integrated into the flow of teaching and learning, to be motivating and relevant, and to show the relevance of biology to students’ lives, so it uses real issues rather than abstract ones.
It also draws together the learning outcomes and the cross-cutting themes of Health, Sustainability and Technology, which run through every strand of the course.

It lets you pursue your own interests in biology, make your own investigative decisions, gain a depth of conceptual understanding and self-regulate your learning (plan, monitor and adjust it yourself).

The specification stresses that research and experimentation are “more about engaging with and learning from the process, rather than seeking a perfect answer”. This is why an experiment that does not go to plan can still be valuable.

You should give an authentic account of how your investigative work unfolded, discuss and explain the outcomes, and say how you might revise aspects of the process. There is more on this in Reflecting on investigations.
Every year the SEC publishes a brief, the document that tells you exactly what the investigation must cover. It is the starting point for everything you do.
The SEC publishes an Investigation Brief every year, in term two of Year 1 (fifth year) of the course, so you have time to plan; the brief for the 2027 examination was issued in January 2026.
The 2027 brief is set on membranes, osmosis and food preservation.
The brief sets out the specific requirements of the investigation for that year, so it is the final word on what you must do.
It allows you to develop your thinking and ideas on areas related to the brief that you would like to pursue.
It helps teachers and students plan, and includes stimulus material (articles, data or images) to set a context for the investigation.

It allows you to develop an investigative log (a running record of your work and decisions) that you can draw on as you complete the investigation. There is more on this in Reflecting on investigations.
The work has two parts, followed by an evidence-based argument and a submitted report. Using both research and an experiment is what makes it more than just a lab write-up.

Part 1 is scientific research on an issue related to the brief, so you start by reading, not experimenting. You gather, process and evaluate information from secondary sources (work done by others, such as articles and reports), and what you learn may help to inform your experimental work.
Evaluating how reliable those sources are, including checking for bias, matters because a weak source weakens your whole argument. There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.

Part 2 is an experiment related to an issue within the brief, which gives you primary data of your own. You generate a hypothesis (a testable prediction), plan and design the experiment, carry it out and gather primary data, then analyse the data and form conclusions.
The skills for Part 2 are in Questioning and predicting, Designing and conducting investigations, Objectivity and data quality and Producing and analysing data.

You then develop an evidence-based argument in response to the brief, drawing on both your research and your experiment, so each part supports your case, because research gives the background and the experiment gives your own evidence.

On completion you submit a report of the investigation in Year 2, in a format prescribed by the SEC. General report-writing skills are in Communicating results, but the SEC sets the actual format, so follow its instructions rather than your own layout.

Schools have a high degree of autonomy in planning and organising the completion of the investigation. A separate document, Guidelines for the Biology in Practice Investigation, gives guidance on its organisation, implementation and oversight.
The specification sums up what the investigation asks of you in four requirements. They are also the reasons the descriptors of quality look the way they do.
It requires you to consider issues related to real-world applications of biology, such as how biological ideas are used in health, sustainability or technology.
It requires you to demonstrate investigative skills, such as the planning, practical and analysis skills used to answer a scientific question.
It requires you to relate your investigative work to the work of scientists in society, for example by asking how professionals would tackle the same question.
It requires you to communicate your findings appropriately and effectively.
The SEC brief sets the report's headings, limits and format, and allocates the 200 marks in four blocks of 50. The descriptors of quality that follow describe the standard expected within them.
Criterion A, 50 marks: title and introduction, research question and hypothesis, background research and evaluation of secondary data, and references.
Criterion B, 50 marks: designing and planning, and conducting the experiment, including safety, fairness, accuracy and choice of equipment.
Criterion C, 50 marks: primary data and its presentation, data analysis, and conclusions.

Criterion D, 50 marks: scientific literacy, so it rewards good writing and thinking throughout (communication, coherence, relevance and a reflective approach), which is judged across the whole report rather than in one section.
Besides the marks, the 2027 brief fixes exactly how the report must look and how it is handed in. Following these rules is part of doing the task properly.

The report uses seven numbered headings, each on a new page: Title and Introduction; Background Research; Designing and Planning; Conducting the Experiment; Data and Data Analysis; Conclusions; References.
The report body is no more than 1,500 words, so you must be concise (references, data tables, formulae, equations and labels are not counted), with no more than 20 images and no video.
Text is Arial and black, with 14-point bold headings and 12-point body text at 1.5 line spacing, portrait pages, 20 mm margins with nothing in them, and page numbers at the bottom centre.
The experiment and primary data collection are carried out under the direct supervision of the biology teacher, and every source, including any use of AI, is referenced.

The completed SEC cover page goes first. The report is converted to PDF, printed and proof-read, then given to the teacher by Friday 26 February 2027 with Authentication Form P.2 signed by the student, teacher and principal.
The SEC judges the quality of your work against four descriptors, each with a high, moderate and low level. The first is about how well you understand the biology behind your investigation.

High: you engage thoroughly with the concepts being investigated; explain clearly and accurately, using appropriate means, the biological phenomena involved; and, where applicable, pose a testable hypothesis that is underpinned by biological theory and clearly describe the purpose of the investigation.
Moderate: you show good engagement with the concepts; describe the biological phenomena involved; and, where applicable, pose a testable hypothesis and outline the purpose of the investigation.
Low: you show limited engagement with the concepts; outline the biological phenomena involved; and are provided with a testable hypothesis to investigate rather than making your own.
The second descriptor is about how well you planned and carried out the experiment, because good data can only come from a good design.

High: you use clear, thorough and appropriate investigative design and methods to collect primary data, leading to high quality data, presentation and analysis, because good data can only come from a good method.
Moderate: you use clear and appropriate design and methods, leading to good quality data, presentation and analysis.
Low: your design and methods are unclear, leading to limited data, presentation and analysis.
The third descriptor is about what you do with your results: whether your conclusions follow from the data and whether you recognise the weaknesses in your own design.

High: you draw valid conclusions that are justified by the data and relate to any hypotheses made, and thoroughly evaluate the investigation, acknowledging sources of error in the investigative design, so your evaluation must be honest and specific.
Moderate: you draw conclusions that relate to any hypotheses made, and identify potential sources of error in the investigative design.
Low: you draw limited conclusions, and potential sources of error in the investigative design are not identified.
The fourth descriptor looks beyond your own experiment. It asks how your findings connect to what scientists do and to wider issues in society.
High: you offer a considered reflection that locates the outcomes of the investigation within broader issues relating to the work of a scientist or science and society.
Moderate: you reflect on how the outcomes relate to the work of a scientist or science and society.
Low: you make limited links between the outcomes and the work of a scientist or science and society, so your findings stay isolated from the wider picture.
This is study advice drawn from the wording of the descriptors, not an SEC rule. Reading the four descriptors side by side shows what moves work from one level to the next.

The differences between levels are in the verbs and qualifiers: “explain clearly and accurately” against “describe” against “outline”; “thoroughly evaluate” against “identify” against not identifying errors; and “considered reflection” within “broader issues” against “limited links”.
Posing your own testable hypothesis, grounded in biological theory, is a feature of the high and moderate levels. Being given a hypothesis is described at the low level.

Acknowledging and evaluating sources of error in the design is expected for high achievement. A perfect result is not required, but an honest evaluation is, because it shows you understand how reliable your results are. This fits the specification’s stress on learning from the process.

The fourth descriptor needs explicit links between your own findings and the work of scientists or wider issues in science and society, for example how scientists would investigate the same issue on a larger scale, or the health, sustainability or technology issue in the brief.

Every news story, advert or social media post about science makes a claim, and a claim is only as good as the evidence behind it. To judge that evidence you ask three questions: is it relevant, is it accurate, and is it biased?
Evidence is the information (observations, measurements, results of studies) used to support or refute a claim, which means to back it up or to count against it.
A claim is a statement that something is true, e.g. “vitamin C prevents colds”. The claim is what you are testing; the evidence is what you test it with.

Relevance asks whether the evidence actually addresses this claim. Evidence about a different organism, population, dose or situation may not apply, so a study in mice, or on cells in a dish, does not show the same effect in humans.
A study of elite athletes may not apply to the general population, because their bodies and training are unusual. A study of a pure chemical may not apply to a food that contains only a little of it.

Accuracy asks whether the evidence is correct and reported correctly. Check whether it comes from a reliable method, whether it has been reproduced (repeated by others with the same result), and whether the numbers in a report match the original study.
Also check whether the conclusion goes further than the data allow. A report can quote accurate numbers and still claim more than those numbers show.

Bias asks whether the evidence, or the way it is presented, has been pushed in one direction. The types of bias in sources are funding, conflict of interest, cherry-picking, publication bias, confirmation bias, sampling bias and political bias. Here you apply them to the evidence behind an argument.

Not all evidence is equally convincing. Scientists rank the types of evidence by how well each can rule out chance and other explanations, so you can say how far a claim is supported. The list runs from weakest to strongest.

Anecdote or personal testimony (“it worked for me”) is the weakest. One person’s experience can be due to chance, the placebo effect (feeling better because you expect to), natural recovery or other causes. It can prompt a proper study, but it is not evidence that a treatment works.
Expert opinion without data, or a single case report (a description of one patient), is weak. It is useful for raising a question that can then be tested.
Laboratory studies on cells or animals are useful for finding mechanisms (how something works), but they may not apply to humans, so the result is relevant only with caution.

Observational studies of large groups of people, e.g. following thousands of people and comparing smokers with non-smokers, are good for finding links (correlations). They cannot on their own show cause and effect, because other factors may differ between the groups.

Randomised controlled trials place people randomly in a treatment group or a control group, usually double-blind. Random placement spreads other factors evenly between the groups, so these are the strongest single study for showing that a treatment causes an effect.
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses combine all good-quality studies on a question. They are the strongest overall evidence because they do not rely on one study, which might be a fluke.
Scientific consensus is the agreed view of most experts in a field, reached after many studies, e.g. that human activity is causing climate change and that vaccines do not cause autism.
A single new study rarely overturns a consensus, because it needs to be reproduced first. One surprising result is more likely to be a chance or a flaw than the end of a well-tested idea.
Even real evidence can be misused. These are the mistakes that most often turn a modest result into a dramatic headline, and each one is a point you can raise when evaluating a claim.

Correlation presented as causation: media reports often say that a food, drug or habit “causes” or “prevents” a disease when a study found only a correlation (two things occurring together). A link alone does not show that one produces the other.

In large health studies, experiments on people are often impossible or unethical, so a link is accepted as causal only when several kinds of evidence agree. The cause comes before the effect, and more exposure gives more effect (a dose–response pattern).
The same link must also be found in many independent studies in different populations, and a biological mechanism must explain it.
Smoking and lung cancer met all of these tests, which is why smoking is accepted as a cause of lung cancer.
Small samples: results from few individuals are more likely to be due to chance, because one or two unusual people can change the average.
No control group: without a comparison, an improvement may have happened anyway, so you cannot tell whether the treatment did anything.

Relative and absolute risk: a headline saying a food “doubles the risk” of a disease may describe a rise from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000. This is an arithmetic illustration, not real data, and the absolute increase is small. Always ask “doubled from what?”
Extrapolating beyond the data: assuming that a trend continues outside the range tested, or that the effect of a high dose applies to a low dose, because nobody tested those conditions.

Media include newspapers, television, radio, websites, podcasts, social media and advertising. Most people learn about science from them rather than from journals, so media reports shape public opinion and decisions on health, the environment and technology. Understanding how reports get distorted helps you spot the problem.

Headlines exaggerate to attract readers or clicks (sensationalism). A single preliminary study may be reported as a breakthrough or a “cure”, and animal or cell results may be reported as if they apply to humans.
Uncertainty and limitations are often left out, which makes results sound firmer than they are. Press releases from universities and companies may themselves exaggerate.
False balance: giving equal time to a fringe view and to the scientific consensus, e.g. one climate scientist debating one climate-change denier, makes the evidence seem evenly split when it is not.
Misinformation is false or misleading information spread without intent to deceive. Disinformation is false information spread deliberately to deceive, e.g. for profit or political gain.

Social media spread both quickly, because posts that provoke emotion are shared more and algorithms show people more of what they already engage with, creating echo chambers (feeds where you mostly meet views you already hold).

Persuasion techniques to recognise: appeal to authority (a celebrity or a doctor speaking outside their expertise); appeal to nature (“natural means safe”, though many natural substances are poisonous, e.g. deadly nightshade); emotive language and images; testimonials instead of data.
Two more techniques: “scientists are hiding the truth” conspiracy claims, which cannot be tested, and scientific-sounding words used to sell a product.

Responsible science reporting does the opposite: it names the study and where it was published, gives the sample size and type of study, states the limitations, separates evidence from opinion, and includes comment from independent experts.

This is a method you can apply to any article, advert or post about science or technology. Work through the steps in order, and finish with a judgement, because “evaluate” means deciding how far the evidence supports the claim and noting its limits.
1. Identify the claim and who is making it, so you know exactly what must be supported and what the speaker stands to gain.
2. Find the original evidence: is a study named, and was it peer reviewed? A claim with no traceable source cannot be checked.
3. Check relevance: who or what was studied, and does it apply to the claim? Mice, cells, elite athletes or a pure chemical may not match the situation in the claim.

4. Check the strength of the evidence: the type of study, the sample size, whether there was a control group, and whether the result has been reproduced. Anecdotes, small samples and missing controls all weaken it.
5. Check accuracy: does the report match the study? Is correlation presented as causation? Is the risk given as relative or absolute?
6. Check bias: who funded the study and the report, what is their purpose, and are other views or limitations mentioned?
7. Check what other reliable sources and the scientific consensus say, because one report that disagrees with many others needs explaining.
8. Make a judgement: how far the evidence supports the claim, and what further evidence is needed.
This case shows the checklist at work on a real claim. One weak study, a hidden conflict of interest and wide media coverage combined to damage public health.

The claim: in 1998 Andrew Wakefield and colleagues published a paper in The Lancet on 12 children, suggesting a link between the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine and autism. The paper suggested a link; later evidence showed there is none.
Relevance and strength: the sample was tiny and had no control group, so there was nothing to compare against. At most, the paper showed a coincidence in timing, not a cause.
Bias: Wakefield had an undisclosed conflict of interest. He had been paid by lawyers acting for parents who wanted to sue vaccine manufacturers.
Media: the claim was reported widely, often with false balance, so the public saw a fringe view presented as an equal to the consensus.

Investigation: the journalist Brian Deer found that the children’s medical details had been misrepresented. The Lancet retracted (formally withdrew) the paper in 2010, and Wakefield was struck off the UK medical register in 2010.
Later evidence: large studies found no link, e.g. a 2019 Danish study of over 650,000 children.
Effect: vaccination rates fell in the UK and Ireland and in other countries, and measles outbreaks followed.

The case shows how one weak study, amplified by the media, can harm public health long after it has been disproved. The paper was published in a peer-reviewed journal, so peer review alone did not prevent the harm.
Claims about technology, like claims about medicine, can be tested with the same checklist. A company selling a product has a reason to make it sound better than it is.

Technology claims need the same checklist. For example, a claim that a new app “detects cancer”, or that a gene test “predicts your ideal diet”, should be tested by asking what evidence shows that it works, in whom, how accurately, and who profits from it.

Scientists add to society in several ways, and the words 'discovery' and 'invention' mean different things. Knowing the difference, and how research is organised and paid for, lets you describe any scientist's contribution accurately.

A discovery is finding something that already exists in nature but was not known, for example the structure of DNA, or that a mould kills bacteria. The thing was always there; the scientist is the first to find and describe it.
An invention is creating a new device, process or product that did not exist before, for example the electron microscope, PCR (a method of copying small samples of DNA) or a vaccine.
Discoveries often lead to inventions. The discovery of penicillin's effect on bacteria led to the invention of methods to mass-produce it, so that it could be given to many patients.
Basic (pure) research aims to understand nature with no particular use in mind. Applied research aims to solve a practical problem, such as finding a cure for a disease.

Many applications come from basic research done decades earlier. For example, the enzymes used in PCR and in DNA profiling (identifying people from their DNA) came from the study of bacteria, long before anyone planned such uses.

Most discoveries are now made by teams, often international, working in universities, hospitals, public research institutes and companies. They are funded by governments, the EU, charities and industry, and who funds research influences which questions are studied. There is more on this in Science as a global enterprise.

Scientists also contribute by advising governments, for example with public health advice in a pandemic (a disease outbreak spreading across many countries). They assess the risks of new technologies, communicate with the public, and warn about problems, as Rachel Carson did in the DDT case study.

To evaluate the impact of a scientific contribution is to judge it using evidence. Four factors give you a checklist: economic, social, sustainability and ethical. Each comes with questions you can ask about any discovery or technology.
Economic means the costs and benefits in money and jobs. Ask who pays for the research and the product, and who profits (companies, through patents). Ask whether it creates jobs or industries.

Economic questions also cover savings and affordability. Ask whether it saves money, for example fewer days lost to illness or higher crop yields, and whether poorer people and countries can afford it.

Social means the effects on people's health, lives and communities, and on how people live. Ask who benefits and who is harmed, and whether it changes life expectancy or quality of life. Ask whether it increases or reduces inequality, and how the public accepts it.

Sustainability means meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Ask what the effects are on the environment, biodiversity, resources and climate, and whether the benefits are long-lasting.
Sustainability questions also cover side effects. Ask whether it causes problems such as resistance (pests or bacteria no longer killed by a chemical or drug) or pollution.

Ethical means whether something is right or wrong. Ask whether it is fair (justice) and whether it does good and avoids harm. Ask whether people were informed and gave consent, whether animals were used and, if so, whether their use was justified, and who decides.

Ethical questions are answered by reasoning about values, informed by evidence. This means science alone cannot settle them: the facts can show what happens, but people must decide what is acceptable.

Ethical questions in biology are not left to opinion alone. Researchers and doctors use a small set of agreed principles to decide what is acceptable, and these give you the vocabulary for the ethical factor.

The four principles of medical ethics are autonomy (respecting people's right to decide for themselves, through informed consent, which means agreeing after being told the risks and benefits), beneficence (doing good), non-maleficence (doing no harm) and justice (treating people fairly and sharing benefits and burdens fairly).

For animal research, the 3Rs were proposed by Russell and Burch in 1959. Replacement means using non-animal methods where possible, Reduction means using as few animals as possible, and Refinement means minimising pain and distress.

The precautionary principle says that where an action might cause serious harm and the science is uncertain, you should take care or not proceed until there is more evidence. In other words, uncertainty is a reason for caution, not for going ahead.
International research conventions, for example the Declaration of Helsinki, set ethical rules for research across countries. There is more on this in Science as a global enterprise.

Penicillin is an antibiotic (a medicine that kills bacteria), and it began the era of antibiotics. Its story shows a discovery turning into an invention through the work of different scientists, and how its benefits are now at risk.

What happened: in 1928 Alexander Fleming, at St Mary's Hospital in London, noticed that a mould (Penicillium) contaminating a culture plate (a dish in which bacteria are grown) of Staphylococcus bacteria had killed the bacteria around it.
Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, at the University of Oxford, purified penicillin and showed that it cured infections, from 1940. It was mass-produced during the Second World War.

Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945. Fleming did not purify or mass-produce penicillin; Florey and Chain did, so Fleming made the discovery and the Oxford team turned it into a usable drug.

Social impact (positive): bacterial infections that were often fatal, such as infected wounds, pneumonia and sepsis (blood poisoning), became curable. Surgery and childbirth became much safer, and the era of antibiotics began.
Economic impact (positive): penicillin created a large pharmaceutical industry, healthier workers and fewer deaths, and antibiotics are cheap to make.

Sustainability impact (negative): overuse and misuse of antibiotics in medicine and farming have selected for resistant bacteria, such as MRSA, by natural selection. This threatens to make infections untreatable again, and Fleming warned of this in his Nobel lecture in 1945. There is more on this in Evidence for evolution.

Ethical impact: access is unequal in poorer countries. Using antibiotics to make farm animals grow faster, which has been banned in the EU since 2006, raises resistance for everyone. Prescribing responsibly, known as antibiotic stewardship, is now an ethical duty.
Judgement: one of the most beneficial discoveries in medicine, whose benefits are now threatened by the way it has been used.

Insulin is the hormone that lowers blood glucose, and people with type 1 diabetes cannot make enough of it. This case study shows a discovery that saved lives, a decision to give up profit, and a later invention that changed how the medicine is made.
What happened: in 1921 at the University of Toronto, Frederick Banting and Charles Best extracted insulin from the pancreases of dogs and showed that it lowered blood glucose in diabetic dogs.

In 1922 insulin was first used to treat a person with type 1 diabetes, a 14-year-old boy named Leonard Thompson. Social impact (positive): type 1 diabetes changed from a fatal disease to a manageable condition.

Banting and John Macleod received the Nobel Prize in 1923. The discoverers sold the patent (the legal right to profit from an invention) to the University of Toronto for a token sum so that insulin could be made widely available.

Insulin was extracted from cattle and pig pancreases until 1982, when human insulin made by genetically modified bacteria became the first genetically engineered medicine approved for use. There is more on this in Genetic engineering.
Economic impact: a large global insulin industry has grown. In some countries, notably the USA, high insulin prices mean that some patients cannot afford enough.
Sustainability impact (positive): making insulin in bacteria in fermenters (large tanks where microbes are grown) gives an unlimited, consistent supply without relying on slaughterhouse animals.

Ethical impact: experiments on dogs should be assessed using the 3Rs. Animal-derived insulin raised religious and vegetarian concerns that human insulin from bacteria removes. Fair access is a justice issue.
Judgement: overwhelmingly positive, but access is unequal.

DDT is a chemical that kills insects. It saved lives, but it also did lasting damage to wildlife. This case study shows how a scientist can contribute by warning society about a problem, and how one technology can have major benefits and major harms.

What happened: in 1939 Paul Müller discovered that the chemical DDT is a powerful insecticide. He received the Nobel Prize in 1948. DDT was used to control insects that spread malaria and typhus, and to protect crops.
In 1962 the American biologist Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, presenting evidence that DDT and other pesticides were harming wildlife, especially birds.

DDT is not broken down quickly, so it builds up in food chains and reaches high concentrations in top predators such as birds of prey. There it causes thin eggshells that break. There is more on this in Energy and nutrient transfer.
The USA banned most uses of DDT in 1972. The Stockholm Convention (2001) restricts it worldwide but allows its use to control malaria-carrying mosquitoes.

Social impact (positive): millions of people were protected from malaria and typhus, and food production increased. Economic impact: DDT was cheap and effective, so it raised crop yields, but chemical companies attacked Carson's work.

Sustainability impact (negative): persistence and build-up in food chains harmed birds of prey and other wildlife, and insects evolved resistance to DDT. Silent Spring helped to start the modern environmental movement.

Ethical impact: weighing human lives saved from malaria against harm to wildlife and long-term ecological damage, applying the precautionary principle, and respecting the public's right to be told the risks.
Judgement: the same scientific contribution can have major benefits and major harms, and scientists also contribute by evaluating technologies.

Ivermectin is a drug against parasitic worms, developed with the help of an Irish scientist. It shows how basic research on soil microorganisms can lead to a medicine, and how a company can share a discovery with people who cannot pay for it.
What happened: William Campbell, born in 1930 in Ramelton, Co. Donegal, and a graduate of Trinity College Dublin, worked at the drug company Merck in the USA.

Satoshi Ōmura in Japan isolated a soil bacterium, a Streptomyces species, that produced useful compounds. Campbell's team found that one of them, avermectin, killed parasitic worms, and developed the drug ivermectin from it. Ōmura isolated the bacterium; Campbell did not.

Ivermectin is used against river blindness (onchocerciasis), caused by a parasitic worm spread by the bites of blackflies, and against lymphatic filariasis. Social impact (positive): it has protected many millions of people in Africa and Latin America from river blindness and other parasitic diseases.
Campbell and Ōmura shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Tu Youyou, who discovered the antimalarial drug artemisinin.
Economic impact: the drug was first sold as a veterinary drug for livestock and pets, which made it highly profitable. Healthier people can work and attend school.

Ethical impact (positive): since 1987 Merck has donated the human form, Mectizan, free for as long as it is needed, through the Mectizan Donation Program. This is a model of a company sharing a discovery with people who cannot pay.
Sustainability impact (negative): heavy use in livestock has led to resistance in some livestock parasites, and residues in animal dung can harm dung-feeding insects.
Judgement: a discovery from basic research on soil microorganisms, with an enormous health benefit, shared ethically.

Thalidomide shows what can go wrong when a drug is released without enough testing. Unlike the other case studies, its main lesson is a warning, and its legacy is the strict system of drug testing we have today.
What happened: thalidomide was sold from 1957, first in West Germany and then in many countries including Ireland and the UK, as a sedative. It was given to pregnant women for morning sickness.
It had not been tested for effects on the developing foetus. It caused severe birth defects, especially shortened or missing limbs, in more than 10,000 babies before it was withdrawn in 1961.
In the USA, Frances Kelsey, a reviewer at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), refused to approve it because the safety evidence was inadequate. Her refusal shows why independent review matters.

Social impact (negative): lifelong disability for survivors and their families, and loss of public trust in medicines. Economic impact: compensation costs, and new regulation made developing drugs slower and more expensive.
Ethical impact (negative): patients were harmed by a drug released without adequate testing. Survivors campaigned for decades for compensation and an apology.
Lasting effect: much stricter laws on testing drugs before sale, including testing for effects in pregnancy, and systems to report side effects.
Thalidomide is now used, under strict controls, to treat leprosy complications and a blood cancer, multiple myeloma.
Judgement: shows why scientists and regulators must test new technologies carefully, and why independent review matters.
The syllabus asks you to research a scientist's contribution and present it, not just recall case studies. This is the method to follow, whichever scientist or team you choose.
1. Choose a scientist or team and their discovery or invention.

2. Research using reliable sources (sources you can trust, such as scientific journals and established institutions): who the scientists were, the problem, what they did and how, the evidence, and how the work was received. There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
3. Describe the impact under the four factors (economic, social, sustainability and ethical), positive and negative, using specific evidence.
4. Make and justify a judgement: say whether the overall impact was positive or negative, and give your reasons.
5. Present the work for the audience, for example as a poster, a slide presentation or a short report, with references so that others can check your sources.

Biology is not just a list of separate chapters. Three cross-cutting themes, Health, Sustainability and Technology, link the chapters to the real world, and they are the way the exam asks you to use what you know.

The three cross-cutting themes are Health, Sustainability and Technology. They are not separate topics: they run through all three contextual strands (Organisation of Life; Structures and Processes of Life; Interactions of Life), and are shown in the specification’s diagram as a ring around them.
Each theme is a lens: a way of looking at any piece of biology to ask how it applies to a real issue today. The same topic can be viewed through more than one lens.
For example, genetically engineered insulin is a health issue (treating diabetes) and a technology issue (recombinant DNA, meaning DNA made by joining pieces from different sources).

The examination asks students to apply biology to issues linked to the themes, often using unfamiliar stimulus material (the new information given in a question) such as a news report, data or a case. This is why you must be able to bring knowledge from any chapter to the issue.

The Health lens asks how biology explains health and disease, how disease is prevented, diagnosed and treated, and how lifestyle and environment affect health. The specification frames health as promoting health and reducing the risk of disease. The first group of examples is about infection and illness.
Vaccination and immunity: vaccinating enough people protects those who are not immune, because the disease cannot spread easily through a mostly protected population.
Emerging infectious diseases (new or newly spreading diseases): how they spread, and the reproduction number, R₀, which is the average number of people one infected person passes the disease on to.
Cancer: its causes, prevention and treatment, for example avoiding smoking and excess UV light, which both damage cells and raise cancer risk.
Vaccination against the human papillomavirus (HPV), which causes most cervical cancers, is a prevention example. It protects against HPV but you should not claim it prevents all cervical cancer.

The gut microbiome (the community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract) has a role in digestion, immunity and metabolic health. There is more on this in “Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment”, “Emergence and spread of infectious disease”, “Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer” and “The microbiome”.

The second group of Health examples covers how lifestyle, the body’s chemical signals and medical care affect health. Each is taught in its own chapter, so here you only need to know that it belongs under this lens.
Diet: a balanced diet supports health, while diet-related conditions include obesity and vitamin deficiencies (too little of a vitamin the body needs).
Dopamine, endorphins, exercise and addiction: these chemical signals link behaviour to mood and reward, so they connect lifestyle choices to health.
Prenatal and postnatal care: looking after health before birth and after birth, for the mother and the baby.
Blood groups and safe transfusion: matching blood groups between donor and recipient makes transfusion safe.

Hormonal treatments, such as insulin and the contraceptive pill, use hormones (chemical messengers in the blood) to treat or control a condition. There is more on this in “Diet”, “Vitamins”, “Dopamine and endorphins”, “Prenatal and postnatal care”, “Blood” and “Hormonal manipulation”.

Sustainability means meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The Sustainability lens asks how human activity affects ecosystems, biodiversity, resources and climate, and how biology can help people live within the planet’s limits.
Biodiversity loss (fewer species and less variety of life) happens through habitat destruction, pollution, invasive species and climate change. Conservation is the effort to protect it.

The carbon cycle, carbon sinks (stores that take in more carbon than they release) and climate change, including Ireland’s peat bogs, which store large amounts of carbon as peat and release it as CO₂ when drained or burned.
The nitrogen cycle matters because excess fertiliser or slurry washing into rivers and lakes causes eutrophication: algal blooms that use up oxygen when they decay, killing fish.
Decomposers and soil microbiomes recycle nutrients, so nutrients are returned to the soil for plants to reuse instead of being lost.
Sustainability is not only about damage. Biology also offers ways to reduce human impact, from plants taking in carbon to enzymes that cut energy use.
Photosynthesis is a carbon sink, because plants take CO₂ from the air and build it into carbohydrates, removing carbon from the atmosphere.
Enzymes (biological catalysts) are used in biofuels, and in detergents that wash at lower temperatures, which saves energy.
The role of biology in a post-fossil-fuel world: using biological resources and processes to meet energy and material needs when fossil fuels are no longer burned.

Technology is the application of scientific knowledge to make tools, techniques and products. The Technology lens works in two directions: how technology lets biologists find out more, and how biological knowledge is used to make new technologies.
Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their parts, such as enzymes, to make useful products or carry out processes.
Technologies that extend what biologists can study include light and electron microscopes, which show cells and structures too small to see by eye.
DNA sequencing and genome databases use computers to analyse huge amounts of genetic data, which would be impossible to read by hand.

Data loggers and sensors in investigations record measurements automatically, and digital tools are used for modelling and analysing data. There is more on this in “Microscopy”, “DNA sequencing” and “Bioinformatics: genome databases”.
Biotechnologies are the technologies built from biological knowledge. They show the second direction of the Technology lens, and each is taught in detail elsewhere.
Genetic engineering, for example human insulin made by bacteria, so that insulin can be produced in large amounts.
PCR and DNA profiling are used in forensics (solving crimes) and paternity testing (finding a child’s father).
Immobilised enzymes (enzymes fixed in place) and bioreactors (vessels in which living cells or enzymes make a product) are used in industry.
Microorganisms are used in pharmaceutical, agricultural, medical and food industries.
Antenatal screening (tests during pregnancy) and fertility treatment are biotechnologies applied to reproduction.

Stem cells and gene technologies raise ethical questions, which are discussed in “Ethics of genetic technologies”. There is more on this in “Genetic engineering”, “DNA profiling”, “Industrial enzymes”, “Microorganisms in industry”, “Prenatal and postnatal care” and “Fertility control and infertility”.
A new technology is never just a benefit. Evaluating one means asking what it costs and who it affects.
New technologies raise questions as well as benefits: cost and access (who can afford it), safety, the privacy of genetic data, and effects on the environment.
The factors for evaluating technologies and the scientists behind them are in “Science, scientists and society”.
In the exam you are often given an unfamiliar issue and asked to discuss it. A fixed method means you can start from the biology you know and build an answer step by step.
1. Identify the biology behind the issue: the structures, processes or organisms involved.
2. Say which theme or themes it relates to, and why.
3. Explain the issue’s causes or mechanism using that biology.
4. Give its benefits or problems, with evidence, so your points are backed up by data or facts from the question.
5. Suggest actions or solutions based on the biology.
6. Note the links to the other themes, because most issues fit more than one lens.
Antibiotic resistance touches all three themes, so it shows the method at work. Follow the steps: biology first, then each lens, then actions.
Biology: bacteria with mutations that let them survive an antibiotic survive and reproduce, so resistant strains increase by natural selection.
Health: infections such as MRSA (an antibiotic-resistant bacterium) become hard or impossible to treat.
Sustainability: overuse of antibiotics in medicine and in farming speeds this up. Antibiotics are a resource that is being used up faster than new ones are found.
Technology: rapid diagnostic tests show whether an infection is bacterial, genome sequencing tracks resistant strains, and new antibiotics are sought.
Actions: prescribe antibiotics only for bacterial infections, take them exactly as prescribed, improve hygiene and vaccination to reduce infections, and limit antibiotic use in farm animals.
Irish peatlands are mainly a Sustainability issue with a Technology link. The method starts with why peat forms, then shows what happens when it is disturbed.
Biology: in waterlogged, acidic, low-oxygen bogs, decomposers work very slowly, so dead plant material, mainly Sphagnum moss, builds up as peat, storing carbon.
Sustainability: draining and cutting bogs for fuel lets oxygen in, so the peat decomposes or is burned, releasing CO₂. Bogs are also habitats for specialised species.
Action: Bord na Móna ended industrial peat harvesting in 2021, and drained bogs are being rewetted to stop carbon loss and restore habitats.
Technology: satellite and sensor monitoring of water levels and greenhouse-gas release.
Health link: burning peat and other solid fuels pollutes the air.

Biologists rarely study a living system directly, so they work with models instead. A model is a stand-in that is easier to handle than the real thing, and it is only useful if you know what it keeps and what it leaves out.
A model is a simplified representation of an idea, structure, process or system, used to describe, explain or predict how it behaves.

Models are needed because real biological systems are too small (molecules, cells), too large (ecosystems, the biosphere), too slow (evolution), too fast (nerve impulses), too complex (the human body), or too dangerous or unethical to study directly.

Every model is simplified: it keeps the features that matter for its purpose and leaves out others. A model is judged by how useful it is for its purpose, not by whether it is a perfect copy, because no model is complete.

Every model rests on assumptions, which are things taken to be true so that the model can work. For example, a Punnett square assumes that fertilisation is random. If an assumption does not hold, the model’s predictions fail.
Models can be modified as more data become available. When new observations do not fit, the model is changed or replaced (worked examples 1 and 2 below show this happening).
Models can predict. A good model predicts how the system will behave in new conditions, and testing those predictions is how models are checked (worked example 3 below).
A model can take many forms, from a sentence to a computer program. The form is chosen to suit what the model has to show, and each one leaves different things out.
Words (verbal or descriptive models), e.g. a written description of natural selection as variation, competition, survival of the better adapted, and inheritance.
Diagrams, e.g. a food web, a diagram of the carbon or nitrogen cycle, a labelled diagram of a cell, a flowchart of a negative-feedback loop, or a pyramid of numbers.
Equations, e.g. the balanced equation for photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. It models what goes in and comes out, but not the many steps in between.
The reproduction number R₀ (the average number of people one infected person infects) is an equation-based quantity used in models of disease spread.

Physical (concrete) models, e.g. Watson and Crick’s model of DNA, a bell-jar model of the lungs, a plastic model of the heart, and ball-and-stick models of molecules. You can handle them and see the structure in three dimensions.

Simulations, often computer models, e.g. models of how an infectious disease spreads through a population, climate models, and computer models of protein folding. Simulations can run “what if” scenarios quickly and safely.

Model organisms are a different use of the word: species studied in detail because they are easy to keep and breed and share much biology with others, e.g. the bacterium Escherichia coli, yeast, the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, the plant Arabidopsis thaliana, and the house mouse.
The assumption behind a model organism is that what is true of it is true of other organisms. The limitation is that results do not always transfer to humans.
Models are built and improved in a cycle: observe, represent, predict, test, then revise. Each step exists so that the model stays tied to real data.
Generating a model: 1. Observe the system and collect data, because a model must start from real observations.
2. Identify its key parts and how they interact, so that you know what the model must include.
3. Represent them simply, often by analogy with something familiar, e.g. “lock and key”, which compares an enzyme and its substrate to a lock and its key.
4. Use the model to make predictions, for example about what will happen if one part changes.
5. Test the predictions against new data, which is how you find out whether the model works.
6. Keep, modify or replace the model, depending on whether the predictions held.
Once a model exists, it has to be judged. The same questions apply to any model, whether it is a diagram, an equation or a simulation.
Evaluating a model asks: what does it show, and for what purpose? What does it leave out? What assumptions does it make?

It also asks: does it fit the data? Can it explain and predict? How could it be improved? Answers about a model should always name at least one strength and one limitation, so that you give a balanced evaluation.
A model is not the same as a theory. A theory is a broad, well-tested explanation; a model is a representation that may be used to explain part of a theory or to make its predictions concrete.
Two different models of the same thing can both be useful for different purposes, because each is built for a different job. There is more on theories in “The nature of scientific knowledge”.

Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions, and the part of the enzyme where the reaction happens is the active site. The way biologists have pictured the active site has changed as new data arrived, which makes it a good example of a model being modified. The Higher Level detail of enzyme structure is in “Enzyme structure and specificity”.

Lock-and-key model, proposed by Emil Fischer in 1894: the enzyme’s active site has a rigid shape that exactly fits its substrate (the molecule the enzyme acts on), as only one key fits a lock. It explains why enzymes are specific, so that each catalyses one reaction.

Its assumption is that the active site is rigid. Some enzymes act on several similar substrates, and later structural studies, e.g. X-ray crystallography (which reveals the 3D shape of molecules), showed that some enzymes change shape when the substrate binds.
For example, the enzyme hexokinase closes around glucose. A rigid lock cannot do this, so the new data did not fit the model.

Induced-fit model, proposed by Daniel Koshland in 1958: the active site is flexible. When the substrate enters, the active site changes shape slightly to mould tightly around it, like a glove around a hand.
This strains the substrate’s bonds and helps the reaction, so induced fit explains how the enzyme speeds the reaction up as well as why it is specific.
The induced-fit model replaced lock and key as the better model, although lock and key is still useful as a simple first explanation of specificity.

Diagram: two rows of three stages. Row one, lock and key: enzyme with rigid active site and substrate, then enzyme–substrate complex, then products released with the enzyme unchanged. Row two, induced fit: same stages, active site changing shape as substrate binds. Label active site, substrate, enzyme–substrate complex, products.
The cell membrane is the thin boundary that controls what enters and leaves a cell. Its structure was first modelled as a simple layered sandwich, then new evidence forced a rethink.

The earlier model, proposed by Hugh Davson and James Danielli in 1935, was a phospholipid bilayer (a double layer of fat-based molecules) sandwiched between two continuous layers of protein. Its assumption was that proteins form uniform layers on each surface.

New data did not fit. Membrane proteins vary greatly in type and amount between membranes, which a uniform protein layer cannot explain. Freeze-fracture electron microscopy, which splits a membrane down the middle of the bilayer, showed proteins embedded in and passing through the bilayer.

In 1970 Larry Frye and Michael Edidin fused a mouse cell and a human cell whose membrane proteins had been labelled differently. The proteins mixed over the surface of the combined cell, showing that membrane components move.
The fluid mosaic model replaced the sandwich. It pictures proteins scattered through a moving bilayer rather than lying in sheets on its surfaces.

The fluid mosaic model, proposed by Seymour Singer and Garth Nicolson in 1972, describes a phospholipid bilayer with hydrophilic (water-attracting) phosphate heads facing the watery fluid inside and outside the cell, and hydrophobic (water-repelling) fatty-acid tails facing inwards.

Proteins are scattered in the bilayer like tiles in a mosaic, some on the surface and some passing right through, as channel and carrier proteins do. The phospholipids and many proteins move sideways, so the membrane is fluid.
Animal cell membranes also contain cholesterol, and many proteins and lipids carry carbohydrate chains (glycoproteins and glycolipids) on the outer surface.

The model explains why small non-polar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂ diffuse straight through the bilayer, while ions and glucose need protein channels or carriers. Transport is taught in “Diffusion, osmosis and active transport”.
It also explains why membranes can fuse and re-seal, e.g. in endocytosis (the cell taking in material by folding its membrane around it), because the fluid bilayer can break and rejoin.

Limitations: the fluid mosaic model is still being refined, so it is not final. Membranes are not uniformly fluid, and some proteins are held in place by the cytoskeleton (the cell’s internal protein scaffold).
Membranes are also more crowded with protein than the usual diagram shows, and small regions of the membrane, called lipid rafts, differ in composition.

Diagram: a section of membrane showing the phospholipid bilayer with heads and tails labelled hydrophilic and hydrophobic, a channel protein passing through, a surface protein, a glycoprotein with its carbohydrate chain on the outside, and cholesterol.

Watson and Crick’s DNA model shows a model doing its most important job: pulling existing data together and then predicting something new that was later tested. DNA structure itself is taught in “Nucleotides, DNA and RNA”.
In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick, at the University of Cambridge, built a physical model of DNA from metal plates and rods.

They used X-ray diffraction images of DNA (patterns showing its structure) made by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling at King’s College London, including the image known as Photo 51, and data from Maurice Wilkins.
They also used Erwin Chargaff’s finding that in DNA the amount of adenine equals that of thymine, and the amount of cytosine equals that of guanine, which a model of the base pairing had to explain.

The model showed two strands wound into a double helix, with a sugar–phosphate backbone on the outside and bases paired inside: adenine with thymine, and cytosine with guanine. It explained Chargaff’s data and the X-ray pattern.
Prediction: complementary base pairing suggested that each strand could act as a template for a new strand, so that DNA could copy itself. Watson and Crick noted this in their 1953 paper.

In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl showed experimentally that DNA replication is semi-conservative (each new DNA molecule keeps one old strand), as the model predicted. Replication is taught in “DNA replication and mitosis in the cell cycle”.

Limitations: the model shows one short, straight, static section. In cells, DNA is extremely long, is wound around histone proteins and coiled into chromosomes, and moves and unwinds. Atoms are shown as solid shapes.

Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962. Franklin had died in 1958, and the prize is not awarded after death. Her contribution is now widely recognised, and the case is an example of how credit is shared in science.
Models turn up throughout the course. For each one, know what it represents and at least one assumption or limitation, because that is how models are evaluated.

Bell-jar model of breathing: a bell jar represents the chest, balloons the lungs, a rubber sheet the diaphragm and a tube the trachea. Pulling the sheet down increases the volume in the jar, lowering the pressure, so air enters the balloons.

Limitations of the bell jar: its walls are rigid, whereas the ribs move; there are no intercostal muscles (the muscles between the ribs); and the rubber sheet is pulled down, whereas the diaphragm contracts and flattens.
The balloons also have no alveoli (the air sacs of the lungs). There is more on this in “Gas exchange and the breathing mechanism”.
Punnett square: predicts the expected ratios of offspring genotypes (the alleles they carry) and phenotypes (their observable features).
Assumptions of the Punnett square: one gene controls the trait; each gamete (sex cell) carries one allele; fertilisation is random; all offspring survive.

Limitations of the Punnett square: the ratios are only probabilities, so small families often differ from them; and it does not apply to traits controlled by many genes or by the environment. There is more on this in “Monohybrid crosses” and “Benefits and limitations of Mendelian genetics”.
Diagrams and equations model whole systems, such as ecosystems, matter cycles and outbreaks. Each shows the pattern but leaves out detail.

Food chains, food webs and pyramids of numbers model feeding relationships and energy flow. Limitations: real feeding relationships are more complex, and pyramids of numbers can be inverted, e.g. many insects on one tree. There is more on this in “Energy and nutrient transfer” and “Pyramids of numbers”.

Carbon and nitrogen cycle diagrams model how matter moves between living things and the environment. They show processes but not their rates or amounts, so they cannot tell you how fast carbon moves or how much is stored.
There is more on these cycles in “The carbon cycle” and “The nitrogen cycle”.

Disease-spread models use R₀, the average number of people one infected person infects in a population with no immunity. They predict that an outbreak grows if R₀ is above 1 and dies out if it is below 1, and how many people must be immune to stop spread.

Assumptions of disease models: people mix randomly and R₀ stays constant. In reality, behaviour, vaccination, seasons and new variants change it, so predictions are updated as new data come in. There is more on this in “Emergence and spread of infectious disease”.
Homeostasis (keeping the body’s internal conditions steady) is modelled as a stimulus–response model, with negative feedback. There is more on this in “Homeostasis as a stimulus-response model”.
Biology covers an enormous range of material, but a few big ideas keep turning up. Learning to use them as tools lets you explain almost any living thing or event, whichever chapter it comes from.
A biological phenomenon is any observable event or feature of living things, e.g. a person sweating on a hot day, bread going mouldy, or a population of rabbits crashing.
Explaining a phenomenon means giving its causes and mechanism (how it happens, step by step), not just describing what you can see. A description says what happened; an explanation says why and how.

Biologists explain phenomena using a small number of big ideas that apply across all of biology: systems; interdependence; the unity and diversity of life; form fits function; and the transfer of information, matter and energy.

The most important further idea is evolution by natural selection, which explains both unity and diversity. The list of big ideas is open-ended, and evolution is the one that ties the others together.

Evolution is the unifying explanation. All living things share common ancestors, so they share features (unity). Natural selection acting on variation in different environments has produced adaptations and many species (diversity).
A living thing is not a pile of separate parts. It is a set of parts that work together, and thinking of it as a system explains why a problem in one part can show up somewhere else.
A system is a set of interacting parts that work together as a whole. A system has inputs and outputs, and its behaviour depends on how the parts interact, not just on the parts themselves.
Properties that appear only from the interactions of parts are called emergent properties. For example, consciousness arises from interacting neurons (nerve cells), not from any single neuron.

Biological systems exist at every level of organisation: molecules, organelles (the working parts inside a cell), cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, organisms, populations, communities, ecosystems and the biosphere (all life on Earth together).

Examples: the circulatory system, in which the heart, vessels and blood together transport materials; the digestive system; the nervous system; an ecosystem, in which living and non-living parts interact; and a cell, whose organelles work together.

Systems are regulated by feedback. Negative feedback reverses a change and keeps the system stable, e.g. the control of blood glucose and of thyroxine (a hormone). There is more on this in Homeostasis as a stimulus-response model.

Systems thinking means looking at how a change in one part affects others. For example, a fall in red blood cell count (anaemia) reduces oxygen delivery, so cells respire less aerobically (using oxygen), causing tiredness.
Organ systems also depend on each other. Breathing supplies oxygen, which the circulatory system transports to respiring cells, so a fault in either system affects the same cells.
No organism lives alone. Each depends on other organisms and on its non-living surroundings, so a change to one reaches others, sometimes in surprising ways.
Interdependence means that organisms depend on each other and on their non-living environment, so a change to one affects others.
Feeding relationships in food webs are an example: removing a predator can let its prey increase and overgraze (eat too much of what they feed on).
Pollination of flowers by insects is an example: the insects get nectar, and the flowers get their pollen carried to other flowers. Seed dispersal by animals is another.
Decomposers recycle nutrients that plants need, so plants depend on them for the minerals they take up. This is part of the carbon and nitrogen cycles.

Nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in the root nodules (small swellings on the roots) of legumes such as clover. The gut microbiome (the community of microbes in the gut) and its human host also depend on each other.
Between organisms and the environment, plants depend on light, water, CO₂ and minerals.
Photosynthesis and respiration link organisms through the carbon cycle: producers release the oxygen that consumers use, and consumers release the CO₂ that producers use.
Within an organism, organ systems depend on each other. Muscles need the nervous system to stimulate them, and the circulatory system to supply glucose and oxygen.
Living things look wildly different, yet at the cellular and molecular level they share the same basic features. That sameness is evidence that they all descend from a common ancestor.
Unity means that all living things share basic features, which is evidence that they share a common ancestor.
All living things are made of cells, with a phospholipid membrane (the thin surface layer around the cell), cytoplasm (the jelly-like contents) and ribosomes (the structures that build proteins).
All use DNA as their genetic material. The genetic code is almost universal: the same codons (three-base units of the code) code for the same amino acids in nearly all organisms.
Because the code is shared, a human gene can be expressed (used to make its protein) in bacteria in genetic engineering. This is why the same code is read correctly in both.
All use ATP to transfer energy, all build proteins from the same set of 20 amino acids, and all use enzymes (biological catalysts).
All show the characteristics of life, the set of features that define a living thing.
If life shares so much, why are there so many different kinds? Diversity is the other half of the picture, and it has identifiable causes.
Diversity means the great variety of living things, at the levels of genes (variation within a species), species, and ecosystems (biodiversity).
Mutation (a change in DNA) creates new alleles (versions of a gene), which is where new variation first comes from.
Sexual reproduction, through meiosis (the cell division that makes gametes) and random fertilisation, shuffles alleles into new combinations. There is more on this in Variation.
Natural selection in different environments favours different adaptations, so populations in different places change in different directions. Populations that are separated can become new species.
Biologists organise diversity by classification into three domains (Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryota) and six kingdoms, based increasingly on genetic evidence.
Unity and diversity are explained together by evolution: shared ancestry gives unity, and adaptation and speciation (the formation of new species) give diversity.

For example, the forelimbs of humans, bats and whales have the same set of bones, which shows unity from a common ancestor. They have different shapes for grasping, flying and swimming, which shows diversity from adaptation.

In living things, the shape or structure of a part (its form) matches the job it does (its function). Spotting that match, and saying how it works, is one of the most reliable ways to explain a feature.

Form fits function means that the structure of a molecule, cell, organ or organism suits the job it does. Natural selection explains why: individuals whose structures did the job better survived and reproduced more.
Adaptations do not arise because organisms need them. Variation already exists, and natural selection favours the better-adapted individuals.

Molecules: an enzyme’s active site (the part where the reaction happens) has a shape complementary to its substrate, so it catalyses one reaction. The DNA double helix, with complementary base pairs, allows accurate copying.

Red blood cells are biconcave discs with no nucleus, giving a large surface area and more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen. Neurons have long axons and a myelin sheath that carry impulses quickly over long distances.

Root hair cells have long extensions that increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals. Sperm cells have a tail for swimming and many mitochondria to supply energy. Guard cells change shape to open and close stomata (the pores in leaves).

Alveoli (the air sacs in the lungs) have walls one cell thick, a moist lining, a large total surface area and a rich blood supply, for fast gas exchange. Villi in the small intestine increase the surface area for absorption.

Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand high pressure, while veins have thinner walls and valves to stop backflow. Xylem vessels are hollow, dead tubes strengthened with lignin to carry water.
The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right because it pumps blood all round the body.
Living things run on instructions and signals. Information is passed between generations, between cells and around the body.
Genetic information passes from DNA to RNA to protein, so genes control traits. There is more on this in Genes, proteins and traits.
Information passes from parent to offspring through gametes (sex cells), and from cell to daughter cells by DNA replication (copying the DNA) and mitosis (the division that makes identical cells).
Information is also transferred within the body by nerve impulses, which are fast, and by hormones, which are slower.
Between cells, information is transferred by chemical signals, e.g. neurotransmitters (chemicals that cross the gap between neurons).
Living things are built from atoms that are not made new. The same atoms are passed around again and again.
Matter is not created or destroyed but is recycled. Atoms of carbon, nitrogen and other elements cycle between organisms and the environment through feeding, excretion, death and decomposition.
Within organisms, matter is taken in by digestion and absorption, gas exchange and root uptake.
