Matter is then transported in blood, xylem and phloem, and built into new molecules (anabolism) or broken down (catabolism).
Energy behaves differently from matter. It enters ecosystems from the Sun, moves through living things and leaves as heat, so it must be constantly resupplied.
Energy flows through living systems in one direction and is not recycled. Light energy from the Sun is converted to chemical energy in glucose by photosynthesis.
Respiration releases that energy and stores it in ATP, which transfers it to cell activities.
At each step some energy is lost as heat, so energy decreases at each feeding level of a food chain. This limits food chains to a few links.
Contrast: matter cycles, whereas energy flows through the system and is lost as heat.

Diagram: a simple ecosystem. Energy as a one-way arrow from the Sun through producers, consumers and decomposers, with heat-loss arrows at each level. Matter (carbon) as a loop from decomposers to air and soil and back to producers.
Most real questions need more than one idea. This five-step method gives a reliable way to build a full explanation.
1. Describe the phenomenon precisely, so you know exactly what you are explaining.
2. Choose the ideas that apply. More than one usually does.
3. Explain the mechanism step by step, naming the structures and processes involved.
4. Link structure to function, and cause to effect, using words such as “so” and “which allows”.
5. If asked, use evolution to explain why the feature exists.
Why do breathing and heart rate rise when you exercise? Four of the big ideas combine to explain it.
Transfer of energy: muscles need more ATP, so they respire faster.
Transfer of matter: more oxygen must be supplied and more CO₂ removed.
Systems and interdependence: the breathing, circulatory and muscular systems work together. The brain detects the rise in CO₂ in the blood and increases the breathing rate, a feedback response.
Form fits function: alveoli and capillaries (the smallest blood vessels) suit fast exchange. There is more on CO₂ control in CO₂ as a controlling factor in breathing.
Why can removing a top predator (an animal at the top of a food chain) reduce plant diversity? Follow the change through the food web.
Interdependence: the predator’s prey, e.g. a herbivore, increases because fewer are eaten.
Transfer of matter and energy: more energy flows to the herbivores, which eat more of the producers (the plants).
Systems: one change spreads through the food web.
Diversity: the plants that the herbivores prefer decline, so species diversity can fall.

Biology is the study of living things, called organisms. No single feature separates living from non-living, so the specification lists eleven characteristics: organisation, response, respiration, nutrition, excretion, reproduction, growth, metabolism, homeostasis, heredity and cellular basis. Together they define life.

An organism shows all eleven characteristics at some stage of its life, though not necessarily all at once. A dormant seed or a hibernating animal shows very little response or growth, but it is still alive.
Some non-living things show one or two characteristics. A crystal grows, but only by adding material to its outside, not by making new material inside cells.
A fire seems to 'use oxygen', 'release energy' and 'spread', but it has no cells, no heredity and no control of its reactions, so it is not alive.
Something is alive only if it shows the full set, not just one or two features. Viruses are the main borderline case. There is more on this in Viruses.

Living things are not random mixtures of chemicals: they are built in an ordered way, and the basic building block is the cell. Two of the eleven characteristics, organisation and cellular basis, describe this.

Organisation: living things have a highly ordered structure. In multicellular organisms (those made of many cells), cells are grouped into tissues, tissues into organs and organs into organ systems, each level carrying out particular jobs.
Even a single cell has organised parts called organelles (small structures inside a cell, each with its own job). There is more on this in Levels of organisation.
Cellular basis: all living things are made of one or more cells. The cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all the processes of life, so it is the basic unit of structure and function.

Unicellular organisms (e.g. bacteria, yeast, Amoeba) are one cell that carries out every life process. Multicellular organisms (e.g. humans, oak trees) have many specialised cells, each adapted to one job.

All cells share a cell membrane, cytoplasm (the jelly-like fluid inside the cell), ribosomes (which make proteins) and DNA as their genetic material. This shared basis is evidence that all life has a common origin.
All cells arise only from pre-existing cells, by cell division. New cells are never made from non-living material.

These points form the cell theory, developed in the 19th century. Matthias Schleiden concluded that all plants are made of cells (1838); Theodor Schwann extended this to animals (1839); Rudolf Virchow stated that all cells come from pre-existing cells (1855).

Every organism needs a supply of food to stay alive and to build and repair its body. Nutrition is how it gets that food, and organisms fall into two groups depending on whether they make it or take it in.
Nutrition: the way an organism obtains food, which supplies the energy and the raw materials (e.g. carbon, nitrogen, minerals) it needs.

Autotrophic nutrition: the organism makes its own food from simple inorganic substances (ones not made by living things, such as carbon dioxide and water). Photosynthetic autotrophs (plants, algae, some bacteria) use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
A few bacteria are chemosynthetic: instead of light, they use energy from chemical reactions to make their food, so they can live where there is no sunlight.
Heterotrophic nutrition: the organism takes in ready-made food made by other organisms, e.g. animals eat plants or other animals.
Fungi and many bacteria are also heterotrophs: they absorb food from dead matter (saprophytes) or from a living host (parasites). There is more on this in Microorganisms.
Food is only useful once its stored energy can be released in a form cells can use. Respiration does this inside every living cell, and it is easily confused with breathing.

Respiration: the controlled release of energy from food, mainly glucose, inside every living cell. The energy is trapped in ATP (the molecule cells use to carry energy), which powers the cell's activities.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy. It releases much more energy per glucose than anaerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen and releases less energy, because the glucose is only partly broken down.
In human muscle, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid. In yeast and plant cells it produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Respiration is not the same as breathing. Breathing is the movement of air into and out of the lungs (gas exchange), while respiration is a chemical process in cells.
Plants respire all the time, day and night, because every living cell needs energy continuously. There is more on this in Respiration.
Living cells carry out thousands of chemical reactions at once. Metabolism is the name for all of them, and they fall into two types: those that build up and those that break down.
Metabolism: the sum of all the chemical reactions in an organism. Every reaction is controlled by an enzyme (a protein that speeds up a reaction).
Anabolic reactions build large molecules from smaller ones and need energy, e.g. photosynthesis (glucose made from carbon dioxide and water) and protein synthesis from amino acids.
Catabolic reactions break large molecules into smaller ones and release energy, e.g. respiration, and the digestion of starch to maltose.
In short, anabolic means building up and using energy, while catabolic means breaking down and releasing energy. There is more on this in Biomolecules — The Chemicals of Life.
Chemical reactions in cells make some products that the body cannot use. Excretion removes them before they cause harm.
Excretion: the removal of the waste products of metabolism, which are substances made in cells that are harmful or not needed. If they built up they would poison cells or upset conditions such as pH.

Human examples: carbon dioxide from respiration is excreted by the lungs. Urea, made in the liver from excess amino acids, is excreted by the kidneys in urine. Excess water and salts are excreted by the kidneys and in sweat.
Plant examples: oxygen from photosynthesis and carbon dioxide from respiration diffuse out through the stomata (the tiny pores in leaves). Some waste is stored in old leaves and lost when they fall.
Excretion is not egestion. Egestion is the removal of undigested food (faeces), which was never inside body cells and so is not a product of metabolism.
Cells work properly only when the conditions around them stay within narrow limits, even if the outside world changes. Homeostasis is the control that keeps them steady.

Homeostasis: the maintenance of a relatively constant internal environment, such as body temperature, blood glucose concentration, water and salt balance and pH, despite changes outside or inside the organism.
It matters because enzymes work only within narrow ranges of temperature and pH, so a large change would slow or stop the reactions of metabolism.
For example, human core body temperature is kept at about 37 °C, and insulin lowers blood glucose after a meal. There is more on the mechanism, negative feedback, in Homeostasis.
Organisms must cope with a changing environment and must also produce new individuals, because every organism eventually dies. Response and reproduction cover these two needs.
Response: the ability to detect a change in the internal or external environment (a stimulus) and react to it, which helps the organism survive.
Animals respond quickly through the nervous system (e.g. pulling a hand away from a hot object) and more slowly with hormones (chemical messengers carried in the blood).

Plants respond more slowly, mainly through chemicals and their structure, e.g. guard cells close the stomata when water is short, which reduces water loss. There is more on this in Structures and systems for response.
Reproduction: the production of new individuals of the same species. Every organism eventually dies, so reproduction is needed for the species to continue.
Asexual reproduction: one parent and no gametes (sex cells). The offspring are genetically identical to the parent (clones), e.g. binary fission in bacteria and budding in yeast.

Sexual reproduction: two gametes fuse at fertilisation to form a zygote (the first cell of the new organism). The offspring are genetically different from the parents and from each other, which gives variation, e.g. humans and flowering plants.
Organisms get bigger as they develop, and they pass their features on to the next generation. Growth and heredity describe these two processes.

Growth: a permanent increase in size and mass. It happens from within, by making new materials (anabolism, the building reactions of metabolism), by cell division (mitosis) increasing the number of cells, and by cells enlarging and becoming specialised.
Plants keep growing throughout life at regions of dividing cells at the root and shoot tips. Most animals grow to a fixed adult size.

Heredity: the passing of genetic information, carried by genes made of DNA, from parents to offspring, so offspring inherit their parents' characteristics. 'Like produces like', e.g. a cat's offspring are always kittens.

Genes code for proteins, which control an organism's traits (its characteristics). Variation arises from sexual reproduction and from mutations (changes in DNA). There is more on this in Genetic Inheritance.
Here is the full set in one place for quick revision. An organism shows all eleven at some stage of its life.
Organisation: highly ordered structure, from cells up to organ systems.
Response: detecting a stimulus and reacting to it.
Respiration: releasing energy from food inside cells.
Nutrition: obtaining food for energy and raw materials.
Excretion: removing the waste products of metabolism.
Reproduction: producing new individuals of the same species.
These are the remaining five characteristics, covering growth, chemistry, stability, inheritance and cells.
Growth: a permanent increase in size and mass.
Metabolism: all the chemical reactions in an organism.
Homeostasis: keeping the internal environment relatively constant.
Heredity: passing genetic information from parents to offspring.
Cellular basis: made of cells, which arise only from pre-existing cells.
Living things are organised in levels of increasing complexity. Each level is made of units of the level below working together, so a whole organism can be understood by building up from its cells.
The order is cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism. Learn it as a ladder: each step up combines the units of the step below.

Below the cell, cells are built of organelles (small structures inside the cell, each with a job), which are built of biomolecules (e.g. proteins, lipids). There is more on this in Structures and organelles of animal and plant cells.
Cell: the basic unit of life. In a multicellular organism (one made of many cells) cells are specialised (differentiated), so that the structure of each cell suits one job.
Tissue: a group of similar cells with the same structure, working together to carry out a particular function. Because the cells are alike, the tissue does one job well.
Organ: a structure made of several different tissues working together to carry out one or more functions. Having different tissues is what separates an organ from a tissue.
Organ system: a group of organs working together to carry out a major function, such as digesting food.
Organism: an individual living thing, whose organ systems work together to keep it alive.

Diagram: a five-step flow chart from cell to organism, with a human example at each level (muscle cell → muscle tissue → stomach → digestive system → human) and a plant example (xylem vessel → vascular tissue → leaf → shoot system → plant).
A specialised cell has a structure that suits its particular job. Cells in a multicellular organism are specialised, and each example below links a feature of the cell to its function.
Unicellular organisms (those made of a single cell), e.g. Amoeba, yeast and bacteria, carry out every life process in one cell, so that cell is not specialised for a single job.
Differentiation: in a multicellular organism, all body cells contain the same DNA, but each cell type uses (expresses) only some of its genes, so cells become specialised.
Unspecialised cells that can still become several cell types are called stem cells. There is more on their uses in Genetic Engineering.

Red blood cell: no nucleus and a biconcave disc shape (a disc dipped in on both faces), giving more room for haemoglobin (the pigment that carries oxygen) and a large surface area for carrying oxygen.
Nerve cell (neuron): long thin extensions carry impulses (electrical signals) over long distances quickly, which suits a cell that links distant parts of the body.
Sperm cell: a tail for swimming, and many mitochondria in the middle section to release the energy that powers the tail.
Root hair cell: a long extension gives a large surface area for absorbing water and minerals from the soil.

Palisade cell of a leaf: packed with chloroplasts (the green structures where photosynthesis happens) for photosynthesis. Guard cells change shape to open and close the stomata (the pores in the leaf surface).
Animal bodies are built from four main tissue types. Each is a group of similar cells doing one kind of job.
Epithelial tissue lines and covers surfaces, e.g. the lining of the gut and the skin surface.
Connective tissue supports and connects other tissues, e.g. bone, cartilage and blood. Blood counts as a connective tissue.
Muscle tissue contracts (shortens) to cause movement. There are three types: skeletal, smooth and cardiac (heart muscle).
Nervous tissue carries impulses, e.g. in the brain, spinal cord and nerves.
Plants also have tissue types, each a group of similar cells with one job. Together they build plant organs such as the leaf.
Dermal tissue is the epidermis, a protective outer layer covering the plant.
Vascular tissue carries materials around the plant: xylem carries water and minerals; phloem carries food.
Ground tissue makes up the bulk of the plant, carrying out photosynthesis and storage, e.g. the mesophyll (the inner tissue) of a leaf.
Meristematic tissue consists of dividing cells at root and shoot tips, where growth happens, so new cells for growth are made there.
A leaf contains dermal, ground and vascular tissue, which shows that an organ is made of several tissue types. Plant organs are root, stem, leaf and flower.
Organs are made of several tissue types, and organs that cooperate form organ systems. Each system has one major function.
The stomach is an organ containing epithelial tissue lining it, smooth muscle that churns food, connective tissue and nervous tissue. Four different tissues working together make it an organ.
Other human organs include the heart, lungs, kidneys and brain.
Digestive system: breaks down and absorbs food. Circulatory system: transports materials around the body.
Breathing system: gas exchange (taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide). Nervous system: fast coordination.
Endocrine system: hormonal coordination. Musculoskeletal system: support and movement.
Urinary system: excretion (removing wastes) and water balance. Reproductive system: reproduction. Immune system: defence.
Plants have two systems. The root system anchors the plant and absorbs water and minerals.
The shoot system (stem, leaves and flowers) carries out photosynthesis, transport and reproduction.
Size changes how a living thing gets what it needs. The bigger an organism, the harder it is to supply every cell, which is why large organisms need specialised systems.
As an organism gets bigger, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so its surface area to volume ratio falls.
Worked example: a 1 cm cube has a surface area of 6 cm² and a volume of 1 cm³, a ratio of 6:1. A 2 cm cube has a surface area of 24 cm² and a volume of 8 cm³, a ratio of 3:1.
A unicellular organism has a large surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion across its membrane is enough to supply oxygen and food and to remove wastes.
In a large multicellular organism most cells are far from the surface, so diffusion alone is too slow to reach them.

Multicellular organisms therefore need specialised exchange surfaces (lungs, gut lining, root hairs, leaves) to take in materials, and transport systems (blood and heart; xylem and phloem) to carry them to every cell.
They also need coordination systems (nervous and hormonal) that link all the parts and keep conditions constant (homeostasis).
Division of labour: each cell type does one job very efficiently, but no cell can survive alone, so the cells depend on each other.
Being made of many specialised cells brings benefits, but it also has costs. Comparing the two shows why both unicellular and multicellular life exist.
Advantage: a larger size, which means fewer predators and access to light or food.
Advantage: cells inside the body are protected from the environment, because they are surrounded by other cells.
Advantage: efficiency from specialisation, since each cell type does one job well.
Advantage: the organism can survive the death of individual cells, which are replaced.
Disadvantage: more energy and resources are needed to build and maintain the body.
Disadvantage: damage to one vital organ or system can kill the whole organism, because the other cells depend on it.
Disadvantage: growth to reproductive age takes longer than for unicellular organisms, which can divide within hours.

A virus is far simpler than any cell. It is a tiny, non-cellular particle (not made of cells) built of nucleic acid inside a protein coat, and it cannot do anything much until it gets inside a living cell.
A virus can reproduce only inside a living host cell (the cell it infects), so it is an obligate intracellular parasite: it must live inside cells and cannot survive and multiply on its own.
Viruses have no cytoplasm, no ribosomes (the structures that build proteins), no cell membrane of their own and almost no enzymes.
Because of this, a virus must use the host cell's ribosomes, enzymes, ATP (the cell's energy carrier) and raw materials to make copies of itself. There is more on this in Viruses: replication.
Every virus has the same basic plan: a core of genetic information wrapped in protein, and in some viruses an extra outer layer. Each part has its own job.
Nucleic acid core: either DNA or RNA, never both. It carries the genes (instructions) for making new virus particles, and it may be single- or double-stranded.
Protein coat (capsid): made of many repeating protein subunits (capsomeres). It protects the nucleic acid inside it.

The proteins of the coat attach to specific receptor molecules on the surface of the host cell, a bit like a key fitting a lock. This is why each virus infects only particular species and particular cell types (host specificity).
Envelope (some viruses only, e.g. influenza virus and HIV): an outer lipid membrane (a layer of fats) taken from the host cell's membrane as the virus leaves the cell.
The envelope is studded with viral proteins called spikes, which help the virus attach to and enter new cells.
Viruses are extremely small and come in a few characteristic shapes, which is useful for recognising and naming them.
Size: most viruses are about 20–300 nm across, much smaller than a bacterium (about 1–10 µm). This is why they pass through filters that trap bacteria.
Because they are so small, viruses can be seen only with an electron microscope, not with a light microscope.
Rod-shaped or helical viruses, e.g. tobacco mosaic virus.
Many-sided or polyhedral viruses, e.g. adenovirus.
Spherical and enveloped viruses, e.g. influenza virus.
Complex viruses with a head and tail: bacteriophages, which are the viruses that infect bacteria.
Diagram: draw a bacteriophage and label head (protein coat), nucleic acid (DNA) inside the head, tail, tail fibres. Then draw an enveloped virus and label envelope, spike proteins, protein coat, RNA.
Viruses are hard to classify because they show some features of living things and lack others. First, the features that make them look alive.
They contain genetic material (DNA or RNA) that uses the same genetic code as cells, so their genes are read in the same way.
They reproduce, making many copies of themselves, but only inside a host cell.
They show heredity, passing genes on to new viruses.
They mutate and evolve by natural selection. For example, new strains of influenza appear every year, which is why the flu vaccine is updated.
Against that evidence, viruses lack many of the features that all cells have. Weighing both sides gives the conclusion examiners expect.
They are not made of cells (they are acellular), so they do not fit the cell theory, which says living things are made of cells.
They have no metabolism (chemical reactions) of their own: no respiration, no nutrition and no excretion.
They do not grow and do not respond to stimuli.
They cannot reproduce outside a host cell, and outside a host they are inert particles, meaning they do nothing.
Some viruses can be crystallised like a chemical and remain infectious afterwards. Wendell Stanley crystallised tobacco mosaic virus in 1935.

Conclusion: viruses are usually described as on the border between living and non-living. Most biologists do not count them as living organisms, so they are not placed in any of the three domains or six kingdoms. There is more on this in Classification.
Others argue that a virus is alive only while it is inside a host cell, using the cell's machinery.
Viruses cause some of the most common and most serious human diseases. Their biology also explains why some usual treatments fail.
Viruses cause many human diseases: common cold (rhinoviruses), influenza (flu), measles, mumps, chickenpox, COVID-19 (caused by SARS-CoV-2), AIDS and hepatitis B.
AIDS is caused by HIV, which destroys helper T cells of the immune system (the white blood cells that coordinate the body's defence).
Some viruses cause cancer. Human papillomavirus (HPV) causes most cervical cancers, and a vaccine against HPV protects against them. There is more on this in Cell Division and Cancer.
Antibiotics do not work against viruses, because antibiotics target structures and processes that viruses do not have, such as bacterial cell walls and ribosomes.
Viral infections are treated with antiviral drugs, which are fewer and more specific than antibiotics, and are prevented by vaccination and hygiene.
Misusing antibiotics for viral infections contributes to antibiotic resistance in bacteria, since the bacteria are exposed to the drug for no benefit.
Although viruses cause disease, scientists have turned their features to medical use. This is one source of the beneficial uses that exam questions ask for.
Vaccines are made from weakened or inactivated viruses or from viral proteins, which train the immune system without causing the disease.
Harmless modified viruses are used as vectors (carriers) to deliver genes into human cells, in gene therapy and in some vaccines.
For example, some COVID-19 vaccines used a harmless adenovirus to carry the gene for a coronavirus spike protein.
Bacteriophages can be used to kill bacteria that are resistant to antibiotics. This is called phage therapy.
Viruses affect money as well as health. They damage farming and cost society a great deal, yet they are also used as tools and in industry.
Plant viruses reduce crop yields, e.g. tobacco mosaic virus (tobacco, tomatoes), potato viruses, and barley yellow dwarf virus in cereals, which is spread by aphids.
Animal viruses such as foot-and-mouth disease (cattle, sheep and pigs) and avian influenza (bird flu, poultry) lead to culling of infected herds and flocks, bans on exports and movement restrictions.
Costs to society: health-care costs, lost working days and, in a pandemic, the closure of businesses, schools and travel, e.g. COVID-19 from 2020.
Economic benefits: viruses are used as tools in genetic engineering, as vectors that carry genes into cells.
Viruses are used in biological control of pests (using a living organism to reduce a pest). Myxoma virus was released in Australia in 1950 to control rabbits.
Vaccine production is a major pharmaceutical industry.

Living things are sorted into ranks, from broad groups down to single species. A domain is the highest, broadest rank in the classification of living things, above kingdom. All cellular life is placed in three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya (the specification calls the last one eukaryota).

The system was developed by the American microbiologist Carl Woese. In 1977, with George Fox, he showed that archaea are a separate group from bacteria. In 1990 Woese and colleagues formally proposed the three domains.

Before this, all prokaryotes (cells with no nucleus) were placed in one group, the kingdom "Monera" in the five-kingdom system. Archaea look like bacteria under the microscope, so the difference could only be found from their molecules.

Genetic basis: Woese compared the base sequences of ribosomal RNA (rRNA), specifically the RNA of the small ribosome subunit. Every cell has ribosomes (the structures that build proteins), and the rRNA does the same job in all of them.
rRNA is a good tool for comparing all life because its sequence changes very slowly over evolutionary time, so even distantly related organisms still have sequences that can be lined up and compared.
The more similar two organisms' rRNA sequences are, the more closely related they are. This is how a molecule can be used to work out family relationships between organisms that look nothing alike.
The results showed three deep branches of life, not two (prokaryote and eukaryote). Archaea differ from bacteria about as much as either differs from eukaryotes.
In several genetic features archaea are more similar to eukaryotes than to bacteria, so archaea and eukaryotes share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either does with bacteria.

Diagram: a three-domain tree with one common ancestor at the base; one branch to Bacteria; and a second branch that splits into Archaea and Eukarya. Label the four eukaryotic kingdoms (Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia) on the Eukarya branch.
Bacteria are the first prokaryotic domain, and the one most people picture when they think of microbes. They live almost everywhere and do very different jobs.
Bacteria are prokaryotic: they have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, so their DNA lies loose in the cell rather than inside a nuclear membrane.

Bacteria have a single circular chromosome without histone proteins (the proteins eukaryotes wind their DNA around), and their cell walls contain peptidoglycan, a strengthening molecule found in bacterial walls.

Bacteria are found almost everywhere. They include decomposers, nitrogen-fixing bacteria, photosynthetic cyanobacteria and pathogens (disease-causing organisms) such as Streptococcus and some strains of Escherichia coli.
Many bacteria are killed by antibiotics, which is why bacterial infections can often be treated with them.

Archaea look like bacteria, but their chemistry is different, and in several ways it is closer to that of eukaryotes. Archaea are not "ancient bacteria" and not a type of bacterium, even though the old name was "archaebacteria".
Archaea are prokaryotic and single-celled, similar in size and shape to bacteria. This is why they were once classified with bacteria.
Their cell walls lack peptidoglycan, and their membrane lipids (the fats that make up the cell membrane) have a different chemical structure from those of all other organisms.

Their DNA is wound around histone-like proteins, and their enzymes for copying DNA and making RNA are more like those of eukaryotes. This is part of the evidence that archaea and eukaryotes are closer relatives.
Most antibiotics that kill bacteria do not affect archaea, because archaea have different cell walls and different molecular machinery for the antibiotics to target.

Many archaea are extremophiles (organisms living in extreme conditions). Thermophiles live in hot springs and deep-sea hydrothermal vents; halophiles live in very salty water such as salt lakes, e.g. Halobacterium.
Methanogens live where there is no oxygen, e.g. in bogs, rice paddies and the digestive systems of cattle, and make methane.
Archaea are also common in ordinary soil and the oceans. Archaea are not restricted to extreme environments, and no archaea are known to cause disease in humans.
The third domain contains every organism whose cells are built on the more complex eukaryotic plan, from single-celled protists to plants, fungi and animals.
Eukarya are all organisms whose cells have a nucleus enclosed by a membrane and membrane-bound organelles (compartments with their own membrane), e.g. mitochondria.
Eukaryotic cells have several linear chromosomes, with DNA wound around histones, unlike the single circular chromosome of bacteria.
Eukarya are unicellular or multicellular. The domain contains the kingdoms Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, which are the four kingdoms that sit on the Eukarya branch of the tree.

Putting the domains side by side shows what separates them. Two features (peptidoglycan and the type of membrane lipid) set bacteria and archaea apart, while archaea share others, such as histone-like proteins, with eukaryotes.
Nucleus: absent in bacteria, absent in archaea, present in eukaryotes. The two prokaryotic domains therefore keep their DNA unenclosed.
Membrane-bound organelles: absent in bacteria, absent in archaea, present in eukaryotes.
Peptidoglycan in the cell wall: present in bacteria, absent in archaea, absent in eukaryotes. So peptidoglycan is a feature unique to bacteria.
Membrane lipids: bacterial-type in bacteria, a unique archaeal type in archaea, bacterial-type in eukaryotes. Archaea are the odd one out here.
Histones: absent in bacteria, histone-like in archaea, present in eukaryotes. This is one feature in which archaea resemble eukaryotes more than bacteria.
Ribosome size: 70S in bacteria, 70S in archaea, 80S in the cytoplasm of eukaryotes. Ribosomes are the structures that build proteins, and the S number is explained below.
Sensitivity to common antibiotics: many bacteria are affected, archaea are generally not, and eukaryotes are not affected.
Examples: Escherichia coli and Streptococcus for bacteria; Halobacterium and methanogens for archaea; the kingdoms Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia for Eukarya.
The ribosome sizes in the comparison (70S and 80S) are written in S units, so you need to know what the S means.

The S number (Svedberg unit) measures how fast a particle settles in a centrifuge (a machine that spins samples at high speed). A larger number means a larger particle, which is why 80S eukaryotic ribosomes are the larger type.
The three domains change how we picture the living world, and they show how classification changes as new evidence arrives.
The biggest division in life is not plant versus animal, or even prokaryote versus eukaryote, but these three lineages. Animals, plants and fungi are just three small branches of one domain.
The domain system is based on genetic evidence, which reflects evolutionary relationships, rather than on appearance. This is why archaea, which look like bacteria, are placed in a separate domain.
It is an example of how new technology (gene sequencing, which reads the order of bases in DNA or RNA) changes classification. There is more on this in Classification.

There are so many kinds of living thing that biologists sort them into groups, the way a library sorts books into sections, shelves and titles. The groups sit inside one another in a fixed set of levels.
Classification is the grouping of organisms according to their shared characteristics. Taxonomy is the science of naming, describing and classifying organisms.
Organisms are placed in a hierarchy of ranks (taxa, the levels of grouping), from broadest to narrowest: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Moving down the ranks, each group has fewer members, which share more features and are more closely related. This is why two species in the same genus are far more alike than two in the same kingdom.
Worked example, human: domain Eukarya, kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Mammalia, order Primates, family Hominidae, genus Homo, species Homo sapiens.
The species is the smallest rank, so it needs a clear definition and a universal name. Every species gets a two-part scientific name, which is called binomial nomenclature.

A species is a group of organisms with similar features that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring (young that can themselves reproduce). A horse and a donkey can mate, but their offspring, a mule, is infertile, so they are different species.

Limitation of the species definition: it cannot be applied to organisms that reproduce only asexually (e.g. bacteria), because they do not interbreed at all, or to fossils, because dead organisms cannot be tested for interbreeding.

Binomial nomenclature: every species has a two-part scientific name, the genus name (capital first letter) followed by the species name (lower case), printed in italics or underlined when handwritten.
Examples of binomial names: Homo sapiens (human), Escherichia coli (a gut bacterium), Rhizopus stolonifer (black bread mould).
The Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature; his Species Plantarum (1753) used it for all plants.
Species in the same genus are closely related, which is why they share the first part of their name. The lion (Panthera leo) and tiger (Panthera tigris) share the genus Panthera.

Before sorting living things into kingdoms, biologists ask one basic question about their cells: is there a nucleus (the compartment that holds the DNA) or not? The answer splits cellular life into two big groups.

The first division of cellular life is by cell type. Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles (the small working parts of a cell). Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus surrounded by a membrane, and membrane-bound organelles. There is more on this in Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
Two kingdoms are prokaryotic, Bacteria and Archaea, each forming its own domain. Four kingdoms are eukaryotic, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, all in the domain Eukarya.
The distinction became clear only once the electron microscope showed cell interiors, because the details inside prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells are too small to see with a light microscope.

Both prokaryotic kingdoms are single-celled with no nucleus, so cell structure alone does not separate them. One way of telling them apart is the chemistry of their cell walls, and another is rRNA. Each is described by cell type, number of cells, cell wall, nutrition and examples.
Bacteria: prokaryotic and unicellular, with cell walls of peptidoglycan (a mesh of sugars and amino acids). They reproduce by binary fission (one cell splits into two).

Bacterial nutrition varies. Bacteria are autotrophic (make their own food), either photosynthetic or chemosynthetic, or heterotrophic (take in food made by others), either saprophytic (feeding on dead matter) or parasitic (feeding on a living host).
Bacteria examples: Escherichia coli, Lactobacillus (used to make yoghurt) and Streptococcus.
Archaea: prokaryotic and unicellular, with cell walls that have no peptidoglycan. This difference in cell wall is one way of telling them apart from bacteria. Many live in extreme environments.
Archaea examples: methanogens (methane-producing archaea) in cattle digestive systems, and Halobacterium in salt lakes.
The four eukaryotic kingdoms all have a nucleus. They are separated by how many cells they have, what their cell walls are made of, how they get food and how they store carbohydrate.

Protista: eukaryotic and mostly unicellular, though some are multicellular algae such as seaweeds (kelp). They have no tissues (groups of similar cells doing one job) of the kind found in plants and animals. Some are photosynthetic (algae) and some are heterotrophic.

Protista includes eukaryotes that do not belong in the other three eukaryotic kingdoms. Examples: Amoeba, Paramecium, Plasmodium (causes malaria) and Phytophthora infestans (causes potato blight, which caused the Great Famine in Ireland, 1845–1849).

Fungi: eukaryotic and mostly multicellular, made of thread-like hyphae forming a mycelium (a tangled mass of threads), though yeasts are unicellular. They have no chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise, and their cell walls are made of chitin.

Fungi are heterotrophic: they secrete enzymes onto food and absorb the digested products, living as saprophytes or parasites. They store carbohydrate as glycogen and reproduce by spores. Examples: Rhizopus (bread mould), yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), mushrooms and Penicillium.

Plantae: eukaryotic and multicellular, with cell walls of cellulose and chloroplasts (where photosynthesis happens). They are autotrophic by photosynthesis, store carbohydrate as starch, and mostly do not move. Examples: mosses, ferns, conifers, and flowering plants such as the daisy and oak.

Animalia: eukaryotic and multicellular, with no cell walls. They are heterotrophic, taking in (ingesting) food, and store carbohydrate as glycogen. Most can move and have nerves and muscles. Examples: sponges, earthworms, insects, fish and mammals.
Classification by kingdom and domain only works for things made of cells. Viruses fall outside it.
Viruses are not in any kingdom or domain, because they are not cells. There is more on this in Viruses.
Grouping by appearance can mislead, so modern classification also asks which organisms share a recent ancestor. This evolutionary family-tree approach is called phylogeny.

Phylogeny is the evolutionary history of a group of organisms. Phylogenetic classification groups organisms by how closely related they are by descent from common ancestors, rather than by appearance alone.

A phylogenetic tree shows these relationships. Each branch point (node) represents a common ancestor, and the closer two species' branches join, the more recent their common ancestor and the more closely related they are.
Species in the same genus share a very recent common ancestor; genera in the same family share an older one. This is how the ranks of the hierarchy reflect evolutionary history.
Example: the lion and tiger (genus Panthera) are more closely related to each other than either is to the domestic cat (Felis catus), but all three are in the cat family (Felidae).
The dog (Canis familiaris, also written Canis lupus familiaris) is in a different family, Canidae, and all four animals are in the order Carnivora.

Evidence used to work out phylogeny includes shared anatomical structures with the same basic plan, e.g. the five-digit limb of mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians; embryology (the study of early development); and fossils. There is more on this in Evolution: The Origins of Life.

The most powerful evidence is comparison of DNA base sequences and protein amino-acid sequences: the fewer the differences, the more closely related the organisms, because less time has passed for differences to build up.
Appearance can mislead. Whales and dolphins look like fish but are mammals: they breathe air with lungs, are warm-blooded and feed their young on milk.
Diagram: a phylogenetic tree for lion, tiger, domestic cat and dog, with the nodes for genus Panthera, family Felidae and order Carnivora labelled.

Classification is not fixed. Each time scientists gained a new tool for looking at living things, the groupings were redrawn, which is why you will meet different numbers of kingdoms in the history of the subject.
Early systems had two kingdoms, plants and animals. Linnaeus, in the 18th century, classified organisms by visible features.
Microscopes revealed single-celled organisms that fitted neither kingdom. In 1866 Ernst Haeckel proposed a third kingdom, Protista.
In 1969 Robert Whittaker proposed five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. Monera held all the prokaryotes.
Fungi were separated from plants in Whittaker's system because they have chitin walls, no chlorophyll and absorb their food.
rRNA sequencing (reading the sequence of a molecule found in ribosomes) by Carl Woese showed that prokaryotes form two very different groups. This gave three domains (1990).
The six kingdoms used in this course followed, with Monera split into Bacteria and Archaea. There is more on this in Domains of life.

Systems change because new technology provides new evidence, e.g. the light microscope, the electron microscope, biochemistry and DNA sequencing. Classification is revised to reflect evolutionary relationships more accurately. It is a model that scientists keep testing and improving.
DNA sequencing, reading the order of bases in an organism's DNA, is now the strongest tool for classification. It is still moving organisms between groups and adding new ones.

DNA sequencing and whole-genome comparisons are now the main evidence for classification, and have moved many organisms. Phytophthora (potato blight) was long classed as a fungus because it grows as threads. Its DNA and its cellulose cell walls show that it belongs with the protists (water moulds).
DNA evidence placed the giant panda in the bear family.

Environmental DNA sequencing, which sequences all the DNA in a soil or water sample, has revealed huge numbers of microorganisms that have never been grown in a laboratory. These add new branches to the tree of life.
Asgard archaea were first reported in 2015 from DNA in sediment near the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vents in the Arctic Ocean. They share many genes with eukaryotes.
Some scientists argue that eukaryotes arose from within the archaea, which would mean only two primary domains. This is still debated, so classification remains a work in progress.
DNA barcoding uses a short standard gene sequence to identify species quickly, e.g. to identify species from tiny samples or to detect mislabelled food.

A dichotomous key is a tool for naming an unknown organism by answering a series of either/or questions about what you can see. The worked key below identifies six invertebrates (animals without backbones).

A dichotomous key identifies an organism by a series of steps. Each step gives a choice between two contrasting statements (a couplet) about a visible feature. Each statement leads either to a name or to the number of the next couplet.
Worked example: a key to six invertebrates.
1. Legs present → go to 2; legs absent → go to 4.
2. Three pairs of legs → ladybird (an insect); more than three pairs of legs → go to 3.
3. Four pairs of legs → spider; seven pairs of legs → woodlouse.
4. Shell present → snail; no visible shell → go to 5.
5. Body divided into rings (segments) → earthworm; body not divided into rings → slug.
To use a key, start at couplet 1 and follow the numbers until you reach a name. Practise tracing a route for each organism so you can do it in the exam.
Using the key: an animal with eight legs goes 1 (legs present) → 2 (more than three pairs) → 3 (four pairs) → spider. Eight legs means four pairs, which is why it ends at spider.
Write the route for one more organism: the slug goes 1 → 4 → 5 → slug, because it has no legs, no visible shell and a body that is not divided into rings.
You may have to build a key of your own, or use the features of the kingdoms to place an unknown organism. Both rely on picking features that give a clear yes or no.
To construct a key, list the organisms, choose a feature that splits them into two groups, and keep splitting each group in two until each organism is on its own.

Use features that are easy to observe and do not vary between individuals or seasons, e.g. number of legs, not size or colour, because size and colour change with age and season and would give unreliable answers.
A key for n organisms needs n − 1 couplets. For example, the six-invertebrate key above has five couplets.
To classify an unknown organism to a kingdom, use the features in order. Does it have a nucleus? If not, it is a bacterium or an archaeon, separated by cell-wall chemistry or rRNA.
If it has a nucleus, ask further questions. Is it multicellular with tissues? What is its cell wall made of? Is it autotrophic or heterotrophic?
Worked example: a newly found organism is eukaryotic, is made of hyphae with chitin walls, and absorbs food from dead leaves. It is in the kingdom Fungi.
Classification is more than tidy labelling. It makes biology easier to study, communicate and apply to health, farming and conservation.
It organises the enormous diversity of life into manageable groups, making it easier to study and to find information.

Scientific names are universal and unique, which avoids the confusion of common names. The robin of Europe (Erithacus rubecula) and the robin of North America (Turdus migratorius) are different species in different genera.
It shows evolutionary relationships, so features of a new organism can be predicted from its relatives. For example, relatives of a plant that produces a useful drug may produce similar compounds.
Health: correctly identifying a pathogen (a disease-causing organism) decides the treatment. A bacterial infection may respond to an antibiotic, but a fungal or viral one will not.

Agriculture and the environment: identifying pests, invasive species and endangered species is needed for control and conservation, and for measuring biodiversity (the variety of living things in an area).
Biologists sort all cells into two types, depending on whether the DNA is enclosed in a nucleus. The names themselves tell you the difference, and you need the units to talk about how big cells are.

A prokaryotic cell has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles (compartments wrapped in their own membrane). Its DNA lies free in the cytoplasm, the jelly-like fluid that fills the cell. “Pro” means before and “karyon” means kernel or nucleus. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes.

A eukaryotic cell has its DNA enclosed in a nucleus surrounded by a double membrane (the nuclear envelope), and it has membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria. “Eu” means true, so eukaryote means “true nucleus”. Protists, fungi, plants and animals are eukaryotes.
Cells are far too small for millimetres to be a handy unit, so their sizes are given in micrometres. 1 mm = 1000 µm (micrometres) and 1 µm = 1000 nm (nanometres). Cell sizes are given in µm.
Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells look very different, but both are living cells that must do the same basic jobs. So they share a core set of features.
Both have a cell membrane that controls what enters and leaves the cell, and cytoplasm, the fluid where many of the cell's reactions take place.
Both have ribosomes (the tiny structures that make proteins), and both use DNA as the genetic material, reading it with the same genetic code.
Both respire, releasing energy from food, and both use ATP (the molecule cells use to carry energy) as the energy currency.
These shared features suggest that all cells evolved from a common ancestor, because such an unusual set of identical features is unlikely to have arisen separately.
The most important difference between the two cell types is how the DNA is stored. This affects where the DNA sits, what shape it has and what it is packed with.

Nucleus: prokaryotes have none. Their DNA is concentrated in a region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid, which has no membrane around it. Eukaryotes have a true nucleus with a nuclear envelope and nuclear pores (small channels through the envelope).
Number and shape of chromosomes: prokaryotes have one circular chromosome (a closed loop of DNA). Eukaryotes have several linear chromosomes (DNA with two ends).
Packaging: eukaryotic DNA is wound around histone proteins, which help to pack it. In bacteria the circular chromosome is not wound around histone proteins.

Prokaryotes often also have plasmids, small extra rings of DNA separate from the main chromosome. Plasmids can carry genes such as antibiotic resistance, which is why resistance can spread between bacteria.
Plasmids are found in prokaryotes (and in yeast), not in all eukaryotes, so do not say that eukaryotes have none or that all have them.
Eukaryotic cells divide their work between membrane-bound organelles, whereas prokaryotes have to do everything without them. Ribosomes are the one structure both have, but they differ in size.

Membrane-bound organelles: prokaryotes have none, so no mitochondria, no chloroplasts and no other membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotes have mitochondria, and plants and algae also have chloroplasts.
Without organelles, prokaryotes carry out respiration and, in photosynthetic bacteria, photosynthesis on the cell membrane or on infoldings of it (folds of the membrane that increase its area).
Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain their own small circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, like a prokaryote. This is one more way these organelles resemble prokaryotic cells.
Ribosomes: both cell types have them, but prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller (70S) than those in eukaryotic cytoplasm (80S). The S number is a measure of size.
Many antibiotics work by blocking 70S ribosomes, so they stop bacteria making proteins and harm bacteria but not human cells, which use 80S ribosomes in their cytoplasm.
The remaining differences are about the whole cell: how big it is, what surrounds it, and how the organism is built and reproduces.
Size: prokaryotic cells are small, most about 1–10 µm long. Eukaryotic cells are usually about 10–100 µm, so they are roughly ten times larger in length.
Cell wall: almost all prokaryotes have one, made of peptidoglycan in bacteria. Among eukaryotes, plant cells have cellulose walls, fungal cells have chitin walls, and animal cells have none.
Some prokaryotes have extra outer structures: a capsule (slime layer) for protection, and a flagellum, a whip-like tail, for movement. There is more on the full bacterial cell in Microorganisms.

Organisation: prokaryotes are almost all unicellular (made of a single cell) and divide by binary fission, in which one cell splits in two. Eukaryotes can be unicellular or multicellular and divide by mitosis.
Examples: prokaryotes are bacteria and archaea. Eukaryotes are protists, fungi, plants and animals.

How a cell looks in a micrograph (a photograph taken through a microscope) depends on the microscope, because a light microscope cannot show very small structures but an electron microscope can. Knowing what each shows lets you identify a cell.
Under a light microscope at ×400, a bacterium appears as a tiny dot, rod or spiral with no visible internal structure. It is too small (about 1–10 µm) for the light microscope to show its parts.

Under a light microscope, eukaryotic cells show the nucleus (especially when stained), the cytoplasm and the cell membrane as a line. Plant cells also show the cell wall, a large vacuole (a fluid-filled sac) and chloroplasts.
Electron micrographs show what the light microscope cannot. In prokaryotes they show the nucleoid, ribosomes as tiny dots, plasmids and the layers of the wall.
In eukaryotes, electron micrographs show the double nuclear envelope and its pores, the internal membranes of mitochondria and chloroplasts, and ribosomes.

Diagram: side-by-side labelled diagrams of a generalised prokaryotic cell (cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleoid with circular DNA, plasmid, ribosomes, capsule, flagellum) and a eukaryotic animal cell (cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, nuclear envelope, nuclear pore, mitochondria, ribosomes), with the eukaryotic cell drawn much larger.
You may be given a micrograph and asked whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic, and to justify the answer. Work through the same checks in order.
1. Check for a nucleus. If one is present, the cell is eukaryotic, because only eukaryotes enclose their DNA in a nucleus.
2. Check the scale bar or stated magnification to estimate size. A cell of about 1–10 µm suggests a prokaryote, since eukaryotic cells are usually about 10–100 µm.
3. Look for membrane-bound organelles, which only eukaryotes have.

4. For a eukaryote, look for a cell wall, a large vacuole and chloroplasts, which mean a plant cell, or their absence, which suggests an animal cell. There is more on this in Structures and organelles of animal and plant cells.
Microscopes do two different jobs: they make things look bigger, and they let you see fine detail. Students often mix these up, but only the second one limits what a light microscope can show.
Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the real object, so a ×100 image is 100 times the real size.
Resolution (also called resolving power) is the ability to show two points that are close together as separate points. It decides how much detail can be seen.
Magnifying an image beyond the resolution limit only makes it bigger and blurrier, not more detailed, because the two close points have already merged into one blur.
Total magnification of a light microscope = eyepiece lens magnification × objective lens magnification. For example, a ×10 eyepiece with a ×40 objective gives ×400.
The light (optical) microscope passes light through a thin specimen and uses glass lenses to enlarge the image. These parts form the image and bring it into focus.
Eyepiece (ocular) lens: the lens you look through. It magnifies the image from the objective, usually ×10.

Objective lenses: mounted on a revolving nosepiece so they can be swapped. They are usually ×4 (scanning), ×10 (low power) and ×40 (high power), sometimes ×100 (oil immersion). They produce the first magnified image.
Stage with clips: the platform that holds the slide in place over the hole through which light passes.
Coarse focus knob: moves the stage (or tube) a long way quickly, so it is used for focusing at low power only.
Fine focus knob: moves the stage or tube a small distance to give a sharp image. It is the only focus used at high power.
Light has to reach the specimen in the right amount and direction, and the instrument needs a stable frame. These parts do that.
Light source: a built-in lamp, or a mirror that reflects light up through the specimen.
Condenser: a lens under the stage that focuses light onto the specimen.
Diaphragm (iris): adjusts the amount of light reaching the specimen. Less light often improves contrast for pale, unstained cells, which are nearly transparent and look washed out in bright light.
Arm and base: support the microscope. The arm is used for carrying it.

Diagram: a light microscope labelled eyepiece, body tube, revolving nosepiece, objective lenses, stage, clips, condenser, diaphragm, light source (or mirror), coarse focus knob, fine focus knob, arm and base.
The method is built to protect the slide and the lenses. You always start on the lowest power, which has the widest view and the most room between lens and slide.
1. Carry the microscope with one hand on the arm and the other under the base, so its weight is supported.
2. Switch on the light and turn the lowest-power objective into place.
3. Clip the slide on the stage with the specimen over the hole, so light can pass through it.
4. Looking from the side, use the coarse focus to bring the objective close to the slide without touching it. Watching from the side stops you grinding the lens into the slide.
5. Looking through the eyepiece, focus by moving the objective and slide apart until the image is clear.
6. Use the fine focus to sharpen the image, and the diaphragm to adjust the light.
7. Move the part to be studied to the centre of the field of view (the circle of specimen you can see), so it stays in view when you increase magnification.
8. Turn the next objective into place and use only the fine focus.
9. Record the total magnification with every drawing.
The image behaves in predictable ways as you change objective, and one safety rule matters for your eyes.
The image is inverted, meaning upside down and reversed left to right. This means moving the slide to the left moves the image to the right.
At higher magnification the field of view is smaller and the image is dimmer, so more light is needed.
At high power the objective is very close to the slide, which is why the coarse focus must not be used: it could crash the lens into the slide.
Never use a mirror to reflect direct sunlight into the microscope, as it can damage the eye.
To view a specimen with light passing through it, you mount it on a glass slide. The technique below is the general method that any slide uses.
A wet mount: the specimen is placed in a drop of water or stain on a clean glass slide and covered with a coverslip (a thin square of glass).
The specimen must be very thin, ideally one layer of cells thick, so that light can pass through it and the cells do not overlap.

Stains add contrast to transparent structures by colouring some parts more than others. Iodine solution is used for plant cells: it stains the nucleus yellow-brown and turns starch blue-black. Methylene blue is used for animal cells: it stains the nucleus dark blue.

Lowering the coverslip: touch one edge of the coverslip to the liquid at an angle of about 45° and lower it slowly with a mounted needle. This pushes air out ahead of it and avoids air bubbles, which appear as black-edged circles and can hide cells.
The coverslip keeps the specimen flat, stops it drying out, and protects the objective lens from the liquid. Excess liquid is removed by touching filter paper or a paper towel to the edge.

Stain can also be added after the coverslip is on. Put a drop at one edge and draw it under the coverslip with filter paper held at the opposite edge (irrigation). There is more on the full procedures in Investigation: plant and animal cells.
A light microscope cannot resolve anything much smaller than 0.2 µm. Electron microscopes get round this by using electrons instead of light, so they show far finer detail.
An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light, focused by electromagnets instead of glass lenses. Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, so resolution is far better.

The specimen is in a vacuum, because air would scatter the electrons, so it must be dead. The image is viewed on a screen and recorded digitally. It is black and white, and colour is added afterwards (false colour).

Transmission electron microscope (TEM): electrons pass through an extremely thin, stained section of a specimen. It gives a flat (2D) image of internal structure at the highest magnifications, e.g. mitochondria, ribosomes, nuclear pores and viruses.

Scanning electron microscope (SEM): a beam of electrons scans across the surface of a specimen coated with a very thin layer of metal, e.g. gold. Electrons bouncing off it form an image. It gives a 3D image of surfaces, e.g. the surface of cells, pollen grains and insects.
The SEM has lower resolution than the TEM and shows no internal structure unless the specimen is broken open.
The first electron microscope was built in Germany in 1931 by Max Knoll and Ernst Ruska.
The two types differ in how they work, what they can resolve and what they demand of the specimen. Compare them point by point.
Radiation: light for the light microscope, electrons for the electron microscope. Lenses: glass for the light microscope, electromagnets for the electron microscope.
Maximum useful magnification: about ×1000–1500 for the light microscope, compared with hundreds of thousands of times or more for electron microscopes.
Resolution: about 0.2 µm (200 nm) for the light microscope, compared with less than 1 nm for the TEM, roughly a thousand times better.

So the light microscope shows the nucleus, cell wall, vacuole and chloroplasts. Ribosomes, nuclear pores, the inner structure of mitochondria and viruses are too small and need an electron microscope.
Specimens: the light microscope can view living or dead specimens, with colour visible. The electron microscope needs dead specimens in a vacuum, and its images are black and white.

Preparation and cost: light microscopes are simple, quick, cheap and portable. Electron microscopes need complex preparation (thin sectioning, metal coating) that can create artefacts, structures that are not really in the living cell. They are very expensive, large, and need trained operators.
Microscopy has a long history and is still developing. Newer techniques tag, scan or freeze specimens to reveal what older methods could not.
Robert Hooke described and named “cells” from thin slices of cork in his book Micrographia (1665).
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, using his own single-lens microscopes, was the first to see and describe bacteria and other single-celled organisms, in the 1670s.

Fluorescence microscopy: specific molecules are tagged with fluorescent dyes or fluorescent proteins that glow when lit with a particular colour of light. This shows exactly where a protein is in a living cell.
Green fluorescent protein (GFP), from a jellyfish, earned the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded to Osamu Shimomura, Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien.
Confocal laser scanning microscopy: a laser scans one thin plane of the specimen at a time, giving sharp images that a computer combines into a 3D model.

Super-resolution fluorescence microscopy overcomes the light microscope’s normal resolution limit. It earned the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded to Eric Betzig, Stefan Hell and William Moerner.

Cryo-electron microscopy: samples are flash-frozen in a thin layer of ice instead of being dried and stained, so molecules keep their natural shape. It shows the structure of proteins and viruses in near-atomic detail.
Cryo-electron microscopy earned the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded to Jacques Dubochet, Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson.
Cryo-electron microscopy was used to show the structure of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, which helped vaccine design.
Microscopes are everyday tools in medicine, research and forensics, and modern imaging adds automation.

Uses in health and technology: examining blood smears and biopsies to diagnose disease, including spotting cancer cells; identifying pathogens; research into how cells and viruses work; and forensic science, e.g. comparing hairs and fibres.
Digital cameras and computer image analysis now allow images to be measured, shared and analysed automatically.
Every cell needs a boundary that holds it together and controls what gets in and out. Plant cells have two layers of boundary: a tough cell wall outside and a thin cell membrane just inside it.
Cell wall: a rigid layer outside the cell membrane, made mainly of cellulose fibres in plants. It is fully permeable, so water and dissolved substances pass through it freely.

The cell wall gives strength, support and a fixed shape. It stops the cell bursting when it takes in water by osmosis (water moving in across the membrane), so the cell becomes firm (turgid), which supports non-woody plants.
Cell walls are found in plant cells, in fungi (where they are made of chitin) and in bacteria, but not in animal cells. The cell wall is visible with the light microscope.

Cell membrane (plasma membrane): a very thin, flexible boundary around every cell, made of a double layer of phospholipids (fatty molecules) with proteins in it. It is selectively permeable, so it controls which substances enter and leave, and it holds the cell contents together.
Proteins in the cell membrane act as receptors that recognise hormones and other signals, and as markers that let cells recognise each other.
The cell membrane is found in all cells, and lies inside the wall in plant cells. With the light microscope it is seen only as a line. There is more on this in Transport Across Membranes.

Inside the membrane, the cell's contents sit in a watery fluid, and plant cells also have a large fluid-filled sac that helps hold them firm. Together these provide the setting for the cell's chemistry and its support.

Cytoplasm: everything inside the cell membrane except the nucleus. It is a watery, jelly-like fluid (cytosol) containing dissolved nutrients, salts and enzymes (proteins that speed up reactions), in which the organelles (the cell's specialised working parts) are suspended.

The cytoplasm is the site of many metabolic reactions (the chemical reactions of the cell), for example the first stage of respiration (glucose broken down to pyruvate) and anaerobic respiration (respiration without oxygen). It is also where proteins are made at free ribosomes. It is found in all cells.

Vacuole: a fluid-filled sac surrounded by a single membrane. A mature plant cell has one large permanent central vacuole filled with cell sap, which is water containing sugars, salts and sometimes pigments, for example the red of beetroot.

The plant vacuole stores water, food and waste. It takes in water by osmosis and pushes the cytoplasm against the wall, which keeps the cell turgid and the plant upright. When water is lost, plants wilt.
Animal cells have only small, temporary vacuoles, for example food vacuoles. Some single-celled protists such as Amoeba have contractile vacuoles that pump out excess water.
The plant vacuole is visible with the light microscope.
Cells need a constant supply of usable energy. Mitochondria are the organelles that release it from food, so cells with high energy demands are packed with them.
Mitochondrion (plural mitochondria): a rod- or sausage-shaped organelle with a double membrane. The outer membrane is smooth, and the inner membrane is folded into cristae.
The folds of the cristae give a large surface area for the enzymes of the later stages of aerobic respiration (respiration using oxygen). The fluid inside the inner membrane is the matrix.
Function: the site of most of aerobic respiration, releasing energy from food to make most of the cell's ATP (the molecule that carries energy for cell activities).
Mitochondria are found in almost all eukaryotic cells (cells with a nucleus), in plants as well as animals. Plant cells respire as well as photosynthesise, so they need mitochondria too.
Cells that need a lot of energy have many mitochondria, for example muscle cells, liver cells, nerve cells and the middle section of sperm.
Mitochondria contain their own DNA and ribosomes. They are too small to show detail with the light microscope, so their structure is seen with the electron microscope.
Diagram: a mitochondrion in section labelled outer membrane, inner membrane, cristae and matrix.
Plants make their own food by photosynthesis, and the organelle that does this is the chloroplast. Its green pigment captures light, and its fluid interior builds sugar.
Chloroplast: a disc-shaped organelle with a double membrane. It contains stacks of flattened membrane sacs (thylakoids; a stack is a granum) that carry the green pigment chlorophyll.
The chloroplast is surrounded by a fluid called the stroma, and starch grains may be stored in the stroma.

Function: the site of photosynthesis. Chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes absorbs light energy (the light-dependent stage). The stroma contains the enzymes that use this energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide (the light-independent stage).
The many stacked membranes give a large surface area for absorbing light. There is more on this in Photosynthesis.
Chloroplasts are found only in plant cells (and algae), in parts exposed to light, especially the palisade cells of leaves and guard cells.
Not all plant cells have chloroplasts. They are not found in root cells or in onion bulb cells, which are not exposed to light, and they are never found in animal cells.
Chloroplasts are visible as green discs with the light microscope. They contain their own DNA and ribosomes.
Diagram: a chloroplast labelled double membrane, thylakoids, granum, stroma and starch grain.

The nucleus is the cell's control centre. It holds the instructions for making proteins, and nuclear pores are the gateways that let the right materials move between the nucleus and the rest of the cell.

Nucleus: usually the largest organelle, round or oval, surrounded by a double membrane called the nuclear envelope. It contains the cell's DNA as chromatin, which is DNA wound around histone proteins.
Function: the nucleus controls the cell's activities, because its DNA carries the genes that code for the cell's proteins, including the enzymes that control every reaction.
The nucleus is where DNA is copied before cell division, and where genes are copied into messenger RNA (mRNA, the working copy of a gene that carries the code out to the ribosomes).
The nucleolus is a dense region inside the nucleus where ribosomes are made.
The nucleus is found in all eukaryotic cells except a few that lose it, for example mature human red blood cells. It is visible with the light microscope, especially when stained.
Nuclear pore: one of many openings through the nuclear envelope, each lined with proteins that control what passes through it.

mRNA and ribosome parts pass out to the cytoplasm. Proteins such as enzymes and histones, nucleotides (the building blocks of DNA and RNA) and ATP pass in. The DNA is too large to leave, so it stays protected in the nucleus.
Nuclear pores are seen only with the electron microscope, because they are too small for the light microscope.
The DNA in the nucleus is not a loose tangle. It is organised into chromosomes, which carry the genes and are passed on when cells divide and when organisms reproduce.
Chromosome: a long thread of DNA wound around proteins (histones), carrying many genes (sections of DNA that code for proteins).
For most of the cell's life the chromosomes are long, thin and spread out as chromatin, which is why they cannot be seen.
Before division the chromosomes coil up tightly, becoming short and thick, and can then be seen with the light microscope when stained.
Human body cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs).
Function: chromosomes carry genetic information and pass it to new cells and offspring. There is more on this in Genetic Inheritance, and division is in Cell Division and Cancer.
Proteins are made on tiny organelles called ribosomes, which read the code carried by mRNA. Every cell needs them, so they are one of the few organelles found in all cells.
Ribosome: a very small organelle with no membrane, made of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and protein, in two subunits.
Function: the ribosome is the site of protein synthesis, where amino acids (the building blocks of proteins) are joined in the order coded for by mRNA.
Ribosomes are found in all cells, prokaryotic (without a nucleus) and eukaryotic, free in the cytoplasm. There are many in cells making a lot of protein.
Ribosomes are seen only with the electron microscope, as dots, because they are very small. There is more on this in DNA Replication, Protein Synthesis and Mutations.
RNA but no DNA is found in ribosomes and in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells. DNA is in the nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts.

Some proteins are not used inside the cell but are exported, such as digestive enzymes. The endoplasmic reticulum is the first stage of the assembly line that folds and transports them, and it also makes lipids.

Endoplasmic reticulum (ER): a network of membrane-bound flattened sacs and tubes running through the cytoplasm, continuous with the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope. It forms channels that transport materials through the cell.

Rough ER is covered with ribosomes. Proteins made at these ribosomes enter the ER, where they are folded and transported. These are mainly proteins that will be secreted from the cell (for example digestive enzymes made by pancreas cells, and antibodies) or built into membranes.
Proteins made at free ribosomes stay in the cytoplasm. Cells that secrete a lot of protein have a lot of rough ER, as in pancreas cells secreting digestive enzymes.
Smooth ER has no ribosomes. It makes lipids, including phospholipids for membranes and steroid hormones. In liver cells it helps to break down (detoxify) drugs and alcohol.
The ER is found in plant and animal cells, and is seen only with the electron microscope.
The Golgi apparatus is the second stage of the assembly line: it modifies, sorts and packages proteins from the ER and ships them out of the cell.
Golgi apparatus (Golgi body): a stack of flattened, curved membrane sacs, usually near the nucleus, with small membrane bubbles (vesicles) budding off it.

The Golgi apparatus receives proteins from the ER in vesicles, modifies them (for example adding carbohydrate to make glycoproteins), and sorts and packages them into vesicles that carry them to where they are needed.
Secretory vesicles move to the cell membrane, fuse with it and release their contents outside the cell (exocytosis). In plant cells the Golgi apparatus also makes materials for the cell wall.
The Golgi apparatus is found in plant and animal cells, and is seen only with the electron microscope.
Secretory pathway, in order: gene in the nucleus, then mRNA leaves through a nuclear pore, then protein is made at a ribosome on the rough ER, then folded and carried in the ER.

The protein then moves in a transport vesicle to the Golgi apparatus (modified and packaged), then in a secretory vesicle, which fuses with the cell membrane, and the protein is released, for example a digestive enzyme.
Diagram: add rough ER (with ribosomes), smooth ER and the Golgi apparatus (with vesicles) to the animal-cell diagram, with arrows showing the secretory pathway.
Plant and animal cells share the same core set of organelles, but plant cells have three extra structures that suit a life of making food and standing upright without a skeleton.
Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus with nuclear pores and chromosomes, mitochondria and ribosomes.
Only plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, a large permanent central vacuole, and chloroplasts in green parts.
Plant cells usually have a fixed, regular (often rectangular) shape, because the rigid wall holds them in place, and they store carbohydrate as starch.
Animal cells have a flexible, irregular or rounded shape, no wall, only small temporary vacuoles, and store carbohydrate as glycogen.
Seen with the light microscope: the cell wall, vacuole, chloroplasts and nucleus, with the cell membrane seen only as a line. Mitochondria, nuclear pores and ribosomes need the electron microscope.
Diagram: a typical animal cell as seen with the electron microscope, labelled cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, nuclear envelope, nuclear pore, nucleolus, chromatin, mitochondrion and ribosomes.

Diagram: a typical plant cell (for example a palisade cell) as seen with the electron microscope, labelled cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, large vacuole, chloroplast, mitochondrion, nucleus, nuclear pore and ribosomes.

This investigation compares plant cells with animal cells. You gather first-hand (primary) data with a light microscope, then add second-hand (secondary) data from scanning electron microscope images. A fair comparison needs a clear aim, a prediction and tight control of variables.

Aim: to observe and compare the structures of plant cells (onion epidermis, the thin outer skin layer) and animal cells (human cheek cells) using a light microscope, and to use scanning electron microscope (SEM) images to see structures the light microscope cannot show.
Hypothesis (a testable prediction): plant cells will show a cell wall and a large vacuole, which animal cells lack. Both will show a cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus.
Independent variable (the one thing you change): the type of cell, plant or animal.
Dependent variable (what you observe or measure): the structures observed, whether present or absent, and their shape and arrangement.

Controlled variables (kept the same so the comparison is fair): the same microscope and total magnification (×100 and ×400), the same light setting, a fresh thin specimen one cell layer thick, and the same volume of stain and staining time.

Control: an unstained wet mount (specimen in a drop of water) of each cell type, viewed in the same way. It shows what the stain adds, meaning which structures become visible, and that the structures seen are in the cells and not produced by the stain.

You need a short list of apparatus, and several of the items carry real hazards: sharp blades, stains, thin glass and body cells. Good practice is part of the method, so know the precaution for each hazard.

Equipment: light microscope; clean glass slides and coverslips; onion; scalpel or knife and white tile; forceps; mounted needle; dropper (pipette); filter paper or paper towel; iodine solution; methylene blue stain; sterile cotton buds; beaker of disinfectant for used buds; distilled water; gloves and safety glasses; pencil and paper for drawings.
