Use only your own cheek cells, with a new sterile cotton bud. Put used buds, and slides after use, into disinfectant to prevent spreading infection, and wash hands afterwards.
Iodine solution and methylene blue stain skin and clothes and can irritate eyes, so wear gloves and safety glasses and wipe up spills.
Cut away from your fingers on a white tile with the scalpel, and carry scalpels pointing down so the blade cannot injure anyone if you trip.
Hold slides and coverslips by their edges. Coverslips are very thin and break easily, so dispose of broken glass in the glass bin, not the ordinary bin, where it could cut someone.
Keep water away from the microscope's electric lamp and cable to avoid electric shock. Never point a microscope mirror at direct sunlight, as this can damage the eye.

Onion epidermis peels off in a layer only one cell thick, so light passes through it and the cells can be seen clearly. The steps below prepare a stained slide and an unstained control. There is more on lowering the coverslip and focusing in Microscopy.
1. Place a few drops of water in the centre of a clean slide.
2. Cut an onion into quarters and remove one fleshy scale leaf.
3. Snap the scale leaf and use forceps to peel the thin, transparent epidermis from its inner (concave) surface.
4. Cut a piece about 1 cm square and lay it flat in the water, unfolding it with the mounted needle so there are no folds or overlaps.
5. Add one or two drops of iodine solution and leave it for a few minutes to stain.
6. Lower a coverslip at 45° with the mounted needle, which avoids trapping air bubbles, then blot excess liquid from the edges with filter paper.
7. Prepare an unstained slide the same way, using water only, as the control.
8. Examine under low power (×100), then high power (×400). Make a labelled pencil drawing of a few cells and record the total magnification.

Cheek cells are collected by scraping the lining of your mouth, then stained so they show up. Because they come from a person, hygiene steps are built into the method. There is also an alternative for schools that do not use cheek cells.
1. Gently rub the inside of your own cheek with a clean, sterile cotton bud.
2. Smear the bud across the centre of a clean slide in a thin layer.
3. Immediately put the used bud into the beaker of disinfectant to prevent spreading infection.
4. Add one or two drops of methylene blue and leave for one to two minutes.
5. Lower a coverslip at 45° and blot the excess with filter paper.
6. Prepare an unstained slide with a drop of water, as the control.
7. Examine under low power, then high power. Look for flat, separate cells, avoiding clumps, which are hard to interpret. Make a labelled pencil drawing and record the magnification.
Alternative where a school does not use cheek cells: a prepared (commercial) slide of human cheek cells or another animal tissue, examined in the same way.
Onion bulb cells have no chloroplasts (the green structures where photosynthesis happens), so this optional extension uses a leaf instead.
Mount a single leaf of a moss or of Elodea (Canadian pondweed) in a drop of water, without stain. These leaves are only one or two cells thick, so light passes through them.
The green chloroplasts are visible without any stain, which onion bulb cells do not have.
The stains make the nucleus and cytoplasm stand out, and the shape of the cells tells you whether they are plant or animal. You should be able to describe what each slide looks like and explain why.
Onion epidermis: cells are regular, brick-shaped or rectangular, and fitted closely together in rows. Each cell is outlined by a clear, rigid cell wall.

In onion cells the nucleus is stained yellow-brown by iodine and is often seen near the edge of the cell. The cytoplasm stains pale yellow and forms a thin layer pushed to the edge by a large central vacuole (a fluid-filled sac), which looks clear.
Onion cells have no chloroplasts, because the bulb grows underground and does not photosynthesise.
Cheek cells: cells are flat and irregular in shape, rounded or many-sided, lying singly or in small overlapping groups. Each has a cell membrane but no cell wall.
In cheek cells the nucleus is small, central and stained dark blue, and the cytoplasm stains pale blue. There is no large vacuole and no chloroplasts.

Unstained controls: the cells are almost transparent. The onion cell walls are faintly visible but the nucleus is hard to see, and the cheek cells are barely visible. So stains make the nucleus and cytoplasm visible by adding contrast.
Structures the light microscope cannot show: ribosomes, the internal detail of mitochondria, and nuclear pores. Mitochondria are too small to see clearly at ×400.

Diagram: pencil drawings of (i) a few onion epidermis cells labelled cell wall, cell membrane (pressed against the wall), cytoplasm, vacuole and nucleus, and (ii) two or three cheek cells labelled cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus, each with the total magnification (e.g. ×400) written beside it.

Secondary data is information collected by someone else, here scanning electron microscope (SEM) images. They reveal detail the light microscope cannot, but they have limits of their own. You also need to be able to work out real cell size from an image.

Sources: published SEM images (micrographs) of onion epidermis, of cheek (epithelial) cells, and of other cells, from textbooks or reputable scientific image libraries. Each has a scale bar or magnification. Record the source of each image so others can check it.
What SEM images add: a three-dimensional view of the cell surface, at much higher magnification and resolution (the ability to separate fine detail) than the light microscope.
For example, SEM images show the regular, box-like shape of the onion cells and the outlines of their walls, and the flat, thin, overlapping shape of cheek cells and the texture of their surfaces.

Limits of SEM images: they show surfaces only, not internal organelles, which need TEM (transmission electron microscope) images. They show dead, metal-coated cells, so preparation can create artefacts (features that are not really in the living cell). Any colour is false colour added afterwards.
Measuring size from an image: actual size = image size ÷ magnification. Measure the image with a ruler in mm and convert to µm (1 mm = 1000 µm).
Worked example: an onion cell measures 40 mm long on an image magnified ×200. 40 ÷ 200 = 0.2 mm = 200 µm.
With a scale bar, measure the bar, then calculate: actual size = (image size of the cell ÷ image length of the bar) × the length the bar represents.

Comparing the data: the light microscope shows living-cell features in colour (with stain) and at low cost. The SEM confirms the shapes and surfaces in 3D at much greater detail. Using both gives a fuller and more reliable picture than either alone.
Your results can now be compared with the hypothesis. The differences between the two cell types fit what each cell does, so you should be able to link structure to function.
Both cell types have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus, so both are eukaryotic (their DNA is enclosed in a nucleus).

The onion cells have a cell wall, which gives their fixed, regular shape and support, and a large vacuole, which keeps the cell turgid (firm and full of water). The cheek cells have neither, so they have a flexible, irregular shape. This supports the hypothesis.
The cheek cells are lining (epithelial) cells: flat and thin, forming a protective layer that is continually rubbed off and replaced, which is why they come away easily.
The onion epidermis is a protective outer layer of tightly fitting cells with strong walls.
The onion has no chloroplasts because the bulb is a food store, not a photosynthetic organ.
Slide preparation is fiddly, and small mistakes give misleading images. For each problem, know what you would see and how to fix it.
Air bubbles (black-edged circles) can be mistaken for cells or can hide them. Lower the coverslip at 45°.
Folded or overlapping tissue, or a thick smear, makes cells hard to see because light cannot pass through. Use a flat piece of epidermis one cell layer thick, and a thin smear.
Too much stain darkens everything and hides detail; too little gives poor contrast. Use one or two drops and blot the excess.
The specimen drying out under the lamp distorts the cells. Add a drop of water at the edge of the coverslip.
Poor focus or wrong light settings: focus with the fine focus at high power and adjust the diaphragm (which controls how much light reaches the specimen).

Drawings depend on the observer, so compare them with other students' slides and with the SEM images. Examine several cells and several fields of view, not just one, so your conclusion does not rest on a single unusual cell.
Living things are built from and run by a small set of chemical families. Knowing which family a molecule belongs to, and what food provides, is the starting point for all of cell chemistry.
A biomolecule is a molecule made by living organisms. The four main groups are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.

All four are organic, which means they are built around chains or rings of carbon atoms bonded to hydrogen. Water and minerals are also chemicals of life but are inorganic, so they do not count as biomolecules. There is more on this in Water and Minerals.
The particular elements found in each biomolecule are listed in Structures of biomolecules.

Food supplies three things: energy, released in respiration (the chemical reactions in cells that release energy from food) mainly from carbohydrates and lipids; raw materials for growth and repair, mainly proteins; and substances that regulate body processes, namely vitamins and minerals.
The body does not take in enzymes and hormones ready made. It makes its own enzymes and hormones from the food it takes in.

Cells build big molecules by joining small ones together, and break big molecules down again by splitting them. The words monomer, polymer, condensation and hydrolysis name these units and these two opposite reactions.
A monomer is a small unit molecule. A polymer is a large molecule made of many monomers joined in a chain.
Monosaccharides (single sugar units) are the monomers of polysaccharides. Amino acids are the monomers of polypeptides and proteins. Nucleotides are the monomers of nucleic acids.
A triglyceride (a fat or oil) is built from glycerol and three fatty acids, but it is not a repeating polymer, because it is not a long chain of identical repeating units.
Condensation: two molecules join and a molecule of water is removed. Glucose units join in this way to form starch, glycogen and cellulose, and amino acids join to form proteins.

Hydrolysis is the reverse: a large molecule is split into smaller ones by adding water, for example starch is hydrolysed to maltose and proteins are hydrolysed to amino acids. Condensation removes water; hydrolysis adds it.

Digestion is hydrolysis catalysed by enzymes (proteins that speed up reactions), which is how food molecules are split into units small enough to absorb. There is more on this in The Digestive System.

Cells assemble biomolecules into the structures they are made of. Cellulose fibres form plant cell walls; phospholipids and proteins form every cell membrane; keratin forms hair and nails; collagen forms skin, tendons and the framework of bone.
Diagram: a chain of linked glucose units. Draw an arrow labelled condensation (water out) joining two units, and an arrow labelled hydrolysis (water in) splitting them. Label monomer and polymer.
Inside every cell many reactions are going on at once. Together they are called metabolism, and they fall into two opposite kinds: reactions that build up and reactions that break down.
Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions in an organism. Each reaction is controlled by a specific enzyme. Metabolism is one of the characteristics of life.
Anabolism: reactions that build larger, more complex molecules from smaller ones. They need (absorb) energy, because forming bigger molecules is an uphill process.

Anabolic examples: photosynthesis, in which glucose is made from carbon dioxide and water; joining glucose into starch in plants or glycogen in the liver and muscles; and joining amino acids into proteins.
Catabolism: reactions that break larger molecules into smaller ones. They release energy.
Catabolic examples: respiration, in which glucose is broken down to carbon dioxide and water; digestion of starch to maltose and glucose; and breakdown of glycogen to glucose.

Energy transfer: energy released by catabolic reactions such as respiration is used to drive anabolic reactions. It is carried between them by the transfer molecule ATP, a small molecule that delivers energy where the cell needs it.
Catabolism and anabolism therefore depend on each other: catabolism supplies the energy that anabolism needs. There is more on this in Transfer Molecules.
Cells do not only build and break down. They also convert one biomolecule into another, so that a single food or product can supply whatever the cell is short of.
Cells convert one biomolecule into another to meet their needs.
Plants make starch for storage, cellulose for cell walls, sucrose for transport and oils (for example stored in seeds) from the glucose made in photosynthesis.
Plants absorb nitrogen from the soil as nitrate. Glucose contains no nitrogen, so they use the nitrate, together with glucose, to make amino acids and proteins.
In humans the liver converts excess glucose to glycogen, a storage carbohydrate, and excess carbohydrate is converted to fat for storage.
The two types of metabolism are mirror images of each other. Setting them side by side makes the differences easy to remember.
Direction: anabolism joins small molecules into large ones; catabolism breaks large molecules into small ones.
Energy: anabolism needs an input of energy; catabolism releases energy, which is why the two are linked.
Examples: photosynthesis and protein synthesis are anabolic; respiration and digestion are catabolic.
Carbohydrates are the first of the four main biomolecules, the large carbon-based molecules of living things. They share one simple pattern in their formula and fall into three groups by size.
Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. Their general formula is Cx(H₂O)y, so hydrogen and oxygen are in the ratio 2 : 1, as in water. Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is an example.
The name means “hydrated carbon” because of that ratio, but the molecule does not contain water molecules. The H and O atoms are simply bonded into the sugar in the same 2 : 1 proportion.
There are three groups by size: monosaccharides (one sugar unit), disaccharides (two units) and polysaccharides (many units).
Mono- and disaccharides are sugars: sweet, soluble in water and crystalline.
Polysaccharides are not sweet and are insoluble or only slightly soluble, which suits them to storage and structure, because a molecule that does not dissolve stays put inside a cell or in a wall.
Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates: a single sugar unit. They are the monomers (single building-block units) from which every other carbohydrate is made.
Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is the main respiratory substrate (the molecule broken down in respiration to release energy) and the product of photosynthesis.
Fructose, the fruit sugar found in fruit and honey, has the same formula, C₆H₁₂O₆, but a different arrangement of atoms. Two molecules can share a formula and still be different sugars.
Galactose also has the formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and is a unit of lactose, the sugar in milk.
Glucose, fructose and galactose are all six-carbon sugars (hexoses).
Ribose and deoxyribose are five-carbon monosaccharides (pentoses). Ribose is found in RNA nucleotides and deoxyribose in DNA nucleotides. There is more on this in DNA, RNA and the Genetic Code.
Diagram: glucose drawn as a simple six-sided ring (hexagon) labelled glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆. Atom-by-atom structural formulas are not needed.
Two monosaccharides can be joined to make a disaccharide. The way they join is the same reaction that later builds starch and other large molecules.
A disaccharide forms when two monosaccharides join by condensation, a reaction that releases one molecule of water. The link between the sugar units is a glycosidic bond.
Disaccharides have the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, which is 2 × C₆H₁₂O₆ minus H₂O, because one water molecule is lost when the two units join.
Hydrolysis (splitting a bond by adding water) splits a disaccharide back into monosaccharides. It is the reverse of condensation.
Maltose (malt sugar) is glucose + glucose. It forms when starch is digested by amylase (an enzyme that breaks down starch) and is found in germinating grain.
Sucrose (table sugar, cane or beet sugar) is glucose + fructose. It is the form in which plants transport sugar in the phloem (the tissue that carries sugars around the plant).
Lactose (milk sugar) is glucose + galactose and is found in milk.
Diagram: two hexagons joined, with H₂O removed by condensation and returned by hydrolysis; label maltose = glucose + glucose.

A polysaccharide is a very long chain of sugar units. Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all made of glucose, yet they do very different jobs because of how the units are linked and whether the chain branches.

A polysaccharide is a polymer (a long molecule made of many repeating units) of many monosaccharide units, often thousands, joined by condensation. Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all polymers of glucose; they differ in how the glucose units are linked and whether the chains branch.

Starch is the storage carbohydrate of plants, held as starch grains in cells of potato tubers, seeds and cereal grains. It is a mixture of amylose, an unbranched chain that coils into a helix, and amylopectin, a branched chain.
Being insoluble, starch does not draw water into cells by osmosis (water moving in towards a more concentrated solution), and its compact shape stores much glucose in a small space.

Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate of animals and fungi, stored mainly in the liver and muscles. It is more highly branched than amylopectin, so it has many chain ends from which glucose can be released quickly when energy is needed.

Cellulose is the structural carbohydrate of plants, forming the cell wall. Its glucose units are linked in a different orientation from starch, giving long, straight, unbranched chains that lie side by side. Many hydrogen bonds (weak attractions between neighbouring chains) hold them together, forming strong fibres.
Humans have no enzyme to digest cellulose, so it passes through the gut as dietary fibre (roughage). There is more on cellulose in Biomolecules and metabolism.
Chitin is a polysaccharide that contains nitrogen. It forms the cell walls of fungi and the exoskeletons (hard outer coverings) of insects and other arthropods.
Diagram: a chain of hexagons for starch (unbranched amylose and branched amylopectin), a more branched chain for glycogen, and parallel straight chains linked by cross-links for cellulose fibres.
Lipids are the second biomolecule group. The triglyceride, one of the main kinds, is built from just two kinds of smaller molecule joined by condensation.

Lipids are fats, oils and related compounds such as phospholipids. They contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with much less oxygen in proportion to carbon and hydrogen than carbohydrates, so they are not of the form Cx(H₂O)y. Phospholipids also contain phosphorus.
Lipids are insoluble in water but dissolve in organic solvents such as ethanol.
A triglyceride is one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acids. Glycerol is a small molecule with three carbons, each carrying an –OH group, so it can bond to three fatty acids.
A fatty acid is a long hydrocarbon chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms with an acid (carboxyl, –COOH) group at one end.
Each fatty acid joins to glycerol by condensation, so forming one triglyceride releases three water molecules. The bond formed is an ester bond.
Hydrolysis by lipase (an enzyme that digests fats) reverses this, giving glycerol and fatty acids. There is more on this in The Digestive System.
Diagram: a triglyceride drawn as an E shape, with a vertical glycerol bar and three horizontal fatty acid tails, labelled glycerol, fatty acid and 3 H₂O removed.
Fats and oils have the same basic unit, the triglyceride. They differ in the fatty acids attached, and that decides whether they are solid or liquid at room temperature.

There are many different fatty acids, varying in chain length and in whether they contain carbon–carbon double bonds. Glycerol combines with different fatty acids to give many different fats and oils.
Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds, so the chain holds the maximum hydrogen. Their straight chains pack closely, so fats rich in them are solid at room temperature.
Saturated examples are butter, lard and the fat on meat. These are mostly animal fats.
Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more C=C double bonds, which put kinks (bends) in the chain. Kinked chains pack loosely, so oils are liquid at room temperature.
Unsaturated examples are olive oil, sunflower oil and fish oils. These are mostly from plants and fish.
A phospholipid is a triglyceride with one change: a phosphate group takes the place of a fatty acid. That small change gives the molecule one end that likes water and one that avoids it.
A phospholipid is glycerol joined to two fatty acids and a phosphate-containing group in place of the third fatty acid.
The phosphate head is hydrophilic (attracted to water). The two fatty acid tails are hydrophobic (repelled by water).
In water, phospholipids arrange themselves in a double layer (bilayer), with the heads facing the watery fluid on each side and the tails pointing inwards, away from the water.
This bilayer is the basis of every cell membrane. There is more on this in Transport Across Membranes and The Unit of Life — The Cell.
Diagram: a phospholipid drawn as a circle (head) with two wavy tails, labelled hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails; and a section of a bilayer.
Proteins are the third biomolecule group. Every protein is a chain built from the same 20 kinds of amino acid, joined by peptide bonds.

Proteins contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, and sometimes sulfur, phosphorus or other elements. Sulfur is in some amino acids such as cysteine and methionine, phosphorus is in casein (the main protein of milk), and iron is in haemoglobin. There is more on this in Minerals.
Proteins are made of amino acids. There are 20 different amino acids in the proteins of living things.

Each amino acid has a central carbon atom bonded to an amino group (–NH₂), an acid (carboxyl, –COOH) group, a hydrogen atom and a variable side group (R group). Only the R group differs between amino acids.
Humans cannot make some amino acids (essential amino acids), so these must be taken in from food.
Amino acids join by condensation between the –COOH group of one and the –NH₂ group of the next, releasing water. The bond formed is a peptide bond.
Two amino acids form a dipeptide; a short chain is a peptide; a long chain is a polypeptide. A protein is one or more polypeptides folded into a particular shape.
The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide (its primary structure) is set by a gene. Because 20 amino acids can be arranged in any order and length, a vast number of different proteins is possible.
Diagram: the general structure of an amino acid, a central carbon with –NH₂, –COOH, –H and –R attached; and two amino acids joined by a peptide bond with H₂O released.
A polypeptide chain does not stay straight. It folds into a precise shape, and that shape is what lets a protein do its job. Damage the shape and the job is lost.

The chain coils into a helix or folds into a pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds (secondary structure). This folds further into a precise three-dimensional shape (tertiary structure), held by bonds between R groups, including sulfur bridges between cysteine units.
Some proteins consist of several polypeptides fitted together (quaternary structure). Haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains.
The shape determines the function, because other molecules must fit it. An enzyme’s active site or an antibody’s binding site fits only particular molecules.

Heat, extremes of pH and some chemicals break the bonds holding the shape, so the protein loses its shape and function. This is denaturation, usually permanent, e.g. egg white turns solid and white when cooked. There is more on this in Enzymes.
Fibrous proteins are long strands, insoluble and structural, such as keratin (hair, nails) and collagen (skin, tendons).
Globular proteins are folded into compact, roughly spherical shapes and are usually soluble, e.g. enzymes, antibodies, haemoglobin and insulin.
Nucleic acids are the fourth biomolecule group. Like the other groups, they are built from repeating units, which are called nucleotides.

Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide contains a sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base, so nucleic acids contain C, H, O, N and P. There is more on this in DNA, RNA and the Genetic Code.
Putting the four groups side by side makes the differences easy to compare: which elements each contains, what its units are, which bond joins them and an example.
Carbohydrate: C, H, O; monosaccharides; glycosidic bond; glucose, sucrose, starch.
Lipid: C, H, O (plus P in phospholipids); glycerol and fatty acids; ester bond; triglycerides, phospholipids.
Protein: C, H, O, N (sometimes S, P or other elements); amino acids; peptide bond; enzymes, keratin.
Nucleic acid: C, H, O, N, P; nucleotides; DNA, RNA.

Carbohydrates do far more than supply energy. Glucose is fuel, a product of photosynthesis and a building block for storage molecules, and other carbohydrates give structure and carry sugar around organisms.

Respiratory and catabolic role (catabolic means breaking molecules down): glucose is the main respiratory substrate, the fuel respiration uses. It is broken down to release energy, which is trapped as ATP, the cell's energy carrier. There is more on this in Respiration.
The brain relies mainly on glucose for its energy, so a steady supply of glucose in the blood matters.

Photosynthetic role: glucose is the product of photosynthesis, the anabolic process (anabolic means building molecules up) in which plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
Almost all the carbohydrate in food chains therefore comes from photosynthesis, because plants are the producers that make it first and every consumer depends on them.
Anabolic and storage role: excess glucose is built up into storage polysaccharides (long chains of sugar units), which are starch in plants and glycogen in the liver and muscles of animals.
These stores are broken down again (catabolism) when glucose is needed, so the organism can release it back as fuel.

Structural role: cellulose forms plant cell walls, and chitin forms fungal cell walls and insect exoskeletons (the hard outer body casing). The pentose (five-carbon) sugars ribose and deoxyribose are part of RNA and DNA nucleotides.
Transport role: plants move sugar from the leaves to other parts as sucrose, carried in the phloem (the tissue that transports food in plants).
Lipids (fats, oils and related molecules) are used for energy storage, but their uses go much further. They insulate, protect, build membranes, waterproof surfaces and act as regulators.
Respiratory and catabolic role: fats are respired to release energy, especially when glucose and glycogen run low.
A gram of fat releases about twice as much energy as a gram of carbohydrate or protein, so lipid is a compact long-term energy store.
Storage (anabolic): excess food is built into triglycerides (the main type of fat molecule) and stored as fat in adipose tissue, under the skin and around organs in animals.
Plants store oils in seeds, such as sunflower seeds, and in fruits, such as olives.
Insulation: fat under the skin reduces heat loss, as in the thick blubber of whales and seals. The myelin sheath around nerve fibres is rich in lipid and insulates them.
Protection: fat around organs such as the kidneys and heart cushions them against physical damage.
Structural role: phospholipids form the bilayer (double layer) of all cell membranes, including the membranes inside chloroplasts and mitochondria.

Photosynthetic role: the light-absorbing pigments of photosynthesis are held in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast, which are built of phospholipids. Plants also convert some of the glucose made in photosynthesis into oils.
Two further roles of lipids come from their water-repelling nature and from their chemistry as signalling molecules.
Waterproofing: waxes, which are lipids, form the waxy cuticle on leaves, reducing water loss. They also waterproof feathers and fur.
Regulators: steroid hormones such as testosterone, oestrogen and progesterone are lipids, which means not all hormones are proteins.
Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed with dietary fat. There is more on this in Vitamins.
Proteins have many different jobs in the body, from speeding up reactions to defence, movement and transport. Each role below has a named protein you can give as an example.

Enzymes: almost all enzymes are proteins. They are biological catalysts that speed up the reactions of metabolism (all the chemical reactions in a cell) without being used up, for example amylase digests starch to maltose.
Hormones: some hormones are proteins, for example insulin, made by the pancreas, which lowers blood glucose. Other hormones are lipids.

Immunity: antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes (B cells, a type of white blood cell). Each binds to a specific antigen (a marker molecule) on a pathogen (a disease-causing organism), marking it for destruction.
Transport of substances in the body: haemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen.
Movement: actin and myosin are the contractile proteins of muscle, which means they shorten to make the muscle contract.
Energy: protein is respired only when carbohydrate and fat are in short supply.
Excess amino acids (the units proteins are made of) cannot be stored. The liver removes their amino group (deamination), forming urea, which is excreted.
Growth and repair: proteins are the main raw material for new cells and tissues, so children, pregnant women and people recovering from injury need more.
Many proteins sit in the cell membrane (the phospholipid bilayer around every cell) and decide what crosses it and how cells respond to signals. The specification names four kinds.
Membrane proteins are embedded in the phospholipid bilayer. They control what enters and leaves cells and how cells communicate.

Channel proteins form water-filled pores through the membrane that let specific ions or molecules pass by diffusion (movement from high to low concentration), for example the sodium and potassium channels of neurons, which allow nerve impulses.
Transporters (carrier proteins) bind a specific molecule and change shape to move it across the membrane.

Some transporters use energy from ATP to move substances against a concentration gradient (active transport), for example the sodium-potassium pump. There is more on this in Transport Across Membranes.

Receptors are proteins on the cell surface, or inside the cell, with a shape that fits one signalling molecule such as a hormone or neurotransmitter. When the signal binds, the cell responds, for example insulin receptors on liver and muscle cells.
This is why a hormone affects only its target cells: only cells with the matching receptor can respond.

Structural proteins give strength and support. Keratin forms hair, nails and the outer skin, and collagen forms skin, tendons, ligaments, cartilage and bone. Proteins also form the cytoskeleton, the internal scaffold of cells.
Diagram: a section of cell membrane (phospholipid bilayer) showing a channel protein, a carrier protein, and a receptor protein with its signalling molecule. Label each.
Hormones link the metabolic roles of proteins and lipids, because they are made from both. They let one part of the body control the activity of another.

A hormone is a chemical messenger made by an endocrine gland and carried in the blood to target cells, where it regulates their activity. Hormones regulate growth, development, metabolism and reproduction.
Hormones are biomolecules from two groups: proteins, such as insulin, and steroid lipids, such as testosterone and oestrogen. There is more on this in The Endocrine System.
Hormones work only on cells with the matching receptor proteins, so only target cells respond.
Plants also make chemical regulators, called plant growth regulators, for example auxin.
Knowing the roles of each biomolecule is only half the story. You also need to name the foods that supply each one.
Carbohydrate sources, sugars: fruit, honey, jam, sweets and fizzy drinks, and lactose (milk sugar) in milk.
Carbohydrate sources, starch: bread, pasta, rice, potatoes and breakfast cereals.
Carbohydrate sources, fibre (cellulose): vegetables, fruit, wholegrain cereals and brown bread, and beans.
Lipid sources, fats (mostly saturated): butter, cream, cheese, lard and fatty meat.
Lipid sources, oils (mostly unsaturated): olive and sunflower oils, nuts and seeds, avocados, and oily fish such as salmon and mackerel.
Protein sources, animal: meat, fish, eggs, milk, cheese and yoghurt. Protein sources, plant: beans, peas, lentils, nuts, soya and tofu, and cereals.

Animal proteins contain all the essential amino acids (those the body cannot make). Many single plant foods lack one or more, so vegetarian and vegan diets combine a range of plant proteins, for example beans with cereal.
What we eat affects both our health and the environment, so food sources link back to the roles of each biomolecule.
Diets high in saturated fat are linked to raised blood cholesterol and heart disease.
Diets high in free sugars are linked to tooth decay, obesity and type 2 diabetes.
Producing plant protein generally needs less land and water, and causes lower greenhouse gas emissions, than producing meat. There is more on balanced diets in The Digestive System.

Living things are built mostly from carbon-based molecules, but they also need a small supply of simple chemical elements. These are the minerals, and they are taken in from the environment because the organism cannot make them.
Minerals are inorganic elements (not carbon-based compounds), usually taken in as ions dissolved in water, that organisms need in small amounts for normal functioning. Organisms cannot make them.
Animals get minerals from food and drink. Plants absorb them as ions dissolved in soil water through their root hairs, the tiny extensions of root cells that give a large surface area for absorption.

Some minerals are built into biomolecules or structures: iron in haemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying protein of red blood cells), magnesium in chlorophyll, phosphorus in phospholipids, DNA and ATP, sulfur in some amino acids, iodine in thyroxine, and calcium (as calcium phosphate) in bone and teeth.
Many minerals are not built into biomolecules. They work as free ions in body fluids, such as sodium (Na⁺), potassium (K⁺), chloride (Cl⁻) and calcium (Ca²⁺) ions, so the mineral itself does the job.
Minerals differ from vitamins: minerals are inorganic elements, while vitamins are organic compounds. Neither supplies energy, so neither can replace carbohydrates, lipids or proteins as a fuel.
Minerals do far more than build bones. Even when they are not part of a larger molecule, ions dissolved in body fluids keep chemical conditions steady and switch key processes on and off.

pH balance: phosphate and hydrogencarbonate ions act as buffers (chemicals that resist pH change) in cells and blood. They take up or release hydrogen ions so that pH stays almost constant; blood is kept at about pH 7.4. This matters because enzymes work only in a narrow pH range.

Regulation of enzyme systems: many enzymes need a mineral ion to work, acting as a cofactor or activator (a helper that the enzyme needs). Magnesium ions are needed by many enzymes that use ATP, zinc is part of many enzymes, and chloride ions activate salivary amylase.
Without its ion an enzyme is inactive, so the level of a mineral helps control which metabolic pathways (chains of enzyme-controlled reactions) can run.

Nerve impulse transfer: a nerve impulse travels as sodium ions move into and potassium ions move out of the neuron (nerve cell) through channel proteins, which are pores in the cell membrane. There is more on this in The Nervous System.
Calcium ions entering the end of a neuron trigger the release of neurotransmitter, the chemical messenger that carries the signal across the synapse (the gap between neurons).

Muscle contraction: after a nerve impulse arrives, calcium ions are released inside a muscle fibre (a muscle cell). They allow the proteins actin and myosin to interact, so the muscle contracts. There is more on this in The Musculoskeletal System.
Osmoregulation: sodium and chloride ions in body fluids affect the movement of water by osmosis, so they help control how much water is in cells and fluids.
Other roles: structure, where calcium and phosphate form bones and teeth; oxygen transport, through iron in haemoglobin; and blood clotting, which needs calcium.
Each mineral the body needs has a job, a set of foods that supply it, and a deficiency disease when it runs short.
Calcium forms bones and teeth as calcium phosphate, and is needed for muscle contraction, nerve transmission and blood clotting. Its absorption needs vitamin D.
Calcium sources: milk, cheese, yoghurt, green leafy vegetables, and tinned fish eaten with the bones, such as sardines, because the soft bones are rich in calcium.

Calcium deficiency weakens bones, because there is too little calcium to build and maintain them. This shows as rickets in children (linked to low vitamin D) and as a risk of osteoporosis, brittle bones, in later life.
Iron is part of haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells.
Iron sources: red meat, liver, eggs, green leafy vegetables such as spinach, beans and lentils, and fortified breakfast cereals (cereals with iron added).
Vitamin C helps the gut absorb iron from plant foods, so eating vitamin C-rich foods alongside plant sources of iron improves the supply.
Iron deficiency causes anaemia: too little haemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen. This causes tiredness, weakness and pale skin.
Women who menstruate need more iron than men, because they lose iron-containing blood each month.
Sodium and potassium work as a pair. They are free ions on either side of cell membranes, and the balance between them drives nerve signals and fluid balance.
Sodium is needed for nerve impulses and controls water balance in body fluids, because water follows sodium by osmosis.
Sodium sources: table salt, processed foods, crisps, bacon and cheese.
Most people take in more sodium than they need, and excess salt is linked to high blood pressure.
Potassium works with sodium in nerve impulses and muscle function, and controls fluid balance inside cells, whereas sodium mainly controls the fluid outside them.
Potassium sources: bananas, potatoes, vegetables, fruit and milk.
Some minerals are needed for one specific job. Iodine is needed to make a hormone, and fluoride protects the teeth.

Iodine is needed to make the hormone thyroxine in the thyroid gland, a gland in the neck. Thyroxine controls metabolic rate, the rate at which the body's chemical reactions run. There is more on this in The Endocrine System.
Iodine sources: seafood, seaweed, milk and iodised salt (table salt with iodine added).
Iodine deficiency causes goitre, a swollen thyroid gland, and a low metabolic rate, because without iodine the body cannot make enough thyroxine.
Fluoride hardens tooth enamel, the outer layer of the tooth, making it more resistant to decay.
Fluoride sources: fluoridated public water, as in Ireland, toothpaste and tea.
Phosphorus and magnesium each turn up in many places in the body, so they have several roles. Both are found in bone, and magnesium also helps enzymes and nerves work.

Phosphorus, as phosphate, forms part of bones and teeth, ATP (the cell's energy carrier), DNA, RNA and phospholipids (the lipids of cell membranes), and helps buffer pH, as phosphate ions do in cells and blood.
Phosphorus sources: milk, cheese, meat, fish, eggs and nuts.
Magnesium is needed for bones, activates many enzymes, and is needed for muscle and nerve function.
Magnesium sources: green leafy vegetables, nuts and wholegrain cereals.
Plants cannot eat, so they take every mineral they need from the soil. Each one has a job, and a shortage shows up quickly in how the plant looks.

Plants absorb minerals from soil water as ions through root hairs, often by active transport (using energy to move ions into the root against a concentration gradient). The minerals then travel up the xylem, the water-carrying tubes, in the water stream.

Nitrogen, absorbed as nitrate, is needed to make amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids. A shortage gives stunted growth and yellow leaves. There is more on how nitrogen reaches the soil in Nutrient Cycling.
Magnesium is part of chlorophyll, the green pigment that traps light for photosynthesis. A shortage causes yellowing leaves, with less chlorophyll and so less photosynthesis.
Phosphate is needed for ATP, DNA and phospholipids, and for root growth.
Calcium forms calcium pectate, which holds neighbouring plant cell walls together.
Farmers add minerals, mainly nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, to soil in fertilisers, so that crops have enough for healthy growth.
Excess fertiliser washed into rivers and lakes causes eutrophication, an over-enrichment of the water with nutrients that harms the ecosystem.
Your body needs a handful of chemicals in tiny amounts that it cannot build for itself. These are the vitamins, and without them key processes stop working properly.

Vitamins are organic compounds (carbon-based molecules made by living things) needed in very small amounts for normal metabolism, growth and health. The body cannot make them, or cannot make enough, so they must come from the diet.
Vitamins supply no energy and are not used to build tissues in bulk. This is what separates them from carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, which are needed in large amounts.
Many vitamins act as coenzymes (helper molecules that enzymes need) or help enzymes work. For example, the B vitamins help release energy from food in respiration.
Some vitamins are needed to make particular substances, such as vitamin C for collagen (a structural protein). Others act as antioxidants that protect cells from damage (vitamins C and E).
Vitamin D controls the absorption of minerals: it controls how much calcium is taken in from food.
A lack of a vitamin causes a deficiency disease with characteristic symptoms. The disease is cured or prevented by supplying the vitamin.
Vitamins are grouped by what they dissolve in. Water-soluble: vitamin C and the B group. Fat-soluble: vitamins A, D, E and K.

Whether a vitamin dissolves in water or in fat decides how it is absorbed, carried, stored and lost, and so how often you must eat it and whether it can build up to harmful levels. Compare the two groups point by point.
Absorption: water-soluble vitamins dissolve in the watery contents of the gut and are absorbed directly into the blood. Fat-soluble vitamins dissolve in dietary fat and are absorbed along with it.
So a very low-fat diet, or a condition that prevents fat absorption, can cause a deficiency of vitamin A, D, E or K, because these vitamins cannot be absorbed without fat.
Transport: water-soluble vitamins travel dissolved in the blood plasma (the watery liquid part of blood). Fat-soluble vitamins are carried with lipids.

Storage of water-soluble vitamins: any excess is excreted by the kidneys in urine and most are not stored. They must therefore be eaten regularly, ideally daily, and a deficiency develops within weeks or months.
Storage of fat-soluble vitamins: they are stored in the liver and fatty tissue, so the body can draw on these reserves and they need not be eaten every day.
Toxicity (harmfulness): because excess water-soluble vitamins are excreted, overdose is rare. Fat-soluble vitamins can build up in the liver to harmful levels if large supplements are taken.
Too much vitamin A is toxic, which is why pregnant women are advised not to eat liver or take vitamin A supplements.

Cooking: water-soluble vitamins leach (dissolve) out of food into the cooking water, and vitamin C is also destroyed by heat and by long storage. Vegetables lose vitamin C when boiled for a long time; steaming, microwaving or eating them raw keeps more. Fat-soluble vitamins are not lost into cooking water.
Vitamin C is the standard example of a water-soluble vitamin. Its main job is to help build collagen, so a shortage weakens the body's connective tissue.
Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, is water-soluble.

Roles: it is needed to make collagen, the protein of connective tissue in skin, gums, blood vessel walls, bones and scar tissue. It also helps wounds heal, acts as an antioxidant, helps the gut absorb iron from plant foods, and supports the immune system.

Sources: citrus fruits (oranges, lemons, limes, grapefruit), kiwi fruit, strawberries, blackcurrants, peppers, broccoli, tomatoes and potatoes. It is best eaten fresh and raw, because it leaches into cooking water and is destroyed by heat and long storage.
Deficiency disease: scurvy. Without vitamin C, collagen is not made properly, so connective tissue weakens. This is why the symptoms involve gums, blood vessels and wounds.
Scurvy symptoms: swollen, bleeding gums and loose teeth; easy bruising and bleeding under the skin; wounds that heal slowly or reopen; tiredness and aching joints.
Untreated, scurvy can be fatal. It is cured quickly by vitamin C.

History (Health and Nature of Science link): scurvy killed many sailors on long voyages without fresh food. In 1747 James Lind, a Scottish naval surgeon, gave different treatments to groups of sailors with scurvy and found that those given oranges and lemons recovered. This was an early controlled trial.
Vitamin D is the standard example of a fat-soluble vitamin. Its main job is to help the gut take in calcium, which bones and teeth need to harden.
Vitamin D, also called calciferol, is fat-soluble.

Role: it increases the absorption of calcium, and phosphate, from food in the small intestine. It is therefore needed for the formation and hardening of bones and teeth. It also helps muscle function and the immune system.

Sources: the skin makes vitamin D when it is exposed to ultraviolet light in sunlight. Dietary sources are oily fish (e.g. salmon, mackerel and sardines), fish-liver oils such as cod-liver oil, egg yolk and liver, and fortified foods such as some milks, spreads and breakfast cereals.
Deficiency disease: rickets in children. Bones do not harden, so they stay soft and weak. The leg bones bend under the body's weight, giving bowed legs; growth is poor and the bones are painful.
In adults the equivalent condition is osteomalacia, which means softening of the bones. Low vitamin D also raises the risk of osteoporosis (thinning, brittle bones) in later life.

People at risk are those who get little sunlight: people living at northern latitudes like Ireland, where winter sunlight is too weak for the skin to make vitamin D, and people who stay indoors or cover their skin.
Other people at risk are people with darker skin living at high latitudes, older people, and babies. Irish health advice recommends a vitamin D supplement for babies in their first year.
You may choose other vitamins to answer questions on the role, source and deficiency of a vitamin. These three are fat-soluble, so they are stored in the body and absorbed with dietary fat.
Vitamin A (retinol) is fat-soluble and is needed for vision in dim light and for healthy skin and linings. Deficiency causes night blindness.
Vitamin A sources: liver, dairy produce, eggs and oily fish. Carrots and other orange and dark green vegetables contain beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Vitamin K is fat-soluble and is needed for blood clotting. Sources: green leafy vegetables. It is also made by bacteria in the large intestine.
Newborn babies have little vitamin K, so they are given it soon after birth to prevent bleeding.
Vitamin E is fat-soluble and is an antioxidant that protects cell membranes from damage. Sources: vegetable oils, nuts and seeds. No named deficiency disease is needed.
The B-group vitamins are water-soluble, so they are not stored well and must be eaten often. Several have a named deficiency disease and two are needed for healthy red blood cells.
The B-group vitamins are water-soluble and help enzymes release energy from food. Sources: wholegrain cereals, meat, eggs, dairy produce and beans.
Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency causes beriberi; vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency causes pellagra.
Folic acid (folate, a B vitamin) and vitamin B12 are needed to make red blood cells. A lack of either causes a form of anaemia (too few healthy red blood cells).
Vitamin B12 is found naturally only in animal foods, so vegans need fortified foods or supplements.

Women are advised to take folic acid before and in early pregnancy, as it reduces the risk of neural tube defects (faults in the development of the baby's spine and brain) such as spina bifida in the baby.
Some groups of people struggle to get enough of a vitamin from their normal diet. Two measures are used to protect them.

Food fortification, adding vitamins to foods such as breakfast cereals and milk, and taking supplements are used to prevent deficiency diseases in groups at risk. An example is the vitamin D supplement advised for babies in their first year.

Water is the most abundant substance in living things, and almost every role it plays comes from the shape and charge of its molecule. Learn the properties here first, because the later blocks all rely on them.
Water is the most abundant substance in living things. It makes up about 60% of the mass of an adult human body and most of the mass of cytoplasm (the jelly-like contents of a cell).
Many plant tissues and jellyfish are over 90% water. Organisms die quickly without water, which shows how much of life depends on it.
A water molecule, H₂O, is polar, meaning it has uneven charge: the oxygen end carries a slight negative charge (δ−) and the hydrogen ends carry slight positive charges (δ+).
Because of these opposite charges, neighbouring water molecules are attracted to each other by hydrogen bonds, weak attractions between the δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and the δ− oxygen of another.

Because it is polar, water is an excellent solvent: ions (e.g. Na⁺, Cl⁻) and polar molecules (e.g. glucose, amino acids) dissolve in it, as the charged water molecules surround them. Lipids are non-polar and do not dissolve.

Hydrogen bonding gives water a high specific heat capacity, so it takes a lot of energy to raise its temperature, because the energy must first break hydrogen bonds. It also gives water a high latent heat of vaporisation, so a lot of energy is absorbed when it evaporates.
Hydrogen bonding makes water molecules stick to each other (cohesion) and to other surfaces (adhesion).
Diagram: two or three water molecules with δ+ on the hydrogens, δ− on the oxygen, and a dotted hydrogen bond between them.
Chemical reactions in cells need the reacting molecules to meet. Water gives them a place to do that, and it also takes part in some of the reactions itself.

Almost all metabolic reactions (the chemical reactions of life) take place in solution in water, in the cytoplasm and inside organelles. This is because dissolved molecules can move, collide and meet enzymes.

Water is also a reactant, meaning it is used up in a reaction. It is split in photosynthesis, releasing oxygen, and it is used in every hydrolysis reaction (breaking a bond by adding water), including digestion.
Water is a product, meaning it is made by a reaction, in respiration and in every condensation reaction (joining molecules together with the loss of water).
Because so many substances dissolve in water, it can carry them from place to place. This works in animals and plants, and also across the surface of every cell.

In animals, blood plasma (the liquid part of blood) is mainly water. It carries dissolved glucose, amino acids, mineral ions, hormones, urea and carbon dioxide around the body; lymph and tissue fluid are also watery.
Urea (a waste product) and excess salts are excreted dissolved in water as urine, so water carries waste out of the body as well as supplies in.
In plants, water carries dissolved minerals up the xylem (the vessels that carry water) from the roots to the leaves. Sucrose and amino acids move through the phloem (the vessels that carry food).
Cohesion between water molecules holds the column of water together in the xylem, so it can be pulled upwards as one continuous stream. There is more on this in Transport in Plants.
Substances move into and out of cells by diffusion through the watery fluid around them, because dissolved substances can spread out through water.
Living things work best within a narrow temperature range. Water helps keep them there, thanks to its high specific heat capacity and high latent heat of vaporisation.

High specific heat capacity: water heats up and cools down slowly, so the water in an organism's body buffers it against sudden temperature changes. Lakes and seas give aquatic organisms a stable temperature.

Cooling by evaporation: because water absorbs a lot of heat when it evaporates, sweating in mammals cools the skin, panting cools dogs, and transpiration (evaporation of water from leaves) cools leaves. There is more on sweating in Homeostasis.
Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats and forms an insulating layer on ponds and lakes, letting organisms survive beneath it in winter.
Enzymes only work properly at the right pH, so cells need to keep acidity steady. Water is the medium in which this control happens.

pH depends on the concentration of hydrogen ions (H⁺) in a solution; pure water is neutral, at pH 7. Acids and bases exert their effects only when they are dissolved in water, because that is when they release ions.
Buffers, such as hydrogencarbonate and phosphate ions, work dissolved in body water. They keep the pH of cells and blood almost constant, so enzymes keep their shape and activity.
Water is the medium by which excess H⁺ ions are removed. The kidneys excrete them dissolved in urine.
Carbon dioxide, which forms an acid in solution, is carried in the blood plasma to the lungs and breathed out, so the acid does not build up in the blood.

Water moves in and out of cells by osmosis, so cells can swell or shrink if the surrounding fluid changes. Osmoregulation is how organisms keep this under control, and animals and plants deal with it differently.
Osmoregulation is the control of the water and salt (solute) concentration of body fluids.

Water moves into or out of cells by osmosis, from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration, through a selectively permeable membrane. There is more on this in Transport Across Membranes.
Animal cells placed in pure water swell and may burst; in strong salt solution they shrink. So the concentration of the blood and tissue fluid must be kept steady.
In humans the kidneys do this, adjusting the volume of water in urine under the control of ADH (a hormone).

Plant cells have a strong cell wall, so water entering by osmosis makes them turgid (swollen and firm) instead of bursting. Turgor pressure supports non-woody plants and leaves and opens stomata (the pores in leaves).
When water is lost, plant cells become flaccid (soft and limp) and the plant wilts.
Single-celled freshwater organisms such as Amoeba constantly gain water by osmosis, because their surroundings are more dilute than their cytoplasm. They expel the excess with a contractile vacuole.
Beyond reactions, transport, temperature, pH and osmoregulation, water has several further roles in living things.
Lubrication: synovial fluid lubricates joints, and mucus and saliva help swallowing.
Support: the fluid pressure of a hydrostatic skeleton supports soft-bodied animals such as earthworms, because water cannot easily be compressed.
Habitat: water is the habitat of aquatic organisms.
Fertilisation: some organisms need water for fertilisation. Moss and fern sperm swim in water to reach the egg.

Food tests are a fair, planned investigation, not just a set of recipes. Before testing anything you decide what you are trying to find out, what you predict, and what you will change, measure and keep the same.

Aim: to find out which nutrients (starch, reducing sugar, protein and lipid) are present in a range of food samples. The investigation is qualitative, which means you record whether a nutrient is present or absent, from a colour change or other observation, not how much of it there is.

Hypothesis, e.g.: “Potato contains starch but not lipid; milk contains reducing sugar (lactose), protein and lipid.” Students predict the result for each food from what the food is, so the results can later support or contradict the prediction.
Independent variable (the one you change): the food sample tested. Dependent variable (the one you observe): the result of each test, the colour or observation, recorded as present or absent.

Controlled variables (kept the same so the test is fair): the volume of food solution and of reagent, the concentration of the reagents, the water-bath temperature and heating time for Benedict's, and clean apparatus for every test to avoid carry-over from one sample to the next.
Every test needs two controls. A negative control uses distilled water in place of the food and shows the colour when the nutrient is absent.
A positive control uses a known pure sample, such as starch solution, glucose solution, egg-white (albumen) solution or vegetable oil, and shows the colour when the nutrient is present.
Results for the foods are judged against these controls, so you can tell a real colour change from the reagent's starting colour, and know the test itself is working.
Choose foods that you expect to be rich in each nutrient, and gather the equipment and reagents (the chemicals that react with a nutrient to give a visible result) before you start.

Example food samples: potato, bread, rice or flour (starch); glucose, honey, grapes, fruit juice and milk (reducing sugar); egg white, milk, meat or cheese (protein); butter, vegetable oil, nuts, crisps and cheese (lipid); and table sugar, which gives a negative Benedict's result.

Equipment: test tubes and rack, test-tube holder, droppers, graduated pipettes or syringes (to measure equal volumes), spotting tile, mortar and pestle or knife and chopping board, beaker of distilled water, filter funnel and filter paper.
Also needed: a hot water bath (a beaker of near-boiling water from a kettle, or an electric water bath) with a thermometer, brown paper, labels, safety glasses and gloves.
Reagents: iodine solution (iodine dissolved in potassium iodide), Benedict's solution, biuret reagent (or sodium hydroxide solution and dilute copper sulfate solution) and Sudan III stain.
Most tests work on a liquid, so solid foods must first be turned into a food solution. This preparation is common to all the tests.
1. Crush or grind a solid food with a little distilled water using a mortar and pestle. Crushing breaks open the cells so the nutrients can mix into the water.
2. Add more water, stir, and filter or let the solid settle, then use the liquid food solution for the tests.
3. Test liquid foods such as milk and juice directly, or dilute them.
4. Label each tube with the food and the test, so the results cannot be mixed up.
Starch is the carbohydrate plants store, and iodine solution is the quickest way to detect it. It needs no heating and gives a result at once.

Method, step 1: place a few drops of food solution, or a small piece of solid food, on a white spotting tile, or place 2 cm³ of food solution in a test tube. The white tile makes the colour easy to see.
Step 2: add a few drops of iodine solution. Step 3: observe the colour at once. No heating is needed.
Step 4: repeat with water as the negative control and starch solution as the positive control.
Result: iodine solution is yellow-brown (orange-brown) at the start. It turns blue-black if starch is present and stays yellow-brown if starch is absent.
Some sugars can react chemically with Benedict's solution and others cannot. This test detects the ones that can, and it is the one food test that needs heat.
A reducing sugar is one that can reduce (give electrons to) the blue copper(II) ions in Benedict's solution. Glucose, fructose, galactose, maltose and lactose are reducing sugars; sucrose is not.
Method, step 1: place 2 cm³ of food solution in a test tube. Step 2: add an equal volume, 2 cm³, of Benedict's solution and mix; the mixture is blue.
Step 3: place the tube in a hot water bath (near boiling, at least about 80 °C) for about 5 minutes. Never heat the tube directly in a Bunsen flame, because the liquid can spurt out.
Step 4: observe the colour. Step 5: run water as the negative control and glucose solution as the positive control, in the same water bath at the same time so the conditions are identical.

Result: if a reducing sugar is present, the blue solution turns green, then yellow, then orange, and finally a brick-red precipitate (solid particles) forms. It stays blue if no reducing sugar is present.

The reducing sugar reduces blue copper(II) ions to copper(I) oxide, the brick-red precipitate. The colour reached gives a rough idea of how much sugar is present: green for a little, brick red for a lot. There is more on this in Investigation: reducing sugars, quantitatively.

Fehling's test is an alternative: equal volumes of Fehling's solutions A and B are mixed with the sample and heated in a water bath. A blue mixture turns to a brick-red precipitate if a reducing sugar is present.

Extension: sucrose stays blue. To show it is made of reducing sugars, boil a sucrose solution with a few drops of dilute hydrochloric acid to hydrolyse it to glucose and fructose. Neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate until fizzing stops, then do the Benedict's test: it now turns brick red.
Biuret detects the bonds that join amino acids together in a protein. Like iodine, it works at room temperature with no heating.
Method, step 1: place 2 cm³ of food solution in a test tube. Step 2: add 2 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution and mix (or add biuret reagent, which already contains it).
Step 3: add a few drops of dilute copper sulfate solution, one drop at a time, shaking gently. Step 4: leave for a few minutes and observe. No heating is needed.
Step 5: run water as the negative control and egg-white solution as the positive control.

Result: the blue colour turns purple (violet or lilac) if protein is present, and stays blue if protein is absent. The copper ions react with the peptide bonds (the links between amino acids) in the protein, so the test detects peptide bonds, not single amino acids.
Lipids (fats and oils) do not dissolve in water, and two simple tests use this. They are alternatives, so you can use either one.
Grease-spot (brown paper) test, method: rub a small amount of food on a piece of brown paper, or place a drop of liquid food on it. Place a drop of water on another part of the paper as a control.
Leave the paper to dry, or warm it gently away from flames, then hold it up to the light.

Grease-spot result: a translucent (see-through), greasy spot that does not disappear when the paper dries shows that lipid is present. The water spot also looks translucent at first but disappears as it dries, which is why the paper must dry before the result is judged.
Sudan III test, method: place 2 cm³ of food solution, or a little crushed food in 2 cm³ of water, in a test tube. Add a few drops of Sudan III, a red dye that dissolves in lipid but not in water.
Shake gently and leave to stand for a minute. Run water as the negative control and vegetable oil in water as the positive control.

Sudan III result: if lipid is present, a red-stained oily layer forms on top of the water, because lipid is less dense than water and does not mix with it. With no lipid, the dye spreads through the water or settles as red specks, with no red oily layer.
Several reagents here are corrosive, harmful or flammable, and the Benedict's test uses near-boiling water. Safe practice is part of any investigation.

Wear safety glasses throughout. Sodium hydroxide (biuret test) is corrosive and especially harmful to the eyes. Benedict's and copper sulfate solutions are harmful if swallowed or splashed. Wash any splash off the skin with plenty of water.

Heat Benedict's tests only in a water bath, never directly over a flame, because the liquid can boil suddenly and spurt out of the tube. Use a test-tube holder, point the tube away from people, and take care with near-boiling water.
Sudan III stain is usually dissolved in ethanol, an alcohol that is highly flammable, so keep it away from flames. Do not warm brown paper near a flame.
Iodine solution stains skin and clothes; wear gloves if possible.
Never taste or eat food in the laboratory. Be aware of food allergies (e.g. to nuts) among the class. Clean up spills and wash hands after the practical.
Your observations are the primary data (results you collected yourself). A clear table lets you compare every food with the controls and draw a conclusion from the evidence.
Record primary data in a results table: one row per food and one column per test, recording the colour observed and whether the nutrient is present or absent (or + or −). Include the control rows.

Expected results: potato shows starch; glucose, honey and grapes show reducing sugar; table sugar is Benedict's negative, as sucrose is non-reducing; egg white shows protein; vegetable oil and butter show lipid; milk shows reducing sugar, protein and lipid; distilled water is negative for all tests.
Conclusion: state which nutrients each food contains, supported by the results compared with the controls, and say whether this supports the hypothesis. The tests show presence only, not the amount.
Food tests are simple, so small mistakes easily give a wrong result. Knowing the common errors, and how to reduce them, makes the conclusion more reliable.
Colour judgements are subjective, so different people may see different shades. Compare each tube with the controls against a white background, and have two people check the result.
Coloured foods, such as dark fruit juice, can mask a colour change. Dilute or filter them, or use a control of the food without the reagent.
Contamination: reusing a dropper or test tube can carry a nutrient from one sample to another, giving a false positive.
A very small amount of nutrient may not give a visible change, which is a false negative. Some nutrients are inside cells, so the food must be well crushed.
Benedict's detects reducing sugars only, so a food rich in sucrose can give a negative result even though it contains sugar.
Repeat each test, e.g. three times, to check that the results are repeatable.
Diagram: a test tube of food solution with Benedict's solution standing in a beaker of hot water, with a thermometer, labelled.

A food test that only says "reducing sugar present" is qualitative. This investigation goes a step further and compares how much reducing sugar (a sugar that reduces the copper(II) ions in Benedict's solution) different foods contain, by checking each food against glucose solutions of known concentration.
Aim: to compare the concentration of reducing sugar in a range of food samples, by comparing their Benedict's results with those of glucose solutions of known concentration.
Hypothesis, for example: "Grape juice contains a higher concentration of reducing sugar than milk." A prediction that ranks the foods in order is also acceptable.

Principle: the more reducing sugar in a sample, the more blue copper(II) ions are reduced to brick-red copper(I) oxide. The colour therefore moves further along the scale blue, green, yellow, orange, brick red.
More precipitate (solid that forms in the tube) appears as well. There is more on the colour scale in Investigation: food tests.
This works only if Benedict's is in excess, meaning there is more than enough to react with all the sugar. Then the colour keeps changing as sugar concentration rises, right across the range tested.
A fair test changes one thing at a time and keeps everything else the same. Here the standards give a reference scale and the controls show that any colour change really comes from the sugar.

Independent variable (the thing you change): the food sample, and for the standards the known glucose concentration. Dependent variable (the thing you measure): the concentration of reducing sugar, judged from the colour, or measured as absorbance with a colorimeter.

Controlled variables (kept the same, so the test is fair): the mass of food and the volume of water used to make each extract; the volume of sample and of Benedict's solution; the concentration of Benedict's; the water-bath temperature; the heating time; and the time before the colours are compared.
Negative control: a tube of distilled water with Benedict's solution (0%, no reducing sugar) stays blue, which shows the reagent alone does not change colour.
Positive controls: the standard glucose solutions, which are known to contain reducing sugar. They also act as the reference scale that the food tubes are compared against.

Equipment and materials: glucose powder, electronic balance, volumetric flask or graduated cylinder, beakers, distilled water, graduated pipettes or syringes, test tubes and rack, labels, mortar and pestle, filter funnel and paper.
Also needed: hot water bath with thermometer, test-tube holder, timer, Benedict's solution, white tile or card and safety glasses. Optionally a colorimeter with cuvettes and glucose test strips.

Example food samples: grape juice, apple juice, orange juice, honey, milk, onion, a sports drink, and a table-sugar solution. The table-sugar solution is expected to stay blue because sucrose is non-reducing.

To read a food's sugar level you need a scale of solutions whose concentration you know exactly. You make these by diluting (adding water to) a single stock solution, which is a stronger solution you start from.
1. Make a stock solution of 1% glucose by dissolving 1 g of glucose in distilled water and making it up to 100 cm³.
2. Dilute the stock with distilled water to make a range of known concentrations, for example 1%, 0.5%, 0.25%, 0.1% and 0% (distilled water only).

Worked dilutions: 5 cm³ of 1% stock plus 5 cm³ of water gives 0.5%, because the same amount of glucose is spread through twice the volume. 2.5 cm³ of stock plus 7.5 cm³ of water gives 0.25%, and 1 cm³ of stock plus 9 cm³ of water gives 0.1%.
3. Label each tube with its concentration. Any evenly spread range is acceptable; a serial dilution, halving the concentration each time, also works.
The Benedict's test needs a clear liquid, and every food must be prepared in the same way so that differences in colour reflect sugar content and not the preparation.
1. Weigh the same mass of each solid food, for example 5 g, on an electronic balance.
2. Crush it with a mortar and pestle in the same volume of distilled water, for example 50 cm³, so that the sugar dissolves out of the food.
3. Filter to give a clear extract, because solid pieces would cloud the tube and hide the colour.

4. Dilute liquid foods by the same factor, for example 1 cm³ of juice plus 9 cm³ of water, so that very sweet samples fall within the range of the standards. Record the dilution so the original concentration can be worked out.
All the standards and food extracts are now treated in exactly the same way, so the colours can be compared directly. The standards, once heated, form a colour scale that you match each food against.
1. Place 2 cm³ of each standard and 2 cm³ of each food extract in separate labelled test tubes.
2. Add 2 cm³ of Benedict's solution to every tube and mix.
3. Place all the tubes in the same hot water bath (near boiling, at least about 80 °C) at the same time, and heat them for exactly the same time, for example 5 minutes.
4. Remove all the tubes at the same time and place them in a rack in front of a white background, which makes the colours easier to judge.
5. Arrange the standards in order to form a colour scale. 6. Compare each food tube with the scale and record the standard it matches most closely, or the two it lies between.
7. Repeat the whole test three times for each food and use the most common or average result, because repeats show whether the result is reliable.
Do not tie an exact colour to each concentration, as the colour depends on the Benedict's volume and heating time.

Diagram: a row of test tubes of the standards after heating, labelled 0%, 0.1%, 0.25%, 0.5% and 1%, colours from blue at 0% through green, yellow and orange to brick red at the highest, and a food tube matched against them.
Judging colour by eye is a matter of opinion. A colorimeter replaces the eye with a measurement, so the result is a number that can be plotted and compared.
A colorimeter measures how much light of a chosen colour passes through a solution (transmission) or is absorbed by it (absorbance). It gives a number instead of a judgement by eye.

Method: after heating, let the precipitate settle, or filter or centrifuge (spin to separate solids) each tube, to leave the remaining blue solution. Zero the colorimeter with a cuvette (a small clear holder for the liquid) of distilled water.
Measure the absorbance of each standard's solution using a red filter, because blue solutions absorb red light.
The more reducing sugar that was present, the more copper(II) ions were used up. The remaining solution is paler blue, so its absorbance is lower and its transmission higher.

Plot a calibration curve (a graph of readings from known solutions): absorbance on the y-axis against known glucose concentration on the x-axis for the standards, with a line or smooth curve of best fit. The curve falls as concentration rises.
Measure the absorbance of each food extract and read its concentration from the curve, then multiply by any dilution factor to give the concentration in the original food.
Glucose test strips are a quick alternative that uses an enzyme instead of Benedict's solution. Because enzymes are specific, the strips behave differently from Benedict's.
A glucose test strip has a pad containing the enzymes glucose oxidase and peroxidase and a dye. When dipped in a solution, the pad changes colour according to the glucose concentration.
The colour is matched to a chart on the container that gives the concentration. Test the standards first to check the strips.

Limitation: the enzyme is specific to glucose, so strips detect glucose only, not other reducing sugars such as fructose, lactose or maltose. Milk, for example, gives a negative or low strip result but a positive Benedict's result, because its sugar is lactose.
Strips have a limited range, so samples may need diluting to bring them within the chart.
Technology and health link: similar strips and electronic glucose meters are used by people with diabetes to monitor their glucose. There is more on this in The Endocrine System.
This investigation uses Benedict's solution, which is harmful if swallowed or splashed in the eyes, along with near-boiling water and food in a lab, so each risk needs a specific precaution.
Wear safety glasses. Benedict's solution is harmful if swallowed or splashed in the eyes; wash splashes off with water.
Heat only in a water bath, never directly in a flame, because the mixture can boil suddenly and spurt. Use a test-tube holder, and take care with near-boiling water and hot tubes.
Do not eat or taste any food in the lab. Note allergies, and clean up spills: sugar solutions make benches sticky and floors slippery.
The results are primary data (measurements you collected yourself), and the conclusion must be built from them. Because the match is made by eye, the answer is a range, not an exact figure.

Record primary data in a table: food sample; colour after heating; matching standard, as an estimated percentage of reducing sugar; repeats; and, with a colorimeter, absorbance and the concentration read from the curve.
Expected pattern: honey and grape juice give orange to brick red, showing high reducing sugar, mostly glucose and fructose. Other fruit juices and sports drinks give yellow to orange.

Milk gives green to yellow, because of its lactose. The table-sugar solution and water stay blue, because sucrose is non-reducing. Actual results depend on the products used, so exact percentages are not given here.

Conclusion: rank the foods by reducing-sugar concentration, give each an estimated range, for example "between 0.25% and 0.5%", state whether the results support the hypothesis, and refer to the primary data.
This method is semi-quantitative: it estimates a range rather than an exact value, because matching colours by eye is a judgement. The colorimeter gives a more precise and objective value.
Every step above can introduce error. For each weakness, state the problem and the matching improvement, and repeating the test is the general safeguard.
Judging colour by eye is subjective. Improve it with a colorimeter, or by having several people judge independently.

Unequal heating, such as tubes put in or taken out at different times, or a water bath that cools, changes the colour. Heat all tubes together for the same time, and check the bath temperature with a thermometer.
If Benedict's is not in excess, all the copper(II) ions are used up and every concentrated sample looks brick red, so they cannot be told apart. Dilute the samples or use more Benedict's.
Coloured or cloudy food extracts affect the colour. Filter them and dilute coloured juices.
The precipitate settles over time, changing the appearance. Compare all the tubes at the same time after heating.
Inaccurate measuring of volumes and masses. Use graduated pipettes or syringes and an electronic balance.
Too few standards give a coarse scale. Use more standards spread over the range, and repeat each test at least three times to check repeatability.
A transfer molecule carries energy, or electrons and hydrogen, from the reaction that releases them to the reaction that uses them.
A transfer molecule is not used up: after handing on its load it returns to be recharged, like a rechargeable battery, so a cell needs only a small amount of each one, recycled continuously.
ATP is the main energy-transfer molecule in all living cells, from bacteria to humans, which is why it is called the energy currency of the cell: it is the common 'money' every reaction accepts.
Metabolism is all the chemical reactions in a cell. These reactions fall into two types, catabolic and anabolic.
Catabolic reactions break large molecules into smaller ones and release energy, e.g. respiration, which breaks down food such as glucose.
