Anabolic reactions build large molecules from smaller ones and need energy, e.g. protein synthesis and photosynthesis.

ATP links the two: catabolic reactions make ATP, and anabolic reactions and other cell work use it, so energy released in one place can be spent in another. There is more on this in Biomolecules and metabolism.
ATP is a small molecule with three parts, and its name tells you what they are. Knowing the parts matters because the exam asks you to name them and draw them.
ATP stands for adenosine triphosphate. It is made of three parts: the nitrogenous base adenine, the five-carbon sugar ribose, and a chain of three phosphate groups attached to the ribose.
Adenine joined to ribose is called adenosine; 'tri' means three phosphates. So adenosine triphosphate is adenosine with three phosphates attached.
ATP is a modified nucleotide, built to the same plan of base, sugar and phosphate as an RNA nucleotide (a building block of RNA). There is more on this in Nucleotides, DNA and RNA.
ADP (adenosine diphosphate) has only two phosphate groups, one fewer than ATP.
Pi (inorganic phosphate) is a single free phosphate group, not attached to any larger molecule.

Diagram: ATP drawn as a box labelled adenine, joined to a pentagon labelled ribose, joined to a chain of three circles labelled phosphate, with the bond to the third (end) phosphate marked as the one broken to release energy; a second sketch showing ADP + Pi.
A cell gets energy from ATP by removing its end phosphate. The reaction is simple, but its features explain why ATP is such a useful energy source.
Energy is released when the end phosphate is removed: ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pi + energy. So the products of ATP breakdown are ADP, Pi and energy.
The reaction uses water to split the molecule, so it is a hydrolysis reaction. It is catalysed (sped up) by an enzyme called ATPase.
The bond to the end phosphate is often called a high-energy bond: it is easily broken, and the reaction releases about 30 kJ per mole of ATP (30.5 kJ/mol) under standard conditions.
The energy is released in one quick step, in a small packet that suits a single reaction and is available right where the cell needs it.

Often the released phosphate is attached to another molecule, such as a carrier protein or a reactant (a molecule taking part in a reaction). This makes it more reactive or changes its shape so that it can do work.
ATP is not used up for good. Once its end phosphate has been removed, the cell puts a phosphate back on to ADP, which needs an input of energy.
ATP is remade by adding a phosphate group back on to ADP: ADP + Pi + energy → ATP + H₂O.
Adding phosphate is called phosphorylation. It is catalysed by enzymes, mainly ATP synthase, the enzyme that makes most of the cell's ATP.

In all living cells, the energy to make ATP comes from respiration, the breakdown of food such as glucose. Some ATP is made in the cytoplasm and most in the mitochondria. There is more on this in Respiration.
In plants and algae, ATP is also made in the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis in the chloroplasts, using light energy. This ATP is used inside the chloroplast to make glucose.
Breaking down ATP and remaking it are two halves of one loop. Because the loop runs all the time, a cell can keep spending energy without running out of ATP.
ATP is continuously broken down to ADP + Pi to release energy for cell work, and ADP + Pi are continuously rebuilt into ATP using energy from respiration (or light). This loop is the ATP/ADP cycle.
Cells hold only a small store of ATP at any time. Each molecule is recycled many times, so ATP must be made constantly while a cell is alive.
When respiration stops, for example after a long time without oxygen or in the presence of a poison that blocks respiration, ATP runs out within minutes and cell processes fail.

Diagram: the ATP/ADP cycle as a circle, with ATP at the top and ADP + Pi at the bottom; one arrow down labelled energy released for cell work: muscle contraction, active transport, synthesis; one arrow up labelled energy in from respiration (and light in photosynthesis).
Almost every energy-demanding job in a cell runs on ATP. The main uses are movement, moving substances across membranes and building molecules.

Muscle contraction: ATP provides the energy for protein filaments in muscle fibres to slide past each other, shortening the muscle. Very active muscle cells therefore contain many mitochondria, to make plenty of ATP.

Active transport: carrier proteins in the cell membrane use energy from ATP to pump substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration), e.g. root hair cells taking in mineral ions from dilute soil water.
The sodium–potassium pump in nerve cells uses ATP to restore the ion balance after an impulse. There is more on this in Transport Across Membranes.
Synthesis (anabolic reactions): ATP is needed to join amino acids into proteins at ribosomes, to make DNA when it is copied before cell division, and to make glycogen and starch from glucose.
The light-independent stage of photosynthesis uses ATP to build glucose from carbon dioxide.

Other uses: cell division (moving chromosomes), movement of cilia and flagella (hair-like and whip-like projections), and the light produced by fireflies (bioluminescence), where the enzyme luciferase uses ATP.
Glucose holds a lot of energy, yet cells do not run reactions straight from it. They first use its energy to make ATP, and this is the better arrangement for several reasons.
Breaking down one glucose molecule releases far more energy than any single reaction needs, and it does so over many steps.
ATP releases a small, manageable amount, matched to one reaction, in a single step, so less energy is wasted as heat.
ATP is available instantly where it is needed and is easily recycled. One type of molecule can supply energy to every kind of reaction in the cell.
ATP is a short-term energy carrier, not a store. Long-term energy is stored in starch (plants), glycogen (animals and fungi) and fats and oils, which respiration uses to make ATP when needed.
Fireflies make light using ATP, and this has been put to practical use. Because the light needs ATP, it can reveal whether living material is present.
Because every living cell contains ATP, hygiene tests in food factories and hospitals swab a surface and add luciferase, the firefly enzyme that gives off light when ATP is present.
Light given off shows that ATP is present, and therefore that living or recently living material, such as bacteria or food residue, is on the surface.

Cells need a way to move electrons and hydrogen from the reactions that release them to the reactions that need them. NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ do this job: they are electron carriers, transfer molecules that carry electrons and hydrogen between reactions.
NAD⁺ is nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide. NADP⁺ is nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate, which is the same molecule with one extra phosphate group.
Both are made in the body from niacin (vitamin B3), which is why niacin is needed in the diet. There is more on this in Vitamins.

Both pick up high-energy electrons, together with hydrogen, in one reaction and hand them on to another reaction, then return to pick up more. In this way they work like shuttle buses that run the same route again and again.
Gaining electrons is reduction and losing electrons is oxidation (OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain).
NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ are the oxidised forms, the empty carriers that have no electrons to give. NADH and NADPH are the reduced forms, the loaded carriers that have gained electrons.
A carrier is useful only if it can be filled, emptied and filled again. The electrons it carries also hold energy, and that energy is what the cell uses.
Loading: each carrier accepts two electrons and a proton (H⁺, a hydrogen ion): NAD⁺ + 2e⁻ + H⁺ → NADH, and NADP⁺ + 2e⁻ + H⁺ → NADPH.
In respiration, enzymes called dehydrogenases remove electrons and hydrogen from food molecules and pass them to NAD⁺, which is how the NAD⁺ gets loaded.
Unloading: NADH and NADPH give up their electrons and hydrogen to the next reaction and become NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ again. This means the same small supply is reused over and over, like ATP.
The electrons carry energy. When NADH's electrons pass along an electron transport chain (a series of proteins that pass electrons on), the energy released is used to make ATP.
When NADPH's electrons are added to carbon dioxide, they help build glucose. This reducing power (the ability to hand over electrons) is what makes the carriers useful.

Respiration is a catabolic pathway, meaning one that breaks glucose down to release energy. NAD⁺ is the carrier that collects the electrons released along the way and delivers them where ATP is made. There is more on this in Respiration.

NAD⁺ collects electrons and hydrogen released as glucose is broken down. This happens first in glycolysis in the cytoplasm, then in the Krebs (citric acid) cycle in the mitochondrial matrix (the fluid inside the mitochondrion). NAD⁺ becomes NADH.

NADH carries the electrons to the electron transport chain on the inner membrane of the mitochondrion. The energy released as the electrons pass along the chain is used to make most of the cell's ATP.

At the end of the chain, the electrons, with hydrogen ions, are passed to oxygen, the final electron acceptor (the last molecule to receive the electrons), which forms water. NAD⁺ is released to collect more electrons.

Without oxygen, the chain stops and NADH cannot unload there. In fermentation, NADH passes its hydrogen to pyruvate (the end product of glycolysis), forming lactic acid in animals and some bacteria, or ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast and plants.
This regenerates NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can continue making a little ATP, which is why fermentation keeps cells going when oxygen is absent.

Photosynthesis is an anabolic pathway, meaning one that builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water. NADP⁺ is the carrier that moves electrons and hydrogen from the light-capturing stage to the glucose-building stage. There is more on this in Photosynthesis.

In the light-dependent stage, on the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast (the flattened sacs inside it), light energises electrons in chlorophyll. These high-energy electrons pass along an electron transport chain to NADP⁺.
NADP⁺ also takes up protons (H⁺) from the photolysis of water (the splitting of water by light), which releases oxygen. NADP⁺ becomes NADPH.

NADPH carries the electrons and hydrogen to the light-independent stage in the stroma of the chloroplast (the fluid around the thylakoids). There they are added to carbon dioxide to make glucose, using energy from ATP.
NADP⁺ and ADP + Pi then return to the light-dependent stage to be loaded again, so none of them is used up.
NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ are very alike in structure but serve opposite kinds of pathway. Comparing them point by point shows how each fits its job.
Process: NAD⁺ works in respiration; NADP⁺ works in photosynthesis.
Type of pathway: NAD⁺ in a catabolic (breaking-down) pathway; NADP⁺ in an anabolic (building-up) pathway.

Where loaded: NAD⁺ in the cytoplasm and mitochondrial matrix, with electrons from glucose; NADP⁺ on the thylakoid membranes, with electrons from chlorophyll, which are replaced by electrons from water.

Where unloaded and final electron acceptor: NADH at the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane, with oxygen as the final acceptor, forming water; NADPH in the stroma, with carbon dioxide as the final acceptor, forming glucose.
Use of the electrons' energy: NADH's energy is used to make ATP; NADPH's energy is used to build glucose.
Structure: NADP⁺ has one extra phosphate group, which lets enzymes tell the two apart. This means the carriers for breaking down and for building up are kept separate.
ATP compared with both: ATP transfers energy, carried as a phosphate group, while NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ transfer electrons and hydrogen. All three are reused, not used up.

Diagram: two loops. Respiration: NAD⁺ → (electrons, hydrogen from glucose; glycolysis, Krebs cycle) → NADH → (electron transport chain, ATP made, electrons to oxygen) → NAD⁺. Photosynthesis: NADP⁺ → (electrons from chlorophyll, H⁺ from water; light-dependent) → NADPH → (light-independent, CO₂ to glucose) → NADP⁺.

Cells need a way to store instructions for building and running themselves. They use nucleic acids, long molecules made by joining many small units, and the unit that is repeated is the nucleotide. There are four kinds of nucleotide, which differ in their base.
Nucleic acids, DNA and RNA, are large molecules (polymers) built from many small units called nucleotides joined in a chain, much as beads are threaded on a string.
DNA is deoxyribonucleic acid; RNA is ribonucleic acid. Both contain the elements carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus.
Each nucleotide has three parts: a five-carbon (pentose) sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base (a nitrogen-containing molecule) attached to the sugar.
The sugar is deoxyribose in DNA and ribose in RNA. Deoxyribose has one fewer oxygen atom than ribose, which is where its name comes from: deoxy means an oxygen has been removed.
Each nucleic acid has four bases. DNA: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G). RNA: adenine (A), uracil (U), cytosine (C) and guanine (G); uracil takes the place of thymine.
Adenine and guanine are larger, double-ringed bases, called purines; cytosine, thymine and uracil are smaller, single-ringed bases, called pyrimidines.

A nucleotide is the building block of DNA and RNA, and its base is one letter of the genetic information. The order, or sequence, of bases along a strand carries the information, just as the order of letters makes a word.
Modified nucleotides also carry energy. There is more on this in ATP.
Diagram: one nucleotide drawn as a circle (phosphate) joined to a pentagon (sugar) joined to a rectangle (base), labelled phosphate, deoxyribose or ribose, and nitrogenous base.
One nucleotide holds one letter of information, so to store a whole message the cell must link many of them together. The way they link leaves a strong chain with the bases free to carry the code.
Nucleotides join by bonds between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next. These bonds are made in condensation reactions, in which a molecule of water is removed for each bond.
The repeating sugar–phosphate–sugar–phosphate chain is the sugar–phosphate backbone. The bonds within it are strong covalent bonds, not hydrogen bonds.

The bases stick out from the backbone, one per sugar. The backbone is the same in every DNA molecule; only the sequence of bases differs, so the bases carry the information and the backbone gives strength and support.
DNA is not one chain but two, held together in a regular pattern. This shape explains how DNA can store information and be copied accurately.
DNA is double-stranded: two strands of nucleotides lie side by side, with the sugar–phosphate backbones on the outside and the bases pointing inwards, like the rails and rungs of a ladder.
The bases pair up: adenine always pairs with thymine (A–T) and cytosine always pairs with guanine (C–G). These are complementary base pairs.
Each pair is one purine with one pyrimidine, so every rung is the same width and the ladder stays an even shape.
The bases in a pair are held together by hydrogen bonds (weak attractions between molecules): two between A and T, and three between C and G.
Each hydrogen bond is weak, so the strands can be separated, or unzipped, when DNA is copied or read. There are millions of hydrogen bonds, so the molecule as a whole is stable.
The two linked strands are twisted around each other into a spiral called a double helix, like a twisted ladder.
Because pairing is fixed, the two strands are complementary: the sequence of one strand decides the sequence of the other. For example, the strand ATGCCTAG pairs with TACGGATC.

Diagram: a short section of DNA drawn as a straight ladder of about four base pairs, labelled sugar (deoxyribose), phosphate, sugar–phosphate backbone, base pairs A–T and C–G, and hydrogen bonds; with a sketch of the twisted double helix.
Because A always pairs with T and C always pairs with G, the amounts of the bases in double-stranded DNA are linked. This lets you work out the percentage of every base from just one.
In double-stranded DNA the amount of A equals the amount of T, and the amount of C equals the amount of G, because every A is paired with a T and every C with a G.
For example, if 20% of the bases in a DNA sample are adenine, then 20% are thymine. That leaves 60% shared equally between cytosine and guanine, so each is 30%.
The order of bases in DNA is the cell's set of instructions. DNA is kept in different places in different kinds of cell.
DNA stores the genetic information (genes) that controls the cell's activities by coding for proteins. There is more on genes and proteins in Genes, proteins and traits.
DNA is copied before a cell divides, so each new cell receives the full set of information, which means that it is passed from parents to offspring.
In eukaryotic cells (cells with a nucleus), DNA is found mostly in the nucleus, in the chromosomes, with small amounts in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
In bacteria, DNA forms a loop in the cytoplasm and is also found in small rings called plasmids.
The structure of DNA was worked out by combining physical evidence with model building. It is a good example of how scientists build on each other's data.

The double-helix model was published by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953. It was based on X-ray diffraction images of DNA (patterns made when X-rays pass through DNA, which reveal its shape) made by Rosalind Franklin, working with Maurice Wilkins.
DNA stays safe in the nucleus, so the cell needs a working copy of its instructions to take out and use. That working copy is RNA, a similar molecule with a few key differences.
RNA is usually single-stranded: one chain of nucleotides with its own sugar–phosphate backbone. RNA molecules are much shorter than DNA molecules.
RNA nucleotides contain ribose instead of deoxyribose, and uracil instead of thymine. Uracil pairs with adenine (A–U) whenever RNA pairs with DNA or with another RNA.
A single strand can fold back on itself where its bases pair up, giving some RNA molecules a fixed shape.
RNA uses the information in DNA to make proteins, so it acts as the go-between for DNA and the protein-making machinery.
Three main types of RNA are named here, with no more detail. Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries a copy of a gene from the nucleus to a ribosome (the structure that makes proteins).
Transfer RNA (tRNA) brings amino acids to the ribosome; ribosomal RNA (rRNA) forms part of the ribosome. There is more on this in DNA Replication, Protein Synthesis and Mutations.
RNA is made in the nucleus and works in the cytoplasm, so it carries information out to where proteins are made. It is found in the nucleus (including the nucleolus), the cytoplasm and the ribosomes.
Diagram: a short single RNA strand of about four nucleotides, labelled ribose, phosphate, backbone and bases, including uracil.
Put side by side, DNA and RNA differ in structure, stability and job. The differences fit their roles: DNA is a long-term store and RNA is a short-lived working copy.
Strands: DNA is a double-stranded helix, which suits long-term storage; RNA is usually single-stranded.
Sugar: DNA contains deoxyribose; RNA contains ribose.
Bases: DNA has A, T, C and G; RNA has A, U, C and G, with uracil instead of thymine.
Pairing: A–T in DNA; A–U in RNA.
Size and life span: DNA is very long and stable and is kept for the life of the cell; RNA molecules are shorter and are broken down after use, so each copy is only a temporary message.
Location: DNA is mainly in the nucleus, with some in mitochondria and chloroplasts; RNA is in the nucleus, the cytoplasm and the ribosomes.
Function: DNA stores the genetic information; RNA carries and uses that information to make proteins.

Three words link what is written in DNA to what an organism looks like and does: gene, protein and trait. Getting each one clear is the first step, because exam answers lose marks when they are mixed up.

A gene is a section of DNA that contains the instructions, or code, for making a particular protein (strictly, a polypeptide, which is a chain of amino acids). A gene is not itself a protein: it is the recipe for one.
Genes are carried on chromosomes (the long DNA molecules in the nucleus), and each chromosome holds many genes, so one chromosome carries the instructions for many different proteins.
A protein is a chain of amino acids folded into a particular shape. About 20 different amino acids are used to make proteins, and different orders of them give different proteins.

A trait is an inherited characteristic of an organism, such as eye colour, blood group, seed shape in peas, or whether a person can make a particular enzyme. The trait is not the protein: it is the visible or measurable result of what the protein does.
A gene's code is turned into a working protein in a fixed chain of events. The order of the code decides the protein's shape, and the shape decides what the protein can do.

The sequence of bases in a gene (the order of the chemical letters along the DNA) determines the sequence of amino acids in the protein it codes for. Change the order of the bases and the order of amino acids can change.
The sequence of amino acids determines how the chain folds, and so the protein's three-dimensional shape. This is why every protein folds into its own shape rather than a random tangle.

The shape determines the protein's function, because other molecules can only fit or bind to the right shape. Examples are the active site of an enzyme (the pocket where the reaction happens) and the binding site of a receptor (the spot that a signal molecule attaches to).

The cell's machinery reads the gene. The code is copied into a messenger molecule, mRNA, which travels from the nucleus to a ribosome (a tiny structure that builds proteins), where the amino acids are joined in the correct order.
Information therefore flows in one direction: DNA (gene) → mRNA → protein → trait. There is more on how the copying and joining work in DNA Replication, Protein Synthesis and Mutations.

Proteins are the link between a gene and a trait because they do most of the work in cells and build much of their structure. Different versions of a gene can therefore give different versions of a trait, and different cells use different genes.
Enzymes (proteins that speed up reactions) control the chemical reactions that make substances such as pigments. If the enzyme is missing or faulty, the substance is not made and the trait changes.
Structural proteins build hair, skin, muscle and connective tissue, for example keratin (hair, nails, skin) and collagen (connective tissue, skin, tendons).
Transport and channel proteins move substances, for example across membranes or around the body. Hormones such as insulin, and receptor proteins, carry signals between cells.

Different versions of a gene, called alleles, have slightly different base sequences. They can give a protein with a different amino acid sequence, a different shape, or no working protein at all, which produces a different version of the trait.

Every body cell contains the same genes, but each cell type uses, or expresses, only some of them. For example, the insulin gene is used to make insulin only in cells of the pancreas, and haemoglobin is made only in developing red blood cells.
Four examples show the whole chain in action, each as gene → protein → trait. In each one, a change to the protein changes the trait that you can see.

Albinism (one form): the gene for the enzyme tyrosinase → tyrosinase is needed to make the dark pigment melanin → people with two non-working copies make little or no melanin, so they have very pale skin, white or very fair hair and light-sensitive eyes.
In albinism the gene codes for the enzyme, not for the pigment: the pigment (melanin) is not a protein, and it is missing only because the enzyme that makes it does not work.

Cystic fibrosis: the CFTR gene → the CFTR protein, a channel in cell membranes that lets chloride ions out of cells → a faulty channel causes thick, sticky mucus in the lungs and pancreas, leading to lung infections and poor digestion.

Haemoglobin: the haemoglobin genes → haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen → normal oxygen transport. There is more on how the change arises in DNA Replication, Protein Synthesis and Mutations.
A changed form of one of the haemoglobin genes gives sickle-cell haemoglobin, which makes red blood cells sickle-shaped when oxygen is low. This causes sickle-cell anaemia.
Seed shape in peas (Mendel's trait): the gene for starch-branching enzyme → the enzyme helps convert sugar into starch in the developing seed → seeds with a working copy are round.
Seeds with two non-working copies (rr) make less starch and keep more sugar. They take up more water while developing, and so wrinkle as they dry out.
Diagram: DNA (gene) → mRNA → protein (amino acid chain folded into a shape) → trait, with the albinism example written under it.
The chain from gene to protein to trait is a useful model, but real traits are often more complicated. Genes are not the only thing that shapes an organism.
Many traits are controlled by several genes acting together, such as height and skin colour in humans, so there is no single gene for a trait. Each gene adds a small part of the final result.
The environment also affects many traits. A person's height depends on diet as well as genes, and a plant's height depends on light and nutrients.
The trait, or phenotype (what the organism is actually like), results from genes and environment together. This is why two organisms with the same genes can still look different.

A gene is a stretch of DNA, but a cell needs proteins, which are chains of amino acids. The genetic code is the translation key between the two, and the cell's machinery reads it to build each protein.
The genetic code is the set of rules by which the sequence of bases in DNA, copied into mRNA (messenger RNA, the working copy of a gene), is converted into the sequence of amino acids in a protein.

The code is read in groups of three bases. A codon is a sequence of three bases on mRNA that codes for one amino acid or for a stop signal. The matching three bases on DNA are called a triplet here, although some textbooks also call these codons.
Why three: there are 4 bases but about 20 amino acids. Reading one base at a time gives only 4 combinations, and two at a time gives only 16 (4 × 4), which is not enough.
Three bases at a time gives 64 combinations (4 × 4 × 4), which is more than enough to code for about 20 amino acids.
Of the 64 codons, 61 code for amino acids and 3 are stop codons, which code for no amino acid and end the message.

The code is read by cellular machinery: the mRNA is read at a ribosome (the cell's protein-making structure) one codon at a time. Transfer RNA molecules bring the matching amino acids, which are joined in order. There is more on this in DNA Replication, Protein Synthesis and Mutations.
The code has a set of features that exams ask you to name and explain. Each one tells you something about how a cell reads a gene, or what happens when a base changes.

Start codon: AUG is the usual signal to start reading a gene's message. It sets where the groups of three begin, and it also codes for the amino acid methionine, so most new proteins begin with methionine.
Stop codons: UAA, UAG and UGA code for no amino acid. They signal the end of the protein, and the finished chain is released.

Non-overlapping and without gaps: the code is read three bases at a time from the start codon, each base belonging to only one codon, with no separators (like commas) between codons. Adding or removing a single base therefore shifts every codon after it, a frameshift mutation.
Degenerate, or redundant: most amino acids have more than one codon, because 61 codons code for only 20 amino acids. Glycine, for example, is coded by GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG.
Often only the third base differs between codons for the same amino acid, so some changes in a base still give the same amino acid and the protein is unchanged.
Specific, or unambiguous: each codon codes for only one amino acid. Degenerate means one amino acid can have several codons, but never the reverse, so the message is read the same way every time.

Universal: almost all living things, from bacteria to plants and humans, use the same code, with a few minor exceptions. In mitochondria, for example, UGA codes for tryptophan in humans instead of acting as a stop signal.

The shared code is evidence that all life shares a common ancestor. It also allows a human gene to be put into bacteria and read correctly, so that genetically modified bacteria make human insulin. There is more on this in Genetic Engineering.
A codon on mRNA does nothing by itself. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules act as adaptors, each reading one codon and delivering the amino acid it codes for.
An anticodon is a sequence of three bases on a transfer RNA (tRNA) molecule that is complementary to an mRNA codon. Codons are on mRNA and anticodons are on tRNA, never on DNA.
Each tRNA carries one specific amino acid, matching its anticodon. The anticodon pairs with the codon by complementary base pairing (A–U and C–G), so the right amino acid is brought for each codon.
For example, the codon AUG pairs with the anticodon UAC, and that tRNA carries methionine.
No tRNA has an anticodon for a stop codon, so when a stop codon is reached no amino acid is added and the chain ends.

Diagram: a short strip of mRNA divided into codons, for example AUG | CCU | AAA, with tRNA below, each anticodon paired to a codon and its amino acid attached at the other end. Draw tRNA simply, as a block or T-shape. Labels: codon, anticodon, mRNA, tRNA, amino acid.
Exam questions give you a DNA or mRNA sequence and a codon table, and ask for the mRNA, the amino acids and the anticodons. Follow the same steps every time and the answer falls out.
Method: 1. Write the mRNA complementary to the DNA strand being read (A → U, T → A, C → G, G → C).
2. Split the mRNA into codons, starting from the start codon.
3. Find each amino acid in the codon table given in the question.
4. Stop at a stop codon, because no amino acid is added after it. 5. The anticodons are complementary to the codons.
Only AUG and the three stop codons need to be memorised; the other codons come from the codon table given in the question.

Worked example: the DNA strand being read is TAC GGA TTT ACT. The mRNA is AUG CCU AAA UGA, which codes for methionine, proline and lysine, then stops. The tRNA anticodons are UAC, GGA and UUU, with none for UGA.
Notice the anticodons have the same sequence as the DNA strand being read, with U in place of T.

Counting: each amino acid needs one codon of three bases, so a protein of 100 amino acids needs at least 300 bases of coding mRNA, plus three for the stop codon, giving 303. A stretch of 90 coding bases codes for 30 amino acids.

A chromosome is DNA together with protein, and it carries genes in a fixed linear order. Knowing what it is made of, how it looks in a resting and a dividing cell, and how big it is explains why cells need to pack their DNA.

A chromosome is a single, very long molecule of DNA together with proteins. It is found in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell (a cell with a nucleus) and carries many genes in a fixed linear order along its length.

Chromatin is the name for the DNA and protein material of the chromosomes when the cell is not dividing. The chromosomes are then long, thin and uncoiled, spread through the nucleus, so they cannot be seen as separate threads.

Before a cell divides, the chromatin coils and folds up tightly (condenses), so each chromosome becomes short and thick and is visible under the light microscope when stained. In other words, chromatin and chromosomes are the same material in two states.

Human body cells are diploid (two sets of chromosomes), with 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes (chromosomes that are not sex chromosomes) and one pair of sex chromosomes, XX in females and XY in males. There is more on this in Sex determination.

Homologous chromosomes are the two chromosomes of a pair. They are the same length, have the centromere (the narrowed region of the chromosome) in the same position and carry the same genes at the same positions, with one chromosome of each pair coming from each parent.
The chromosome number is fixed for a species (46 in humans); a different number does not mean a more complex organism, so you cannot judge complexity by counting chromosomes.

The human genome (all the DNA in one set of 23 chromosomes) is about 3 billion base pairs. The DNA in one human body cell, stretched out, would be about 2 m long, yet it fits in a nucleus a few micrometres across, which is why DNA must be packed.
Prokaryotes (bacteria) differ: a bacterial cell has one circular chromosome in the cytoplasm, not wound around histones (the packing proteins of eukaryotes), plus plasmids (small extra rings of DNA).
Histones are the proteins that pack eukaryotic DNA into a small space. Without them, about 2 m of DNA per cell could not fit in the nucleus or be moved safely when the cell divides.

Histones are small proteins around which the DNA of a eukaryotic chromosome is wound. They are positively charged, while the phosphate groups of the DNA backbone are negatively charged, so DNA binds tightly to them.
The DNA wraps nearly twice around a core of eight histone proteins, forming a bead called a nucleosome. Nucleosomes are joined by short stretches of linker DNA, like beads on a string.
The string of nucleosomes coils and loops further, and before division it condenses into the visible chromosome.
Histones do three jobs: they pack a very long DNA molecule into a small nucleus, they protect the DNA and keep it untangled during division, and they help control which genes can be read.
DNA wound tightly around histones cannot be reached by the enzymes that read genes, so those genes are switched off; loosely packed regions are active, which means their genes can be read.
Chemical changes to histones are one of the epigenetic mechanisms (ways of switching genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence). There is more on this in Genetic and epigenetic mechanisms.
Diagram: DNA double helix wound around histone cores to form nucleosomes, then the coiled chromatin fibre, then a condensed chromosome; label DNA, histone, nucleosome, chromatin and chromosome.
Before a cell divides it copies its DNA, so each chromosome ends up as two joined copies. Chromatids and the centromere are the names for those copies and for the point that holds them together.

Before a cell divides, each chromosome's DNA is copied, a process called replication. The two identical copies stay joined together; each copy is a chromatid. There is more on this in DNA replication and mitosis in the cell cycle.
A replicated chromosome therefore consists of two identical sister chromatids, each containing one complete DNA molecule with the same genes and the same alleles (versions of a gene).

The centromere is the constricted (narrowed) region of a chromosome where the two sister chromatids are held together. Spindle fibres (protein threads that move chromosomes in division) attach at the centromere and pull the chromatids apart to opposite poles of the cell.
Once separated, each chromatid is a chromosome in its own right.

The centromere is in a fixed position for each chromosome, dividing it into two arms of equal or different length, so it is not always in the middle. Its position, together with length and banding pattern, is used to identify each chromosome.

Before replication, a chromosome is one DNA molecule and one chromatid. After replication it is still one chromosome but has two chromatids, the X shape usually drawn; the two arms of the X are chromatids, not separate chromosomes.
Homologous chromosomes (a pair, one from each parent) may carry different alleles, whereas sister chromatids are identical copies of each other, so they always carry identical alleles.

Diagram: an unreplicated chromosome (single rod) beside a replicated chromosome (X shape); label chromatid, sister chromatids, centromere, arm, and a gene locus marked as a band at the same position on both chromatids. Optionally add a homologous pair of replicated chromosomes, same locus marked on each, labelled homologous chromosomes.

A gene is the unit of heredity, the piece of information that is passed on from cell to cell and parent to offspring. Genes sit at fixed places on chromosomes and, through the proteins they code for, control traits.
A gene is a section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a protein. This means a chromosome is not simply a string of genes: genes are sections of its DNA.
Each gene has a fixed position on a particular chromosome, called its locus (plural loci). The locus of a gene is the same in every member of a species.

A gene carries the information to make one protein, although some genes code instead for RNA molecules that are used directly, such as ribosomal RNA and transfer RNA. So not every gene codes for a protein.
Through the protein it codes for, a gene controls a trait (a characteristic of the organism). The gene is copied and passed to daughter cells in division and to offspring in gametes (sex cells).
Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes spread across the 23 kinds of chromosome; each chromosome carries hundreds to thousands of genes.

Because homologous chromosomes carry the same genes, a body cell has two copies of each autosomal gene. These may be the same or different versions, called alleles. There is more on this in Key concepts of information transfer.
Most of the DNA in a human cell does not code for protein. Separating the small coding part from the large non-coding part shows that a chromosome is far more than a list of protein recipes.
Coding DNA is DNA whose base sequence is used to make a protein: the protein-coding parts of genes. Only about 1–2% of human DNA is coding DNA.
Non-coding DNA is all DNA that does not code for protein, about 98% of the human genome. It includes several kinds of sequence, listed in the next points.
Regulatory sequences beside genes act as switches, controlling when, where and how much a gene is expressed (used to make its product).
Genes for functional RNA (rRNA and tRNA) are non-coding DNA, as are introns, the non-coding sections within genes, which are copied into mRNA but removed before it is used to make protein.

Repeated sequences, such as the DNA at centromeres and at the ends of chromosomes (telomeres), protect the chromosome and help it divide correctly. Some non-coding DNA has a function that is still unknown.
Non-coding DNA was once called 'junk DNA', but much of it is now known to have functions, especially in regulating genes. Changes in regulatory DNA can change a trait without changing any protein.
Repeated non-coding sequences vary greatly in length between people, which is why they are used in DNA profiling (identifying individuals from their DNA).

Diagram: a stretch of a chromosome's DNA drawn as a line, with two genes shown as boxes (each with a regulatory region at one end and coding sections separated by an intron), and the DNA between genes labelled non-coding; label gene, coding DNA, non-coding DNA, regulatory sequence and intron.
Inheritance starts with a few basic ideas: what counts as one kind of organism, what is passed on, and what carries it. These terms are used throughout genetics.

A species is a group of organisms with similar features that can interbreed in natural conditions to produce fertile offspring (offspring that can themselves reproduce). A horse and a donkey can mate, but their offspring, the mule, is sterile, so horses and donkeys are different species.

The species definition has limits: it cannot be applied to organisms that reproduce only asexually, because they never interbreed, or to fossils, because dead organisms cannot be tested for interbreeding. There is more on how new species form in Evidence for evolution.

Heredity is the passing of characteristics (traits), by means of genes, from parents to offspring, that is, from one generation to the next. A gene is a section of DNA that carries the instructions for a trait.
Genetics is the study of heredity (how traits are passed on) and of variation (the differences between individuals).

A chromosome is the structure that carries genes from one generation to the next. Body cells carry chromosomes in homologous pairs (two matching chromosomes, one from each parent), and each gamete carries one chromosome from each pair.
Parents pass genes on through special sex cells. Following the chromosome number from parent to gametes to zygote shows how each generation gets its genes and why the number stays constant.
A gamete is a sex cell: a sperm or egg in animals, or in flowering plants the male gamete nucleus in the pollen grain and the egg cell in the ovule.

Gametes are haploid, with one set of chromosomes (one from each pair), so a human gamete has 23 chromosomes. They are made by meiosis. Gametes must be haploid because fertilisation adds the two sets together, so otherwise the chromosome number would double every generation.

Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of two gametes, usually from two parents. The offspring receive half their chromosomes from each parent, so they are genetically different from both parents and from each other. There is more on this in Variation.
Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no gametes, so it produces genetically identical offspring, called clones.

Fertilisation is the fusion of the nucleus of a male gamete with the nucleus of a female gamete to form a diploid zygote (a cell with two sets of chromosomes), the first cell of the new organism. It restores the diploid number: in humans 23 + 23 = 46 chromosomes.
The zygote divides by mitosis, so every body cell carries the same set of chromosomes.

Diagram: life-cycle flow: parent (2n = 46) → meiosis → gametes (n = 23, sperm and egg) → fertilisation → zygote (2n = 46) → mitosis → offspring; label haploid, diploid, meiosis, fertilisation and mitosis.
A gene is a section of DNA for one trait, such as seed shape. Genes come in slightly different versions, and these versions, called alleles, are what make individuals differ.

An allele is one of the alternative forms of a gene, found at the same locus (position) on homologous chromosomes. Alleles differ slightly in base sequence, as they arise by mutation, so they may produce different versions of the trait.
In peas, the gene for seed shape has an allele for round seeds (R) and one for wrinkled seeds (r).
A diploid organism has two alleles for each autosomal gene (a gene on a non-sex chromosome), one on each homologous chromosome, one inherited from each parent.

A population may have more than two alleles of a gene, but each individual carries only two, because it has only two homologous chromosomes. The human ABO blood-group gene has three alleles (A, B and O) in the population.
Homozygous means having two identical alleles of a gene (RR or rr). A homozygous organism is also called pure-breeding, because it passes on the same allele in every gamete.
Heterozygous means having two different alleles of a gene (Rr). A heterozygous organism is also called a hybrid for that gene.

Diagram: a pair of homologous chromosomes with one gene locus marked, one chromosome carrying R and the other r (heterozygous); a second pair carrying r and r (homozygous); label homologous chromosomes, locus and allele.
Two terms separate what an organism's genes are from what it looks like or does. They are not always the same, because the environment and dominance both play a part.
Genotype is the genetic make-up of an organism: the alleles it has for a particular trait, written with letters, such as RR, Rr or rr.
Phenotype is the observable (physical, chemical or behavioural) characteristics of an organism that result from its genotype, such as round or wrinkled seeds, or blood group A.
Phenotype = genotype + environment. The genotype sets the possible range, and the environment affects how it is expressed.
Identical twins have the same genotype but may differ in mass because of diet and exercise, so the same genes can give different phenotypes.
Hydrangea plants of the same variety have blue flowers in acid soil and pink flowers in alkaline soil, so soil pH changes the phenotype.
A plant with the genes for chlorophyll is pale yellow if grown in the dark, because the environment (no light) stops the pigment forming.

Different genotypes can give the same phenotype: RR and Rr are both round, because one allele is dominant. So the phenotype does not always reveal the genotype. There is more on how to find the genotype (the test cross) in Monohybrid crosses.
When an organism is heterozygous, the two alleles do not always show equally. Dominant and recessive describe which allele is seen in the phenotype and which is hidden.
A dominant allele is expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote, masking the effect of the other allele. It is written with a capital letter (R), and a dominant trait shows in both RR and Rr.
A recessive allele is expressed in the phenotype only when no dominant allele is present, that is, only in the homozygous condition (rr). It is written with the lower-case letter (r).
In a heterozygote, a recessive allele is present but hidden, and it can still be passed on to offspring. It does not disappear and is not weaker.
Often the dominant allele codes for a working protein and the recessive allele for a non-working one. One working copy makes enough protein, so Rr looks the same as RR.
In peas, R codes for a working starch-branching enzyme; rr seeds make less starch and wrinkle. There is more on this chain in Genes, proteins and traits.
Dominant does not mean common or better. The allele causing Huntington's disease is dominant but rare, and harmful.
Cystic fibrosis and albinism are caused by recessive alleles, so two carriers (heterozygotes) can have an affected child.
A carrier is a heterozygous individual who carries a recessive allele for a condition but does not show it.
Having a gene is not the same as using it. Gene expression is how a cell turns the information in a gene into something that affects the organism.
Gene expression is the process by which the information in a gene is used to make its product (a protein or a functional RNA), so that the gene affects the phenotype.
A gene that is being used is switched on (expressed); one that is not is switched off.
Every body cell has the same genes, but each cell type expresses only some of them, which is why cells become specialised.

Expression is controlled by regulatory DNA (stretches of DNA that switch genes on or off), by signals such as hormones, and by the environment: some genes are switched on only in response to a stimulus.
There is more on how the environment and behaviour change expression in Genetic and epigenetic mechanisms.
Four more terms extend the basic vocabulary. Each has a short definition and, where there is one, a named example.

Epigenetic expression is a change in gene expression that is not caused by a change in the DNA base sequence, but by chemical tags on the DNA or on the histones (the proteins DNA is wound around) that switch genes on or off.
Epigenetic tags can be caused by the environment and behaviour, can be passed on when cells divide, and some are reversible.

Incomplete dominance means neither allele is dominant over the other, so the heterozygote has a phenotype intermediate between the two homozygotes. For example, red-flowered and white-flowered snapdragons give pink-flowered heterozygotes. This contrasts with complete dominance, where the heterozygote looks like the dominant homozygote.
Linkage: genes located on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, because they do not separate into different gametes. Linked genes do not assort independently.

Sex-linkage: a gene located on a sex chromosome (in humans almost always the X chromosome) is sex-linked, so the trait's inheritance pattern differs between males and females. Examples are red–green colour blindness and haemophilia, which are much more common in males.

Most of your genes sit on the chromosomes inside the nucleus of each cell, and nuclear inheritance is how those genes pass from parents to offspring. It follows a tidy, predictable route from the parent's nucleus to the child's.
Nuclear inheritance is the inheritance of genes carried on the chromosomes in the nucleus. Nearly all of an organism's genes are nuclear; in humans, about 20,000 protein-coding genes.
1. The DNA in the nucleus is copied before division, so each new cell can receive a full set of genetic information.

2. Meiosis (the division that makes gametes, the sex cells) separates each homologous pair (the two matching chromosomes, one from each parent). Each gamete therefore receives one chromosome of every pair, and so one allele (version) of each gene.
3. At fertilisation the nuclei of a male and a female gamete fuse, so the zygote (the first cell of the new individual) receives one set of chromosomes from each parent.
4. Mitosis (ordinary cell division) then passes the full set of chromosomes to every body cell as the zygote grows.

Both parents contribute equally: the offspring inherits one allele of each autosomal gene (a gene on a non-sex chromosome) from its mother and one from its father. So for nuclear genes it does not matter which parent carries an allele.
For example, a tall male crossed with a short female gives the same results as a short male crossed with a tall female (reciprocal crosses). The exception is genes on the sex chromosomes.

Each gamete gets only one allele of each pair, chosen at random, so nuclear genes are inherited in the predictable ratios described by Mendel's laws, and new combinations of alleles arise in every generation. There is more on this in Monohybrid crosses.
The nucleus is not the only place in a cell that holds DNA. Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry a little of their own, and genes in this DNA are inherited by a different route from nuclear genes.

Non-nuclear (also called extranuclear or cytoplasmic) inheritance is the inheritance of genes carried in DNA outside the nucleus. This DNA is in mitochondria, which are found in all eukaryotes, and in chloroplasts, which are found in plants and algae only.

Each mitochondrion and chloroplast contains several copies of its own small, circular DNA molecule, like the DNA of a bacterium. It is not wound around histones (the proteins that nuclear DNA is wrapped around). Each organelle also has its own small (70S) ribosomes.
A cell contains many such organelles, so it has hundreds to thousands of copies of the organelle DNA, compared with two copies of each nuclear gene.

Organelle genes code for some of the proteins the organelle needs: for mitochondria, some proteins of aerobic respiration (releasing energy from food using oxygen); for chloroplasts, some proteins of photosynthesis. They also code for the organelle's own rRNA and tRNA (the RNA parts of its ribosomes and protein-making machinery).
Most proteins in these organelles are coded by nuclear genes and imported, so the organelle depends on both its own genes and the nuclear genes.

Mitochondria and chloroplasts are thought to be descended from bacteria that came to live inside an ancestral cell, which is why they have their own DNA. Evidence includes their circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, double membrane and division by splitting in two.

New mitochondria and chloroplasts come only from the division of existing ones; the cell does not make them from scratch. This is why the organelle DNA is passed on only along with the cytoplasm that holds the organelles.

Chromosomes are moved around by a precise mechanism, but organelles are not. This difference, together with the way the egg and sperm differ in size, explains why non-nuclear genes usually come from the mother only.

Organelles lie in the cytoplasm (the cell contents outside the nucleus), and they are shared out between daughter cells at random when the cytoplasm divides, not by the spindle (the fibres that pull chromosomes apart) as chromosomes are.
Their genes therefore do not segregate (separate into different gametes) in meiosis, and do not follow Mendel's laws or Mendelian ratios.

In humans and most animals, the egg contributes nearly all the cytoplasm of the zygote, including its mitochondria. The sperm contributes almost only its nucleus; the few sperm mitochondria, in its midpiece, that enter the egg are destroyed.
So mitochondrial genes are inherited from the mother only. In most flowering plants, chloroplasts (and mitochondria) are likewise inherited through the egg cell, from the female parent.
Consequence 1: all the offspring of a mother share her mitochondrial DNA, whatever the father.
Consequence 2: reciprocal crosses give different results, with the offspring resembling the female parent for the trait, unlike nuclear genes where reciprocal crosses give the same results.
Consequence 3: mitochondrial DNA does not mix between two parents, so it changes only by mutation and passes down the female line almost unchanged.
An early experiment on plants showed non-nuclear inheritance in action. It is a worked example of offspring copying the female parent rather than following Mendel's ratios.

In 1909 Carl Correns studied the four-o'clock plant (Mirabilis jalapa), which has branches bearing green, white or variegated (green-and-white) leaves. The white areas lack working chloroplasts, so they cannot photosynthesise.
Seeds from flowers on green branches gave green seedlings, and seeds from flowers on white branches gave white seedlings, which soon died.
Seeds from variegated branches gave a mixture of seedlings, whatever branch the pollen came from.

The offspring took the leaf type of the female parent. Leaf colour was inherited through the chloroplasts in the egg's cytoplasm, which made this one of the first demonstrations of non-nuclear inheritance.
Human mitochondrial DNA is tiny, but because of maternal inheritance it has medical and scientific uses. Faults in it cause disease, and its unmixed female line makes it a useful record.

Human mitochondrial DNA is about 16,600 base pairs long and carries 37 genes. By comparison, there are about 20,000 protein-coding genes on nuclear chromosomes of up to hundreds of millions of base pairs each.

Mutations in mitochondrial DNA can cause diseases that mostly affect tissues with high energy demands, such as muscle, nerves, brain and eyes, because they reduce aerobic respiration, the process that supplies those tissues' energy. Example: Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), which causes loss of central vision, usually in young adults.

An affected mother can pass a mitochondrial disease to all her children, sons and daughters, because every child gets its mitochondria from her egg. An affected father passes it to none, because his mitochondria are not passed on. Sons inherit their mother's mitochondria too, but only daughters pass them on.
Severity varies: a cell may contain a mixture of normal and mutant mitochondria, and the proportion passed to each egg varies, so children of the same mother can be affected to different degrees.

Mitochondrial donation (“three-parent IVF”) replaces a mother's faulty mitochondria with healthy mitochondria from a donor egg, keeping the nuclear DNA of both parents. In 2015 the UK became the first country to allow it by law.
In mitochondrial donation the child's nuclear DNA comes from its two parents and its small amount of mitochondrial DNA from the donor. There is more on the ethics in Ethics of genetic technologies.
Because mitochondrial DNA passes down the female line without mixing and changes only by mutation, it is used to trace maternal ancestry and human migration and evolution.
It is also used to identify remains when nuclear DNA is too damaged, since there are many copies per cell and it survives better.

Putting the two systems side by side shows how a difference in where the DNA is kept leads to differences in how it is passed on. Each point below pairs nuclear inheritance with non-nuclear inheritance.
Location: nuclear DNA is in chromosomes in the nucleus; non-nuclear DNA is in mitochondria and chloroplasts in the cytoplasm.
Form: nuclear DNA is long, linear molecules wound around histones; non-nuclear DNA is small, circular molecules without histones.
Amount: most of the genes are nuclear (about 20,000 protein-coding genes in humans); few are non-nuclear (37 in human mitochondria), coding mainly for the organelle's own proteins and RNA.
Copies: two copies of each autosomal gene in a diploid cell (one with two sets of chromosomes); hundreds to thousands of copies of organelle DNA per cell.
Parents contributing: both parents equally for nuclear genes; usually the mother only for non-nuclear genes (maternal inheritance).
Distribution to gametes and daughter cells: chromosomes are separated precisely by the spindle in meiosis and mitosis; organelles are shared out randomly when the cytoplasm divides.

Patterns: nuclear inheritance follows Mendel's laws with predictable ratios, and reciprocal crosses give the same results; non-nuclear inheritance gives no Mendelian ratios, and reciprocal crosses give different results.
Variation between generations: nuclear inheritance gives new combinations of alleles from both parents each generation; non-nuclear DNA does not mix, and changes only by mutation.
Despite their differences, the two kinds of DNA are the same kind of molecule working in the same way. A comparison answer should say what they share as well as how they differ.
Both are DNA, using the same genetic code (with minor differences in mitochondria) and the same base pairing, so the same rules read and copy them.
Both are copied before cell division, so that each daughter cell or organelle receives genetic information.
Both can mutate and so cause inherited disease, such as LHON for mitochondrial DNA.

Diagram: sperm and egg fusing. Egg large, nucleus plus many mitochondria in cytoplasm; sperm nucleus in head, few mitochondria in midpiece. Arrows: nuclear DNA from both parents, mitochondria from egg only. Labels: nucleus (nuclear DNA, both parents), mitochondria (mitochondrial DNA, mother).

Genetic inheritance is the passing of instructions from one generation to the next, and it works by passing on DNA itself. Here is how that information is stored, copied and changed, and where it falls short of explaining everything.

Genetic inheritance works by passing on DNA: the sequence of bases (the letters A, T, C and G) in the genes is copied when cells divide and passed to offspring in the gametes (sex cells). There is more on this in Nuclear and non-nuclear inheritance.
The information is stored in the base sequence itself. DNA is copied very accurately, so the information is stable over many generations.
It changes only by mutation, a change in the base sequence or in the chromosomes. There is more on this in Variation.
A mutation is usually permanent: it is copied into every cell descended from the cell where it happened and, if it is in a gamete, into the offspring.

The genetic code is the same in every body cell, so genetic mechanisms alone cannot explain why cells with the same DNA become different (a liver cell and a nerve cell, for example), or why identical twins grow more different with age. Epigenetic mechanisms explain these.

Every body cell carries the same DNA, yet cells behave differently because different genes are active in them. Epigenetics is the study of how that activity is controlled without altering the DNA sequence.
Epigenetics is the study of changes in gene expression (which genes are switched on or off, and how strongly) that are not caused by changes in the DNA base sequence.
'Epi-' means 'on top of': the changes are chemical marks added on top of the DNA. The full set of marks in a cell is its epigenome.

Epigenetic marks are caused by development and by the environment and behaviour, such as diet, stress, smoking, exposure to pollutants and other chemicals, and temperature. In insects, the food a larva is given is a trigger.

The marks are copied when a cell divides by mitosis, so a change can last for the rest of an organism's life. This is why they keep specialised cells specialised: a liver cell's daughter cells are liver cells.
Some epigenetic changes are reversible, because marks can be added and removed by enzymes, for example in response to a change in diet or lifestyle.

In humans, smokers' blood cells show changed patterns of marks on some genes, and some of these changes partly reverse after a person stops smoking. This shows behaviour can change the epigenome, and quitting can partly undo it.

Epigenetic marks can last through a lifetime, but whether they reach the next generation is a separate question. The answer differs between mammals and plants, and twins show how the environment reshapes the epigenome with age.
In mammals most marks are erased and reset in the gametes and early embryo, so epigenetic changes are usually not passed on. Some escape erasure and are inherited, as in agouti mice.
In plants, marks are more often passed on through seeds, as in toadflax. Passing marks to the next generation in this way is epigenetic inheritance.

Identical twins have the same DNA, and when young their epigenetic marks are very similar. In older twins, especially those who have lived apart or had different lifestyles, the marks are much more different, matching differences in health.
The environment changes the epigenome over a lifetime. This is why twins with identical DNA grow more different with age.
Epigenetic marks work by controlling how easily a gene can be read. There are two main kinds of mark, one placed on the DNA itself and one on the proteins it is wound around.
DNA methylation: an enzyme adds a small chemical group, a methyl group (CH₃), to cytosine bases in the DNA, especially in the control region at the start of a gene.
Methylation usually switches the gene off (silences it), because the cell's machinery can no longer read it. Removing the methyl groups can switch it back on.
The base sequence is unchanged: a methylated C still pairs with G. This is why methylation is not a mutation.
Histone modification: chemical groups are added to or removed from the histone proteins that the DNA is wound around, like thread on spools. There is more on this in Chromosome structure and genes.
Adding acetyl groups loosens the packing so the genes there can be read and are switched on; other changes tighten the packing so the genes cannot be read and are switched off.
Tightly packed, heavily methylated DNA is inactive; loosely packed, unmethylated DNA is active. So the same DNA can give different phenotypes depending on its marks.

Diagram: the same gene twice. Left: DNA loosely wound on histones, no methyl groups, arrow 'gene read → protein made → gene switched on'. Right: DNA tightly packed, methyl groups as small flags, cross through 'gene read → gene switched off'. Label DNA, histone, methyl group, gene on, gene off.
Genetic and epigenetic mechanisms both affect the phenotype, but they differ in what changes, what causes it, how long it lasts and whether it is inherited. Learn them as paired points.
What changes: the DNA base sequence (genetic) versus gene expression, through chemical marks on the DNA and histones (epigenetic). The base sequence is unchanged in epigenetic change.

Cause: mutation, from random copying errors or mutagens (agents that cause mutations) such as radiation (genetic), versus the environment, behaviour and development, such as diet, stress, chemicals and temperature (epigenetic).
Reversibility: usually permanent (genetic) versus often reversible (epigenetic).
Speed: genetic change in a population is slow, spreading over many generations, whereas epigenetic change can happen within an organism's lifetime, in response to its surroundings.

Inheritance: reliably passed on in every generation through the gametes, following Mendel's laws for nuclear genes (genetic), versus usually erased in the gametes and early embryo in mammals (epigenetic). Epigenetic marks are sometimes passed on, more often in plants, and often fade over a few generations.
Within one organism: the same in all body cells, except for new mutations (genetic), versus different in different cell types and tissues (epigenetic).
Similarities: both change the phenotype by changing which proteins are made, and both are copied when cells divide by mitosis.

Both can be involved in disease. For example, some cancers involve both mutations and abnormal methylation that silences genes which normally control cell division. There is more on this in Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer.
A honeybee colony shows how diet can switch on different sets of genes in animals with identical DNA. The marks last through the bee's life, but they are not passed to her offspring.

The queen (large, fertile, lays the eggs, lives for years) and the workers (smaller, sterile females that forage and care for the larvae, living for weeks in summer) develop from genetically identical female larvae.
Trigger: diet. All young larvae are fed royal jelly, a secretion of worker bees, for the first few days.
A larva fed royal jelly throughout its development, in a special large cell, becomes a queen; the rest are switched to a diet including pollen and honey and become workers.
Mechanism: the different diets produce different patterns of DNA methylation in the developing bee, switching on different sets of genes.

Evidence: in 2008, researchers in Australia reduced the activity of the enzyme that adds methyl groups to DNA in newly hatched larvae. Most of these larvae developed into queens with working ovaries, as if they had been fed royal jelly.
What it shows: one genotype gives two very different phenotypes because the environment (food) changes gene expression during development.
The marks are passed on through every cell division in the developing bee, but the caste is not passed to the queen's offspring, because each larva's caste is decided by its own diet.
Agouti mice show a clear link between a mother's diet, methylation of one gene and the colour and health of her offspring. They are also a true case of epigenetic inheritance in a mammal.

The agouti gene in mice normally controls fur colour, giving brown fur. In mice with a variant called agouti viable yellow, an extra stretch of DNA inserted beside the gene can switch it on in every cell all the time.
When that region is unmethylated, the gene is always on: the mice have yellow fur and become obese, with a higher risk of diabetes and cancer.
When it is heavily methylated, the gene is switched off and the mice are brown and lean; partly methylated mice are mottled. Genetically identical mice in the same litter can be any of these.

Effect of the mother's diet: in a study published in 2003 (Robert Waterland and Randy Jirtle), pregnant mothers given extra methyl-donor nutrients (folic acid, vitamin B12, choline and betaine) had more brown, healthy offspring, because more methyl groups were added to the gene in the embryos.
In later work, exposing pregnant mothers to the plastics chemical bisphenol A (BPA) reduced methylation and gave more yellow offspring. Methyl-donor supplements cancelled this effect.
Inheritance: the offspring's coat colour tends to resemble its mother's, because the marks on this gene are not fully erased when the eggs are made. So it is a true example of epigenetic inheritance.
The effects can be changed (reversed) by diet.
The Dutch Hunger Winter is a human case of the environment before birth leaving a lasting epigenetic mark. It is clear evidence within one lifetime, but weaker evidence for inheritance.
In the winter of 1944–1945, during the Second World War, a German blockade cut food supplies to the occupied western Netherlands. Food rations fell well below 1,000 kilocalories a day.
About 20,000 people died before the region was liberated in May 1945.

The famine had a clear start and end, and records of births were kept, so scientists could study people who were in the womb during it. Those whose mothers were starved in early pregnancy had higher rates of obesity, heart disease and some other conditions as adults.

A study published in 2008 found that, about 60 years later, people exposed to the famine around conception had less methylation of a growth gene, IGF2 (insulin-like growth factor 2), than their brothers or sisters of the same sex who were not exposed.
The environment before birth left a lasting mark on gene expression, even decades later.
Some studies report effects on the next generation (the grandchildren of the starved mothers), but this evidence is weaker and debated.
So this is clear evidence of a lasting epigenetic effect of the environment in humans, and possible but uncertain evidence of inheritance across generations.
Some plants use an epigenetic 'memory' of winter to decide when to flower. The mark is remembered for the rest of that plant's life, but it is reset in the next generation.

Vernalisation is the need of some plants to experience a long period of cold (winter) before they can flower. It stops them flowering in autumn and makes them flower in spring, when conditions suit seed production.
In thale cress (Arabidopsis thaliana), a small wild plant, a gene called FLC (FLOWERING LOCUS C) blocks flowering.
During weeks of cold, histone modifications gradually switch FLC off, and the longer the cold lasts, the more cells have FLC switched off.
FLC stays switched off after the weather warms, because the marks are copied through all later cell divisions, so the plant flowers in spring.
The change is epigenetic: the FLC gene's base sequence is unchanged.

The change is reset in each generation: FLC is switched back on in the seeds, so each new plant must go through its own winter. This is an epigenetic memory within one plant's life, not inheritance to offspring.
Many crops, such as winter wheat, need vernalisation, which is why they are sown in autumn.

Common toadflax shows a natural variant caused by an epigenetic mark rather than a mutation, and it is passed on to the next generation. Together with agouti mice, it is a main example of epigenetic inheritance.
Common toadflax (Linaria vulgaris), a wild plant, normally has flowers with one plane of symmetry (bilaterally symmetrical) and a single spur.
A natural variant, the peloric form, has radially symmetrical flowers (the same all the way round) with five spurs. Carl Linnaeus first described it in the 1740s.

In 1999, Enrico Coen's group at the John Innes Centre in Norwich showed that peloric plants have the same base sequence in the key flower-symmetry gene (Lcyc) as normal plants, but the gene is heavily methylated and switched off.
This is an epigenetic change (sometimes called an epimutation), not a mutation, because the DNA sequence is the same.
The methylated, switched-off state is passed on through the seeds to the next generation, so the peloric form is inherited in wild populations.
Occasionally the methylation is lost and branches with normal flowers appear, showing the change is reversible.
This is a heritable natural variation, noticed for more than 250 years, caused by an epigenetic mark rather than a change in DNA sequence.
Research one example of epigenetic inheritance in detail, using the steps below. Following the same order every time makes sure you cover trigger, mechanism, effect and evidence.
1. Choose an example and find reliable sources (scientific organisations, universities and review articles). There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
2. Identify the organism and the trait.
3. Identify the environmental or behavioural trigger.
4. Identify the gene and the epigenetic change (methylation or histone modification), if known.
5. Describe the effect on the phenotype.
6. Describe the evidence that the change is epigenetic (same DNA sequence, different marks).
7. State whether it is reversible and whether it is passed to offspring.
8. Evaluate the strength of the evidence, for example animal studies versus observational studies in humans.

Worked model, agouti mice: mouse fur colour; the mother's diet; methylation of the agouti gene; yellow obese or brown lean mice; genetically identical mice with different methylation; passed on partly through the mother, and reversed by methyl donors.

A genetic cross predicts what offspring a pair of parents can have. It works only because of how alleles (the different versions of a gene) are shared out when gametes (sex cells) are made and joined.
Each body cell carries two alleles of each gene, one on each chromosome of a homologous pair (two matching chromosomes, one inherited from each parent).
Each gamete carries only one of the two alleles, because meiosis (the cell division that makes gametes) separates the two chromosomes of each homologous pair.
At fertilisation the zygote (the first cell of the new organism) again has two alleles, one from each parent, so the pair is restored.

There is more on this in the subsections on chromosome structure and genes, mitosis and meiosis, and the key concepts of information transfer, where allele, homozygous, heterozygous, pure-breeding and carrier are defined.

Before you can set out any cross you must work out which gametes each parent can make. This depends only on whether the parent is homozygous (two identical alleles) or heterozygous (two different alleles).
A homozygous individual (TT or tt) makes only one type of gamete for that gene: T from TT, or t from tt, because both of its alleles are the same.
A heterozygous individual (Tt) makes two types of gamete, T and t, in equal numbers, half of its gametes each, because the two chromosomes separate at random in meiosis.
True-breeding is another name for pure-breeding (homozygous): crossed with one like itself, it always gives offspring with the same trait.
A monohybrid cross is the simplest kind of genetic cross, because it follows just one characteristic at a time. Labels for the generations let you say clearly which individuals you mean.
A monohybrid cross follows the inheritance of one trait, controlled by one gene with two alleles.
Unlinked means the gene is considered on its own, without other genes on the same chromosome affecting the result. There is more on this in Linkage.
P (parental generation) are the parents crossed.
F1 (first filial generation) are their offspring, for example the plants grown from the seeds of the P cross.
F2 (second filial generation) are the offspring of crossing F1 individuals with each other.
“First generation” means the offspring of the cross being modelled, so you only need to work out the offspring of one cross.
Symbols are shorthand for alleles. A key at the start tells the examiner what each symbol means, so your answer can be read without guessing.
Use the first letter of the dominant trait: a capital for the dominant allele and a lower-case letter for the recessive allele, e.g. T = tall, t = dwarf.
Use the letters a question gives, because the marking scheme is written with them.
Avoid letters whose capital and lower case look alike when handwritten, because the examiner cannot tell which allele you mean: C/c, O/o, S/s, W/w, P/p, K/k, V/v, X/x, Z/z.
Always state a key first, e.g. “T = allele for tall, t = allele for dwarf”.
Every line is shown, in this order, because marks are given for each. Working in the same sequence every time also stops you missing a step.
Step 1: the key, so that the examiner knows what each letter means.
Step 2: the parents' phenotypes (the visible traits), e.g. tall × dwarf.
Step 3: the parents' genotypes (the alleles they carry), e.g. TT × tt.
Step 4: the gametes, each different allele each parent can pass on, written once and usually circled (T from TT; t from tt; T and t from Tt).
Step 5: the Punnett square (a grid that combines the gametes), or fertilisation lines joining every gamete of one parent to every gamete of the other.
Step 6: the offspring genotypes, with their ratio, such as 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.
Step 7: the offspring phenotypes, with their ratio, such as 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
A Punnett square is a grid that shows every possible fertilisation between the gametes of two parents. It makes sure you do not miss a combination.
One parent's gametes go across the top and the other parent's gametes down the side.
Each box takes the allele from its column and the allele from its row, with the dominant allele written first (Tt, not tT), so that identical genotypes are always written the same way.
Each box is one equally likely outcome of fertilisation; with two gametes from each parent, each box is a 1 in 4 (25%) chance.

Diagram: a 2 × 2 Punnett square for Tt × Tt: gametes T and t across the top (labelled “gametes of parent 1”), T and t down the side (labelled “gametes of parent 2”); boxes TT, Tt, Tt, tt; each box labelled with its phenotype (tall, tall, tall, dwarf).
A cross predicts chances, not certainties. Each fertilisation is a separate chance event, so the ratio describes what is expected on average.
A ratio is a prediction of the proportions expected, not an exact count.
Each fertilisation is independent, so in a family where the first child is affected, the chance for the next child is unchanged.
A 3 : 1 ratio is a probability, not a guarantee that a family of four has exactly one affected child.
Ratios can be given as a ratio (3 : 1), a fraction (3/4), a percentage (75%) or a probability (0.75, or “a 3 in 4 chance”).
Observed results come close to the predicted ratio only with large numbers of offspring (e.g. hundreds of pea plants), not in a small human family, because chance has more effect on small samples.
Pea plants: tall (T) is dominant to dwarf (t). Here two heterozygous tall plants are crossed, and every line of the standard layout is shown.
Parents' genotypes: Tt × Tt (both heterozygous, so each makes two types of gamete).
Gametes: T, t × T, t, because each heterozygous parent makes both types.
Punnett square: TT, Tt / Tt, tt.
Offspring genotypes: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, because Tt arises in two boxes of the square.
Offspring phenotypes: 3 tall : 1 dwarf (75% tall, 25% dwarf), because TT and both Tt boxes are tall.
Of the tall offspring, 1/3 are homozygous (TT) and 2/3 heterozygous (Tt), because the three tall offspring are TT, Tt and Tt.
In the cross above there are two different ratios, one for genotypes and one for phenotypes. They differ because of dominance.
The genotype ratio (1 : 2 : 1) differs from the phenotype ratio (3 : 1) because TT and Tt look the same: the dominant allele masks the recessive one.
A recessive trait reappears in offspring of parents who both show the dominant trait only if both parents are heterozygous, because only then can each parent pass on a recessive allele.
Crossing a true-breeding tall plant with a true-breeding dwarf plant is the simplest case, because each parent makes only one type of gamete.
