Parents' phenotypes: true-breeding tall × true-breeding dwarf.
Parents' genotypes: TT × tt (both homozygous, so true-breeding).
Gametes: T × t, because each parent makes only one type.
Offspring genotypes: all Tt (heterozygous), because each gets T from one parent and t from the other.
Offspring phenotypes: all (100%) tall, because the dominant T masks t.
This is Mendel's P → F1 cross; crossing these F1 plants together (Tt × Tt) gives the F2 result of the heterozygous × heterozygous example above, in which the dwarf trait reappears.
Mendel's own figures are in Mendel's Laws.
In this cross a heterozygous tall plant is crossed with a dwarf plant. It gives a different ratio from the first example, because one parent can pass on only the recessive allele.
Parents' genotypes: Tt × tt (one heterozygous parent, so only the Tt parent makes two types of gamete).
Gametes: T, t × t, because the tt parent can give only t.
Punnett square (2 × 1, or 2 × 2 with t written twice): Tt, tt.
Offspring phenotypes: 1 tall : 1 dwarf (50% each), because Tt is tall and tt is dwarf.
With one gene and two alleles there are only three genotypes, TT, Tt and tt, so only six different crosses are possible. Knowing all six lets you recognise any monohybrid cross quickly.
Cross 1: TT × TT → all TT → all tall, because both parents can only pass on T.
Cross 2: TT × Tt → 1 TT : 1 Tt → all tall.
Cross 3: TT × tt → all Tt → all tall, because T masks t.
Cross 4: Tt × Tt → 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt → 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
Cross 5: Tt × tt → 1 Tt : 1 tt → 1 tall : 1 dwarf.
Cross 6: tt × tt → all tt → all dwarf, because both parents can only pass on t.
You can also work from the offspring back to the parents. The ratio of offspring tells you which genotypes the parents must have had.
Offspring in a 3 : 1 ratio mean both parents are heterozygous, because only Tt × Tt gives this ratio.
A 1 : 1 ratio means one parent is heterozygous and the other homozygous recessive, so only one parent makes two kinds of gamete.
Any offspring showing the recessive trait mean each parent carries at least one recessive allele, because an offspring needs two recessive alleles, one from each parent.
An organism showing the dominant trait could be TT or Tt, and you cannot tell by looking. A test cross finds out by crossing it with a recessive organism.
A test cross finds the unknown genotype of an organism showing the dominant trait (TT or Tt) by crossing it with a homozygous recessive (tt) organism.
The tt parent can give only t, so each offspring's phenotype shows directly which allele came from the unknown parent.
If all offspring show the dominant trait (all tall), the unknown parent is almost certainly TT (TT × tt → all Tt).
If any offspring show the recessive trait (about half dwarf), the unknown parent is Tt (Tt × tt → 1 : 1), because it must have passed on a recessive allele.
Many offspring are needed to be confident that a TT result is not chance.
Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disorder that follows the same rules as the pea plants. Two parents who do not have the disease can still have an affected child, if both are carriers.
Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele of a gene on an autosome (a chromosome that is not a sex chromosome).
Key: F = normal allele, f = cystic fibrosis allele, with the normal allele dominant.
Parents: two unaffected carriers (people who carry the recessive allele but do not have the disease).
Gametes: F, f × F, f, because each carrier makes both types.
Offspring phenotypes: 3 unaffected : 1 with cystic fibrosis, because only ff has the disease.
Each child has a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of having cystic fibrosis, a 1 in 2 (50%) chance of being a carrier, and a 1 in 4 chance of being neither.
Why the mutation causes the disease is in Mutations, and its use in genetic counselling is in Benefits and limitations of Mendelian genetics.

With complete dominance, one allele (a version of a gene) hides the other in a heterozygote (an organism carrying two different alleles). With incomplete dominance, neither allele hides the other, and the results of crosses look different.
The heterozygote's phenotype (its observable feature) lies between those of the two homozygotes (organisms with two identical alleles), e.g. pink snapdragons from red × white.
There are three phenotypes rather than two, so each genotype (the pair of alleles an organism carries) can be recognised just by looking at the phenotype.
With complete dominance the heterozygote looks like the homozygous dominant (Tt is as tall as TT), so there are only two phenotypes and a tall plant could be TT or Tt.
The AB blood group is not an example of incomplete dominance: both the A and B antigens are fully made side by side, rather than giving an in-between result.
The pink colour has a simple molecular cause, which also shows that the alleles themselves are never altered.
In snapdragon flower colour, the red allele codes for a working enzyme that makes red pigment, and the white allele codes for no working pigment enzyme.
A plant with two red alleles has two working copies, so it makes enough pigment to be red.
A heterozygote has only one working copy, so it makes less pigment and is pink. A plant with two white alleles makes none and is white.
The alleles are not mixed or changed: red and white flowers reappear in the next generation, which shows the genes themselves do not blend.
Genetics questions need a key for the allele letters. A capital and lower-case pair suggests one allele is dominant, so incomplete dominance needs a different choice.
Neither allele is dominant, so don't use a capital and a lower-case letter of the same kind as if one were dominant.
Use the letters the question gives.
If choosing, use two different capital letters, e.g. R = allele for red, W = allele for white (so RR red, RW pink, WW white), and state in the key that the alleles show incomplete dominance.
Questions sometimes use B and b with a statement that B is incompletely dominant; follow the question's key.
Snapdragon flower colour. Crossing a true-breeding red plant with a true-breeding white plant is the simplest cross, and it shows where the pink phenotype comes from.
Key: R = red, W = white, incomplete dominance.
Gametes (sex cells, each carrying one allele): R × W.
Offspring genotypes: all RW, because every offspring gets one R from one parent and one W from the other.
Crossing two pink plants brings the parental colours back, which is the classic test of incomplete dominance. Set it out in the standard layout, line by line.
Gametes: R, W × R, W, because each parent can pass on either of its two alleles.
Punnett square (a grid showing every possible combination of gametes): RR, RW / RW, WW.
Offspring phenotypes: 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white (25% red, 50% pink, 25% white).
Diagram: draw the 2 × 2 Punnett square for RW × RW. Labels: gametes R and W on each side; boxes RR, RW, RW, WW; each box labelled red, pink, pink or white (or shaded red, pink, white).
The offspring ratio of a heterozygote × heterozygote cross tells you which kind of dominance a trait shows.
The phenotype ratio (1 : 2 : 1) is the same as the genotype ratio, because each genotype has its own phenotype.
With complete dominance the same cross gives 3 : 1, because the heterozygote looks like the dominant homozygote and the two classes merge.
If a cross of two parents that look the same gives three phenotypes in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, the trait shows incomplete dominance.
A pink plant can also be crossed with a red or a white one. Only two genotypes are possible in the offspring, so there are two phenotypes in a 1 : 1 ratio.
Gametes: R, W × W, because the homozygous parent can only pass on W.
Pink × red: RW × RR gives 1 RR : 1 RW, so 1 red : 1 pink.
Chickens give a second example of incomplete dominance, with a practical consequence for breeders.
In Andalusian chickens, feather colour shows incomplete dominance.
Homozygous black × homozygous white gives all offspring with grey-blue feathers, called 'blue'.
Blue × blue gives 1 black : 2 blue : 1 white.
If black were instead completely dominant to white, the same blue-type (heterozygous) cross would give 3 black : 1 white.
Blue Andalusians can never be true-breeding (always producing offspring like themselves), because every blue bird is heterozygous and its offspring include black and white.
Breeders get all-blue chicks by crossing black with white birds.
Real organisms carry many genes at once, so a cross can follow an incompletely dominant gene together with a completely dominant one.
A cross can combine an incompletely dominant gene with a completely dominant one, e.g. snapdragon flower colour with plant height.
This is a two-gene cross. There is more on this in Dihybrid crosses, which has the worked example.
Mendel bred pea plants in a monastery garden and worked out the basic rules of inheritance long before anyone knew about genes, chromosomes or DNA.
Gregor Mendel (1822–1884) was an Augustinian friar, later abbot, at the monastery of St Thomas in Brno (then Brünn, in the Austrian Empire; now in the Czech Republic).
He bred garden pea plants (Pisum sativum) between 1856 and 1863, presented his results in 1865 and published them in 1866.
His work was largely ignored until 1900, when it was rediscovered independently by other botanists, including Hugo de Vries and Carl Correns.

He worked before chromosomes, meiosis (the cell division that makes gametes) or DNA were understood, so he called the units of inheritance “factors”. We now call them genes, and their different versions alleles.
Mendel's choice of organism was part of why his experiments worked. Garden peas had four features that made clean, countable results possible.
Peas had many varieties with clear contrasting forms of a trait (for example tall or dwarf, with nothing in between), so every offspring could be sorted into one group or the other.
Peas normally self-pollinate (a flower pollinates itself), so true-breeding lines were available. True-breeding means offspring always look like their parents, generation after generation.

They can be cross-pollinated by hand: the anthers (pollen-producing parts) of one flower are removed and its stigma (the pollen-receiving part) is dusted with pollen from another. This lets the experimenter choose the parents.
They grow quickly and produce many seeds, giving large numbers to count, which is needed to see clear ratios.
Mendel's method was careful and quantitative, which is why his results were clear. He followed simple, clear-cut traits and treated inheritance as something to be counted and calculated.

The seven traits he studied, dominant form first: seed shape (round / wrinkled), seed colour (yellow / green), flower colour (purple / white), pod shape (inflated / constricted), pod colour (green / yellow), flower position (axial, along the stem / terminal, at the tip), stem length (tall / dwarf).
He started with true-breeding parents and studied one trait at a time, then two. Looking at one trait at a time kept the results simple enough to interpret.
He counted large numbers of offspring, because small samples can give misleading ratios by chance.
He recorded results over several generations: P (the parents), F1 (their offspring) and F2 (the offspring of the F1 crossed with each other).
He used mathematics (ratios) to analyse the results, and repeated each cross for several traits to check that the pattern held.
Mendel's crosses gave the same pattern every time. That pattern led him to the idea that each trait is controlled by two factors, one of which can hide the other.
Crossing true-breeding tall with true-breeding dwarf gave an F1 that was all tall; none were dwarf and none were in between.
Self-pollinating the F1 gave an F2 of tall and dwarf in about 3 : 1.
F2 figures: 787 tall : 277 dwarf (2.84 : 1); 5474 round : 1850 wrinkled seeds (2.96 : 1); 6022 yellow : 2001 green seeds (3.01 : 1). Large numbers bring the ratio very close to 3 : 1.
The dwarf trait disappeared in the F1 and reappeared in the F2, so the dwarf “factor” must have been present, hidden, in the F1.
He concluded that each plant has two factors for each trait, one from each parent, and that one (dominant) can mask the other (recessive).
Mendel's first law explains the 3 : 1 ratio. It is about the two alleles of a single gene, and what happens to them when gametes (sex cells) are made.
Statement: “The two alleles (factors) of a gene separate (segregate) from each other during gamete formation, so that each gamete receives only one allele of each gene.”
Shorter accepted form: “Inherited traits are controlled by pairs of factors (alleles), which separate during gamete formation.”
A heterozygous tall plant (Tt, carrying two different alleles) forms two types of gamete, T and t, in equal numbers, so half the gametes carry T and half carry t.
Random fertilisation of these gametes in Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt and 3 tall : 1 dwarf, the 3 : 1 Mendel observed. There is more on this in Monohybrid crosses.

Chromosome basis (Mendel did not know this): the two alleles of a gene lie at the same locus (position) on the two chromosomes of a homologous pair, the matching pair of chromosomes, one from each parent.
In meiosis the homologous chromosomes separate into different cells, carrying one allele each into each gamete. This is why the alleles segregate.

Diagram: a diploid cell with one homologous pair, one chromosome carrying T and the other t at the same position, dividing by meiosis into gametes, half with T and half with t. Labels: homologous pair, allele T, allele t, locus, meiosis, gametes (haploid).
Mendel's second law deals with two different genes at once. It says that how one gene's alleles are shared out into gametes does not affect how another gene's alleles are shared out.
Statement: “When gametes form, the alleles of one gene separate independently of the alleles of another gene, so either allele of one gene can combine at random with either allele of another gene.”
Equivalent: “Each member of a pair of factors can combine randomly with either member of another pair.”
The law applies to genes on different chromosomes (unlinked genes). Genes close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together and break this rule.
A plant heterozygous for seed shape and seed colour (RrYy) forms four types of gamete, RY, Ry, rY and ry, in equal numbers (1/4 each).
This is because whether a gamete gets R or r has no effect on whether it gets Y or y.
Chromosome basis: when homologous pairs line up in meiosis, the way one pair lines up is independent of the way another pair lines up.
With R and Y on different chromosome pairs, half the cells put R with Y (giving RY and ry gametes) and half put R with y (giving Ry and rY gametes), so all four types are made in equal numbers.

Diagram: a cell with two homologous pairs (a long pair carrying R and r, a short pair carrying Y and y) in the two possible arrangements. Arrangement 1 gives RY and ry; arrangement 2 gives Ry and rY. Labels: homologous pairs, alleles, two equally likely arrangements, four gamete types.
A dihybrid cross follows two traits at the same time. Mendel's results from one showed that the two traits were inherited independently of each other.
Mendel's dihybrid cross: true-breeding round yellow × wrinkled green gave an F1 that was all round yellow.
Self-pollinating the F1 gave an F2 of 315 round yellow : 108 round green : 101 wrinkled yellow : 32 wrinkled green (total 556), close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

The new combinations (round green and wrinkled yellow) can only arise if the two genes are inherited independently, because neither parent had those pairings of traits. There is more on this in Dihybrid crosses.
Mendel's biggest contribution was a new way of thinking about heredity. His laws still underpin how we predict the outcome of genetic crosses.
Mendel showed that inheritance is particulate: traits are passed on by separate units that stay unchanged from generation to generation, rather than by blending of the parents' characteristics.
A blended trait could never reappear unchanged, as the dwarf trait did in the F2, so the reappearance is evidence for separate units.
His laws are the basis of the predictions in Benefits and limitations of Mendelian genetics.
A monohybrid cross follows one gene. A dihybrid cross follows two genes at once, which is how you predict offspring when two traits are inherited together.
A dihybrid cross follows the inheritance of two different traits (two genes) at the same time, e.g. seed shape and seed colour in peas.

“Unlinked” means the two genes are on different chromosomes, so they assort independently (are sorted into gametes without affecting each other) and every combination of their alleles is equally likely in the gametes. There is more on genes on the same chromosome in Linkage.
Key for the worked examples: R = round seed, r = wrinkled; Y = yellow seed, y = green. Capital letters are dominant alleles (the version that shows when present), lower case are recessive.

A genotype always has two letters for each gene (four letters in all), written with the two alleles of one gene together and the dominant first: RrYy, not RYry. Keeping each gene's pair together stops you mixing the genes up.
Before you can fill in a Punnett square you need the gametes (sex cells) each parent can make. This is a short method you can use on any two-gene genotype.
Each gamete gets one allele of each gene, so every gamete has two letters, one for each gene; never two of the same gene: RY, not Rr.
Method: pair each allele of the first gene with each allele of the second gene.

For RrYy: R with Y, R with y, r with Y, r with y, giving RY, Ry, rY, ry, in equal numbers. This equal mixing is the Law of Independent Assortment: the alleles of one gene are sorted into gametes independently of the other gene.
The number of gamete types depends on how many genes are heterozygous (have two different alleles): RRYY gives one type (RY); RRYy gives two (RY, Ry); Rryy gives two (Ry, ry).
RrYy, heterozygous for both genes, gives four (RY, Ry, rY, ry); rryy gives one (ry). Write each different gamete once, however many times it could be made.
The first step in Mendel's style of cross is to breed two pure lines together. The offspring, the F1 (first filial) generation, are all identical, which sets up the F2.
Parents' phenotypes (the visible traits): round yellow × wrinkled green (both true-breeding, meaning homozygous, so they always pass on the same alleles).
Parents' genotypes: RRYY × rryy, so each parent is homozygous for both genes.
Gametes: RY × ry, because each parent has only one type of gamete.
F1 genotype: all RrYy, as every offspring gets one dominant and one recessive allele of each gene.
F1 phenotype: all round yellow (both dominant traits), because the dominant alleles hide the recessive ones.

Crossing two F1 plants is the core dihybrid cross. Both parents are heterozygous for both genes, so each makes four types of gamete and the Punnett square (a grid showing every possible gamete pairing) is 4 × 4.
Parents (F1): round yellow × round yellow. Genotypes: RrYy × RrYy, so both are heterozygous for both genes.
Gametes: RY, Ry, rY, ry × RY, Ry, rY, ry.
Punnett square: 4 × 4 = 16 boxes, each a 1/16 chance, because every gamete pairing is equally likely.
Punnett square, row by row (gametes RY, Ry, rY, ry across the top and down the side). Row 1 (gamete RY): RRYY, RRYy, RrYY, RrYy. Row 2 (gamete Ry): RRYy, RRyy, RrYy, Rryy.
Row 3 (gamete rY): RrYY, RrYy, rrYY, rrYy. Row 4 (gamete ry): RrYy, Rryy, rrYy, rryy.
F2 genotypes (nine kinds): 1 RRYY, 2 RRYy, 2 RrYY, 4 RrYy, 1 RRyy, 2 Rryy, 1 rrYY, 2 rrYy, 1 rryy (total 16). Count repeated genotypes from the squares to get these numbers.
The 16 boxes contain nine genotypes but only four phenotypes, because a dominant allele hides the recessive one. Counting those phenotypes gives the famous dihybrid ratio.
F2 phenotypes: 9 round yellow (at least one R and at least one Y) : 3 round green (at least one R, yy) : 3 wrinkled yellow (rr, at least one Y) : 1 wrinkled green (rryy).

The ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 is the signature of a dihybrid F2 with two unlinked genes, each with complete dominance (the heterozygote looks the same as the dominant homozygote). There is more on Mendel's F2 counts, close to this ratio, in Mendel's Laws.
Look at the F2 phenotypes against the original parents. Some combinations of traits appear that neither the P nor the F1 plants showed.
Two of the four F2 phenotypes (round green and wrinkled yellow) are new combinations, found in neither the P nor the F1 generation.
They appear because the genes assort independently, so any seed shape allele can end up with any seed colour allele. They are a source of variation in offspring.

Diagram: the full 4 × 4 Punnett square of the F1 × F1 cross, with gametes labelled on both sides, and the boxes coloured or marked by phenotype (9 round yellow, 3 round green, 3 wrinkled yellow, 1 wrinkled green).
A 16-box square is slow and easy to miscount. Because the two genes are independent, you can work out each gene separately and multiply, which gives a quick check.
Because the genes are independent, the dihybrid result is the two monohybrid results multiplied.
Rr × Rr gives 3/4 round and 1/4 wrinkled; Yy × Yy gives 3/4 yellow and 1/4 green, so each gene is treated as its own monohybrid cross.
So round yellow = 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16, round green = 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16, wrinkled yellow = 3/16, wrinkled green = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.
Use this to check a Punnett square; show the full square in an exam answer when asked for a genetic cross.

A test cross crosses an individual showing the dominant traits with one that is homozygous recessive for both genes. The recessive parent makes only one type of gamete, so the offspring reveal exactly which gametes the other parent makes.
Round yellow (RrYy) × wrinkled green (rryy) is the dihybrid test cross.
Gametes: RY, Ry, rY, ry × ry, because rryy can only make ry.
Offspring genotypes: RrYy, Rryy, rrYy, rryy (1 : 1 : 1 : 1).
Phenotypes: 1 round yellow : 1 round green : 1 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green (25% each), because each of the four gametes has a 1/4 chance.
A 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 result shows that the dominant-looking parent was heterozygous for both genes and that the genes assort independently. There is more on the same cross with linked genes in Linkage.

The same pattern with other traits: in peas with tall (T) dominant to dwarf (t) and yellow (Y) dominant to green (y), TtYy × ttyy gives 1 tall yellow (TtYy) : 1 tall green (Ttyy) : 1 dwarf yellow (ttYy) : 1 dwarf green (ttyy).
Not every cross has two double heterozygotes. Here one parent is heterozygous for only one gene, so it makes just two gamete types and the square is 4 × 2.
Round yellow × round green: RrYy × Rryy, so the second parent is homozygous recessive for colour and heterozygous for shape.
Gametes: RY, Ry, rY, ry × Ry, ry.
Punnett square: 4 × 2 = 8 boxes; column Ry: RRYy, RRyy, RrYy, Rryy; column ry: RrYy, Rryy, rrYy, rryy.
Phenotypes: 3 round yellow : 3 round green : 1 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green (3 : 3 : 1 : 1).
Check: 3/4 round × 1/2 yellow = 3/8 round yellow, matching the 3 round yellow out of 8 boxes.
When one gene shows incomplete dominance, the heterozygote has a blend in between the two homozygotes. This changes the phenotype count but the method for crossing two genes stays the same.
Snapdragons: tall (T) is dominant to dwarf (t); red (R) and white (W) flower colour show incomplete dominance (RW = pink).
Parents' phenotypes: homozygous dwarf red × tall pink (heterozygous for height). Parents' genotypes: ttRR × TtRW.
Gametes: tR × TR, TW, tR, tW, because the ttRR parent can only make tR while the TtRW parent makes four types.
Offspring: TtRR (tall, red), TtRW (tall, pink), ttRR (dwarf, red), ttRW (dwarf, pink), in a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio.
So 50% of the offspring have pink flowers (two of four genotypes) and 50% are tall.
To the second generation: TTRR × ttWW gives an F1 of all TtRW (tall pink).
F1 × F1 gives 3 tall red : 6 tall pink : 3 tall white : 1 dwarf red : 2 dwarf pink : 1 dwarf white (out of 16).
These are found by multiplying 3/4 tall and 1/4 dwarf by 1/4 red, 1/2 pink and 1/4 white, because the two genes are independent.
Genes that sit on the same chromosome are passed on together, because a chromosome goes into a gamete as one piece. This is called linkage.
Each chromosome carries many genes in a fixed order along one DNA molecule, and a chromosome passes into a gamete (a sex cell) as one unit, so any two genes on it travel together.
Linked genes are not joined to each other in any special way. They are simply on the same DNA molecule, which is why they are inherited together.
All the genes on one chromosome form a linkage group, so there are as many linkage groups as there are chromosome pairs.

Linked genotypes show the alleles (versions of a gene) on each chromosome together, with a line or slash for the pair of chromosomes. AB/ab means one chromosome carries A and B and its homologue (the matching chromosome of the pair) carries a and b.
Diagram: two vertical bars (a homologous pair), one labelled with A above B, the other with a above b, at matching positions; label “homologous chromosomes”, “linked genes” and “locus”.

Independent assortment means the alleles of one gene are sorted into gametes without affecting the alleles of another gene. That only works if the genes are on separate chromosomes, so linkage is an exception to it.
The Law of Independent Assortment holds only for genes on different chromosomes. The Law of Segregation still applies to each gene, so linkage is an exception to one law, not a refutation of Mendel.
Linked genes do not assort independently: the alleles on one chromosome move together into the same gamete when the homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis (the cell division that makes gametes).
A double heterozygote (heterozygous for both genes) with linked genes, AB/ab, produces only two types of gamete, AB and ab, in equal numbers.

An unlinked double heterozygote produces four types (AB, Ab, aB, ab) instead. The gametes Ab and aB (new combinations) are not formed when the genes are linked, because A and B stay together on one chromosome.
Offspring show only (or mostly) the parental combinations of traits, while the new combinations seen with unlinked genes are missing (or rare).
So linkage gives fewer types of offspring and less variation, and the ratios differ from 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 and 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.

In real organisms, linked genes are occasionally separated, so a small number of offspring with new combinations can appear. The reason is crossing over, and genes are more likely to stay together the closer they lie on the chromosome.

Diagram: side by side, (a) unlinked genes: two chromosome pairs (A/a on one, B/b on the other) giving four gamete types AB, Ab, aB, ab; (b) linked genes: one chromosome pair, A and B on one homologue, a and b on the other, giving two gamete types AB and ab.
A test cross mates an individual of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive one, so the offspring reveal which gametes it makes. With linked genes, only two kinds of offspring appear.
Key: A = dominant allele of gene 1, a = recessive; B = dominant allele of gene 2, b = recessive; A and B on the same chromosome.
Parents' phenotypes: AB/ab shows both dominant traits; ab/ab shows both recessive traits. Parents' genotypes: AB/ab × ab/ab.
Gametes: AB, ab × ab. The recessive parent can only give ab, so each offspring's type shows which gamete came from the other parent.
Offspring genotypes: AB/ab (AaBb) and ab/ab (aabb), 1 : 1. Offspring phenotypes: 1 showing both dominant traits : 1 showing both recessive traits.
If the genes were unlinked, the same cross (AaBb × aabb) would give four phenotypes, 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. Linkage removes the two new combinations.

The arrangement matters. If the double heterozygote has the dominant allele of one gene with the recessive allele of the other on each chromosome (Ab/aB), its gametes are Ab and aB, and the test cross gives 1 Aabb : 1 aaBb, i.e. only the two mixed phenotypes.
Always read which alleles are on the same chromosome, because AB/ab and Ab/aB are different genotypes that give different offspring.
Crossing two linked double heterozygotes (the F1, or first-generation offspring) shows how linkage changes the familiar dihybrid ratio.
Gametes: AB, ab × AB, ab. Each parent makes only two gamete types because the genes are linked.
Punnett square: AB/AB, AB/ab / AB/ab, ab/ab.
Phenotypes: 3 both dominant : 1 both recessive (3 : 1), compared with 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 if the genes were unlinked, because no offspring show a dominant and a recessive trait together.
The fruit fly gives a real case of two genes inherited together. Both genes sit on the same chromosome, so the results of a test cross do not match the unlinked pattern.
In the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, the genes for body colour (grey dominant to black) and wing shape (normal wings dominant to vestigial wings) are on the same chromosome.

A test cross of a fly heterozygous for both (with grey and normal on one chromosome) with a black, vestigial fly gives mostly grey normal-winged and black vestigial-winged offspring, the parental combinations.
Only a few grey vestigial or black normal flies appear, not the 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 expected for unlinked genes, because the genes are usually inherited together.
In an exam you may be given offspring results and asked whether the genes are linked. You decide by comparing them with the ratios expected for unlinked genes.
A dihybrid cross (a cross following two genes) whose offspring show mainly the parental combinations suggests that the two genes are linked.

Fewer phenotype classes than expected, or a ratio far from 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (F1 × F1) or 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 (test cross), also suggests that the two genes are linked, because linked alleles stay together instead of mixing.
Whether a person is female or male depends on one pair of chromosomes out of 23. Knowing what that pair looks like in each sex is the starting point for working out how sex is inherited.

A human body cell has 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes (the chromosomes that are the same in both sexes) and one pair of sex chromosomes, which decide the person's sex. There is more on this in Chromosome structure and genes.
Females have two X chromosomes (XX); males have one X and one Y (XY). Every body cell carries this pair, not just the gametes (sex cells).
The X is a large chromosome carrying roughly 800–900 protein-coding genes, so it carries many genes for the body generally.
The Y is much smaller and carries well under 100 genes, most of them concerned with male development and sperm production.
A karyotype is a photograph or diagram of a cell's chromosomes arranged in their pairs by size; it shows the sex chromosomes as XX or XY, so the sex of the person can be read straight from it.
Diagram: a simplified karyotype of 22 numbered autosome pairs plus the sex-chromosome pair, with a female (XX) and a male (XY) version of pair 23, the Y drawn clearly smaller than the X.

Body cells have two sex chromosomes, but gametes are made by meiosis (the cell division that halves the chromosome number), so each gamete gets only one. Writing out which gametes each parent makes lets you model the cross and predict the sexes of the children.
Gametes are haploid (they have half the usual chromosome number), with 23 chromosomes: 22 autosomes and one sex chromosome.
All of a woman's eggs carry an X (23,X), because she has only X chromosomes to pass on.
A man's sperm carry either an X (23,X) or a Y (23,Y), in equal numbers, because the X and Y separate into different cells in meiosis.
Parents' phenotypes (what they are): female × male.
Parents' genotypes (their sex chromosomes): XX × XY.
Punnett square (a grid showing every possible gamete combination): XX, XX / XY, XY (or 2 × 1: XX, XY). Offspring genotypes: 1 XX : 1 XY. Offspring phenotypes: 1 female : 1 male (50% each).
Diagram: the Punnett square of this cross, with the mother's egg (X) on one side and the father's sperm (X and Y) on the other, each box labelled with genotype and sex.
The cross shows that every egg is the same but sperm come in two kinds. So the result of fertilisation, when a sperm and egg fuse, depends on which sperm wins.
The sex of a child is decided at fertilisation by the sperm: an X-carrying sperm gives a girl (XX); a Y-carrying sperm gives a boy (XY).
So the father's gamete decides the sex; the mother always gives an X, so her egg cannot make the difference.
Every pregnancy has an independent 1 in 2 chance of a girl or a boy, whatever the sex of earlier children, because each fertilisation is a fresh chance event.
Across a large population the sex ratio is close to 1 : 1, because X and Y sperm are made in equal numbers.
A boy receives his X from his mother and his Y from his father; a girl receives one X from each parent.
This is why X-linked traits (traits carried by genes on the X) pass from mother to son. There is more on this in Sex-linked traits.
Having XY or XX is only the start. The Y chromosome carries a particular gene that sets an embryo on the male path, and without it development follows the female path.
The Y chromosome carries the SRY gene (sex-determining region of the Y).

In an XY embryo, from about the sixth to seventh week of development, SRY switches on the development of the undifferentiated gonads (gonads that have not yet become either testes or ovaries) into testes.
The testes then make testosterone, which brings about the development of the male reproductive system.
In an XX embryo, with no Y and so no SRY, the gonads develop into ovaries and the female reproductive system develops.
So it is the presence of a Y (SRY), not the number of X chromosomes, that makes the embryo male.

Some genes sit on the sex chromosomes rather than on the other chromosomes, and this changes how they are inherited. Because males and females carry different sex chromosomes, the same allele can have a different effect in each sex.
Sex-linked genes are almost all on the X chromosome (X-linked), because the Y carries very few genes.
A sex-linked trait is a trait controlled by such a gene. The Y has no matching allele for most X-linked genes, so in males the X-linked gene has no second copy to pair with.
Females (XX) have two copies of each X-linked gene, so they can be homozygous (two identical alleles) or heterozygous (two different alleles).
A heterozygous female with one recessive allele is a carrier (she carries the allele but does not show the trait), because her dominant allele masks it.
Males (XY) have only one copy, so whatever allele their single X carries is expressed, with no second allele to mask it.
This is why a male cannot be a carrier, and why one recessive allele is enough for him to show the trait.
X-linked recessive conditions are therefore much more common in males than in females.
A female shows the condition only if she inherits the recessive allele from both parents, which means an affected father and a carrier or affected mother.

To predict who inherits an X-linked allele, follow the sex chromosomes. A child's sex is decided by the sex chromosome the father contributes, and that also decides where the X-linked allele comes from.
A father passes his X to all his daughters and his Y to all his sons.
So an affected father never passes an X-linked condition to his sons, because sons get his Y, which carries no allele for the gene.
All his daughters are at least carriers, because each receives his X with the recessive allele.
A son's X-linked allele always comes from his mother, since his only X is the one she gave him.
Genetics questions use a fixed way of writing X-linked genotypes so that the sex and the alleles are both clear at a glance.
Write the allele as a superscript on the X, and the Y with no allele, because the Y has no matching allele for these genes.
Colour blindness: Xᴮ = normal colour vision, Xᵇ = colour blind. Haemophilia: Xᴴ = normal clotting, Xʰ = haemophilia.
Colour-blindness genotypes: female XᴮXᴮ (normal), XᴮXᵇ (carrier), XᵇXᵇ (colour blind); male XᴮY (normal), XᵇY (colour blind).
Use the letters a question gives.
Red-green colour blindness is the standard example of an X-linked recessive condition, and the one most often used in crosses.
Red-green colour blindness is an X-linked recessive condition in which a person has difficulty telling red and green apart.

The genes for the red- and green-sensitive light-absorbing pigments of the cone cells of the retina (the colour-detecting cells at the back of the eye) are on the X chromosome. The recessive allele gives a pigment that is missing or works abnormally.
It affects about 1 in 12 men (8%) and about 1 in 200 women (0.5%) of northern European ancestry. The difference fits the pattern that males need only one recessive allele.
It is detected with coloured-dot test charts (Ishihara plates).
It is not treatable, but most people adapt to it.
Haemophilia is the second named X-linked recessive condition. It shows how a single faulty gene can affect the whole body, because it removes one step in blood clotting.
Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive condition in which blood does not clot properly because a clotting protein is missing or faulty.
Haemophilia A lacks clotting factor VIII; haemophilia B lacks factor IX.
Bleeding after injury lasts much longer, and bleeding can occur into joints and muscles.
Haemophilia A affects about 1 in 5,000 male births.
It is treated by injections of the missing clotting factor, now mostly produced by genetically engineered cells. There is more on this in Genetic engineering.
Haemophilia in European royal families is a well-known real case of an X-linked allele passing through carrier daughters to affected grandsons.
Queen Victoria (1819–1901) was a carrier of haemophilia.
Her son Leopold had haemophilia. Through two of her daughters, who were carriers, it passed into the royal families of Russia (Tsarevich Alexei, son of Tsar Nicholas II) and Spain.
Haemophilia and colour blindness are not the only X-linked recessive conditions. A third example is useful when a question asks for one other than haemophilia.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy is another X-linked recessive condition, caused by a lack of the muscle protein dystrophin, which causes progressive muscle weakness (muscles get steadily weaker over time).
It is almost always in boys, which fits the pattern for X-linked recessive conditions.
A mother who is a carrier of colour blindness has a partner with normal vision, so we can work out what their children could inherit.
Parents' phenotypes: normal-vision (carrier) female × normal-vision male.
Parents' genotypes: carrier female XᴮXᵇ × normal male XᴮY.
Gametes (each carries one sex chromosome with its allele): carrier female Xᴮ, Xᵇ × normal male Xᴮ, Y.
Punnett square: XᴮXᴮ, XᴮY / XᴮXᵇ, XᵇY.
Offspring genotypes and phenotypes: 1 normal female (XᴮXᴮ) : 1 carrier female (XᴮXᵇ) : 1 normal male (XᴮY) : 1 colour-blind male (XᵇY).
Half the sons are expected to be colour blind and half the daughters carriers; no daughters are colour blind, because every daughter gets the father's normal Xᴮ. 25% of all children are colour blind.

Diagram: the Punnett square for this cross, with the mother's gametes Xᴮ and Xᵇ on one side and the father's Xᴮ and Y on the other, each box labelled with genotype and phenotype (normal female, carrier female, normal male, colour-blind male).
Here the father has haemophilia and the mother has two normal alleles. This cross shows what an affected father passes on.
Parents' phenotypes: normal female × affected male.
Parents' genotypes: normal female XᴴXᴴ × affected male XʰY.
Gametes: normal female Xᴴ × affected male Xʰ, Y.
Offspring: XᴴXʰ (carrier daughters) and XᴴY (normal sons), 1 : 1.
All daughters are carriers, because each gets the father's Xʰ. No children have haemophilia, because the sons get his Y and the mother's normal Xᴴ.
When both parents contribute a recessive allele, a daughter can be affected. This cross shows how that happens.
Parents' phenotypes: carrier female × colour-blind male.
Parents' genotypes: carrier female XᴮXᵇ × colour-blind male XᵇY.
Gametes: carrier female Xᴮ, Xᵇ × colour-blind male Xᵇ, Y.
Offspring: XᴮXᵇ (carrier female), XᵇXᵇ (colour-blind female), XᴮY (normal male), XᵇY (colour-blind male), 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.
Half the daughters and half the sons are colour blind. This is how a colour-blind daughter can arise: she inherits Xᵇ from both her mother and her father.
This cross reverses the sexes of the affected parent. It shows that an affected mother passes the condition to every son.
Parents' phenotypes: affected female × normal male.
Parents' genotypes: affected female XʰXʰ × normal male XᴴY.
Gametes: affected female Xʰ × normal male Xᴴ, Y.
Offspring: XᴴXʰ (carrier daughters) and XʰY (sons with haemophilia).
All sons are affected, because their only X comes from the mother; all daughters are carriers, because they also get the father's normal Xᴴ.
Females with haemophilia are very rare; this cross is used to show the pattern.
A pedigree shows how a trait passes through several generations of a family. Before you can use one, you need to know what its symbols and lines mean.
A pedigree is a family-tree diagram showing which members of a family have a trait.
Symbols: square = male; circle = female; shaded = affected; half-shaded (or a dot in the centre) = carrier.
A horizontal line joining a male and a female = parents; a vertical line down to a horizontal line = their children, in birth order from left to right.
Generations are numbered I, II, III and individuals 1, 2, 3 within each, so every person can be named, for example II-2.
Four features of a pedigree point to an X-linked recessive trait. Each follows from the rules on how X chromosomes are passed on.
Many more affected males than females, because a male needs only one recessive allele.
Affected males usually have unaffected parents, because the mother is a carrier.
The trait can skip a generation, passing from an affected man through his carrier daughters to his grandsons.
It is never passed from father to son, because a son gets his father's Y, not his X.
To give the genotype of a named person, or the chance that a child is affected or a carrier, work through the pedigree in a fixed order. This starts with the people whose genotype is certain.
1. Write XY for every male and XX for every female.
2. Fill in the alleles of affected males (XʰY) and unaffected males (XᴴY), which follow directly from their phenotype.
3. Any daughter of an affected male is at least a carrier; any mother of an affected son is a carrier or affected.
4. Use these to fill in the remaining females.
5. Then work any further cross with a Punnett square.

Diagram: a three-generation X-linked recessive pedigree. Generation I: normal man, carrier woman. Generation II: affected son, normal son, carrier daughter, normal daughter. Generation III: the carrier daughter's children with a normal man, including an affected grandson. Label symbols and generations.
Genes on the Y chromosome follow a different pattern from X-linked genes, because only males have a Y.
Genes on the Y chromosome (for example SRY) are passed only from father to son and are found only in males. There is more on SRY in Sex determination.

Gregor Mendel worked out simple rules for how single genes are passed from parents to offspring. Mendelian genetics is the set of ideas built on those rules, and you need to know them before you can judge where they work and where they fail.
Mendelian genetics is the study of how traits controlled by single genes are inherited, using Mendel's principles.
Principle 1: each organism has two alleles (versions) of each gene, one from each parent, and the two alleles separate into different gametes (sex cells), so each gamete carries only one.
Principle 2: one allele can be dominant over the other, meaning it decides the trait when both are present.
Principle 3: alleles of different genes are inherited independently of one another.
Because the rules are so regular, Mendelian genetics predicts offspring ratios using genetic crosses. There is more on this in Monohybrid crosses.
A Mendelian (single-gene) trait is controlled by one gene with clear alternative forms.
This gives discontinuous variation, which means an individual falls into one category or another with nothing in between, for example tall or dwarf pea plants, or having cystic fibrosis or not.

The main strength of Mendelian genetics is predictive power: if you know the parents' genotypes, you can work out the chances for their children. Medicine uses this idea in genetic counselling for single-gene disorders.

Predicting offspring: knowing the parents' genotypes, a cross predicts the probability of each genotype and phenotype in the offspring. For example, two carriers of cystic fibrosis (people with one faulty recessive allele who are not themselves affected) have a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child.
Genetic counselling and screening in medicine: families with a history of a single-gene disorder can be told the risks to future children, so they can make informed decisions.
Carrier testing tells people whether they carry a recessive allele before they have children, which matters because carriers usually show no symptoms.
Cystic fibrosis is an important example in Ireland, which has the highest rate of cystic fibrosis in the world; about 1 in 19 Irish people is a carrier.
Sickle-cell anaemia is a single-gene disorder inherited as a recessive trait, so both parents must pass on the faulty allele for a child to be affected.
Huntington's disease is dominant, so one faulty allele is enough: an affected heterozygous parent has a 1 in 2 chance of passing it to each child.

Haemophilia and colour blindness are sex-linked (carried on the sex chromosomes), but their inheritance still follows Mendel's rules once that is allowed for. There is more on this in Sex-linked traits.
Mendel's rules also let us work backwards from what we can see to what is hidden, and forwards to design organisms with useful combinations of traits. Both uses matter in medicine and farming.

Identifying an unknown genotype: a test cross or a pedigree (a family tree showing who has a trait) reveals whether an individual carries a hidden recessive allele. For example, a breeder can check whether a breeding animal carries an allele for an inherited disease before it is used for breeding.
Plant and animal breeding: breeders use Mendel's principles to produce true-breeding varieties, which always pass on the same trait because they carry identical alleles.

Breeders can also combine desirable traits from two parents into one variety, for example a high yield from one variety with disease resistance from another, and predict how many offspring of each kind to expect.
New combinations of traits arise from independent assortment, which is why breeding for two traits at once can work. There is more on this in Dihybrid crosses.
Mendel's work did more than explain pea plants. His idea of separate units of inheritance opened the way to later discoveries, and it is still used to interpret modern genetic tests.

Mendel's idea that traits are passed on by separate, unchanging units (genes) that segregate in gametes is the basis of later discoveries, such as genes being carried on chromosomes, DNA being the genetic material, and gene mapping.

It also explains how hidden recessive alleles keep variation in a population, because they are carried unseen by heterozygotes. Natural selection acts on this variation. There is more on this in Variation.
Genetic databases and testing: modern genetic tests and genome databases identify alleles known to cause single-gene diseases.

Mendel's rules then turn a test result into a risk for a person's children, so the database finding becomes useful advice for a family. There is more on database searches in Bioinformatics: genome databases.
Mendel's laws work best for traits controlled by one gene. Most traits are more complicated, because many genes combine, genes affect each other, and the environment also plays a part.
Complex traits involve multiple gene interactions (polygenic traits): most traits are controlled by many genes, each with a small effect, for example human height, skin colour and eye colour.

Polygenic traits show continuous variation (a range of values, not a few categories), so they don't give simple ratios such as 3 : 1 and can't be predicted with a Punnett square (a grid used to show the possible offspring of a cross).

Genes interacting with one another: the effect of one gene can depend on other genes. For example, a gene that blocks all pigment production (as in albinism) hides the effects of the other genes for colour.
Because of this, the offspring ratios no longer match the simple Mendelian ratios.
Environmental factors: the phenotype (the observable trait) results from the genotype and the environment together, not the genotype alone.
A person's height depends on diet and health in childhood as well as genes; identical twins, with the same genotype, can differ in height and weight.
The flowers of some hydrangea plants are blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil; a plant grown in poor light or poor soil is shorter than its genotype allows.
So Mendelian ratios can't predict traits strongly affected by the environment.
Many of the diseases people worry about most are not caused by a single gene. They arise from genes and lifestyle together, and the environment can even alter how genes are switched on.

Common diseases are multifactorial (caused by several factors together): conditions such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes and most cancers depend on many genes plus lifestyle and environment (diet, exercise, smoking).
So a person's risk can be estimated but not predicted from a simple cross. There is more on this in Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer.

Epigenetic effects: environment and behaviour can switch genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence, and some such changes can be passed on, which Mendel's laws don't account for. There is more on this in Genetic and epigenetic mechanisms.
Even some single-gene situations break the patterns Mendel described. Each exception below has its own pattern, so a simple 3 : 1 prediction fails.
Linked genes on the same chromosome don't assort independently, because they tend to be inherited together. There is more on this in Linkage.
With incomplete dominance neither allele fully hides the other, so the heterozygote is intermediate and the F2 (second generation) gives 1 : 2 : 1 not 3 : 1.
Sex-linked genes (on the sex chromosomes) give different results in sons and daughters.
Many genes have more than two alleles in a population, for example the ABO blood group gene has three (A, B and O). This is multiple alleles, which is different from polygenic inheritance.
Not all genes sit in the nucleus, and even for nuclear genes Mendel's ratios are only chances. Both facts limit how far a prediction can be trusted.

Non-nuclear inheritance: genes in mitochondria (and chloroplasts) are passed on mainly through the egg's cytoplasm, so they are inherited from the mother only and don't follow Mendel's rules. There is more on this in Nuclear and non-nuclear inheritance.
Predictions are probabilities: a ratio describes chances, not exact outcomes, and is reliable only for large numbers of offspring.
Human families are small, so a couple with a 1 in 4 risk may have no affected children or several.
Mendelian genetics also can't say which child will be affected.
Putting the benefits and limitations together gives a balanced judgement. Mendel's work is still valuable, but it is not the whole story of heredity.
Mendelian genetics remains accurate and useful for single-gene traits, in genetic counselling, carrier testing and breeding.
Most human traits and common diseases are complex, so Mendel's rules alone cannot predict them.
Modern genetics adds polygenic risk, gene–environment interaction, epigenetics and whole-genome sequencing (reading all of a person's DNA) to Mendel's principles rather than replacing them.
No two members of a species are exactly alike. These differences are called variation, and they have two very different origins: the genes an organism inherits and the conditions it lives in.
Variation is the differences between individuals of the same species, such as in height, eye colour, blood group or resistance to a disease.
Genetic (inherited) variation is caused by differences in alleles (the different versions of a gene) and genes, so it can be passed to offspring in the DNA.

Environmental (acquired) variation is caused by the conditions an organism lives in, e.g. a scar, a suntan, muscles built by exercise, or a plant's size in poor soil. It is not passed on through the DNA, so a parent's exercised muscles do not appear in its children.
Most characteristics depend on both causes: phenotype (the observable trait) = genotype (the alleles an organism carries) + environment. For example, height is set by genes but also depends on diet.
Only genetic variation matters for evolution, because only it can be inherited and acted on by natural selection (the survival and reproduction of the best-suited individuals).

Traits vary in two patterns. Some sort individuals into a few clear groups, while others spread them along a smooth range. The pattern tells you how many genes are involved and how much the environment matters.
Discontinuous variation: individuals fall into a few distinct groups with no in-between forms, e.g. the human ABO blood group, round or wrinkled pea seeds, or albinism (lack of pigment).

Discontinuous traits are usually controlled by one or a few genes, with little effect from the environment, so a person cannot change their blood group by diet or lifestyle. The data are shown in a bar chart, because each group is a separate category.
Continuous variation: individuals show a smooth range between two extremes, e.g. human height, mass, skin colour or leaf length.

Continuous traits are usually controlled by many genes together with the environment, so there are many small steps between the extremes. Most individuals are near the middle, giving a bell-shaped (normal) distribution shown in a histogram.

Diagram: a bar chart of the four ABO blood groups (discontinuous) beside a bell-shaped histogram of height in a class (continuous). Labels: blood group or height class on the x-axis; number of people on the y-axis.

Sexual reproduction does not make new genes. It reshuffles the alleles already in the population, and it does so so thoroughly that each offspring is a new combination. Asexual reproduction, with no shuffling, shows what is lost without it.
Sexual reproduction does not create new alleles. It produces new combinations of existing alleles in every generation, so every offspring (except identical twins) is genetically unique.

Independent assortment: which chromosome of each homologous pair (the two matching chromosomes, one from each parent) enters a gamete (sex cell) is random and independent of the other pairs. One person can therefore make 2²³, about 8.4 million, different combinations of chromosomes in their gametes.

Random fertilisation: any one of the father's millions of sperm types can fertilise any one of the mother's egg types. Two parents can therefore produce about 8.4 million × 8.4 million, about 70 trillion (7 × 10¹³), different combinations of chromosomes, before other sources of variation are counted.
Two parents: each offspring combines alleles from two different individuals, so alleles that arose in different family lines come together. The choice of mate also varies, which adds further variety.

Asexual reproduction has one parent and no gametes. Cells divide by mitosis (bacteria divide by binary fission), so offspring are genetically identical clones, e.g. bacteria, potato tubers and strawberry runners. Their only source of genetic variation is mutation.
A population of clones may all be destroyed by the same disease or change in the environment, because none has a different allele that could resist it.

Example of the risk: the potatoes grown in Ireland before the Great Famine were mostly a single variety, the Lumper, propagated from tubers, so the plants were almost genetically identical. When potato blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, arrived in 1845, none was resistant and the crop failed across the country.

Diagram: two homologous pairs (one long, one short, coloured to show the chromosome from the mother and from the father) in a cell, the two possible ways they can line up before separating, and the four resulting kinds of gamete. Labels: homologous pair, gamete, maternal chromosome, paternal chromosome.
Sexual reproduction can only shuffle alleles that already exist. Mutation is the only source of new alleles, so it is the original source of all genetic variation.
A mutation is a change in the DNA: in the base sequence of a gene (the order of its chemical letters), or in the structure or number of chromosomes.
Mutations happen spontaneously, mainly as rare copying errors when DNA is replicated (copied before a cell divides).
Mutagens, such as ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays), ultraviolet light and certain chemicals, e.g. some in tobacco smoke, increase the rate of mutation.
Mutations are random: mutagens change the rate but not the direction. The environment does not cause a mutation that helps the organism adapt, and a need for a change does not make it happen.
Each gene mutates rarely, but there are many genes and many individuals, so new mutations arise in every generation.

Organisms that reproduce very fast, such as bacteria, accumulate mutations quickly because they pass through so many generations. Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is an example: a mutation that lets a bacterium survive an antibiotic is quickly passed on to its many descendants.
Mutations are grouped by the size of the change. A gene mutation alters the letters of one gene, while a chromosome mutation changes a whole stretch of a chromosome, or the number of chromosomes.
Gene (point) mutation: a change in the base sequence of one gene, e.g. one base replaced by another, or a base added or lost. It creates a new allele of that gene.
Example of a gene mutation: sickle-cell anaemia is caused by a change of a single base in a gene for haemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells).

Chromosome mutation: a change in the structure of a chromosome, such as a section lost (deletion), copied (duplication), turned around (inversion) or moved to another chromosome (translocation). It affects many genes at once, because a chromosome carries many genes.

Changes in chromosome number also cause variation. Down syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes in total instead of 46). It is a change in number, not one of the four structural changes above.
In plants, whole extra sets of chromosomes (polyploidy) are common; bread wheat has six sets.
A mutation is a random change, so it has no built-in tendency to help or harm. Its effect depends on what the change does and on the environment the organism lives in.

Most mutations are neutral (no effect, e.g. in non-coding DNA, or a change that gives the same amino acid) or harmful; a few are beneficial in a particular environment. So it is false to say a mutation always has a negative effect.
Chromosome mutations are usually harmful in animals, but polyploidy is often tolerated in plants, and many crop plants are polyploid.

Beneficial example, lactase persistence: most mammals stop making lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, after weaning (when they stop drinking milk). A mutation in the DNA controlling the lactase gene keeps it switched on in adults.
The lactase mutation became common in populations with a long history of dairy farming, such as northern Europe including Ireland, because adults who could digest milk had an advantage.
A mutation only matters for the next generation if it reaches the gametes. The cell in which it happens decides whether it is inherited.
Only mutations in cells that make gametes (or in a gamete) are inherited, because only gametes join to form the next generation.
A mutation in a body cell (a somatic mutation), e.g. a skin cell damaged by ultraviolet light, affects only the cells descended from it and may cause cancer, but is not passed to offspring.
Both processes produce genetic variation, but in different ways. Set side by side, they show why natural selection needs both.
What it does: sexual reproduction shuffles existing alleles into new combinations; mutation creates new alleles or new chromosome arrangements.
How often: sexual reproduction happens in every generation, in every offspring; mutation happens rarely and at random.

Effect on the individual: sexual reproduction makes every offspring different, but each allele in the new combination was already present and working in a parent. Most mutations are neutral or harmful, and a few are beneficial.
Organisms: sexual reproduction occurs only in sexually reproducing organisms; mutation occurs in all organisms, including those that reproduce asexually.
Together, mutation supplies new alleles and sexual reproduction spreads them into new combinations, giving the variation on which natural selection acts.
Evolution is the big idea of this chapter, and natural selection is the process that drives it. Adaptation is the link between the two: it is the kind of feature that selection favours.
Evolution is the change in the inherited characteristics of a population (a group of the same species living in one place) over many generations. Over long periods it can produce new species.
In genetic terms, evolution is a change in how common particular alleles (versions of a gene) are in a population.

An adaptation is an inherited feature that increases an organism's chance of surviving and reproducing in its environment. Because it is inherited, it can be passed to offspring, which is what lets selection act on it.
Structural adaptations are body features, for example a cactus's leaves reduced to spines, which reduces water loss.
Behavioural adaptations are ways of acting, for example birds migrating to warmer regions in winter.
Physiological adaptations concern the chemistry of the body, for example lactase (the enzyme that digests milk sugar) made by adults. There is more on this in Variation.

Natural selection is the process by which individuals with inherited characteristics better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more than others, so those characteristics become more common in the next generation. It is the main mechanism of evolution.
A rationale is the reasoning behind an idea. Darwin did not start with a theory: he started with observations on a long sea voyage that the idea of fixed species could not explain.
Charles Darwin (1809–1882), an English naturalist, sailed around the world on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836.

He observed that species varied from place to place: the finches and giant tortoises of the Galápagos Islands differed from island to island and resembled species on the nearby South American mainland.
On the same voyage he found fossils (preserved remains) of extinct animals in South America that resembled living species there, which suggested the living species were related to the extinct ones.

The observations the theory had to explain were: variation within species; the fit between organisms and their environments; species on islands resembling those on the nearest mainland; and fossils of extinct species resembling living ones.
Darwin and Wallace needed an explanation for these observations because the older idea of fixed, separately created species did not explain them.
Observations alone were not enough. Ideas from geology, economics and farming gave Darwin the pieces of his explanation, and a second naturalist reached it independently.
Charles Lyell, a geologist, argued that the Earth is very old and is shaped by slow processes over vast time, which gave time for gradual change in living things.
Thomas Malthus argued that populations tend to grow faster than their food supply, so there is a struggle for existence (not everyone can survive).
Breeders of pigeons, dogs and farm animals showed that selection over generations could change a species greatly. This is artificial selection (humans choosing which animals breed).
Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), working in the Malay Archipelago, reached the same idea independently and wrote to Darwin.
Papers by both were read together at the Linnean Society of London on 1 July 1858. Darwin then published On the Origin of Species in November 1859, giving the evidence in detail.
The theory rests on six numbered steps, from observation to inference, and on one point about what selection acts on. Each step follows from the one before it.

1. Overproduction: organisms produce more offspring than can survive (for example a single cod releases millions of eggs; an oak tree produces thousands of acorns), yet population sizes stay fairly stable over time.
2. Struggle for existence: resources such as food, water, space and mates are limited, so individuals compete, and many die from predation, disease or harsh conditions before reproducing.
3. Variation: individuals of a species differ, and many of the differences are inherited (they come from sexual reproduction and mutation, so offspring are not identical to their parents).

4. Survival of the fittest: individuals whose inherited variations suit them better to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce. Fittest means best adapted to that environment, with the greatest reproductive success, not the strongest. The phrase was coined by Herbert Spencer and later used by Darwin.

5. Inheritance: the survivors pass the favourable alleles to their offspring, so these alleles and characteristics become more common in the next generation, and less favourable ones become less common.

6. Over many generations the population becomes better adapted to its environment. Different populations in different environments change in different ways and, given time and isolation, may become separate species (this is called speciation).
Selection acts on individuals, since they survive or not, but it is populations that evolve; an individual's genes do not change during its life.

Diagram: a flow chart of the six numbered steps, or a three-panel sequence for the peppered moth: a mixed population on a soot-darkened tree, birds eating the visible pale moths, and the next generation mostly dark.
The peppered moth is the classic worked example of natural selection. It shows every step of the theory, and shows that selection follows the environment.

The peppered moth (Biston betularia) rests on tree trunks by day and is eaten by birds. It has a pale, speckled form and a dark (melanic) form; the difference is controlled by one gene, and the dark allele arose by mutation.
Before the Industrial Revolution, tree trunks in England were pale and thick with lichens, and almost all moths were pale, so they were camouflaged; the rare dark moths were easily seen and eaten.

In the 1800s, air pollution from coal killed the lichens and blackened tree trunks with soot near industrial cities such as Manchester. Now the dark moths were camouflaged and the pale ones were eaten more.
So dark moths survived and reproduced more, passing on the dark allele, and the dark form became the most common in industrial areas.

After clean-air laws in the 1950s reduced pollution, the trunks became paler again and the pale form again became the most common. Selection changed direction when the environment changed; evolution is not a fixed march in one direction.
A good theory explains what we already see. Natural selection explains why all living things resemble each other in some ways, and why some organisms are so narrowly specialised.

Common origins: the theory explains why all living things share features such as cells, DNA, the same genetic code and ATP (the energy-carrying molecule), because they are all descended from common ancestors.

More closely related species share a more recent common ancestor. This is the basis of classification by phylogeny (grouping organisms by their evolutionary relationships). There is more on this in Classification.
Highly specialised organisms are the result of natural selection over many generations in a particular, stable environment, producing close adaptation to a narrow way of life.
Examples: the giant panda's diet is almost entirely bamboo, and the koala's is almost entirely eucalyptus leaves.
A good theory also makes predictions. Because natural selection depends on the environment, the theory lets us predict which organisms will cope when conditions change, and which will change fastest.
If the environment changes, the theory predicts that organisms will adapt (if suitable variation exists and there is time), move, or become extinct. They do not change simply because they need to.

Highly specialised organisms, which depend on one food or habitat and often reproduce slowly, are most at risk of extinction when that resource or habitat is lost, because they have no alternative food or home and cannot evolve quickly enough.
Generalists, which can use many foods and habitats, are more likely to survive change, because if one resource disappears they can switch to another.
Organisms with short generation times (little time between birth and reproducing) and large populations are predicted to evolve fastest, because new variation arises and spreads quickly.

Examples: bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics, insects evolve resistance to pesticides, and the influenza virus changes so much each year that the flu vaccine must be updated annually. These predictions are borne out. There is more on antibiotic resistance in Evidence for evolution.
Artificial selection (selective breeding) is the process by which humans choose which individuals breed, so that characteristics useful or attractive to humans become more common over generations.
Dogs: all dog breeds, from the Chihuahua to the Great Dane, were bred from wolves.
Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi were all bred from the wild cabbage (Brassica oleracea), each by selecting a different part or feature of the plant.
Dairy cows have been bred for high milk yield, and modern wheat for large grains that stay on the plant until harvested.

Darwin used artificial selection as evidence that selection over generations can produce large changes, and as an analogy for natural selection: humans select in the farm, the environment selects in the wild.
Both kinds of selection work in the same way, with some individuals reproducing more than others. They differ in who does the choosing and in what is chosen.
Who or what selects: the environment (predators, climate, food supply, disease) in natural selection; humans in artificial selection.

Characteristics favoured: those that increase survival and reproduction in the wild, versus those wanted by humans, which may harm the organism. For example, flat-faced dog breeds such as pugs and bulldogs have breathing problems.
Speed: natural selection is usually slow, over many generations; artificial selection is relatively fast, because humans choose strongly.
Outcome: natural selection leads to adaptation to the environment and, eventually, new species; artificial selection leads to new breeds and varieties of the same species (all dogs are one species).

Genetic variation: usually maintained in large wild populations, but often reduced in artificial selection, because a few chosen individuals are bred and inbred, making the population more vulnerable to disease. The Irish potato example is in Variation.
Similarity: both depend on inherited variation and on some individuals reproducing more than others.
When Darwin proposed the theory it had real gaps, and the main one was inheritance. Later discoveries in genetics filled the gaps and strengthened the theory.
Darwin did not know how characteristics were inherited or where new variation came from.
Many people then believed in blending inheritance (offspring being a mixture of both parents), which would dilute any favourable variation within a few generations.

Mendel published his work on inheritance in 1866, but it was widely recognised only from 1900. It showed that inheritance is by discrete units (genes) that are not blended, so favourable alleles are not diluted away.
Later, the discovery of DNA and mutation explained the source of new variation. There is more on this in Variation.

Combined with genetics in the early 20th century, the theory became the modern synthesis: evolution is a change in allele frequencies in populations, caused mainly by natural selection acting on variation that comes from mutation and sexual reproduction.
Critics in Darwin's day also challenged the evidence for the theory, and it caused controversy beyond science. Later evidence answered the scientific criticisms.
Critics in Darwin's time said there were too few transitional fossils (fossils showing a stage between one type of organism and another), and that the Earth was too young for such slow change.

Since then many transitional fossils have been found, and radiometric dating (dating rocks by the decay of radioactive atoms in them) shows the Earth is about 4.6 billion years old, which gives plenty of time for slow change. There is more on this in Evidence for evolution.
The theory caused controversy because it conflicted with the religious belief, then widespread, that species were created separately in their present form.
Why evolution is accepted as the best explanation is in The importance of the theory.
Fossils are the actual remains or traces of organisms that lived long ago. To use them as evidence you need to know how they form and how old they are.
A fossil is the preserved remains or traces of an organism that lived long ago, for example bones, shells, teeth, footprints or impressions of leaves.

Most fossils form when an organism is quickly buried in sediment (mud or sand) in water. Its soft parts decay, and minerals gradually replace the hard parts as the sediment becomes sedimentary rock (rock formed from compacted sediment).
Whole organisms are occasionally preserved in amber (hardened tree resin), ice or peat, which is why these finds are rare and valuable.
In undisturbed layers of sedimentary rock, deeper layers are older, because new sediment settles on top of old. So fossils in deeper layers are older than those above them.
Radiometric dating measures the decay of radioactive elements in rocks, and gives ages in years rather than just older or younger.
The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. The oldest widely accepted fossils, of simple bacteria-like cells, are about 3.5 billion years old.

Diagram: a cross-section of rock layers with fossils, the deepest layer labelled oldest and the top labelled youngest, showing simpler forms in the lower layers; optionally, three horse feet from Hyracotherium to the modern horse showing toe reduction.
Laid out in order of age, the fossils show a pattern: life changes over time in a consistent direction. This is what evolution predicts and is why the record counts as evidence.
The oldest rocks contain only simple, single-celled life, so complex organisms had not yet appeared.
More complex organisms appear in younger rocks in a consistent order, for example fish before amphibians, and reptiles before birds and mammals.
Most species that ever lived are extinct, so the living world is only a small part of the history of life.
In many groups a series of fossils shows gradual change over time, which is what you would expect if one form slowly gave rise to another.
Some fossils show features of two different groups. These are called transitional fossils, and Archaeopteryx and Tiktaalik are two examples.
Archaeopteryx was found in Germany in 1861, two years after On the Origin of Species, and is about 150 million years old.
It had feathers and wings like a bird, but also teeth, a long bony tail and clawed fingers like a reptile (a dinosaur). So it shows features of both groups.
Tiktaalik was found in 2004 on Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic and is about 375 million years old. It was a fish with scales, fins and gills.
It also had a flat head, a neck, and fin bones like the bones of a limb, so it was intermediate between fish and the first four-limbed land animals.
The team searched rocks of that age because the theory predicted such an animal should have lived then, and the prediction was confirmed. There is more on this in The importance of the theory.
A long series of horse fossils shows gradual change in one group. The record is also incomplete, so you need to know why gaps exist and why they do not weaken the case.
The horse series runs over more than 50 million years, from Hyracotherium, a small animal about the size of a dog with four toes on its front feet, to the modern horse.
The modern horse is much larger, stands on a single toe (the hoof), and has teeth suited to grazing. This matches a change from forest to open grassland.
The fossil record is incomplete, because fossils form only in rare conditions and soft-bodied organisms seldom fossilise.
Many fossils have also been destroyed by erosion or movements of the Earth, and many have not yet been found.
The gaps do not contradict evolution, and every new fossil found has fitted the expected order.
Comparing the bodies of different species shows similarities that are hard to explain unless the species share ancestors. Structures with the same basic plan but different jobs are called homologous.
Homologous structures have the same basic structure because they were inherited from a common ancestor, but are adapted for different functions.
The pentadactyl (five-digit) limb is the classic example: the human arm (grasping), bat wing (flying), whale flipper (swimming) and horse leg (running).
All of them have one upper bone (humerus), two lower bones (radius and ulna), wrist bones (carpals), palm bones (metacarpals) and finger bones (phalanges), differently shaped and sized.
This is divergent evolution: one ancestral form adapted in different directions, so the same bones were modified for different uses.
Diagram: the forelimbs of a human, a bat and a whale side by side, each bone group shaded the same way in all three; label humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges.
Not every similarity points to a shared ancestor, and some structures have lost their original job. Analogous and vestigial structures show two different things.

Analogous structures have the same function but different structures and origins, for example the wing of a bird (bones and feathers) and the wing of an insect (a thin membrane of chitin with no bones).
Analogous structures are not evidence of common ancestry. They show that similar environments select similar solutions, which is called convergent evolution.
Vestigial structures are reduced, with little or no function, but were functional in the organism's ancestors.

Examples are the human coccyx (the remains of a tail), the human appendix (a much-reduced part of the gut, larger in plant-eating mammals), the small pelvic and leg bones inside some whales, and the tiny wings of flightless birds such as the kiwi.
Vestigial structures make sense only if the organism descended from ancestors that used them.
