Embryos (animals in the earliest stages of development) can reveal ancestry that adult bodies hide. Vertebrates, the animals with backbones, are a good example.

Comparative embryology compares the development of embryos. The early embryos of all vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals) look very similar: all have a tail and a series of pouches in the throat region (pharyngeal pouches).
In fish these pouches develop into gills; in humans they develop into parts of the ear, jaw and throat, and the tail is reduced to the coccyx.
The shared early stages suggest that all vertebrates inherited the same basic plan of development from a common ancestor, which was then modified in each group.
Limitations: the similarity is in early development, not in adult structures, and embryos do not pass through the adult forms of their ancestors.
In the 19th century Ernst Haeckel published drawings that exaggerated the similarity of embryos; modern photographs confirm the shared features but not the exaggeration.
Diagram: early embryos of a fish, a chicken and a human side by side, labelled tail and pharyngeal pouches.
Evolution predicts that the more closely two species are related, the more similar their DNA and proteins should be. Comparing these molecules tests that prediction independently of anatomy.
Phylogeny is the evolutionary history of a group; phylogenetic trees show which species share the most recent common ancestors. There is more on this in Classification.
Species closely related by anatomy and fossils should also have the most similar DNA and proteins, because they have had less time to accumulate differences since their common ancestor.
All living things use DNA, the same four bases, almost the same genetic code and the same ATP (the energy-carrying molecule of cells). This is evidence that all life shares one origin.
Human and chimpanzee DNA is about 98–99% identical in comparable sequences; human DNA is less similar to that of a mouse, and less again to that of a fish.
Cytochrome c is a protein used in aerobic respiration in nearly all eukaryotes (organisms whose cells have a nucleus). Its amino-acid sequence is identical in humans and chimpanzees.
It differs by one amino acid between humans and rhesus monkeys, and differs more in more distantly related organisms such as yeast.
The trees built from DNA and proteins largely agree with those built from anatomy and fossils. Independent lines of evidence giving the same pattern are strong support for evolution.
Molecular evidence has also corrected some classifications based on appearance, for example the domains of life (the three largest groupings of living things).
Bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics, and the way this happens is natural selection taking place in front of us. Once you can describe the steps, you can explain it in an exam.

An antibiotic is a drug that kills or stops the growth of bacteria; antibiotics have no effect on viruses. Antibiotic resistance is the ability of bacteria to survive an antibiotic that would normally kill them.

1. A bacterial population varies: a few bacteria carry a mutation (or a resistance gene on a plasmid, a small ring of DNA) that makes them resistant, for example by producing an enzyme that breaks down the antibiotic.
2. The antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria.
3. The resistant bacteria survive and, with less competition, reproduce rapidly by binary fission (splitting in two), as often as every 20 minutes in ideal conditions.
4. They pass the resistance gene to their offspring, and can pass plasmids carrying it to other bacteria, even of other species.
5. The population soon becomes mostly resistant, and the antibiotic no longer works.

Diagram: four panels of a bacterial population: mostly non-resistant cells with a few resistant ones (shaded), then antibiotic added and non-resistant cells die, then resistant cells multiply, then the population is mostly resistant.
A common mistake is to think antibiotics create resistance. The evidence shows that resistance is already there, and that selection simply favours it.
The resistance mutations are present before the antibiotic is used: the antibiotic selects them but does not cause them.
In 1952 Joshua and Esther Lederberg showed this by growing bacteria that had never met the antibiotic and finding resistant colonies already among them.
MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is resistant to many common antibiotics and causes infections that are hard to treat, especially in hospitals.
Natural selection is observed directly, within years, because bacteria have huge populations and very short generation times.

Overuse of antibiotics, for example prescribing them for viral infections or in farm animals, speeds up resistance by applying selection more often. There is more on this in Science, scientists and society.
Natural selection can be seen in wild populations too, and the way species are spread across the world supports common descent.
Peter and Rosemary Grant studied the medium ground finch on the Galápagos island of Daphne Major. In a drought in 1977, small soft seeds became scarce and mainly large, hard seeds were left.
Most finches died, but birds with deeper (larger) beaks, which could crack the hard seeds, survived more, and their offspring had, on average, deeper beaks than the generation before.
Natural selection was measured happening in one generation.

Biogeography (the distribution of species): species on oceanic islands resemble those on the nearest mainland rather than those on islands with similar conditions elsewhere. The Galápagos species resemble South American species.
This is explained by colonisation from the mainland followed by evolution, not by separate creation for each environment.
Speciation is the formation of new species, and it is evidence that evolution can produce the diversity of life. One route to speciation is when a population is split by a physical barrier.

A species is a group that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring, so a new species has formed when two populations can no longer interbreed: they are reproductively isolated. There is more on this in Key concepts of information transfer.
1. A population is split by a barrier, such as a sea, a mountain range or a river, so the two groups no longer interbreed.
2. Different mutations arise in each group.
3. The environments differ, so natural selection favours different characteristics in each.
4. Over many generations the two populations become so different that they could not interbreed even if they met; they are now separate species.
Diagram: a flow diagram of geographical speciation: one population, then a barrier divides it, then different mutations and selection on each side, then two species that can't interbreed.
The finches of the Galápagos show geographical speciation in a real place. Different islands acted as separate environments.
More than a dozen species of finch on the Galápagos are descended from a common ancestor that arrived from the South American mainland.
Populations on different islands, eating different foods, evolved beaks of different shapes, for example large, deep beaks for cracking seeds and thin, pointed beaks for catching insects.
Why it is evidence: new species have been seen to form, and the pattern of species (groups of similar species on neighbouring islands) is what the theory predicts.
A barrier is not always needed. In plants, a change in the number of chromosomes can make a new species almost at once.

In plants, a new species can form in one or a few generations when a change in chromosome number (polyploidy, having extra sets of chromosomes) makes offspring unable to breed with the parent species. There is more on this in Variation.
The cordgrass Spartina anglica arose in southern England in the late 1800s from a cross between a native European cordgrass and an introduced American one.
The chromosomes then doubled, which made the hybrid fertile. It is now a separate, widespread species, including on Irish coasts.
Each source of evidence has weak points, but together they make a strong case because they are independent of each other.
Each source has limitations: an incomplete fossil record, embryos similar only early on, and analogous structures that can mislead.
The sources are independent of each other and all point to the same conclusion: common descent with change over time, driven largely by natural selection.

Antibiotic resistance, the finch beaks, the peppered moth and new species such as Spartina anglica show evolution happening now. There is more on the peppered moth in The theory of evolution by natural selection.

In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation, not a guess. Evolution by natural selection (the process by which better-suited individuals survive and reproduce more) meets every part of that definition.

Evolution by natural selection is a broad explanation of a huge range of observations, including the diversity of life, adaptation, shared features, the fossil record and the distribution of species, so one idea accounts for many different kinds of evidence.
It is supported by evidence from many independent sources and it makes testable predictions. It could be shown false by evidence, but no such evidence has been found.

It is falsifiable (open to being proved wrong). Finding fossils of mammals in rocks older than the first fish, or finding that the DNA of closely related species was no more similar than that of distant species, would contradict it.

The everyday meaning of theory (a guess or hunch) is not the scientific meaning. Saying evolution is only a theory misunderstands the word: in science, a theory is the highest status an explanation reaches.
The cell theory (all living things are made of cells) and the germ theory of disease (microorganisms cause many diseases) are theories in the same sense, and nobody calls them guesses.

Two parts should be distinguished. The fact of evolution is that living things have changed over time and share common ancestors, which the evidence shows directly. The theory of natural selection is the explanation of how that change happens.
Acceptance of evolution rests on how often it has been tested and how well it has survived. Each new kind of evidence was a chance for it to fail, and it did not.

It has been tested for over 160 years, since 1859 (the year Darwin published On the Origin of Species), by scientists in every field of biology, and also in geology, chemistry and physics, for example radiometric dating of the Earth.

Evidence that was not known to Darwin has confirmed it: genetics (Mendel's work, recognised from 1900), the structure of DNA (1953), molecular comparisons of DNA and proteins, and many transitional fossils (fossils showing features intermediate between two groups).
Each new kind of evidence could have contradicted the theory, and did not. This is why independent confirmation counts for so much.
Its predictions have been confirmed. Tiktaalik, a transitional fossil, was found in rocks of the age the theory predicted, and trees built from DNA match those built from anatomy.
Evolution can also be seen happening: bacteria evolve resistance to new antibiotics and insects evolve resistance to pesticides, as the theory predicts.

It is accepted by almost all biologists and by scientific academies around the world, and is the framework used in all biological research. Acceptance is based on evidence, not on authority or majority opinion.

Like all theories, it has been refined: it was combined with genetics into the modern synthesis. Scientists still debate details such as how fast evolution happens and the roles of chance and of epigenetics (chemical changes that switch genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence).
Debate about details within the theory is normal science, not doubt about evolution itself.
Darwin was not the first to propose that species change. Comparing his explanation with an earlier rival, Lamarck's, shows why natural selection is the better one.

Lamarck's theory (Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, 1809) said that organisms change during their lives through the use or disuse of body parts, and pass these acquired characteristics to their offspring. For example, giraffes stretching to reach leaves would have offspring with longer necks.

Acquired characteristics are not passed on through DNA, the molecule that carries inherited information, so they do not reach the next generation. A weightlifter's children are not born with large muscles.
In the 1880s August Weismann cut off the tails of mice over several generations, yet their offspring still had normal tails. This was direct evidence against inheritance of acquired characteristics.
Natural selection works with variation that already exists in a population, so it explains adaptation without any need for the organism to try. It is also supported by genetics.

Darwin's explanation of the giraffe: giraffes with slightly longer necks, through inherited variation, reached more food in times of shortage, so they survived and reproduced more and passed on the alleles (versions of a gene) for longer necks.
Epigenetic inheritance is a small, limited exception, in which some chemical changes to genes can be passed on. It does not restore Lamarck's theory.
A scientific explanation has to be testable. Comparing natural selection with special creation shows why evolution counts as the best available explanation.
Special creation, the belief that species were created separately in their present forms, is a matter of religious faith rather than a scientific theory, because it makes no testable predictions.

Special creation does not explain the evidence, such as homologous structures (similar bone layouts in different species), vestigial structures (reduced structures with little or no use), the order of fossils, or the pattern of DNA similarity.
Many religious people and organisations accept evolution. Science and faith answer different kinds of questions, so accepting one does not require rejecting the other.
Evolution by natural selection explains all the evidence together, with one mechanism, and makes predictions. No other explanation does this, so it is the best available explanation.

Evolution is not just something that happened in the distant past. It can be observed today, especially in organisms with short generations (so changes build up quickly) and large populations (so there is plenty of variation).

Examples of evolution observed now include antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA, the Galápagos finches' beaks after the 1977 drought, the peppered moth, and the new cordgrass species Spartina anglica.

Viruses evolve fast. New variants of the virus that causes COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2), such as Delta and Omicron, spread because their mutations helped them spread or escape immunity, so vaccines were updated.
Flu vaccines are updated every year for the same reason: the flu viruses change, so last year's vaccine may no longer match.
Pests and weeds evolve resistance to the pesticides and herbicides used against them, because the few resistant individuals survive and breed.
Cancer cells in a tumour can evolve resistance to the drugs used to treat them, by the same process of selection.

Human activity is now a strong selection pressure (a factor that decides which individuals survive): antibiotic and pesticide use, climate change and habitat loss. Highly specialised species with slow reproduction are least able to evolve fast enough.
Evolution is the idea that ties the rest of biology together. The geneticist Theodosius Dobzhansky wrote in 1973 that “nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution”.
It explains the unity of life (shared cells, DNA, genetic code and ATP, from common ancestry) and its diversity (adaptation and speciation, the formation of new species).
Classification: modern classification is based on evolutionary relationships (phylogeny), so species are grouped by how closely they are related, and new DNA evidence keeps refining it.
Form and function: it explains why structures suit their functions, since natural selection favoured individuals whose structures did the job better.

Genetics and technology: comparing the genomes (complete sets of DNA) of different species to find which genes are shared and what they do depends on evolutionary relationships. There is more on this in Bioinformatics: genome databases.

Limits of the theory: it explains how life changed and diversified once it existed. How the first living cells arose from non-living chemicals is a separate question, still being researched, and is not part of the theory of natural selection.
Evolutionary thinking has practical uses. It helps people in medicine, agriculture and conservation to predict and manage change in living things.

Medicine and health: it guides the responsible use of antibiotics to slow resistance (antibiotic stewardship), the yearly updating of flu vaccines, the tracking of new virus variants, and the treatment of cancers that evolve drug resistance.
Because of shared ancestry, studies of other organisms can tell us about human biology and disease. For example, mice share many genes with humans.
Agriculture and food: selective breeding of crops and animals (artificial selection, where people choose which individuals breed), and managing pesticide use to slow resistance.
Keeping varied crop genes protects against disease, because a variable crop is unlikely to be wiped out by one pathogen. This is the lesson of the Irish potato.

Conservation and sustainability: it shows why genetic variation in a population matters for its survival when the environment changes, since some individuals may carry alleles that suit the new conditions.

Small, inbred populations of endangered species are at risk because they have little variation. Specialised species are vulnerable to climate change and habitat loss because they cannot adapt quickly.

Cells carry out thousands of chemical reactions, and left alone most of them would be far too slow to keep a cell alive. Catalysts speed reactions up, and enzymes are the catalysts that living things make for themselves.
A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up or permanently changed by it, so it can be used again and again.
A catalyst does not change which products form or how much product is made in the end; it only makes the reaction reach that point faster.
An enzyme is a biological catalyst: a catalyst made by a living cell.

Almost all enzymes are globular proteins (proteins folded into a compact, rounded ball), folded into a precise three-dimensional shape. That shape decides what the enzyme can do. There is more on protein structure in Structures of biomolecules.
Because enzymes are proteins, they are made at ribosomes (the tiny structures in a cell where proteins are built), following the instructions in a gene (the length of DNA that codes for the protein).
Because an enzyme is a protein that is reused rather than consumed, it has a set of properties that follow from that.
Enzymes are needed only in small amounts, because each molecule is reused many times; catalase, among the fastest, breaks down millions of hydrogen peroxide molecules per second.
Enzymes are unchanged at the end of the reaction, which is why the same molecule can start work on another substrate straight away.
Enzymes are specific: each acts on one reaction or one type of reaction, because only a substrate of the right shape fits the enzyme's active site (the region where the substrate binds).

Enzyme activity is affected by temperature and pH, and enzymes are denatured (their shape is changed so that they stop working) by heat and by extremes of pH. There is more on this in Investigation: rate of enzyme activity.
Enzyme names usually give away the job the enzyme does. Enzymes also work in different places, depending on whether their job is inside or outside the cell.

Most enzyme names end in -ase, and many are named after their substrate (the molecule the enzyme acts on), so the name tells you the job: maltase acts on maltose, lipase on lipids, protease on proteins, sucrase on sucrose.
Some older names, such as pepsin and trypsin, don't follow this rule, so don't assume that every enzyme name ends in -ase.

Most enzymes work inside the cell that made them (intracellular), for example the enzymes of respiration (releasing energy from food) in the cytoplasm and mitochondria and of photosynthesis (making food using light) in chloroplasts.

Some enzymes are secreted to work outside the cell (extracellular), for example digestive enzymes released into the gut and the enzymes that fungi and bacteria release onto their food. There is more on this in The Digestive System.
Even a reaction that releases energy overall needs a push to get started. An enzyme works by making that push smaller, not by adding energy.
Activation energy is the minimum energy that reacting molecules need before a reaction can start: the energy needed to break or strain existing bonds.
Think of activation energy as an energy hill that must be climbed even when the reaction releases energy overall.

Without a catalyst, most reactions of metabolism (the chemical reactions of life) have such a high activation energy that, at body temperature (37 °C), they would happen far too slowly to keep a cell alive.
Heating would supply the energy, but high temperatures would damage cells and their proteins, so heating is not an option for living things.

An enzyme provides an alternative route for the reaction with a lower activation energy, so many more molecules have enough energy to react at the temperature of the cell, and the reaction is many times faster.
The overall energy change of the reaction (energy released or taken in) stays the same; only the hill to be climbed gets lower.
Diagram: energy-profile graph, energy on the y-axis, progress of reaction on the x-axis. Reactants high on the left, products lower on the right.
Draw two humps, a tall one labelled without enzyme and a lower one labelled with enzyme. Mark each activation energy with a vertical arrow from the reactants to the top of its hump.
Every enzyme reaction has two partners: the enzyme and the molecule it works on. One small region of the enzyme does the work, and its shape is what makes the enzyme selective.
The substrate is the molecule an enzyme acts on; the products are the molecules made.
Example: catalase acts on its substrate hydrogen peroxide: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂.
The active site is a small region of the enzyme, a pocket or groove on its surface, where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place.
The active site's shape, and the chemical charges in it, are complementary to the substrate, meaning the two fit together like matching pieces.
The active site is a part of the enzyme, not of the substrate. The substrate's shape is complementary to the active site, not the same as it.
Once the substrate meets the active site, the reaction follows three steps. Together they make the active-site (lock-and-key) model of enzyme action.
1. The substrate collides with the enzyme and binds to the active site, forming an enzyme–substrate complex (the enzyme and substrate joined together).
Enzyme and substrate molecules meet by random movement, so anything that increases collisions (more substrate, more enzyme, higher temperature) increases the rate, up to a point.

2. While the substrate is held in the active site, the enzyme lowers the activation energy, for example by straining the bonds that must break, or by holding two substrate molecules close together in the right position to react.
The substrate is then converted to products, forming an enzyme–product complex.
3. The products have a different shape, no longer fit the active site, and are released.
The active site is then free and unchanged, ready to bind another substrate molecule, which is why one enzyme molecule can be used again and again.
In summary: enzyme + substrate → enzyme–substrate complex → enzyme + products.

Diagram: three stages in a row: enzyme with active site and complementary substrate approaching; enzyme–substrate complex; unchanged enzyme with two products leaving. Label enzyme, active site, substrate, enzyme–substrate complex and products. A matching diagram for a joining reaction is optional.
The same active-site mechanism works whichever way a reaction runs. Metabolism has reactions that break molecules down and reactions that build them up, and enzymes catalyse both.
In catabolic reactions one substrate is split into smaller products, for example amylase splits starch into maltose.
In anabolic reactions two or more substrates are joined into a larger product. For example, DNA polymerase joins nucleotides (the building blocks of DNA) into a new DNA strand when DNA is copied.
Another anabolic example is ATP synthase, which joins ADP and phosphate into ATP, the molecule cells use to carry energy.

A cell contains thousands of different molecules but does not react them all at random. Enzymes are selective: each one picks out its own substrate, and that selectivity comes from the shape of the active site.
Specificity means that each enzyme catalyses only one reaction, or one type of reaction, because only a substrate with the complementary shape fits its active site.
This is what selective catalysts means: amylase digests starch but not protein or fat; pepsin digests protein but not starch.
The lock-and-key model is the simplest explanation: the substrate (the key) fits only the active site (the lock) of the right shape.
The lock-and-key model was later refined to the induced-fit model, in which the active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds. There is more on this in Enzyme structure and specificity.
Because enzymes are specific, a cell needs thousands of different enzymes, one for each of its reactions, and it can control a reaction by making, or not making, the one enzyme that catalyses it.
Anything that changes the shape of the active site stops the substrate fitting, so the enzyme stops working: for example high temperature or extreme pH (denaturation).
A change in the enzyme's amino-acid sequence (the order of the amino acids that make up the protein), caused by a mutation in its gene, also changes the active site and stops the substrate fitting.
Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions in a living thing. Enzymes make these reactions possible, and they usually work in sequences called pathways.
Every reaction of metabolism is catalysed by its own specific enzyme.
Without enzymes, the reactions that keep cells alive (respiration, photosynthesis, protein synthesis, DNA copying, digestion) would be far too slow at the temperatures and pH inside living things.
Most processes are metabolic pathways: a sequence of reactions, each catalysed by a different enzyme, in which the product of one reaction is the substrate of the next.
Respiration and photosynthesis are such pathways. There is more on this in Respiration and Photosynthesis.
Diagram: a pathway written as A → B → C → D, with enzyme 1, enzyme 2 and enzyme 3 written over the arrows.
Because every step in a pathway needs its own enzyme, a cell controls its chemistry by controlling its enzymes.
A cell controls which reactions happen, and how fast, by switching on or off the genes for particular enzymes and by activating or inhibiting enzymes already made.
If one enzyme in a pathway is missing, the pathway stops at that step: its substrate builds up and the later products are not made.
Many enzymes need a non-protein helper to work: a mineral ion (for example magnesium for many enzymes that use ATP) or a coenzyme made from a vitamin. There is more on this in Minerals.
Because each reaction depends on one enzyme, blocking or losing that enzyme has serious effects. Some poisons act this way, and some inherited or common conditions come from a missing enzyme.

Some drugs and poisons work by blocking an enzyme: for example some insecticides and nerve agents inhibit the enzyme that breaks down a neurotransmitter (a chemical messenger between nerve cells). There is more on this in Conduction across the synaptic cleft and its disruption.

Lactose intolerance: many adults make little lactase, the enzyme that digests lactose (milk sugar), so undigested lactose passes to the large intestine, where bacteria ferment it, causing bloating, wind, cramps and diarrhoea.
Lactose-free milk is made using lactase, which digests the lactose in the milk before it is drunk.

Phenylketonuria (PKU): an inherited lack of the enzyme that converts the amino acid phenylalanine into another amino acid (tyrosine), so phenylalanine builds up in the blood and damages the developing brain.
PKU is detected by the heel-prick test given to newborn babies in Ireland, and is controlled by a diet low in phenylalanine.

An enzyme is a protein, and the way its chain is folded decides what it can do. Folding builds a small pocket called the active site (the region where the substrate, the molecule the enzyme acts on, binds and is converted).

An enzyme's three-dimensional shape is set by the sequence of amino acids in its polypeptide chain (its primary structure), and that sequence is set by its gene, so the gene ultimately decides the shape.

The chain coils and folds (secondary structure), then folds further into a precise globular (rounded) shape (tertiary structure); some enzymes are made of more than one polypeptide (quaternary structure).
The active site is formed by folding: it is made of a small number of amino acids, often far apart in the chain, that folding brings together into a pocket or cleft.
Most of the rest of the enzyme holds these few active-site amino acids in exactly the right positions, so the whole molecule matters even though only a small part touches the substrate.

The R groups (side groups, the part of each amino acid that differs from the others) of the active-site amino acids give the site its shape and its pattern of charges and of water-attracting and water-repelling regions.
The R groups bind the substrate by weak attractions (hydrogen bonds and ionic attractions between opposite charges), and some take part directly in the reaction.

An enzyme acts only on particular substrates, a property called specificity. It comes from the active site's shape and chemistry, and that shape is only as stable as the bonds that hold the protein folded.

Specificity depends on two things: the shape of the active site (only a substrate of complementary shape fits) and its chemistry (only a substrate with matching charges and groups is held in the right position).
A molecule of similar shape but with the wrong charges is not catalysed, because its groups are not held in the correct position.
The shape is held by hydrogen bonds, by ionic bonds between charged R groups, and by attractions between water-repelling R groups; these are all weak bonds.
Disulfide (sulfur) bridges between cysteine units (cysteine is an amino acid that contains sulfur) are strong covalent bonds that also hold the shape.
Because most of these bonds are weak, the shape is easily changed, which is why enzymes are sensitive to conditions.

Diagram: a folded polypeptide chain drawn as a looping ribbon, with three or four amino acids (circles) from distant parts of the chain meeting to form a labelled active site; label polypeptide chain, R groups of active-site amino acids, active site, a hydrogen bond and a disulfide bridge.
An enzyme works only while its active site keeps its exact shape. Anything that alters the shape of the protein, or the amino acids that make it, changes how well it works.
Activity depends on the active site keeping its shape.
Heat makes the enzyme molecule vibrate until weak bonds break; a change in pH changes the charges on R groups (by adding or removing hydrogen ions), breaking ionic and hydrogen bonds.

Either way the active site loses its shape, the substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme is denatured (permanently changed in shape and unable to work). The effects on rate, and the investigations, are in “Investigation: rate of enzyme activity”.
A change in a single amino acid can change the shape or charge of the active site, so a mutation in the gene can make an enzyme work less well or not at all.
Example: in phenylketonuria the enzyme that converts phenylalanine is faulty, so the conversion does not happen properly.
Some enzymes need a cofactor, such as a metal ion, held in or near the active site to complete its shape or chemistry; without it the enzyme is inactive.
Enzymes differ in how narrowly they choose a substrate. Some enzymes also have structures that keep their shape in conditions that would ruin most others.
Some enzymes act on only one substrate (absolute specificity): for example, urease acts only on urea, breaking it into ammonia and carbon dioxide.

Others act on a group of substrates that share the same type of bond (group specificity): for example, lipase acts on many different triglycerides, and proteases such as pepsin break peptide bonds in many different proteins.
A rigid lock-and-key active site does not explain group specificity well, because one fixed shape cannot fit many different substrates; the induced-fit model does.

Enzymes that work in extreme conditions have structures that hold their shape there: for example, Taq polymerase, from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus, stays active at temperatures that denature human enzymes.
Pepsin keeps its shape in the strong acid of the stomach, where most enzymes are denatured.
The induced-fit model describes an active site that is flexible, not a fixed mould. It explains how an enzyme grips its substrate, strains it and releases the products, then is ready to go again.

The induced-fit model says the active site is flexible, not rigid. Before binding, its shape is close to, but not exactly, complementary to the substrate; binding of the substrate induces (causes) a change in the enzyme's shape that produces a close fit.
1. The substrate collides with the enzyme and starts to bind to the active site through weak attractions to its R groups.
2. Binding causes the enzyme to change shape: the active site moulds itself around the substrate, like a glove taking the shape of a hand, forming a tightly fitting enzyme–substrate complex.
3. The change in shape puts strain on particular bonds in the substrate, or brings reacting groups of two substrates close together in the correct orientation.

3 (continued). The R groups of the active site may lend or take hydrogen ions or electrons, which lowers the activation energy (the energy needed to start the reaction), and the substrate is converted to products.
4. The products no longer fit the active site closely, so they are released.
5. The enzyme returns to its original shape, unchanged and ready to bind another substrate molecule.
The earlier lock-and-key model treated the active site as rigid. Induced fit replaced it because it explains observations that a rigid site cannot.
Example: the enzyme hexokinase (used in the first stage of respiration) closes around its substrate glucose like a clamp when glucose binds; structural studies of enzymes showed this change of shape.
Induced fit explains why some enzymes act on several similar substrates: a flexible site can mould around each of them.
Induced fit explains how binding itself helps catalysis: the shape change strains the substrate's bonds, lowering the activation energy.
Induced fit explains why molecules of similar shape may bind but not react: they do not induce the correct change of shape.
Lock and key remains a useful simple model of specificity.

Diagram: induced fit in four labelled stages: (1) an enzyme whose active site does not quite match the approaching substrate; (2) substrate binding and the active site changing shape around it, forming the enzyme–substrate complex, with arrows showing the change.

Diagram (continued): (3) products formed in the active site; (4) products released and the enzyme back in its original shape. Label enzyme, active site, substrate, change in shape, enzyme–substrate complex and products.
Diagram (contrast): include a one-line sketch of lock and key, with a rigid active site that already fits the substrate exactly.
The two models differ in whether the active site can move. Setting them side by side shows why induced fit explains more.
Active site: rigid, with a fixed shape that exactly matches the substrate (lock and key); flexible, changing shape when the substrate binds (induced fit).
Fit: an exact fit before binding (lock and key); a close fit only after binding (induced fit).
Role of binding: it holds the substrate only (lock and key); the change of shape itself helps the reaction by straining bonds (induced fit).
Specificity explained: absolute specificity only (lock and key); both absolute and group specificity (induced fit), because a flexible site can mould around several similar substrates.
An enzyme is a biological catalyst, so what we want to know in an investigation is how fast it works. That speed is called the rate, and it is always measured against time.
The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction is the amount of substrate (the molecule the enzyme acts on) converted into product per unit time, e.g. cm³ of oxygen produced per minute.
The rate can be measured either by how fast a product appears or by how fast the substrate disappears, whichever is easier to detect for that reaction.
Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide (2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂); the rate is measured by the oxygen released, as foam or as a volume of gas.
Amylase digests starch to maltose; the rate is measured by the time taken for the starch to disappear, tested with iodine.
Rate = amount of product ÷ time: e.g. 30 cm³ of foam in 2 minutes gives a rate of 15 cm³ per minute.

Where the time taken to reach an end-point (such as the starch disappearing) is measured, rate = 1 ÷ time: starch gone in 120 s gives a rate of 1/120 = 0.0083 s⁻¹, often written as 1000/time to give whole numbers.
A shorter time means a faster rate, because the same change has been completed more quickly.
Measure the initial rate, at the start of the reaction (e.g. in the first one or two minutes), because the reaction slows as substrate is used up.
Primary data are the results you collect yourself. Presenting them clearly in a table and a graph is how you show the pattern in your results.
A results table has the independent variable (the factor you change) in the first column, then the repeat readings, the mean and the rate, each column headed with its unit.
A graph has the independent variable on the x-axis and the rate on the y-axis, with points plotted accurately and joined by a smooth curve or line of best fit.
All five investigations use the same small set of enzymes, substrates and equipment. Knowing what each is for makes the methods easy to follow.
Catalase is found in almost all cells that use oxygen, where it breaks down hydrogen peroxide, a toxic by-product of metabolism. Good sources are celery, potato, liver and yeast.

Catalase extract: blend a fixed mass of chopped celery (e.g. 20 g) with distilled water (e.g. 100 cm³), then filter through muslin or filter paper. Make one batch and use it for every test, so the enzyme is the same each time.
Amylase: a commercial (e.g. fungal) amylase solution made up at a fixed concentration; starch solution (e.g. 1%) is its substrate. Saliva contains amylase but is avoided for hygiene reasons.
Equipment for measuring: 100 cm³ graduated cylinders, syringes or graduated pipettes for measuring volumes, thermometer to check temperatures, stopwatch to time each run, electronic balance.

Other equipment: test tubes and boiling tubes, blender or mortar and pestle, knife and chopping board, filter funnel, spotting tile and droppers, conical flask with bung and delivery tube, trough, labels.
Water baths can be thermostatically controlled electric baths, or beakers of water warmed with kettle water or cooled with ice, checked with a thermometer.

Reagents: hydrogen peroxide solution (one stock of fixed concentration), buffer solutions or buffer tablets of known pH, washing-up liquid, distilled water, starch solution, amylase solution and iodine solution.

Four ideas recur across the investigations: a buffer to hold pH steady, washing-up liquid to make the oxygen measurable in the foam methods, a waiting time so the mixture reaches the right temperature, and a control to prove the enzyme is responsible.
A buffer is a solution that keeps the pH constant even when acids or alkalis are produced or added.
A buffer at pH 7 (or at the enzyme's optimum) is added in every investigation except the pH investigation, so that pH is a controlled variable (kept the same each time).
In the foam methods, a drop of washing-up liquid traps the oxygen released by catalase as a foam, so its volume can be read in a graduated cylinder; the same amount is added every time.

Reaching temperature (equilibration): the enzyme and the substrate are placed in the same water bath, in separate containers, for about 5 minutes before they are mixed, so the reaction starts at the chosen temperature.
A control in each investigation uses enzyme that has been boiled (denatured), or distilled water in place of the enzyme, with everything else the same.
The control shows that the oxygen (or the loss of starch) is caused by the enzyme and not by the substrate breaking down on its own.
The chemicals and equipment here are mostly mild, but several can harm skin, eyes or clothes if handled carelessly.
Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidising agent that irritates or burns the eyes and skin; wear safety glasses (and gloves), measure it with a syringe, and wash any splash off with plenty of water.
Buffers of very low or very high pH are irritants, so wear safety glasses.
Use tongs or a test-tube holder and take care with boiling water and hot water baths; keep electrical water baths and blenders away from spilt water.
Take care with knives and blender blades. If liver is used, treat it as raw meat: wear gloves, keep it off benches used for other work and wash hands afterwards.
Iodine solution stains skin and clothes, so handle it with care. Never eat or drink in the laboratory, because chemicals could be swallowed.
Here we vary how much hydrogen peroxide (the substrate) the same amount of catalase has to work on, and see how the rate of oxygen production changes.
Aim: to investigate the effect of substrate (hydrogen peroxide) concentration on the rate of catalase activity, by changing only the substrate so any change in rate must be due to it.

Hypothesis: “Increasing the concentration of hydrogen peroxide increases the rate of oxygen production, because more substrate molecules collide with active sites per second, until all the active sites are occupied and the rate levels off.”

Independent variable: hydrogen peroxide concentration, made by diluting the stock with distilled water to 0%, 20%, 40%, 60%, 80% and 100% of the stock (e.g. 2 cm³ stock + 8 cm³ water = 20%), always to the same total volume (e.g. 10 cm³).
Dependent variable (the one you measure): volume of oxygen collected in the first minute (cm³), giving the rate in cm³ per minute.

Controlled variables: volume of the same celery extract (so enzyme concentration is constant), temperature (water bath at e.g. 25 °C), pH (same volume of pH 7 buffer), total volume of solution, timing and apparatus.
Control: the 100% hydrogen peroxide with boiled extract (or with water in place of the extract), which gives little or no oxygen; the 0% tube also shows that no oxygen forms without substrate.
The oxygen given off is collected in an upturned cylinder of water, so its volume can be read directly.
1. Fill a graduated cylinder with water and turn it upside down in a trough of water, with no air at the top.

2. Put 10 cm³ of the first hydrogen peroxide dilution and 2 cm³ of pH 7 buffer in a conical flask (or boiling tube) in the water bath, with 2 cm³ of celery extract in a separate tube beside it, for about 5 minutes.
3. Place the end of the delivery tube under the mouth of the upturned cylinder.
4. Add the extract to the flask, immediately put in the bung with the delivery tube, and start the stopwatch.
5. Read the volume of oxygen collected in the cylinder after 1 minute (or every 30 seconds for 3 minutes).
6. Rinse the flask and repeat for each concentration. Do each concentration three times and calculate the mean rate.
Alternatives: a gas syringe connected to the flask measures the oxygen volume more accurately than collection over water; or the foam method used in the pH investigation can be used.

Another alternative: filter-paper discs soaked in catalase extract are dropped into each concentration and the time for each disc to rise to the surface (buoyed by oxygen bubbles) is timed, with rate = 1 ÷ time.

Diagram: a conical flask in a water bath, with a bung and delivery tube leading under an upturned graduated cylinder full of water in a trough. Label hydrogen peroxide + buffer + catalase extract, water bath, thermometer, delivery tube, oxygen collecting, trough of water.

The results follow a typical curve: a steep rise, then a plateau. Each part has its own explanation, and the plateau is caused by saturation of the active sites, not by the enzyme being denatured or used up.

Expected results: no oxygen at 0%; at low concentrations the rate rises steeply, roughly in proportion to concentration; at high concentrations it rises less and levels off into a plateau. The boiled-enzyme control gives little or no oxygen.

The rise is explained by collisions: more substrate molecules in the same volume means more collisions with active sites (the part of the enzyme where the substrate binds) per second, so more enzyme–substrate complexes form and more product is made per minute.

The plateau is explained by saturation: at high substrate concentration every active site is occupied at any moment, so the enzyme (saturated) works at its maximum rate, and adding more substrate cannot increase the rate.
At the plateau the amount of enzyme is the limiting factor (the thing holding the rate back); adding more enzyme would raise the rate again.
Within the range used in a school investigation the plateau may not be reached if the enzyme is in excess.
Conclusion: state the trend shown by the mean rates, whether it supports the hypothesis, and the concentration above which the rate stopped increasing, if one was found.

Diagram: a graph of rate (y-axis) against substrate concentration (x-axis); a curve rising from the origin, steep at first and then levelling off, with the plateau labelled all active sites occupied (saturated).

Now the substrate stays the same and the amount of enzyme changes. Amylase digests starch, and the end-point is found with iodine, which turns blue-black with starch and stays yellow-brown when starch is absent.
Aim: to investigate the effect of enzyme (amylase) concentration on the rate at which starch is digested.
Hypothesis: “Increasing the concentration of amylase increases the rate of starch digestion, because more active sites are available to bind starch molecules, as long as starch is in excess.”
Independent variable: amylase concentration, made by diluting the stock amylase solution with distilled water to 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of the stock, always to the same volume.
Dependent variable: time taken for the starch to disappear (the iodine test no longer turns blue-black), converted to rate = 1 ÷ time.

Controlled variables: volume and concentration of starch solution, volume of amylase solution, temperature (water bath at e.g. 37 °C), pH (buffer at pH 7), volume of iodine in each well, and the sampling interval.

Control: starch solution with distilled water (0% amylase) or with boiled amylase in place of the amylase; it stays blue-black with iodine for the whole investigation, showing that the starch does not disappear without active enzyme.
Drops of the reacting mixture are tested with iodine at regular intervals until the blue-black colour no longer appears.
1. Put a drop of iodine solution into each well of a spotting tile (a white tile with small hollows), so each sample can be tested as soon as it is taken.
2. Put 5 cm³ of starch solution and 1 cm³ of pH 7 buffer into a test tube, and 2 cm³ of the first amylase dilution into another, then stand both in the water bath for 5 minutes.
3. Pour the amylase into the starch, mix, and start the stopwatch.
4. Every 30 seconds, take one drop of the mixture with a clean dropper and add it to the next well of iodine.
5. Note the time at which a drop first leaves the iodine yellow-brown (no blue-black): this is the end-point, when all the starch has been digested.
6. Repeat for each amylase concentration, three times each, so that a mean can be calculated and a one-off error does not mislead you; then calculate the mean time and the rate.

Alternative: with catalase, vary the volume of celery extract (e.g. 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 and 2.5 cm³, each made up to the same total volume with distilled water) or the number of equal-sized celery discs, and measure the foam or oxygen volume in a fixed time.

Diagram: a spotting tile with a row of wells, the first wells blue-black and the later wells yellow-brown, labelled with sampling times; and the starch–amylase tube in a water bath with a thermometer.
With more enzyme, the starch disappears sooner. Unlike the substrate investigation, the graph is a straight line, as long as there is plenty of substrate.
Expected results: the higher the amylase concentration, the shorter the time for the starch to disappear, so the faster the rate; the 0% and boiled-enzyme controls never reach the end-point.
A graph of rate against enzyme concentration is a straight line through the origin: doubling the enzyme roughly doubles the rate.
Explanation: more enzyme molecules means more active sites, so more substrate molecules can be bound and converted at the same time, and more product is made per unit time.

The straight line continues only while substrate is in excess (more than the enzyme can use). If the enzyme concentration becomes very high, substrate becomes the limiting factor and the line levels off.
Diagram: a graph of rate (y-axis) against enzyme concentration (x-axis); a straight line rising from the origin, labelled substrate in excess.
Each enzyme works best at a particular pH. Here, buffers set the pH, and the volume of foam produced by catalase shows how active it is at each one.
Aim: to investigate the effect of pH on the rate of catalase activity.
Hypothesis: “Catalase has an optimum pH at which its rate is highest, and the rate decreases at pH values above and below it, because the shape of the active site is changed.”
Independent variable: pH, set with buffer solutions (e.g. pH 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10), which hold each pH steady so it does not drift as the reaction proceeds.
Dependent variable: volume of foam produced in 2 minutes (cm³), giving the rate in cm³ per minute.

Controlled variables: temperature (water bath at e.g. 25 °C), volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide, volume of the same celery extract (or mass of celery), volume of buffer, one drop of washing-up liquid, time and size of cylinder.
Control: at each pH (or at pH 7), boiled celery extract (or water) in place of the extract, giving no foam.
The foam is built up in a graduated cylinder, so its height can be read at the end of a fixed time.
1. Into a 100 cm³ graduated cylinder put 10 cm³ of pH 4 buffer, 2 cm³ of celery extract (or a fixed mass of chopped celery) and one drop of washing-up liquid.
2. Stand the cylinder in the 25 °C water bath, with a boiling tube of hydrogen peroxide beside it, for 5 minutes.
3. Note the starting volume of liquid in the cylinder, so the foam volume can be found by subtraction.
4. Add 2 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide with a syringe and start the stopwatch.
5. After 2 minutes, read the volume at the top of the foam, at eye level; the foam volume is this reading minus the starting volume.
6. Wash the cylinder and repeat with each buffer, three times each, and calculate the mean rate.

Diagram: a graduated cylinder standing in a water bath with a thermometer, containing buffer, celery extract and washing-up liquid at the bottom and a column of foam above, with a syringe adding hydrogen peroxide. Label each part and the foam height being read.
The rate rises to a peak at one pH and falls on both sides. The explanation lies in how pH affects the shape of the active site.

Expected results: the most foam forms at around pH 7 (the optimum for celery and liver catalase), with less in more acidic and more alkaline buffers and very little at the extremes. The control gives no foam.
The optimum pH is the pH at which the active site has the shape and charges that best fit the substrate.

A higher or lower hydrogen ion concentration, in more acidic or more alkaline conditions, changes the charges in the active site and the bonds holding the enzyme's shape, so the substrate fits less well and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.
Small changes from the optimum are reversible; extreme pH denatures the enzyme permanently.

Each enzyme's optimum suits the place where it works: pepsin in the acid stomach has an optimum of about pH 2; salivary amylase in the mouth about pH 7; trypsin in the alkaline small intestine about pH 8.

Diagram: a graph of rate (y-axis) against pH (x-axis); a peaked, bell-shaped curve with its peak labelled optimum pH at about 7 for catalase; optionally a second curve peaking at about pH 2, labelled pepsin.

Temperature has two opposite effects on an enzyme: it speeds up collisions, but too much heat destroys the enzyme. This investigation measures catalase activity across a range of water-bath temperatures.
Aim: to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of catalase activity.

Hypothesis: “As temperature increases, the rate of catalase activity increases up to an optimum temperature, because molecules move faster and collide more often; above the optimum the rate falls sharply because the enzyme is denatured.”
Independent variable: temperature, set with water baths at e.g. 0 °C (ice water), 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and 70 °C, each checked with a thermometer because baths drift from their set temperature.
Dependent variable: volume of foam in 2 minutes (cm³), giving the rate in cm³ per minute.
Controlled variables: pH (same volume of pH 7 buffer), volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide, volume of the same celery extract, one drop of washing-up liquid, time and size of cylinder.
Control: boiled celery extract (or water) in place of the extract at each temperature, giving no foam.
The temperature method reuses the foam method from the pH investigation, with the buffer fixed and the water bath changed.

Method: follow the pH investigation method, but with pH 7 buffer in every cylinder, and with each cylinder (buffer, extract and washing-up liquid) and its tube of hydrogen peroxide left in a water bath at the chosen temperature for 5 minutes before the peroxide is added.
Check the bath temperature with the thermometer during the 2 minutes, because it can drift; repeat three times at each temperature and calculate the mean rate.
The same method works with amylase and starch, timing the starch's disappearance at each temperature, as in the enzyme concentration investigation.
Diagram: the pH set-up, with a row of water baths at different labelled temperatures.
The curve rises slowly to a peak and then drops steeply. The rise and the fall have different causes.

Expected results: little foam at 0 °C; the rate increases as temperature rises, to a maximum at the optimum temperature; above the optimum the rate falls steeply, with little or no activity at the highest temperatures tested.
The graph is not symmetrical: a gradual rise and a steep fall. For human enzymes the optimum is about 37 °C, body temperature.

Explanation of the rise: as temperature increases, enzyme and substrate molecules have more kinetic energy (movement energy), move faster and collide more often, and more collisions have enough energy to react, so more enzyme–substrate complexes form per second.
Over the lower part of the range, the rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise (an approximate pattern, not an exact law).

Explanation of the fall: above the optimum, the enzyme molecule vibrates so much that the bonds holding its shape break, the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits: the enzyme is denatured.
As temperature rises further, more enzyme molecules are denatured, so the rate falls even though collisions are more frequent.

At low temperature the enzyme is inactive, not denatured: the molecules move too slowly for many collisions, but the active site keeps its shape, so activity returns when the enzyme is warmed (shown in the heat denaturation investigation).

Diagram: a graph of rate (y-axis) against temperature in °C (x-axis); a curve rising gradually to a peak labelled optimum temperature, then falling steeply to zero, with the falling part labelled enzyme denatured.
Heat can do more than slow an enzyme: it can destroy its shape for good. This investigation shows that boiled catalase stays inactive even after it is cooled.
Aim: to investigate the effect of heat denaturation on the activity of catalase.
Denaturation is the permanent loss of an enzyme's shape, and so of its active site and its activity, caused by high temperature or extreme pH.
Hypothesis: “Catalase that has been boiled will not break down hydrogen peroxide, even when cooled, because its active site has been permanently changed.”
Independent variable: whether the extract has been boiled (heat-treated) or not. Dependent variable: volume of foam in 2 minutes (cm³).

Controlled variables: both extracts tested at the same temperature (e.g. 25 °C) and pH (pH 7 buffer), with the same volumes of extract, buffer and hydrogen peroxide, the same drop of washing-up liquid and the same time.
Control: the unboiled extract, which shows how much foam active catalase produces under the same conditions, so the boiled result has something to be compared with.
Half the extract is boiled and half is not; both are then tested at the same temperature, so any difference is due to boiling alone.
1. Divide the celery extract between two labelled boiling tubes, A and B.
2. Place tube A in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes; leave tube B at room temperature.
3. Cool tube A, then stand both tubes in the 25 °C water bath for 5 minutes, so the boiled extract is tested at the same temperature as the unboiled.
4. Set up two graduated cylinders, each with 10 cm³ of pH 7 buffer, a drop of washing-up liquid and 2 cm³ of extract A or B.
5. Add 2 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide to each and read the foam after 2 minutes. Repeat three times.

Expected results: the boiled extract gives little or no foam; the unboiled extract gives a large column of foam. Any small amount of foam from the boiled extract comes from hydrogen peroxide breaking down slowly on its own, or from catalase that was not fully denatured.

Conclusion: boiling denatured the catalase; its activity did not return on cooling, so the change is permanent. This supports the hypothesis and explains why boiled enzyme is used as the control in the other investigations.

Extension: extract kept in ice water for 10 minutes and then warmed to 25 °C gives as much foam as unchilled extract, showing that cooling makes an enzyme inactive without denaturing it, whereas heating denatures it.

The same investigation works with amylase: boiled amylase added to starch leaves the iodine test blue-black at every sampling time, while unboiled amylase digests the starch so the iodine stays yellow-brown.
Secondary data are results that someone else collected. They let you check and extend your own conclusions, and the specification requires conclusions supported by both primary and secondary data.
Secondary data are data collected by someone else: results pooled from other groups in the class, published tables, textbooks or research papers, or online databases.
Uses: compare your optimum with published optima (the optimum pH of digestive enzymes and the optimum temperature of human enzymes given in the pH and temperature investigations).
Uses: check whether your trend agrees with other groups' (reproducibility), and extend a conclusion beyond the range you could test.

Secondary data on enzymes from extreme environments support the link between structure and conditions: Taq polymerase, from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus, works best at about 72 °C and is not denatured at temperatures that denature human enzymes.

When using secondary data, record its source, check that it was measured under comparable conditions (same enzyme source, substrate, pH or temperature), and judge whether the source is reliable. There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
Every method has weaknesses. Knowing where the error comes from tells you how to reduce it.

Foam volume is imprecise: bubbles burst, the top of the foam is uneven, and foam may stick to the cylinder walls. Read at eye level at exactly the same time each run; collecting the oxygen in a gas syringe is more accurate.
Gas is lost in the time between adding the enzyme and inserting the bung, or through leaks; some oxygen dissolves in the water when it is collected over water.
Water-bath temperatures drift, especially in beakers of hot water or ice; check with a thermometer throughout or use a thermostatically controlled bath.
The reaction mixture may not reach the bath temperature if equilibration is too short, so allow the full time.
Some errors come from the enzyme and reagents themselves, or from judging a colour change. Repeating and averaging makes results more reliable.

Enzyme activity varies between celery samples and falls as an extract stands, so make one batch, keep it cool and use it quickly for all the tests; a fresh batch for a repeat can give different values.
Hydrogen peroxide slowly breaks down on standing, especially in light, so its concentration may fall during the session: use one fresh stock kept in a dark bottle.

The iodine end-point is a judgement of colour, and sampling every 30 seconds means the time is only known to within 30 seconds; sample more often near the end-point, compare against a control well, or use a colorimeter.
Measure volumes with syringes or graduated pipettes rather than by eye, and use a clean syringe or dropper for each solution to avoid contamination.
Repeat each value three times, calculate the mean, and identify and investigate any anomalous result; pool class data to check reproducibility.
Use at least five values of the independent variable so the shape of the graph (peak or plateau) can be seen.

Industry needs reactions that are fast, clean and cheap. Enzymes (biological catalysts, which speed up reactions without being changed) often do this better than the chemical catalysts used in factories.
Specificity: an enzyme catalyses one reaction, so it makes the wanted product with few unwanted by-products. This gives a purer product that needs less purification.

Mild conditions: enzymes work at moderate temperatures (often 30–60 °C), normal pressure and near-neutral pH (neither strongly acidic nor alkaline), whereas many chemical catalysts need high temperatures and pressures.
Mild conditions save energy and money, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and make the process safer, because there are no very hot, high-pressure vessels.

Enzymes are efficient catalysts that are not used up, so a small amount can be used repeatedly. They are also biodegradable (broken down naturally), so they leave less harmful waste than many chemical catalysts.

Industry has to get its enzymes from living things, and enzymes have weaknesses as well as strengths. Knowing both explains how enzymes are produced and why the conditions in a factory are tightly controlled.

Most industrial enzymes are made by microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) grown in large vessels called fermenters or bioreactors. They are used because they grow fast, can be grown on cheap nutrients, and many release (secrete) their enzymes into the medium, where they are easy to collect.
Many industrial enzymes are now made by genetically modified microorganisms, which carry the gene for the enzyme. There is more on this in Genetic engineering.
A few enzymes come from plants (e.g. papain from papaya) or from animals, such as rennet (from calves' stomachs).
Limitation: enzymes are denatured (their shape is permanently changed so they stop working) by high temperatures and extreme pH, so conditions must be carefully controlled.
Limitation: enzymes can be expensive to produce and purify.
Limitation: free enzymes (ones simply dissolved in the mixture) are lost in the product after one use. Immobilisation, covered below, solves this.
Limitation: enzyme dust can cause allergies. In the early years of biological detergents, some factory workers developed allergies, so enzymes are now sealed in granules.

Enzymes from microorganisms that live in hot springs or in alkaline conditions are chosen or engineered for processes that need tougher enzymes, because they already work where normal enzymes would be denatured.
Milk is a good example of how industry uses single, specific enzymes. One enzyme turns milk into cheese, and another removes the sugar that some people cannot digest.
Cheese-making: chymosin (rennin), the active enzyme in rennet, clots the milk protein casein, so the milk separates into solid curds (made into cheese) and liquid whey.
Rennet was traditionally extracted from the stomachs of young calves. Much of the chymosin used today is made by genetically modified microorganisms, which suits vegetarians and needs no animals.
Lactose-free milk: lactase breaks lactose (the sugar in milk) down into glucose and galactose, so people with lactose intolerance (who cannot digest lactose) can drink the milk.
Lactose-free milk tastes sweeter, because glucose and galactose are sweeter than lactose. Lactase is often used immobilised.
Plant materials such as fruit and grain are full of structural and storage carbohydrates. Carbohydrate-digesting enzymes release the useful sugars and make processing easier.
Fruit juice: pectinase breaks down pectin, which helps hold plant cell walls together, so more juice is released from crushed fruit and the juice is clearer (less cloudy).
Sugar syrups: amylases break starch (e.g. from maize) into glucose syrup. Immobilised glucose isomerase then converts glucose into fructose, which is much sweeter.
High-fructose syrup is used to sweeten soft drinks and processed foods, so less is needed for the same sweetness.

Brewing and baking: amylases break starch in grain into maltose and glucose, which yeast ferments to make ethanol and carbon dioxide. In baking, the carbon dioxide helps the dough rise. There is more on fermentation in Respiration.
Proteases (enzymes that digest protein) are used to clear haze from beer.
Proteases, lipases and amylases digest the three main food molecules: protein, fat and starch. This is why they are useful both in sweets and meat and in household cleaning.
Proteases such as papain tenderise meat by breaking down muscle proteins.
Invertase (sucrase) converts sucrose into glucose and fructose, to make the soft centres of chocolates and other sweets.
Household link: biological washing powders contain proteases, lipases and amylases that digest protein stains (blood, egg, grass), fat and grease, and starch.
Biological washing powders work at low washing temperatures (e.g. 30–40 °C), saving energy. They are not used at very high temperatures, where the enzymes would be denatured.
Biofuels are fuels made from living material. Enzymes are needed to turn the carbohydrates and oils in plants into forms that yeast or chemistry can convert into fuel.
Bioethanol from starch crops: amylases break the starch of crops such as maize and wheat into glucose, which yeast ferments to ethanol. The ethanol is blended with petrol as a fuel.
Bioethanol from cellulose (a second-generation biofuel): cellulases break down the cellulose in straw, wood chips and other crop waste into glucose for fermentation.
Cellulose is tightly packed and hard to digest, so these enzymes are slow and costly and are an active area of research. There is more on cellulose in Structures of biomolecules.

Biodiesel: lipases can catalyse the conversion of vegetable oils and waste cooking oils into biodiesel. This is an alternative to chemical catalysts that works at lower temperatures and leaves less waste.
Biofuels are often described as green, but the picture is more complicated. Exams ask you to weigh the benefits against the costs.
For: biofuels are renewable, because the crops can be regrown.
For: the carbon dioxide released when they burn was taken in by the crop during photosynthesis, so they add less to atmospheric CO₂ than fossil fuels.
For: using waste materials (straw, waste oil) adds value to waste.
Against: growing fuel crops uses land that could grow food, which can raise food prices.
Against: clearing forests for fuel crops destroys habitats and releases carbon.
Against: fertilisers, machinery and processing use fossil-fuel energy, so the saving is smaller than it first appears.

Cellulose-based and waste-based biofuels avoid most of the competition with food, because they use parts of the plant or waste that people do not eat. Carbon cycle and climate detail is in Nutrient Cycling.
Because enzymes are so specific, they are used in medicine to detect substances, break down harmful ones, and replace enzymes that the body fails to supply.
Diagnosis: glucose oxidase is used in blood-glucose test strips and electronic biosensors used by people with diabetes, and in urine test strips.
Glucose oxidase is specific to glucose, so other sugars do not interfere. The reaction produces a colour change or an electrical signal in proportion to the amount of glucose.

Dissolving blood clots: clot-dissolving enzymes such as streptokinase (from bacteria) and tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) are given soon after a heart attack or a stroke caused by a clot, to break down the clot and restore blood flow.
Enzyme replacement: people with cystic fibrosis often cannot release enough digestive enzymes from the pancreas, so they take capsules of pancreatic enzymes (lipase, protease and amylase) with meals.
Lactase tablets help people with lactose intolerance, because they supply the missing enzyme.
Cancer treatment: the enzyme asparaginase is used to treat a type of childhood leukaemia (acute lymphoblastic leukaemia).
The leukaemia cells cannot make enough of the amino acid asparagine and take it from the blood. The enzyme breaks down asparagine in the blood, starving the cancer cells.

Medical technologies built on enzymes (named only here): restriction enzymes and DNA ligase in genetic engineering (see “Genetic engineering”); Taq polymerase in PCR for DNA profiling and diagnostic testing (see “Generating a DNA profile”).
Making drugs chemically can be wasteful and use harsh conditions. Enzymes can make the same drugs more precisely and more cleanly.

Making antibiotics: immobilised penicillin acylase converts natural penicillin, made by the Penicillium mould, into a starting molecule (6-APA) from which semi-synthetic penicillins, such as amoxicillin, are made.
Semi-synthetic penicillins can treat infections that the natural form does not.
Making single-form drugs: many drug molecules exist in two mirror-image forms, of which only one works (the other may be useless or harmful).
Because enzymes are specific, they make only the wanted form, avoiding wasteful separation. For example, an engineered enzyme (a transaminase) is used to manufacture the diabetes drug sitagliptin.

Enzymes allow drug manufacture at mild temperatures with less toxic solvent waste than chemical methods (“green chemistry”). Human insulin made by genetically modified bacteria depends on enzymes used to insert the gene (see “Genetic engineering”).
Free enzymes mix into the product and are lost after one use. Fixing the enzyme in place solves this, and it is a central idea in industrial enzyme use.

An immobilised enzyme is an enzyme (or a whole cell containing it) fixed to, or trapped in, an inert, insoluble material. It is held in place while the substrate solution passes over or through it, so it does not mix freely with the product.
Entrapment: the enzyme is trapped in a gel bead, such as calcium alginate.
Adsorption: the enzyme is stuck to the surface of an insoluble support, such as glass beads, resin or charcoal.
Covalent bonding: the enzyme is chemically bonded to a support.
Enclosure: the enzyme is enclosed behind a partially permeable membrane.
Examples: glucose isomerase for high-fructose syrup; lactase for lactose-free milk; penicillin acylase for semi-synthetic penicillins.
Immobilisation brings clear benefits in cost and purity, but it also adds complications. Exams ask for both sides.
Advantage: the enzyme can be recovered and reused many times, cutting costs.
Advantage: the product is not contaminated with enzyme, so it needs no purification.
Advantage: the enzyme can be packed in a column for a continuous-flow process, with substrate fed in at the top and product collected at the bottom.
Advantage: immobilised enzymes are often more stable, being less easily denatured by changes in temperature or pH. The reaction can be stopped at once by removing the enzyme.
Disadvantage: immobilising costs money and equipment to set up, and some activity is lost, as part of the active sites (where the substrate binds) may be blocked or altered.
Disadvantage: the reaction can be slower, because the substrate must diffuse into the bead to reach the enzyme. Enzyme may also leak out of the support.
Disadvantage: immobilised enzymes are unsuitable where the substrate molecules are too large to enter the beads.
This is the school method for immobilising an enzyme. Yeast is used because its cells contain the enzyme sucrase (also called invertase), which acts on sucrose.
1. Mix sodium alginate solution with a suspension of yeast (which contains the enzyme sucrase, also called invertase) or with an enzyme solution.
2. Draw the mixture into a syringe and drop it, one drop at a time, into calcium chloride solution: each drop forms a bead of insoluble calcium alginate gel trapping the yeast.
3. Leave the beads to harden for about 15–20 minutes.
4. Sieve them out and rinse them with distilled water to remove the calcium chloride and any free yeast.
5. Place the beads in a separating funnel (or a syringe barrel with a tap) as a column.
Safety: calcium chloride irritates the eyes, so wear safety glasses and wash spills.

Diagram: (a) a syringe dripping the alginate–yeast mixture into a beaker of calcium chloride solution, with beads forming, labelled; (b) a separating funnel or column packed with beads, with sucrose solution added at the top, a tap, and product (glucose and fructose) collected below, labelled.

Once the column is made, sucrose solution is passed through it and the liquid that comes out is tested. A control and a comparison with free yeast show that the beads do the work and that immobilisation helps.
Using the beads: pour sucrose solution through the column and collect the liquid that drips out. Test it with a glucose test strip.
A positive glucose result shows that the sucrose has been converted to glucose and fructose. The sucrose solution tested before it enters the column gives a negative result.
Control: beads made without yeast (alginate only). Their product gives no glucose, so the conversion is due to the yeast and not the beads.

The product from the beads is clear, while sucrose mixed with free yeast becomes cloudy with yeast cells that must be removed, showing the advantage of immobilisation. The beads can be rinsed and used again.
Enzymes and cells work best when conditions are right. A bioreactor is the vessel that holds those conditions steady in industry.

A bioreactor is a vessel in which cells or enzymes carry out a reaction under controlled conditions: temperature, pH, oxygen (or its absence), nutrient supply, mixing and sterility are monitored and kept at the values that suit the enzyme.
A column of immobilised enzyme is a simple bioreactor. There is more on growing microorganisms in bioreactors, and on batch and continuous culture, in Microorganisms in industry.
The uses above fall into three themes that link enzymes to health, sustainability and technology. Exams may ask you to draw these together.
Health: diagnostic strips and biosensors, clot-busting and replacement enzymes, and lactose-free foods.
Sustainability: lower energy use and less chemical waste; low-temperature washing; biofuels and the arguments about them; more juice from the same fruit.
Technology: genetic modification of microorganisms to make enzymes, engineered enzymes, immobilisation and continuous-flow bioreactors.

Photosynthesis is how plants make their own food. They capture energy from light and use it to build glucose, a sugar, out of two simple substances they take from their surroundings: carbon dioxide and water.

Green plants, algae and some bacteria, such as cyanobacteria, photosynthesise. They use light energy, absorbed by the green pigment chlorophyll, to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, and they release oxygen as a by-product.

Because they make their own food from simple inorganic substances, these organisms are called autotrophs (self-feeders). Animals and fungi can't do this, so they must eat food that was made by an autotroph.

The key change is an energy conversion: light energy becomes chemical energy, stored in the bonds of the glucose molecule. Almost every food chain starts with this conversion, so nearly all the energy living things use was first captured by photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis is also where the oxygen in the air comes from. Without it, there would be no oxygen for aerobic respiration.
Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with light energy and chlorophyll written above the arrow, because both are needed for the reaction but neither is a reacting substance.

Balanced equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, with light energy and chlorophyll above the arrow. Each side has 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 18 oxygen atoms. Six CO₂ molecules are needed because each one supplies one of glucose's six carbon atoms.
Every reaction in a cell either builds molecules up or breaks them down. Photosynthesis is a building-up reaction, and the exam expects you to say why in two parts.
An anabolic reaction builds a large molecule from smaller ones and takes in energy to do it. Photosynthesis fits both parts of that definition.
First, it builds a large organic molecule, glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆), from small inorganic molecules, carbon dioxide and water.
Second, it takes in energy rather than releasing it. The energy comes from light, and it ends up stored in the glucose.
Respiration is the opposite, catabolic process: it breaks glucose back down into carbon dioxide and water and releases the stored energy. There is more on this in Respiration as a catabolic process.
A plant has to gather carbon dioxide, water and light, and then deal with the oxygen and glucose it makes. Each one has a definite route into or out of the leaf.
