Carbon dioxide diffuses from the air into the leaf through the stomata, small pores found mainly on the lower surface. It moves through the air spaces inside the leaf to the mesophyll cells, where photosynthesis happens. Some also comes from the plant's own respiring cells.
Plants that live under water can't take gas from the air, so they absorb carbon dioxide dissolved in the water, partly as hydrogencarbonate ions.

Water is absorbed from the soil by root hair cells, by osmosis, and carried up the stem to the leaves in the xylem (the plant's water-carrying tubes). Only a tiny fraction of this water is used in photosynthesis; most evaporates from the leaves in transpiration.
Light comes from the sun, or from artificial lights in greenhouses and laboratories.
Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green light. This is why leaves look green: green is the colour the plant isn't using.
Oxygen is partly used by the plant's own cells for respiration. The rest diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata into the air, or into the water for aquatic plants.

The oxygen released comes from splitting water molecules, not from carbon dioxide. This was shown in the 1940s: when plants were given water containing a heavy form (isotope) of oxygen, ¹⁸O, the oxygen gas they released contained ¹⁸O.
Glucose is partly used straight away in the plant's own respiration, which releases its energy as ATP for the cell's work. The rest is turned into sucrose, starch and cellulose.
Glucose is a good fuel, but it isn't ideal for moving around the plant, storing or building with. So plants convert it into three other carbohydrates, each suited to one job.

Sucrose (for transport): glucose is joined to fructose to form the disaccharide sucrose. Sucrose is carried from the leaves in the phloem (the plant's food-carrying tubes) to growing tips, roots, fruits and storage organs.

Sucrose suits transport because it is soluble, so it travels dissolved in the phloem, and less reactive than glucose. It is not a reducing sugar, so it isn't used up by the cells it passes on the way.

Starch (for storage): glucose is joined into long chains to form the polysaccharide starch. Starch grains build up in the chloroplasts during the day, and longer-term stores are kept in storage organs and seeds, such as potato tubers and cereal grains.
Starch suits storage because it is insoluble, so large amounts can be stored without drawing water into the cell by osmosis, and it is compact.

Cellulose (for building): glucose is joined into the polysaccharide cellulose, which forms the strong walls around plant cells. Because every plant cell has a wall, cellulose is the most abundant organic compound on Earth.
Plants also use glucose to make lipids, such as the oils in seeds, and, combined with nitrates taken from the soil, amino acids for proteins.
When a plant photosynthesises, it pulls carbon out of the air and locks it inside its own body. This is why forests, bogs and the oceans matter in the fight against climate change.
A carbon sink is anything that takes in more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases, and stores it. Photosynthesis is the only major biological process that removes carbon dioxide from the air.
The carbon from CO₂ is fixed (built into organic molecules) as glucose, then as sucrose, starch, cellulose and the rest of the plant's body, its biomass.

The carbon stays locked away for as long as the biomass lasts: for decades or centuries in the wood of trees, and for thousands of years in peat bogs, because waterlogged, acidic conditions slow down decomposition.
Algae and phytoplankton (tiny floating photosynthesisers) in the oceans also fix carbon, and some of it is locked up in ocean sediments when they die.
Respiration, decomposition and burning return the stored carbon to the air as CO₂.

Forests, peatlands and the oceans' algae and phytoplankton are the main natural carbon sinks. Cutting down forests, draining or burning peat and burning fossil fuels all release stored carbon and add to the CO₂ that drives climate change.
Fossil fuels are themselves stored photosynthesis: coal, oil and gas hold carbon that plants and algae fixed millions of years ago, which is why burning them adds extra CO₂ to the air.

Photosynthesis happens inside chloroplasts, and it doesn't happen in one go. It runs as two linked stages in two different parts of the chloroplast: the first captures energy from light, and the second uses that energy to build glucose.
In a leaf, most chloroplasts are in the palisade mesophyll cells, just below the upper surface, because that is where light is strongest. Spongy mesophyll cells and guard cells also have some.
Stage 1, the light-dependent stage, takes place on the thylakoid membranes, the flattened sacs inside the chloroplast that are stacked into piles called grana.
2. The energy is used to split water molecules into oxygen, protons (H⁺) and electrons. This splitting is called photolysis, meaning splitting by light.
3. The oxygen is released as a by-product.
4. The energy is trapped in ATP, and the protons and high-energy electrons are picked up by a hydrogen carrier molecule, ready for stage 2.
Stage 2, the light-independent stage, takes place in the stroma, the fluid that fills the chloroplast around the thylakoids.

1. Carbon dioxide enters the stroma. 2. It is combined with the hydrogen (protons and electrons) brought from stage 1. 3. Energy from the ATP made in stage 1 drives these reactions. 4. Glucose is formed.

The two stages are like a factory with a delivery service between them. Stage 1 loads up carriers with energy and hydrogen, stage 2 unloads them to build glucose, and the empty carriers go back to be reloaded.
Stage 1 supplies the two things stage 2 needs: energy, as ATP, and hydrogen, on the hydrogen carrier.
Stage 2 returns the spent carriers to stage 1: ATP comes back as ADP, and the carrier comes back empty, so both can be reused.
The reactions of stage 2 are controlled by enzymes, which is why this stage, and so the whole process, is affected by temperature.
The light-independent stage doesn't use light directly, but it stops soon after dark, because stage 1 stops and the supply of ATP and hydrogen runs out.
Older books call the light-independent stage the dark stage. That name is misleading: the stage happens in the light, at the same time as stage 1.

Diagram: a chloroplast outline with stage 1 on a thylakoid stack (inputs light and H₂O; output O₂) and stage 2 in the stroma (input CO₂; output glucose → sucrose, starch, cellulose). Arrows: ATP and hydrogen to the stroma; ADP and the empty carrier back.
Before measuring anything, you need to know what "rate" means and which conditions can speed photosynthesis up or hold it back. This theory is what every hypothesis in the investigation rests on.

The rate of photosynthesis is the amount of product made, or reactant used, per unit time. It is usually measured as the rate of oxygen production, in bubbles per minute or cm³ of gas per minute, but it can also be measured as the rate of CO₂ uptake.
Oxygen is a good thing to measure because it is a product: it comes from the splitting of water in the light-dependent stage (the first stage, which needs light).

Light intensity: light supplies the energy for the light-dependent stage, so more light means more ATP (the cell's energy carrier) and hydrogen are made per minute and the rate rises, until another factor holds it back.
Carbon dioxide concentration: CO₂ is the raw material of the light-independent stage (the second stage, which builds glucose), so more CO₂ raises the rate, until another factor holds it back.

Temperature: the light-independent stage is controlled by enzymes. Raising the temperature increases the rate, because molecules move faster and collide more often with the enzymes' active sites (the part of the enzyme where the reaction happens), up to an optimum.
Above the optimum the rate falls quickly, because the enzymes are denatured (their shape is permanently changed, so they stop working). There is more on this in Enzymes as catalysts.

A limiting factor is the factor in shortest supply, which holds back the rate of a process even when the other factors are increased. At any moment the rate is limited by whichever of light intensity, CO₂ concentration or temperature is furthest from its best value.
Raising a limiting factor increases the rate. Raising a factor that is not limiting has no effect, because something else is still holding the rate back.
The bubbles you count are not the whole story. A plant is also respiring, and respiration uses oxygen, so what you measure is a net result.
A plant respires all the time, using some of the oxygen it makes, so the oxygen given off is photosynthesis minus respiration. This is called the net (apparent) rate.
In very dim light the two processes are equal and no oxygen is given off, because all the oxygen made is used up. This is the compensation point.
In darkness there is no photosynthesis, so the plant takes in oxygen for respiration.
A good investigation changes one thing and measures one thing. Planning starts with a clear aim, a prediction for each factor, and a plant that lets you see the result.

Aim: to investigate the effect of light intensity (or CO₂ concentration, or temperature) on the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed. Write one investigation per factor, changing only that factor, so you know which one caused any change.

Hypothesis for light: as light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases until it levels off. This rests on the theory that light drives the light-dependent stage until something else becomes limiting.
Hypothesis for CO₂: as CO₂ concentration increases, the rate increases until it levels off. This rests on CO₂ being the raw material of the light-independent stage.
Hypothesis for temperature: the rate increases with temperature up to an optimum and then decreases, because the enzymes of the light-independent stage work faster until they are denatured.

Elodea (Canadian pondweed) is the standard school plant. It is aquatic, so the oxygen it gives off appears as visible bubbles from the cut stem, which can be counted or collected. It is also easy to obtain, grows quickly and photosynthesises rapidly.
Next you decide what to change, what to measure and what to hold steady, and gather the apparatus. The variables below are for the light-intensity investigation.
The independent variable (the one you change) is light intensity, set by the lamp's distance from the plant or measured with a light meter in lux.
The dependent variable (the one you measure) is the rate of oxygen production, as bubbles per minute or cm³ of gas per minute.

Controlled variables (kept the same, so they cannot affect the result): temperature (water bath), CO₂ concentration (same sodium hydrogencarbonate concentration), the same pondweed (species, length, leaves), the same lamp and bulb, the adjustment time and the counting period.
For the other factors, swap the independent variable for CO₂ concentration or temperature, and keep light intensity constant.

Control: an identical set-up kept in darkness (lamp off, tube covered with foil), or a tube with no plant, gives no bubbles. This shows that the bubbles come from photosynthesis by the plant in the light, not from gas leaving the solution.

Equipment: fresh Elodea, scalpel or scissors, boiling tube or test tube, paper clip to weigh the pondweed down, beaker as a water bath (or an electric water bath), thermometer, bench lamp (an LED bulb gives out less heat), metre stick, stopwatch, and a light meter (optional).
Chemicals: sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO₃) powder, or solutions of known concentration, which supplies the plant with CO₂, in water that has been boiled and cooled.
For measuring volume: a funnel and graduated tube, or a capillary tube attached to a syringe, called a photosynthometer. A glowing splint is optional, for testing the gas.
This basic set-up is used for all three investigations. Only the factor you change differs, so learn it once and adapt it.

1. Fill a boiling tube with water containing a set concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate. It dissolves to supply CO₂ to the plant, so that CO₂ is not limiting (except in the carbon dioxide investigation).
2. Cut a healthy shoot of pondweed about 5 to 8 cm long, cutting the stem cleanly and slantwise under water.
3. Place it in the tube upside down, with the cut end at the top, weighed down with a paper clip.
4. Stand the tube in a beaker of water at a constant temperature, for example 25 °C, checked with a thermometer, so the temperature stays steady.
5. Carry out the investigation in a darkened room, so that the lamp is the only light source.

Counting: let the plant adjust to each new condition for about 5 minutes, then count the bubbles leaving the cut end in one minute. Repeat the count three times at each setting and calculate the mean.

Collecting (more accurate): place an inverted funnel over the pondweed in a beaker, with a water-filled graduated tube over its stem, and record the gas collected in a set time, for example 5 minutes. Alternatively, draw the gas up a capillary tube with a syringe and measure the bubble's length.

Volume per unit time is more accurate than counting, because bubbles vary in size. Optional gas test: it relights a glowing splint, so it is rich in oxygen, but not pure oxygen, since dissolved nitrogen and carbon dioxide also come out.
Here the independent variable is light intensity, which you change by moving the lamp. The challenge is changing the light without also changing the temperature.
1. Set up as in the basic set-up.
2. Place the lamp 10 cm from the pondweed, measured with a metre stick from the bulb to the plant.
3. Allow 5 minutes to adjust, then count the bubbles per minute three times.
4. Move the lamp to 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm, and repeat.
5. Check the water temperature at each distance and keep it constant, by adding cold or warm water to the bath.

A lamp close to the plant also heats it, which would change two variables at once. Use an LED bulb, or place a beaker or flat-sided tank of water between the lamp and the plant as a heat shield, and check the thermometer.

Moving the lamp further away lowers the light intensity as the inverse square of the distance (light intensity ∝ 1/d²): doubling the distance gives a quarter of the light intensity. It does not fall in simple proportion.
So plot the rate against 1/d² to show the relationship with light intensity, or measure the light intensity at each position with a light meter.
Here the independent variable is CO₂ concentration, which you change by using sodium hydrogencarbonate solutions of different strengths. Light and temperature are held constant.

1. Make up a series of sodium hydrogencarbonate solutions of increasing concentration, for example 0%, 0.25%, 0.5%, 0.75% and 1%, using water that has been boiled and cooled. Boiling removes dissolved CO₂, so the 0% tube has very little.
2. Keep the lamp at a fixed distance close to the plant, for example 10 cm, and keep the temperature constant, so that CO₂ is the only thing that changes.
3. Place the same pondweed in each solution in turn, allow 5 minutes to adjust, and count the bubbles per minute three times.
4. Calculate the mean for each concentration.
Here the independent variable is temperature, changed with water baths. Light and CO₂ are held constant.
1. Set up as in the basic set-up, with a fixed lamp distance and a fixed sodium hydrogencarbonate concentration.
2. Place the tube in a water bath at a range of temperatures, for example 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C, using ice or warm water or electric water baths, and check each with a thermometer.
3. Let the tube reach the bath temperature, about 5 minutes, then count the bubbles per minute three times.
4. If the first pondweed stops producing bubbles, use a fresh piece for the higher temperatures, and note that you have done so.
Warm water holds less dissolved gas, so some bubbles at high temperatures can come from gas leaving the solution. The darkness control at each temperature checks this.
This investigation mixes electricity, water, heat and sharp tools, so each hazard needs its own precaution.
Electricity and water: keep the lamp, its cable and plug away from the water bath, dry your hands before touching switches, and do not move a lamp while it is on and hot.
Lamp bulbs, other than LEDs, get very hot and can burn, so let them cool before moving them.
Take care with the scalpel: cut on a tile, away from the body. Take care with hot water baths and glassware.
Wash your hands after handling pondweed and pond water.

Elodea canadensis is a non-native invasive species (one that spreads and harms native wildlife) in Ireland. Never put leftover pondweed or its water into ponds, lakes, rivers or drains; dispose of it in compost or general waste.
The results table and graph turn counts into a relationship you can explain. For each factor the shape of the graph tells you what is limiting the rate.

Record the primary data (the results you collect yourself) in a table: the independent variable (distance in cm and 1/d², concentration in %, or temperature in °C), the three counts and the mean number of bubbles per minute.
Plot the mean rate on the y-axis against the independent variable on the x-axis, with units, and join the points with a smooth curve or straight lines.

Light intensity: as the lamp moves closer, the rate increases, so it falls as distance increases. At high intensity the curve levels off in a plateau, because another factor, CO₂ concentration or temperature, has become limiting.
CO₂ concentration: the rate increases with CO₂ concentration and then levels off, because light intensity or temperature becomes limiting. At 0% (boiled water) there are few or no bubbles.

Temperature: the rate rises up to an optimum, then falls steeply above it, as the enzymes of the light-independent stage are denatured. Bubbling may stop at the highest temperatures. The curve is not symmetrical: the fall is steeper than the rise.
Conclusion: state the relationship shown by the primary data and whether it supports the hypothesis. On the levelling-off part of the graph, name the factor that is now limiting.
Examiners often ask you to draw the apparatus or sketch the expected graphs. Learn the labels for each.

Diagram: the set-up. Labels: lamp, metre stick, heat shield, beaker water bath, thermometer, boiling tube of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, upside-down pondweed with bubbles at the cut end (or the funnel and graduated collecting tube).

Diagram: two sketch graphs. (a) Rate against light intensity, rising then levelling off, plus a higher curve labelled higher CO₂ concentration; label the rise light limiting and the plateau CO₂ or temperature limiting. (b) Rate against temperature, rising to an optimum then falling steeply.
Your own results are only one source. You can also use other people's data to support a conclusion, and apply the idea of limiting factors to growing crops.

Secondary data are results collected by others: other groups' class results, textbook or published graphs, or data-logger results from an oxygen or CO₂ sensor. Pooling class results increases the sample size and checks reproducibility (whether others get the same result).

Interpreting a graph of rate against light intensity at two CO₂ concentrations (or two temperatures): where the two curves overlap, light is the limiting factor, because raising CO₂ makes no difference.
Where the two curves separate and each levels off, CO₂ (or temperature) is limiting, because raising it raises the plateau.

Applying limiting factors: commercial glasshouse growers raise the yield of crops such as tomatoes and lettuce by supplying extra light (artificial lighting), heat and CO₂. Burning paraffin or propane gives both heat and CO₂, or CO₂ gas can be added.
Each factor is kept just high enough that it is not limiting. Raising a factor that is not limiting wastes fuel and money and adds to emissions.
No school investigation is perfect. Knowing where the errors come from tells you how to reduce them.
Bubbles vary in size and can be missed or merge when the rate is fast, so counting is imprecise. Collecting the volume of gas is more accurate.
Other light in the room, such as daylight or other groups' lamps, changes the light intensity, so work in a darkened room.
Temperature can drift, especially with a hot bulb close to the plant, so check it and adjust it.
The gas is not pure oxygen, and some oxygen dissolves in the water instead of forming bubbles, so the bubbles underestimate the true rate. The measured rate is also a net rate, after respiration.
The carbon dioxide from sodium hydrogencarbonate is used up over time, and the plant's response may change, so use fresh solution, a fresh plant for each run if needed, and repeat the whole series.
Allowing too little time to adjust after each change gives rates that still reflect the previous setting.
Repeat each reading at least three times and calculate a mean, so a single odd count has less effect. Compare your results with other groups' results.

The light-dependent reactions start when light hits a leaf. Before any chemistry can happen, the plant has to catch that light energy and channel it to one special chlorophyll molecule, which uses it to fire off an electron.
Light travels as tiny packets of energy called photons. A pigment is a molecule that absorbs light of particular colours (wavelengths).

The thylakoid membranes hold several pigments: chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, and yellow and orange pigments called carotenoids. Each absorbs slightly different colours, so having several widens the range of light the plant can use.

The pigment molecules sit in clusters of hundreds, called light-harvesting or antenna complexes, around a reaction centre. The cluster works like a satellite dish, collecting light over a wide area and focusing it on one point.
When any pigment in the cluster absorbs a photon, the energy is passed from one pigment molecule to the next until it reaches the reaction centre, a special chlorophyll a molecule.

At the reaction centre, the energy raises (excites) one of the chlorophyll's electrons to a high energy level. This energised electron leaves the chlorophyll and is taken up by an electron acceptor, the first carrier of an electron transport chain.

Because an electron carries a negative charge, losing one leaves the reaction-centre chlorophyll positively charged. It must get an electron back before it can fire off another one, and in the non-cyclic pathway it takes that electron from water.

The energised electron now has to go somewhere useful. In the non-cyclic pathway, it travels one way, from water to NADP⁺, and along the way its energy is used to make the two things the second stage of photosynthesis needs: ATP and NADPH.
1. Light energy reaches the reaction centre, and energised electrons leave the chlorophyll.

2. The electrons are passed along an electron transport chain, a series of electron carriers in the thylakoid membrane. At each hand-over they lose a little energy, like a ball bouncing down a staircase, and this released energy is used to make ATP from ADP and phosphate (Pi).
3. At the end of the chain, the electrons, now at lower energy, are passed to NADP⁺, a hydrogen carrier. Each NADP⁺ takes two electrons and one proton (H⁺) to form NADPH: NADP⁺ + 2e⁻ + H⁺ → NADPH.

4. The chlorophyll is still positively charged, so it strongly attracts electrons and pulls them from water molecules. This splits the water, a step called photolysis (splitting by light, because the energy for it ultimately came from light): 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂.
5. The electrons from water replace the ones the chlorophyll lost, so it is neutral again and ready to absorb more energy.

The protons (H⁺) from photolysis are used to form NADPH, and they also build up inside the thylakoid, where this crowd of protons is used to power ATP-making. There is more on this in The chloroplast's internal structure.
The oxygen from photolysis is a by-product. It is used in the cell's respiration or released through the stomata.

It is called non-cyclic because the electrons go one way only, from water through the chlorophyll and the chain to NADP⁺, and never return to where they started. The electrons aren't used up; they end up on NADPH.
Products of the non-cyclic pathway: ATP, NADPH and oxygen.
Sometimes the energised electrons take a shortcut. In the cyclic pathway they loop back to the chlorophyll they came from, making ATP on the way but nothing else.

In the cyclic pathway, some energised electrons leaving the reaction-centre chlorophyll pass along carriers of the electron transport chain and then return to the same chlorophyll molecule, instead of going on to NADP⁺.
As they pass along the carriers, they give up their extra energy, which is used to make ATP from ADP and Pi.
Because the electrons come back, the chlorophyll is neutral again without needing electrons from water. So water is not split, no oxygen is released and no NADPH is made.
Products of the cyclic pathway: ATP only.

Why the plant needs it: the light-independent reactions use more ATP than NADPH, 3 ATP for every 2 NADPH for each CO₂ molecule fixed (built into sugar) in the light-independent reactions, the second stage that makes glucose. The cyclic pathway tops up the extra ATP.
It also runs when NADP⁺ is in short supply because most of it is already loaded as NADPH. The energised electrons then still have somewhere to go.
Exams ask you to tell the two pathways apart. The differences all come back to one thing: where the electrons end up.
Route of the electrons: non-cyclic goes one way, from water to NADP⁺; cyclic goes from the chlorophyll round the carriers and back to the same chlorophyll.
Final electron acceptor: NADP⁺ in the non-cyclic pathway; the chlorophyll molecule itself in the cyclic pathway.
Water: split by photolysis in the non-cyclic pathway, to replace the lost electrons; not needed in the cyclic pathway, because the electrons come back.
Products: non-cyclic makes ATP, NADPH and oxygen; cyclic makes ATP only.

What they share: both start with light energy reaching the reaction centre and an energised electron leaving the chlorophyll, both pass electrons along carriers to make ATP, and both happen on the thylakoid membranes.

Older Irish textbooks and past papers call the cyclic pathway pathway 1 and the non-cyclic pathway pathway 2, and describe NADP⁺ first picking up two electrons (becoming NADP⁻) and then a proton. Recognise these names, but learn the single step to NADPH given above.

Diagram: one energy diagram with chlorophyll at the bottom receiving light from pigment molecules; the electron rising to an acceptor; a downhill chain (ATP made) ending at NADP⁺ → NADPH; water entering below the chlorophyll; a loop back to the chlorophyll for the cyclic pathway (ATP made).
Put together, the light-dependent reactions turn light into a form of energy the rest of the chloroplast can use, and hand it on to the second stage.
Location: the thylakoid membranes (grana) of the chloroplast, because that is where the pigments and electron carriers are held.
Inputs: light energy, water, ADP + Pi and NADP⁺.
Outputs: ATP and NADPH, which pass into the stroma for the light-independent reactions, and oxygen, released as a by-product.
Energy conversion: light energy becomes chemical energy, stored in ATP and in the high-energy electrons carried by NADPH.

The two products have different jobs: ATP carries energy, and NADPH carries electrons and hydrogen to reduce carbon dioxide to glucose. After use, they return as ADP + Pi and NADP⁺ to be reloaded. There is more on this in The light-independent reactions.

The second stage of photosynthesis is where glucose is actually built. It uses the ATP and NADPH made in the first stage as its energy and hydrogen supply, and in return sends the empty carriers back.

Location: the stroma (the fluid that fills the chloroplast), which contains the enzymes for these reactions. The reactions need no light directly, but they depend on the ATP and NADPH made in the light-dependent reactions on the thylakoids.

1. Carbon dioxide diffuses into the stroma, from the air spaces of the leaf through the cell and the chloroplast's membranes. It is taken up, or fixed, by combining with a carbon dioxide-accepting compound already present in the stroma.
2. NADPH and ATP from the light-dependent reactions enter the reactions, because they supply the hydrogen and the energy that CO₂ needs to become glucose.

3. Protons and electrons, that is hydrogen, are transferred from NADPH to the carbon compounds made from CO₂. This adds hydrogen to the carbon, which is reduction, turning CO₂ into carbohydrate. NADPH becomes NADP⁺.
4. The energy to achieve this conversion comes from ATP, which is broken down to ADP + Pi (phosphate).

5. Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is the product. Six molecules of CO₂ are fixed for each molecule of glucose, because each supplies one of its six carbon atoms. The glucose is then used, or converted to sucrose, starch and cellulose.
6. ADP + Pi and NADP⁺ return to the light-dependent reactions on the thylakoid membranes, where they are reloaded to ATP and NADPH and can be re-used.
The reactions form a cycle, the Calvin cycle. Most of the carbon compounds made regenerate the CO₂-accepting compound, so the cycle can keep fixing CO₂, and the rest is built into glucose.
Once you know the inputs and outputs, you can explain why this stage responds to temperature and CO₂ and why it stops soon after dark, even though it uses no light directly.
Summary in words: carbon dioxide + hydrogen (from NADPH) + energy (from ATP) → glucose, with NADP⁺ and ADP + Pi released, so the carriers are free to be reloaded.

Every step is catalysed by enzymes in the stroma, so the rate rises with temperature up to an optimum, and falls when the enzymes are denatured. This is why temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis.
CO₂ is the raw material of this stage, so its supply directly limits the rate of glucose production.
In darkness the light-dependent reactions stop, so ATP and NADPH run out within a short time. The light-independent reactions then stop too, even though they do not use light directly.
Photosynthesis is best understood as two linked stages joined by recycled carrier molecules. Modelling it means showing what goes in and out of each stage and what the carriers move between them.

Stage 1, the light-dependent reactions on the thylakoid membranes (the flattened sacs inside the chloroplast): light energy, absorbed by chlorophyll, splits water and drives electron transfer. This produces O₂, which is released, and loads the transfer molecules: ADP + Pi → ATP and NADP⁺ → NADPH.

Stage 2, the light-independent reactions in the stroma: the transfer molecules are unloaded, which is why this stage needs stage 1. NADPH gives its protons and electrons to CO₂, and ATP gives the energy, producing glucose. NADPH → NADP⁺ and ATP → ADP + Pi.
The transfer molecules link the two stages. They carry energy (ATP) and electrons and hydrogen (NADPH) from stage 1 to stage 2, and return empty, as ADP + Pi and NADP⁺, from stage 2 to stage 1.
Because the transfer molecules are recycled, the chloroplast needs only a small supply of each.
Tracing the atoms: the oxygen gas comes from water (stage 1). The carbon and the oxygen in glucose come from CO₂ (stage 2). The hydrogen in glucose comes from water, carried by NADPH.

Diagram: thylakoid (stage 1) beside stroma (stage 2). Stage 1: in light, H₂O; out O₂. Stage 2: in CO₂; out glucose. Two loops between them: ATP across and ADP + Pi back, NADPH across and NADP⁺ back, each arrow labelled energy, or protons and electrons.
Photosynthesis happens inside the chloroplast, and its two stages happen in different parts of it. Each internal part has a structure that suits its job.

Envelope: two membranes, an outer and an inner, surround the chloroplast. The inner membrane controls which substances enter and leave, such as CO₂ going in and the products of photosynthesis going out, so the stroma (the fluid inside the envelope) keeps its enzymes and conditions separate from the cytoplasm.
Thylakoids are flattened membrane sacs inside the chloroplast, separate from the envelope. Each one encloses a fluid-filled space called the thylakoid space, or lumen.

Thylakoids are stacked like piles of coins into grana (singular: granum). Grana are joined by single, unstacked thylakoid membranes called intergranal lamellae, so the whole system is one connected network of membranes.

The thylakoid membranes hold the pigments (molecules that absorb light, such as chlorophyll) in their clusters and reaction centres, the electron transport chains (chains of electron carriers) and the enzyme ATP synthase. This is why they are the site of the light-dependent reactions, the first stage of photosynthesis.

The stroma contains the enzymes of the light-independent reactions, the second stage of photosynthesis, so it is the site of those reactions. It also holds starch grains, which are a temporary store of glucose, lipid droplets, ribosomes (the small structures that make proteins) and a small loop of DNA.

The chloroplast makes some of its own proteins, including some of the proteins of the thylakoid membrane and of the light-independent reactions, using its own DNA and ribosomes. There is more on this in Nuclear and non-nuclear inheritance.

Diagram: an electron-microscope-level drawing of a chloroplast in section, labelled outer membrane, inner membrane, stroma, granum, thylakoid, thylakoid space, intergranal lamella, starch grain, ribosomes and DNA.
The light-dependent reactions need a chain that moves electrons along and releases their energy bit by bit. In the chloroplast, this chain is built into the thylakoid membrane.

An electron transport chain is a series of electron carriers that pass electrons from one to the next, each at a slightly lower energy level. It releases energy in small steps that can be used, such as water running downhill in stages, losing height and so energy at each step.

In the thylakoid membrane, the chain is made of a number of large protein complexes (large groups of proteins that work together) embedded in, or spanning, the membrane. Smaller mobile electron carriers that move within or along the membrane link the complexes, carrying electrons from one to the next.

Some protein complexes contain the clusters of pigment molecules and the reaction-centre chlorophyll, the special chlorophyll molecule that loses electrons when light hits it. Others pass electrons on and use their energy.

NADP⁺, a carrier that takes up electrons and hydrogen, is reduced (gains electrons) to NADPH, as NADP⁺ + 2e⁻ + H⁺ → NADPH, on the stroma side of the membrane. This means NADPH is made right where the light-independent reactions use it.

Embedding the complexes in a membrane holds them in a fixed order and close together, so electrons pass quickly and in the right sequence. The energy released can move protons across the membrane, setting up a proton gradient (a difference in proton concentration across it) that drives ATP making.
The energy released by the electron transport chain is used to move protons (H⁺) into a small enclosed space. The protons then flow back out through an enzyme, and this flow powers the making of ATP.

As electrons pass along the chain, protons (H⁺, hydrogen ions) are moved from the stroma into the thylakoid space. Protons released by the photolysis of water (splitting water using light energy) are also released there, so the small, enclosed thylakoid space builds up a high concentration of protons.
Photolysis happens on the thylakoid-space side of the membrane, and its equation is 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂, so the protons it makes go straight into the thylakoid space.

The protons flow back out of the thylakoid space into the stroma through ATP synthase in the thylakoid membrane. The enzyme uses this flow to make ATP from ADP and phosphate (Pi), as ADP + Pi → ATP, on the stroma side, where the light-independent reactions need it.
The same mechanism makes ATP in mitochondria. There is more on this in The mitochondrion's internal structure and ATP synthase.
Exams ask how the structure of the chloroplast suits it to photosynthesis. The key idea is that each feature gives the reactions more room to work, or keeps them in the right place.

Large surface area: the many stacked thylakoids give a huge area of membrane for pigment clusters, electron transport chains and ATP synthase, so more light can be absorbed and more ATP and NADPH can be made.

Organisation of pigments: grouping many pigment molecules around each reaction centre funnels the energy of photons absorbed over a wide area, and over a range of colours, to the reaction centres. This means more of the light energy reaches the reaction centres.

Separate compartments: the thylakoid space is a small, enclosed compartment, so protons can be concentrated in it to drive ATP synthase. The thylakoid membrane is not freely permeable to protons, so the gradient is kept.

Two stages side by side: the light-dependent reactions on the membranes and the light-independent reactions in the stroma are next to each other, so ATP and NADPH are released into the stroma directly where they are used. ADP + Pi and NADP⁺ return only a short distance.

The stroma holds all the enzymes of the light-independent reactions in one compartment, with their substrates (the substances they act on), so they meet easily. It stores its glucose temporarily as starch.
Own DNA and ribosomes let the chloroplast make some of its own proteins on the spot, such as the membrane and enzyme proteins its two stages need.
Related: the palisade mesophyll, the leaf cells that do most photosynthesis, are packed with chloroplasts, which can move within the cell towards or away from the light.

Diagram: a thylakoid membrane, stroma above and thylakoid space below. Draw pigment clusters, protein complexes and electron carriers with electron arrows, water splitting and H⁺ building up inside, and ATP synthase making ATP in the stroma. Label thylakoid membrane, thylakoid space, stroma, protein complex, mobile electron carrier, ATP synthase.

Every living cell needs a constant supply of usable energy. Respiration is the process that gets it, by breaking down food molecules and transferring the energy they hold to ATP, the cell's energy carrier.

Respiration is the controlled, enzyme-catalysed breakdown of food, mainly glucose, in every living cell. The energy released is transferred to ATP, so respiration releases energy rather than making it.

Respiration is catabolic, meaning a large molecule such as glucose is broken down into smaller molecules and energy is released. The products are CO₂ and H₂O, or lactic acid, or ethanol and CO₂, depending on the conditions.
Photosynthesis is the matching anabolic process, because it builds small molecules up into large ones and takes in energy, whereas respiration breaks large ones down.

The energy is released in many small enzyme-controlled steps rather than all at once, as in burning. This is why much of it can be trapped as ATP instead of being lost as heat. Energy not trapped as ATP is released as heat, which keeps birds and mammals warm.
The ATP made is used for cell activities such as muscle contraction, active transport (moving substances across a membrane using energy) and building large molecules.
Carbon release: the carbon atoms of glucose leave the cell as CO₂, returning to the atmosphere (or water) the carbon that photosynthesis fixed (built into sugar).
Respiration by plants, animals and decomposers, together with burning, balances the uptake of carbon by photosynthesis in the carbon cycle. There is more on this in Nutrient Cycling.

Glucose is the main respiratory substrate (the molecule that is broken down). Glycogen (in animals) and starch (in plants) are first broken down to glucose, and fats and, when needed, proteins can also be respired.

Aerobic (with oxygen) respiration breaks glucose down completely, releasing energy. Knowing where the glucose and oxygen come from, and where the carbon dioxide and water go, shows how organisms and their surroundings are linked.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and breaks glucose down completely to carbon dioxide and water. Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.
Balanced equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy. Its chemicals are those of the photosynthesis equation reversed, but it releases energy (as ATP and heat) instead of taking in light energy.

Source of glucose in plants: photosynthesis, or stored starch and sucrose transported in the phloem (the tissue that carries sugars around the plant). In animals: digested food absorbed into the blood, or glycogen stored in the liver and muscles.
Source of oxygen in humans: the air, taken in through the lungs and carried to the cells by red blood cells, which is how it reaches every cell.

Source of oxygen in plants: the air, entering through stomata (leaf pores) and lenticels (pores in woody stems); soil air, taken in by the roots; and the plant's own photosynthesis. In aquatic organisms it is oxygen dissolved in water.

Fate of carbon dioxide: it diffuses out of cells. In humans it is carried in the blood to the lungs and breathed out; in plants it diffuses out through stomata or, in the light, is used in photosynthesis.
Fate of water: it joins the cell's water and is used in the cell or excreted. Some is breathed out as water vapour.
When oxygen is scarce or absent, cells can still release some energy from glucose, but not nearly as much. The products depend on the organism.

Anaerobic respiration releases energy from glucose without oxygen. Because the glucose is only partly broken down, much of the energy stays in the products, so much less energy is released per glucose and much less ATP is made than in aerobic respiration.

In animals, such as human muscle during intense exercise, and in some bacteria, the product is lactic acid. Word equation: glucose → lactic acid + energy. Balanced equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + energy. No CO₂ is produced.

In yeast, and in plant cells short of oxygen such as roots in waterlogged soil, the products are ethanol and carbon dioxide. Word equation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy. Balanced equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy.

Anaerobic respiration in microorganisms is called fermentation. In baking, yeast's CO₂ makes dough rise and the ethanol evaporates in the oven. In brewing and wine-making, yeast's ethanol is the useful product. In making yogurt and cheese, bacteria's lactic acid is the useful product.
In human muscle during hard exercise, the lungs and blood cannot supply oxygen fast enough, so some respiration is anaerobic. Lactic acid builds up and the muscles tire.

Oxygen debt: after exercise, extra oxygen is needed to remove the lactic acid. It is carried in the blood to the liver, where much of it is converted back to glucose, and the rest is respired aerobically. This is why breathing and heart rate stay high after exercise.
Obligate anaerobes respire only anaerobically and are poisoned by oxygen, for example the bacteria that cause tetanus. Yeast can respire either way, so it is a facultative anaerobe.
Respiration happens in two stages in different parts of the cell. Stage 1 is the same whether or not oxygen is present, and what happens next depends on oxygen.

Stage 1, glycolysis, takes place in the cytoplasm (cytosol, the fluid inside the cell) of every cell and does not need oxygen. 1. Glucose, with 6 carbon atoms, is split into two molecules of pyruvate, each with 3 carbon atoms. 2. A small amount of ATP is made.
With oxygen, stage 2 takes place in the mitochondria (the organelles where aerobic respiration is completed). 3. Pyruvate enters a mitochondrion and is broken down completely to CO₂ and water.
4. Hydrogen removed from it is passed to oxygen, forming water, and a large amount of ATP is made. Stage 2 needs oxygen.

Without oxygen, pyruvate stays in the cytoplasm and is converted to lactic acid (in animals and some bacteria) or to ethanol and CO₂ (in yeast and plants). No further ATP is made, so anaerobic respiration is glycolysis followed by this conversion, all in the cytoplasm.
Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no mitochondria, so their aerobic respiration takes place in the cytoplasm and on the cell membrane.

Diagram: flow diagram. Glucose (cytoplasm), then glycolysis (small ATP), then 2 pyruvate. Oxygen present: mitochondrion, then CO₂, water, large ATP. No oxygen: cytoplasm, then lactic acid (animals) or ethanol and CO₂ (yeast, plants). Label cytoplasm, mitochondrion, stage 1, stage 2.

Aerobic and anaerobic respiration start the same way but differ in how far glucose is broken down and how much ATP results. Respiration also contrasts with photosynthesis: respiration is catabolic and happens in all living cells, while photosynthesis is anabolic and happens only in cells with chloroplasts.
Oxygen: needed in aerobic respiration; not needed in anaerobic respiration.
Location: aerobic respiration takes place in the cytoplasm and the mitochondria; anaerobic respiration takes place in the cytoplasm only.
Breakdown of glucose: complete, to CO₂ and H₂O, in aerobic respiration; incomplete, to lactic acid or to ethanol and CO₂, in anaerobic respiration.
Energy: a large amount of ATP in aerobic respiration; a small amount, only the ATP made in glycolysis, in anaerobic respiration, because the glucose is only partly broken down.
Stages: stage 1 followed by stage 2 in aerobic respiration; stage 1 followed by conversion of pyruvate in anaerobic respiration.
Respiration is catabolic, releases energy, uses O₂ and releases CO₂. It happens in all living cells all the time, in the cytoplasm and mitochondria.
Photosynthesis is anabolic, takes in light energy, uses CO₂ and releases O₂. It happens only in cells with chloroplasts, and only in the light.

Fermentation is a way of releasing energy from sugar without oxygen. This investigation asks what a fermenting microorganism needs before it will do it: sugar, living cells, no oxygen and a suitable temperature.

Fermentation is anaerobic respiration (respiration without oxygen) by microorganisms. Yeast, a single-celled fungus, ferments sugar to ethanol and carbon dioxide; lactic acid bacteria ferment sugar to lactic acid.
The two products of yeast fermentation are the evidence looked for in this investigation: CO₂, shown by bubbles and by limewater turning milky, and ethanol, shown by the iodoform test.
Condition 1, sugar: it is needed because it is the respiratory substrate (the molecule that is broken down), so it is the source of energy for fermentation.
Condition 2, living microorganisms: they are needed because their cells contain the enzymes (biological catalysts) that carry out fermentation. Dead cells have no working enzymes.
Condition 3, an anaerobic environment (no oxygen): yeast with oxygen respires mainly aerobically, producing CO₂ and water instead of ethanol, so oxygen must be kept out to make the cells ferment.
Condition 4, a suitable temperature: it lets the enzymes work at a good rate, because enzymes are slow when cold and denatured (permanently changed in shape, so no longer working) when too hot.

Yeast is a facultative anaerobe, meaning it can respire with or without oxygen, so the conditions decide which kind of respiration it carries out. There is more on this in Respiration as a catabolic process.

A fair test changes one thing at a time. Here you build one flask that has all four conditions and then a set of flasks that each differ from it in a single condition, so any difference in the result can be blamed on that condition.
Aim: to investigate the conditions necessary for fermentation by yeast: the presence of sugar, the presence of living yeast, the absence of oxygen and a suitable temperature.

Hypothesis (example): yeast will ferment glucose, producing carbon dioxide and ethanol, only when sugar and living yeast are present, oxygen is absent and the temperature is warm. Fermentation will be fastest at about 30–40 °C and will stop at high temperature, e.g. 60 °C.
Design: set up one full fermentation flask that meets all four conditions, then a series of flasks each identical except that one condition is missing or changed.
Independent variable (the one you change): the condition changed, which is sugar (present or absent), microorganism (living, dead or none), oxygen (present or absent) or temperature.

Dependent variable (the one you measure): the amount or rate of fermentation, measured as the rate of CO₂ production (bubbles per minute, or cm³ of gas in a set time), whether limewater turns milky, and whether ethanol is present at the end.

Controlled variables (kept the same so the test is fair): the volume and concentration of glucose solution, the mass of yeast, the volume of the flask, the time allowed, and the temperature, except in the temperature series.

Control: a flask with glucose solution and yeast that has been boiled for a few minutes and cooled, set up identically. It shows that the CO₂ and ethanol come from living yeast, not from the glucose solution itself.
The apparatus has to do four jobs: hold the mixture, keep air out while letting gas escape, hold the temperature steady, and detect the two products.

Core equipment: conical flasks or boiling tubes; fermentation locks or rubber bungs fitted with delivery tubes; test tubes of limewater (calcium hydroxide solution); a balance and graduated cylinders; a hot plate or kettle to boil water; a water bath or incubator; a thermometer; a stopwatch; labels.
Materials: dried or fresh baker's yeast; glucose or sucrose; distilled water; liquid paraffin or vegetable oil, which will form a layer that keeps air out.
For the ethanol test: a filter funnel and filter paper, test tubes, potassium iodide solution, sodium hypochlorite solution (dilute bleach) and a water bath.
Optional: a gas syringe, or an inverted measuring cylinder in a trough of water, to collect the gas so its volume can be measured.
The full flask is the reference set-up that meets all four conditions. Every other flask is a copy of it with one condition removed or changed, so follow the steps in order.
1. Boil distilled water for a few minutes and allow it to cool to about 30 °C. Boiling drives out dissolved oxygen and kills unwanted microorganisms; cooling stops the hot water killing the yeast.
2. Dissolve glucose in the cooled, boiled water to make a glucose solution (e.g. 10 g in 100 cm³). Place it in a conical flask, add a set mass of yeast (e.g. 2 g) and swirl to mix.
3. Gently pour a layer of liquid paraffin or vegetable oil on top of the solution, about 1 cm deep, to stop oxygen from the air dissolving in it. This makes the conditions anaerobic.
4. Fit a fermentation lock containing water, or a bung with a delivery tube leading into a test tube of limewater, so that gas can escape but air cannot get in.
5. Place the flask in a water bath or incubator at about 30 °C, and set up the control flask beside it.

6. After the yeast has had time to start, about 10–15 minutes, count the bubbles passing through the fermentation lock or into the limewater in one minute, three times. Note when the limewater turns milky.
Alternatively, collect the gas over a set time in a gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder.
7. Leave the flasks until bubbling stops, a day or more, then test for ethanol.
To show that a condition is needed, remove it from the full flask and see what stops. Each flask below differs from the full flask in one condition only.

Sugar: a flask with yeast in boiled, cooled water only, with no glucose, under oil, at 30 °C. Expected result: very few or no bubbles, limewater stays clear and there is no ethanol. Conclusion: sugar is needed.

Microorganisms: a flask with glucose solution and boiled, dead yeast (the control), and, if wished, a flask with glucose solution only. Expected result: no bubbles, limewater stays clear and there is no ethanol. Conclusion: living microorganisms are needed.
Anaerobic environment: a flask with glucose solution and yeast, made with unboiled water, with no oil layer, open to the air or with air bubbled through it (using an aquarium pump), or shaken often.
Expected result: CO₂ is still produced, from aerobic respiration and often faster, but little or no ethanol is detected. Conclusion: ethanol is made when oxygen is absent.
Suitable temperature: identical full flasks placed at about 5 °C (fridge), 20 °C (room), 30 °C, 40 °C and 60 °C (water baths), each checked with a thermometer.
Expected result: very slow bubbling at 5 °C, where the enzymes are slowed but not denatured and speed up if warmed; faster at 20 °C; fastest at about 30–40 °C.
At 60 °C there is no fermentation, because the enzymes are denatured and the yeast killed, and fermentation does not restart on cooling. Conclusion: a suitable warm temperature is needed.

Bubbles prove only that CO₂ is made, which also happens in aerobic respiration. To show that fermentation really happened you must detect ethanol, and the iodoform test does this by making a visible solid.
1. When bubbling has stopped, filter a sample of the liquid from each flask into a clean test tube, about 3 cm³. Filtering removes the yeast cells.
2. Add about 3 cm³ of potassium iodide solution.
3. Add about 5 cm³ of sodium hypochlorite solution and mix.
4. Warm the tube gently in a water bath at about 60 °C for a few minutes.
5. Allow the tube to cool and observe. Test water as a negative control and a little dilute ethanol as a positive control, so you know what no ethanol and definite ethanol look like.
Result: pale yellow crystals of iodoform (triiodomethane), with an antiseptic, hospital smell, form if ethanol is present; no crystals form without ethanol.
Alternative test: acidified potassium dichromate solution turns from orange to green when warmed with ethanol. Many schools avoid it because potassium dichromate is toxic.
The syllabus names bacteria as well as yeast, so the same four conditions can be tested with lactic acid bacteria. The product is different, so the way you detect fermentation changes too.
The specification allows bacteria. Lactic acid bacteria ferment the sugar lactose in milk to lactic acid, as in making yogurt.

Set up warm milk with a spoonful of live natural yogurt, the source of the bacteria, in clean, closed containers kept warm in an incubator or water bath. Compare with milk without yogurt, and with boiled yogurt.

Measure the fall in pH over several hours, with a pH meter, pH probe or universal indicator, because lactic acid makes the milk more acidic. The milk also thickens as the acid makes its protein clump.
No CO₂ is produced in lactic acid fermentation, so limewater is not used. The same four conditions can be tested.
This practical uses boiling water, corrosive chemicals, flammable ethanol and living cultures. Each hazard has a simple precaution.

Wear safety glasses. Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) is corrosive and irritant to skin and eyes; wash splashes off with plenty of water. Potassium dichromate, if used, is toxic and must be handled with gloves.
Take care with boiling water, the hot plate and water baths, and let the water cool before adding yeast.
Never seal a fermenting flask with a solid bung and no outlet: CO₂ builds up pressure and can force out the bung or crack the glass.
Ethanol is flammable, so keep it away from flames. Never taste the products; laboratory glassware and solutions are not food-safe.
Treat microorganisms with care: wash hands after the practical, and dispose of yeast and bacterial cultures as the teacher directs. Never eat the yogurt made in the laboratory.
Once the flasks have run, record the primary data (the results you collected yourself), compare each flask with the full flask, and decide whether the hypothesis is supported.

Record primary data in a table with one row per flask, giving the condition, the mean bubbles per minute (or volume of gas), whether limewater is milky or clear, and the ethanol test result (crystals or none).
For the temperature series, plot the mean rate on the y-axis against temperature on the x-axis.

Expected results: the full flask bubbles steadily, its limewater turns milky and its iodoform test is positive. The flasks without sugar or without living yeast show no CO₂ and no ethanol. The aerated flask gives CO₂ but little or no ethanol.
Also expected: the rate rises with temperature to a peak at about 30–40 °C and stops at 60 °C. The control shows no activity.

Conclusion: fermentation, the production of ethanol and CO₂, takes place only when sugar and living yeast are present, oxygen is absent and the temperature is suitable. State whether the results support the hypothesis.

Diagram: the fermentation set-up. A conical flask in a water bath, with a thermometer, containing glucose solution and yeast under a layer of oil, fitted with a fermentation lock or a delivery tube into a test tube of limewater.
Label each part. Optionally draw beside it the control flask with boiled yeast.

Your own results are primary data. Secondary data is information collected by others, and using it alongside yours shows whether your conclusion holds up. The conditions you tested are also the ones used in real fermentation.

Pool class results, or compare with published data, to check reproducibility (whether others get the same result). CO₂ production rates can be measured with a CO₂ sensor and data logger, or by the mass lost by a fermenting flask on a balance as CO₂ escapes.

Applications of the conditions: brewers and wine-makers exclude air so that yeast makes ethanol, and control the temperature; bakers keep dough warm so that yeast makes CO₂ quickly to raise it; yogurt makers incubate milk warm with bacteria. There is more on industrial uses in Microorganisms.
Each weakness below would make the results less reliable or the conclusion less certain. For each one, know what goes wrong and how to improve it.
Oxygen can enter if the water was not boiled, the oil layer is broken or the fermentation lock leaks. Some respiration is then aerobic and less ethanol is made.

Yeast can still ferment some sugar when oxygen is present if plenty of sugar is available, so the aerated flask may give a weak positive ethanol test. Compare the amount of crystals, not just their presence.
Bubbles vary in size and some CO₂ dissolves in the solution, so bubble counts are imprecise and underestimate the gas produced. Collecting the gas, or weighing the mass lost, is more accurate.
Limewater turns milky slowly in air, and very large amounts of CO₂ make the milkiness clear again. Set up a limewater tube open to the air for comparison, and observe at set times.
Temperature can drift, so check the water bath regularly. Yeast takes time to start, so begin timing after the same period in every flask.
Yeast samples differ. Use yeast from the same batch, mixed well, for every flask, and repeat each set-up at least three times so a mean can be taken.

Respiration starts with glycolysis, a short pathway that partly breaks down glucose before the cell knows whether oxygen is available. It is the first stage of both aerobic respiration (with oxygen) and anaerobic respiration (without oxygen).

Glycolysis means 'sugar splitting'. It takes place in the cytoplasm (cytosol, the fluid part of the cell outside the organelles), is controlled by about ten enzymes working in sequence, and needs no oxygen.
1. Activation: two ATP molecules are used to add phosphate groups to the glucose (C₆, a six-carbon sugar). This makes the glucose more reactive, so it is an investment of energy that is repaid later.
2. Splitting: the six-carbon sugar is split into two three-carbon molecules.

3. Oxidation: hydrogen, as electrons and protons, is removed from each three-carbon molecule by dehydrogenase enzymes and picked up by NAD⁺ (a carrier molecule that accepts hydrogen), forming NADH. Two NADH are made per glucose.
4. ATP generation: four ATP are made as phosphate groups are transferred to ADP. Net gain: 4 made minus 2 used, so 2 ATP per glucose.
5. Product: two molecules of pyruvate (pyruvic acid, C₃) per glucose. Pyruvate still holds most of the energy of the glucose, which is why much more energy can be released from it later.
Summary: glucose + 2 ADP + 2 Pi + 2 NAD⁺ → 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP (net) + 2 NADH. No CO₂ is released in glycolysis, because the carbons all stay in the two pyruvate molecules.
Glycolysis happens in almost every living cell, and it is not limited to glucose from food.

Glycolysis happens in almost every living cell, prokaryotic (no nucleus) and eukaryotic (with a nucleus). This suggests it evolved early in the history of life, before there was oxygen in the atmosphere, which fits with it needing no oxygen.
Other six-carbon sugars, such as fructose, and the glucose from glycogen or starch enter the same pathway.
Two transfer molecules, ATP and NAD⁺, carry energy and hydrogen through glycolysis. How each one is used explains why the cell must have a way to carry on without oxygen.

ATP: two are used to activate the glucose and four are made by transferring phosphate from the sugar molecules directly to ADP. The net 2 ATP is all the energy anaerobic respiration releases per glucose.
NAD⁺: the cell has only a small supply. Glycolysis converts NAD⁺ to NADH, so glycolysis stops if NADH is not turned back into NAD⁺, because there would be no NAD⁺ left to accept hydrogen.

The fate of NADH depends on oxygen. With oxygen, it passes its electrons to the electron transport chain in the mitochondrion (the organelle where the second stage of respiration happens). There is more on this in Second-stage process.
Without oxygen, NADH passes its hydrogen to pyruvate instead, a process called fermentation. Either way, NAD⁺ is regenerated, so glycolysis can carry on.
Without oxygen, pyruvate is not passed to the mitochondrion, and glycolysis would stop if NADH were not turned back into NAD⁺. Fermentation solves this problem, and it works in the cytoplasm.

When oxygen is absent or too scarce, pyruvate is not passed to the mitochondrion. Instead, in the cytoplasm, NADH passes its hydrogen to pyruvate, or to a product made from it. This regenerates NAD⁺, so glycolysis can keep running and keep making its 2 ATP per glucose.
The purpose of fermentation is to regenerate NAD⁺, not to make more ATP. No ATP is made after glycolysis.

Lactic acid fermentation, in animal muscle cells and in lactic acid bacteria such as those used to make yogurt: pyruvate (C₃) takes hydrogen from NADH and becomes lactic acid (lactate, C₃). This is one step, and no CO₂ is released.
Overall for lactic acid fermentation: glucose → 2 lactic acid, with a net 2 ATP.

Alcoholic (ethanol) fermentation, in yeast and in plant cells short of oxygen, such as waterlogged roots: pyruvate (C₃) first loses one carbon as CO₂, forming a two-carbon compound. This then takes hydrogen from NADH and becomes ethanol (C₂).
Alcoholic fermentation is two steps, with one CO₂ released per pyruvate. Overall: glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 CO₂, with a net 2 ATP.
Lactic acid has three carbons, like pyruvate; ethanol has two, because one carbon is lost as CO₂.
Whether fermentation happens, and what it produces, depends on the organism and on the conditions. Fermentation also releases far less energy than aerobic respiration.
The product depends on the organism's enzymes. Animals and many bacteria make lactic acid, while yeast and plants make ethanol.

Whether fermentation happens at all depends on conditions. Yeast and muscle respire aerobically when oxygen is available and switch to fermentation when it is not. There is more on the conditions in Investigation: conditions for fermentation.
Fermentation releases little energy because glucose is only partly broken down. Lactic acid and ethanol still contain much of the original energy; ethanol is a fuel, for example in biofuels.

Diagram: flow chart. Glucose (C₆), 2 ATP used, 4 ATP made, 2 NAD⁺ → 2 NADH, gives 2 pyruvate (C₃). Branches: (a) oxygen: mitochondrion; (b) no oxygen, animals, some bacteria: lactic acid (C₃); (c) no oxygen, yeast, plants: CO₂, ethanol (C₂). NADH → NAD⁺ loops to glycolysis. Label cytoplasm, mitochondrion.

Glycolysis (the first stage of respiration, in the cytoplasm) only splits glucose part of the way and ends with pyruvate. If oxygen is available, the cell passes pyruvate on to the second stage, and the first job there is a short link step that prepares it for the citric acid cycle.

When oxygen is present, each pyruvate (a 3-carbon molecule, C₃) made in glycolysis moves from the cytoplasm into the matrix of a mitochondrion. The matrix is the fluid-filled space inside the inner membrane.
In the matrix, pyruvate is broken down. One carbon atom is removed as one molecule of carbon dioxide, and hydrogen is removed and picked up by NAD⁺ (a hydrogen carrier), which turns it into NADH.
The remaining two-carbon (acetyl) group is joined to coenzyme A, a carrier molecule, forming acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl CoA, C₂). Per pyruvate: pyruvate + coenzyme A + NAD⁺ → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH.
Each glucose gives two pyruvate, so this link step happens twice per glucose, producing 2 CO₂ and 2 NADH.

Acetyl CoA is the fuel for the citric acid cycle, which strips the carbon from the acetyl group off as CO₂ and loads hydrogen onto carriers. Because the cycle rebuilds its starting compound every turn, it can keep running as long as acetyl CoA keeps arriving.
The citric acid cycle, also called the Krebs cycle, is a cycle of enzyme-controlled reactions in the matrix of the mitochondrion, not on the cristae (the folds of the inner membrane).

1. The acetyl CoA passes its two-carbon acetyl group into the cycle, where it joins a four-carbon compound to form citric acid (C₆), which gives the cycle its name. Coenzyme A is released to collect another acetyl group.
2. In a series of steps, citric acid is broken down back to the four-carbon compound. This is regenerated to accept the next acetyl group, which is why it is a cycle.
3. During each turn, two carbon atoms are removed as two molecules of CO₂, so the carbon of the acetyl group leaves as CO₂.
4. Hydrogen, as protons and electrons, is removed at several steps and loaded onto NAD⁺, forming NADH. A small amount of ATP, one per turn, is also made directly.

The cycle turns twice for each glucose, once per acetyl CoA. With the link step, all six carbon atoms of glucose have now left as six molecules of CO₂, matching the 6CO₂ in the respiration equation. Glycolysis releases none.

The specification's products are CO₂ and H₂O. The CO₂ is released directly. The hydrogen removed is carried by NADH to the electron transport chain, where it ends up in water, so water is not made in the cycle itself.
The cycle does not need oxygen directly, but it stops without oxygen, because NADH cannot be unloaded and NAD⁺ runs out.

Most of the energy in glucose is still locked up in the hydrogen carried by NADH. The electron transport chain releases it in small steps and uses it to make ATP, which is why far more ATP per glucose is made in the second stage than the net 2 ATP of glycolysis. Aerobic respiration (respiration with oxygen) therefore releases many times more energy per glucose than fermentation.
The electron transport chain is a series of electron carriers (protein complexes and mobile carriers) in the inner mitochondrial membrane, especially on the folds called cristae.
1. NADH from glycolysis, the link step and the citric acid cycle delivers its high-energy electrons and protons to the start of the chain. NAD⁺ is released to collect more.
2. The electrons are passed from carrier to carrier, each at a lower energy level. The energy released at each transfer is used to make ATP from ADP and Pi (phosphate).

3. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor. At the end of the chain, low-energy electrons combine with oxygen and protons (H⁺) to form water: 4e⁻ + 4H⁺ + O₂ → 2H₂O. It is the only step of respiration using oxygen directly, and the source of the 6H₂O in the equation.

4. If oxygen is absent, electrons cannot leave the end of the chain, so the whole chain stops. NADH cannot be unloaded, so the citric acid cycle and the link step stop too, and the cell can then only carry out glycolysis and fermentation.
Cyanide is a poison because it blocks the last complex of the chain, which has the same effect as having no oxygen: the chain stops and aerobic ATP production collapses.
5. The ATP made is exported from the mitochondrion to the cytoplasm and used for other biochemical reactions in the cell, such as synthesis of proteins, active transport and muscle contraction.
Most of the ATP from aerobic respiration is made here, via a proton gradient and ATP synthase. There is more on this in The mitochondrion's internal structure and ATP synthase.

Respiration can be modelled as two stages joined by carrier molecules that shuttle electrons, hydrogen, acetyl groups and energy around the cell. Putting the stages together shows where each product comes from and where each reactant is used. There is more on the membrane comparison with photosynthesis in The mitochondrion's internal structure and ATP synthase.
Stage 1, glycolysis, takes place in the cytoplasm: glucose becomes 2 pyruvate, a net 2 ATP is made directly, and NAD⁺ is converted to NADH.

Stage 2 takes place in the mitochondrion. The link step and the citric acid cycle, in the matrix, turn pyruvate into acetyl CoA and then into CO₂, converting NAD⁺ to NADH and making a little ATP directly.
The electron transport chain, on the inner membrane (cristae), unloads NADH to NAD⁺, passes electrons to oxygen to form water, and makes most of the ATP from ADP and Pi.

Transfer molecules carry energy and electrons between the stages. NAD⁺/NADH carries electrons and hydrogen from the breakdown of glucose (glycolysis, link step and cycle) to the electron transport chain, and returns empty. Coenzyme A carries the acetyl group into the cycle and returns.
ATP carries energy from the mitochondrion and cytoplasm to the cell's activities, returning as ADP + Pi to be reloaded. All the transfer molecules are recycled, so only small amounts are needed.

Tracing the atoms: the carbon of glucose leaves as CO₂ in the link step and the cycle. The hydrogen of glucose ends up in water, formed by combining with oxygen breathed in at the electron transport chain. The oxygen breathed in therefore ends up in water, not in CO₂.

Comparison with photosynthesis: in photosynthesis, NADPH and ATP are made in stage 1, using light energy, and used in stage 2 to build glucose. In respiration, NADH is made as glucose is broken down and is used at the end of stage 2 to make ATP.

Diagram: cytoplasm and a mitochondrion (outer membrane, inner membrane with cristae, matrix). Label: glucose, 2 pyruvate, NAD⁺ → NADH, acetyl CoA, CO₂, citric acid cycle (acetyl group + C₄ → citric acid (C₆) → back to C₄), electron transport chain, O₂ + H⁺ → H₂O, ATP, NAD⁺; what each carrier carries.
A mitochondrion is an organelle (a specialised compartment inside a cell). Its inside is divided into distinct regions by two membranes, and each region has a job.
Outer membrane: smooth, it surrounds the mitochondrion and is permeable to small molecules such as pyruvate, ADP and ATP, so these can move freely in and out.

Inner membrane: folded into many cristae (singular crista), which greatly increase its surface area. It holds the electron transport chains and ATP synthase (the enzyme that makes ATP). It is impermeable to protons except through ATP synthase.

Intermembrane space: the narrow space between the outer and inner membranes, into which protons are moved. This is the space "outside the inner membrane" in the specification's wording, not outside the mitochondrion.
Matrix: the fluid inside the inner membrane. It contains the enzymes of the link step and the citric acid cycle (the earlier stages of respiration that deliver electrons to the chain).
The matrix also holds the mitochondrion's own small loop of DNA and its ribosomes (the structures that build proteins), so the mitochondrion makes some of its own proteins.

Diagram: electron-microscope-level drawing of a mitochondrion in section. Label outer membrane, inner membrane, cristae, intermembrane space, matrix, DNA, ribosomes, and ATP synthase drawn as small knobs on the matrix side of the cristae.
The electron transport chain is the machinery that passes electrons along a series of steps, releasing energy at each one. It is built into the inner membrane, so the membrane's structure matters.
The chain is made of a number of large protein complexes embedded in, and spanning, the inner membrane (reaching from one side to the other).
Smaller mobile electron carriers link the complexes. They move within or along the membrane and carry electrons from one complex to the next, so the electrons are handed on step by step.
NADH (the carrier that brings electrons from earlier stages of respiration) delivers electrons to the first complex. The electrons then move from complex to complex, each at a lower energy level.
At the last complex the electrons are passed to oxygen, forming water. There is more on this in Second-stage process.

The electrons do not make ATP directly. Their energy is used to build up a store of protons on one side of the inner membrane, and the protons' flow back drives ATP synthase. The sequence runs in seven steps.

1. Electrons arrive: high-energy electrons from NADH are transferred to a protein complex in the inner membrane. Electrons are negatively charged, so their arrival gives the complex a negative charge, a charge difference.

2. Protons are attracted: the charge difference attracts positively charged protons (H⁺) to the complex. The protons are given by donor molecules: NADH releases a proton when it gives up its electrons, and more protons come from the solution in the matrix.

3. Protons are moved out: the protons pass through the complex from the matrix side to the outside of the inner membrane, into the intermembrane space. Energy from the electrons drives this. It happens at several complexes along the chain as the electrons pass from one to the next. Textbooks call this proton pumping.

4. A gradient builds: protons accumulate in the narrow intermembrane space, giving a high concentration of protons outside the inner membrane and a low concentration in the matrix. This proton (concentration) gradient is a store of energy, like water held behind a dam. It also makes the intermembrane space more positive and more acidic than the matrix.

5. Protons flow back: the inner membrane lets protons through only at the enzyme ATP synthase. They flow back down their gradient, from the intermembrane space across the inner membrane into the matrix, through a channel in ATP synthase. They do not pass back through the electron transport complexes.

6. ATP is made: ATP synthase harnesses the flow of protons. It turns part of the enzyme, like a water wheel or turbine, and uses the energy to join ADP and Pi (inorganic phosphate) into ATP on the matrix side.

7. Oxygen keeps the system running: oxygen accepts the electrons and protons at the end of the chain, forming water, so electrons keep flowing and protons keep being moved out. Without oxygen, the gradient is not maintained and ATP synthase stops.

Diagram: inner membrane, matrix below, intermembrane space above. Show NADH → NAD⁺ + H⁺ + 2e⁻; electron arrow; many H⁺ up; ½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O; H⁺ down ATP synthase, ADP + Pi → ATP. Label protein complex, mobile electron carrier, inner membrane, intermembrane space, matrix, ATP synthase, proton gradient.
The process in the last block has a name, and its history shows how a new scientific idea can win acceptance.
Making ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane is called chemiosmosis.

Nature of Science: the idea was proposed by the British biochemist Peter Mitchell in 1961 and was at first widely doubted. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1978, once experiments had supported it.
Each feature of the mitochondrion's structure suits the way the proton gradient is built and used. Linking a feature to its effect is how you answer structure-and-function questions.

Cristae: folding gives a large area of inner membrane, which holds very many electron transport chains and ATP synthase molecules, so more ATP can be made. Mitochondria in very active cells, such as heart and flight muscle, have more densely packed cristae.
Narrow intermembrane space: its small volume means that protons moved into it quickly build up a high concentration and a steep gradient.
Impermeable inner membrane: the gradient is kept, and protons can return only through ATP synthase, so their energy is not wasted.
Complexes embedded in the membrane in a fixed order: electrons pass quickly and in sequence, and protons are moved in one direction only, across the membrane.

Matrix next to the inner membrane: the enzymes of the link step and the citric acid cycle are right beside the chains, so NADH is delivered quickly. ATP is made into the matrix, from where it is exported to the cytoplasm.
Double membrane: separates the matrix's enzymes and conditions from the cytoplasm. The outer and inner membranes together create the intermembrane space.

Own DNA and ribosomes: the mitochondrion makes some of its own proteins, including some of the chain's, and can divide to make more mitochondria when a cell needs more energy, for example in muscles during training.

Chloroplasts (the organelles where photosynthesis happens) make ATP using a very similar mechanism, built into their thylakoid membranes (flattened internal membrane sacs). The two organelles are alike in several ways, then differ in the details.
Both have electron transport chains of protein complexes and mobile electron carriers embedded in a membrane.
Both use the energy of electrons passing along the chain to move protons across the membrane, building a proton gradient, and both make ATP as protons flow back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis).
Both have a large membrane area, from cristae in the mitochondrion or stacked thylakoids in the chloroplast, so each can hold many chains and ATP synthase molecules.
Both organelles have their own DNA and ribosomes.
The shared mechanism is fed by different energy and electron sources, and it sits in different membranes and compartments. Compare each feature as a pair.
Source of energy: the mitochondrion uses chemical energy from food (glucose), delivered as electrons by NADH; the chloroplast uses light energy, absorbed by chlorophyll.
Source of electrons: NADH, from glucose, in the mitochondrion; water, via the reaction-centre chlorophyll, in the chloroplast.
Final electron acceptor: oxygen, forming water, in the mitochondrion; NADP⁺, forming NADPH, in the chloroplast (non-cyclic pathway).
Oxygen: used at the end of the chain in mitochondria; released by photolysis (the splitting of water) in chloroplasts.
Which membrane: the inner membrane of the envelope (cristae) in the mitochondrion; the thylakoid membrane, a separate internal membrane system, in the chloroplast, not its envelope.
Where protons build up: in the intermembrane space, between the inner and outer membranes, in the mitochondrion; inside the thylakoid space in the chloroplast.
