Where ATP is made and used: in the matrix, then exported for use all over the cell, in the mitochondrion; in the stroma (the fluid around the thylakoids), where it is used in the light-independent reactions, in the chloroplast.

Diagram: side-by-side sketches of a section of the inner mitochondrial membrane and a section of the thylakoid membrane. Each shows its chain, the direction of proton movement, the high-proton compartment (intermembrane space; thylakoid space) and ATP synthase. Label the electron source and final acceptor on each.
Before you can follow the cell cycle you need to know what is being copied and shared out: the chromosomes. How many a cell has, and how they are arranged, decides whether it is diploid or haploid.
A chromosome is one long DNA molecule wound around proteins, carrying many genes (the units of inheritance). There is more on this in Chromosome structure and genes.

Between divisions the chromosomes are long, thin and spread out as chromatin (DNA with its proteins). Before division they coil up (condense) and become short and thick, so they can be seen with the light microscope when stained.

Homologous chromosomes are a pair of chromosomes of the same size and shape, with the same genes at the same positions, one inherited from each parent; the alleles (versions of a gene) on them may differ. Human body cells contain 23 such pairs.
Diploid (2n): a cell or organism with two sets of chromosomes, so that its chromosomes lie in homologous pairs. Human body (somatic) cells are diploid, 2n = 46. The 46 counts chromosomes, not pairs.

Haploid (n): a cell with one set of chromosomes, one chromosome from each homologous pair. Human gametes (sperm and egg cells) are haploid, n = 23. Haploid means one complete set, not half a chromosome.
When two haploid gametes fuse at fertilisation, the zygote (the first cell of the new organism) is diploid again (23 + 23 = 46), so the chromosome number stays the same from generation to generation.
Haploid cells are made by meiosis, a division that halves the chromosome number; mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same. There is more on this in Mitosis and meiosis.
Each species has its own chromosome number: human 2n = 46, the fruit fly Drosophila 2n = 8, the garden pea 2n = 14. The number does not reflect how complex an organism is.
Cells don't just divide and stop: each one lives through a repeating sequence of events called the cell cycle. It shows how a cell prepares for division and then carries it out.
The cell cycle is the sequence of events in the life of a cell, from the time it is formed by division until it divides itself into two daughter cells.
It has three main activities, in this order. First, growth: the cell makes new proteins and organelles (the working parts of a cell) and gets bigger.
Second, DNA synthesis: every chromosome is copied, so the cell has two copies of its genetic information to hand out.
Third, division: the nucleus divides so that each new nucleus gets one copy of every chromosome, then the cytoplasm divides to give two cells.
The phase between divisions, when growth and DNA synthesis happen, is interphase. A cell spends most of its life in interphase, about 90% of the cycle, so division is short.
In many human cells grown in the laboratory, one cycle takes about 24 hours.
Interphase is not a resting stage. The cell is very active, carrying out its normal functions as well as preparing to divide.
One cycle, including division, produces two daughter cells, each with the same number and type of chromosomes as the parent cell and genetically identical to it.
Not every cell divides at the same pace, and no cell divides without being told it is safe to. Whether a cell cycles depends on its job and on control checks built into the cycle.
Some cells leave the cycle once they are specialised and stop dividing, for example most mature nerve cells. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and can't divide.

Other cells divide often throughout life, for example cells of the skin, the lining of the gut and the bone marrow, and in plants the cells at root and shoot tips (meristems, regions where growth happens).

The cycle is controlled. Proteins inside the cell check at several points (checkpoints) that the cell is large enough, that the DNA has been copied correctly and is undamaged, and that the chromosomes are attached correctly before the cell moves on.
Signals from other cells (growth factors, chemical messages) tell a cell whether to divide. There is more on how loss of this control leads to cancer in Cancer.

Diagram: the cell cycle as a circle. Large sector: interphase (cell growth and DNA replication). Small sector: division (mitosis, then cytokinesis). Arrow for direction. Higher Level: also label G1, S, G2 and the four stages of mitosis.
Interphase is long and busy, and it has three parts: G1, S and G2. Together they prepare the cell so that division can be quick and accurate.
G1 (first growth phase): the cell grows, makes proteins (including the enzymes needed to copy DNA) and organelles, and carries out its normal job.
S (synthesis) phase: DNA replication, so each chromosome now consists of two identical copies called sister chromatids, joined at the centromere (the narrow point where they are held together).

G2 (second growth phase): further growth and more organelles, for example mitochondria. The proteins of the spindle (the fibres that later pull chromosomes apart) are made, and ATP is stored for division.
A cell that stops dividing leaves the cycle from G1 into a non-dividing state (sometimes called G0), for example mature nerve cells.
Throughout interphase the nuclear membrane (envelope) is intact, the nucleolus is visible and the chromosomes are uncoiled as chromatin, so individual chromosomes can't be seen.
Mitosis is the division of the nucleus. It runs as one smooth process, but it is split into four stages to make it easier to describe, and each stage has a characteristic look and job.

Nuclear division (mitosis) is a continuous process, divided for convenience into four stages in this order: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. It is followed by cytokinesis, which is division of the cytoplasm and not a stage of mitosis.

Prophase: the chromosomes condense (shorten and thicken) and become visible, each as two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. The nucleolus disappears, the nuclear membrane breaks down, and spindle fibres (protein tubes called microtubules) begin to form.
In animal cells, two centrioles move to opposite ends (poles) of the cell and the spindle forms between them. Plant cells have no centrioles but still form a spindle.
Metaphase: the chromosomes line up singly on the equator (middle) of the spindle; each is attached by its centromere to spindle fibres from both poles.
Anaphase: the centromeres split and the spindle fibres shorten, pulling the sister chromatids apart to opposite poles, centromere first, which gives a V shape.
Once separated, each chromatid is called a chromosome, so each pole now has a full set of identical chromosomes. Energy for the movement comes from ATP, the cell's energy carrier.

Telophase: the chromosomes reach the poles and uncoil back into chromatin; a nuclear membrane forms around each set; the nucleoli reappear; the spindle breaks down. There are now two nuclei, each genetically identical to the original.

Diagram: the four stages of mitosis in an animal cell, 2n = 4 (one long and one short homologous pair, shaded to show the two parents). Labels: chromosome, sister chromatids, centromere, spindle fibres, centriole, pole, equator, nuclear membrane (breaking down, re-forming), cell membrane, cleavage furrow (end of telophase).
You can tell which stage a cell is in just by looking at how its chromosomes are arranged under the microscope. Counting dividing cells then tells you how fast a tissue is dividing.

In stained cells from a growing root tip (for example onion or garlic) viewed at ×400, most cells are in interphase, seen as a nucleus with no visible chromosomes, because interphase is the longest part of the cycle.
Dividing cells are identified by the arrangement of their chromosomes: condensed and scattered for prophase; in a line across the middle for metaphase.
Two groups moving apart is anaphase; two groups at opposite ends, with new nuclei forming, is telophase.
The mitotic index is the percentage of cells in a sample that are dividing. For example, 24 dividing cells out of 200 gives (24 ÷ 200) × 100 = 12%.
A high mitotic index shows a tissue that is dividing rapidly, such as a root tip or a tumour.
After the nucleus has divided, the cell still has to split in two. Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, and plant and animal cells do it differently because plant cells have a rigid wall.
Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm to form two separate daughter cells. It usually starts during late telophase. Organelles such as mitochondria are shared between the two cells.
In animal cells the cell membrane is pulled inwards around the middle of the cell, forming a groove (cleavage furrow) that deepens until the cell pinches into two.
In plant cells the rigid cell wall can't pinch in. Instead, vesicles (small membrane sacs) from the Golgi apparatus collect across the middle of the cell and fuse to form a cell plate.
The cell plate grows outwards to the sides and becomes the new cell membranes and cell wall between the two cells.
Diagram: an animal cell with a cleavage furrow beside a plant cell with a cell plate forming, each labelled.
When a cell divides, its genetic information has to go somewhere. In mitosis the information is passed on unchanged, so the new cells are exact genetic copies of the cell they came from.

Mitosis is nuclear division (division of the nucleus, which holds the chromosomes) that produces two nuclei, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent nucleus and genetically identical to it.
A diploid cell (one with two sets of chromosomes) gives two diploid cells (2n to 2n). A haploid cell (one with a single set), in organisms that have haploid stages, gives haploid cells (n to n).

Every chromosome is copied exactly before mitosis. During mitosis the two identical copies of each chromosome are separated, so each new nucleus receives one copy of every chromosome. This is one division giving two daughter cells.
Homologous chromosomes (the matching pair, one from each parent) do not pair up in mitosis. There is more on this in 'DNA replication and mitosis in the cell cycle'.
Cells produced by mitosis from one parent cell form a clone: a group of genetically identical cells or organisms.
Mitosis on its own produces no genetic variation, because the information is copied exactly. The only source of difference is a rare mistake in copying, called a mutation.

Sexual reproduction needs cells with half the usual number of chromosomes, and it also produces variety. Meiosis does both: it halves the chromosome number and shuffles the genetic information, so no two cells are alike.

Meiosis is nuclear division that halves the chromosome number, producing four haploid nuclei from one diploid nucleus (2n to n). It involves two divisions, one after the other, after the DNA has been copied once.

In the first division, homologous chromosomes pair up and then separate, one of each pair going to each new cell, so each cell receives one complete set. In the second division the two copies of each chromosome separate.

The four cells differ from each other and from the parent because the homologous pairs line up and separate independently of one another (random, or independent, assortment). Each gamete (sex cell) therefore receives a random mixture of maternal and paternal chromosomes.

With 23 pairs, one person can make 2²³ (more than 8 million) different combinations of chromosomes in their gametes. This is the basis of Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment. There is more on this in 'Mendel's Laws'.
Homologous chromosomes can also exchange matching segments during the first division (crossing over), mixing their alleles (versions of a gene) further.

Random fertilisation adds further variation, since any one of a huge number of different sperm may fuse with any one of a huge number of different eggs. So offspring of sexual reproduction differ from their parents and from each other, except identical twins. Variation from sexual reproduction and its role in evolution are in 'Variation'.

Meiosis keeps the chromosome number constant across generations: gametes are haploid, so the zygote (the cell formed at fertilisation) is diploid (n + n = 2n). Without meiosis the number would double every generation.
A unicellular organism is a single cell, so when it divides it is reproducing. Mitosis gives it a fast way to reproduce, and meiosis gives some of them a way to add variation.

In unicellular eukaryotes (organisms made of one cell with a nucleus) such as Amoeba and yeast, mitosis followed by division of the cell is asexual reproduction: one organism becomes two genetically identical organisms. In yeast this happens by budding.
Asexual reproduction is fast, needs only one parent and passes on a successful set of genes unchanged, so a population can grow quickly when conditions are good.
The drawback is that all the offspring are alike, so one change in conditions, such as a new disease, can affect them all.

Some unicellular eukaryotes also reproduce sexually, using meiosis to produce varied haploid cells, often when conditions become poor. For example, starved diploid yeast cells undergo meiosis to form four haploid spores, which can survive harsh conditions.
The variation from meiosis makes it more likely that some offspring survive a changed environment.

Prokaryotes (bacteria, which have no nucleus) have neither mitosis nor meiosis. They copy their single circular chromosome and divide by binary fission. There is more on this in 'Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells'.
A multicellular organism uses mitosis to build and maintain its body, and meiosis only to make cells for sexual reproduction. Keeping these jobs separate matters for what offspring inherit.
Mitosis for growth: a multicellular organism develops from a single cell, the zygote, by repeated mitosis, so every body cell has the same genetic information as the zygote.
In plants, growth by mitosis is concentrated at the tips of roots and shoots (regions called meristems).

Mitosis for repair and replacement: cells that wear out or are damaged are replaced, for example when a cut heals, when skin cells and the cells lining the gut are replaced, and when new blood cells are made in the bone marrow (stem cells there divide by mitosis).

Mitosis for asexual reproduction: some multicellular organisms, including many plants, also reproduce asexually by mitosis, producing clones of the parent. Methods of asexual reproduction in plants are not on the specification.

Meiosis for sexual reproduction takes place only in the reproductive organs. In humans it happens in the testes (forming sperm) and the ovaries (forming eggs). There is more on how human gametes form in 'Gametes and fertilisation'. In flowering plants it happens in the anthers and the ovules, leading to the pollen grains and the egg cell.

Because body cells are made by mitosis and gametes by meiosis, a change to the DNA of a body cell, such as a skin cell, is not passed to offspring. A change in a cell that gives rise to gametes can be.
There is more on this in 'Mutations', which is Higher Level only.
Both divisions share machinery but do different jobs. Comparing them point by point shows how mitosis keeps information the same and meiosis varies it.

Similarities: both are nuclear divisions of eukaryotic cells; both follow DNA replication (copying of the DNA) in interphase (the period between divisions); both use a spindle (a structure of fibres) to separate chromosomes; both are followed by cytokinesis (division of the cytoplasm).
Number of divisions and cells: mitosis has one division and gives two cells; meiosis has two divisions and gives four cells.
Chromosome number: mitosis keeps it the same (2n to 2n); meiosis halves it (2n to n), so its cells are haploid.

Genetic make-up of the cells produced: mitosis gives cells identical to each other and to the parent; meiosis gives cells that differ from each other and from the parent. Homologous chromosomes do not pair in mitosis; in meiosis they pair and then separate.
Where it happens: mitosis in body cells throughout the organism; meiosis only in the reproductive organs (testes, ovaries, anthers and ovules).
Role of meiosis: it produces gametes or spores for sexual reproduction, giving variation and keeping the chromosome number constant across generations.
Role in unicellular and multicellular organisms: mitosis serves growth, repair, replacement and asexual reproduction in both.

Diagram: two flow diagrams for a cell with 2n = 4 (one long, one short homologous pair, parents' chromosomes shaded differently). Mitosis: two cells, 2n = 4, same shading as the parent. Meiosis: four cells, n = 2, different shadings. Label diploid, haploid, homologous pair.

Before a cell divides, it has to copy its DNA, the molecule that carries its genetic instructions. This copying is called DNA replication, and it is what lets one cell become two with the same instructions.
DNA replication is the process by which a DNA molecule makes an exact copy of itself, giving two identical DNA molecules.

In eukaryotic cells (cells with a nucleus) it happens in the nucleus during interphase, the growing phase before the cell divides. It is the DNA-synthesis part of the cell cycle, the repeating sequence of events in a dividing cell.
Every chromosome in the nucleus is copied once, and only once, per cell cycle, so the DNA is doubled exactly one time before each division.

Replication is needed because a cell that divides must give each daughter cell a complete and identical set of genetic instructions. Without replication each daughter cell would receive only half the DNA.

A DNA molecule is a double helix (a twisted ladder) made of two strands held together by pairs of bases. Replication works by pulling the two strands apart and using each one as a pattern for a new partner strand. Follow the steps in order.

1. Enzymes (proteins that speed up reactions) unwind the double helix and separate, or unzip, the two strands by breaking the weak hydrogen bonds between the base pairs. The strong bonds of each sugar–phosphate backbone are not broken, so each strand stays intact.
2. Each separated single strand acts as a template (pattern) for building a new strand, because its exposed bases decide which nucleotides can attach.
3. Free DNA nucleotides in the nucleus line up against the exposed bases of each template strand by complementary base pairing: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G.
4. Enzymes join the new nucleotides to each other to form a new sugar–phosphate backbone, making a complementary strand; hydrogen bonds form between the new and old bases.
5. Each new DNA molecule winds back into a double helix. The result is two DNA molecules, each made of one original (parent) strand and one new strand.

This is why replication is described as semi-conservative: half of each new molecule is conserved from the parent. There is more on the evidence for this in Modelling DNA replication and information flow.
Replication has to be accurate, because any error is passed on to every daughter cell. Fixed base pairing and checking enzymes are what keep the copies exact.
Because base pairing is fixed, each new strand is an exact complement of its template, so both new molecules have the same base sequence as the original.

For example, a section of DNA with one strand ATTGCA and the other strand TAACGT separates: ATTGCA is a template for a new TAACGT, and TAACGT is a template for a new ATTGCA, giving two molecules identical to the original.
Enzymes make replication fast and accurate; they also check the new strands and correct most mistakes. A rare uncorrected mistake changes the base sequence, which is a mutation (a change in the DNA).

Diagram: a short section of DNA (about four base pairs) as a ladder: parent molecule, strands separating with free nucleotides pairing, two daughter molecules each with one old strand (dark) and one new strand (light). Label parent strand, new strand, hydrogen bonds broken, free nucleotide, complementary base pair, enzyme.

Replication copies the DNA, but copying alone does not make two cells. Mitosis (the division of the nucleus) and cytokinesis (the division of the rest of the cell) then share the copies out, so each new cell ends up with a full set.

Replication in interphase doubles the DNA. Afterwards each chromosome consists of two identical copies joined together, so the cell temporarily has twice the normal amount of DNA. A human cell still has 46 chromosomes, but each one is double.

Mitosis then separates the two copies of every chromosome, sending one copy to each end of the cell, so each daughter nucleus receives one copy of every chromosome: 46 chromosomes in each human daughter cell, with the same number and the same genes as the parent.
Cytokinesis then divides the cell, so the amount of DNA in each daughter cell returns to the amount in the parent cell before replication. Each daughter cell can then grow and repeat the cycle.

Replication and mitosis together keep the genetic information the same in every cell of a multicellular organism, and pass identical copies to offspring in asexual reproduction. There is more on these roles in Mitosis and meiosis.

Order matters: replication must be complete before mitosis begins, which the cell checks, and it happens only once per cycle. Otherwise daughter cells would get missing or extra DNA. When this control fails, cells can be damaged or become cancerous.

Diagram: a graph of DNA per cell (y-axis, arbitrary units) against time (x-axis) over two cell cycles. DNA is steady at one level in early interphase, rises to double during replication, stays double until the end of mitosis, then drops back at cytokinesis. Label interphase, DNA replication, mitosis, cytokinesis.
Your body replaces and repairs tissue by mitosis (cell division that makes two identical cells), and it keeps this tightly controlled. Cancer is what happens when that control fails.
Cancer is a group of diseases in which some body cells lose control of mitosis. They divide too often (the rate of division is abnormal) and too many times (the number of divisions is not limited).
Cancer cells can also invade nearby tissues and spread to other parts of the body, which is what makes cancer more than just extra cells.
There are over 200 kinds of cancer, named after the organ or tissue where they start, e.g. lung, breast, skin, bowel and blood.
Carcinomas are the group that start in epithelial tissues (the tissues that line or cover organs), e.g. most lung, breast and bowel cancers.
Sarcomas start in bone, muscle or connective tissue (the supporting tissue that holds other tissues together).
Leukaemias start in the blood-forming cells of the bone marrow, and lymphomas start in the lymphatic system (the network of vessels and nodes that drains fluid and carries immune cells).
Cancer starts from a single cell whose DNA has changed (mutated). All the cancer cells in a tumour are descended from that one cell by mitosis, so they all carry its mutation.
To see how cancer starts, you first need to know how healthy cells stay in check. Normal cells divide only when told to, and have built-in ways to stop damaged cells from dividing.
Normal cells divide only when they receive signals to divide (growth factors, chemical messengers from other cells), and stop when signals tell them to stop.
Checkpoints in the cell cycle (the ordered series of stages a cell goes through to divide) halt the cycle if the DNA is damaged or not copied correctly, so errors are not passed on.
Two groups of genes control this. Proto-oncogenes code for proteins that stimulate the cell cycle, so they are the accelerator, e.g. growth factor receptors (proteins that detect the growth signal).
Tumour suppressor genes code for proteins that stop the cycle at checkpoints, so they are the brakes. They also repair damaged DNA or make a badly damaged cell destroy itself.
Apoptosis is programmed cell death: a damaged or unwanted cell breaks itself down in a controlled way, without harming neighbouring cells. It removes cells with damaged DNA before they can divide.

TP53 is an example of a tumour suppressor gene. It codes for the protein p53, which stops the cell cycle when DNA is damaged so that the DNA can be repaired, or triggers apoptosis if the damage is too great.
p53 is called the guardian of the genome because it protects the DNA. TP53 is mutated in about half of all human cancers, which shows how important its protection is.
Contact inhibition: normal cells in a tissue, and in a culture dish, stop dividing when they touch neighbouring cells, so they form a single layer.
Most normal human cells can divide only a limited number of times before they stop, because the protective caps at the ends of their chromosomes (telomeres) shorten with each division.
Cancer develops when the genes that control division are damaged by mutation (a change in the DNA). The damage affects the accelerator, the brakes, or both, and it builds up step by step.
1. A mutation in a proto-oncogene can turn it into an oncogene, which is permanently switched on and keeps telling the cell to divide even with no signal, like an accelerator stuck down.
2. A mutation that inactivates a tumour suppressor gene removes the brakes: damaged cells keep dividing instead of stopping, being repaired or dying by apoptosis.
Usually both copies (alleles) of a tumour suppressor gene must be inactivated before control is lost, because one working copy can still make enough of the protein.
3. One mutation is usually not enough. Several mutations in different control genes must build up in the same cell, often over many years.
This is why the risk of most cancers rises with age, and why anything that increases the rate of mutation raises the risk.

4. Once one cell has lost control, every daughter cell inherits the same mutations. As they divide faster and faster, further mutations arise, and the cells that divide fastest or survive best take over, so the cancer cells become more abnormal over time.
5. The immune system (the body's defence against disease) destroys many abnormal cells before they form a tumour. People whose immune system is weakened have a higher risk of some cancers.
Cancer cells differ from normal cells in many ways. Most of the differences come straight from the lost controls on division, and they are best learned as pairs.
Division: normal cells divide only when signalled, at a controlled rate. Cancer cells divide rapidly and continuously without signals, and ignore signals to stop.

Lifespan: normal cells divide a limited number of times and die by apoptosis when damaged. Cancer cells avoid apoptosis, and many keep their telomeres long by using the enzyme telomerase, so they can divide indefinitely (immortal cells).
Contact inhibition is lost: cancer cells ignore contact with neighbours and pile up into a mass, whereas normal cells stop at contact.
Specialisation: normal cells are specialised (differentiated) for a job. Cancer cells are unspecialised (poorly differentiated), so they don't carry out the tissue's function.

Appearance under the microscope: cancer cells vary in size and shape and have large, irregular, darkly staining nuclei, often with abnormal numbers of chromosomes, and many are seen dividing. This is how cancer is diagnosed from a biopsy (tissue sample) or smear.
Blood supply: cancer cells can release signals that make new blood vessels grow into the tumour (angiogenesis), supplying the oxygen and nutrients needed for further growth.
Attachment: normal cells stick to their neighbours and stay in place. Cancer cells can lose this adhesion (stickiness), break away and move.

HeLa cells are a famous example of immortal cancer cells. They were taken in 1951 from a cervical cancer of Henrietta Lacks at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, USA, without her knowledge or consent.

They were the first human cells to keep dividing indefinitely in the laboratory, and they are still used in research worldwide, including in developing the polio vaccine. Her case is a well-known example of the ethics of consent in research.
Not every lump of abnormal cells is cancer. What decides it is whether the cells stay put or invade and spread.
A tumour is an abnormal mass of cells produced by uncontrolled division.
A benign tumour grows slowly, is usually enclosed in a capsule (a layer of tissue around it), does not invade surrounding tissue or spread, and its cells look fairly normal.

A benign tumour is usually removable by surgery and not life-threatening, though it can be dangerous if it presses on a vital organ such as the brain. Examples are most moles and warts. A benign tumour is not cancer.
A malignant tumour, which is a cancer, grows quickly, has no capsule, invades and destroys surrounding tissue, can spread around the body, and has abnormal cells.

Benign and malignant tumours differ in rate of growth (slow or quick), capsule (present or absent), invasion (none or destructive), spread (none or around the body) and appearance of cells (fairly normal or abnormal).
They also differ in danger: a benign tumour is usually not life-threatening, while a malignant tumour is a cancer and can be life-threatening because it invades and spreads.
A cancer becomes dangerous when it spreads beyond where it began. These are the steps from one mutated cell to tumours in other organs.
1. A cell mutates and divides without control, producing a clone (a group of identical cells) of abnormal cells.
2. Further mutations and division form a small tumour in the tissue of origin, the primary tumour.
3. Angiogenesis (the growth of new blood vessels) supplies the tumour with blood, so it grows larger.
4. Cancer cells invade the surrounding tissue.
5. Some cells break away, enter blood vessels or lymph vessels, and are carried around the body.
6. They leave the vessels in another organ and divide there to form secondary tumours, called metastases.

Diagram: draw normal tissue (a neat single layer), then one mutated cell, a primary tumour with a vessel growing in, cells entering a vessel, a secondary tumour elsewhere. Labels: normal cells, cancer cell with large nucleus, primary tumour, blood vessel, invasion, metastasis, secondary tumour.
Spread is what makes cancer so serious, and the harm tumours do comes from their size, position and appetite for nutrients.
Metastasis is the spread of cancer from the primary tumour to form secondary tumours elsewhere.
Secondary tumours contain the same type of cells as the primary tumour: breast cancer that spreads to the bones is still breast cancer cells, not bone cancer.
Metastasis makes cancer much harder to treat, because the cells are in many places, which is why early detection matters. There is more on this in Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer.
Tumours harm the body by pressing on and damaging organs, and by blocking tubes such as the airways, gut or blood vessels.
They also destroy normal tissue and stop it working, e.g. leukaemia cells crowd out normal blood-forming cells in the bone marrow, causing anaemia (too few red blood cells) and infections.
Tumours use up the body's nutrients, causing weight loss.
Cancer is rarely down to one thing. The ideas of risk and carcinogens set out here are the ones the later blocks on infections, environment and genes all use.

Most cancers have no single cause. They result from several mutations (changes in DNA) building up in one cell, so anything that damages DNA, makes cells divide more often or weakens the body's defences raises the risk.
A factor that increases the chance of developing a disease is a risk factor.

A carcinogen is any agent that can cause cancer. Most carcinogens are mutagens: they damage DNA, causing mutations in proto-oncogenes (genes that promote cell division) or tumour suppressor genes (genes that restrain it).

The three kinds of cause in the specification are infectious agents, environmental factors (including lifestyle) and genetic susceptibility (an inherited tendency). They often act together in the same person.
Risk is a probability, not a certainty. A risk factor makes cancer more likely, but not everyone exposed develops cancer, and some people with no known risk factor do.
Cancer itself is not infectious, but some infections raise the risk of it. For each agent, learn the route: the agent, how it pushes cells towards cancer, and which cancer results.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a virus spread by sexual contact. Some high-risk types infect cells of the cervix (neck of the womb). The virus's DNA enters the cells and its proteins switch off the cell's tumour suppressor proteins, including p53, so infected cells divide without control.
Persistent HPV infection causes most cervical cancers, and two types, HPV 16 and HPV 18, cause about 70% of them. HPV also causes some cancers of the throat, anus, penis and vulva.
Most HPV infections are cleared by the immune system and cause no harm, so infection raises the risk of cancer but does not mean cancer. There is more on HPV as a virus in Viruses.

Hepatitis B and hepatitis C viruses infect liver cells. Long-term infection causes repeated liver damage and inflammation, and the repeated cell division needed to repair the liver gives more chances for mutations. They cause liver cancer.

Helicobacter pylori is a bacterium that lives in the stomach lining, causing long-term inflammation and ulcers. Long-term infection raises the risk of stomach cancer. It can be cleared with antibiotics.

Epstein–Barr virus, the virus that causes glandular fever, is linked to some lymphomas (cancers of lymph tissue), e.g. Burkitt's lymphoma, and to cancer of the nose and throat (nasopharyngeal cancer).

Infections raise cancer risk in three ways. Some viruses insert their own genes, whose proteins interfere with control of the cell cycle (HPV). Long-term inflammation and repeated repair division increase the chance of mutation (hepatitis viruses, H. pylori).
Third, infections that weaken the immune system let abnormal cells escape destruction. Remember that cancer itself is not infectious: it cannot be caught from another person.
Tobacco is the largest single avoidable cause of cancer. It shows clearly how a chemical in the environment can cause mutations.
Tobacco smoke contains many carcinogens. Tar contains benzo[a]pyrene, a chemical that binds to DNA and causes mutations, including in TP53, the gene for the tumour suppressor protein p53.
Smoking is the main cause of lung cancer. It also causes cancers of the mouth, throat, larynx, oesophagus, pancreas, bladder, kidney and cervix.
Second-hand (passive) smoke, breathed in by people near a smoker, also causes lung cancer.

The risk of smoking-related cancer rises with the number of cigarettes and the number of years of smoking, which is called a dose–response relationship (more exposure, more risk). The risk falls after stopping.
Some radiation carries enough energy to damage DNA directly. The two types to know are ultraviolet (UV) light and ionising radiation, and they are different.

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun and from sunbeds is absorbed by DNA in skin cells. It makes neighbouring thymine bases on a strand bond together (thymine dimers), which distorts the DNA and causes mutations if not repaired.

UV causes skin cancers, including melanoma, the most dangerous type. Skin cancer is the most common cancer in Ireland. People with fair skin that burns easily are at greatest risk, and sunburn, especially in childhood, raises the risk.
Ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays and radioactive substances) has enough energy to break DNA strands.

Radon is a natural radioactive gas that comes from uranium in rocks and soil and seeps into buildings. It is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking. Parts of Ireland have high radon levels, so homes can be tested and fitted with a radon sump or barrier.

After the Chernobyl nuclear accident in 1986, released radioactive iodine caused a large increase in thyroid cancer in children in the surrounding area. Medical X-rays use the lowest effective dose for this reason.
Chemicals at work, what we drink and eat, body weight and simply getting older all change cancer risk. Each works by damaging DNA or by making cells divide more.

Asbestos fibres, once used in building insulation, lodge in the lungs and cause mesothelioma (a cancer of the lining of the lungs) and lung cancer. Smokers exposed to asbestos have a far greater risk than the two risks added together, because the factors multiply.
Alcohol is broken down in the body to ethanal (acetaldehyde), which damages DNA. Drinking raises the risk of cancers of the mouth, throat, oesophagus, liver, bowel and breast.
The risk from alcohol rises with the amount drunk, and there is no completely safe level for cancer risk.

Processed meat (e.g. bacon, ham and sausages) was classified by the World Health Organization's cancer agency, IARC, in 2015 as a cause of bowel cancer, and red meat as probably causing it. A diet high in fibre, from wholegrains, fruit and vegetables, lowers the risk of bowel cancer.

Obesity raises the risk of several cancers, e.g. bowel, breast after the menopause, womb, kidney and oesophagus, partly because fat tissue releases hormones and growth signals that stimulate cell division. Regular physical activity lowers the risk of bowel and breast cancer.
Age is the strongest single risk factor. Most cancers are diagnosed in older people, because mutations build up over a lifetime.
Some people start life with a head start towards cancer because they inherit a faulty gene. This is a minority of cases, but it shows clearly how mutations lead to cancer.

Most mutations that cause cancer arise during a person's life in body cells (acquired, or somatic, mutations) and are not inherited. Only about 5–10% of cancers are strongly linked to an inherited faulty gene.
A person who inherits one faulty copy of a tumour suppressor gene has it in every cell, so only one more mutation, in the other copy, is needed in a cell to lose that brake.
This is why inherited cancers often appear at a younger age, in more than one family member, and sometimes in both of a pair of organs, e.g. both breasts.

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumour suppressor genes whose proteins repair damaged DNA. An inherited faulty copy greatly increases the lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer in women, and raises the risk of prostate and breast cancer in men.
Either parent can pass on a faulty BRCA gene, with a 50% chance for each child, which is a dominant pattern of inheritance (one faulty copy is enough to raise risk).
Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited faulty copies of genes that repair copying errors in DNA. It greatly raises the risk of bowel cancer and of cancer of the womb.

People with a strong family history can be tested for these faulty genes. Those who carry one can have more frequent or earlier screening, and some choose surgery to reduce risk, e.g. removal of the breasts or ovaries.

The actress Angelina Jolie publicly described her choice of a preventive double mastectomy in 2013, after testing positive for a faulty BRCA1 gene. Her account greatly increased the number of women seeking testing. There is more on genetic testing in Ethics of genetic technologies.
Evaluating means weighing how strong the evidence is and what can be done about each factor. Each point below is a short argument you can use.
Avoidable or unavoidable: smoking, alcohol, diet, body weight, sun and sunbed exposure, radon and some infections can be changed or prevented, but age and inherited genes cannot.
The World Health Organization estimates that between 30% and 50% of cancers could be prevented by avoiding risk factors and using existing prevention strategies.

Size of effect: tobacco is the largest single avoidable cause of cancer. A strong effect, consistent across many studies, with a dose–response relationship and a known mechanism, is strong evidence of cause.
The link between smoking and lung cancer was first shown by Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill, in a study of lung-cancer patients in Britain published in 1950.

Factors interact: a person's risk depends on several factors together. Smoking and asbestos multiply each other's effects, and alcohol and smoking together raise the risk of mouth and throat cancer more than either alone.
An inherited BRCA mutation raises risk, but lifestyle still matters. So it is hard to say what caused any one person's cancer.

Time lag: cancers usually appear many years or decades after exposure, e.g. mesothelioma after asbestos and lung cancer after smoking. This makes causes harder to identify and means the benefits of prevention appear only years later.

Individual or public action: individuals can change their behaviour, but laws and public-health measures often have larger effects. Arguments against heavy regulation include personal freedom and cost; arguments for it include protecting others, e.g. from second-hand smoke, and reducing health-care costs.
Knowing a factor is linked to cancer is not the same as knowing it causes cancer. The kind of evidence behind a claim decides how far to trust it.

Much of the evidence is correlational. Most evidence about diet and lifestyle comes from observing large populations, which shows links but must rule out other explanations, e.g. people who eat more vegetables may also smoke less.
Laboratory and animal studies can show a mechanism, but results in animals don't always apply to humans. Media reports of single studies are often unreliable.
Laws and free programmes can lower cancer risk across a whole population, which is why public action is often more effective than asking individuals to change.
In 2004 Ireland became the first country in the world to ban smoking in all enclosed workplaces, including pubs and restaurants. This protects workers and customers from second-hand smoke.
Sunbed use by under-18s is banned in Ireland, which limits exposure to UV radiation during the years when sunburn does most harm.
Vaccination and screening programmes are free, so cost does not stop people taking part.
Prevention is better than treatment. Vaccines remove infections that cause cancer, and lifestyle changes remove the avoidable risk factors met earlier.

The HPV vaccine protects against infection by the HPV types that cause most cervical cancers, and some other cancers. It works best if given before any exposure to the virus, so it is offered free in Ireland to girls and boys in first year of secondary school.
A large Swedish study published in 2020 found that girls vaccinated before age 17 had close to 90% lower risk of invasive cervical cancer than unvaccinated women.
The HPV vaccine does not protect against every HPV type, so cervical screening is still needed. There is more on how vaccines work in Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment.
The hepatitis B vaccine is given to babies in Ireland as part of the 6-in-1 vaccine. By preventing hepatitis B infection it prevents many cases of liver cancer.
There is no vaccine against hepatitis C, but hepatitis C can now be cured with antiviral drugs.

Lifestyle changes that lower risk: don't smoke, and avoid second-hand smoke; keep a healthy body weight; be physically active; eat plenty of wholegrains, fibre, fruit and vegetables, and limit processed and red meat; limit alcohol.
Also protect skin from the sun with shade, clothing, a hat and sunscreen, and don't use sunbeds; test the home for radon; take part in vaccination and screening.
Finding cancer early gives the best chance of cure. Early detection includes screening of healthy people, self-checks, and diagnosis once something is suspected.

A cancer found early is usually small and has not spread (no metastasis), so it can often be removed completely and treatment is much more likely to succeed. Screening can also find pre-cancerous changes, which can be treated before cancer develops.
Screening means testing healthy people with no symptoms. Ireland's free national programmes are BreastCheck, which offers mammograms (X-rays of the breast) to women aged 50–69 every two years.
CervicalCheck screens women and people with a cervix aged 25–65. The sample is first tested for high-risk HPV, and only HPV-positive samples are examined under the microscope for abnormal cells.
BowelScreen is a free home test kit that detects hidden traces of blood in a stool sample, followed by a colonoscopy (a camera examination of the bowel) if positive.

Self-examination and symptoms: check breasts and testicles for lumps, and check moles using the ABCDE rule: Asymmetry, irregular Border, more than one Colour, Diameter more than 6 mm, and Evolving or changing.
Go to a doctor about warning signs such as an unexplained lump, unexplained weight loss, a persistent cough, or blood in the urine or stool.

Diagnosis: a biopsy, a small sample of tissue, is examined under the microscope for cancer cells. Scans (X-ray, CT, MRI and ultrasound) show where tumours are and whether they have spread. Blood tests can detect some cancers or the substances they release.

Limits of screening: no test is perfect. A false positive causes worry and unnecessary further tests; a false negative gives false reassurance; and some screening finds slow-growing cancers that would never have caused harm (overdiagnosis). So screening is offered to the age groups where the benefits are greatest.
Treatment depends on the type and spread of the cancer. For each treatment, learn how it works, its advantage and its disadvantage.

Surgery removes the tumour with a margin of surrounding normal tissue, and sometimes nearby lymph nodes. It is most effective for a solid tumour that has not spread; it is not possible for leukaemias (cancers of the blood) or widespread cancer.

Radiotherapy aims beams of ionising radiation at the tumour, damaging the DNA of the cancer cells so that they die. Rapidly dividing cells with faulty repair are especially vulnerable. Side effects come from damage to nearby normal tissue, e.g. sore skin and tiredness.

Chemotherapy uses drugs carried in the blood throughout the body to kill dividing cells, usually by damaging DNA or stopping DNA replication or mitosis. Unlike surgery, it can reach cancer cells that have spread.

Two chemotherapy drugs act on mitosis. Vincristine, from the Madagascar periwinkle plant, stops the spindle (the fibres that pull chromosomes apart) forming; paclitaxel (Taxol, first obtained from the bark of the Pacific yew tree) stops the spindle breaking down. Either way, chromosomes can't be separated.

Because chemotherapy also kills normal rapidly dividing cells, its side effects include hair loss (hair follicles), nausea and mouth ulcers (gut lining), and anaemia and infections (bone marrow). It is given in cycles to let normal tissues recover.

Hormone therapy is used for cancers that need a hormone to grow. Many breast cancers have oestrogen receptors, and the drug tamoxifen blocks the receptors, so oestrogen can't stimulate the cancer cells to divide.

A bone-marrow (stem cell) transplant is used for some leukaemias. After high-dose treatment destroys the diseased bone marrow, healthy blood-forming stem cells from a matched donor, or the patient's own cells collected earlier, are given to rebuild it.
Newer treatments and tests aim to hit cancer more precisely and find it sooner. For each, know what it is, what it offers and its limits.

Targeted therapy uses drugs designed to act on the protein made by a particular mutated gene in the cancer, so they harm normal cells less. Targeted drugs work only for cancers with that target, and cancers can become resistant.

Imatinib (Glivec) blocks the abnormal protein made by the BCR-ABL gene in chronic myeloid leukaemia. This gene is formed by the Philadelphia translocation, and the drug has turned a fatal leukaemia into one most patients live with for many years.
Trastuzumab (Herceptin) is an antibody that attaches to the HER2 receptor on breast cancer cells that have too many of these receptors.

Immunotherapy helps the patient's own immune system destroy cancer cells. Checkpoint-inhibitor drugs release the brakes that cancer cells use to switch off T lymphocytes (immune cells that kill abnormal cells). The 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to James Allison and Tasuku Honjo for this work.

Checkpoint inhibitors have produced long-lasting responses in some people with advanced melanoma and lung cancer. In CAR-T cell therapy, a patient's T cells are genetically modified to recognise their cancer cells, multiplied and returned to the body; it is used for some leukaemias and lymphomas.
Immunotherapy works in only some patients, can cause the immune system to attack healthy organs, and is very expensive.

Personalised (precision) medicine: sequencing the DNA of a patient's tumour shows which genes are mutated, so doctors can choose the drug most likely to work for that tumour rather than for the organ in which it started.

Personalised mRNA cancer vaccines, made to match the mutated proteins of one patient's tumour, train the immune system to attack it. They are in clinical trials, e.g. for melanoma, and are not yet routine.
Biopsies normally need a tissue sample taken by a procedure. A newer approach uses only a blood sample.
A liquid biopsy is a blood test that detects small fragments of DNA released by tumours into the blood, so no tissue needs to be removed.
This may allow cancers to be found earlier, and relapse (the cancer coming back) to be detected, without surgery. The tests are still being evaluated for accuracy.

Before a cell divides it must copy all of its DNA, a process called replication, so that each new cell gets a complete set of genetic instructions. Knowing where, when and how fast this happens is the starting point for the model.

Replication takes place in the nucleus (the compartment that holds the DNA) during the S phase of interphase, the stage of the cell cycle between divisions when the cell copies its DNA. There is more on this in The cell cycle.
In eukaryotes (cells with a nucleus) replication begins at many points along each chromosome at once, so the very long DNA molecules are copied quickly.
Bacteria start replication at one point on their circular chromosome, because their DNA is a single, much smaller loop.
Replication needs energy, which is supplied by ATP (the cell's energy-carrying molecule) and by the nucleotides themselves as they are added.

Replication uses each old strand of DNA as a pattern for a new one, and two key enzymes (proteins that speed up a chemical reaction) do the main jobs. Learn the stages in order and name the enzyme that does each job.

1. The enzyme DNA helicase unwinds the double helix and separates the two strands by breaking the hydrogen bonds (the weak links) between complementary bases. This opens a Y-shaped replication fork where copying happens.

2. Each exposed strand acts as a template, a pattern to copy. Free DNA nucleotides, which are made in the cell and are present in the nucleus, pair with the exposed bases by complementary base pairing (A–T, C–G).

3. The enzyme DNA polymerase joins each new nucleotide to the growing strand, forming the sugar–phosphate backbone of the new strand. It adds nucleotides only where they pair correctly with the template, so the copy matches the original.
4. DNA polymerase also proofreads: it checks each new base pair and removes and replaces most wrongly paired nucleotides. Other repair enzymes correct many of the rest.
A mistake that is not corrected becomes a permanent change in the base sequence, a point mutation (a change to one base in the DNA). There is more on this in Mutations.
5. Each new DNA molecule, made of one template strand plus its new complementary strand, twists into a double helix. The two new molecules are identical to each other and to the original.

The two new molecules remain joined as two sister chromatids (identical copies of a chromosome) at a centromere, the narrow point where they are held together, until they separate at anaphase of mitosis.

Diagram: a replication fork, labelled: parent (original) DNA double helix, DNA helicase at the fork, hydrogen bonds being broken, the two template strands, free nucleotides, DNA polymerase adding nucleotides, the new complementary strands, and the two daughter molecules, each with one old strand (dark) and one new strand (light).

Once the base-pairing structure of DNA was known, there was more than one way the copying could work. Scientists had to decide between three models, and the one that proved correct is called semi-conservative.
Semi-conservative replication: each new DNA molecule contains one strand from the original molecule (conserved, meaning kept) and one newly made strand. This is why it is called half-conserving.
Watson and Crick predicted this in 1953 from the base-pairing model, because each strand can act as a template for its partner. There is more on this in Models.
Conservative replication: the original double helix stays intact, and a completely new molecule is made.
Dispersive replication: each new molecule is a patchwork of old and new pieces in both strands, so old and new DNA are mixed along each strand.

In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl tested the three models by labelling DNA so that old and new strands could be told apart by their weight. Learn the method and the results, because you may be asked to interpret them.
1. They grew the bacterium E. coli for many generations in a medium whose only nitrogen was the heavy isotope ¹⁵N (a heavier form of nitrogen), so all its DNA was “heavy”.
2. They moved the bacteria to a medium containing only normal, light ¹⁴N, so any new DNA strand would be built from light nitrogen.
3. After each generation they extracted the DNA and spun it at high speed in a caesium chloride solution, which forms a density gradient, so DNA settles as a band at a level that matches its density.
Before the transfer there is one heavy band, because all the DNA is made with ¹⁵N.
After one generation there is one band of intermediate density, so conservative replication, which would give one heavy and one light band, is ruled out.

After two generations there are one intermediate band and one light band, of equal size. This rules out dispersive replication, which would give a single band at every generation, becoming lighter each time.
Only the semi-conservative model fits both results.

Diagram: three centrifuge tubes side by side (generation 0, 1, 2) showing band positions heavy; intermediate; intermediate and light; with a strand diagram under each showing heavy strands dark and light strands pale.

The semi-conservative model is precise enough to make exact predictions about base sequences and numbers of nucleotides. Because A always pairs with T and C with G, you can work these out step by step.
Predicting daughter molecules: given a parent molecule with strands ATGCCA and TACGGT, the strands separate.
ATGCCA is the template for a new TACGGT, and TACGGT is the template for a new ATGCCA, because each base can only pair with its partner.
The two daughter molecules are identical to the parent, each with one old strand and one new strand.
Counting nucleotides: copying a DNA molecule of 1,000 base pairs makes two new strands of 1,000 nucleotides each, so 2,000 free nucleotides are used.
If 30% of the parent's bases are adenine, then 30% of the free nucleotides used are A and 30% are T.
The remaining free nucleotides are 20% C and 20% G, because A = T and C = G in double-stranded DNA. There is more on this in Nucleotides, DNA and RNA.

Two more skills use the model: working out how many molecules exist after several rounds of replication, and building a hands-on model to show how copying works. A good model also has limits that you should be able to name.
Generations: one DNA molecule replicated three times gives 2³ = 8 molecules, because the number of molecules doubles each time.
In a Meselson–Stahl-type experiment only 2 of these 8 still contain an original heavy strand, because each original strand is kept whole and never broken up.
Physical model: build a short double strand from paper or plastic nucleotide pieces in four colours, one per base, that fit only their correct partners.
Separate the strands, add free pieces to each, and compare the two products with the original. Use two shades for old and new pieces to show semi-conservation.
Strength of the physical model: it shows templates, base pairing and identical products.
Limitations of the physical model: it is flat and short, and does not show the helix, the enzymes, the energy needed, or the speed and accuracy of copying in cells. There is more on this in Models.

A gene is a section of DNA that carries the instructions for one protein. The instructions are not used directly: they are first copied into a molecule of RNA, and that copy is then used to build the protein.
Genetic information flows from DNA to mRNA to protein: DNA → transcription → mRNA → translation → protein. Replication, by contrast, copies DNA to DNA.
Francis Crick called this one-way flow from nucleic acid to protein the “central dogma” of molecular biology.
Transcription: in the nucleus, the base sequence of one gene is copied into a molecule of messenger RNA (mRNA), using one DNA strand as the template.

The mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore (a small channel in the nuclear envelope) and travels to a ribosome in the cytoplasm, either free or attached to rough endoplasmic reticulum. The DNA stays in the nucleus.
Translation: at the ribosome (the structure that builds proteins), the mRNA's codons (groups of three bases) are read, and transfer RNA molecules bring the matching amino acids.

The amino acids are joined in the order set by the codons to make a specific polypeptide (a chain of amino acids), which folds into a functional protein. There is more on this in Transcription and translation.

Diagram: a eukaryotic cell showing a gene on DNA in the nucleus → transcription → mRNA passing through a nuclear pore → ribosome in the cytoplasm → translation → polypeptide folding into a protein. Label: nucleus, DNA, gene, mRNA, nuclear pore, ribosome, tRNA bringing amino acid, polypeptide.
The ribosome works from an mRNA copy of a gene rather than from the DNA itself, for three reasons. There is also one well-known exception to the usual direction of flow.
The DNA is kept safe in the nucleus and is not damaged by being used directly.
Many mRNA copies can be made from one gene, and each is read by many ribosomes, so a lot of protein can be made quickly.
mRNA is broken down after use, so the cell can switch protein production on and off.
Exception: retroviruses such as HIV carry RNA and use the enzyme reverse transcriptase to make DNA from their RNA, so information flows from RNA to DNA. There is more on this in Viruses: replication.
Information never flows from protein back to nucleic acid.
A cell can't send its DNA out to the ribosomes, so it makes a working copy of the gene instead. Three molecules are involved in making and carrying that copy: DNA, the enzyme RNA polymerase and mRNA.
DNA holds the gene, the base sequence (the order of A, T, C and G) that codes for the protein.
In transcription only one of the two strands of the gene is read, the template strand. The DNA is not used up or changed, and it stays in the nucleus, so the original instructions stay safe.

RNA polymerase is the enzyme that carries out transcription. It binds to the DNA at the start of a gene, unwinds and separates the two strands there, and joins free RNA nucleotides into a strand complementary to the template.
RNA polymerase moves along the gene until it reaches the end, building the new strand as it goes.
mRNA (messenger RNA) is a single-stranded copy of one gene's code, a series of codons (groups of three bases), and it carries the code from the nucleus to a ribosome.
mRNA is short-lived and is broken down after use, so a cell can stop making a protein by no longer making its mRNA.

Translation (turning the mRNA code into a chain of amino acids) needs a delivery molecule for the amino acids and a workbench to assemble them on. These are tRNA and the ribosome, which is built from rRNA. Together with mRNA, these are the three types of RNA in protein synthesis.
tRNA (transfer RNA) is a small RNA molecule in the cytoplasm that carries one specific amino acid to the ribosome.
Each tRNA's anticodon (three bases) pairs with a matching codon on the mRNA, so tRNA is the molecule that “translates” codons into amino acids.
tRNA brings amino acids to the ribosome; it does not make them.
rRNA (ribosomal RNA) makes up the ribosome together with proteins. It holds the mRNA and tRNAs in position.
The rRNA of the large subunit also catalyses the formation of peptide bonds (the bonds that join amino acids), so it acts as an enzyme.
The ribosome is the site of translation, made of rRNA and protein in two subunits: a small subunit that binds the mRNA and a large subunit with room for two tRNAs at a time.
The ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, reading the code in order.

Ribosomes are free in the cytoplasm, making proteins used in the cell, or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (a membrane network studded with ribosomes), making proteins for export or for membranes. There is more on this in Endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus.
Transcription is the making of an mRNA copy of a gene, and it takes place in the nucleus. It works by complementary base pairing, where each base on the DNA attracts one particular partner base.
1. RNA polymerase attaches to the DNA at the start of the gene, unwinds the double helix there and separates the two strands by breaking the hydrogen bonds between the base pairs.
2. One strand, the template strand, is read.
2. Free RNA nucleotides pair with its exposed bases by complementary base pairing: A on DNA pairs with U on RNA, T with A, C with G, and G with C. RNA has U (uracil) where DNA has T.
3. RNA polymerase joins the RNA nucleotides into a strand of mRNA as it moves along the gene, so the mRNA grows one nucleotide at a time.
3. Behind it, the DNA strands re-join and rewind, so the DNA is left unchanged.
4. At the end of the gene, RNA polymerase detaches and the finished mRNA is released.
4. The mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore (a gap in the nuclear envelope) and goes to a ribosome.

Diagram: a section of DNA unwound by RNA polymerase, with the template strand and the mRNA strand growing alongside it; label DNA, template strand, RNA polymerase, free RNA nucleotides, mRNA, base pair A–U, direction of movement.
A tRNA has to do two jobs: carry the right amino acid and recognise the right codon. Its folded shape has one end for each job.

A tRNA is a single strand of about 80 RNA nucleotides that folds back on itself, so some regions lie side by side and can base-pair. Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases in some regions hold the folded molecule in shape.
The folded molecule is a clover-leaf in two dimensions and folds further into an L shape in three dimensions.
At one end is the amino-acid attachment site, where one specific amino acid is attached by a specific enzyme, using energy from ATP.
At the opposite end is a loop with the anticodon: three unpaired bases that pair with a complementary codon on mRNA.
The code is read in codons of three bases, so each tRNA has an anticodon of exactly three bases and matches one codon (three bases of mRNA).
Each tRNA brings one amino acid. The attachment of a specific amino acid to each tRNA with a specific anticodon is what links each codon to its amino acid.
The ribosome holds two tRNAs side by side on neighbouring codons, so the code is read three bases at a time without gaps or overlaps.
Diagram: a clover-leaf tRNA, labelled: single RNA strand, regions of base pairing (hydrogen bonds), anticodon loop with three bases, amino-acid attachment site, amino acid.

Translation is the making of a polypeptide (a chain of amino acids) from the code in mRNA, and it takes place at ribosomes in the cytoplasm. It begins by assembling the ribosome on the mRNA and joining the first two amino acids.
1. Start: the small ribosomal subunit attaches to the mRNA and moves along it to the start codon, AUG.
1. A tRNA with the anticodon UAC, carrying methionine, pairs with the start codon, and the large subunit then joins.
2. A second tRNA, whose anticodon is complementary to the next codon, arrives carrying its amino acid and pairs with that codon in the second position in the ribosome.
3. A peptide bond forms between the two amino acids, a condensation reaction that releases water. It is catalysed by the rRNA of the ribosome.
3. The first tRNA's amino acid is now attached to the second amino acid.
Once two amino acids are joined, the same cycle repeats along the mRNA until a stop signal is reached. Cells also run many ribosomes at once to make protein quickly.
4. The ribosome moves along the mRNA by one codon, three bases. The first tRNA, now without its amino acid, is released into the cytoplasm, where it can pick up another of the same amino acid.
4. A new tRNA pairs with the codon now in the empty position, because the move has exposed the next codon.
5. Steps 2 to 4 repeat, the chain growing by one amino acid each time, in the order set by the codons.
6. End: when a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA) is reached, no tRNA matches it, and a protein release factor binds instead.
6. The polypeptide is released, and the ribosome's subunits separate from the mRNA.
Many ribosomes can translate the same mRNA at once, one behind the other, forming a polysome, so many copies of the protein are made quickly.
Translation also needs energy, both to attach amino acids to their tRNAs (from ATP) and to move the ribosome along the mRNA.

Diagram: a ribosome on an mRNA strand, with two tRNAs paired to neighbouring codons, a growing polypeptide on one, a peptide bond forming and a released tRNA leaving; label mRNA, codon, anticodon, tRNA, amino acid, peptide bond, ribosome (large and small subunits), polypeptide, direction of movement.
A newly made polypeptide is only a chain. It becomes a working protein when it folds into a particular three-dimensional shape, and the shape is set by its amino-acid sequence.
The sequence of amino acids (the primary structure) determines how the chain folds.
Bonds form between amino acids in different parts of the chain, such as hydrogen bonds and, in some proteins, sulphur bridges, giving the protein its particular three-dimensional shape.
Some proteins are made of more than one polypeptide, for example haemoglobin, which has four.
The shape determines the function, for example the active site of an enzyme or the binding site of an antibody or receptor. There is more on this in Genes, proteins and traits.
A change in the amino-acid sequence can change the shape and stop the protein working, because the bonds that fold the chain form in different places.

Proteins made on the rough endoplasmic reticulum are folded and modified there and in the Golgi apparatus, then packaged into vesicles (small membrane sacs) for export, such as digestive enzymes and insulin.

In prokaryotes, which have no nucleus, so no nuclear envelope separates the steps, transcription and translation both take place in the cytoplasm, and ribosomes can begin translating an mRNA while it is still being transcribed.
Both processes copy DNA using complementary base pairing, so they are easy to confuse. They differ in what is copied, which enzymes do it, and what happens to the product.
Product: replication makes a complete copy of all the DNA, giving two DNA molecules; transcription makes an RNA copy of one gene, the mRNA.
Strands used: replication uses both strands as templates, so both new molecules are complete; transcription uses only one strand of the gene.
Enzymes: DNA helicase and DNA polymerase in replication; RNA polymerase in transcription, so the enzyme names tell the two processes apart.
Nucleotides and pairing: DNA nucleotides contain deoxyribose (a sugar) and pair A with T; RNA nucleotides contain ribose, and A on DNA pairs with U.
When: replication happens once per cycle, in S phase; transcription happens throughout the cell's life, for whichever genes are needed, many times.
Fate of the product: new DNA stays in the nucleus, but mRNA leaves for the cytoplasm and is broken down after use.
Exam questions often give a DNA sequence and ask for the mRNA, tRNA anticodons and amino acids. You can do this with a fixed five-step method.
1. Write the mRNA complementary to the template strand (A → U, T → A, C → G, G → C).
2. Divide the mRNA into codons from the start codon, because the ribosome reads three bases at a time.
3. Write the tRNA anticodon complementary to each codon, because the anticodon pairs with the codon.
4. Use the codon table given to find the amino acids.
5. Stop at a stop codon, because no amino acid is added there.
Here is the method applied to one short template strand, showing each product in turn.
Template DNA TAC AAA CCG ATT gives mRNA AUG UUU GGC UAA, by pairing T with A, A with U and C with G.
The anticodons are UAC, AAA and CCG, with none for the stop codon UAA, because no tRNA matches a stop codon.
The polypeptide is methionine, phenylalanine and glycine, and then the chain stops.
Three codons code for amino acids, so the worked example gives three amino acids joined by two peptide bonds.
You can also model the two processes with paper and cards. A model makes the order of events clear, but it leaves out some of the real chemistry.
Paper strips for DNA, in a “nucleus” area, are copied onto mRNA strips that are carried to a “ribosome” area.
Cards for tRNA have a three-base anticodon on one side and an amino acid on the other, so each card shows what a real tRNA does.
In the role-play, students match anticodons to codons in order and link the amino acids with clips to represent peptide bonds.
Limitations of the role-play: it is slow and flat, and ignores the enzymes, energy and folding, so it shows the order of events but not how they happen chemically.

DNA is copied every time a cell divides, and the copying is not perfect. A mutation is what is left when a change in the DNA is not put right, and it matters because it is the raw material for new traits.
A mutation is a permanent change in the DNA: either in the base sequence of a gene, called a point or gene mutation, or in the structure of a chromosome, called a chromosomal mutation.
A mutation that changes a gene produces a new allele (a different version of that gene).
Mutations arise spontaneously, mainly as uncorrected errors in base pairing during DNA replication (the copying of DNA before a cell divides), when a wrong base is paired and nobody fixes it.
Mutagens (agents that increase the rate of mutation) include ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays, radioactive substances) and ultraviolet light, which damage DNA directly.
Other mutagens are chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, and some viruses.
Repair enzymes correct most damage, so only the errors that escape repair become permanent mutations. There is more on mutagens and cancer in Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer.

Whether a mutation matters to a family depends on which cell it happens in. What it does to the organism depends on whether it changes a protein, and for evolution it matters because mutation creates new alleles.
Body-cell (somatic) mutations affect only the individual and the cells descended from the mutated cell, so they are not inherited; they can lead to cancer.
Mutations in cells that form gametes (germ-line mutations) can be passed to offspring, and are then present in every cell of the child because every cell grows from the fertilised egg.
Most mutations are neutral, either because they fall in non-coding DNA (DNA that does not code for a protein) or because they are silent, meaning the protein is not changed.
Many mutations are harmful, because they change or stop a protein.
A few mutations are beneficial in a particular environment, for example lactase persistence (being able to digest milk sugar as an adult).
Mutations giving antibiotic resistance help bacteria survive antibiotics, so they are beneficial to the bacteria in the presence of the drug.
Mutation is the only source of new alleles, and so the ultimate source of variation for natural selection to act on. There is more on this in Variation.

A point mutation is a tiny change at one spot in a gene. Because the genetic code is read in codons (groups of three bases, each coding for one amino acid), the effect depends on exactly what changes. The simplest case is a substitution.
A point mutation is a change in the nucleotide sequence at one point in a gene, usually of one or a few base pairs. This includes small deletions and insertions, not only substitutions.
It occurs when a wrong nucleotide pairs during replication and is not corrected, or when a nucleotide is added or missed out.
At the next replication the change is copied into both strands, so it becomes permanent.
In a substitution one base is replaced by another, so only one codon changes.
Silent substitution: the new codon codes for the same amino acid, because the code is degenerate (several codons can code for the same amino acid), so the protein is unchanged.
Missense substitution: the new codon codes for a different amino acid, which may or may not change the protein's shape and function.
Nonsense substitution: the codon becomes a stop codon (a signal to end translation), so the polypeptide is cut short and usually does not work.
Adding or losing bases is more dangerous than swapping one, because it can shift the way the whole rest of the gene is read.

Insertion or deletion of one base, or of any number of bases that is not a multiple of three, is a frameshift: every codon after the change is read differently, because the code is read in threes without gaps from the start codon.
After a frameshift many amino acids are wrong, and a stop codon often appears early or is lost, so the protein usually does not work.
A frameshift near the start of a gene is more damaging than one near the end, because more of the protein is changed.

Insertion or deletion of three bases adds or removes one amino acid without a frameshift, so the rest of the protein is normal, but even one missing amino acid can change the folding, as in cystic fibrosis.

To model a mutation, write the mRNA in codons, apply the change, then read each new codon with the codon table. Start with the normal mRNA AUG UUU GGC AAA UAA, which codes for methionine, phenylalanine, glycine and lysine, then stops.
Substitution, silent: GGC changed to GGA; still glycine, so the protein is unchanged.
Substitution, missense: UUU changed to UCU; serine instead of phenylalanine.
Substitution, nonsense: AAA changed to UAA, a stop codon; the chain ends after glycine.

Insertion of G after AUG: AUG GUU UGG CAA AUA A… gives methionine, valine, tryptophan, glutamine, isoleucine…; every amino acid after the start is changed and the original stop codon is lost from the reading frame.
Deletion of the first U of UUU: AUG UUG GCA AAU AA… gives methionine, leucine, alanine, asparagine…; this is a frameshift, because the groups of three have moved along.
Deletion of the whole codon UUU: AUG GGC AAA UAA gives methionine, glycine, lysine; one amino acid is missing and the rest is unchanged, so there is no frameshift.

Word analogy for revision: THE CAT ATE THE RAT; substitution THE CAT ATE THE HAT changes one word; insertion THE CXA TAT ETH ERA T gives nonsense words after the change; deletion THE ATA TET HER AT shifts every word after it.
Sickle-cell anaemia shows how a change in a single base can alter a protein and so a whole disease. It is a substitution.
Sickle-cell anaemia is a substitution in the gene for beta-globin, one of the polypeptides of haemoglobin, on chromosome 11.
One base change alters the codon for the sixth amino acid from GAG to GUG in mRNA (CTC to CAC in the DNA strand being read), so valine replaces glutamic acid.
The changed haemoglobin, haemoglobin S, molecules stick together into long fibres when oxygen is low, distorting red blood cells into a rigid sickle shape.
Sickled cells block small blood vessels, causing pain and organ damage, and are destroyed quickly, causing anaemia.
Sickle-cell is recessive: people with two copies have the disease; people with one copy (sickle-cell trait) are usually healthy and are more resistant to malaria.
This is why the sickle-cell allele is common in parts of Africa where malaria is common, an example of natural selection.
Cystic fibrosis is the example of a point mutation that is a small deletion. It shows that losing even one amino acid can ruin a protein.
Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7, which codes for a chloride-ion channel protein in cell membranes.
The most common cystic fibrosis mutation, F508del (delta F508), is a deletion of three bases, which removes one amino acid, phenylalanine, at position 508 of the protein.
The faulty protein folds wrongly, is broken down by the cell and does not reach the membrane, giving thick, sticky mucus in the lungs and pancreas.
Cystic fibrosis is recessive, and Ireland has the highest rate of cystic fibrosis in the world.
Newer CFTR modulator drugs help the faulty protein fold and work, which shows how knowing the mutation leads to treatment.
Cystic fibrosis is one of the conditions tested for in the newborn heel-prick screening offered to every baby in Ireland. There is more on this in Prenatal and postnatal care.
A chromosomal mutation changes a large piece of a chromosome, so many genes are affected at once, unlike a point mutation. A letter model makes the four types easy to follow.
A chromosomal mutation is a change in the structure of one or more chromosomes that affects many genes at once.

It occurs when chromosomes break, for example from ionising radiation or chemicals, or from errors when chromosomes are copied or separated in meiosis (the cell division that makes gametes), and the broken pieces are lost or rejoin in the wrong place.
Large changes can be seen under the light microscope in a karyotype (a picture of a cell's chromosomes).
Model: write a chromosome as A B C • D E F G H, where the letters are genes or groups of genes and • is the centromere (the constricted point where the two halves of a chromosome are joined).
A different, non-homologous chromosome (one that is not its partner in a pair) is written M N O • P Q R.
Two of the four types change how many copies of a section there are, one by losing it and one by repeating it.
Deletion: a section breaks off and is lost, so its genes are missing: A B C • D E F G H becomes A B C • D E H, with F and G lost.
Deletion is usually harmful, because a whole set of genes is missing.
Duplication: a section is copied twice, so its genes are repeated: A B C • D E F G H becomes A B C • D E F E F G H.
Extra copies can upset the balance of gene products (the proteins the genes make); over evolutionary time, duplicated genes can mutate to take on new functions.
