The other two types move genes without necessarily losing any. An inversion turns a section around in the same chromosome; a translocation moves a section to another chromosome.
Inversion: a section breaks out, turns through 180 degrees and rejoins, so its genes are in reverse order: A B C • D E F G H becomes A B C • D G F E H.
No genes are lost, so an inversion often has no effect on the person, unless a break falls inside a gene; it can cause problems in meiosis, leading to gametes with missing or extra genes.
Translocation: a section of one chromosome breaks off and joins a different, non-homologous chromosome; in a reciprocal translocation two chromosomes swap sections.
In a reciprocal translocation, A B C • D E F G H and M N O • P Q R become A B C • D E F Q R and M N O • P G H.
If no genes are lost the person may be healthy, but a break can join two genes into a new hybrid (fusion) gene, and carriers can produce gametes with unbalanced sets of genes.
Diagram: each of the four mutations drawn as a chromosome with lettered bands and a centromere, before and after, with the translocation shown between two chromosomes of different sizes.
Each structural type has a real disorder that illustrates it.
Deletion: cri du chat syndrome (French for “cry of the cat”) is caused by deletion of part of the short arm of chromosome 5.
Babies with cri du chat have a high-pitched cry like a cat's, a small head and low birth weight, and later intellectual disability and delayed development.
Duplication: Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 1A is caused by duplication of a small section of chromosome 17 containing the PMP22 gene.
The extra copy disrupts the insulating myelin sheath of nerves in the limbs, causing gradual weakness of the muscles of the feet and lower legs.
Inversion: an inversion within the gene for blood-clotting factor VIII on the X chromosome breaks the gene and causes nearly half of all cases of severe haemophilia A.
By contrast, a common inversion in chromosome 9 usually has no effect, because no genes are broken. There is more on haemophilia as a sex-linked trait in Sex-linked traits.
The Philadelphia chromosome shows how swapping pieces between chromosomes can create a gene that causes cancer.
The Philadelphia chromosome is found in chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), a cancer of white blood cells.
A reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, in a bone-marrow stem cell, joins part of the ABL gene from chromosome 9 to the BCR gene on chromosome 22.
This forms a BCR-ABL fusion gene on a shortened chromosome 22, the Philadelphia chromosome.
The fusion gene codes for an enzyme that is permanently switched on and drives the cell to divide uncontrollably, so it is an oncogene (a gene that causes cancer).
CML is caused by a somatic mutation and is not inherited, because it happens in a body cell and not in a gamete-forming cell.
The Philadelphia chromosome was discovered in Philadelphia, USA, in 1960 by Peter Nowell and David Hungerford; Janet Rowley showed in 1973 that it arises by translocation.
The drug imatinib blocks the BCR-ABL enzyme. There is more on this in Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer.
Some conditions come from having the wrong number of chromosomes, not from a change in structure. They are therefore not examples of deletion, duplication, inversion or translocation.
Some conditions are caused by a change in the number of chromosomes, not in their structure, so they are not deletion, duplication, inversion or translocation.
They usually result from non-disjunction: a homologous pair, or two copies of a chromosome, fails to separate during meiosis, so a gamete has one chromosome too many or too few.
Down syndrome: in about 95% of cases there are three copies of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), giving 47 chromosomes, after non-disjunction, usually during egg formation.
The risk of Down syndrome rises with the mother's age.
Features of Down syndrome include a characteristic facial appearance, some degree of intellectual disability and a higher risk of heart defects.
A few per cent of Down syndrome cases are caused instead by a translocation that attaches extra chromosome-21 material to another chromosome; only those cases involve a structural change.
Sex chromosomes can also be gained or lost, and a karyotype is the tool that shows number changes and large structural changes.
Turner syndrome is a change in number with 45 chromosomes, X: one X and no second sex chromosome, female.
Klinefelter syndrome is a change in number with 47 chromosomes, XXY, male.
A karyotype is a photograph of a cell's chromosomes, taken during mitosis when they are condensed, and arranged in homologous pairs by size and shape.
A karyotype shows changes in number (for example three chromosome 21s) and large structural changes (for example the shortened chromosome 22).
The two kinds of mutation differ in size, in how they arise, and in how they are detected. Comparing them in pairs is the quickest way to answer a distinguish question.
Scale: a point mutation changes one or a few bases in one gene; a chromosomal mutation changes the arrangement or number of copies of a large section with many genes.
How they arise: point mutations mainly from mispairing during replication; chromosomal mutations from breakage and wrong rejoining of chromosomes, often during meiosis.
Detection: point mutations need DNA sequencing (reading the order of bases), because they are too small to see; large chromosomal mutations can be seen in a karyotype under the light microscope.

Examples: sickle-cell anaemia (substitution) and cystic fibrosis (three-base deletion); cri du chat (deletion), Charcot–Marie–Tooth type 1A (duplication), severe haemophilia A (inversion), and the Philadelphia chromosome in CML (translocation).
The musculoskeletal system is the framework of bones and joints together with the muscles that move it. Between them they let the body respond to a stimulus (a change in the surroundings) by moving.
The skeleton is the bones, together with the cartilage and ligaments that join them at joints (the places where two bones meet).
The skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tendons, which are the other part of the system.
Muscles provide the force, bones act as rigid levers, and joints are the pivots where movement happens, so a muscle pulling on a bone moves it at a joint.
The parts are only named here. There is more on the bones in "The axial skeleton" and "The appendicular skeleton", and on the joints and muscle pairs in "Muscles and joints".
The adult human skeleton has 206 bones, which are divided into two groups.
80 of these form the axial skeleton: the skull, vertebral column (backbone), ribs and sternum (breastbone), which make up the central axis of the body.
The other 126 form the appendicular skeleton: the pectoral girdle (shoulders), the pelvic girdle (hips) and the limbs attached to them.
Bones look like lifeless sticks, but bone is a living tissue made of cells. Its structure explains why it is both hard and tough.
Bone is a living connective tissue, which means a tissue that supports and holds the body together.
Bone cells lie in a hard matrix (the material around the cells) of calcium phosphate, which gives bone its hardness and resists compression (being squashed).
Collagen fibres in the matrix give bone some flexibility and resist bending and snapping, so bone is not brittle like chalk.
Bone has a blood supply and nerves, can grow and repair itself, and changes shape slowly in response to the forces put on it.
The skeleton does much more than hold us up. It has five functions, and each one can be illustrated with an example.

Support: the skeleton is a rigid framework that holds the body up, gives it its shape and supports soft organs. The vertebral column supports the head and trunk, and the leg bones carry the body's weight.

Protection: bones surround delicate organs so that knocks do not damage them. The skull protects the brain, the ribs and sternum protect the heart and lungs, the vertebrae protect the spinal cord, and the pelvic girdle protects the bladder and reproductive organs.
Movement: bones provide attachment points for muscles and act as levers that the muscles pull on, moving the body at joints.
Making blood cells: red bone marrow, found in spongy bone (the light, honeycomb-like bone), makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
In adults, red marrow is mainly in the flat bones (skull, ribs, sternum, vertebrae and pelvis) and in the ends of long bones such as the femur (thigh bone) and humerus (upper arm bone).
Yellow marrow fills the hollow shafts of long bones and stores fat.
Storing minerals: bone stores calcium and phosphate.

When blood calcium falls, calcium is released from bone under the control of parathyroid hormone, which helps keep blood calcium constant. This matters because nerves and muscles need calcium to work. There is more on this in "Glands, locations and hormones".
The body has three types of muscle, and they differ in where they are, whether you can control them, how they look and how they contract. Only one of them belongs to the musculoskeletal system.

Skeletal muscle is attached to bones by tendons and is the only muscle type in the musculoskeletal system. It is under voluntary (conscious) control as well as reflex control, and its cells look striped (striated) under the microscope.
Skeletal muscle contracts quickly and powerfully but tires (fatigues), which is why you cannot keep sprinting indefinitely.
Smooth muscle is found in the walls of the gut, blood vessels, bladder and uterus. It is involuntary (not under conscious control) and not striped.
Smooth muscle contracts slowly and can stay contracted for a long time, as in peristalsis (the waves of squeezing that push food along the gut).

Cardiac muscle is found only in the wall of the heart. It is involuntary and striped, and it contracts rhythmically throughout life without tiring. There is more on the heart in "The Circulatory System and Blood".

A skeletal muscle is the effector that carries out a response, in the same way as the other effectors (the parts that act on a nerve message) such as glands. There is more on this in "Structures and systems for response". To see how it works, start with what it is made of.
A skeletal muscle is made of bundles of long cells called muscle fibres.
Each fibre contains many nuclei and many mitochondria, so it has plenty of control and plenty of energy supply for contraction.
Each fibre is packed with two kinds of protein filament: thin filaments of actin and thick filaments of myosin.
The filaments are arranged in repeating units that give the striped appearance of skeletal muscle.
A skeletal muscle never contracts on its own. It contracts only when it is stimulated by a motor neuron (a nerve cell that carries impulses to a muscle), and the contraction follows a fixed sequence.

1. Skeletal muscle contracts only when it is stimulated by a motor neuron. A voluntary movement starts in the brain; a reflex movement starts in the spinal cord. There is more on this in "The reflex action".
2. Impulses travel along the motor neuron to its ending on the muscle fibre, a synapse (a gap between nerve and target) called the neuromuscular junction.
3. At the neuromuscular junction the neurotransmitter (chemical messenger) acetylcholine is released, crosses the gap and binds to receptors on the muscle fibre, starting an impulse in the fibre.
4. The impulse causes calcium ions (Ca²⁺) to be released from stores inside the fibre.
5. The calcium allows myosin filaments to attach to actin filaments and pull them inwards, so the filaments slide past each other and the fibre shortens.
6. Energy for this comes from ATP, the energy carrier of the cell, which is made in the many mitochondria by respiration.
Contraction is only half the story. The muscle must also relax, and the nervous system must be able to vary how hard the muscle pulls.
When the impulses stop, calcium is pumped back into its stores, the filaments detach and the muscle relaxes.
A relaxed muscle does not lengthen by itself: it is pulled back to its full length by an opposing muscle, which is why muscles work in pairs. There is more on this in "Muscles and joints".
A muscle can only pull by contracting; it can never push.
The force is passed through a tendon to a bone, which moves at a joint. This movement is the response.
Strength of response: the more motor neurons that fire and the more muscle fibres that contract, the stronger the contraction, so movements can be gentle or forceful.
Muscle tone: a slight, continuous partial contraction of muscles holds the body's posture without conscious effort.

Diagram: a flow diagram of a voluntary response: brain, spinal cord, motor neuron, neuromuscular junction, skeletal muscle (contracts), tendon, bone moves at joint. Also a sketch of a skeletal muscle cut open to show bundles of muscle fibres, with one fibre enlarged to show actin and myosin filaments, all labelled.
Because skeletal muscle is attached to bones, the system produces a wide range of responses, from obvious movements to constant small adjustments you never notice.
Movement of the whole body (locomotion: walking, running, swimming) to find food, escape danger or move to better conditions.
Movement of parts of the body, such as grasping or turning the head towards a sound.
Maintaining posture and balance: muscles of the back, neck and legs make constant small adjustments, in response to information from receptors, to keep the body upright.
Breathing: the diaphragm and intercostal muscles (the muscles between the ribs) move the ribs. There is more on this in "Gas exchange and the breathing mechanism".
Speech, facial expression, chewing and swallowing all depend on skeletal muscle.
Shivering: rapid involuntary contractions that release heat when the body is cold.
Muscles and bones cannot respond alone. They depend on other body systems to start the contraction, to supply fuel and to prepare them for action.
Nervous system: every contraction of a skeletal muscle is started by a motor neuron.
Receptors in muscles and joints send information back to the brain about the position of the limbs, so that movements can be coordinated.
Circulatory and breathing systems: active muscles need more oxygen and glucose for respiration, and must remove more carbon dioxide and heat, so heart rate and breathing rate rise during exercise.
When oxygen cannot be supplied fast enough, muscle fibres respire anaerobically (without oxygen), producing lactic acid and much less ATP, and soon tire (fatigue).
The lactic acid is removed afterwards, when oxygen is available again; this is one reason breathing stays fast after exercise. There is more on this in "Respiration".
Endocrine system: adrenaline (a hormone) increases blood flow to skeletal muscles and raises blood glucose, preparing them for action.
Health: regular weight-bearing exercise, such as walking or running, strengthens bones and muscles.
A diet with enough protein (for muscle), calcium and vitamin D (for bone) supports the system.

The skeleton has two parts, and the axial skeleton is the one that forms the central axis (the upright line) of the body. The appendicular skeleton, the limbs and the girdles that attach them, is attached to it. There is more on this in The appendicular skeleton.
The axial skeleton is made of four parts: the skull, the vertebral column (the vertebrae, which are the individual back bones, plus the discs between them), the ribs and the sternum (breastbone).
Its main jobs are protecting the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs, which are soft and easily damaged, and supporting the head and trunk (the body without the head and limbs).
The skull is the bony case of the head. It protects the brain and the sense organs, and it is built from two parts with different jobs.
The skull has two parts. The cranium is a dome of curved, flat bones that encloses and protects the brain.
The facial bones form the face, hold the teeth, and form the eye sockets (orbits) and the nasal cavity (the space inside the nose).

The bones of the cranium are joined by sutures: wavy, interlocking joints filled with fibrous tissue that allow no movement, so the cranium acts as one rigid, strong box. Its domed shape also spreads the force of a blow.
The lower jaw (mandible) is the only skull bone that moves. It joins the cranium at a freely movable joint on each side, allowing chewing and speech.
The skull also protects the sense organs: the eyes sit in the bony orbits, and the inner ear is enclosed in bone.
A large opening at the base of the cranium, the foramen magnum, lets the spinal cord pass down from the brain. The skull rests on the first vertebra.

In a newborn baby the cranial bones are not yet fused (joined into one). Soft, membrane-covered gaps called fontanelles allow the skull to change shape slightly during birth and allow the brain to grow; they close in the first two years.
Diagram: side view of the skull, labelling cranium, sutures, orbit (eye socket), facial bones, upper jaw, lower jaw (mandible), teeth and foramen magnum (or opening for spinal cord).

The vertebral column is the backbone. It is made of many small bones stacked in a line, so it is strong enough to carry the body yet flexible enough to bend. It is divided into five regions, each suited to its job.
The vertebral column (backbone or spine) is a flexible column of 33 vertebrae stacked one on another, from the skull to the pelvis.
It supports the head and trunk, protects the spinal cord, provides attachment for ribs and muscles, and joins the axial skeleton to the pelvic girdle (the hip bones).
The 7 cervical vertebrae (neck) are small and light, so they can support the head and allow it to nod and turn.
The 12 thoracic vertebrae (chest) each join a pair of ribs.
The 5 lumbar vertebrae (lower back) are the largest and strongest. They carry most of the weight of the upper body and allow bending.
The 5 sacral vertebrae are fused into one bone, the sacrum, which is joined to the pelvic girdle and passes the body's weight to the legs.
About 4 coccygeal vertebrae are fused to form the coccyx (tailbone), which anchors some muscles; the number varies from 3 to 5.
Vertebrae get larger from the neck to the lower back, because each one carries the weight of everything above it.
The top two vertebrae are shaped differently from the rest so that the head can move in two ways. Seen from the side, the whole column also bends in an S shape.
The atlas (first cervical vertebra) carries the skull and allows the head to nod.
The axis (second cervical vertebra) has a peg on which the atlas turns, allowing the head to rotate from side to side.
The column has an S-shaped curve when seen from the side: forward in the neck, back in the chest and forward in the lower back.
The curves act like a spring, absorbing shock when walking and running, and keep the body's weight balanced over the legs.
Diagram: side view of the vertebral column labelling the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and coccyx regions, the S-shaped curves and the discs between vertebrae.
A typical vertebra has a heavy part at the front to take weight, and a ring of bone at the back to protect the spinal cord. Each part of its structure suits its job.
The centrum (body) is a thick cylinder of bone at the front of the vertebra. It bears the body's weight.
The neural arch at the back surrounds the neural canal (vertebral canal), through which the spinal cord runs, so the cord is enclosed in bone.

The spinous process at the back and a transverse process on each side are projections that provide attachment for muscles and ligaments (tough bands that join bone to bone), acting as levers for the back muscles.
Facets are smooth surfaces that form small joints with the vertebrae above and below, guiding and limiting movement. In thoracic vertebrae, extra facets form the joints with the ribs.
Between neighbouring vertebrae there are small gaps on each side through which the spinal nerves leave the spinal cord. There is more on this in CNS and PNS.
Diagram: top view of a single lumbar or thoracic vertebra labelling centrum, neural arch, neural canal with spinal cord, spinous process, transverse processes and facets.
Bone on bone would be painful and would wear away, and it would not bend. Between the vertebrae lie intervertebral discs (inter means between), which solve these problems.
Position: an intervertebral disc lies between the centra of each pair of neighbouring vertebrae, from below the axis down to the sacrum, joining them together.
There are no discs within the fused sacrum and coccyx, because those vertebrae are fused into single bones and do not move against each other.
Structure: each disc is a pad of cartilage with a tough outer ring of fibrocartilage (fibrous cartilage) surrounding a soft, jelly-like centre.
Shock absorption: the discs compress under load and spring back, cushioning the vertebrae and the brain against the jolts of walking, running and jumping.
Preventing friction and wear: the discs stop the bones of neighbouring vertebrae rubbing against each other.

Flexibility: each disc allows a small amount of movement between two vertebrae, so the joints between vertebrae are slightly movable. Added together along the column, these small movements let the back bend forwards, backwards and sideways, and twist.
Holding the column together: the discs, with the ligaments, bind the vertebrae into one column while allowing it to bend.
The discs are squeezed slightly during a day of standing and sitting and recover while lying down, so a person is slightly taller in the morning than in the evening.

The ribs and sternum together form the rib cage, a bony cage around the chest. It must be strong enough to protect the organs inside but also able to move, because the chest changes size when we breathe.
There are 12 pairs of ribs: curved, flat bones that form the rib cage around the chest. At the back, every rib is joined to a thoracic vertebra by small joints that let it move.
The first seven pairs (true ribs) are joined directly to the sternum by strips of flexible costal cartilage.
Pairs 8 to 10 (false ribs) are joined to the cartilage of the rib above them.
Pairs 11 and 12 (floating ribs) are attached only at the back, to the vertebrae, and are free at the front.
The rib cage protects the heart and lungs, and partly the liver, stomach and kidneys.

Because the ribs are curved and joined by flexible cartilage, the cage can absorb blows and can move. The intercostal muscles between the ribs raise and lower the rib cage, changing the volume of the chest in breathing. There is more on this in Gas exchange and the breathing mechanism.

The sternum (breastbone) is a long, flat bone in the centre of the front of the chest. It protects the heart and anchors the ribs, through the costal cartilages, and the clavicles (collarbones). Like other flat bones, it contains red bone marrow.
Diagram: front view of the rib cage labelling the sternum, ribs, costal cartilage, true, false and floating ribs, thoracic vertebrae (behind), and the position of the clavicles.

The appendicular skeleton is the skeleton of the limbs and of the two girdles that attach them to the axial skeleton (the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum). It is the part of the skeleton that lets you reach, walk and run.
A girdle is a ring or half-ring of bones that anchors a pair of limbs to the trunk. The pectoral (shoulder) girdle attaches the arms, and the pelvic (hip) girdle attaches the legs.

Its main job is movement, because the limb bones act as levers for the muscles that pull on them. The legs and pelvic girdle also bear the body's weight, so they are built for strength as well as movement.
Most of the limb bones are long bones, and their structure shows how a bone can be both strong and light. Knowing the layers of a long bone also lets you label a section through one.
The limb bones named in the specification, except the patella, are long bones: a long shaft with a wider end at each joint. The patella is a small flat bone, so it is the exception.
The shaft is a hollow tube of dense compact bone. A tube is nearly as strong as a solid rod of the same width but much lighter, so the limb is strong but light enough to move quickly.
The wider ends are made of spongy bone, a lattice of thin bony struts that is light but strong along the lines of force, and that contains red bone marrow.
The central cavity of the shaft (the marrow cavity) contains yellow marrow.
The ends are covered with smooth articular cartilage (cartilage covering the joint surface) where they form joints. There is more on this in Muscles and joints.
Apart from the joint surfaces, the whole bone is covered by a tough membrane, the periosteum, to which tendons (which join muscle to bone) and ligaments (which join bone to bone) attach.

Diagram: a long bone (the femur) in longitudinal section, labelling compact bone, spongy bone, marrow cavity with yellow marrow, red marrow in the spongy bone, articular cartilage, periosteum and shaft.
The pectoral girdle is the shoulder girdle that hangs the arm from the trunk. Its design favours freedom of movement over strength, which is the opposite of the pelvic girdle.
The pectoral girdle is formed on each side by a clavicle and a scapula. It attaches the arm to the axial skeleton and is built for a wide range of movement rather than for bearing weight.
The clavicle (collarbone) is a slender, S-shaped bone running across the top of the chest from the sternum (breastbone) to the scapula.
The clavicle acts as a strut, holding the shoulder out to the side so the arm can swing freely, and passes forces from the arm to the axial skeleton.
Its joint with the sternum is the only bony connection between the arm and the axial skeleton, which is why the arm is so mobile.
The scapula (shoulder blade) is a large, flat, triangular bone lying on the back of the rib cage.
The scapula is not joined to the ribs or vertebrae but is held in place by muscles, so it can slide and rotate, increasing the range of movement of the arm.
Its large flat surface and ridges give a large area for attachment of shoulder and arm muscles, including the biceps and triceps. There is more on this in Muscles and joints.

The scapula has a shallow socket into which the rounded head of the humerus (the upper arm bone) fits, forming the shoulder joint, a ball-and-socket joint. The shallow socket allows the arm to move in almost every direction, including rotation, but makes the joint less stable than the hip.
The pelvic girdle is the hip girdle that joins the legs to the trunk. Because the legs carry the whole body, it is built for stability and strength rather than range of movement.
The pelvic girdle (pelvis) is a strong, bowl-shaped ring formed by the two hip bones, joined firmly to the sacrum (the base of the vertebral column) at the back and to each other at the front.
Each hip bone is made of several bones fused together; the names of these bones are not required.

The pelvic girdle is joined firmly to the vertebral column through the sacrum, so it is rigid. It carries the weight of the upper body and passes it to the legs, which makes it much stronger and less movable than the pectoral girdle.
It has a deep, cup-shaped socket on each side into which the head of the femur (the thigh bone) fits, forming the hip joint, a ball-and-socket joint.
The deep socket makes the hip very stable and suited to bearing weight, but it gives a smaller range of movement than the shoulder.
The pelvic girdle protects the organs of the lower abdomen: the bladder, lower intestine and reproductive organs, including the uterus.
Its broad surfaces anchor the large muscles of the legs and trunk.
The female pelvis is wider and shallower, with a larger, rounder central opening than the male pelvis, so that a baby's head can pass through during birth.
The two girdles do different jobs, and each difference in structure explains a difference in function. Set them side by side to answer comparison questions.
Attachment: the pectoral girdle is loosely attached to the axial skeleton by muscles, so the arm is free to move; the pelvic girdle is fused to the sacrum, so it is rigid.
Socket: the pectoral girdle has a shallow socket, which allows a wide range of movement; the pelvic girdle has a deep socket, which holds the femur firmly.
Function: the pectoral girdle gives mobility; the pelvic girdle gives stability and carries weight.
The arm has one bone in the upper arm and two in the forearm. Each joint between them is a different type, which gives the arm both stability and mobility.
The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm. Its rounded head fits into the socket of the scapula at the shoulder, a ball-and-socket joint.

The lower end of the humerus meets the radius and ulna at the elbow, a hinge joint (a joint that bends in one direction only). Its long shaft gives attachment to the muscles that move the shoulder and elbow.
The ulna is the longer forearm bone, on the little-finger side.
The upper end of the ulna hooks around the end of the humerus, forming the main part of the elbow hinge and the point of the elbow, which stops the arm bending backwards beyond straight.
The triceps (the muscle at the back of the upper arm) is attached to the ulna. There is more on this in Muscles and joints.
The radius is the shorter forearm bone, on the thumb side. It forms most of the joint with the wrist.

At the elbow, the rounded head of the radius turns against the ulna in a pivot joint, so the radius can rotate around the ulna to turn the palm up or down. The biceps (the muscle at the front of the upper arm) is attached to the radius.
The two forearm bones make the hand both strong and highly mobile: the ulna gives a stable hinge at the elbow, and the radius allows rotation of the hand.
The leg has one bone in the thigh and two in the lower leg, plus the patella at the knee. These bones carry the body's weight and drive walking, running and jumping.
The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone in the body.
The rounded head of the femur fits into the deep socket of the pelvic girdle at the hip. Its lower end forms the knee joint, a hinge joint, with the tibia.
The thick shaft of compact bone carries the body's weight, and it gives attachment to the large thigh muscles used in walking, running and jumping.
The patella (kneecap) is a small, flat, roughly triangular bone at the front of the knee, embedded in the tendon of the quadriceps, the large muscle at the front of the thigh.
The patella protects the front of the knee joint and holds the tendon away from the joint, improving the leverage of the quadriceps when it straightens the leg.

The tibia (shinbone) is the larger, inner bone of the lower leg, on the big-toe side. It forms the knee joint with the femur and the ankle joint below, and carries almost all the weight passed down from the femur.

The fibula is the thin outer bone of the lower leg. It is not part of the knee joint and carries little weight, but it provides attachment for muscles of the lower leg and helps form and stabilise the outer side of the ankle.

The wrist, hand, ankle and foot bones are not named in the specification; label them on diagrams as wrist bones, hand bones, ankle bones and foot bones. Many small bones give the hands their fine, flexible movements and give the feet a flexible, weight-spreading base.
The arm and the leg look different, but they follow the same basic plan. This similarity is a useful pattern to spot on a skeleton diagram.

The arm and the leg are built to the same plan: one bone in the upper part (humerus; femur), two in the lower part (radius and ulna; tibia and fibula), then many small bones in the wrist or ankle and five digits.

The same plan in the forelimbs of other vertebrates is evidence of common ancestry, because it suggests the animals inherited the pattern from a shared ancestor. There is more on this in Explaining biological phenomena.
Putting the axial and appendicular parts together on one diagram shows how the girdles and limbs attach to the central skeleton.

Diagram: front view of the whole human skeleton, labelling the axial parts (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum) and the appendicular parts named in the specification (clavicle, scapula, pelvic girdle, humerus, radius, ulna, femur, patella, tibia and fibula), with the wrist, hand, ankle and foot bones labelled as groups.
Bones only help the body move where they meet other bones. These meeting places are called joints, and they are grouped by how much movement they allow.
A joint is a place where two or more bones meet. Joints are grouped by how much movement they allow, from none at all to a wide range.

Fixed (immovable) joints join bones with fibrous tissue and allow no movement, so they protect and hold structures rigid, for example the sutures of the cranium (the joins between the bones of the skull).

Slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints join bones with cartilage (a firm, flexible tissue) and allow a little movement, for example between vertebrae, which are joined by intervertebral discs. There is more on this in The axial skeleton.
Freely movable (synovial) joints have bones separated by a fluid-filled cavity and allow a wide range of movement, for example the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee.
Not all freely movable joints move in the same way. Their types are named after the shape of the surfaces and the movement this allows.
Ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip): a rounded head fits into a cup, so movement is possible in all directions and the limb can also rotate.
Hinge joints (elbow, knee): movement is in one plane only, bending and straightening, like a door opening and closing on its hinge.

Pivot joints: one bone rotates around another, for example the atlas (the top vertebra) turning on the axis (the second vertebra) to turn the head, and the radius turning against the ulna to rotate the forearm.
Gliding joints: flat surfaces slide over each other, for example between the small wrist and ankle bones, so only small sliding movements are possible.

A synovial joint has to move smoothly thousands of times without the bone ends wearing away. Three parts working together make this possible: the cartilage on the bone ends, the membrane that makes the fluid, and the fluid itself.
Articular cartilage (hyaline cartilage) is a smooth, slippery, slightly compressible layer covering the ends of the bones inside the joint.
Articular cartilage reduces friction so the bones glide over each other, absorbs shock to cushion the bones against impact, and prevents the bone ends from wearing each other away.
Cartilage has no blood vessels, so it gets its nutrients from the synovial fluid and heals slowly if it is damaged.
The synovial membrane is a thin membrane lining the inside of the joint capsule, but it does not cover the cartilage. It secretes synovial fluid into the joint cavity.
Synovial fluid is a thick, slippery fluid filling the joint cavity. It lubricates the joint, reducing friction and wear, and helps absorb shock.
Synovial fluid also supplies oxygen and nutrients to the cartilage and removes its wastes, which is how cartilage stays alive without a blood supply of its own.

Smooth surfaces are not enough: the joint must also be held together and be moved by muscles. The capsule and ligaments hold the bones in place, tendons connect the muscles that move them, and in the knee fibrocartilage pads add extra cushioning.
The joint capsule is a tough, fibrous sleeve that encloses the joint, holds the synovial fluid in and helps hold the bones together. It is strengthened by ligaments.
Ligaments are tough, strong bands of fibrous connective tissue, mainly collagen with some elastic fibres, that join bone to bone across the joint.

Ligaments hold the bones of the joint together and keep them in line. Being slightly elastic, they allow the joint to move in its normal directions while limiting movement in others, which prevents dislocation (the bones being forced out of position).
Some ligaments lie outside the capsule and some inside the joint, for example inside the knee.

Tendons are tough, strong, inelastic (non-stretchy) cords of fibrous connective tissue, mainly collagen, that join muscle to bone. The Achilles tendon, for example, joins the calf muscle to the heel bone.
A tendon transmits the pull of a contracting muscle to the bone, so the bone moves at the joint. Because it does not stretch, all of the muscle's pull goes into moving the bone.
Pads of fibrocartilage (cartilage with extra tough fibres) inside some joints, the menisci in the knee, deepen the joint surfaces, spread the load and absorb shock.

Diagram: a generalised synovial joint (or the knee or hip) in section, labelling the two bones, articular cartilage, joint cavity with synovial fluid, synovial membrane, joint capsule, ligament, and a tendon attaching a muscle to one bone.
The knee shows how every part of a synovial joint has its own job and how they combine to let the leg move without the joint falling apart.
At the knee, articular cartilage on the femur (thigh bone), tibia (shin bone) and the back of the patella (kneecap), together with the synovial fluid, lets the bones glide over each other.
Ligaments inside and outside the joint keep the femur and tibia aligned and stop the knee bending sideways or backwards.
The quadriceps tendon, which contains the patella, passes the pull of the thigh muscle to the tibia to straighten the leg.
Ligaments, tendons and cartilage are all tough tissues found at joints, so they are easily confused. They differ in what they join, how much they stretch and the job they do.
What each joins: a ligament joins bone to bone; a tendon joins muscle to bone; cartilage either covers the ends of bones (articular cartilage) or joins bones (discs).
Elasticity: a ligament is slightly elastic, allowing some movement; a tendon is inelastic, so it transmits force without wasting it; cartilage is firm but compressible, so it absorbs shock.
Main function: a ligament holds the joint together and prevents dislocation; a tendon moves the bone when the muscle contracts; cartilage reduces friction and absorbs shock.
Muscles can only do one thing: shorten. That limitation is why the body arranges muscles in opposing pairs around each joint.
A muscle can only contract and pull, never push, so each movement at a joint needs a second muscle to pull the bone back.
An antagonistic pair is two muscles that produce opposite movements at the same joint: when one contracts, the other relaxes and is stretched.
The flexor bends a joint (flexion); the extensor straightens it (extension).
Each muscle is attached by tendons at both ends. The origin is the attachment to the bone that stays still; the insertion is the attachment to the bone that moves.
When the muscle contracts it shortens (and becomes fatter), pulling the insertion towards the origin and so moving the bone.
The biceps and triceps in the upper arm are the standard example of an antagonistic pair, and the thigh muscles at the knee are a second one.
At the elbow, the biceps lies at the front of the upper arm, with its origin on the scapula (shoulder blade) and its insertion on the radius.
The triceps lies at the back of the upper arm, with its origin on the scapula and humerus and its insertion on the ulna.
Bending the arm (flexion): the biceps contracts and shortens, pulling the radius and forearm up, while the triceps relaxes and is stretched. The biceps is the flexor.
Straightening the arm (extension): the triceps contracts, pulling the ulna and forearm down, while the biceps relaxes and is stretched. The triceps is the extensor.
A second example is the knee: the quadriceps (front of the thigh) contracts to straighten the leg, as the extensor, and the hamstrings (back of the thigh) contract to bend it, as the flexor.
The arm works as a lever, and the nervous system controls the pair so that movement is smooth or the joint is held still.
Lever action: the forearm acts as a lever with the elbow joint as the pivot (the fixed point it turns around).
The biceps is inserted close to the elbow, so a small shortening of the muscle moves the hand through a large distance quickly, at the cost of needing a large muscle force.
Coordination: the nervous system sends impulses to one muscle of the pair while the other is allowed to relax, so movements are smooth.
Both muscles of a pair contracting slightly together hold a joint steady in one position, for example when holding a weight still.

Diagram: two drawings of the arm, bent and straight, showing scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, elbow joint, biceps and triceps with their tendons, each muscle labelled contracted or relaxed in each position, with arrows showing the direction of pull.
A simple model of the arm lets you see antagonistic muscles work. Each part of the model stands for a real part of the arm.

A simple physical model uses two strips of stiff card or wood to represent the upper arm (humerus) and the forearm (radius and ulna), joined at one end by a split pin, which represents the elbow hinge joint.

Two pieces of string, elastic bands or long balloons represent the biceps and triceps. Each is fixed to the upper arm at one end (origin) and to the forearm at the other (insertion), one on the front and one on the back, with their ends standing for tendons.
Pulling (shortening) the front string raises the forearm while the back string slackens. This shows the biceps contracting and the triceps relaxing in flexion.
Pulling the back string lowers the forearm, showing extension.
Pushing on a string does nothing, which shows that a muscle can only pull.

The model shows that muscles work in pairs with opposite effects, that a muscle must be attached on both sides of a joint to move it, and that an insertion close to the joint gives a large movement of the forearm end (the lever action).
No model is perfect. Judging a model means saying what it leaves out or gets wrong compared with the real arm.
Real muscles shorten actively by contracting and get fatter, while the model's strings are pulled by hand.
The model has no articular cartilage, synovial fluid or ligaments, so it does not show how the joint surfaces glide or how the bones are held together.
A split pin allows movement in only one plane and does not show the rotation of the radius.
The model has no nervous control and no energy supply (ATP), whereas real muscles need impulses to contract and ATP as their energy source.
Real tendons are inelastic, while elastic bands stretch.

The nervous system detects stimuli (changes in the surroundings or inside the body) and coordinates responses by carrying nerve impulses. To do this it is split into two divisions: one that makes decisions and one that carries messages.
The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord, the control centre of the body.
The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is all the nerves outside the CNS, so it reaches every part of the body.
The CNS receives information, processes it and sends out instructions, which is why it is the part that decides what to do.
The PNS carries impulses between the CNS and the rest of the body, so it is the communication line that links the CNS to receptors and effectors.
A neuron is a nerve cell; a nerve is a bundle of many neuron fibres wrapped in connective tissue, so one nerve carries many separate signals at once.
A nerve impulse is an electrochemical signal travelling along a neuron, which is how information moves around the body.
Information has to travel into the CNS and instructions have to travel out again. The PNS does both jobs using two kinds of neuron, and its fibres run through the body bundled in nerves.
Sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors (cells that detect stimuli) to the CNS, so the CNS learns what is happening.
Motor neurons carry impulses from the CNS to effectors, which are muscles and glands, so the CNS's instructions produce a response such as a movement or a secretion.
Nerve fibres of the PNS run through the body inside nerves, which carry them to almost every tissue.
Humans have 31 pairs of spinal nerves, which leave the spinal cord between the vertebrae (the bones of the backbone).
Each spinal nerve joins the cord by two roots, short branches that attach it to the spinal cord, so sensory and motor fibres enter and leave by separate routes.
The dorsal (back) root carries sensory fibres into the spinal cord.
The ventral (front) root carries motor fibres out of the spinal cord.

A neuron's cell body (the part containing the nucleus) can sit in different places depending on the type of neuron. Knowing where each type lies tells you which part of the nervous system it belongs to.
Sensory neuron cell bodies lie in the dorsal root ganglion, a swelling on the dorsal root just outside the spinal cord.
Motor neuron cell bodies lie in the grey matter of the CNS, inside the cord, and their fibres leave through the ventral root.
Interneurons (neurons that link one neuron to another) lie entirely within the CNS, so they never leave the brain or spinal cord.
The spinal cord runs from the base of the brain down the back, inside the vertebral column, which protects it. It is the main route between the brain and the rest of the body.
The spinal cord relays impulses between the body and the brain, so sensory information travels up to the brain and instructions travel back down.
It carries out spinal reflexes, which are fast automatic responses, such as the withdrawal reflex when you touch something painful. There is more on this in The reflex action.

Cut straight across (a transverse section), the spinal cord shows a clear pattern of grey and white tissue around a central canal. The two tissues differ because they are made of different parts of neurons.
A central canal, containing cerebrospinal fluid (a watery fluid that cushions the CNS), lies at the centre of the cord.
Around the canal is an H- or butterfly-shaped core of grey matter.
White matter surrounds the grey matter.
Grey matter is made of cell bodies and unmyelinated interneurons (interneurons without a fatty myelin sheath), which is why it looks grey.
White matter is made of myelinated axons (long fibres coated in myelin); it is white because myelin is fatty.
In the brain the arrangement is reversed: the cerebral cortex is grey matter on the outside, with white matter beneath.
Diagram: transverse section of the spinal cord labelling central canal, grey matter, white matter, dorsal root, dorsal root ganglion, ventral root and spinal nerve.
The brain and spinal cord control the whole body, so they need strong protection. The CNS is protected by bone, membranes and fluid.
The brain is protected by the skull (cranium), a rigid bony case.
The spinal cord is protected by the vertebrae, which form a bony tunnel around it.
Three membranes, the meninges, surround the brain and spinal cord.
Cerebrospinal fluid lies between the inner meninges and fills the brain's cavities and the central canal.
Cerebrospinal fluid cushions the CNS against shock, so a knock to the head or back is absorbed, and it supplies the CNS with nutrients.
Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, usually caused by bacterial or viral infection.
The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and the part that handles most of its higher functions, such as thought and voluntary movement.
The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain, divided into left and right cerebral hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum.
The cerebral cortex, its outer layer, is grey matter deeply folded to increase its surface area, and so the number of neurons.
Each cerebral hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body, so the left hemisphere controls the right side and vice versa.
The cerebrum controls voluntary movement (movement you choose to make) and interprets the senses.
It also governs memory, thought, language, intelligence and personality.
Smooth, accurate movement needs a part of the brain dedicated to coordinating it. That is the cerebellum.
The cerebellum lies at the back of the brain, below the cerebrum, and also has a folded surface.
It coordinates muscular movement and controls balance and posture.
Some vital actions must carry on without you thinking about them, even during sleep. The medulla oblongata controls these.
The medulla oblongata lies at the base of the brain, where it joins the spinal cord.
It controls involuntary actions (those that happen without conscious control), including breathing rate, heart rate and blood pressure.
It controls reflexes such as swallowing, coughing and sneezing.
The hypothalamus is a small region that keeps conditions in the body steady and connects the nervous system to the hormone system.
The hypothalamus lies below the cerebrum and above the pituitary gland, to which it is connected.
It controls homeostasis (keeping the internal environment steady): body temperature, water balance, hunger and thirst. There is more on this in Homeostasis.
It links the nervous and hormonal systems by controlling the pituitary gland, so nerve signals can lead to hormone release.
You may be asked to label the brain, so know where each part sits relative to the others.
Diagram: vertical section of the brain labelling cerebrum, cerebral cortex, corpus callosum, cerebellum, medulla oblongata, hypothalamus and pituitary gland, with the spinal cord continuing below.

Every reflex, and every nervous response, is built from the same three parts: something that triggers it, something that detects it and something that acts. A reflex begins with a stimulus that a receptor detects and ends with a response from an effector.
A stimulus is a change in the internal or external environment that can be detected, such as heat on the skin or an object approaching the eye.
A receptor detects the stimulus. It is a cell or nerve ending that is sensitive to that particular type of change, and it starts the impulse.
An effector, a muscle or a gland, carries out the response. A muscle responds by contracting; a gland responds by secreting.
Some situations need a response so quickly that there is no time to think. A reflex action is the body's built-in solution: a response that is fixed and does not wait for a decision.
A reflex action is a rapid, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, happening without conscious thought. Involuntary means you do not choose it or control it.
Reflexes protect the body from harm, for example pulling a hand from a hot object or blinking when something approaches the eye, so damage is limited before you even notice.
Reflexes also maintain posture and normal body functions; coughing and sneezing clear the airways, for example.
Reflexes are inborn, so they are not learned. You are born able to do them.
The same stimulus always produces the same response, which is what makes a reflex automatic and predictable.
A reflex works because the nerve pathway involved is short and fixed. The reflex arc is the pathway an impulse (the electrical signal carried by nerve cells) follows in a reflex action.

The pathway runs receptor, sensory neuron, interneuron in the grey matter of the spinal cord, motor neuron, effector. The sensory neuron carries the impulse in, the motor neuron carries it out, and the interneuron connects them.
The sensory neuron enters the spinal cord through the dorsal root (the back root of the spinal nerve); its cell body lies in the dorsal root ganglion, a swelling on that root.
The motor neuron leaves the spinal cord through the ventral root (the front root), carrying the impulse out to the effector.

Diagram: reflex arc drawn through a transverse section of the spinal cord, labelling receptor in the skin, sensory neuron, dorsal root ganglion, interneuron, grey matter, white matter, motor neuron, ventral root and effector muscle, with arrows showing the direction of the impulse.
Touching a hot object shows the whole reflex arc at work. Follow the impulse from the finger to the muscle that pulls the hand away.
1. Pain and heat receptors in the skin of the finger are stimulated by the hot object.
2. An impulse travels along a sensory neuron to the spinal cord.
3. It passes across a synapse (the tiny gap between two neurons) to an interneuron in the grey matter.
4. It passes across a synapse to a motor neuron.
5. The motor neuron carries the impulse to the biceps, the effector.
6. The biceps contracts and the hand is pulled away from the object.
A reflex is faster than a voluntary action because of the route it takes. The brain is not left out, though: it is told what happened a moment later.
The impulse takes a short route through the spinal cord, crossing few synapses. Each synapse adds a small delay, so fewer synapses means a faster response.
It does not wait for a decision by the brain, which is why reflexes are rapid.
Interneurons also carry impulses up the spinal cord to the brain, so pain is felt just after the hand has moved.
The brain can sometimes override a reflex, for example when a person holds on to a hot plate to avoid dropping it.
The knee-jerk (patellar) reflex is the simplest reflex arc, because it leaves out the interneuron. It is a useful contrast with the withdrawal reflex.
Tapping the tendon below the kneecap stretches the thigh muscle, which is the stimulus.
The sensory neuron synapses directly with the motor neuron in the spinal cord, with no interneuron, so the pathway has only one synapse.
The leg kicks. Doctors use this reflex to test the nervous system, because a normal response shows the reflex pathway is working.
Not every reflex passes through the spinal cord. Some are controlled by the brain instead, but they are still rapid, automatic and involuntary.
Some reflexes are controlled by the brain rather than the spinal cord.
Examples are blinking, coughing, sneezing and the pupil narrowing in bright light.

Your body has to pass information quickly between receptors (cells that detect changes), the brain and spinal cord, and muscles and glands. Neurons are the cells that do this job, and there are three types, each with its own role.
A neuron, or nerve cell, is the basic unit of the nervous system; it carries electrochemical nerve impulses (tiny electrical-and-chemical signals that travel along the cell).
Neurons are long and thin, so a single cell can connect distant parts of the body, for example the skin of the foot and the spinal cord.
Sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors (cells that detect a stimulus) to the CNS (the central nervous system: brain and spinal cord).
Motor neurons carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands, which carry out the response).
Interneurons, also called relay or connector neurons, carry impulses between neurons within the CNS, so they link the incoming and outgoing pathways.
Every neuron is built from the same three main regions: a cell body, branched dendrites that receive signals, and an axon that sends them on. The shape of each region suits its job.
The cell body contains the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm and organelles, which keeps the cell alive.
The cell body also makes the neurotransmitter (the chemical that passes the signal to the next cell) and the proteins the neuron needs.
Dendrites are short, branched extensions that receive impulses from other neurons or receptors and carry them towards the cell body.
Branching gives dendrites a large surface, so one neuron can receive signals from many others.
The axon is a long single fibre that carries impulses away from the cell body.
The axon's length lets impulses reach distant effectors, for example a muscle in the foot.
Many axons are wrapped in a fatty coat that makes impulses travel faster. Fast conduction matters because the body must respond quickly, for example when you pull your hand from something hot.
The myelin sheath is a fatty insulating layer around many axons, so the impulse does not leak away along the way.
It speeds up the impulse, which jumps between the small gaps in the sheath called nodes of Ranvier.
Schwann cells are cells that wrap around the axon in the PNS (the peripheral nervous system: the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord), their membrane forming the myelin sheath.
At its far end an axon has to hand the impulse on to the next cell, whether another neuron, a muscle or a gland. The axon terminals are built for this hand-over.
The axon ends in swollen synaptic knobs, also called axon terminals.
Neurotransmitter vesicles are tiny sacs in the synaptic knobs that store neurotransmitter, so a supply is ready to be released.
The neurotransmitter is released to pass the impulse to the next cell. There is more on this in Neurotransmission.
A motor neuron carries the command from the CNS out to an effector. Its structure is arranged to collect many inputs inside the CNS and then send one signal a long way out.
A motor neuron has its cell body at one end, inside the CNS, with many dendrites.
Its many dendrites receive input from many interneurons, so one motor neuron can combine signals from many sources.
It has one long axon, which ends in axon terminals on a muscle or gland, so the axon reaches the effector wherever it lies in the body.
A sensory neuron brings information in from a receptor to the CNS. It has a different layout from a motor neuron, with its cell body off to one side.
A sensory neuron has a long fibre, the dendron, which carries impulses from the receptor to the cell body. A dendron is not the same as a dendrite, which is short and branched.
Its cell body sits to one side of the fibre, in a ganglion (a cluster of cell bodies) outside the CNS.
A shorter axon carries the impulse on into the CNS.
The long dendron reaches from a receptor, for example in the skin of the foot, to the spinal cord.
The cell body lies off the main pathway, so it does not slow the impulse.
Between the sensory and motor neurons sits a third type that links them. Interneurons make the CNS a network rather than a set of separate wires.
Interneurons are short, with many branched connections, so each can link with many other neurons.
They are found only in the CNS.
They connect sensory neurons to motor neurons and link many neurons together.
You are often asked to label a neuron diagram or to say which type is shown. Practise drawing both types so that you can place every part and show the direction of the impulse.

Diagram: a motor neuron and a sensory neuron, labelling cell body, nucleus, dendrites, dendron (sensory), axon, myelin sheath, Schwann cell, node of Ranvier, axon terminals, neurotransmitter vesicles, and an arrow for the direction of the impulse.
The importance of myelin shows when it is damaged. Multiple sclerosis is a disease in which this happens.
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease (the immune system attacks the body's own tissue) in which the body's immune system damages the myelin sheath in the CNS.
Damaged myelin slows or blocks impulses, because the insulation that lets them jump between the nodes of Ranvier is lost.
Symptoms include problems with movement, balance and vision.

A nerve impulse (a signal carried by nerve cells, called neurons) rarely travels through just one neuron. It passes along a chain of neurons from receptor to effector, and the signal changes form along the way.

The chain runs receptor (detects the stimulus), sensory neuron (carries the signal towards the central nervous system), interneuron or interneurons (link neurons inside the central nervous system), motor neuron (carries the signal outwards), effector (the muscle or gland that responds).
Within a single neuron the impulse is electrical: a wave of electrical change along the membrane, caused by ions (charged particles) moving in and out of the neuron.
Between neurons the impulse is passed on chemically, across a synapse (the junction between two neurons). So the signal is electrical inside each neuron and chemical in the gaps between them.
The neurons in a chain do not physically touch, so something must carry the signal from one to the next. That job is done at the synapse, using a chemical messenger.
A synapse is the junction between two neurons, or between a neuron and an effector such as a muscle fibre (a single muscle cell).
The two cells do not touch; a tiny gap called the synaptic cleft separates them, which is why the electrical impulse cannot simply carry on across.
The neuron before the cleft is the presynaptic neuron; the one after it is the postsynaptic neuron. Pre means before and post means after.
The presynaptic axon (the long fibre of the neuron) ends in a swollen synaptic knob containing mitochondria, which supply energy, and vesicles (small membrane sacs) of neurotransmitter.
A neurotransmitter is a chemical released by a neuron that carries the impulse across a synapse.
Examples of neurotransmitters are acetylcholine, noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin.
A labelled synapse diagram is a common exam task, and it also shows you where each part sits relative to the cleft.

Diagram: synapse labelling presynaptic neuron, synaptic knob, mitochondria, vesicles, neurotransmitter molecules, synaptic cleft, receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane, postsynaptic neuron, and an arrow for the direction of the impulse.
Crossing the cleft is a sequence of steps in which the electrical impulse is converted into a chemical signal and then back into an electrical one. Learn the steps in order.
1. The impulse arrives at the synaptic knob.
2. This causes calcium ions (Ca²⁺) to move into the knob.
3. The calcium ions trigger vesicles to move to the presynaptic membrane, fuse with it and release neurotransmitter into the cleft.
4. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft. The gap is tiny, so this is quick.
5. It binds to specific receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane; each receptor fits only its own neurotransmitter, like a key in a lock.
6. Binding opens ion channels in the postsynaptic membrane, ions move in, and a new impulse starts in the postsynaptic neuron if enough neurotransmitter binds.
Mitochondria in the knob supply ATP (the cell's energy currency) for making and releasing neurotransmitter.
Synapses are not just gaps to cross. Because the signal is chemical, they control how signals travel and which ones get through.
Impulses cross in one direction only, because only the presynaptic side has vesicles and only the postsynaptic side has receptors. The neurotransmitter therefore cannot send a signal backwards.
A weak stimulus may release too little neurotransmitter to start a new impulse, so synapses filter out unimportant signals.
One neuron can synapse with many others, so impulses can be spread to many cells or combined from many cells.
Many drugs act at synapses, since the chemical step can be altered. There is more on this in Conduction across the synaptic cleft and its disruption.

A synapse is the junction where one neuron passes a signal to the next across a tiny gap, the synaptic cleft. The signal crosses the gap as a chemical, a neurotransmitter, and the release of that chemical is switched on by ions.

Release is triggered by ions: calcium ions entering the synaptic knob (the swollen tip of the presynaptic neuron, the neuron sending the signal) are the trigger for the neurotransmitter to be let out.
Release lasts only a short time, so each impulse produces a brief burst of neurotransmitter rather than a steady flow.

This brief burst passes the impulse to the next neuron, and because it is short, each impulse arriving at the knob gives its own separate signal. There is more on how the release happens in Neurotransmission.
Once the neurotransmitter has done its job of passing on the impulse, it cannot be left in the cleft. An enzyme (a biological catalyst) in the cleft inactivates it.
After it has passed on the impulse, the neurotransmitter is inactivated by an enzyme in the synaptic cleft, so its message stops being delivered.
Example: the enzyme acetylcholinesterase breaks the neurotransmitter acetylcholine down into choline and ethanoic acid (acetate).
Removing the neurotransmitter is not tidiness. It is what lets a synapse carry a series of separate signals.
If the neurotransmitter stayed in the cleft, it would keep binding to the receptors on the postsynaptic neuron (the neuron receiving the signal), so that neuron would keep firing.
The signal could not be switched off, so repeated signals could not be told apart: one long continuous signal would replace a series of separate ones.
Neurons do not waste neurotransmitter. The presynaptic neuron takes back either the breakdown products or the intact neurotransmitter and reuses them.
The breakdown products are reabsorbed by the presynaptic neuron and used to make new neurotransmitter; for example, choline from the breakdown of acetylcholine is reabsorbed.

Serotonin and dopamine are mainly reabsorbed whole by transporter proteins (proteins in the membrane that carry a substance across it) in the presynaptic membrane, a process called reuptake. This is why they are cleared mainly by reuptake rather than by an enzyme.
Putting the pieces together, a synapse works as a loop. The same neurotransmitter is released, removed and then remade, ready for the next impulse.
1. An impulse arrives at the synaptic knob, and calcium ions enter the knob.
2. Vesicles (small membrane-bound sacs) release neurotransmitter into the cleft.
3. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft.
4. It binds to receptors (proteins that the neurotransmitter fits) on the postsynaptic membrane.
5. A new impulse starts in the postsynaptic neuron.
6. An enzyme breaks the neurotransmitter down, or it is taken back by reuptake.
7. The presynaptic neuron reabsorbs the breakdown products or the neurotransmitter, and new neurotransmitter is made and stored in vesicles, ready for the next impulse.
Diagram: a synapse showing the presynaptic knob, vesicles, cleft and postsynaptic membrane with receptors. Label: enzyme in the cleft, reuptake arrows into the presynaptic knob.
Because the synapse depends on several steps working together, a fault at any step changes how signals pass. The result can be a disorder.
Disruption can come from too little or too much neurotransmitter, faulty receptors, or blocked breakdown or reuptake.
Disruption can cause short-term (acute) or long-term (chronic) disorders, depending on whether the fault is brief or lasting.
A quick, severe disorder shows how much depends on removing neurotransmitter. A poison that stops the removal step affects the synapses between nerves and muscles within a short time.
Nerve agents and organophosphate insecticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine.
Acetylcholine then builds up at synapses with muscles, because it is no longer broken down, causing continuous muscle contraction and paralysis.
In severe cases death follows from failure of the breathing muscles.
Long-term disorders involve a lasting change in the neurons or the signalling that a neurotransmitter carries. Each example below involves a different neurotransmitter.
In Alzheimer's disease, neurons that use acetylcholine are lost, contributing to memory loss.
Depression is associated with altered signalling by serotonin and noradrenaline. Its causes are complex, so it should not be described as simply caused by low serotonin or as a chemical imbalance.
In Parkinson's disease, dopamine-producing neurons in the brain die, causing tremor, stiffness and slow movement.
A drug inhibits the enzyme that breaks down a neurotransmitter, so the neurotransmitter stays in the cleft longer and its effect is enhanced.

Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, e.g. donepezil, are used to treat the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease: acetylcholine is broken down more slowly, so the remaining acetylcholine-using neurons are stimulated for longer.
Monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors are antidepressants that slow the breakdown of serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine, so these neurotransmitters stay in the cleft longer.
A drug blocks the transporter that reabsorbs a neurotransmitter, so more neurotransmitter stays in the cleft for longer.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), e.g. fluoxetine, are used to treat depression: with serotonin reabsorption blocked, serotonin acts on the postsynaptic neuron for longer.
Neither strategy cures the disorder; both treat symptoms by enhancing the remaining signalling, which means they work with the neurons that are still functioning.
Psychoactive drugs and painkillers work at synapses in similar ways to the treatments above. They block removal, copy a neurotransmitter, or block receptors.
A psychoactive drug alters brain function, affecting mood, perception or behaviour.
Cocaine blocks the reuptake of dopamine, so dopamine builds up in the cleft, producing euphoria. There is more on its effect on mood and addiction in Dopamine and endorphins.
Nicotine mimics acetylcholine, binding to and activating some of its receptors.
Opioid painkillers such as morphine bind to the same receptors as endorphins (the body's own pain-reducing neurotransmitters), mimicking them and reducing the sensation of pain.
A drug may instead block receptors, preventing transmission: curare blocks acetylcholine receptors on muscles, so acetylcholine cannot act on them, causing paralysis.
Every type of disruption ends in one of two outcomes for impulse travel: transmission is reduced or stopped, or it is prolonged or enhanced.
Blocked release or blocked receptors: less or no neurotransmitter acts, so transmission is reduced or stops.
Blocked breakdown or blocked reuptake: the neurotransmitter stays in the cleft, so transmission is prolonged or enhanced.
Mimics: a drug that activates receptors makes transmission occur without the natural neurotransmitter.

Neurotransmitters are the chemical messengers that carry a signal from one neuron (nerve cell) to the next. The ones released in the brain shape how we feel and what we do, so two of them, dopamine and endorphins, are worth knowing in detail.
Neurotransmitters released in the brain affect mood, which is how we feel, and behaviour, which is what we do.
They do this by changing how groups of neurons signal, which means the same brain cells can send stronger, weaker or different messages depending on which chemicals are present.
Because mood and behaviour depend on how neurons signal, anything that changes neurotransmitter levels, such as exercise, diet or drugs, can change how a person feels and acts.
Dopamine is the neurotransmitter behind motivation and movement. The body has to build it from a raw material, which is why diet affects dopamine.
Dopamine is a neurotransmitter made by groups of neurons deep in the brain, from the amino acid tyrosine (one of the building blocks of proteins).
Because tyrosine is the starting material, the amount of dopamine the brain can make depends partly on a supply of this amino acid.
One of dopamine's main jobs is to link an experience to a sense of reward, so that we are drawn to do useful things again. The brain circuit involved is called the reward pathway.
Dopamine is released when we experience or expect something rewarding, such as food, social contact or achievement.
It produces feelings of pleasure and satisfaction and reinforces the behaviour (makes it more likely to happen again), so we are motivated to repeat it.
In short, dopamine is better described by its role in reward and motivation than as a 'pleasure chemical': it drives us to seek out and repeat rewarding behaviour.
Dopamine does more than reward. It also works in the parts of the brain that control movement and in those involved in learning.
Dopamine helps control smooth movement, so the muscles can produce steady, coordinated actions.
It is also involved in learning and attention, which means it helps us focus on and remember what matters.

Loss of dopamine-producing neurons causes Parkinson's disease, a condition where movement becomes difficult because the neurons that make dopamine are lost. There is more on this in Conduction across the synaptic cleft and its disruption.
Endorphins are the brain's own pain-relieving chemicals. The body releases them when it is under strain, so that pain and stress are easier to cope with.
Endorphins are neurotransmitters, specifically peptides (short chains of amino acids), produced in the brain, including by the pituitary gland and hypothalamus, among other brain regions.
They are produced in response to pain, stress and physical exertion, which are the situations where reducing discomfort is most useful.
They bind to opioid receptors (receptor proteins that the endorphin fits into) and reduce the sensation of pain, so they act as the body's natural painkillers.
They also produce a feeling of wellbeing and reduce stress.

Some drugs used for non-medical reasons act directly on the dopamine system. Stimulants (drugs that speed up activity in the nervous system) push dopamine levels in the reward pathway far above normal.
Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake, which means dopamine is not taken back up into the neuron that released it, so it stays active for longer.
Amphetamines increase dopamine release, so more dopamine is put out into the gap between neurons.
Either way, both flood the reward pathway with dopamine, so the result is an intense high.
Stimulants are not the only drugs that act on these systems. Nicotine and alcohol work on dopamine, while opioids work on the endorphin system.
Nicotine and alcohol also increase dopamine release in the reward pathway, so they produce rewarding feelings that encourage repeated use.
Heroin and other opioids bind to endorphin (opioid) receptors, the same receptors natural endorphins use, producing pain relief and euphoria (an intense feeling of wellbeing).
Using a drug repeatedly does not leave the brain unchanged. The brain adapts to the abnormal levels of neurotransmitter, and these adaptations are what lead to addiction.
With repeated drug use the brain adapts, for example by reducing the number of dopamine receptors, so the same amount of dopamine has less effect.
More drug is then needed for the same effect; this is tolerance.
Normal rewards feel less pleasurable, because there are fewer receptors for ordinary dopamine release to act on.
Stopping causes low mood and cravings; this is dependence and withdrawal.
Exercise is a lifestyle choice that raises these neurotransmitters naturally. It links back to the conditions that trigger endorphin release: pain, stress and physical exertion.
Sustained exercise raises endorphin levels and increases dopamine signalling.
This improves mood, reduces stress and anxiety, and reduces the perception of pain during exertion, because endorphins act as natural painkillers and dopamine supports the reward pathway.
What we eat affects dopamine in two ways: some foods trigger its release, and the diet supplies the raw material to make it.
Foods high in sugar and fat trigger dopamine release in the reward pathway, which can drive overeating, because the reward encourages us to repeat the behaviour.
A diet with enough protein supplies tyrosine, the amino acid that dopamine is made from.

A good discussion compares how different lifestyle choices change neurotransmitter levels and what follows from each. The key difference is how far above normal the levels are pushed and what the brain does in response.
Exercise and social contact raise these neurotransmitters in ways that support long-term wellbeing.
Drugs raise them far above normal levels, and the brain adapts in ways that cause dependence.
Mood and behaviour depend on many factors, not on one neurotransmitter, so no single chemical explains how a person feels.
Your body coordinates itself partly with chemical messengers called hormones, which travel in the blood. The glands that release them directly into the blood make up the endocrine system.

A hormone is a chemical messenger made by an endocrine gland, carried in the blood, that acts on specific target cells or organs. Only cells with receptors (molecules that the hormone fits onto) for that hormone respond, so a hormone reaches the whole body but affects only its targets.
Endocrine glands are ductless: they have no tubes, so they secrete hormones directly into the blood, which carries them round the body.
Exocrine glands secrete through ducts (tubes) to the place where the secretion is used, for example the salivary glands and sweat glands.
The pancreas is both: an exocrine gland making digestive enzymes, and an endocrine gland making insulin.
Diagram: outline of the human body showing the position of the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals, pancreas, ovaries and testes.

The pituitary is at the base of the brain, below and attached to the hypothalamus (the part of the brain that controls it). It is called the master gland because several of its hormones control other glands.
TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine, which is how the pituitary controls another gland.
Oxytocin, for example, causes the uterus (womb) to contract during labour, and causes milk to be released from the breasts during breastfeeding.
Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released from the pituitary, so the pituitary acts as its release point rather than its maker.
Three more pituitary hormones control the reproductive organs and the kidney. Each has a different job in females and males, or in a different organ.

FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone): in females, stimulates a follicle (a fluid-filled sac in the ovary containing an egg) to develop an egg and to produce oestrogen; in males, stimulates sperm production in the testes.
LH (luteinising hormone): in females, a surge of LH causes ovulation (release of the egg) and the empty follicle to become the corpus luteum, a temporary structure left in the ovary after ovulation.
LH in males stimulates the testes to produce testosterone, so it acts on the testes as FSH does.
ADH (antidiuretic hormone): makes the collecting ducts of the kidney more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood and a smaller volume of more concentrated urine is produced.
ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the pituitary, like oxytocin. There is more on its role in osmoregulation (controlling the body's water balance) in The Urinary System.
The thyroid controls how fast the body's cells use energy, and it is needed for normal growth and development.
Location: in the neck, in front of the trachea (windpipe), just below the larynx (voice box).
Thyroxine controls the metabolic rate, which is the rate of respiration in cells, so it sets how quickly the body releases energy.
Thyroxine is needed for normal growth and development, so a child lacking it grows abnormally.
Thyroxine contains iodine, so the thyroid needs iodine to make it.
The parathyroids are small glands that keep the calcium level of the blood from dropping too low.
Location: four small glands on the back of the thyroid, which is why they are named parathyroid (beside the thyroid).
Parathyroid hormone raises the calcium level of the blood when it falls.
It does this in three ways: by releasing calcium from bone, by increasing calcium absorption from the gut, and by increasing calcium reabsorption in the kidneys, so less calcium is lost in the urine.
The adrenal glands release adrenaline when you face stress or danger. It prepares the body for fight or flight, the choice between confronting a threat and running from it.
