Location: one on top of each kidney, which is why they are called adrenal (next to the renal, or kidney, region).
Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight in stress or danger, so you can fight the threat or flee from it.
It increases heart rate and breathing rate, so more oxygen reaches the muscles.
It raises blood glucose by causing the liver to convert glycogen (the stored form of glucose) to glucose, giving the muscles more fuel for respiration.
It diverts blood to the muscles, where it is most needed for action, and dilates (widens) the pupils.
The pancreas has an endocrine part that makes insulin, the hormone that brings blood glucose down after a meal.
Location: in the abdomen, behind the stomach, so it sits just behind it.
Clusters of cells called the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin directly into the blood.
Insulin lowers blood glucose by making cells take up glucose from the blood, so the level falls after a meal.
Insulin makes the liver and muscles convert glucose to glycogen for storage, which also removes glucose from the blood.
The testes make sperm and also act as endocrine glands, producing the male sex hormone testosterone.
Location: in the scrotum, outside the abdomen, so they hang in a pouch of skin.
Testosterone causes sperm production to begin at puberty (the stage of life when the body becomes sexually mature).

It causes the male secondary sexual characteristics (features that develop at puberty but aren't needed for reproduction itself): growth of facial and body hair, deepening of the voice and increased muscle growth.
The ovaries release eggs and also act as endocrine glands. They make two hormones, oestrogen and progesterone, which shape female development and prepare the uterus.
Location: in the lower abdomen, one on each side of the uterus (womb), so each ovary sits beside it.
Oestrogen causes the female secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast development and widening of the hips.
Oestrogen repairs and thickens the endometrium (the lining of the uterus) after menstruation.
Progesterone maintains the endometrium and maintains pregnancy, so the lining stays in place to support a developing embryo.
The pituitary is the one gland with five hormones on the syllabus. Each is listed here with its main function, so you can see how a single location serves several jobs.
Pituitary gland: base of the brain; FSH (Higher Level only); in females stimulates the follicle to develop an egg and produce oestrogen, in males stimulates sperm production.
Pituitary gland: base of the brain; LH (Higher Level only); in females causes ovulation and the corpus luteum, in males stimulates testosterone production.
Pituitary gland: base of the brain; oxytocin; causes uterine contraction in labour and milk release in breastfeeding.
Pituitary gland: base of the brain; TSH; stimulates the thyroid to release thyroxine.
Pituitary gland: base of the brain; ADH (Higher Level only); makes the collecting ducts more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed.
The remaining glands each make one or two hormones. This list gives the gland, location, hormone and main function, in the order of the syllabus list.
Adrenal glands: on top of each kidney; adrenaline; fight or flight, raising heart rate and blood glucose.
Thyroid gland: in the neck; thyroxine; controls metabolic rate.
Parathyroid glands: on the back of the thyroid; parathyroid hormone; raises blood calcium.
Pancreas: behind the stomach; insulin; lowers blood glucose.
Testes: in the scrotum; testosterone; sperm production and male secondary sexual characteristics.
Ovaries: in the lower abdomen; oestrogen; female secondary sexual characteristics and thickening of the endometrium.
Ovaries: in the lower abdomen; progesterone; maintains the endometrium and pregnancy.

Hormones are chemical messengers that control growth and body functions. Because they act in tiny amounts, people can change how an organism works by adding hormones or blocking them. This is called hormonal manipulation, and it is used in sport, health and agriculture.
Hormonal manipulation is the deliberate use of natural or synthetic (man-made) hormones, or of drugs that block hormones, to change how an organism grows or functions.
It can work by adding a hormone the body lacks or by supplying extra, or by blocking a hormone's release or action, so the body's own control system is deliberately altered.
The syllabus asks you to recognise the impact of these manipulations on organisms, so for each use you need the benefit and the cost.
Some athletes take hormones to gain a physical edge. Two are misused: anabolic steroids, which build muscle, and EPO, which boosts the blood's oxygen supply. Both are dangerous and banned.
Anabolic steroids are synthetic derivatives of testosterone (the male sex hormone). They increase muscle mass and strength and speed up recovery from training, which is why athletes misuse them.
Anabolic steroids cause liver damage, increase the risk of heart disease, and cause acne and mood changes including aggression.
In males, anabolic steroids reduce sperm production, cause infertility and cause shrinking of the testes.
In females, anabolic steroids cause male characteristics to develop, because the drug is a form of a male hormone.
EPO (erythropoietin) is a hormone made by the kidneys that stimulates red blood cell production.
Athletes misuse EPO to increase the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, because red blood cells carry oxygen, and so their endurance.
Extra red cells thicken the blood, which increases the risk of clots, heart attack and stroke.
The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) bans these substances in competitive sport and tests athletes through urine and blood samples. Their use is unfair to other competitors.

Doctors use hormones to replace ones the body no longer makes enough of, to control fertility and to relieve symptoms of the menopause such as hot flushes. Each treatment fixes a specific hormone problem.
Insulin injections treat type 1 diabetes, in which the pancreas makes little or no insulin, so blood glucose would otherwise rise too high.
Most insulin used today is human insulin made by genetically modified bacteria (bacteria given the human insulin gene). There is more on this in Genetic Engineering.
The contraceptive pill contains synthetic oestrogen and progesterone, or progesterone alone. These are female sex hormones.
The pill inhibits (reduces) the release of FSH and LH, the pituitary hormones that make an egg mature and be released, so no egg matures and ovulation (release of an egg) is prevented.
Fertility treatment uses hormones to stimulate the ovaries to release eggs, which helps women who do not ovulate normally to become pregnant.

Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) supplies oestrogen, often with progesterone, after the menopause (when the ovaries stop producing these hormones) to relieve symptoms such as hot flushes and to reduce bone loss.
For some women, HRT slightly increases the risk of some cancers and of blood clots, so it carries a risk as well as a benefit.
Thyroxine tablets are given to people whose thyroid gland produces too little thyroxine, replacing the missing hormone.

Farmers use hormones to control breeding, boost yields and manage plants. Animal uses raise welfare and food-safety concerns, while plant hormones are used as weedkillers, rooting aids and ripening agents.
Progesterone, given as a vaginal sponge or implant, synchronises the breeding cycles of cattle and sheep, so a herd can be bred and give birth at the same time.
Growth-promoting hormones increase meat production in cattle.
Bovine somatotropin (BST), a growth hormone from cattle, increases milk yield in cattle.
Growth-promoting hormones and BST are banned in the EU, including Ireland, because of concerns about animal welfare and hormone residues (traces left behind) in food. BST is permitted in the USA.
Synthetic auxins such as 2,4-D are selective weedkillers (they kill some plants but not others). They kill broad-leaved weeds in cereal crops by making them grow uncontrollably.
Auxin rooting powder makes cuttings (pieces cut from a plant) form roots, so new plants can be grown from them.
Ethene gas is used to ripen fruit such as bananas in storage after transport, so fruit can be shipped unripe and ripened when needed.
Hormonal manipulation brings real gains but also real harms. To evaluate it, weigh the benefits against the costs for each use.
Benefits: better health, treatment of disease (such as insulin for type 1 diabetes), increased food production and convenience (such as synchronised breeding and ripening on demand).
Costs: side effects (such as those of anabolic steroids, EPO and HRT), an unfair advantage in sport, animal welfare concerns, hormone residues in food and environmental effects of weedkillers.

Every living thing has to cope with a changing world, from a predator appearing to a drop in water supply. Detecting a change and reacting to it is called response, and it is the starting point for every system in this subsection.
Response is a characteristic of all living things: organisms detect stimuli (changes in their internal or external environment) and react to them in ways that help them survive.
The general pathway is stimulus → receptor (detects it) → coordinator (processes the information) → effector (a muscle or gland) → response.
In other words, a receptor notices the change, a coordinator decides what to do, and an effector carries it out, so the body reacts in a useful way rather than at random.
The nervous system is the body's fast communication network. It links the places that detect changes to the places that act on them.
Receptors in the sense organs (such as the skin, eye and ear) detect stimuli. Here sense organs are named only as receptors, with no structure needed.
Neurons (nerve cells) carry fast electrical impulses from the receptors to the brain and spinal cord, which act as the coordinator.
The brain and spinal cord send impulses along neurons to muscles and glands, which act as effectors, so the body can respond.
Nervous responses are fast and short-lived, because electrical impulses travel quickly and stop as soon as the stimulus ends. There is more on this in The Nervous System.
Diagram: a nervous pathway from receptor to coordinator to effector. Label the sense organ, sensory neuron, brain and spinal cord, motor neuron and muscle or gland.
The hormonal system is a second way of coordinating a response. Instead of electrical impulses along neurons, it uses chemical messengers carried in the blood.
Glands release hormones (chemical messengers) directly into the blood, rather than along neurons.
Hormones travel in the blood to the target organs, the organs that have the means to respond to them.
Hormonal responses are slower and longer-lasting than nervous responses, because a chemical has to be carried round the body in the blood and takes time to be cleared away.
Examples: adrenaline, released in danger, and insulin, released after a meal. There is more on this in The Endocrine System.
Diagram: a gland releasing a hormone into a blood vessel, with an arrow to a target organ. Label the gland, hormone, blood vessel and target organ.
Detecting a stimulus and deciding what to do achieves nothing unless the body moves. The musculoskeletal system, made of muscles and bones, does the moving.
Muscles are the effectors of most nervous responses, so most nerve impulses to effectors end at a muscle.
Muscles contract (shorten) and pull on bones at joints, the places where bones meet, to move the body.
Example: withdrawing a hand from heat, carried out by muscles pulling on the bones of the arm. There is more on this in The Musculoskeletal System.
Diagram: a muscle attached to a bone across a joint. Label the bone, the joint and the muscle.
Some stimuli are not changes in temperature or danger from outside but invaders inside the body. The immune system is the response system that deals with them.
The immune system responds to pathogens (disease-causing organisms) and other foreign antigens (molecules the body recognises as not its own).
White blood cells respond in two ways: they engulf bacteria, or they produce antibodies (proteins made against a specific foreign antigen). There is more on this in Immunity.
Responses rarely use just one system. A single danger can involve the nervous, hormonal and musculoskeletal systems one after another.
In danger, the nervous system stimulates the adrenal glands (hormone-releasing glands) to release adrenaline, so a nerve signal triggers a hormone response.
Adrenaline prepares the muscles for action, so the body is ready to act.
The musculoskeletal system then carries out the movement, as the effector.
Plants have no nervous system or muscles. They respond more slowly, mainly through chemicals and through their structure.
Because plants cannot run away from danger, their protection depends on features built into their structure and on chemicals they make.
An anatomical adaptation is a feature of a plant's structure that protects it. These features work against grazing animals, insects and pathogens (disease-causing organisms).
Thorns, spines and prickles deter grazing animals, since they make the plant painful to eat: holly leaves have spines, brambles have prickles and cacti have spines.
A thick waxy cuticle (a waterproof layer on the surface) and bark form barriers to pathogens and to water loss, so microbes find it hard to get in and water stays inside.
Stinging hairs inject irritants into anything that touches them, as in nettles.
Diagram: a labelled leaf showing the waxy cuticle and a spiny leaf margin, such as holly.
Plants also protect themselves by making chemicals. Some make a plant unpleasant or poisonous to eat, and others fight infection.
Toxic or bad-tasting chemicals deter herbivores (plant-eating animals): nicotine in tobacco, caffeine in tea and coffee plants, and tannins in oak leaves.
Nettle stings contain histamine and formic acid, which is why the stinging hairs of nettles act as both an anatomical and a chemical defence.
Some plants produce antimicrobial chemicals when infected, which limit the spread of a pathogen.
Plants also react to changes in their surroundings. Some of these responses are slow and some are quick.
Guard cells (the pair of cells around each stoma, or leaf pore) close the stomata when water is short, reducing water loss. There is more on this in Transport in Plants.
The sensitive plant, Mimosa pudica, folds its leaves rapidly when touched, a fast response by a plant.
Putting the two side by side shows why plants rely on protective adaptations: plants cannot move away from danger, as humans can, and their responses are generally slower.
Speed: human responses can be fast, through nerves, whereas plant responses are generally slower.
Mechanism: humans use nerves and hormones, whereas plants use chemicals and their structure.
Protection: plants cannot move away from danger, so their protective adaptations matter more.

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a relatively constant internal environment despite changes in external or internal conditions. The internal environment is the tissue fluid and blood around the cells, so it is the conditions the cells actually live in that are kept steady.
Factors kept constant include body temperature, blood glucose concentration, water and salt balance, blood pH and carbon dioxide level.
Enzymes (the proteins that speed up the body's chemical reactions) work best within a narrow range of temperature and pH, so a drift outside that range slows or stops reactions.
If the concentration of the fluid around a cell changes, the cell gains or loses water by osmosis (the movement of water across a membrane), which can swell or shrink it.
Steady conditions let cells function whatever the conditions outside the body.
Values fluctuate slightly around a set point (normal level) rather than staying perfectly fixed; for example, normal core body temperature is about 37 °C.

Every homeostatic response follows the same chain: something changes, the change is detected, a decision is made and the body acts. Learning the five named parts lets you analyse any example, however unfamiliar.
Stimulus: a change away from the set point, such as the body getting too hot.
Receptor: detects the change, because the body can only respond to a change it can sense.
Control centre: compares the change with the set point and sends instructions. It is often in the brain, e.g. the hypothalamus (a region at the base of the brain), or in a gland.
Effector: a muscle or gland that carries out the response, because these are the tissues able to act on the instructions.
Response: what the effector does, which returns the factor towards the set point.
In vertebrates, the control centre is linked to receptors and effectors by nervous pathways (neurons, fast) and hormonal pathways (hormones in the blood, slower).

Negative feedback is the way homeostatic systems are kept stable. The word negative means the response works against the change that triggered it, like a thermostat switching the heating off once a room is warm enough.
In negative feedback, the response reverses the original change: a rise is followed by a fall, and a fall by a rise.
Once the factor returns to normal, the stimulus is removed and the response stops, so the body does not overcorrect.
Because the response stops at the set point, the factor oscillates (swings slightly above and below) close to it rather than moving far away.
Diagram: a negative-feedback loop of set point, change, receptor, control centre, effector, response and back towards the set point, with a second branch for a change in the opposite direction.
Positive feedback is the opposite of negative feedback, and knowing it helps you see what makes homeostasis special.
Positive feedback: the response increases the original change, so the change keeps growing, e.g. oxytocin (a hormone) causes stronger and stronger contractions during labour.
Positive feedback is rare and is not used in homeostasis, because it pushes a factor further from the set point instead of holding it steady.

Body temperature is the clearest example of a nervous control system. The hypothalamus is the temperature control centre, and it works with receptors and effectors, linked by fast nervous pathways, that respond to heat or cold.
Stimulus and receptors: receptors in the hypothalamus detect blood temperature, and receptors in the skin detect skin temperature.
Control centre: the hypothalamus compares the temperature with the set point.
Too hot, effector 1: sweat glands produce sweat, which cools the skin as it evaporates (evaporation takes heat from the skin).
Too hot, effector 2: arterioles (small arteries) in the skin widen (vasodilation), so more blood flows near the surface and loses heat.
Too cold, effector 1: muscles shiver, releasing heat from respiration, which warms the body.
Too cold, effector 2: arterioles in the skin narrow (vasoconstriction), so less blood flows near the surface, reducing heat loss.
Behaviour changes, such as adding clothes or seeking shelter, also help restore the temperature.
Blood glucose is kept steady by a hormone rather than by neurons. A hormone is a chemical messenger carried in the blood, so this pathway is slower than the nervous one.
Stimulus: blood glucose rises after a meal, because glucose from digested food enters the blood.
Receptor: cells of the pancreas (a gland beside the stomach) detect the rise.
Response: the pancreas releases insulin, the hormone that lowers blood glucose.
Effect: cells take up glucose, and the liver stores it as glycogen (a storage carbohydrate made from glucose).
Glucose falls back to normal, so less insulin is released. This is negative feedback.
In type 1 diabetes this feedback fails because too little insulin is made, so blood glucose stays high.

In this example the hormone controls its own level. The level of thyroxine (a hormone made by the thyroid gland) is detected, and the thyroxine itself switches off the signal that makes more of it. This makes it a standard example of negative feedback.
Stimulus: thyroxine falls below normal in the blood.
Receptors: the hypothalamus and pituitary gland (a gland at the base of the brain) detect the low level.
Response: the pituitary releases TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), and TSH makes the thyroid release thyroxine.
High thyroxine inhibits the release of TSH by the pituitary, so thyroxine production falls. This is why the level does not keep rising.
The body must also keep the water concentration of the blood steady, which it does through a hormone released from the pituitary gland.
The hypothalamus detects the water concentration of the blood, and the pituitary adjusts the release of ADH (antidiuretic hormone).

ADH changes how much water the kidneys reabsorb (take back into the blood): when the blood is short of water, more ADH is released, so more water is reabsorbed and less is lost in urine. There is more on this in The Urinary System.

A rise in blood carbon dioxide is detected by the brain, which increases the breathing rate. Faster breathing removes carbon dioxide from the blood, which returns its level towards the set point. There is more on this in The Breathing System.
Carbon dioxide level is one of the factors kept constant, and it is controlled by negative feedback: the brain detects a rise and increases the breathing rate.

The cells of the body need to act together when something changes, such as a hot surface or a rise in blood sugar. Coordination is the process of linking stimuli (changes in the surroundings or inside the body) with responses so the body works as a whole. Humans have two coordinating systems: the nervous system and the hormonal (endocrine) system.
The nervous system coordinates using electrical impulses carried along nerve cells (neurons), so it can act within a fraction of a second.
The hormonal system coordinates using chemical messengers called hormones, which are released into the blood and carried around the body.
Both systems link a stimulus to a response, so the body works as a whole rather than as separate cells acting alone.

The two systems do the same job in different ways. The differences come down to what carries the message and where it goes, and from these follow how fast and how long the effect lasts. Each point below is a pair: nervous first, then hormonal.

Nature of the message: nervous coordination uses electrical impulses along neurons, with chemical neurotransmitters (chemicals that pass the message across the gap between neurons) at synapses; hormonal coordination uses chemical hormones.
Route: nervous messages travel along neurons directly to particular cells; hormones travel in the blood to all parts of the body, because the blood reaches every organ.
Speed: nervous coordination is very fast, with impulses arriving in a fraction of a second; hormonal coordination is slower, taking seconds to hours, because hormones must travel in the blood.
Duration: nervous effects are short-lived and end when the impulses stop; hormonal effects are longer-lasting because hormones stay in the blood until they are broken down, mainly in the liver.

Area affected: nervous effects are localised to the muscle or gland the neuron reaches; hormonal effects are widespread, reaching every target cell with receptors for the hormone, possibly in many organs.
Effectors (the parts that carry out the response): nervous coordination acts on muscles and glands; hormonal coordination acts on target cells in organs and tissues.

Typical uses: nervous coordination suits rapid responses such as reflexes and movement; hormonal coordination suits long-term processes such as growth, metabolism, puberty and the menstrual cycle, and steady control of blood glucose.
Despite their differences, the two systems share the same basic design. Both pass information to cells using chemicals, and both keep conditions in the body steady.

Both use chemical messengers that bind to specific receptors (molecules that fit the messenger, like a lock and key) on target cells: neurotransmitters in the nervous system and hormones in the hormonal system.
Both carry information from receptors (which detect a change) or control centres (which decide what to do) to effectors (which carry out the response).
Both take part in homeostasis (keeping the internal environment steady) through negative feedback, in which a change triggers a response that reverses that change.
The two systems are not rivals. They are linked, and many responses use both: the nervous system acts first and fast, and the hormonal system follows with a longer-lasting effect.
The hypothalamus links the two systems: it is part of the brain, which is nervous tissue, but it controls the pituitary gland, which releases hormones.
In danger, nerve impulses stimulate the adrenal glands to release adrenaline, so a fast nervous response is followed by a longer-lasting hormonal one.
Touching a hot plate is nervous coordination: it is a reflex, takes under a second, and affects one arm.
Rising blood glucose is hormonal coordination: the hormone insulin is released, it takes minutes to hours, and it affects cells throughout the body.
Some organisms and particles make us ill, and the biology of disease starts with naming them. A pathogen is an organism or agent that causes disease in its host, the organism it lives in or on.
An infectious (communicable) disease is one caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one host to another, which is why such diseases can spread through a population.
Most microorganisms are not pathogens: many are harmless or useful, so bacteria and fungi should not be lumped together as 'germs'. There is more on this in The microbiome.
Pathogens cause harm in three main ways: they invade and destroy host cells or tissues, they release toxins, or they take nutrients from the host.
Invasion means the pathogen destroys cells: viruses burst the cells they reproduce in, and the malaria parasite bursts red blood cells.
Toxins are poisonous chemicals that damage cells or disturb how they work; the tetanus toxin made by bacteria in a wound causes muscle spasms.
In some diseases the host's own immune response causes much of the damage, for example inflammation of the lungs in pneumonia.
A pathogen only survives if it can keep moving from host to host. So each one is adapted to its host and, often, to a carrier that helps it spread.
Each pathogen is adapted to its host: it must enter the host, survive its defences, reproduce, and leave to infect a new host.

Many pathogens need a vector, an organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another without itself being the disease: the mosquito for malaria and aphids (small sap-sucking insects) for many plant viruses.
The routes by which pathogens pass between hosts are called routes of transmission. There is more on this in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.

A prion is an infectious protein particle. It contains no nucleic acid (no DNA or RNA), so it is neither a cell nor a virus. It is the odd one out among pathogens, because a protein alone causes the disease.
The name comes from proteinaceous infectious particle, a term coined by Stanley Prusiner in 1982 (Nobel Prize 1997).
A prion is a misfolded form of a normal protein, the prion protein, which is found on nerve cells, especially in the brain.
When a prion meets a normal prion protein, it causes the normal one to fold into the abnormal shape too, so the misfolded protein builds up in a chain reaction.
Clumps of misfolded protein kill nerve cells, leaving tiny holes so that the brain looks like a sponge under the microscope. This is why the diseases are called spongiform encephalopathy.
Prion diseases take years to appear, are always fatal and have no cure.
Prion diseases have been found in cattle, sheep and humans. Because prions are very hard to destroy, prevention depends on keeping infected material out of the food chain.
Bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE, mad cow disease) in cattle spread when cattle were fed meat-and-bone meal made from infected animals.
Variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (vCJD) in humans is linked to eating BSE-infected beef and was first described in the UK in 1996.
Scrapie affects sheep. Kuru affected the Fore people of Papua New Guinea and spread by eating the brains of dead relatives at funeral rites.
Prions are not destroyed by normal cooking, by the usual sterilisation temperatures or by many disinfectants.
The immune system does not attack prions, because they are the body's own protein in a different shape, so the body has no defence against them.

Prevention therefore keeps prions out of the food chain: meat-and-bone meal is banned from the feed of farm animals, and the brain and spinal cord of cattle are removed from food as specified risk material.

A virus is a non-cellular particle of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) in a protein coat. It is an obligate intracellular parasite, meaning it can reproduce only inside a living host cell. There is more on this in Viruses.
Viruses cause disease by destroying the cells they reproduce in, or by changing how those cells work.

Each virus attaches to particular receptor proteins (molecules on the cell surface that it fits onto), so it infects only certain hosts and tissues: HIV infects helper T cells and influenza viruses infect cells lining the airways.
Human viral diseases include influenza, the common cold, measles, chickenpox, COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) and AIDS (HIV).
Animal viral diseases include foot-and-mouth disease, which affects cattle, sheep and pigs, and avian influenza, which affects birds.
Plant viral disease: tobacco mosaic virus infects tobacco and tomatoes.
Antibiotics don't affect viruses, because viruses have no cell structures for the drugs to target and reproduce inside host cells.

Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes with no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, about 1–10 µm long. Only some bacteria are pathogens, but those that are can multiply very quickly inside the body.
Pathogenic bacteria reproduce rapidly by binary fission (one cell splitting into two) in host tissues, so numbers rise fast.
Most bacteria cause harm by releasing toxins; some invade and destroy tissue.
Most bacterial diseases can be treated with antibiotics, which target structures bacteria have and human cells lack. There is more on this in Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment.
Antibiotic-resistant strains (bacteria no longer killed by the drug) are increasing, for example MRSA.
Each bacterial disease has a named bacterium and a usual route of spread. Learn them as pairs, and note the plant and cattle examples as well as the human ones.
Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spreads in airborne droplets and mainly affects the lungs.
Food poisoning is caused by Salmonella, which spreads through contaminated food such as undercooked chicken or eggs.
Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae in water contaminated with faeces, and causes severe diarrhoea.
Tetanus is caused by Clostridium tetani. Its spores in soil enter a wound, and its toxin causes muscle spasms, known as lockjaw.
Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi and is passed on by tick bites, so the tick is the vector.
In plants, fire blight of apple and pear trees is caused by Erwinia amylovora.
In cattle, bovine TB is caused by Mycobacterium bovis.
Fungi are eukaryotes (their cells have a nucleus) with cell walls of chitin. Most are made of thread-like hyphae, and some, such as yeasts, are single cells. Parasitic fungi feed on living hosts.
Parasitic fungi grow hyphae into or over host tissue and secrete enzymes that digest it, and the fungus absorbs the products.
Fungi spread by spores, which are often carried by wind, water or contact.
Athlete's foot and ringworm are skin infections caused by fungi that feed on keratin (the protein in skin); ringworm is a fungus, not a worm.
Thrush is caused by the yeast Candida albicans in the mouth or vagina, often after antibiotics have killed the bacteria that normally keep it in check.
Fungal infections are most dangerous in people with weakened immune systems.
Antibiotics don't work on fungi, because fungi are eukaryotic and have no peptidoglycan cell wall or 70S ribosomes; antifungal drugs are used instead.
Fungi infect plants and animals as well as people. The examples below affect trees, cereal crops and amphibians.
Ash dieback, caused by the fungus Hymenoscyphus fraxineus, is killing ash trees across Europe.
Dutch elm disease, caused by the fungus Ophiostoma novo-ulmi, is spread by elm bark beetles, which act as vectors.
Cereal rusts such as wheat rust are caused by Puccinia species.
Chytrid fungus (Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis) infects the skin of frogs and other amphibians. There is more on this in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.

Protists are eukaryotes, mostly single-celled, that are neither animals, plants nor fungi (kingdom Protista). Parasitic protists often have complex life cycles with more than one host. Malaria is one example.
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, which is passed to humans by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, the vector.
The parasite reproduces first in the liver and then in red blood cells, which burst together, causing repeated fevers and anaemia (too few red blood cells).

Malaria is controlled with insecticide-treated bed nets, insecticides, draining of standing water where mosquitoes breed, and antimalarial drugs such as artemisinin. There is more on this in Science, scientists and society.
Other protists cause gut and blood diseases in people, and one protist-like organism caused a famine in Ireland.
Amoebic dysentery is caused by Entamoeba histolytica, which spreads in water or food contaminated with faeces.
African sleeping sickness is caused by Trypanosoma brucei, which is spread by tsetse flies, the vector.
Potato late blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans, a water mould (oomycete). It looks like a fungus, being thread-like and spread by spores, but it is classed with the protists.
Its spores spread on wind and rain splash in mild, wet weather, and it rots leaves and tubers.
Potato late blight caused the Irish Great Famine from 1845, because potatoes were the main crop and the disease destroyed them. There is more on this in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.

A parasite lives in or on another organism, its host, feeding on it and harming it. Parasitic animals are multicellular and much larger than microorganisms; most are worms or arthropods. Endoparasites live inside the host.
Tapeworms (e.g. Taenia) live in the small intestine, absorbing digested food through their body surface and attaching by hooks and suckers.
Humans become infected with tapeworms by eating undercooked infected pork or beef.
Liver fluke (Fasciola hepatica) is a flatworm of sheep and cattle that damages the liver.
The liver fluke needs a freshwater mud snail as a second host, so it is common on wet pasture in Ireland.
Onchocerca volvulus is a roundworm spread by blackflies that causes river blindness. There is more on this in Science, scientists and society.
Ectoparasites live on the outside of the host. Worms inside the body are treated with drugs, and prevention targets how the parasite reaches us.
Head lice are ectoparasites that feed on blood from the scalp.
Ticks feed on blood and can also act as vectors, carrying the bacterium that causes Lyme disease.
Parasitic worms are treated with anthelmintic drugs that kill them, e.g. ivermectin.
Prevention: cook meat thoroughly, maintain sanitation, and control the second host or vector, because breaking the life cycle stops the parasite spreading.

The six types of pathogen differ in whether they are cells, what genetic material they carry, their size and how they are treated. The treatment follows from the structure, which is why antibiotics work only on bacteria.
Prion: not cellular; no nucleic acid; a single protein molecule; no treatment.
Virus: not cellular; DNA or RNA; about 20–300 nm; treated with antivirals, not antibiotics.
Bacterium: prokaryotic cell; DNA; about 1–10 µm; treated with antibiotics.
Fungus: eukaryotic; DNA; from single cells to large networks of hyphae; treated with antifungals.
Protist: eukaryotic and mostly single-celled; DNA; treated with antiprotozoal drugs such as antimalarials.
Parasitic animal: multicellular eukaryote; DNA; from millimetres to metres in size; treated with anthelmintics.

Immunity is the body's ability to resist infection by pathogens (disease-causing organisms such as bacteria and viruses). The immune system does this by telling self from non-self, and it has two parts that work at different speeds.

The immune system consists of physical and chemical barriers, white blood cells (made from stem cells in the bone marrow), the lymphatic system (lymph nodes, spleen and thymus) and defence proteins in the blood, such as antibodies and complement.
The body's own cells carry their own marker molecules on their surface, which the immune system normally ignores, so foreign cells and molecules, which lack these markers, are attacked.
Innate immunity, also called non-specific immunity, is present from birth, acts against any pathogen in the same way and acts within minutes to hours.
Adaptive immunity, also called acquired or specific immunity, develops during life after exposure to a particular pathogen and acts against that pathogen only.
Adaptive immunity takes days to develop the first time, but it remembers the pathogen, which is why a later infection is dealt with much faster.
Innate defences are found in all animals and in plants; adaptive immunity, with antibodies and lymphocytes (the white blood cells that run it), is found only in vertebrates.
The best way to deal with a pathogen is to stop it getting in. Skin and the linings of the body's openings form physical barriers that block or trap microorganisms before they can cause infection.
Skin is a tough outer layer of dead, keratin-filled cells (keratin is a tough protein) that pathogens can't easily cross.
Oil (sebum) from skin glands makes the surface slightly acidic, which slows bacterial growth.
Breaks in the skin are sealed by blood clotting, which stops blood loss and blocks pathogen entry.
Mucous membranes line the breathing, digestive, urinary and reproductive tracts. Their sticky mucus traps microorganisms and dust, so these don't reach the cells beneath.
In the trachea and bronchi (the main airways to the lungs), cilia (tiny hair-like projections) beat the mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed or coughed out.
Coughing and sneezing are reflexes (automatic responses) that expel irritants, so trapped microorganisms are blown out of the airways.
Some barriers work by chemistry rather than by physically blocking entry. Acids and enzymes kill or inhibit microorganisms, and harmless resident microorganisms add a living defence of their own.
Hydrochloric acid in the stomach, at about pH 2, kills most microorganisms swallowed with food.
Lysozyme, an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus, breaks down bacterial cell walls, so the bacteria burst or die.
The acidic conditions in the vagina inhibit many pathogens.

Harmless microorganisms living on the skin and in the gut and vagina, the normal microbiota, compete with pathogens for space and nutrients, which leaves pathogens less room to establish an infection. There is more on this in The microbiome.
If a pathogen gets past the barriers, the innate response moves on to cells that destroy it. Phagocytes find the invader, swallow it and digest it in a process called phagocytosis.
Phagocytes are white blood cells that engulf and digest pathogens, and the process is called phagocytosis.
Neutrophils are the most numerous white blood cells and the first to arrive at an infection. Macrophages, formed from monocytes (another type of white blood cell), are larger and longer-lived.
1. The phagocyte is attracted to the pathogen by chemicals released by pathogens and damaged cells.
3. It surrounds the pathogen with extensions of its membrane and takes it into a vesicle (a small membrane-bound sac inside the cell).
4. Digestive enzymes are released into the vesicle and break the pathogen down.
5. The harmless products are absorbed or released.

Diagram: the stages of phagocytosis in four sketches: a phagocyte approaching a bacterium; membrane extensions surrounding it; the bacterium enclosed in a vesicle; the bacterium being digested. Label phagocyte, nucleus, bacterium, vesicle and digestive enzymes.

Inflammation and fever are whole-body or whole-area responses that bring more defences to an infection and make conditions harder for the pathogen. The signs you notice when you are ill are the immune system at work.
Inflammation: damaged cells and mast cells (cells in tissues that release signals when damaged) release histamine and other chemicals, which widen local blood vessels and make capillaries leakier.
More blood flow brings phagocytes and defence proteins to the site, and fluid leaks into the tissue, giving redness, heat, swelling and pain at the site.
Pus is a mixture of dead phagocytes, pathogens and tissue fluid.

Fever: chemicals released by white blood cells reset the temperature set point in the hypothalamus (the brain region that controls body temperature) upwards, raising body temperature. There is more on this in Homeostasis as a stimulus-response model.
A higher temperature slows the reproduction of many pathogens and speeds up the reactions of the immune system, so fever helps the body fight infection.
Besides phagocytes, the innate response uses proteins in the blood and released by infected cells. Plants have no adaptive immunity, so their innate defences have to do all the work.
Complement, a group of blood proteins, coats pathogens so that phagocytes engulf them more easily, and it can punch holes in bacterial membranes, bursting them.
Interferons are proteins released by virus-infected cells that make neighbouring cells resist virus replication, so the infection is slowed before it spreads.
Natural killer cells also act in the innate response, in addition to phagocytes and defence proteins.

Plants have innate defences only: physical barriers (cuticle, bark and cell walls), protective chemicals, and the death of infected cells to wall off a pathogen. There is more on this in Structures and systems for response.

Adaptive immunity depends on recognising a particular pathogen. The molecules it recognises are called antigens, and the immune system's ability to tell them apart from the body's own molecules is what makes the response specific.
An antigen is a molecule, usually a protein or polysaccharide on the surface of a pathogen or on a toxin it releases, that the immune system recognises as foreign.
Antigens trigger a specific immune response, including antibody production.

Each pathogen carries several antigens, so more than one kind of antibody can be made against it. The body's own cell markers are self antigens, which are normally tolerated, so the body doesn't attack itself.
An antibody is the body's protein that matches one antigen. Its Y shape and the shape of its tips explain why each antibody works against only one antigen.
An antibody, also called an immunoglobulin, is a Y-shaped protein made by plasma cells, which are derived from B lymphocytes. It binds to one specific antigen.
An antibody has four polypeptide chains (chains of amino acids), two long heavy chains and two short light chains, held together by disulfide bonds.

The tips of the two arms are the variable regions, which differ between antibodies and form two identical antigen-binding sites. The rest of the molecule is the constant region, which is the same in all antibodies of a class.

Specificity: the shape of the antigen-binding site is complementary to the shape of one antigen, so each antibody binds only that antigen, like a key in a lock. There is more on this in Enzyme structure and specificity.
Diagram: an antibody as a Y shape, labelled heavy chain, light chain, variable region, antigen-binding site (two), constant region and disulfide bonds, with an antigen fitting one binding site.

Once antibodies have bound to an antigen, they can stop the pathogen in four different ways. The Y shape matters again here, because the two arms bind the antigen while the stem is recognised by other defences.
Agglutination: because each antibody has two binding sites, antibodies link pathogens together into clumps that can't spread and are easily engulfed.
Neutralisation: antibodies cover the parts of viruses that attach to cells, or bind to toxins (antitoxins), so that they can't act.
Opsonisation: antibodies coat pathogens, marking them for phagocytes, which have receptors for the antibody's constant region.
Complement activation: antibodies activate complement (the blood proteins of the innate response), which bursts bacterial cells.
The body can't know in advance which pathogen it will meet, so it keeps a huge variety of B cells ready. Only the ones that fit the invader are chosen to multiply, a process called clonal selection.
Lymphocytes are the white blood cells of adaptive immunity, and there are two main kinds.
B lymphocytes (B cells) produce antibodies. This is the antibody-mediated or humoral response, acting on pathogens and toxins in blood and tissue fluid.
T lymphocytes (T cells) act directly on infected body cells in the cell-mediated response (Higher Level).
Clonal selection: the body has millions of different B cells, each with one type of antibody fixed in its membrane as a receptor, made before any infection.

When a pathogen enters, only the B cells whose receptors fit its antigen bind to it. These are selected and, with chemical signals from helper T cells, divide rapidly by mitosis to form a clone of identical cells.
The clone differentiates (becomes specialised) into plasma cells and memory B cells.
Plasma cells secrete large amounts of the matching antibody into the blood, thousands of molecules per second, for a few days, and then die.
Memory cells stay in the body for years, ready to respond to the same antigen.

The first time you meet a pathogen, the response is slow. A second meeting is much faster, because memory cells are already there. This difference is the reason you rarely get the same infection twice.
Primary response, on first exposure: there is a delay of several days, often about a week, while matching B cells are selected and cloned. Antibody levels rise slowly and stay fairly low.
During the primary response the person may become ill, because the pathogen multiplies before enough antibodies are made.

Secondary response, on later exposure to the same antigen: memory cells recognise it at once and quickly produce many plasma cells, so antibodies appear within a few days, reach a much higher level and last longer.
The pathogen is usually destroyed before symptoms appear, so the person is immune. This is the basis of vaccination. There is more on this in Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment.

Diagram: a graph of antibody concentration (y-axis) against time in days (x-axis), with a first exposure giving a small, slow primary peak and a second exposure giving a faster, much taller, longer secondary peak. Label both exposures, the lag phase, and the primary and secondary responses.

Antibodies work in blood and tissue fluid, but some pathogens hide inside body cells. The cell-mediated response uses T cells to find and deal with those infected cells, and it begins with the cell showing that it is infected.
The cell-mediated response is the part of adaptive immunity carried out by T lymphocytes acting directly on cells, not by antibodies.
It is needed because antibodies can't reach pathogens inside body cells, such as viruses and some bacteria, for example the TB bacterium, which lives inside macrophages.
It also destroys cancer cells and cells of transplanted organs, which is why transplant patients take drugs that suppress the immune system.
Antigen presentation: an infected body cell displays fragments of the pathogen's antigens on its surface, held in its self-marker proteins (MHC proteins).
Macrophages and other antigen-presenting cells that have engulfed a pathogen display its antigens in the same way.
T cells can't recognise free antigens, so this presentation is how they detect infection.
Helper T cells act as the managers of adaptive immunity. Once one is activated, it signals to the other cells that need to act, so it links the cell-mediated and antibody responses.

Activation of helper T cells: a helper T cell whose receptor fits the displayed antigen binds to the antigen-presenting cell and is activated. It divides to form a clone of helper T cells, as B cells do.
Helper T cells coordinate the response by releasing chemical signals called cytokines.
Cytokines stimulate the matching killer T cells to divide.
Cytokines also stimulate the matching B cells to divide into plasma cells and memory cells, because B cells need this help to respond fully.
Cytokines also attract and activate macrophages, which increases phagocytosis at the infection.
Helper T cells therefore link the cell-mediated and antibody responses.
After helper T cells give the signal, the killer T cells destroy infected cells, the B cells add antibodies, and suppressor T cells end the response. Memory cells are left behind for next time.

Killer T cells (cytotoxic T cells) of the clone bind to body cells displaying the antigen and kill them, destroying the pathogens inside before they can multiply. There is more on this in White blood cells.
When the infection is cleared, suppressor T cells switch off the response by stopping the activity of killer T cells and B cells, so that healthy tissue isn't damaged.
Memory T cells remain, so a second infection triggers a faster, larger cell-mediated response.
Role of B lymphocytes: B cells act as antigen-presenting cells, taking in the antigen they bind and displaying it to helper T cells.
The antibodies released by the plasma cells of B cells mark infected cells and pathogens for destruction.

Diagram: draw a flow diagram in this order: pathogen; antigen presented by macrophage or infected cell; helper T cell activated and cloned; cytokines; killer T cells cloned, infected cells killed; B cells cloned into plasma cells, antibodies; memory T and B cells formed; suppressor T cells end response.
The two systems differ in speed, specificity and memory, but they are not separate. A comparison of the two is a standard exam question, so learn each as a pair.
Presence: innate immunity is present from birth, while adaptive immunity develops after exposure to a pathogen.
Specificity: innate immunity is non-specific, giving the same response to every pathogen, while adaptive immunity is specific, with each response against one antigen.
Memory: innate immunity gives the same response each time, while adaptive immunity has memory, so a second response is faster and stronger.
Speed: innate immunity acts within minutes to hours, while adaptive immunity takes days on first exposure.

Mechanisms: innate immunity uses barriers, phagocytes (neutrophils and macrophages), inflammation, fever, complement, interferons and natural killer cells; adaptive immunity uses B and T lymphocytes and antibodies.
Distribution: innate defences are found in all animals and in plants, while adaptive immunity is found only in vertebrates.
The two systems work together: macrophages of the innate system present antigens to start the adaptive response, and antibodies of the adaptive system make phagocytosis and complement more effective.

Acquired immunity is the specific (adaptive) protection a person has against one particular pathogen. It can be obtained in two basic ways, depending on who makes the antibodies, and each way can be natural or artificial.

Active immunity: the person's own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells (long-lived cells that remember the pathogen) in response to an antigen, the molecule on a pathogen that the immune system recognises as foreign.
Active immunity takes days to weeks to develop, because the body has to build its response from scratch. It is long-lasting, often for years or for life, because memory cells remain.
Passive immunity: ready-made antibodies from another person or animal are given to the person, so their own immune system does none of the work.
Passive immunity gives immediate protection but is short-lived, lasting weeks to a few months, because the antibodies are gradually broken down and no memory cells are made.
Because passive immunity leaves no memory cells, a later infection with the same pathogen triggers a primary response (the slow first-time response), as if for the first time.
Natural immunity comes from normal life events such as infection, pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Artificial immunity comes from deliberate medical intervention, such as vaccines and antibody injections.
Combining active or passive with natural or artificial gives four routes to acquired immunity. Each has a typical example, and comparing active with passive is a standard exam question.
Active natural immunity, by infection: catching a disease and recovering leaves memory cells against that pathogen. For example, most people who have had chickenpox or measles don't get them again.

Active artificial immunity, by vaccination: a vaccine stimulates the immune system to make antibodies and memory cells without causing the disease, for example the MMR vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella.
Passive natural immunity, from the mother: antibodies (IgG, the main antibody type in blood) cross the placenta into the fetus during pregnancy, so the baby is born with protection it did not make.
After birth, breast milk, especially the first milk (colostrum), contains antibodies, mainly IgA, that protect the baby's gut and breathing passages, where many infections enter.
This passive protection lasts for the newborn's first few months, while its own immune system develops. The baby does not make its own memory cells from breast milk.

Passive artificial immunity, by donor transfer of antibodies: an injection of antibodies collected from donors (human immunoglobulin) or from immunised animals gives instant protection when there is no time for active immunity to develop.

Examples of passive artificial immunity: tetanus immunoglobulin for an unvaccinated person with a dirty wound; rabies immunoglobulin after a bite from a possibly rabid animal; hepatitis B immunoglobulin for babies born to infected mothers; antivenom, made in horses or sheep, for snake bites.

Active immunity uses the person's own antibodies and memory cells, starts slowly and lasts long. Passive immunity uses donor antibodies, starts immediately, forms no memory and is short-lived. Active immunity is used for prevention in advance; passive immunity is used for emergency protection or to protect newborns.
Vaccination gives active immunity without the danger of catching the disease. It works by letting the immune system practise on a harmless version of the pathogen.
A vaccine contains antigens of a pathogen in a form that can't cause disease. Vaccines contain antigens, not antibodies, which is why they produce active immunity.
Given by injection, or by mouth or nasal spray, a vaccine triggers a primary response, so memory cells form.
A later infection meets a fast, strong secondary response (the quicker, bigger response of memory cells), and the disease doesn't develop. There is more on this in Innate and adaptive immunity.
Vaccines differ in what form of the pathogen they contain. Each type is a different way of presenting an antigen safely, and each has typical examples.
Live attenuated vaccines contain a weakened pathogen that reproduces only slightly, so the immune system sees a realistic infection that causes little or no illness, e.g. MMR, and BCG against TB.
Inactivated vaccines contain a killed pathogen, which cannot reproduce at all, e.g. the injected polio vaccine and most injected flu vaccines.
Toxoid vaccines contain an inactivated toxin (a harmful chemical made by a bacterium), so the body learns to neutralise the toxin, e.g. tetanus and diphtheria vaccines.
Subunit vaccines contain only a purified antigen, not the whole pathogen, often made by genetically modified cells, e.g. the hepatitis B and HPV vaccines.
mRNA vaccines contain the genetic instructions (messenger RNA) for a pathogen protein, which the body's cells use to make the antigen themselves, e.g. some COVID-19 vaccines.
Viral vector vaccines use a harmless virus that carries an antigen gene into body cells, which then make the antigen. There is more on this in Viruses.
A single dose may not give lasting protection, and a vaccinated person is not the only one who benefits. Boosters strengthen the individual's immunity, and herd immunity protects the whole community.
Booster doses: a second or later dose of the same vaccine produces a secondary response, raising antibody levels and the number of memory cells, so immunity lasts longer, e.g. tetanus boosters.
A vaccine booster is active immunity, because the person makes their own antibodies; an injection of donor antibodies is passive.
Herd immunity: when a high enough proportion of a population is immune, a pathogen can't find enough susceptible hosts to keep spreading, so people who can't be vaccinated are protected indirectly.
People who can't be vaccinated include newborns, people with weakened immune systems and people allergic to a vaccine component.
The proportion needed depends on how infectious the disease is. The calculation is in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.
Vaccination began as an observation tested in an experiment, and it has since removed a human disease from the world. Like any medical measure it has benefits and some concerns.
In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that infecting a boy, James Phipps, with cowpox, a mild disease, protected him from smallpox. The word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow.
Worldwide vaccination led the World Health Organization to declare smallpox eradicated in 1980, the first human disease to be eradicated.
Benefits: vaccines prevent illness, disability and death, are cheaper than treatment, and protect others through herd immunity.
Concerns: rare side effects, most of them mild, e.g. a sore arm or a low fever.
Live vaccines are not given to people with weakened immune systems, because even a weakened pathogen could cause disease in them.
Misinformation lowers uptake, and outbreaks follow when coverage falls, because herd immunity is lost. The MMR case is in Evaluating evidence.
Prevention is better than cure, so many strategies work by breaking the chain of transmission before a pathogen reaches a person. These three cut off the routes of contact, water and food.
Hygiene: handwashing with soap removes and kills microorganisms on the hands, breaking transmission by contact. The Semmelweis case is in The nature of scientific knowledge.
Covering coughs and sneezes and cleaning surfaces also reduce transmission, because they stop droplets and contaminated surfaces passing pathogens on.
Clean water and sanitation: treating drinking water by filtering and chlorination, and safely disposing of sewage, stops the spread of waterborne diseases such as cholera.
Food safety: cooking food thoroughly kills pathogens, e.g. Salmonella in chicken.
Food safety: refrigeration slows the growth of pathogens.
Food safety: pasteurisation heats milk to about 72 °C for 15 seconds and then cools it quickly, killing pathogens without spoiling the milk.
Food safety: avoiding cross-contamination between raw and cooked food stops pathogens moving from raw food, which may carry them, to food that will not be cooked again.
Other strategies target the carrier of a disease or the route of entry into the body. Each one is matched to how a particular disease spreads.
Vaccination: vaccines given before exposure protect the vaccinated person and, through herd immunity, others. The vaccine types are in the vaccination blocks above.

Vector control (a vector is an organism that carries a pathogen between hosts): insecticide-treated bed nets, insecticide spraying and draining standing water reduce the mosquitoes that carry malaria; controlling ticks reduces Lyme disease.
Barrier methods: condoms reduce the spread of sexually transmitted infections such as HIV by stopping body fluids passing between partners.
Blood safety: donated blood is screened for HIV and hepatitis viruses, and needles are sterile and used once, so blood-borne pathogens are not passed from one person to another.
Pathogens also spread through equipment, between sick and healthy people, and among crops and livestock. These strategies deal with each of those.
Sterilisation: autoclaving, which uses steam under pressure at 121 °C, kills microorganisms and spores (tough resting forms of bacteria) on equipment.
Disinfectants and antiseptics are used on surfaces and skin, to kill or inhibit microorganisms there.
Aseptic technique (working so that no microorganisms are introduced) in surgery prevents wound infection.
Isolation separates people who are ill. Quarantine separates people, or animals and plants, who may have been exposed until it is clear they are not infected.
Contact tracing finds people who have been exposed to a case. Population-level use of isolation and quarantine is in Emerging diseases and society.
In plants and farm animals: resistant varieties and breeds, certified disease-free seed and stock, crop rotation, fungicide sprays (e.g. against potato blight), and good animal housing and hygiene.
Prion diseases (diseases caused by infectious misfolded proteins) are prevented by keeping prions out of feed and food. There is more on this in Pathogens.
Once an infection is established, drugs can treat it. Antibiotics are the main treatment for bacterial disease because bacterial cells differ from human cells in ways a drug can exploit.
Antibiotics are chemicals, originally made by microorganisms, that kill bacteria or stop them growing, without harming human cells.
Antibiotics work because they target structures that bacteria have and human cells lack.
Penicillin stops bacteria building their peptidoglycan cell wall (the strong mesh around a bacterial cell), so growing bacteria burst.
Tetracycline and streptomycin bind to bacterial 70S ribosomes and stop protein synthesis; human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, so human cells are not harmed.
Antibiotics have no effect on viruses, because viruses have no cell wall or ribosomes of their own for the drugs to target.
Responsible antibiotic use: take antibiotics only when prescribed for a bacterial infection, take the full course as directed, and never share them.
Unnecessary use selects for resistant bacteria, because those that survive the drug go on to reproduce. The detail is in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.
Different pathogens need different drugs, and some treatments simply help the body fight on. The drug type must match the type of pathogen.
Antiviral drugs interfere with a stage of virus replication inside the host cell, so each is specific to one virus or a few. Examples and how they act are in Viruses: replication.
There are far fewer antivirals than antibiotics, because viruses use the host cell's own machinery, which a drug must not damage.
Antifungal drugs target structures of fungal cells, e.g. clotrimazole cream for athlete's foot and thrush.
Antiprotozoal drugs treat protist infections, e.g. artemisinin-based drugs for malaria.
Anthelmintics kill parasitic worms, e.g. ivermectin.
Monoclonal antibodies, which are identical antibodies made in the laboratory against one antigen, are used to treat some infections and cancers.
Supportive treatment: rest, fluids and rehydration, e.g. oral rehydration solution of water, salts and sugar for cholera, and reducing fever, while the immune system clears the infection.

A virus is not a cell, so it lacks the machinery that every living cell uses to build new copies of itself. This is why a virus can only reproduce by taking over a host cell (the living cell it infects).
A virus has no ribosomes (the structures that build proteins), almost no enzymes and no energy supply, so it can't make anything by itself.

It reproduces by delivering its nucleic acid (its DNA or RNA) into a host cell. The host cell then makes new virus particles using its own ribosomes, enzymes, ATP (the cell's energy carrier), nucleotides (the building blocks of nucleic acids) and amino acids (the building blocks of proteins).
Every virus follows the same basic cycle of six stages, which ends with new viruses leaving the cell. The first three get the virus's nucleic acid inside the right kind of cell and free to act.
Stage 1, attachment: proteins on the capsid (the protein coat) or the envelope (the outer membrane some viruses have) bind to specific receptor proteins on the host cell membrane.

HIV binds to the CD4 receptor on helper T cells, and the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 binds to the ACE2 receptor on cells lining the airways. Receptor binding decides which cells a virus can infect, because only cells with the matching receptor can be attached to.
Stage 2, entry: a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) injects only its nucleic acid through the bacterial wall, leaving the empty coat outside.
Animal viruses enter whole, either by the host membrane folding in around them (endocytosis) or, for enveloped viruses, by the envelope fusing with the host membrane.
Stage 3, uncoating: inside the cell, the capsid breaks down and releases the viral nucleic acid, so its genes can be read.
Once the viral nucleic acid is free inside the cell, the virus uses the cell's machinery to make its parts, put them together and escape. The new viruses then repeat the cycle in other cells.

Stage 4, replication and synthesis: the viral genes take over the cell. Viral mRNA (the message copied from a gene) is made, and the host's ribosomes translate it into viral proteins, which are capsid proteins and viral enzymes.
In stage 4 the viral nucleic acid is copied many times, and host-cell activities are often shut down so that the cell's resources go into making viruses.
Stage 5, assembly: new nucleic acid and capsid proteins come together to form many new virus particles, often hundreds per cell. Viruses are assembled from parts, not grown or divided.

Stage 6, release: either the cell bursts (lysis), releasing all the viruses at once and killing the cell, or, for enveloped viruses, each new virus pushes out through the membrane and takes a piece of it as its envelope (budding), so the cell can survive for a time.
The new viruses infect neighbouring cells, and the cycle repeats.

Diagram: the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage in five or six sketches in a circle: phage attached by tail fibres; DNA injected; phage DNA copied and proteins made; new phages assembled; cell bursting. Label phage, bacterial cell wall, phage DNA, bacterial chromosome, new phages.
Diagram: an enveloped animal virus, such as influenza, entering a cell by endocytosis or fusion and leaving by budding, with the host membrane forming the new envelope.
A virus does not always burst its host straight away. Some bacteriophages (and some human viruses) can instead hide inside the host for a time, so there are two possible routes after infection.
Lytic cycle: the virus replicates immediately, following the stages above, and the host cell bursts. Example: bacteriophage T4 infecting the bacterium E. coli.
Lysogenic cycle: some viruses insert their DNA into the host cell's chromosome, where it stays inactive and is copied every time the cell divides, so all daughter cells carry it.
In bacteria the inserted DNA is called a prophage. Example: bacteriophage lambda in E. coli.
A trigger, such as stress like UV light, can cut the viral DNA out of the chromosome and start the lytic cycle.
Latency in human viruses: some viruses hide in cells in an inactive state for years and reactivate later.
Herpes simplex virus stays in nerve cells after the first infection and reactivates to cause repeated cold sores.
Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox, stays in nerve cells, and can reactivate decades later as shingles.
A latent virus is hidden from the immune system and from antiviral drugs, because it is not making viral proteins or new viruses that they could target.

Viruses cause disease in several different ways, from simply destroying cells to turning the body's own defences against it. Each mode of action follows from what a virus does to the cells it infects.
Killing cells: lysis destroys infected cells. Influenza destroys cells lining the airways, causing a sore throat and cough, and the cold virus damages cells of the nose and throat.
Disrupting cell function: the virus diverts the cell's ribosomes, enzymes and energy to making viruses, so the cell stops its normal work.
Damaging the immune system: HIV infects and destroys helper T cells, the white blood cells that coordinate the immune response.
As helper T cell numbers fall over years, the immune system can no longer coordinate its responses, and the person develops AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome).
People with AIDS die of opportunistic infections and cancers, which a healthy immune system would control but which take hold when the immune system is weakened.

Causing cancer: some viruses insert genes that interfere with the control of cell division, e.g. human papillomavirus (HPV) and cervical cancer. There is more on this in Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer.
Triggering harmful immune responses: much of the fever, aches and tissue damage in viral illness is caused by the body's own immune response (inflammation) to infected cells.

Viruses are grouped by the type of nucleic acid they carry, and this affects where they replicate, which enzymes they need and how fast they change. Comparing the two groups is a likely exam question.
Genetic material: a DNA virus has DNA as its genetic material; an RNA virus has RNA.
DNA viruses include herpes simplex and varicella-zoster (chickenpox) viruses, human papillomavirus (HPV), adenoviruses, the smallpox virus, and bacteriophages T4 and lambda.
RNA viruses include influenza, measles, mumps, polio, rhinoviruses (the common cold), SARS-CoV-2, HIV, Ebola and tobacco mosaic virus.
Where they replicate: most DNA viruses enter the host nucleus and use the host's own enzymes, such as DNA polymerase and RNA polymerase, to copy their DNA and make mRNA.
Poxviruses such as the smallpox virus are an exception: they replicate in the cytoplasm with their own enzymes.
Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm and must carry or code for their own enzyme, an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, to copy RNA from RNA, because host cells have no enzyme that does this.

Mutation rate: the enzyme that copies RNA has no proofreading (no checking for mistakes), so RNA viruses make many more copying errors and mutate much faster than DNA viruses, whose DNA is copied by host polymerases that proofread.

RNA viruses such as influenza and HIV change their surface antigens quickly, so new strains escape existing immunity. This is why flu vaccines are updated every year, and drug resistance appears quickly.
Once inside the cell, an RNA virus's genes still have to be turned into proteins. RNA viruses do this in one of two ways, depending on the virus.
In some RNA viruses, such as poliovirus and SARS-CoV-2, the RNA acts directly as mRNA when it enters the cell and is translated at once by the host's ribosomes.
In others, such as influenza and measles, the RNA must first be copied into a complementary strand that acts as mRNA.
DNA is a more stable molecule than RNA, which fits with DNA viruses mutating more slowly.
Mutation as a factor in disease emergence is covered further in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.
Retroviruses break the usual rule that information flows from DNA to RNA. HIV is the key example, and its cycle has a few extra steps compared with the general cycle.
A retrovirus is an RNA virus that makes a DNA copy of its RNA inside the host cell, using its own enzyme, reverse transcriptase, which reverses the usual direction of DNA to RNA. HIV is an example.
HIV replication, step 1: its envelope protein binds the CD4 receptor on a helper T cell.
Step 2: the envelope fuses with the cell membrane, and the capsid enters.
Step 3: reverse transcriptase makes double-stranded DNA from the viral RNA.
Step 4: a second viral enzyme, integrase, inserts this DNA into the host's chromosome, where it is called a provirus and can stay hidden for years.
Step 5: when the cell is activated, the provirus is transcribed into viral mRNA and new viral RNA, and viral proteins are made.
Step 6: new viruses assemble and bud from the cell, taking an envelope of host membrane.
Reverse transcriptase makes many errors, so HIV mutates very quickly, which is one reason there is still no effective HIV vaccine.

Diagram: an HIV particle (envelope with surface proteins, capsid, two RNA strands and reverse transcriptase), and a flow of the six steps into and out of a helper T cell. Label receptor, viral RNA, viral DNA, host chromosome (provirus) and budding virus.
Antibiotics don't work on viruses, so viral infections are treated with antiviral drugs that interrupt one stage of the replication cycle. Each drug targets a step that depends on a viral protein.
Antiviral drugs block a step in the cycle that uses a viral protein, so the host cell isn't harmed.
Aciclovir blocks the DNA polymerase of herpes viruses, which treats cold sores and shingles.
Oseltamivir blocks neuraminidase, the influenza enzyme that releases new viruses from the cell surface.
HIV drugs include reverse transcriptase inhibitors, of which zidovudine (AZT), approved in 1987, was the first.
HIV drugs also include protease inhibitors, which stop new viral proteins being cut into their working form.
HIV is treated with a combination of several antiretroviral drugs at once (antiretroviral therapy).
Antiretroviral therapy keeps the virus at very low levels and lets the immune system recover, but it doesn't cure the infection, because the provirus remains in the host DNA.
Using several drugs together makes resistance much less likely, since the virus would need several mutations at once.
The syllabus asks you to model how viruses replicate within cells. A model turns the six stages into something you can draw, handle and use to make predictions, while leaving out some detail.

To model the cycle, first list the stages in order: attachment, entry, uncoating, replication and synthesis, assembly and release. Then draw each as a labelled sketch or box, showing the host-cell part used at that stage (receptor, membrane, ribosomes, enzymes, nucleotides).
Join the stages with arrows into a cycle, because the new viruses go on to infect other cells.
Mark how a DNA virus, an RNA virus and a retrovirus differ at stage 4.
Mark where an antiviral drug would act.
A physical model can use card or modelling clay to represent viruses and cells, to show attachment and budding.
The model shows the order of events, the dependence on host machinery, and why one infected cell releases many viruses. There is more on this in Models.
The model simplifies the timing (a cycle can take minutes to hours), the numbers released, the molecular steps, and the differences between viruses.

Worked prediction: if each infected cell releases 100 viruses and each of those infects a new cell, two cycles from one virus give 100 × 100 = 10,000 viruses. This is an illustrative calculation, not a figure for a real virus.
Diagram: a flow chart of the cycle, with stages as labelled boxes joined by arrows into a loop, and the host-cell part used at each stage marked on it.

The immune system is run by several different kinds of white blood cell, and they all start from the same place. Knowing where each type comes from and matures explains how the body learns to attack invaders but not itself.
White blood cells (leucocytes) are the cells of the immune system. Unlike red blood cells, they have a nucleus, which holds the genes they need to make the proteins for their defensive jobs.
All white blood cells develop from stem cells (cells that can divide and become different cell types) in the red bone marrow, the soft tissue inside some bones.
They travel in the blood and lymph (the fluid that drains from tissues), and many leave the capillaries to enter the tissues, because that is where pathogens (disease-causing organisms) are found.
There are two broad groups. Phagocytes (neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages) engulf pathogens, taking them into the cell.
The second group is the lymphocytes (B cells, T cells and natural killer cells). These are small cells with a large round nucleus filling most of the cell and little cytoplasm.
B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow. T lymphocytes leave the marrow and mature in the thymus, a gland in the chest behind the breastbone (T for thymus).

During maturation, lymphocytes that would attack the body's own cells are removed, so mature lymphocytes respond only to non-self antigens (molecules on a pathogen's surface that the immune system recognises as foreign).

Monocytes are the white blood cells that travel in the blood and then settle in tissues as macrophages. Macrophages are the body's general-purpose cleaners and also the link between the fast, general response and the specific one.
Monocytes are the largest white blood cells, with a large kidney- or bean-shaped nucleus, which makes them easy to tell from lymphocytes under the microscope.
They circulate in the blood for a few days, then move into tissues and develop into macrophages, which can live for months.
Macrophages carry out phagocytosis (engulfing and digesting) of pathogens, dead cells and debris. There is more on the stages in Innate and adaptive immunity.

Macrophages are antigen-presenting cells: they display fragments of engulfed pathogens on their surface to activate helper T cells, so they link innate immunity (the fast, non-specific response) and adaptive immunity (the slower, specific one).
Macrophages release chemicals that cause inflammation and fever and attract other white blood cells to the site of infection.
Diagram: a monocyte (large cell, kidney-shaped nucleus) beside a lymphocyte (small cell, large round nucleus, thin rim of cytoplasm). Label nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane.

Natural killer (NK) cells are a fast first line of attack against body cells that have gone wrong, either because a virus is hiding inside them or because they have become cancerous. They check cells for a missing marker rather than for a particular pathogen.

Natural killer (NK) cells are lymphocytes of the innate system. They are not specific to one antigen and need no earlier exposure, so they act within hours of an infection, before B and T cells have responded.
Healthy body cells display normal self-marker (MHC) proteins on their surface, which tell the immune system the cell belongs to the body.
Many virus-infected cells and cancer cells display fewer of these markers, or display stress molecules instead. NK cells kill cells showing this missing self pattern.
NK cells also kill cells coated with antibodies, the proteins that bind to antigens.
