NK cells release perforin, a protein that makes pores in the target cell's membrane, and enzymes called granzymes that enter through the pores and trigger the cell to self-destruct (apoptosis, programmed cell death).
The dying cell breaks into fragments that macrophages engulf, so the virus inside is destroyed without spreading.
NK cells also release chemicals that activate macrophages, which helps clear the fragments.
B lymphocytes are the cells behind antibodies. Each B cell is committed to one antibody shape, so the body needs a huge range of B cells to cover many different antigens.
B lymphocytes carry antibody molecules in their membrane as receptors, which let them bind a matching antigen. Each B cell and its descendants make only one antibody shape.

B lymphocytes are responsible for antibody-mediated (humoral) immunity, meaning protection by antibodies carried in body fluids. Clonal selection, plasma cells and memory B cells are taught in Innate and adaptive immunity.

Plasma cells, the antibody-secreting form of B cells, are larger than resting B cells, with extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum (a network of membranes studded with ribosomes) to make and secrete large amounts of antibody protein.
Antibodies act on pathogens and toxins outside cells, in blood, tissue fluid and mucus, not on pathogens hidden inside cells, because antibodies cannot get into body cells.

T lymphocytes are the cells that control and carry out cell-mediated immunity, the response that deals with infected body cells. Helper T cells are the coordinators that most of the adaptive response depends on.
All T cells have T-cell receptors on their surface that recognise one antigen, but only when it is displayed on a cell's surface (presented), never as a free molecule.
T cells don't make antibodies. That is the job of plasma cells, which come from B cells.
Helper T cells carry the surface marker CD4.

Helper T cells are the coordinators of the adaptive response, signalling with cytokines (chemical messengers between immune cells). Which cells they activate, and in what order, is taught in Innate and adaptive immunity.
Almost every adaptive response depends on helper T cells, so HIV, which infects and destroys CD4 helper T cells, leaves the body unable to fight many infections.
Killer T cells deal with threats that antibodies cannot reach, because the pathogen is hidden inside a body cell. They destroy the whole infected cell.
Killer T cells (cytotoxic T cells) carry the surface marker CD8.
Killer T cells bind to body cells displaying their matching antigen, such as virus-infected cells, cancer cells and cells of transplanted tissue.
They kill these cells by releasing perforin and granzymes, which triggers apoptosis (the cell's programmed self-destruction).
Killer T cells use the same killing method as NK cells, but only against cells showing their one specific antigen, whereas NK cells look for missing self-markers.
Each killer T cell can kill many target cells in turn.
An immune response needs brakes, and it needs a record of past infections. Suppressor T cells provide the brakes, and memory T cells provide the record that makes a second infection easier to fight.
Suppressor T cells, now usually called regulatory T cells, are the brakes of the immune system.
Suppressor T cells end a response once an infection is cleared, so the body is not damaged by an immune response that carries on. The details are taught in Innate and adaptive immunity.
They also suppress lymphocytes that react to the body's own antigens, helping to prevent autoimmune disease (the body attacking its own tissues) and allergy.
Memory T cells form from the clone of activated T cells (the identical cells that divide from one activated T cell) and remain in the blood and lymph tissue for years or decades.
On re-exposure to the same antigen, memory T cells quickly produce new helper and killer T cells, giving a faster, stronger cell-mediated response. Memory B cells do the same for antibodies.
Memory cells are why vaccination works: the vaccine exposes you to the antigen safely, so memory cells are ready if the real pathogen arrives.

The outcome asks you to compare the roles of different white blood cells. The first comparison is between the fast, general innate cells and the slower, specific adaptive cells, and then between the ways each one destroys pathogens.
Innate versus adaptive: monocytes, macrophages and NK cells are part of innate immunity, which is non-specific, acts quickly and has no memory.
B and T lymphocytes are adaptive: they are specific to one antigen, slower on first exposure, and they form memory cells.
Macrophages engulf and digest pathogens by phagocytosis. NK and killer T cells kill infected body cells by perforin and apoptosis.
B cells, as plasma cells, secrete antibodies. Helper T cells kill nothing themselves but signal to other cells.
Suppressor T cells regulate the response. Memory cells kill nothing but enable a rapid future response.
Cells also differ in what they attack and in how they recognise it. This explains why different cells are needed to cover both free pathogens and pathogens hidden inside body cells.
Where the target is: antibodies from B cells act on pathogens and toxins outside cells, because antibodies cannot enter body cells.
Killer T and NK cells act on pathogens inside body cells by killing the cell. Macrophages engulf free pathogens.
Recognition: B cells recognise free antigens with membrane antibodies, while T cells recognise only antigens presented on cell surfaces.
NK cells recognise missing or abnormal self-markers, not a specific antigen.
Macrophages recognise general features of pathogens and antibody-coated particles, so they need no specific receptor for each pathogen.
This list puts each cell side by side: whether it is innate or adaptive, whether it is specific, its main role, and where it matures. Use it to compare cells quickly.
Monocyte or macrophage: innate; non-specific; main role is phagocytosis and antigen presentation; matures in the bone marrow, then in tissues.
NK cell: innate; non-specific; kills infected and cancer cells; matures in the bone marrow.
B lymphocyte: adaptive; specific; main role is antibodies (via plasma cells) and memory; matures in the bone marrow.
Helper T cell: adaptive; specific; activates B cells, killer T cells and macrophages (CD4); matures in the thymus.
Killer T cell: adaptive; specific; kills infected, cancer and transplant cells (CD8); matures in the thymus.
Suppressor T cell: adaptive; ends responses and prevents attack on self; matures in the thymus.
Memory B and T cells: adaptive; specific; long-lived, giving a fast secondary response.
In a real infection the cells act as a team in sequence. Influenza, a virus that infects the cells lining the airways, shows how the innate and adaptive cells combine.

First, infected cells release interferons (chemical signals that warn neighbouring cells of a virus) and NK cells kill some of them within hours. Macrophages engulf viruses and present antigens, and helper T cells are activated.
Next, killer T cells destroy infected cells while plasma cells release antibodies that neutralise free viruses, so both hidden and free viruses are dealt with.
Finally, suppressor T cells end the response and memory cells remain. Because flu antigens change, memory cells may not recognise next year's strain.
Disease specialists use precise words for how common a disease is and how fast it is changing. You need these terms to describe any outbreak, and they appear throughout the rest of this subsection.
An emerging infectious disease is one that has newly appeared in a population, or one that was known but is rapidly increasing in incidence (the number of new cases) or in geographic range.
A re-emerging disease is one that had declined and is increasing again, e.g. measles where vaccination rates fall, or TB with drug-resistant strains.
Endemic means always present at a fairly steady level in a region, so the number of cases is predictable from year to year.
An epidemic, or outbreak, is a sudden increase in cases above the expected level in a region.
A pandemic is an epidemic that spreads across several continents or worldwide, e.g. COVID-19, which the World Health Organization declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020.
Some terms describe where a pathogen (a disease-causing organism) lives between outbreaks and who can pass it on. These explain why some diseases are so hard to get rid of.
A zoonosis is an infectious disease that passes from animals to humans, e.g. avian influenza or rabies.
Most emerging human diseases are zoonoses, often from wild animals, because people have little immunity to pathogens they have never met. There is more on this in Emerging diseases and society.
A reservoir is a host population in which a pathogen persists and from which it infects others, e.g. badgers for bovine TB in Ireland, or wild birds for avian influenza.
A carrier is an infected individual who shows no symptoms but can pass on the pathogen, so nobody knows to avoid them.
A pathogen can only cause an outbreak if it can get from one host to the next. There are several routes, and each has typical diseases that use it, in both animals and plants.
Airborne droplets and aerosols (tiny particles hanging in the air) from coughs, sneezes and breath spread influenza, TB, measles and COVID-19.
Wind-borne spores spread ash dieback, cereal rusts and potato blight in plants, because spores are light enough to be carried between fields.
Direct contact, touch and skin to skin, spreads ringworm and athlete's foot.
Indirect contact via contaminated objects and surfaces (fomites), hands, tools and clothing spreads disease. In plants, contact with hands and tools spreads tobacco mosaic virus.
Contaminated food and water, the faecal–oral route (pathogens in faeces reach the mouth), spreads cholera, Salmonella food poisoning and amoebic dysentery.
Body fluids spread HIV and hepatitis B through sexual contact, blood (shared needles and unscreened transfusions) and mother to baby.

Vectors are animals that carry pathogens between hosts: mosquitoes (malaria), ticks (Lyme disease), tsetse flies (sleeping sickness), elm bark beetles (Dutch elm disease), aphids (many plant viruses, e.g. barley yellow dwarf virus) and biting midges (bluetongue virus of sheep and cattle).

In plants, rain splash, soil, infected seed, tubers and cuttings also spread disease. Vegetative propagation (growing new plants from parts of old ones) passes viruses and blight to the next crop, and grafting does too.

Diseases spread when infected organisms, or the things they touch, move. Over short distances this happens through everyday contact, and over a whole country it follows the trade and travel routes of animals and people.

Local spread occurs within a household, school, hospital or farm, between neighbouring fields by wind and rain splash, and between neighbouring farms by animals straying, shared equipment, vehicles and people's boots.

Regional spread occurs when farm animals move through marts (livestock markets) and between farms, when plants and animals are traded within a country or the EU, when wild animals move seasonally, and when people commute and holiday.
In the 2001 foot-and-mouth disease epidemic in Britain, infected sheep were moved through markets across the country before the disease was detected, spreading it to many farms.
Control of that epidemic needed a ban on animal movement and the culling of millions of animals, which shows how costly it is once movement has carried a disease widely.
Modern travel and trade mean a pathogen no longer stays where it started. A disease can reach another continent before anyone knows it is there.
Air travel can carry an infected person to any continent within a day, faster than many diseases take to show symptoms, so travellers can carry infection without knowing it.
COVID-19 reached every continent within months of its first identification in Wuhan, China, in December 2019.
International trade moves pathogens and vectors in plants, wood, soil, live animals and goods. Ash dieback spread through Europe partly in imported young ash plants and was found in Ireland in 2012.
The second, more aggressive epidemic of Dutch elm disease reached Britain from the late 1960s in imported elm logs.
The Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus), a vector of several viruses, has spread to many countries in used tyres and plants.
Migrating wild birds carry avian influenza between continents, because infected birds fly long distances without any border controls.
Trade in live animals can move a disease into places where the local species have never met it. Amphibians show how serious this can be.
The pet and wildlife trade spread chytrid fungus (Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis) around the world in the trade in amphibians.
Chytrid is linked to the decline of hundreds of amphibian species and the extinction of some.
Emergence and spread depend on several interrelated factors, and the first is persistence. The longer a host carries a pathogen in a way that can pass on, the more chances it has to infect others.
The longer a host is infectious, the more others it can infect.
Persistence includes long infectious periods, carriers without symptoms, latent infections (the pathogen is present but inactive) that reactivate, and reservoir hosts.
HIV may cause no symptoms for years while the person can still pass it on.
Herpes viruses stay latent in nerve cells for life, so the person is never rid of the virus. There is more on this in Viruses: replication.
TB bacteria can stay dormant (inactive) in the lungs for years and become active later.
Persistence shows up in each kind of host, from a single healthy-looking person to wildlife and crops.

Mary Mallon, known as Typhoid Mary, was born in Co. Tyrone in 1869 and worked as a cook in New York. She carried the typhoid bacterium, Salmonella Typhi, without symptoms and infected many of the families she cooked for.
Health authorities isolated her for most of the rest of her life, because as a carrier she could not be identified by illness.
Bovine TB persists in Irish cattle partly because badgers act as a wildlife reservoir that reinfects herds, so clearing the disease from cattle alone is not enough.
Plant viruses persist in perennial plants (which live for years), weeds and tubers, so infected seed potatoes carry viruses into the next year's crop.
Phytophthora infestans, the cause of potato blight, survives the winter in infected tubers left in the ground or in dumps.
A mutation is a random change in a pathogen's genetic material. Pathogens that reproduce quickly produce huge numbers of changed copies, so some will spread better than the original.
Pathogens with short generation times and large populations produce many mutants, because each new copy is another chance for a change.
RNA viruses mutate fastest because their copying enzyme doesn't proofread (check for copying errors). There is more on this in Viruses: replication.

Antigenic drift: small mutations gradually change a virus's surface antigens (the molecules the immune system recognises), so memory cells and antibodies from earlier infections or vaccines no longer fit well.
Antigenic drift is why influenza returns every winter and why flu vaccines are updated each year.
Mutations likewise produced new SARS-CoV-2 variants, such as Delta and Omicron, that spread faster or partly escaped immunity, causing new waves of COVID-19.
Mutations can also change what a pathogen is able to do, giving it a new host or defeating a crop's defences.
Antigenic shift (influenza): if two different flu viruses infect the same cell, e.g. in a pig, their RNA segments can mix to form a new strain with surface antigens that no human population has met.
Antigenic shift has caused flu pandemics, e.g. the 2009 H1N1 (swine flu) pandemic, because with no existing immunity the new strain spreads easily.
Mutations can let a pathogen infect a new host species (spillover, e.g. a bird virus gaining the ability to infect mammals), become more transmissible, or overcome resistance bred into crops.
The Ug99 strain of wheat stem rust, identified in Uganda in 1999, overcame resistance genes used in most of the world's wheat varieties.

Resistance means a pathogen or pest survives a drug or chemical that used to kill it. It arises by natural selection (survival of the individuals best suited to their conditions), which happens in four steps. There is more on this in The theory of evolution by natural selection.
1. Random mutations, or genes passed between bacteria on plasmids (small rings of DNA), make a few individuals resistant.
2. The antibiotic or chemical kills the susceptible individuals.
3. The resistant survivors reproduce with less competition.
4. The next generation is mostly resistant. The chemical doesn't cause the mutation; it selects it.
Resistance arises by natural selection when a drug or chemical kills susceptible individuals, and some practices make it spread faster. The examples cover people, crops and livestock.
Overuse and misuse of antibiotics speed up resistance: use for viral infections (which antibiotics cannot treat), not finishing courses, and use in farm animals.
Poor infection control in hospitals and heavy repeated use of one pesticide also speed up resistance.
MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is resistant to many antibiotics and spreads in hospitals.
Multidrug-resistant TB, malaria parasites resistant to some antimalarial drugs, and mosquitoes resistant to insecticides, which weakens malaria control.
Fungi that cause crop diseases are resistant to some fungicides, and parasitic worms of sheep and cattle are resistant to some anthelmintics (drugs that kill worms).
Resistant pathogens persist longer in hosts and spread further, linking factors 1 and 3.
A pathogen needs susceptible hosts, meaning individuals with no immunity to it. How many of these there are in a population strongly affects how far and how fast an outbreak goes.

A pathogen spreads only if it can reach susceptible (non-immune) hosts. The higher the proportion of immune individuals, the fewer susceptible hosts there are and the slower the spread. This is herd immunity. There is more on this in Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment.
A pathogen new to a population meets no immunity at all, so it spreads fast and can be very severe, e.g. COVID-19 in 2020, before vaccines.
Smallpox and measles, brought by Europeans to the Americas from the late 1400s, killed very large numbers of Indigenous people, who had never been exposed to them.
Immunity falls when vaccination rates drop, as when measles outbreaks return.

Immunity also falls when protection from vaccination or infection wanes over time, and where many people have weakened immune systems, e.g. from untreated HIV or malnutrition, or the very young and very old.
Plants have no antibody-based immunity like animals, but the same principle applies. What matters is whether any individuals in the crop can resist the pathogen.
In plants, the equivalent is genetic uniformity. A monoculture (a crop of one genetically identical variety) has no resistant individuals, so a pathogen that infects one plant can infect them all.
In Ireland in the 1840s, most of the poor depended on one potato variety, the Lumper, grown from tubers (genetically identical clones) and susceptible to blight.
When Phytophthora infestans arrived in 1845, crops failed across the country in successive years. About one million people died and over a million emigrated in the Great Famine.
The more infected hosts move and mix, the more other hosts they meet, so the further a pathogen travels. Mobility applies to people, livestock, wildlife and vectors.
The more infected hosts move and mix, the more contacts each has and the further the pathogen spreads. The routes are those in local, regional and global spread above.
Crowding in cities, refugee camps, festivals and mass gatherings, travel and migration, and the movement of livestock all increase spread.
Migration of wild animals, such as birds, also moves pathogens into new areas.
Vector mobility: climate warming lets vectors survive further north and for longer each year, carrying disease into new regions.
Bluetongue, a midge-borne virus of sheep and cattle, spread into northern Europe from 2006.

Reducing mobility reduces spread: animal movement bans in foot-and-mouth outbreaks, travel restrictions and quarantine in human epidemics, and import controls on plants. There is more on this in Emerging diseases and society.
To compare outbreaks and predict whether one will grow, scientists use a single number, R₀. It measures how contagious a pathogen is when nobody has immunity.

The basic reproduction number, R₀ ('R nought'), is the average number of new (secondary) infections caused by one infected individual in a population where everyone is susceptible, with no immunity and no control measures.
R₀ greater than 1: each case causes more than one new case on average, so numbers grow and an epidemic can occur.
R₀ equal to 1: numbers stay steady, which is endemic.
R₀ less than 1: each case causes fewer than one new case, so the outbreak dies out.

Each infected person passes the pathogen to R₀ others, so cases multiply by R₀ every generation of infection (one round of people infecting the next). Working through numbers shows why R₀ above or below 1 matters.
Growth example: with R₀ = 2, one case leads to 2, then 4, then 8, then 16 new cases per generation of infection. After 10 generations, one case has led to 2¹⁰ = 1,024 new cases in that generation.
Decline example: with R₀ = 0.5, 100 cases give 50, then 25, then about 12, and the outbreak fades.
Diagram: a branching tree from one case, giving 2, then 4, then 8 cases (R₀ = 2), beside a single chain with one case per generation (R₀ = 1). Label each generation.
R₀ is not a fixed property of a pathogen. It combines features of the pathogen, the host and the environment, which are the factors already covered.
R₀ depends on how long a host is infectious (persistence), so a longer infectious period raises R₀.
R₀ depends on how many contacts an infected host has per day (mobility and crowding), so more contacts raise R₀.
R₀ depends on the chance that a contact passes on the infection (the transmission route, and mutations that make a pathogen more transmissible).
So R₀ is not fixed for a disease: it differs between populations and settings.
In real outbreaks some people are already immune or control measures are in place. The effective reproduction number measures spread under those real conditions.

The effective reproduction number, R (sometimes written Rt), is the average number of new infections per case at a given time, in a population where some people are immune or control measures are in place.
Approximately, R = R₀ × the proportion still susceptible. For example, R₀ = 3 with half the population immune gives R = 3 × 0.5 = 1.5.
Control aims to bring R below 1, so that each case infects fewer than one other person and the outbreak dies out.
If R₀ tells us how contagious a disease is, we can work out how many people must be immune to stop it spreading. The more contagious the disease, the higher that proportion.
Herd-immunity threshold: to stop sustained spread, the proportion immune must be at least 1 − 1/R₀.
Examples: R₀ = 2 needs 1 − ½ = 50% immune; R₀ = 4 needs 1 − ¼ = 75% immune; R₀ = 10 needs 90% immune.
Measles is one of the most contagious diseases, with R₀ usually quoted as 12–18, so about 95% of people must be immune.
The World Health Organization therefore recommends at least 95% coverage with two doses of measles vaccine.
R₀ comes from a simple model, and a model is only as good as its assumptions. Real outbreaks differ in important ways.
The model's assumptions are that everyone is equally likely to meet everyone else and that R₀ stays constant. There is more on this in Models.
Real populations are clustered, behaviour changes during outbreaks and new variants change R₀, so estimates are updated as data come in.
The six factors do not work one at a time. Real outbreaks happen when several combine, and other changes in how we live bring pathogens and new hosts into contact.
The factors act together, not one at a time. A mutation that makes a virus more transmissible raises R₀, and a population with low immunity and high mobility then lets it spread widely.
Long persistence in carriers lets a pathogen reach new areas undetected, and resistance to drugs lets infections last longer, raising R₀ further.
Plant example: a genetically uniform crop (low immunity), a pathogen spread by wind and trade (mobility) and survival in tubers (persistence) together explain the speed of the potato famine.

Other drivers increase contact between pathogens and new hosts: clearing forests and expanding farms into wild areas (more contact with wild animals), intensive farming of large numbers of genetically similar animals kept close together, climate change (vectors' ranges), poverty, poor sanitation, and conflict, which weakens health systems.
A virus can cause a new disease without being new to the world: it only has to be new to the species it infects. Most of the new viruses that infect people come from other animals.
A novel virus is one not previously known to infect a species, usually because it has jumped from another host (a jump called spillover) or has changed by mutation or by mixing of genes.
Most new human viruses come from animals. A disease passed from animals to people is called a zoonosis, and the animals involved are especially bats, birds and other mammals.

Contact between wildlife and people increases when people clear forests, hunt or trade wild animals, or farm animals intensively, because each of these creates new opportunities for a virus to cross from one species to another.
Two viruses that reached people from animals changed the world in very different ways: one spread silently over decades, the other around the globe within months.

HIV crossed into humans from a related virus, SIV (simian immunodeficiency virus), in chimpanzees in central Africa in the early twentieth century, probably through hunting and butchering them for meat.
HIV was identified in 1983 by Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier at the Institut Pasteur, Paris (Nobel Prize 2008).
HIV's long symptom-free period let it spread worldwide unnoticed for decades, because infected people had no reason to suspect they carried it.

There is still no HIV vaccine, but antiretroviral therapy (drugs that stop the virus replicating) has turned it from a fatal disease into a long-term condition. There is more on this in Viruses: replication.

SARS-CoV-2, the coronavirus that causes COVID-19, was first identified in Wuhan, China, in December 2019. It spreads by droplets and aerosols (tiny airborne particles), including from people without symptoms, and air travel carried it worldwide.
Its genome sequence was shared online in January 2020, and vaccines were developed and approved within a year.
Mutations produced more transmissible variants (forms that spread more easily), so vaccines were updated to match them.

Animal viruses show how a virus moves between wildlife, farm animals and people, and what controlled each outbreak. For each one, know what it is, where it came from, how it spread and how it was stopped.

Avian influenza H5N1 is a highly pathogenic (very disease-causing) bird flu virus that kills poultry and wild birds. A strain that spread worldwide from about 2020, carried by migrating wild birds, has infected many mammals, and in 2024 it was found in dairy cattle in the USA.

Human infections with H5N1 are rare and mostly occur in people in close contact with infected birds or animals. The concern is that mutation, or mixing with a human flu virus, could produce a strain that spreads between people.
Avian influenza is controlled by culling infected flocks, keeping poultry housed when the risk is high (which keeps them away from wild birds), and surveillance.

Ebola virus causes severe haemorrhagic fever (fever with bleeding). Fruit bats are thought to be its natural reservoir, the animal host in which the virus normally lives. The 2014–2016 epidemic in West Africa killed more than 11,000 people.

Ebola spreads by contact with the body fluids of sick or dead people, so caring for the sick and traditional burial practices spread it. It was controlled by isolation, contact tracing, safe burials and, later, a vaccine.
Nipah virus emerged in Malaysia in 1998–1999, passing from fruit bats to pigs on farms near fruit trees, and from pigs to pig farmers, causing brain inflammation (encephalitis).
Nipah was controlled by culling over a million pigs. It shows how farming changes create new routes from wildlife to people.

Schmallenberg virus, an animal virus, was identified in 2011 in Germany and is named after the town where it was found. Spread by biting midges, it causes birth defects in lambs and calves when the mother is infected in early pregnancy.
It spread across northern Europe, including Ireland, within about a year.
Plants get emerging virus diseases too. Tomato brown rugose fruit virus (ToBRFV) is a recent example that threatens a major glasshouse crop.
ToBRFV is a tobamovirus, related to tobacco mosaic virus, first identified in the Middle East in the mid-2010s, and it then spread to many countries.
It infects tomatoes and peppers, causing wrinkled, discoloured fruit that can't be sold, so growers lose income.
It spreads by contact (hands, tools and clothing), in infected seed and in the trade in plants and fruit, and it stays infectious on surfaces for long periods.
It is serious because it overcomes the resistance genes bred into tomato varieties to protect them against related viruses, so the older protection no longer works.
Control: EU plant-health rules on imported seed and plants, testing of seed, hygiene and disinfection in glasshouses, destroying infected crops, and breeding new resistant varieties.
Several human activities and natural changes help plant viruses reach new places and crops. Because plants cannot be treated once infected, prevention is the only real defence.

Why plant viruses emerge: global trade in seeds and plants; monocultures of genetically uniform crops (one variety grown over huge areas, so one virus can overcome them all); insect vectors (carriers) spreading into new areas as the climate warms; and mutation overcoming plants' resistance genes.

Plants have no adaptive immune system (the antibody- and T-cell-based defence animals use) and can't be vaccinated or cured of viral infection, so control depends on prevention: clean seed and stock, controlling vectors, removing infected plants, quarantine and resistant varieties.
Economic and food-security importance: crop losses raise food prices and threaten farmers' incomes.
Diseases of staple crops (the main food crops) are most serious for poor countries that depend on one crop, because there is no alternative food if it fails.
The immune system is meant to attack invaders and leave the body alone. In an autoimmune disease it gets this wrong and attacks the body's own tissues.
An autoimmune disease is one in which the immune system attacks the body's own cells or tissues as if they were foreign, because it fails to tell self from non-self.
Normally, lymphocytes (white blood cells that recognise antigens) that react to self are removed during maturation, and the rest are held in check by suppressor (regulatory) T cells.
In autoimmune disease this tolerance (not attacking self) breaks down, and antibodies or killer T cells attack a self antigen, an antigen that is part of the body's own cells.
Each autoimmune disease is defined by which tissue the immune system attacks, and the symptoms follow from the job that tissue does.

Type 1 diabetes: T cells destroy the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas, causing high blood glucose. It is treated with insulin injections for life. There is more on this in Glands, locations and hormones.
Multiple sclerosis: the myelin sheath (the insulating layer) around nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord is damaged, slowing or blocking impulses.
Rheumatoid arthritis: the lining of the joints becomes inflamed, causing painful, swollen and damaged joints.

Coeliac disease: eating gluten, a protein in wheat, barley and rye, triggers an immune attack that damages the villi of the small intestine (the finger-like folds that absorb food), causing poor absorption. Treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet.
Graves' disease: antibodies stimulate the thyroid gland, producing too much thyroxine.
Autoimmune diseases have no single cause. Inherited genes make some people more susceptible, and something in the environment then sets the disease off.
Causes: a combination of inherited susceptibility, since some alleles make these diseases more likely and they run in families, and environmental triggers.
Infections can trigger autoimmunity when a pathogen's antigen resembles a self antigen, so antibodies made against the pathogen also attack the body.
Rheumatic fever: antibodies against Streptococcus bacteria, from a throat infection, attack the heart valves.
Guillain–Barré syndrome is a paralysis that can follow some infections, including Campylobacter food poisoning and Zika virus.
Autoimmune diseases are not infectious, yet they are grouped with emerging diseases because more people have several of them than before. Treatment can manage them but rarely cures them.
Autoimmune diseases are grouped with emerging diseases because the number of people with several autoimmune diseases has been rising in many countries.

The hygiene hypothesis proposes that less early-life exposure to microorganisms leaves the immune system poorly regulated. It is supported by some evidence but not proven, so it remains a hypothesis. There is more on this in The microbiome.
An autoimmune disease is not caught from another person. AIDS is an immune deficiency caused by a virus, not an autoimmune disease.

There is usually no cure. Treatments replace what is lost (insulin, thyroid hormone), avoid the trigger (a gluten-free diet), or suppress the immune system with drugs such as corticosteroids, which relieves symptoms but makes infections more likely.

Knowing which factors make a disease spread lets us target each one. Each strategy below is linked to the factor it acts on, which is how exams expect you to present it. There is more on the factors in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.

Surveillance and early detection: doctors and vets must report notifiable diseases (ones the law requires them to report), and laboratories sequence pathogens' genomes to detect new variants and resistance.
Agencies such as the World Health Organization and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control share data. Early detection lets control start while case numbers are low.

Reducing R (targets R₀, contact and transmission): isolating cases, contact tracing and quarantine reduce the infectious period in the community, because infected people have fewer days in which to pass the disease on.

Masks, ventilation, hand hygiene and physical distancing reduce the chance of transmission per contact, and limiting mass gatherings reduces the number of contacts. The aim is to bring R (the average number of people each case infects) below 1, so the outbreak dies out.

Raising immunity (targets the immunity level): vaccination campaigns aimed at the herd-immunity threshold (the proportion immune that stops an outbreak spreading), with priority for the most vulnerable.
Updating vaccines to match new variants targets mutation.
Other strategies target how pathogens travel, how crops are protected, how resistance develops and how animal viruses reach people in the first place.

Limiting mobility (targets movement): travel restrictions and screening; animal movement bans and culling during outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease or avian influenza; and disinfecting vehicles and footwear at farms.
Plant biosecurity: plant passports and import inspections, quarantine of imported plants, and bans on importing high-risk plants (e.g. ash from infected areas).
Plant biosecurity also uses certified disease-free seed and planting material, removing and destroying infected plants, and breeding resistant varieties, which counters genetic uniformity.

Fighting resistance (targets resistance): antimicrobial stewardship, meaning prescribing antibiotics only when needed; infection control in hospitals; restricting antibiotic use in farm animals; rotating pesticides and fungicides; and developing new drugs.
Reducing spillover: controlling vectors, regulating wildlife trade and markets, protecting habitats, and biosecurity on farms.
The One Health approach treats human, animal and environmental health as linked, and coordinates doctors, vets and ecologists.
Control measures work best when they are chosen using evidence and when the public is willing to follow them.
Research and public information: understanding a new pathogen's transmission and R₀ tells authorities which measures will work, so effort is not wasted on measures that won't help.
Clear public information increases vaccine uptake and cooperation and counters misinformation (false or misleading claims). There is more on this in Evaluating evidence.
Understanding how new diseases arise and spread benefits health, the economy, food supplies, the environment and ordinary citizens.
Health: early recognition and control save lives and prevent disability.
Knowing the factors lets health systems prepare, with stockpiles, hospital capacity and vaccine platforms, before the next outbreak.
Protecting vulnerable groups depends on high immunity in everyone else, which means those who can't be vaccinated are shielded by those who can.
Economic: epidemics close businesses, schools and travel, and cost health systems heavily, as COVID-19 did from 2020.
Animal and plant diseases cause culling, lost exports and crop losses, e.g. the 2001 foot-and-mouth epidemic in Britain. Prevention and early control usually cost far less than a large outbreak.

Food security and the environment: plant and animal diseases threaten the food supply, especially where people depend on one crop. The Irish Great Famine shows the human cost, and there is more on this in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.
Diseases of wild species threaten biodiversity, e.g. chytrid fungus in amphibians, and ash dieback removing a native tree species and the organisms that depend on it.

Informed citizens: understanding how diseases spread, and why vaccines and antibiotics must be used carefully, lets people make informed choices, follow public-health advice and judge claims in the media.
A full discussion gives arguments for, then the costs and tensions of control measures, then a judgement. Examiners expect both sides.
Global cooperation: pathogens ignore borders, so a disease anywhere is a risk everywhere. Sharing data, genome sequences and vaccines between countries benefits all.

Tensions and costs: control measures limit personal freedom, such as quarantine, travel bans and lockdowns, and their social and economic costs, such as lost income and education, isolation and poor mental health, fall unequally.
Culling destroys farmers' livelihoods and healthy animals, vaccine requirements raise questions of consent, and poorer countries have less access to vaccines and drugs.

Acting early on uncertain evidence may later look like over-reaction, while waiting for certainty lets a disease spread. This is the precautionary principle, and there is more on this in Science, scientists and society.
Judgement: knowledge of emerging diseases matters because it allows targeted, proportionate measures, which cost less and do less harm than either doing nothing or applying blanket restrictions.
The more is known about a disease's factors, the more precisely its spread can be limited.
The male reproductive system has two jobs: making sperm and a hormone, and getting the sperm to the female. Knowing the route sperm take makes each organ's role easy to place.

The male reproductive system produces sperm, the male gametes (sex cells), and the hormone testosterone, and delivers sperm into the female's vagina during sexual intercourse, so that a sperm can fertilise an egg.

Sperm pass in order: testis → epididymis → vas deferens → urethra (where fluids from the seminal vesicles and prostate are added) → out through the penis. Sperm are made in the testis, so that is the starting point.
Semen is sperm suspended in seminal fluid. Seminal fluid, made by the seminal vesicles and the prostate, gives the sperm a liquid to swim in and supplies an energy source.
Seminal fluid is slightly alkaline overall, which neutralises the acidity of the vagina and of any urine left in the urethra, because acid damages sperm.
Sperm make up only a small part of the volume of semen, because most of it is seminal fluid.
Sperm cannot be made at normal body temperature, so the testes hang outside the body. The scrotum is the sac that holds them and keeps them at the right temperature.

Scrotum: a sac of skin and muscle hanging outside the abdomen that holds the two testes. Muscles in it pull the testes closer to the body when it is cold, to keep them warm, and relax to let them hang lower when it is warm.
The scrotum keeps the testes about 2–3 °C below core body temperature (37 °C), which sperm production needs; this is why the testes are outside the body.
The testes are where sperm and testosterone are made. Inside, two different tissues do these two jobs.
Testes (singular testis): the two oval male gonads, which are the primary sex organs (the organs that make the gametes).
Each testis is packed with many long, tightly coiled seminiferous tubules, whose walls produce sperm by meiosis (cell division that halves the chromosome number), continuously from puberty.
The coiling packs a very long length of tubule, and so a large sperm-producing surface, into a small organ, because a long tube can fit in little space when coiled.

Between the seminiferous tubules are interstitial cells, which secrete testosterone into the blood; the testes are therefore also endocrine glands (glands that release hormones into the blood, so the hormone reaches the whole body).
Testosterone has roles in puberty, sperm production and the secondary sexual characteristics (the body changes that develop at puberty). There is more on this in Hormones in reproduction.
The testes form inside the abdomen of the foetus and normally descend into the scrotum before birth, which puts them in the cooler position sperm production needs.
A testis that has not descended cannot produce sperm normally, which is a known cause of male infertility.
Once made, sperm travel through a series of tubes. Each one has a different job: storage, transport and exit from the body.
Epididymis: a single, very long, tightly coiled tube lying against the back of each testis.
Sperm from the seminiferous tubules pass into the epididymis, where they are stored and mature, gaining the ability to swim. The coiling gives a long tube for storage in a small space.
Vas deferens (sperm duct; plural vasa deferentia): a muscular tube carrying sperm from the epididymis up into the abdomen and around the bladder, to join the urethra.
During ejaculation the smooth muscle of the vas deferens contracts in waves (peristalsis) to push sperm along, which is why the tube has a thick muscular wall.
The vas deferens is the tube that is cut and tied in a vasectomy, the male sterilisation operation, so that sperm can no longer reach the urethra.
Urethra: the tube running from the bladder through the length of the penis to the outside, so it is the final exit for both urine and semen.
In males the urethra carries both urine and semen, but never at the same time: during ejaculation a ring of muscle (sphincter) at the base of the bladder closes, so urine cannot mix with semen.
In females the urethra carries only urine and opens separately from the vagina. There is more on this in The female reproductive system.
Sperm need a liquid to swim in and an energy source. Two glands add fluids that supply these, so that sperm can swim and reach the egg.
Seminal vesicles: two glands behind the bladder whose ducts join the vasa deferentia.
The seminal vesicles secrete a thick, alkaline fluid rich in the sugar fructose; the sperm's mitochondria respire fructose to release energy for swimming.
This fluid makes up most of the volume of semen, so the seminal vesicles supply the bulk of the liquid sperm swim in.
Prostate gland: a single gland, about the size of a walnut, just below the bladder, surrounding the start of the urethra.
The prostate secretes a thin, milky fluid containing enzymes that keep the semen liquid after ejaculation, so the sperm can swim free.
The secretions of the seminal vesicles and the prostate together form seminal fluid, which is why seminal fluid as a whole is slightly alkaline.
Because the prostate surrounds the urethra, an enlarged prostate, common in older men, can press on the urethra and make urination difficult.
The penis delivers semen into the vagina and also lets urine out. Its tip and the skin covering it have their own roles.
Penis: the male organ that places semen in the vagina during intercourse, and through which urine and semen leave the body via the urethra.

The penis contains spongy erectile tissue. During sexual arousal its blood vessels widen and the spaces fill with blood under pressure, so the penis becomes larger, firm and erect, which allows it to enter the vagina.
Glans: the rounded, sensitive tip of the penis, with many nerve endings; stimulation of these leads to ejaculation.
The urethra opens at the tip of the glans, so semen and urine leave the body there.
Foreskin: a fold of loose skin that covers and protects the glans when the penis is not erect, and pulls back (retracts) during an erection.
The foreskin is removed in circumcision, an operation that leaves the glans uncovered.
Ejaculation: at the peak of sexual stimulation, waves of muscle contraction in the epididymis, vasa deferentia, glands and urethra expel semen from the penis.
The semen from one ejaculation (a few millilitres) contains many millions of sperm, so many sperm are available to reach the egg.
Exams ask you to draw and label this system, so it helps to know where each part sits in relation to the bladder.

Diagram: side view (longitudinal section) with the bladder for orientation. Label testis, scrotum, epididymis, vas deferens (sperm duct), seminal vesicle, prostate gland, urethra, penis, glans, foreskin, bladder. Draw the vas deferens running up from the epididymis and looping up and over the ureter behind the bladder to join the urethra just below the bladder.
Each point gives the part, where it is, what it does and how its structure suits that job. They run in the order of the sperm pathway.
Scrotum – holds the testes outside the abdomen – keeps them 2–3 °C below body temperature – muscles pull the testes closer to the body in cold conditions.

Testis – the sperm-producing organ, inside the scrotum – makes sperm in the coiled seminiferous tubules and testosterone in the interstitial cells – very long coiled tubules give a large surface in a small organ.
Epididymis – on the back of each testis – stores and matures sperm so they can swim – a single very long, coiled tube that stores a lot in a small space.
Vas deferens – from the epididymis, up into the abdomen and around the bladder to the urethra – carries sperm along the route – a muscular tube whose walls contract in peristalsis.
The pathway continues with the glands that add fluid, then the urethra and the penis, which delivers the semen.
Seminal vesicle – behind the bladder – adds a thick, alkaline, fructose-rich fluid that gives energy and makes up most of the semen – a gland whose ducts join the vasa deferentia.
Prostate – below the bladder, around the urethra – adds an enzyme-containing fluid that keeps semen liquid – a gland that surrounds the start of the urethra.
Urethra – from the bladder through the penis – carries semen and urine, never together – a sphincter closes the bladder during ejaculation.
Penis – outside the body – places semen in the vagina – erectile tissue fills with blood so it becomes firm enough to enter the vagina.
Glans – tip of the penis – detects stimulation and leads to ejaculation – many nerve endings in its sensitive tip, and the urethra opens there.
Foreskin – fold of skin over the glans – protects the glans and pulls back during an erection – loose skin that retracts.

The female reproductive system does more than make eggs: it also receives sperm, provides the place where an egg is fertilised, and then looks after the developing baby. Knowing the route an egg and sperm each take makes the position of every organ easier to remember.
The system produces eggs (ova; singular ovum), the female gametes (sex cells), and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone (chemical messengers carried in the blood).
It receives sperm during intercourse, is the site of fertilisation (the joining of egg and sperm), and holds, nourishes and protects the developing baby until birth.
Its organs lie in the lower abdomen (pelvis), where the pelvic bones protect them, except the external parts (the vulva).
Route of an egg: ovary → fallopian tube (where it may be fertilised) → uterus.
Route of sperm after intercourse: vagina → cervix → uterus → fallopian tube, so the two meet in the fallopian tube.
The vulva is the external female genitalia, the only part of the system you can see from outside the body. Its parts protect the openings to the inside and provide sexual sensation.

Vulva: the collective name for the external female genitals, including the labia, the clitoris and the openings of the urethra and the vagina, so it is the outer area while the vagina is the tube inside.
Labia: two pairs of folds of skin around the openings.
The outer labia (labia majora) are fleshier and covered with pubic hair after puberty; the inner labia (labia minora) are thinner.
The labia protect the openings of the vagina and urethra from infection and damage, because the folds close over them like a cover.
Clitoris: a small, very sensitive organ at the front of the vulva where the inner labia meet, with many nerve endings, which is why it is so sensitive.
The clitoris contains erectile tissue that fills with blood during arousal; its function is sexual pleasure. It develops in the embryo from the same tissue as the penis.
In females the urethra (the tube from the bladder) opens separately, in front of the vaginal opening, and carries urine only; it is not part of the reproductive system.
This is the main contrast with the male urethra, which carries semen as well as urine. There is more on this in The male reproductive system.

The vagina is the passage that links the outside of the body to the cervix. It has three jobs, receiving sperm, acting as the birth canal and letting menstrual blood out, and its structure suits each of them.
Vagina: a muscular, elastic tube about 7–10 cm long, leading from the vulva to the cervix.
The vagina receives the penis during intercourse; semen is deposited at its top, near the cervix.
The vagina is the birth canal, which stretches greatly during birth because its wall is muscular and elastic.
Menstrual blood leaves the body through the vagina, because it is the passage that runs from the cervix to the outside.

The vaginal lining is moist and kept acidic by harmless bacteria (lactobacilli), which helps prevent infection by pathogens (disease-causing microbes); this is an innate defence, one present from birth rather than learned. There is more on this in Innate and adaptive immunity.
The cervix is a narrow gateway between the vagina and the uterus. It controls what gets through, and it opens wide only when a baby is born.
Cervix: the narrow neck at the lower end of the uterus, opening into the top of the vagina through a small canal. It is part of the uterus, not part of the vagina.
Glands in the cervix make mucus. For most of the cycle the mucus is thick and blocks sperm and pathogens, so it keeps the uterus protected.
Around ovulation (release of the egg) the mucus becomes thin, clear and slippery, letting sperm pass towards the egg. There is more on this in The menstrual cycle.
During pregnancy a thick mucus plug seals the cervix, so the baby in the uterus stays protected from infection.
In labour the cervix widens (dilates) to about 10 cm to let the baby out.
Cells from the cervix are sampled in cervical screening, a test for early signs of cancer, because the cervix is easy to reach from the vagina.
The uterus is where a pregnancy develops. Its thick muscular wall does the pushing, while its lining, the endometrium, prepares each month to receive an embryo.
Uterus (womb): a hollow, pear-shaped organ, about the size of a fist when not pregnant, with a very thick wall of smooth muscle.
The embryo (the earliest stage of the developing baby) implants (attaches) in the uterus and the foetus develops there.
The muscular wall stretches enormously during pregnancy to hold the growing foetus and contracts powerfully to push the baby out in labour.
Endometrium: the inner lining of the uterus, rich in blood vessels and glands, which supply the embryo with nourishment.
Each month the endometrium thickens under the influence of ovarian hormones, ready to receive an embryo.
If no embryo implants, the outer layer of the endometrium breaks down and is shed with blood in menstruation (the monthly period). There is more on this in The menstrual cycle.
If an embryo implants, the endometrium stays and helps form the mother's part of the placenta (the organ that feeds the foetus).
Only the endometrium is shed in menstruation, not the muscular wall, which is the bulk of the uterus.
The fallopian tubes connect the ovaries to the uterus and are where the egg meets sperm. An egg cannot swim, so the tube has to move it along.
Fallopian tubes (oviducts): two narrow tubes, about 10 cm long, one from each side of the top of the uterus towards an ovary.
The open end near the ovary is funnel-shaped with finger-like projections that sweep the released egg into the tube.
Cilia (tiny hairs) lining the tube beat, and waves of muscle contraction (peristalsis) move the egg, or the early embryo, towards the uterus, because the egg cannot swim.
Fertilisation normally happens in the fallopian tube, because this is where the egg and the sperm travelling up from the uterus meet.
Ectopic pregnancy: if an embryo implants in the fallopian tube instead of the uterus, the tube cannot stretch to hold it and may rupture, which is a medical emergency.
A damaged tube, for example one scarred by infection, raises the risk of an ectopic pregnancy. There is more on this in Fertility control and infertility.
The ovaries are the organs that make eggs and the female sex hormones. They sit beside the uterus but are not attached to the tubes, which affects how the egg is collected.
Ovaries: two almond-sized organs, one on each side of the uterus, close to but not joined to the open end of each fallopian tube.
The ovaries contain follicles, each holding an immature egg. Usually one follicle matures and releases its egg each month, from puberty to menopause; this is ovulation.
The ovaries also secrete oestrogen and progesterone. There is more on this in Glands, locations and hormones.
Because the ovary is not attached to the tube, the egg must be swept in by the funnel.

Exams ask you to draw and label the system or to identify parts on a diagram. Practise two views: the front view shows the organs side by side, and the side view shows their position relative to the bladder and rectum.

Label ovary, fallopian tube (oviduct), uterus, endometrium, muscle wall of uterus, cervix, vagina.

Diagram: side view (longitudinal section) showing the uterus between the bladder in front and the rectum behind, with the vagina, cervix and external parts. Label the ovary, fallopian tube, uterus, endometrium, cervix, vagina, vulva, labia, clitoris, bladder and urethra.
Here is every part in turn, from outside to inside, in the form: where it is, what it does, and how its structure suits that job.
Vulva – external genitals – collective name for the external parts that protect the openings and give sexual sensation.
Labia – around the openings of the vagina and urethra – protect them from infection and damage – folds of skin, the outer pair fleshier.
Clitoris – front of the vulva where the inner labia meet – sexual pleasure – many nerve endings and erectile tissue.
Vagina – from the vulva to the cervix – receives the penis, is the birth canal, and carries menstrual blood – muscular, elastic and stretchy, with an acidic lining.
Cervix – neck of the uterus – controls entry of sperm and pathogens, and dilates in labour – mucus changes through the cycle and the canal is narrow.
Uterus – between the bladder and rectum – holds and nourishes the foetus – thick smooth muscle that stretches and contracts.
Endometrium – inner lining of the uterus – receives the embryo and is shed if there is no pregnancy – rich in blood vessels and glands, so it can nourish an embryo.
Fallopian tube – from the uterus towards each ovary – carries the egg to the uterus and is the site of fertilisation – funnel with finger-like projections, cilia and muscle.
Ovary – one on each side of the uterus, near the fallopian tube – produces eggs and oestrogen and progesterone – contains follicles, each holding an immature egg.
The male and female systems do matching jobs, making gametes and hormones, but they differ in where the gonads sit and how the urethra is used.
Gonads (organs that make gametes): testes in the male; ovaries in the female, so each system has its own gamete factory.
Gamete produced: sperm, made continuously from puberty in the male; one egg a month from puberty to menopause in the female. There is more on this in Gametes and fertilisation.
Main hormones: testosterone in the male; oestrogen and progesterone in the female. There is more on this in Hormones in reproduction.
Gonad position: the testes lie outside the body in the scrotum; the ovaries lie inside the pelvis.
Urethra: shared with the reproductive system in the male, carrying urine and semen; separate in the female, carrying urine only, so it is not a reproductive organ in females.

Gametes are the cells that carry genes from one generation to the next, and they are made by a special kind of cell division. Knowing where this division happens, and which cells do it, is the starting point for sperm and egg production.
A gamete is a haploid sex cell, meaning it has only one chromosome of each pair. In humans the haploid number is 23 (n = 23).

Sperm and eggs are made by meiosis (the cell division that halves the chromosome number), so each gamete carries one chromosome of each pair, and each gamete is genetically different from the others. There is more on this in Mitosis and meiosis.
At fertilisation two haploid gametes fuse to give a diploid zygote (the first cell of a new individual, with both chromosomes of each pair) with 46 chromosomes (2n = 46).
Meiosis happens only in the gonads (the organs that make gametes): in the seminiferous tubules (the coiled tubes inside the testes) for sperm, and in the ovaries for eggs.
The cells that undergo meiosis are diploid. Every other cell in the body divides by mitosis, which keeps the chromosome number the same.
Unlike eggs, sperm are made continuously, in huge numbers, from puberty onwards. The process happens in the testes and finishes in a storage tube beside them.
Sperm production begins at puberty and then continues every day throughout a man's life, though it declines in old age.

Many millions of sperm are made each day in the walls of the seminiferous tubules, from diploid cells that first multiply by mitosis (which keeps a supply of cells available) and then divide by meiosis.
Each cell that completes meiosis gives four sperm, all of equal size.
Half the sperm carry an X chromosome and half carry a Y, because the dividing cell has one X and one Y. There is more on this in Sex determination.
The new sperm move into the epididymis (a coiled tube on the back of each testis), where they are stored and mature, becoming able to swim.
It takes about two to three months for a sperm to be produced and matured, so a change in lifestyle or health affects sperm only after some weeks.
Production needs the lower temperature of the scrotum (the sac that holds the testes outside the body) and the hormones FSH and testosterone.
Egg production runs on a very different timetable from sperm production. A girl's eggs begin forming before she is born, and she never makes more.

Egg production starts before birth: while a girl is a foetus (an unborn baby), her ovaries form all the immature eggs she will ever have, each inside a follicle (a small fluid-filled sac of cells that nourishes the egg).
Each of these eggs begins meiosis but stops part-way.
A baby girl is born with about one to two million immature eggs. Most degenerate (break down), and only about 400–500 are ever released in her life.
No new eggs are made after birth, which is why the supply is fixed.
From puberty, usually one follicle each month develops fully and releases its egg at ovulation (the release of an egg from the ovary). The monthly cycle is dealt with in The menstrual cycle.
Meiosis continues around ovulation but is completed only if a sperm enters the egg, so an egg that is never fertilised never finishes meiosis.
Meiosis in the ovary does not split the cell evenly, and the eggs it makes are as old as the woman herself. Both facts matter for the early embryo and for fertility.
Division in egg production is unequal: almost all the cytoplasm goes to one cell, the egg, and the other products are tiny cells called polar bodies, which degenerate.
So one cell undergoing meiosis gives one egg, not four.
This unequal split gives the egg a large store of cytoplasm, food reserves and organelles (the small working structures inside a cell) to support the early embryo.

Because the eggs are as old as the woman, they age with her. In older women more eggs have errors in chromosome separation, which is why the risk of conditions such as Down syndrome rises with the mother's age. There is more on this in Mutations.
Fertility also falls with age because of these egg changes.
A sperm has one job, to carry the father's haploid nucleus to the egg. Every part of its structure helps it do that, so it is small, streamlined and powered for swimming.
A sperm is a very small, mobile cell, about 0.05 mm long.
The head contains the haploid nucleus (23 chromosomes) and, at its tip, the acrosome, a cap containing enzymes that digest a path through the layers around the egg.
The middle piece is packed with mitochondria that release energy (ATP) by aerobic respiration (respiration using oxygen) to power the tail.
The tail is a flagellum (a whip-like tail) that beats to make the sperm swim.
A sperm has very little cytoplasm, which keeps it small and streamlined for swimming.
Diagram: a sperm cell. Label the head, acrosome, nucleus, middle piece, mitochondria and tail.
The egg has a different job from the sperm. It cannot move, so its structure is built to supply and protect the new life once a sperm arrives.
The egg (ovum) is one of the largest cells in the body, about 0.1 mm across, just visible to the naked eye. It cannot move by itself.

It contains a haploid nucleus (23 chromosomes, always including an X), a cell membrane, and a large volume of cytoplasm holding food reserves and many mitochondria, which feed and power the early embryo.
Around the egg is a thick, clear, jelly-like coat called the zona pellucida, and outside that an outer layer of follicle cells.
Diagram: an egg, drawn much larger than the sperm. Label the nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, zona pellucida (jelly coat) and follicle cells.
Sperm and eggs are both haploid gametes, but their differences follow from their jobs: the sperm travels and delivers, and the egg stores food and waits. Compare them in pairs, one feature at a time.
Size: sperm are tiny, about 0.05 mm long, while the egg is far larger, about 0.1 mm across, with a far greater volume.
Movement: the sperm swims with its tail, but the egg cannot swim and is moved along the fallopian tube by cilia (tiny hair-like structures lining the tube).
Numbers: there are millions of sperm per ejaculation, but usually one egg a month.
Cytoplasm and food: sperm have almost none, but the egg is a large store.
Sex chromosome: a sperm carries an X or a Y, but the egg always carries an X.
Production: sperm are made continuously from puberty, four per meiosis, while eggs begin to form before birth, one per meiosis.

Fertilisation needs sperm and egg to meet in the right place at the right time. Only a tiny fraction of sperm survive the journey, and the timing is tight because both gametes live for a limited time.
During intercourse semen (the fluid containing the sperm) is ejaculated into the top of the vagina, near the cervix (the neck of the uterus).
Sperm swim through the cervical mucus, which is easiest to pass around ovulation when it is thin, then through the uterus and into the fallopian tubes, helped by contractions of the uterus.
Only a few hundred of the millions of sperm reach the egg. Most die in the acidic vagina, are blocked by mucus, or go into the tube with no egg.
Sperm can survive up to about five days in the female tract.
An egg survives only about 12–24 hours after ovulation.
So intercourse in the five days before ovulation, or on the day of ovulation, can lead to fertilisation, because live sperm and a live egg are then present together.
Fertilisation is more than a sperm touching an egg. It is the fusion of two nuclei, and it happens in a set order that stops more than one sperm getting in.
Fertilisation is the fusion of the haploid nucleus of a sperm with the haploid nucleus of an egg to form a diploid zygote.
In humans it normally takes place in the upper part of a fallopian tube, within a day of ovulation.
1. Sperm reach the egg and push between the follicle cells.
2. The acrosome of a sperm releases its enzymes, which digest a path through the zona pellucida. This is called the acrosome reaction.
3. The membrane of one sperm fuses with the egg's membrane, and the sperm's nucleus enters the egg. The tail is left outside, so the sperm's mitochondria stay out.
4. At once the egg's outer layer changes and the zona pellucida hardens, so no other sperm can enter. This ensures the zygote receives only one set of chromosomes from the father.
6. The sperm nucleus and egg nucleus fuse, giving a zygote with 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, one of each pair from each parent.
Fertilisation settles several things at once: the child's sex, where its mitochondria come from, and the start of a new genetically unique individual.

At fertilisation the sex of the child is decided by whether the sperm carries an X or a Y, because the egg always carries an X. The zygote receives its mitochondria from the egg only. There is more on this in Sex determination and in Nuclear and non-nuclear inheritance.
Fertilisation restores the diploid number, which would otherwise halve in every generation.
It combines genetic material from two parents, so the offspring is genetically unique. Together with meiosis, this is a source of variation.
Fertilisation starts the development of the embryo. The zygote begins to divide by mitosis as it moves down the tube. There is more on this in Pregnancy.

Diagram: a sequence showing a sperm entering an egg (the acrosome digesting the zona pellucida), the sperm nucleus inside the egg, and the two nuclei fusing to form the zygote. Label the sperm nucleus, egg nucleus, zona pellucida, zygote, n and 2n.
Twins can arise in two different ways, and the difference explains why some twins are genetically identical and others are not.
Identical twins come from one zygote that splits into two embryos early in development, so they have the same genes.
Non-identical (fraternal) twins come from two eggs released at the same time and fertilised by two different sperm, so they are no more alike genetically than other brothers and sisters.
Once a month, the female reproductive system gets ready for a possible pregnancy and, if none begins, starts over. This repeating pattern is the menstrual cycle.

The menstrual cycle is the series of changes in the ovary (where eggs are stored) and the uterus (the womb) that happens about once a month in a woman from puberty to menopause, except during pregnancy.
Its purpose is to release an egg and to prepare the endometrium (the lining of the uterus) to receive an embryo, so a fertilised egg has somewhere to implant and grow.
The cycle lasts about 28 days on average, but a cycle of about 21 to 35 days is normal, and its length varies between women and from month to month.
Day 1 is the first day of bleeding, so every day number in the cycle is counted from the start of a period.

Two sets of changes run side by side: the ovarian cycle, in which a follicle (a small fluid-filled sac holding an egg) develops, releases its egg and becomes the corpus luteum, and the uterine cycle, in which the endometrium is shed, rebuilt and thickened.
Hormones (chemical messengers carried in the blood) coordinate the two sets of changes, which is why the ovary and uterus stay in step with each other.
The first period (menarche) occurs during puberty, and the cycles end at the menopause. There is more on this in Hormones in reproduction.
The cycle starts with the period, the phase where the lining built up in the last cycle is lost. Counting from day 1, it is the first of the four phases.
Menstruation lasts about days 1–5 of a typical 28-day cycle, although the typical days given for each phase are only approximate.
If no egg was fertilised in the previous cycle, the thickened outer layer of the endometrium is no longer needed, so it breaks down and is shed through the cervix (the neck of the uterus) and vagina.
The shed lining leaves with a small amount of blood. This is a period, and the shedding lasts about 3–7 days.
After the old lining is lost, the body prepares a new egg and rebuilds the lining. This phase is named after the follicles in the ovary that grow during it.
The follicular phase runs from day 1 to about day 13, so it overlaps with menstruation.
In the ovary, several follicles start to develop, and usually one grows into a large, mature, fluid-filled follicle containing the egg, called a Graafian follicle.
In the uterus, after menstruation ends, the endometrium is repaired and grows thicker from about day 6, rebuilding the lining that was lost.
Near the end of this phase the cervical mucus (the fluid made at the cervix) becomes thin, clear and slippery, which lets sperm through.
Ovulation is the high point of the ovarian cycle: the mature egg leaves the ovary.

Ovulation happens at about day 14: the Graafian follicle bursts at the surface of the ovary and releases its egg, which is swept into the fallopian tube (the tube that carries the egg towards the uterus).

This is the most fertile time, because the egg survives only about 12–24 hours, so sperm must already be present or arrive within that short window. There is more on this in Gametes and fertilisation.
After the egg is released, the ovary and the uterus prepare for a possible embryo. What happens next depends on whether an embryo implants.
The luteal phase lasts about days 15–28. The empty follicle turns into a yellow mass of cells, the corpus luteum (Latin for “yellow body”).
The endometrium thickens further, becoming spongy, with more blood vessels and glands, so that it is ready for an embryo to implant (embed in the lining).
If no embryo implants, the corpus luteum breaks down after about 10–14 days and the endometrium is shed, so the next menstruation begins on day 1 of a new cycle.
If an embryo implants, the corpus luteum stays active, so the lining is kept and there is no period. There is more on this in Hormones in reproduction.
Not every woman ovulates on day 14. The timing depends on a fixed gap before the next period, not a fixed day number.
Ovulation happens about 14 days before the next period starts, because the luteal phase is fairly constant at about 14 days.
Differences in cycle length come mostly from the follicular phase, since that is the phase that varies in length.
So in a 35-day cycle ovulation is about day 21, not day 14, because 35 minus 14 gives day 21.
Here is each phase with its days, what the ovary is doing and what the endometrium is doing, for a typical 28-day cycle.
Menstruation: days 1–5; ovary: the corpus luteum of the last cycle has broken down; endometrium: shed.
Follicular phase: days 1–13; ovary: a follicle develops into the Graafian follicle; endometrium: repaired and growing thicker from about day 6.
Ovulation: about day 14; ovary: the Graafian follicle bursts and releases the egg; endometrium: at the thickness built up in the follicular phase.
Luteal phase: days 15–28; ovary: the corpus luteum forms and then breaks down if there is no pregnancy; endometrium: thickens further, becoming spongy, and is shed if no embryo implants.
A timeline puts the ovary and the uterus side by side, so you can see how the two cycles line up day by day.

Diagram: a timeline, day 0 to day 28. Above: the ovary (follicle growing, Graafian follicle, ovulation at day 14, corpus luteum forming then breaking down). Below: endometrium thickness (shed days 1–5, thickening to day 28). Label the four phases along the timeline.
Four hormones coordinate the cycle. Knowing which organ makes each one is the key to explaining the rest of this topic.

FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) and LH (luteinising hormone) are made by the pituitary gland (a small gland at the base of the brain). Oestrogen is made mainly by the developing follicle, and in smaller amounts by the corpus luteum. Progesterone is made by the corpus luteum.
The cycle restarts when progesterone falls, and the follicular phase is then driven by FSH and oestrogen. Each hormone's level explains what happens in the ovary and uterus.
Menstruation: oestrogen and progesterone are both low, because the corpus luteum of the last cycle has broken down.
The fall in progesterone is what causes the endometrium to break down. Low oestrogen alone is not the cause.
Low progesterone no longer holds back the pituitary, so FSH begins to rise.
Follicular phase: FSH stimulates follicles to develop, and one becomes the Graafian follicle. The growing follicle secretes oestrogen, so oestrogen rises steadily.
Oestrogen repairs and thickens the endometrium and makes the cervical mucus thin.
Rising oestrogen at first inhibits (holds back) FSH, so FSH falls back and usually only one follicle completes development.
Ovulation is triggered by a sudden surge of LH, which is itself set off by high oestrogen.
When oestrogen reaches a high peak (around day 12–13), it stimulates the pituitary to release a large surge of LH, with a smaller rise in FSH.
The LH surge causes the Graafian follicle to burst and release its egg about a day later (ovulation, about day 14).
After ovulation the corpus luteum takes over, and progesterone rises. Whether the cycle ends or a pregnancy continues depends on whether the corpus luteum survives.
Luteal phase: LH causes the empty Graafian follicle to develop into the corpus luteum.
The corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and some oestrogen), so progesterone rises to a peak around day 21.
Progesterone maintains and further thickens the endometrium, making it ready for implantation, and makes the cervical mucus thick again.
High progesterone, with oestrogen, inhibits FSH and LH, so no new follicle develops and no further egg is released while the corpus luteum is active. FSH and LH stay low.
End of the cycle: without pregnancy, low LH means the corpus luteum is no longer maintained. It breaks down after about 10–14 days, so progesterone and oestrogen fall.
The endometrium can no longer be maintained and is shed (menstruation). The fall removes the inhibition of FSH, which rises and starts a new cycle.
If an embryo implants, a hormone from the embryo keeps the corpus luteum alive, so progesterone stays high and menstruation does not happen. There is more on this in Hormones in reproduction.
This summary gives the level of each hormone in each phase, with the state of the ovary.
Menstruation: FSH rising, LH low, oestrogen low, progesterone low; a new follicle begins to grow.
Follicular phase: FSH high then falling, LH low, oestrogen rising, progesterone low; a follicle grows to the Graafian follicle.
Ovulation: LH surge, a small FSH peak, oestrogen at its peak then falling, progesterone low; the Graafian follicle bursts.
Luteal phase: FSH and LH low, progesterone high with a peak about day 21, oestrogen at a moderate second, smaller peak, both falling at the end; the corpus luteum active, then breaking down.
The ovary and the pituitary signal each other in a loop, and that feedback is what keeps the cycle going from one month to the next.
The cycle is controlled by feedback, meaning each hormone's level changes the release of the next.

Negative feedback: progesterone, and moderate oestrogen, inhibits the pituitary's release of FSH and LH. This keeps FSH and LH low in the luteal phase, and their fall lets the corpus luteum break down. There is more on negative feedback in Homeostasis as a stimulus-response model.
Positive feedback: high oestrogen just before ovulation causes more LH to be released, giving the LH surge.

Each hormone controls the next: FSH → follicle grows → oestrogen → LH surge → ovulation and corpus luteum → progesterone → FSH and LH inhibited → corpus luteum breaks down → progesterone falls → menstruation and FSH rises.
Technology link: home ovulation test kits detect the LH surge in urine, showing that ovulation is likely within about a day or two.
Technology link: the combined contraceptive pill gives steady oestrogen and progesterone, which by negative feedback keep FSH and LH low, so no follicle matures and no LH surge occurs.
Diagram: this sequence as a loop (a flow chart) linking the pituitary, the ovary and the endometrium, with “+” on the oestrogen-to-LH arrow and “−” on the progesterone-to-FSH/LH arrow.
Exams show graphs of the four hormones across a 28-day cycle. You need to recognise each curve and explain every change by its cause.
How to read the standard graphs of a 28-day cycle: FSH has a rise early in the cycle and a small peak at day 14.
LH is low except for a sharp, tall peak just before day 14.
Oestrogen rises through the follicular phase to a peak just before the LH surge, drops after ovulation, then has a lower second rise in the luteal phase.
Progesterone is low until ovulation, rises to a peak around day 21, then falls to day 28.
Exam answers explain each change by its cause, for example: progesterone rises after day 14 because the corpus luteum secretes it.

Diagram: two graphs on one 28-day time axis, one for FSH and LH (pituitary), one for oestrogen and progesterone (ovarian), lined up with the ovary events and endometrium thickness from the timeline. Label the LH surge, oestrogen peak, progesterone peak and ovulation.
