Pregnancy starts with a single fertilised cell and, within about a week, a ball of cells that must attach itself to the wall of the uterus. The journey and the attachment (implantation) happen in a set order and in set places.

Fertilisation takes place in the fallopian tube (the tube that carries the egg from the ovary towards the uterus) and gives a diploid zygote (a cell with a full set of chromosomes), the first cell of the new individual. There is more on this in Gametes and fertilisation.
The zygote divides repeatedly by mitosis (division that makes identical cells) as cilia (tiny moving hairs lining the tube) and muscle contractions of the tube wall carry it along towards the uterus.
The cells do not grow between divisions, so they become smaller with each division and the ball stays about the size of the egg.
After about five days the ball reaches the uterus, the muscular organ in which the baby will develop, as a small ball of cells.

Implantation: about 6–7 days after fertilisation the ball of cells sinks into the thick, spongy endometrium (the lining of the uterus) and embeds itself there, with enzymes from its outer cells digesting a way in. From implantation the woman is pregnant.
Once the ball of cells is embedded, the endometrium has to stay in place, or it would be shed in a period and the pregnancy would be lost. A hormone from the embryo makes sure it stays.
Implantation needs an endometrium kept thick by progesterone, a hormone made by the corpus luteum (the structure left in the ovary after the egg is released).
After implantation, a hormone from the embryo keeps the corpus luteum alive, so the endometrium is kept and menstruation (the monthly period) stops.
A missed period is often the first sign of pregnancy, and pregnancy tests work by detecting this hormone, hCG, in urine. There is more on this in Hormones in reproduction.
If the ball of cells implants in the fallopian tube instead of the uterus, it is an ectopic pregnancy.

Soon after implantation the embryo needs a way to get food and oxygen from its mother and to get rid of its wastes. The placenta is the organ that does this, and it is built jointly by the embryo and the mother.
After implantation, the outer cells of the embryo grow many finger-like projections (villi) into the endometrium.
The villi, together with the mother's endometrium and the blood spaces around them, form the placenta, a disc-shaped organ attached to the wall of the uterus.
The placenta is therefore made by both the embryo (the villi) and the mother (the endometrium).
The placenta is fully formed by about the end of the third month (12 weeks) and keeps growing until birth.
The foetus (the developing baby) floats in the uterus, away from the placenta. The umbilical cord is the link between them, and it carries blood in two directions.
The umbilical cord connects the foetus to the placenta.
The cord contains two umbilical arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood (blood low in oxygen) with wastes from the foetus to the placenta.
The cord contains one umbilical vein, which carries oxygenated blood with nutrients from the placenta to the foetus.

The vein carries oxygenated blood, the reverse of the adult pattern for most arteries and veins, because arteries are defined by carrying blood away from the heart and veins by carrying it towards the heart. There is more on this in Circulation.

Mother and foetus swap materials at the placenta, but their blood never meets. Everything that is exchanged has to cross a very thin barrier, and the placenta's structure is built to make that crossing quick.
The mother's and the foetus's blood do not mix. They are separated by a thin barrier of the villi, only a few cells thick.
This barrier protects the foetus from the mother's high blood pressure and from her immune cells, and it matters because their blood groups may differ. There is more on this in Blood.
The villi give a very large surface area, and the barrier is very thin, so the distance for diffusion is short.

The foetus's capillaries (tiny blood vessels) in the villi lie close to pools of the mother's blood, and blood flows on both sides, which keeps the concentration gradients high so diffusion carries on.
Substances cross by diffusion (movement from high to low concentration), and some, such as glucose and amino acids, cross by facilitated diffusion or active transport.
Before birth the foetus's own lungs, gut and kidneys cannot do their jobs, so the placenta does them. It also protects and controls the pregnancy.
It supplies oxygen, glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins, minerals and water to the foetus, so it acts as the foetus's lungs and gut.
It removes carbon dioxide and urea, which pass into the mother's blood to be excreted by her lungs and kidneys, so it acts as the foetus's kidneys.

It passes antibodies from mother to foetus, giving passive natural immunity (protection received ready-made, not made by the baby's own body) for the first months after birth. There is more on this in Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment.
It secretes hormones, taking over the production of progesterone and oestrogen from the corpus luteum.
It forms a barrier to many pathogens (disease-causing organisms) and to the mother's blood cells.

The placenta is a barrier to many things, but not to everything. Some harmful substances in the mother's blood can cross to the foetus, which is why what a mother drinks, smokes, takes or catches matters.
Alcohol crosses and can cause foetal alcohol spectrum disorder, with damage to the brain and growth.
Nicotine and carbon monoxide from smoking reduce the oxygen supply to the foetus, and are linked to low birth weight and premature birth.
Many drugs, legal and illegal, cross the placenta; the thalidomide case is a well-known example. There is more on this in Science, scientists and society.
Some viruses cross the placenta. Rubella (German measles) can cause deafness, blindness and heart defects if caught in early pregnancy, and HIV can also cross.
This is why antenatal advice (advice given to women during pregnancy) matters.
The foetus also needs protection from knocks and from drying out or overheating. A fluid-filled sac around it provides that.
The amnion is a thin membrane that forms a fluid-filled sac, the amniotic sac, around the embryo.
Amniotic fluid cushions the foetus against shocks, keeps its temperature steady, lets it move and so develop its muscles and bones, and prevents it sticking to the membranes.
Foetal cells in the fluid can be sampled for testing by amniocentesis. There is more on this in Prenatal and postnatal care.
A labelled drawing of the foetus in the uterus pulls together the placenta, cord and amnion in one picture.

Diagram: a foetus in the uterus, showing the uterus wall and endometrium, the placenta attached to the uterus wall, the umbilical cord with its two arteries and one vein, the amnion and amniotic fluid, and the cervix with its mucus plug. Label each.
Over about nine months one cell becomes a baby with every tissue and organ. This follows a timetable, and the early weeks are the most delicate.

The baby develops by repeated mitosis (increasing cell number), cell growth, and cell differentiation (cells becoming specialised for different jobs), so that one zygote gives rise to all the tissues and organs.

Length of pregnancy (gestation): about 38 weeks from fertilisation, which in practice is counted as about 40 weeks from the first day of the woman's last period, because the date of fertilisation is not known.
The pregnancy is divided into three trimesters of about three months each.
In the first two months all the main organs form, and the heart begins beating by the end of the first month.
By about 12 weeks the baby is recognisably human with all organs present, though tiny.
During the rest of pregnancy the organs grow and mature, the baby moves (felt by the mother from about 16–20 weeks), and fat is laid down under the skin in the last weeks.
The lungs are among the last organs to mature, which is why babies born very early have difficulty breathing. There is more on this in Prenatal and postnatal care.
The first two months are when the baby is most at risk from harmful substances, because that is when the organs are forming; damage then can cause structural birth defects.
The ball of cells on its way to the uterus passes through two named stages. The names describe what the ball looks like at each point.
Zygote: the single diploid cell formed at fertilisation.

Morula: after about 3–4 days of division the zygote has become a solid ball of about 16 or more cells, still inside the zona pellucida (the protective coat around the egg), looking like a mulberry, which is the meaning of "morula".
The morula is still in the fallopian tube or just entering the uterus.
Blastocyst: by about day 5 the cells have rearranged into a hollow ball with a fluid-filled cavity.

The blastocyst has two parts: an outer layer of cells, the trophoblast, which will form the embryo's part of the placenta and its membranes; and a small cluster inside, the inner cell mass, which will form the embryo itself.
The blastocyst hatches out of the zona pellucida and is the stage that implants, trophoblast first.

The cells of the inner cell mass can develop into any type of body cell, which is why they are embryonic stem cells. Their use and the ethical questions they raise are in Ethics of genetic technologies.

Diagram: the sequence zygote → 2 cells → 4 cells → morula → blastocyst; the blastocyst in section (trophoblast, inner cell mass, fluid-filled cavity); and a side view of tube and uterus marking fertilisation, morula (both in the tube) and blastocyst implanting in the endometrium.
Soon after implantation the cells of the embryo sort themselves into three layers. Each layer goes on to form a particular set of tissues and organs.

Germ layers: during the third week after fertilisation the cells of the inner cell mass move and arrange themselves into three layers, the germ layers, each of which gives rise to particular tissues and organs.
Ectoderm (outer layer) forms the epidermis of the skin, hair and nails, the whole nervous system (brain, spinal cord and nerves), and parts of the eye.
Mesoderm (middle layer) forms muscles, bones and cartilage, the heart, blood and blood vessels, the kidneys and the reproductive organs.
Endoderm (inner layer) forms the lining of the digestive system and of the breathing system (trachea, bronchi and lungs), and the liver and pancreas.
Memory aid: ecto = outer skin and nerves; meso = movement, blood and support; endo = inner linings.
From implantation to birth the developing baby has two names. The boundary between them is when the organs have finished forming.
Embryo: the developing individual from implantation, about the second week after fertilisation, until the end of the eighth week, during which all the main organs form (organ formation).
By the end of week 8 the embryo is about 3 cm long and has all its major organs.
Foetus: from the ninth week until birth. No new organs form, but the existing ones grow, mature and begin to work.
The distinction: embryo means organs forming; foetus means organs present and growing.

Summary sequence: zygote (day 0, fallopian tube) → morula (days 3–4) → blastocyst (about day 5; implants about days 6–7) → germ layers form (week 3) → embryo (to the end of week 8; organs form) → foetus (week 9 to birth; growth and maturation).
Labour is the end of pregnancy. It starts when the uterus, which has held the baby for about nine months, begins to push it out.
Labour is the process by which the baby, then the placenta, is pushed out of the uterus.
Labour usually begins at about 40 weeks of pregnancy, when the baby is normally head down.

Hormonal changes start it, and the hormone oxytocin drives the contractions (tightening of the uterus muscle) by positive feedback (a change that leads to more of the same change). There is more on this in Hormones in reproduction.
The first stage prepares the way out. The cervix (the narrow neck at the bottom of the uterus), which stayed closed during pregnancy, has to open wide enough for the baby's head.
The muscle of the uterus wall begins to contract regularly, and the contractions become stronger and more frequent.
The contractions pull the cervix open until it is fully dilated, about 10 cm wide.
The mucus plug (the plug of mucus that sealed the cervix) comes away, and the amnion usually bursts, releasing the amniotic fluid; this is what is meant by "the waters break".
Stage 1 is the longest stage, often many hours in a first birth.
In the second stage the baby is pushed out through the birth canal. As soon as it is born it must switch from relying on the placenta to doing things for itself.

Strong contractions of the uterus, helped by the mother pushing with her abdominal muscles, push the baby, usually head first, out through the cervix and the vagina, the birth canal. This stage is also called expulsion.
The umbilical cord is then clamped and cut; the stump later dries and falls off, leaving the navel.
At birth the baby must start breathing for itself: the first breaths inflate the lungs, and its circulation changes so that blood goes to the lungs for oxygen instead of relying on the placenta.
Labour is not over when the baby is born: the placenta still has to come out. Sometimes a vaginal birth is not safe, and the baby is delivered by surgery instead.
Shortly after the birth, further contractions separate the placenta and membranes from the uterus wall and push them out; this is the afterbirth.
Contraction of the uterus also closes the blood vessels where the placenta was attached, which limits bleeding.

A Caesarean section is the delivery of the baby through a surgical cut in the abdomen and uterus, used when a vaginal birth would be unsafe for the mother or baby, for example a baby lying the wrong way, or a placenta blocking the cervix.
Reproduction is run by chemical messengers (hormones) carried in the blood. Three places make nearly all of them, and in pregnancy a fourth organ joins in.

Reproduction is controlled by hormones from three places: the pituitary gland at the base of the brain, the testes (the male gonads, which make sperm) and the ovaries (the female gonads, which make eggs).
The pituitary gland makes oxytocin and prolactin, and also the hormones that stimulate the gonads, which is how the brain controls the testes and ovaries.
The testes make testosterone, and the ovaries make oestrogen and progesterone. In pregnancy the placenta (the organ that links mother and foetus) also makes oestrogen and progesterone.
Prolactin is made by the pituitary gland, and its main role is to stimulate milk production in the breasts. There is more on where each gland sits in Glands, locations and hormones.
Puberty is the changeover from child to adult body. A hormone signal from the brain switches the reproductive system on.

Puberty is the stage, usually in the early teens, when the reproductive organs mature and become able to produce gametes (sperm or eggs), and the secondary sexual characteristics develop. These are the body changes, apart from the reproductive organs themselves, that mark a person as male or female.
Puberty typically begins between about 8 and 13 in girls, and between about 9 and 14 in boys.

It begins when the brain signals the pituitary to increase its release of the hormones that stimulate the gonads (the testes and ovaries). There is more on these pituitary hormones in the Higher Level block on the gonad-stimulating hormones.
As a result the testes begin to make much more testosterone, and the ovaries much more oestrogen. It is these sex hormones that cause the changes of puberty.
Testosterone at puberty starts sperm production, causes growth of the penis and testes, and causes the male secondary sexual characteristics. It also increases sex drive.
Oestrogen at puberty causes growth of the uterus (womb) and vagina, preparing the body for pregnancy, and the female secondary sexual characteristics.
Oestrogen, working with progesterone, starts the menstrual cycles, so a girl becomes able to ovulate and conceive; the first period is called menarche.
Once puberty has started the gametes, hormones keep them coming. The pattern differs between the sexes: continuous in men, monthly in women.

Testosterone is needed throughout adult life for sperm production in the seminiferous tubules (the coiled tubes inside the testes where sperm are made), and to maintain the male reproductive organs and secondary sexual characteristics.
Testosterone is made by the interstitial cells between the tubules, not by the tubules themselves, which make sperm.
Its level stays fairly steady from day to day, so sperm are made continuously rather than in a cycle, which is why men stay fertile from day to day.

Egg production: each month hormones cause one follicle (a fluid-filled sac holding a developing egg) to mature and release its egg, and prepare the endometrium (the lining of the uterus). There is more on the hormone levels and feedback in The menstrual cycle.
After fertilisation the embryo has to bury itself in the uterus lining (implantation) and the lining must then be kept, not shed. Two hormones make this possible.

Progesterone prepares the endometrium for implantation: it keeps it thick, spongy and well supplied with blood vessels, and makes its glands secrete nutrients for the early embryo before the placenta forms.
Without high progesterone, implantation cannot succeed, because the embryo would have no suitable lining to attach to or feed from.
hCG (human chorionic gonadotrophin) is a hormone made by the outer cells of the embryo from implantation.

hCG keeps the corpus luteum (the structure left in the ovary after ovulation) alive and secreting progesterone, so the endometrium is not shed and menstruation stops. Home pregnancy tests detect hCG in urine, using a monoclonal-antibody test.
The corpus luteum cannot support a whole pregnancy, so the placenta takes over hormone production. Progesterone from it then keeps the pregnancy going in several ways.
From about the end of the third month the placenta takes over from the corpus luteum, making large amounts of progesterone and oestrogen for the rest of pregnancy; the corpus luteum then breaks down.
Progesterone during pregnancy maintains the endometrium and so the placenta, which is attached to it.
Progesterone keeps the muscle of the uterus relaxed, so it does not contract and expel the foetus early.
Progesterone keeps the cervical mucus plug (the mucus that seals the cervix, the neck of the uterus) thick, and prepares the milk-producing glands of the breasts.
Progesterone, with oestrogen, prevents further ovulation and menstruation during pregnancy.
Oestrogen supports the growth of the foetus by building up the mother's tissues, and late in pregnancy it prepares her body for birth.

Oestrogen during pregnancy drives the growth of the foetus: it stimulates growth of the muscle of the uterus so it enlarges with the growing foetus, and increases blood flow to the uterus and placenta, which supplies the foetus.
Oestrogen also develops the milk ducts of the breasts, so they are ready to carry milk after birth.
Late in pregnancy oestrogen makes the uterus muscle more sensitive to oxytocin, preparing it for labour.
Level summary: progesterone and oestrogen rise steadily to very high levels by late pregnancy, far above their levels in the menstrual cycle, and fall sharply after the placenta is delivered.
Birth needs the powerful uterus muscle to contract strongly. A shift in hormone balance and the hormone oxytocin make this happen.
Near the end of pregnancy the balance of hormones changes: oestrogen's effects increase relative to progesterone's, so the uterus muscle becomes more responsive to oxytocin and begins to contract.
Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus (a part of the brain just above the pituitary) and released by the pituitary into the blood.
Oxytocin causes the muscle of the uterus to contract strongly in labour, the process of giving birth.
Labour speeds itself up. Each contraction causes more oxytocin, which causes stronger contractions, a pattern called positive feedback, where a change leads to more of the same change.
1. The baby's head presses on and stretches the cervix.
2. Stretch receptors in the cervix send nerve impulses to the brain.
4. Stronger contractions push the head harder against the cervix, stretching it more.
5. The cycle repeats, building up until the baby is born, which removes the stimulus (the stretching), so the loop stops.
A nervous pathway (the impulses) and a hormonal pathway (oxytocin in the blood) work together here. There is more on this in Nervous vs hormonal coordination.

Diagram: the positive feedback loop as a cycle: baby's head stretches cervix → nerve impulses to brain → pituitary releases oxytocin → uterus contracts more strongly → back to the start; birth ends the loop.
Oxytocin's work does not stop when the baby arrives. It also helps the uterus recover, and doctors use a man-made version of it.
After the birth, oxytocin keeps the uterus contracting, which expels the placenta and closes the blood vessels at its attachment site, reducing bleeding.
Oxytocin also helps the uterus shrink back towards its normal size, because its contractions squeeze the muscle smaller.
Synthetic oxytocin is given by drip in hospital to start (induce) or speed up labour, and to reduce bleeding after birth.
The breasts are prepared during pregnancy, but milk only starts once the placenta has gone. The hormone that actually makes milk is prolactin.
During pregnancy, oestrogen and progesterone develop the breasts' ducts and milk glands, and prolactin rises.
The high levels of oestrogen and progesterone stop milk being produced, even though prolactin is already rising.
When the placenta is delivered, oestrogen and progesterone fall sharply, so prolactin can act and milk production begins.
Prolactin stimulates the milk glands to produce milk, which is why it is called the milk-making hormone.
Suckling by the baby stimulates nerve endings in the nipple, causing the pituitary to release more prolactin, so the more the baby feeds, the more milk is made: supply matches demand.

While a mother breastfeeds frequently, high prolactin suppresses ovulation, so periods often do not return for some months; this is not reliable contraception. There is more on this in Fertility control and infertility.
Making milk is not the same as delivering it. Oxytocin does the second job, so a feed needs both hormones.
Oxytocin causes the milk to be released (called let-down, or milk ejection).
Suckling triggers oxytocin release, which makes muscle cells around the milk glands contract and squeeze milk into the ducts and out of the nipple.
Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin releases it.
The first milk a baby gets is different from the milk that follows. It is tuned to protect a newborn rather than to fatten it.
Colostrum is the first milk, produced for the first few days after birth.
Colostrum is a small volume of thick, yellowish fluid, richer in protein and antibodies than later milk and lower in fat and sugar.

Its antibodies give the newborn passive immunity, which means protection made by the mother rather than by the baby's own immune system. There is more on this in Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment.
Over the following days and weeks it changes to mature milk, with more fat and lactose (milk sugar) for energy and growth.
A woman's fertility does not last for life. Menopause is the point where the ovaries stop responding, and the fall in hormones has effects across the body.
Menopause is the end of a woman's menstrual cycles and of her fertility, confirmed when she has had no period for 12 months.
It usually happens between about 45 and 55 years of age.

Cause: the ovaries run out of follicles that can respond, so ovulation stops and the ovaries make much less oestrogen and progesterone. It is not simply that the eggs are used up by ovulation, because most follicles degenerate without ever ovulating.
Without these hormones the endometrium is no longer built up, so there is nothing to shed and periods stop.
Effects of falling oestrogen in the short term: hot flushes and night sweats, mood changes and poorer sleep, and vaginal dryness.
Effects of falling oestrogen in the longer term: loss of bone density, raising the risk of osteoporosis (brittle bones), and a rise in the risk of heart disease.
Men have no equivalent of the menopause: testosterone falls only slowly with age, and many men can produce sperm into old age, although sperm numbers and quality decline.
There is more on hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in Hormonal manipulation.
One bullet per hormone: its gland, its roles and how its level changes through life.
Testosterone (testes; small amounts also in females): male development before birth, puberty, sperm production and sex drive. There is more on development before birth in Sex determination.
Testosterone level: low in childhood, rises sharply at puberty, high and fairly steady in adult men, and declines slowly in later life.

Oestrogen (ovaries; placenta in pregnancy): female puberty, repair and thickening of the endometrium each cycle, growth of the uterus and breast ducts in pregnancy, preparing the uterus for oxytocin, and keeping bones strong.
Oestrogen level: low in childhood, rises at puberty, rises and falls each cycle, very high in pregnancy, and falls at menopause.
Progesterone (corpus luteum; placenta in pregnancy): maintains the endometrium for implantation and pregnancy, relaxes the uterus muscle, prepares the milk glands and prevents ovulation in pregnancy.
Progesterone level: high only in the second half of each cycle; very high in pregnancy; falls sharply at birth; very low after menopause.
Oxytocin (made in the hypothalamus, released by the pituitary): contractions of the uterus in labour and after birth, and milk let-down. Its level rises sharply during labour and with each feed.
Prolactin (pituitary): milk production. Its level rises during pregnancy, stays high while breastfeeding, rising further with each feed, and falls when breastfeeding stops.
FSH and LH are the two pituitary hormones that stimulate the gonads. In males they hold testosterone steady through negative feedback, and in females they drive the monthly cycle.
At puberty the hypothalamus, the part of the brain above the pituitary, signals the pituitary to increase its release of FSH and LH.
In males these hormones stimulate the testes to make sperm and testosterone; in females they stimulate follicles to develop and the ovaries to make oestrogen, starting the cycles.
In males, FSH stimulates sperm production in the seminiferous tubules, working with testosterone, so without FSH sperm output falls.
In males, LH (sometimes called interstitial-cell-stimulating hormone in males) stimulates the interstitial cells of the testes to secrete testosterone.
Male negative feedback: when testosterone in the blood rises, it inhibits the release of LH and FSH from the pituitary, so less testosterone is made; when testosterone falls, LH rises again.
This keeps testosterone and sperm production steady and continuous, unlike the female cycle.

Example: men who take anabolic steroids (synthetic testosterone) have high testosterone-like levels, which switch off their own LH and FSH, so their testes shrink and sperm production falls. There is more on this in Hormonal manipulation.
In females, FSH stimulates follicle development and oestrogen production, and the LH surge causes ovulation and forms the corpus luteum.
FSH and LH levels follow the state of the ovaries and the other hormones. When oestrogen and progesterone are high they stay low, and when these hormones are lost they rise.
In pregnancy, high progesterone and oestrogen keep FSH and LH low, so no follicles develop and no ovulation happens.
While breastfeeding, high prolactin also suppresses FSH and LH.
After the menopause, FSH and LH rise to high levels, because the ovaries no longer make enough oestrogen and progesterone to inhibit them; a high FSH level in the blood is a sign of the menopause.
Levels summary: FSH and LH are low in childhood and rise at puberty.
In men FSH and LH are fairly steady; in women they vary through each cycle, with an LH surge at ovulation.
In women FSH and LH are low in pregnancy and while breastfeeding, and high after the menopause. The levels and feedback through the month are in The menstrual cycle.
A model shows how a control centre, a hormone, a target organ and feedback fit together. You can then use it to predict what happens when one part changes.

A model of hormonal control shows, in order: the control centre (hypothalamus and pituitary), the hormone released, the target organ, the hormone or effect the target produces, and the feedback, with − for inhibition and + for stimulation.
Use the model to predict effects: blocking testosterone's feedback raises LH; giving steady oestrogen and progesterone, as in the pill, keeps FSH and LH low.
Diagram: two flow charts side by side, male then female. Male: hypothalamus → pituitary → FSH and LH → testes → sperm and testosterone, with a “−” arrow from testosterone back to the pituitary.

Female flow chart: hypothalamus → pituitary → FSH and LH → ovary → follicle, oestrogen, corpus luteum, progesterone → endometrium, with “−” arrows from progesterone (and oestrogen) to the pituitary and a “+” arrow from high oestrogen to the LH surge.

Pregnancy and the first weeks of a baby's life are when many problems can start, and when many can be caught and treated. Health services therefore care for the mother and baby both before and after the birth.
Prenatal (antenatal) care is the health care of a pregnant woman and her developing baby before birth, so it covers the whole of pregnancy.
Postnatal care is the care of the mother and baby after birth, usually for the first six weeks.
Its aims are to keep mother and baby healthy, to find problems early, when they can be treated or managed, and to give the parents information to make decisions.
Care in pregnancy and after birth uses two kinds of test that are easy to mix up. Screening sorts people into higher and lower risk, while diagnosis gives the answer for one person.
A screening test is offered to everyone in a group, such as all pregnant women or all newborns, to find those at higher risk of a condition.
A screening test is quick, cheap and safe, but it is not certain, so it can only say that a condition is more or less likely.
A diagnostic test confirms whether a person actually has the condition; it is more accurate and may carry some risk.
A positive screening result leads to a diagnostic test, because the screen only raises a suspicion that must then be confirmed.
The same distinction is used for cancer. There is more on this in Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer.
At the first visit early in pregnancy, called the booking visit, the mother's blood is tested. The results show what she needs for a safe pregnancy and what could affect the baby.

The mother's blood is tested for her blood group and Rhesus factor. A Rhesus-negative mother carrying a Rhesus-positive baby may be given anti-D injections to protect this and later babies. There is more on this in Blood.
Haemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying pigment in red blood cells) is tested to detect anaemia, which is common in pregnancy and is treated with iron.
Immunity to rubella is checked at booking, because rubella infection in pregnancy can harm the baby.
Infections that can pass to the baby are tested for, including HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis, so that treatment can greatly reduce the chance of passing them on.
Two simple measurements are repeated at every antenatal visit, because some serious pregnancy conditions develop gradually and show up first in blood pressure or in the urine.
At every visit her blood pressure is measured and her urine tested.

High blood pressure with protein in the urine is a sign of pre-eclampsia, a condition in pregnancy that can be dangerous to mother and baby. She is monitored closely and the baby may be delivered early.
Glucose in the urine, or a raised blood glucose in a glucose tolerance test, may show gestational diabetes, which is diabetes that develops in pregnancy.
Gestational diabetes can make the baby grow too large. It is managed by diet and, if needed, insulin.
Much of antenatal care is advice, because what the mother eats, drinks, takes and catches can reach the baby. Following it prevents harm rather than treating it afterwards.

Take folic acid, a B vitamin, daily from before conception until the 12th week, which reduces the risk of neural tube defects (faults in the developing spine and brain) such as spina bifida. There is more on this in Vitamins.
Do not smoke or drink alcohol, eat a balanced diet, and take medicines only on medical advice, because some substances cross the placenta to the baby.
Avoid foods that may carry harmful microorganisms, for example unpasteurised cheese and pâté, which can carry Listeria bacteria.
Avoid undercooked meat, which can carry Toxoplasma, a parasite that can infect the baby.
A mother can be vaccinated during pregnancy to protect herself and, through the placenta, her newborn baby, who is too young to be vaccinated yet.
The flu vaccine and the whooping cough (pertussis) vaccine are recommended in pregnancy.

The mother's antibodies cross the placenta, so the baby is protected from whooping cough in the first weeks of life, before it can be vaccinated itself. This is passive immunity, meaning protection from antibodies made by someone else. There is more on this in Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment.
Ultrasound lets doctors look at a baby before birth without touching it. It is a good example of technology improving prenatal care.
Ultrasound scanning sends high-frequency sound waves into the body. Their echoes from tissues of different density form a moving image on a screen.
Ultrasound uses no ionising radiation, unlike X-rays, which are avoided in pregnancy, so it is regarded as safe for mother and foetus.
Scans are done at different stages of pregnancy, and each is timed to answer particular questions.

A dating scan early in pregnancy, around 11–14 weeks, confirms the pregnancy, the number of babies and the expected date of delivery, and checks for an ectopic pregnancy (one that develops outside the uterus).
An anomaly scan at about 20 weeks checks the baby's organs, for example the heart, spine, brain and kidneys, and its growth, and the position of the placenta.
Later scans check growth and the baby's position before birth.
Finding a problem such as a heart defect before birth allows the birth to be planned in a hospital ready to treat the baby at once.
Labour is the time when a baby is most at risk of not getting enough oxygen, so its condition is watched closely.
During labour the baby's heart rate and the mother's contractions are monitored, for example by a cardiotocograph (CTG).

This means that signs that the baby is short of oxygen are noticed, and the birth can be speeded up, for example by Caesarean section (delivery through a cut in the abdomen and uterus). There is more on this in Pregnancy.
Some conditions are inherited or caused by an extra chromosome. Genetic screening estimates the chance that a baby is affected, and carries no risk to the pregnancy.

Genetic screening tests for genetic conditions, or for carriers of them (people who carry a gene for a condition without having it). There is more on this, including Punnett squares, in Genetic Inheritance.
Before or during pregnancy, couples with a family history of an inherited condition, for example cystic fibrosis, can have carrier testing to find out their chance of having an affected child.
Chromosome conditions such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21, where a person has an extra copy of chromosome 21) are screened for.
The combined test uses an ultrasound measurement of the fluid at the back of the baby's neck (nuchal translucency) together with a blood test of the mother, at about 11–14 weeks.
The combined test gives the chance, a probability, of Down syndrome, taking the mother's age into account.
Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), from about 10 weeks, tests a sample of the mother's blood for small fragments of DNA from the placenta that circulate in it.
NIPT is a much more accurate screening test for trisomy 21, 18 and 13, but a positive result still needs a diagnostic test, because it is still screening.
Neither the combined test nor NIPT harms the pregnancy, since NIPT uses only a blood sample from the mother and the combined test uses an ultrasound scan and a blood sample.

When screening shows a raised chance of a condition, a diagnostic test can confirm it. These tests take cells from the baby's side of the pregnancy, so the baby's own chromosomes or DNA can be examined.

Diagnostic tests take cells from the baby's side of the pregnancy so its chromosomes or DNA can be examined, for example as a karyotype (a picture of all the chromosomes arranged in pairs). There is more on this in Generating a DNA profile.
Chorionic villus sampling (CVS), at about 11–14 weeks, takes a sample of placental tissue with a fine needle through the abdomen or a thin tube through the cervix.
Amniocentesis, from about 15 weeks, uses a fine needle guided by ultrasound to take a sample of amniotic fluid, which contains cells shed by the foetus.
CVS and amniocentesis both give a definite result, but both carry a small risk of miscarriage, well under 1 in 100, so they are offered only when the chance of a condition is raised.

Preimplantation genetic testing: in IVF (fertilisation outside the body), one or a few cells are taken from each early embryo and tested for a known serious genetic condition, and only unaffected embryos are placed in the uterus.
Right after birth, and in the first days, the baby is checked quickly for problems that need action straight away or that can be treated if found early.
Apgar score: at one minute and five minutes after birth, the baby is scored 0, 1 or 2 on each of five signs: heart rate, breathing, muscle tone, reflex response and skin colour, for a maximum of 10.
A low Apgar score shows that the baby needs help, for example with breathing.
Vitamin K is offered to every newborn, usually by injection, to prevent a rare but serious bleeding disorder. There is more on this in Vitamins.

A full physical examination of the newborn checks, for example, the heart, the hips for hip dysplasia (a loose or dislocated hip joint, treatable if found early), the eyes and, in boys, whether the testes have descended.
Newborn hearing screening is offered to all babies in Ireland, so deafness is found early and language development can be supported.
Care does not stop after the first examination. In the following weeks the baby's growth and the mother's recovery and wellbeing are both followed.
Weight, length and head size are recorded on growth charts, so a baby who is growing poorly is noticed early.
A public health nurse visits the family at home in the first weeks.
The mother's recovery and her mental health are checked, because postnatal depression is common and treatable.
Breastfeeding is supported. There is more on this in Hormones in reproduction.
The baby's routine vaccinations begin at 2 months of age.
The heel-prick test is a postnatal screening test done in Ireland. It looks for rare, serious conditions in a baby who looks completely healthy.
Every baby born in Ireland is offered newborn bloodspot screening, the heel-prick test, with the parents' consent.
When the baby is 3 to 5 days old (72–120 hours after birth), a midwife or public health nurse pricks the baby's heel and places drops of blood on a special card.
The card is sent to the national screening laboratory at Children's Health Ireland at Temple Street, Dublin.
The conditions screened for are rare and serious, and show no signs at birth, but early treatment prevents or greatly reduces lasting harm.
A positive screen leads to diagnostic tests, because the heel-prick test is a screening test.

The test is done at 3–5 days because by then the baby has been feeding on milk for a few days, so a substance that the baby cannot break down, such as phenylalanine in PKU, has had time to build up in the blood to a detectable level.
Testing too early can miss the condition, because the substance has not yet built up.
PKU is the condition the heel-prick test was first developed for. It is a clear example of a serious inherited condition that is controlled by diet if it is found in the first days of life.
PKU has been screened for in Ireland since the 1960s. It is the condition for which the blood-spot test was first developed, by Robert Guthrie in the USA; the card is often called a Guthrie card.
The test measures phenylalanine (an amino acid from protein in food) in the blood spot; a high level shows the baby cannot convert phenylalanine. There is more on this in Enzymes as catalysts.
PKU is inherited as a recessive condition.
Treatment is a special diet low in phenylalanine, which means restricting high-protein foods and using special protein substitutes, from the first weeks of life and continued for life.
The sweetener aspartame contains phenylalanine, which is why food labels warn people with PKU.
Treated early, children with PKU develop normally; untreated, phenylalanine builds up and causes severe intellectual disability.
Women with PKU need very strict diet control before and during pregnancy, because high phenylalanine harms the developing foetus.
Other serious conditions are also on the Irish heel-prick screen. Each looks normal at birth, and each can be treated if found early.
Cystic fibrosis is also screened for by the heel-prick test. There is more on this in Mutations.
A raised level of a protein made by the pancreas in the blood spot is followed by DNA testing of the same spot for common CFTR mutations.
Early diagnosis of cystic fibrosis allows early treatment: physiotherapy to clear mucus, antibiotics, pancreatic enzymes with food, and newer drugs, which improve growth and lung health.
Congenital hypothyroidism: the baby's thyroid gland makes too little thyroxine, the hormone that controls growth and development. Untreated, it causes poor growth and intellectual disability.
Treatment for congenital hypothyroidism is a daily dose of thyroxine by mouth, which allows normal development.
Classical galactosaemia: the baby cannot break down galactose, one of the two sugars in lactose (milk sugar), because an enzyme in the pathway is missing.

Galactose builds up as soon as the baby drinks milk and can quickly cause serious illness. Treatment is a diet free of lactose and galactose, for example a soya-based formula instead of breast or cow's milk.
The heel-prick programme also screens for a small number of other rare inherited conditions.
Scans, blood tests and screening mean that problems are found when they can still be managed. This is how technology has improved prenatal and postnatal care.
Problems in the mother, such as anaemia, pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and infections, are found early and managed.
Problems in the baby, such as growth problems, heart and other defects, and the baby's position, are also found early and managed.
Pregnancy and birth are now far safer for mothers and babies than in the past.
Newborn screening prevents intellectual disability and early death in PKU, galactosaemia and congenital hypothyroidism.
Newborn screening gives children with cystic fibrosis early treatment.
Parents and doctors can plan the birth and treatment in advance, for example by choosing a hospital that is ready to treat the baby at once.
Technology also helps once the baby is born, especially for babies born too early. Premature babies are not ready to cope without support.
Neonatal intensive care (specialist care for newborns) allows many premature babies to survive.
Incubators keep the baby warm and protected from infection.
Surfactant, a substance that stops the air sacs in the lungs collapsing, can be given into the lungs, because premature lungs lack it.
Phototherapy, using blue light, breaks down bilirubin (a yellow substance that builds up in the blood) in babies with jaundice.
These treatments link to the late maturing of the lungs. There is more on this in Pregnancy.
Technology brings problems as well as benefits. A full evaluation also covers the errors, risks, costs and difficult choices it creates.
No screening test is perfect: a false positive causes anxiety and further tests, and a false negative gives false reassurance.
Screening gives a chance, not a certainty, which can be hard to understand.
Invasive diagnostic tests, CVS and amniocentesis, carry a small risk of miscarriage.
Finding a condition that cannot be treated can leave parents with difficult decisions.
Equipment, staff and intensive care are expensive, so access is unequal between and within countries.
Some very premature babies who survive have long-term health problems.
These are arguments to weigh; no side is taken.
Parents have the right to information about their pregnancy and to decide whether to have tests (informed consent). There is more on this in Science, scientists and society.
Genetic tests raise questions about who can see the results and how they are stored.
Some people with disabilities and their families argue that screening for conditions such as Down syndrome can send a negative message about people living with them.
Others argue that information from screening lets families prepare.
Newborn blood-spot cards contain the baby's DNA, which raises questions about how long they are stored and who may use them.

Fertility is the ability to produce offspring, but it is not available all the time in everyone. Males and females differ because sperm production runs continuously while egg release happens once per cycle.
A fertile period is the time during which intercourse can lead to pregnancy.

Males are continuously fertile: from puberty, sperm are made every day for the rest of life, declining slowly in old age, and every ejaculation (release of semen) contains millions of sperm. This is why a man is fertile on any day.
Females are cyclically fertile: from puberty to menopause, usually one egg is released per cycle (ovulation), so fertility comes in a short window once each cycle rather than every day.
The egg survives only about 12–24 hours after release, while sperm can survive up to about five days in the female body.
So the fertile window in each cycle is about six days: the five days before ovulation, when sperm already present can wait for the egg, and the day of ovulation.
In a regular 28-day cycle this is roughly days 9 to 14, but because the day of ovulation varies from woman to woman and cycle to cycle, the window cannot be predicted exactly from the calendar alone.
A woman's fertility is not the same at every age. It follows the state of her eggs, which she is born with and which do not renew.
Female fertility is highest in the twenties and falls with age, more steeply after about 35, because the number and quality of the remaining eggs decline.
Female fertility ends at the menopause, the time of life when ovulation and periods stop for good. There is more on this in Hormones in reproduction.

Contraception means stopping a pregnancy from starting. Every method blocks one step on the route from egg release to implantation, and methods differ in how reliable they are and in what else they protect against.
Contraception is the deliberate prevention of pregnancy.

Methods work in one of three ways: by preventing ovulation, by preventing sperm from reaching the egg (preventing fertilisation), or by preventing implantation, the embedding of the embryo in the lining of the uterus.
Methods are grouped as natural, mechanical (barrier), surgical and chemical (hormonal and spermicidal).
Effectiveness with perfect use: the male condom is about 98% effective; the pill, the implant, the coils and sterilisation are each more than 99% effective.

With typical, real-life use, methods that depend on the user remembering or using them correctly every time, namely natural methods, condoms and the pill, fail more often, because people forget or make mistakes.
Long-acting methods, namely the implant, coils and sterilisation, stay above 99% effective with typical use, because there is nothing to remember.
Only condoms, male and female, protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), because they stop body fluids passing between partners.
People using another method need condoms as well to reduce the risk of STIs.
Natural methods use no drugs or devices. They rely on behaviour: avoiding intercourse altogether, or avoiding it on the days when pregnancy is possible.
Abstinence, not having intercourse, is the only method that is completely effective against pregnancy and STIs.
Fertility awareness (natural family planning): the couple avoid intercourse during the fertile window, which they find by combining several signs.
Sign 1, the calendar (rhythm) method: recording cycle lengths over time to estimate when ovulation happens.

Sign 2, body temperature: measured each morning before getting up, it rises by a small amount, a few tenths of a degree Celsius, just after ovulation and stays up for the rest of the cycle, because of the hormone progesterone.
Sign 3, cervical mucus (the fluid made by the cervix, the neck of the uterus): it becomes thin, clear, stretchy and slippery around ovulation.
Home kits that detect the hormone surge before ovulation in urine can also be used, giving a warning that ovulation is near. There is more on this in The menstrual cycle.
Natural methods appeal to some people but are demanding to use and fail more often than other methods in real life. Knowing both sides lets you discuss them fairly.

Advantages of natural methods: no drugs, devices or side effects, and they are acceptable to people whose religious beliefs rule out artificial contraception, for example the teaching of the Catholic Church, which accepts only natural methods.
Limits of natural methods: they need training, daily records and regular cycles, and are much less reliable with typical use.
Natural methods are hard to use after childbirth, when breastfeeding or near the menopause, because cycles are then irregular. They also give no protection against STIs.
Withdrawal of the penis before ejaculation is unreliable, because some sperm may be released before ejaculation.
Breastfeeding delays ovulation but is not reliable contraception, because ovulation can return without warning.

Barrier methods put a physical block between sperm and egg. Of the methods used during intercourse, only the condoms in this group protect against STIs, because they also stop body fluids passing between partners.
Male condom: a thin latex, or non-latex, sheath placed over the erect penis that collects the semen, so sperm cannot enter the vagina.
The male condom also blocks the exchange of body fluids, so it reduces the spread of STIs, including HIV.
The male condom is cheap, widely available and has no hormones; it can tear or slip, and must be put on before any contact.
Female condom: a soft pouch placed in the vagina that lines it and collects semen; it also protects against STIs.

Diaphragm or cap: a dome of soft silicone placed over the cervix before intercourse, used with a spermicide (a sperm-killing chemical) and left in for several hours afterwards; it does not protect well against STIs.
The copper coil is a device rather than a barrier, but it is grouped with mechanical methods because it is a physical object placed in the body. It works without hormones.
Copper coil (copper intrauterine device, IUD): a small T-shaped device with copper, placed in the uterus by a doctor or nurse.
Copper is toxic to sperm and eggs, preventing fertilisation, and it changes the endometrium (the lining of the uterus) so an embryo is unlikely to implant.
The copper coil lasts for 5–10 years, contains no hormones, and can be removed at any time with a quick return to fertility.
The copper coil can also be used as emergency contraception if fitted within five days.
The copper coil can make periods heavier, and gives no protection against STIs.
It is grouped as mechanical because it is a device; the hormonal coil is in the chemical methods.
Sterilisation is a permanent operation that blocks the tubes gametes travel along. In men this is vasectomy, which stops sperm joining the semen without changing anything else about the man.

Vasectomy (male sterilisation): under local anaesthetic, each vas deferens (the tube carrying sperm from the testis) is cut and tied or sealed, so sperm cannot leave the testes. There is more on this in The male reproductive system.
After a vasectomy the man still ejaculates semen, because the fluids come from glands that are untouched; his testosterone and sex drive are unaffected.
The sperm that are still made are broken down and reabsorbed.
A vasectomy is not effective at once, because sperm remain in the ducts beyond the cut; semen tests are needed after some weeks to confirm there are no sperm.
Female sterilisation works on the same principle as vasectomy: the tubes are blocked so egg and sperm cannot meet. Unlike vasectomy, it works straight away.

Tubal ligation (female sterilisation): each fallopian tube, the tube that carries the egg from the ovary to the uterus, is cut, tied or blocked with a clip, usually by keyhole surgery under general anaesthetic, so the egg and sperm cannot meet.
After tubal ligation ovulation and the menstrual cycle continue as before, because the egg is reabsorbed.
Tubal ligation is effective at once.
Sterilisation suits some people very well and others badly. The key issue is that it is meant to be permanent.
Sterilisation is very effective and permanent, with nothing to remember, but it should be treated as irreversible: reversal is difficult and often fails.
Sterilisation carries the small risks of any surgery, and gives no protection against STIs.
It suits people who are sure they want no more children.

Diagram: outline of the male system with the cut in each vas deferens marked, and of the female system with the cut or clip in each fallopian tube marked; label the vas deferens, testis, fallopian tube, ovary, uterus and “cut and tied”.
Chemical methods use hormones or sperm-killing chemicals. The pill is the best known: it is taken by mouth every day and uses synthetic versions of the body's own reproductive hormones.
The combined pill contains synthetic oestrogen and progesterone and prevents ovulation; the detail of how is in Hormonal manipulation. It also thickens the cervical mucus so sperm cannot pass.
The combined pill is taken daily, usually with a break or dummy pills each month, during which a withdrawal bleed (a bleed like a period) happens.
The progestogen-only pill (synthetic progesterone only) works mainly by thickening the cervical mucus, and in some types also stops ovulation; it suits women who cannot take oestrogen.

Some hormonal methods release their hormone slowly over months or years, so the user has nothing to remember daily. This is why the implant and the coils, which are long-acting, stay above 99% effective in real life.
Long-acting hormonal methods release a synthetic progesterone continuously.
The implant is a small flexible rod placed under the skin of the upper arm, lasting about 3 years.
The injection is given every few months.
The hormonal coil (intrauterine system, IUS) is placed in the uterus and lasts several years; it thickens the cervical mucus and thins the endometrium.
The contraceptive patch and vaginal ring release oestrogen and progesterone, like the combined pill.
Some chemical methods are used after the event or alongside another method rather than as a regular choice.

Emergency hormonal pills, taken as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse, work mainly by delaying ovulation, so there is no egg for sperm to meet; one type works within 3 days and another within 5 days.
The copper coil fitted within 5 days is the most effective emergency method. Emergency pills are not for regular use.
Spermicides are chemicals in a gel or cream that kill sperm; they are not reliable alone and are used with a diaphragm or cap.
Hormonal methods are very effective and have extra health benefits, but they act on the whole body, so they also carry side effects and risks.
Hormonal methods are very effective; periods often become lighter, more regular and less painful.
The combined pill lowers the risk of cancers of the ovary and of the endometrium (womb).
Hormonal methods can cause side effects, for example headaches, mood changes and irregular bleeding with progesterone-only methods.
The combined pill slightly raises the risk of blood clots (deep vein thrombosis) and stroke, especially in smokers and women over 35, so it is not prescribed to everyone.
Hormonal methods give no protection against STIs.
The pill must be taken correctly every day; vomiting or some medicines can stop it working.
Some infections spread mainly through sexual contact, and some of them damage the reproductive system. This links contraception to infertility.
An STI (sexually transmitted infection) is an infection passed on mainly by sexual contact.
Bacterial STIs are chlamydia, gonorrhoea and syphilis, which are treated with antibiotics.

Viral STIs are HIV, genital herpes, human papillomavirus (HPV, which causes genital warts and most cervical cancers) and hepatitis B, which can be controlled but is not usually cured. There is more on pathogens in Pathogens.
Chlamydia and gonorrhoea often cause no symptoms, especially in women, but can spread to the uterus and fallopian tubes, causing pelvic inflammatory disease, which scars and blocks the tubes.

Blocked tubes from pelvic inflammatory disease are a major preventable cause of female infertility, because the egg and sperm can no longer meet, and they raise the risk of ectopic pregnancy (a pregnancy that starts outside the uterus).
In men chlamydia and gonorrhoea can inflame the epididymis, the coiled tube on the testis where sperm mature and are stored.
Because many STIs cause no symptoms and can damage fertility, prevention combines protection during sex, testing and treatment, and vaccination.
Prevention: correct use of condoms every time, and fewer sexual partners.

Prevention: regular testing and treatment of infected people and their partners breaks the chain of transmission, because many infected people have no symptoms and would otherwise pass the infection on without knowing.
Prevention: vaccination against HPV and hepatitis B. There is more on HPV in Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer.
For HIV, anti-HIV drugs taken before possible exposure (pre-exposure prophylaxis, PrEP) lower the risk of infection.
Treatment of people with HIV reduces their virus to levels at which it is not passed on sexually.
Gonorrhoea is becoming resistant to antibiotics (the drugs no longer kill it), which makes prevention more important.
Egg freezing (oocyte cryopreservation) lets a woman store her eggs while they are still young and healthy, to be used later. It uses a series of steps similar to the start of IVF.
1. Hormone injections stimulate the ovaries to mature several eggs at once, rather than the usual one.
2. The eggs are collected with a fine needle through the vaginal wall, guided by ultrasound, under sedation.
3. The eggs are frozen very rapidly (vitrification), so that ice crystals, which would damage the cells, do not form, and they are stored in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C.
4. Later the eggs are thawed and fertilised by IVF (fertilisation in a dish) or by ICSI (one sperm injected into an egg).
Egg freezing preserves fertility but cannot promise a baby. Who uses it, and why it is not a guarantee, are the points to know.
Uses: before cancer treatment, because chemotherapy or radiotherapy can destroy the eggs in the ovaries, or by women who wish to delay having children.
Sperm, and embryos made in IVF, can also be frozen; sperm freezing is offered to men before cancer treatment.
Limits: success depends strongly on the woman's age when the eggs are frozen, since younger eggs have fewer chromosome errors and survive freezing better.
Freezing gives no guarantee of a baby, and not every egg survives thawing.
The process involves hormone treatment and a procedure, and it is expensive.
Infertility is common, and its causes can lie with the man, the woman, both, or neither. Finding the cause decides which treatment is suitable.
Infertility is the failure to become pregnant after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse.
The World Health Organization estimated in 2023 that about 1 in 6 people worldwide experience infertility at some point in their lives.
Causes are found in the man, the woman, both, or neither, which is called unexplained infertility.
Male infertility usually comes down to too few sperm, sperm that cannot do their job, or sperm that cannot get out. Lifestyle can also reduce sperm production.
Low sperm count (too few sperm in the semen), and sperm that swim poorly or are abnormally shaped, for example with a faulty tail, reduce the chance that one reaches the egg.
A blockage of the epididymis or vas deferens, for example after infection or vasectomy, stops sperm leaving the testes.
Undescended testes (testes that have not moved down into the scrotum) and low testosterone or low pituitary hormones are also male causes.

Lifestyle and environmental factors reduce sperm production, such as smoking, heavy drinking, obesity, anabolic steroids and overheating of the testes. There is more on steroids in Hormonal manipulation.
Male infertility is diagnosed by semen analysis, which tests sperm count, movement and shape under the microscope.
Female infertility arises when no egg is released, when egg and sperm cannot meet, or when the uterus cannot support an embryo.
Failure to ovulate, caused by a hormone imbalance, for example polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), or by being very underweight or overweight, means no egg is released.
Blocked or damaged fallopian tubes, for example after pelvic inflammatory disease from an STI, stop egg and sperm meeting.
Endometriosis is a condition in which tissue like the endometrium grows outside the uterus and can cause scarring around the tubes and ovaries.
Female causes also include problems of the uterus or cervical mucus, and age, because egg number and quality fall.
Female infertility is diagnosed by blood hormone tests, ultrasound of the ovaries and uterus, and tests that show whether the tubes are open.
If the problem is that a woman does not release eggs regularly, the treatment is to make her ovaries release them. This is a first step before more complex techniques.
Stimulating ovulation is for women who do not ovulate regularly, for example because of PCOS.
Fertility drugs, as tablets or injections, cause the ovaries to mature and release eggs.
The woman is monitored by ultrasound to see how many follicles (the fluid-filled sacs in the ovary that each contain an egg) develop, and intercourse or insemination is timed to ovulation.
Risk: more than one egg may be released, so twins or triplets are more likely.
Risk: the ovaries can over-respond (ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome), becoming swollen and painful, which is occasionally serious.
Lifestyle change, for example weight loss, can restore ovulation in some women.
Fertility drugs work by acting on the same hormone system that controls the menstrual cycle, either by boosting the brain's signals to the ovaries or by supplying them directly.

Some fertility tablets block oestrogen's negative feedback on the brain and pituitary, so the pituitary releases more FSH and LH, which stimulate follicle development and ovulation. There is more on feedback in The menstrual cycle.
Injected fertility drugs contain FSH, often with LH, and act directly on the ovaries to make follicles develop.
A final injection of a hormone that acts like LH triggers the eggs' final maturation and ovulation, imitating the LH surge.
The same injections are used to stimulate the ovaries in IVF and egg freezing.
Artificial insemination helps when the sperm have trouble reaching the egg. It puts sperm into the uterus by hand, so more of them start closer to the egg.

Artificial insemination, or intrauterine insemination (IUI): semen from the partner or a donor is collected, the sperm are washed and concentrated, and they are placed directly into the uterus through the cervix with a thin tube, at the time of ovulation.
This places many active sperm close to the fallopian tubes, where fertilisation happens.
It is used for a mildly low sperm count or poor motility (swimming), cervical mucus that blocks sperm, difficulty with intercourse, and single women or female couples using donor sperm.
The woman's fallopian tubes must be open, because the sperm still have to travel along them to meet the egg.
The same technique is widely used in farming, for example to breed cattle from selected bulls.
IVF takes fertilisation out of the body. Eggs and sperm are brought together in the laboratory, and the resulting embryo is then placed in the uterus.
IVF means “in glass”, that is, fertilisation outside the body.
1. Hormone injections stimulate the ovaries to mature several eggs.
2. The eggs are collected with a needle guided by ultrasound.
3. The eggs are mixed with sperm in a dish in the laboratory, where fertilisation takes place.
4. The embryos are grown in an incubator for 2–5 days, up to the blastocyst stage (a ball of cells ready to implant). There is more on this in Pregnancy.
5. Usually one, sometimes two, embryos are placed in the uterus through the cervix with a thin tube.
6. A pregnancy test about two weeks later shows whether an embryo has implanted.
Spare good-quality embryos can be frozen for later attempts.
IVF is used when simpler treatments will not work or are unsuitable. It was developed in the twentieth century and is now widely used.

IVF is used for blocked or damaged fallopian tubes, unexplained infertility, endometriosis, failure of other treatments, and couples needing preimplantation genetic testing (checking embryos for a genetic condition before transfer). There is more on this in Prenatal and postnatal care.
History: the first baby conceived by IVF, Louise Brown, was born in England on 25 July 1978, after work by the scientist Robert Edwards and the gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe.
Edwards was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2010.
Millions of babies have since been born by IVF worldwide.
ICSI is a version of IVF designed for severe male infertility. Instead of leaving sperm to fertilise the egg in the dish, the laboratory places one sperm inside the egg.
ICSI is the same as IVF except that in step 3 a single sperm is chosen and injected directly into the cytoplasm of each egg with a very fine glass needle, under a microscope.
Because the sperm does not have to swim to or enter the egg itself, ICSI overcomes severe male infertility.
ICSI is used for very low sperm count, sperm that cannot swim or cannot penetrate the egg, and previous failure of fertilisation in IVF.
ICSI is also used when sperm are taken directly from the testis or epididymis by a needle, for example after a vasectomy or a blockage.
ICSI is also used with frozen eggs, which are thawed before the sperm is injected.
A flow chart shows IVF and ICSI together, because they share every step except how the egg is fertilised.

Diagram: a flow chart of IVF with ICSI as a branch: stimulate ovaries → collect eggs → (IVF: mix eggs and sperm in a dish | ICSI: inject one sperm into each egg) → grow embryos for 2–5 days → transfer an embryo to the uterus → pregnancy test.
Discussing contraception means weighing benefits against drawbacks. The benefits range from the individual to the whole planet.
Contraception lets people choose whether and when to have children and how many, and to space pregnancies, which improves the health of mothers and babies.
It prevents unintended pregnancy, including in teenagers.
Condoms reduce the spread of STIs, including HIV, a major public-health benefit.
Hormonal methods can treat heavy or painful periods, and the combined pill lowers the risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer.
At a global scale, access to contraception slows population growth, reducing pressure on food, water and habitats. This is a sustainability link; there is more on this in The cross-cutting themes.
Contraception also has drawbacks, some medical, some personal, and one environmental.
Hormonal methods have side effects and, for some women, a small increased risk of blood clots.
No method except condoms prevents STIs, so a person relying on the pill may still catch one.
User-dependent methods often fail in real life, because they must be used correctly every time.
Sterilisation is effectively irreversible and may be regretted.
Some people object to artificial contraception on religious or moral grounds.
Synthetic oestrogen from the pill, along with natural oestrogens, passes through sewage treatment into rivers, where it has been linked to the feminisation of male fish, an environmental effect.
Treatments for infertility bring benefits that are both personal and medical. Each argument rests on the biology of the technique.
It allows people with infertility to have a child who is genetically their own, relieving much distress.
ICSI lets many men with very few or poorly swimming sperm become fathers.
Egg and sperm freezing preserve fertility for people having cancer treatment.
Preimplantation testing in IVF lets couples who carry a serious genetic condition avoid passing it on.
Donor eggs or sperm allow people without their own gametes to have children.
Research in IVF has increased understanding of fertilisation and early development.
Infertility treatments also raise health, cost and ethical concerns. Some are risks to mother and baby, others are questions of fairness and identity.

Stimulating ovulation and transferring more than one embryo raise the chance of twins and triplets, which are more often born premature and underweight and carry more risk for the mother; this is why single-embryo transfer is now favoured.
Success rates per cycle are limited and fall sharply with the woman's age, so treatment can mean repeated cycles with much stress and cost, and unequal access for those who cannot pay.
ICSI bypasses the natural selection of sperm, so a genetic cause of the father's infertility, for example some changes on the Y chromosome, can be passed to a son.
Spare frozen embryos raise questions about how long they are stored and whether they may be used in research or discarded. There is more on this in Ethics of genetic technologies.
Children conceived with donor gametes may want to know their genetic origins, which raises questions about donor anonymity.
Treatment allows parenthood at older ages, when pregnancy carries more risk, for example a higher chance of chromosome conditions.
Egg freezing gives women more control over timing but is not a guarantee. Weigh the benefits against the limits.
For: it preserves a woman's own eggs before cancer treatment.
For: it gives women more choice over when to have children.
Against: success is uncertain, and lower when eggs are frozen at older ages.
Against: it involves hormone treatment, egg collection and high costs.
Against: it may give a false sense of security that leads to delayed attempts at pregnancy.

Flowering plants reproduce sexually by means of flowers, which produce the gametes (sex cells) and bring about pollination (the transfer of pollen) and fertilisation (the joining of male and female gametes). Three structures carry the process from gamete to new plant: the flower, the seed and the fruit.

The flower is a short shoot whose parts are modified leaves arranged in rings (whorls) on the receptacle, the tip of the flower stalk. Its job is to produce gametes, bring about pollination and fertilisation, and then produce seeds and fruits.

The flower makes the male and female gametes and brings about pollination. It is the only one of the three structures that exists before fertilisation, because the seed and fruit develop from flower parts afterwards.

The seed, a fertilised and developed ovule, contains the embryo (a new plant) with a food store and a protective coat. The fruit, a developed ovary, protects the seeds and helps to disperse them, that is, spread them away from the parent plant.
Seed detail is in Seeds; dispersal is in Fruit and seed dispersal.
Many flowers are bisexual (hermaphrodite), meaning they have both male and female parts in the same flower, e.g. buttercup.

Some plants have separate male and female flowers on the same plant, e.g. hazel, whose male flowers hang in catkins and whose small female flowers have red stigmas. In some species male and female flowers are on different plants, e.g. holly.
A flower is built in rings, listed here from the outside inwards. The outer parts hold the flower together, protect it and, in many species, attract the animals that carry its pollen.

Receptacle: the swollen tip of the flower stalk, to which all the other flower parts are attached, so it holds the flower together. For example, in strawberry it swells to form the fleshy part of the fruit.

Sepal: a small, usually green, leaf-like part in the outer ring; together the sepals form the calyx. Sepals enclose and protect the flower while it is a bud, and some photosynthesise (make food using light).
Petal: inside the sepals; together the petals form the corolla. In insect-pollinated flowers the petals are large, coloured and often scented, which attracts insects.

Many insect-pollinated petals have lines or patches (nectar guides) that lead insects to the nectar. In wind-pollinated flowers petals are small, dull or absent, because there is no need to attract animals.

Nectary: a gland, usually at the base of the petals, that secretes nectar, a sugary liquid that rewards visiting insects so that they keep coming back. Pollen is also eaten by some insects, e.g. bees collect it to feed their larvae.
The male part of the flower is the stamen. Its job is to make pollen, the package that carries the male gametes, and to hold it where a pollinator can pick it up.
Stamen: the male part, made of an anther on a stalk, the filament, so that the pollen is held up where it can be picked up. The stamens together form the androecium.

Anther: produces pollen grains by meiosis (a cell division that halves the chromosome number), so the pollen grains are haploid, with one set of chromosomes. Each pollen grain contains the male gamete nuclei. When ripe the anther splits open to release the pollen.

Filament: the stalk that holds the anther in position, where insects brush against it or out in the wind. It also carries water and nutrients to the anther through a small vascular strand (a thin tube of transport tissue).
Diagram: a stamen drawn on its own. Labels: anther, filament.
The female part of the flower is the carpel. It catches pollen, provides a route for the male gametes to reach the egg cell, and protects the ovules that become seeds.
Carpel: the female part, made of the stigma, style and ovary. A flower may have one carpel or many; the carpels together form the gynoecium.

Stigma: the tip of the carpel that receives (catches) pollen. It is sticky in insect-pollinated flowers, so pollen carried on an insect adheres, and large and feathery in wind-pollinated grasses, so it can catch pollen from the air.
Style: the stalk joining the stigma to the ovary. It holds the stigma in a position to receive pollen, and the pollen tube (the thin tube a pollen grain grows) grows down through it to the ovary.
Ovary: the swollen base of the carpel. It contains one or more ovules and protects them, so the developing seeds are not exposed. After fertilisation the ovary develops into the fruit.

Ovule: a structure inside the ovary that contains the egg cell (female gamete), made by meiosis, so it is haploid. After fertilisation the ovule develops into the seed. The micropyle is a tiny pore at one end of the ovule through which the pollen tube usually enters.
Diagram: a carpel drawn on its own. Labels: stigma, style, ovary.

Diagram: a half-flower (vertical section) of an insect-pollinated flower such as buttercup or wallflower. Labels: receptacle, sepal, petal, nectary, stamen (anther, filament), carpel (stigma, style, ovary), ovule.
Pollination must happen before fertilisation can take place. Flowers can be self-pollinated or cross-pollinated, and several features favour cross-pollination.

Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma of a flower of the same species. It is only the arrival of pollen: fertilisation, the fusion of gamete nuclei in the ovule, comes later.

Self-pollination: pollen is transferred to a stigma of the same flower or of another flower on the same plant. Cross-pollination: pollen is transferred to a stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species.

Cross-pollination combines genes from two different parents, so the offspring show more genetic variation. The species is better able to adapt to change, such as new diseases or climate, and avoids the harmful effects of inbreeding (breeding between close relatives).
Self-pollination needs no second plant or pollinator and is more certain, but it gives less variation. It suits isolated plants and plants in places with few pollinators.

Ways flowers favour cross-pollination: the stamens and stigmas of a flower ripen at different times; self-incompatibility, where pollen landing on a stigma of the same plant fails to grow a pollen tube; separate male and female flowers (hazel) or separate male and female plants (holly).

In primrose two flower forms exist: pin flowers, with a long style and low anthers, and thrum flowers, with a short style and high anthers. Insects carry pollen between the two forms, so the pollen reaches a different plant.

Agents of pollination (the carriers of pollen): insects (most showy flowers), wind (grasses and many trees, e.g. hazel, oak and birch), and less often other animals (birds and bats in other parts of the world) or water. There is more on this in Investigation: insect- and wind-pollinated plants.
The flower's structure matches the agent of pollination, whether an animal or the wind. Each type of flower is built to make the transfer of pollen as reliable as possible.
In insect-pollinated plants the flower attracts the pollinator (colour, scent, nectar guides), rewards it (nectar and pollen), and places its anthers and stigma where the insect's body touches them.
Pollen sticks to the insect at one flower and is rubbed onto the sticky stigma of the next flower of the same species it visits.
Many insects visit only one species on a foraging trip, having learned the flower they are faithful to, so pollen is carried to the right species.

Plant and pollinator both benefit, because the plant is pollinated and the insect is fed: this is a mutualism (a relationship in which both partners gain). There is more on this in Biotic factors and relationships.

In wind-pollinated plants the flower's job is to release very large amounts of pollen into moving air and to catch pollen on a large stigma. There is nothing to attract animals, so there are no showy petals, scent or nectar.
