Sustainability link: many crops (e.g. apples, strawberries and oilseed rape) and wild plants depend on insect pollinators, especially bees. Bee numbers are falling through habitat loss, pesticides and disease.

Ireland's response is the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan, first published in 2015 and coordinated by the National Biodiversity Data Centre. It encourages councils, farmers, schools and gardeners to provide food and nesting places for pollinators, e.g. by leaving wildflowers and mowing less often.
Health link: wind-pollinated plants, especially grasses, release huge numbers of small, light pollen grains that cause hay fever (allergic rhinitis) in early summer.
Once pollen reaches a stigma of the right species, a sequence of events leads to fertilisation. Afterwards the flower parts change into the seed and fruit.
Fertilisation in five steps: 1. A pollen grain of the same species lands on the stigma.
2. It grows a pollen tube down through the style to the ovary, digesting a path with enzymes.
3. The tube enters an ovule, usually through the micropyle, and carries the male gamete nuclei to it.
4. Fertilisation: a male gamete nucleus fuses with the egg cell nucleus to form a diploid zygote (a cell with two sets of chromosomes, the first cell of the new plant).
5. The zygote divides by mitosis (ordinary cell division that makes identical cells) to form the embryo.
Double fertilisation: a second male nucleus fuses with two other nuclei in the ovule (the polar nuclei) to form the endosperm nucleus, which divides to form the endosperm food store.

After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed, and its outer layers (integuments) become the testa, the seed coat. The ovary becomes the fruit, and its wall becomes the fruit wall (pericarp). The petals, stamens and usually the sepals wither and fall off.

Diagram: a carpel in section, with a pollen grain on the stigma, the pollen tube growing down the style and entering an ovule through the micropyle. Labels: pollen grain, pollen tube, style, ovary, ovule, egg cell, micropyle.

A flower's structure follows from how its pollen travels. Insects must be lured in and rewarded, so insect-pollinated flowers advertise; the wind needs no persuading, so wind-pollinated flowers drop the advertising. Each point gives the insect-pollinated flower first and the wind-pollinated flower second, and the flower parts are named as in Flower structure and pollination.
Petals: insect-pollinated flowers have large, brightly coloured petals, often with nectar guides (markings that lead the insect towards the nectar), to attract insects.
Wind-pollinated flowers have small, green or dull petals, or none, because there is no animal to attract and large petals would block pollen in the wind.
Scent and nectar: insect-pollinated flowers are usually scented and have nectaries (the glands that produce nectar, a sugary liquid), so the insect is rewarded for visiting.
Wind-pollinated flowers have no scent and no nectaries, because there is no visitor to reward.
Flowers as a whole: insect-pollinated flowers are usually showy, single or in visible clusters, so that insects can spot them.
Wind-pollinated flowers are small and inconspicuous, often in catkins (dangling spikes of tiny flowers) or spikes held high above the leaves, where the wind can reach them.
Many wind-pollinated trees, e.g. hazel, flower before their leaves open, so the leaves don't block the pollen.
Examples: insect-pollinated plants include buttercup, wallflower, foxglove and primrose; wind-pollinated plants include grasses (e.g. ryegrass), hazel, oak, birch and plantain.

The anther (the pollen-producing part of the stamen, held up on a stalk called the filament) and the stigma (the sticky or feathery top of the carpel that receives pollen) are positioned to suit the carrier. Insects touch the flower's parts; the wind blows past them.
Position of anthers: insect-pollinated anthers are inside the flower, held firmly on short or stiff filaments where a visiting insect brushes against them, so pollen rubs onto its body.
Wind-pollinated anthers hang outside the flower on long, thin, flexible filaments, loosely attached and often swinging freely, so the wind shakes pollen out.
Stigma: insect-pollinated stigmas are small, sticky and inside the flower, where the insect's body touches them and pollen sticks to them.
Wind-pollinated stigmas are large, feathery (branched) and hang outside the flower, giving a big surface area to catch pollen from the air.

Diagram: side-by-side labelled drawings of a buttercup or wallflower half-flower (large petal, nectary, anther inside, small sticky stigma) and a wind-pollinated grass flower (feathery stigmas, anthers on long filaments hanging outside small green bracts). Label bracts only as bracts (small green scales).
The pollen itself also differs. Insects deliver pollen accurately, whereas the wind scatters it at random, and the grains are built for the different journeys.
Amount of pollen: insect-pollinated flowers produce relatively small amounts, because insects carry pollen directly from flower to flower.
Wind-pollinated flowers produce very large amounts, because most pollen carried by the wind never reaches a stigma of the same species, so many grains are needed for a few to land.
Pollen grains: insect pollen grains are larger, often with a sticky or oily coat and a rough or spiky surface that clings to insect hairs.
Wind pollen grains are small, light, dry and smooth, so they are carried easily and far by the wind and don't clump together.
Diagram: an insect pollen grain (larger, with a spiky or sculptured surface) drawn beside a wind pollen grain (smaller and smooth), as seen under the microscope.
This is a comparative observation study, not a controlled experiment. No factor is changed, so there is no treatment and no control group; the two flower types are compared with each other.
Aim: to compare the structures of an insect-pollinated flower and a wind-pollinated flower, and relate each structure to its function in pollination.

Example hypothesis: “The insect-pollinated flower will have larger, coloured petals, nectaries and a sticky stigma inside the flower; the wind-pollinated flower will have small or no petals, anthers and feathery stigmas hanging outside the flower, and smaller, smoother pollen grains.”

What differs and what is recorded: the factor being compared is the method of pollination (insect or wind). Qualitative features (recorded in words) are colour, scent, presence of nectar, whether the stigma is sticky or feathery, whether anthers and stigma are inside or outside the flower, and pollen surface.
Quantitative features (measured as numbers) are the number of each part, the lengths of filaments and styles, petal size and pollen grain diameter.

Keeping the comparison fair: use fully open, mature flowers in which the anthers are shedding pollen, so every flower is at the same stage. Examine several flowers of each species (at least three) and average the measurements, to reduce the effect of one unusual flower.
Measure every flower in the same way, with the same instruments and microscope magnification, so the two types can be compared fairly.

Equipment: fresh insect-pollinated flowers (e.g. buttercup or wallflower) and wind-pollinated flowers (e.g. a flowering grass, or hazel catkins in late winter); white tile; scalpel or sharp blade; forceps; mounted needle; hand lens (×10) or stereo (dissecting) microscope; ruler (mm) or graph paper.
Also needed: microscope slides and coverslips; dropper with water; compound light microscope; clear sticky tape; gloves; pencil and paper.
The method moves from the whole flower, to its separated parts, to the pollen under the microscope, and repeats everything for the second flower type.
1. Examine each whole flower with the hand lens. Record its colour, size and whether it has a scent. Note whether the anthers and stigmas are inside the flower or hang outside it.

2. Remove the parts of the insect-pollinated flower from the outside in, using forceps, laying each ring (sepals, petals, stamens, carpels) in order on the white tile. Count the parts in each ring and record them.
3. Look at the base of the petals for nectaries (shiny or moist patches). Touch the stigma lightly with a mounted needle to see if it is sticky.
4. Measure the length of the filaments, style and petals with a ruler (or on graph paper) for each flower. Repeat for at least three flowers of each species and calculate the means.
5. Repeat steps 1 to 4 with the wind-pollinated flower, using the stereo microscope for the small grass flowers. Note the bracts, the long hanging filaments and the feathery stigmas.
6. Cut a vertical section of the insect-pollinated flower with the scalpel on the tile (a half-flower) and draw it, labelled.

7. Pollen: tap a ripe anther over a drop of water on a clean slide, or press clear sticky tape onto the anther and stick the tape on a slide. Add a coverslip and examine under the light microscope at low, then high, power.

8. Draw a few grains of each type at the same magnification and compare their size and surface; estimate their diameter (e.g. against the field of view or an eyepiece scale). Note how easily pollen comes off the anther and whether it clumps (sticky) or spreads (dry).
Scalpels, pollen, some plants and glass slides each carry a risk, so the practical needs a precaution for each.
Cut away from the body on a white tile with a sharp scalpel; carry and store blades safely, so nobody is cut.
Pollen can trigger hay fever or asthma. Students with pollen allergies should avoid handling wind-pollinated flowers or wear a mask and gloves, and the room should be ventilated.

Some plants are poisonous or irritant: foxglove is poisonous if eaten, and buttercup sap can irritate the skin. Wear gloves, don't put plant material near the mouth, and wash hands after the practical.
Collect only common plants, with the landowner's permission; don't pick protected or rare wild flowers.
Microscope slides and coverslips are fragile glass; dispose of breakages in a glass bin.
Recording results in a table puts the two flowers side by side, so each difference can be seen and then explained.

Results table: one column for each species (insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated), with rows for petal colour and size, scent, nectaries, number of stamens, filament length, anther position, stigma type and position, style length, amount of pollen released, and pollen size and surface.

Expected primary data (collected by you) for the insect-pollinated flower: large coloured petals, nectaries, scent, anthers on short or stiff filaments inside the flower, a small sticky stigma, and larger, sticky, spiky or sculptured pollen grains.

Expected primary data for the wind-pollinated flower: small green bracts or no petals, no nectar or scent, anthers dangling outside the flower on long filaments that shed clouds of dry pollen when tapped, feathery stigmas outside the flower, and smaller, smooth, dry pollen grains.
A conclusion links what was seen to why it matters for pollination, and secondary data add evidence the class could not collect itself.

Conclusion: relate each observed structure to its function, using the adaptations above. For example, the feathery stigma of the grass gives a large surface to catch airborne pollen, and the sticky stigma of the buttercup collects pollen rubbed off an insect's body. State whether the results support the hypothesis.

Secondary data used to support the conclusions: scanning electron micrographs (SEM images) of pollen grains, which show surface detail that a light microscope can't resolve, such as spikes and ridges on insect pollen and smooth surfaces on grass pollen.

Other secondary data: published pollen counts, which show the huge numbers of grass pollen grains in the air in early summer; and labelled diagrams and descriptions of other species in textbooks or plant identification guides.
Primary data are collected by the student through observing and measuring; secondary data are collected by others. There is more on this in Producing and analysing data.
Every practical has weaknesses. Each limitation below has a matching improvement, and you should be able to give both.
Only a few flowers of one or two species are examined, so the results may not represent all insect- or wind-pollinated plants; examine more flowers and more species, and compare with secondary data.
Flowers at different stages (bud, open, withering) differ in size and pollen release; use flowers at the same stage.
Grass flowers are very small, so measurements with a ruler are imprecise; use a stereo microscope or graph paper.
Pollen size estimated against the field of view is approximate; a calibrated eyepiece scale gives more precise sizes.
The light microscope can't show fine surface detail, hence the use of SEM images.
Judgements of colour, scent and stickiness are qualitative and subjective, because different people judge differently; have two people record them.
Damage during dissection can break parts or knock off pollen; handle flowers gently with forceps.

After fertilisation, a flower's ovule (the small structure inside the ovary that holds the female egg cell) develops into a seed. The seed is the package that carries the next generation of a flowering plant.
A seed is a fertilised, mature ovule. It contains an embryo (a new plant in miniature), a food store and a protective coat, the testa.
It is the product of sexual reproduction in flowering plants, because it forms only after a male and a female sex cell have fused.
As the seed matures it loses most of its water and becomes dry and hard, and the activity of the embryo slows almost to a stop. This makes the seed compact and tough.
A seed is built from a few parts, each with one clear job: protect the embryo, be the embryo, or feed it. Learn each part by what it becomes and what it does.
Testa: the seed coat, formed from the outer layers (integuments) of the ovule. It protects the embryo from mechanical damage, from attack by insects, fungi and bacteria, and from drying out.

Embryo: the young plant, which developed from the zygote (the cell formed when the sex cells fuse) by mitosis (cell division that makes identical cells). It is made of the plumule, the radicle and one or two cotyledons.
Plumule: the embryonic shoot of the embryo. It will grow into the shoot (stem and leaves) of the new plant.
Radicle: the embryonic root of the embryo. It will grow into the first root of the new plant, and it points towards the micropyle.
Cotyledon: a seed leaf, part of the embryo. In some seeds the cotyledons absorb and store the food; in others they pass food from the endosperm to the growing embryo.

Endosperm: a food store outside the embryo, formed by double fertilisation. It supplies the embryo with food, mainly starch and also oils and proteins in some seeds, when it starts to grow into a seedling, before the seedling's leaves can photosynthesise.
Micropyle: a tiny pore in the testa, where the pollen tube entered the ovule. Hilum: the scar where the seed was attached to the inside of the fruit.

Food stored in seeds: starch (e.g. cereal grains and beans), oils (e.g. sunflower seeds and oilseed rape) and protein (e.g. peas and beans). These stores make seeds important human foods, such as cereals, pulses and vegetable oils. There is more on this in Metabolic roles and nutritional sources.
Flowering plants split into two groups by how many cotyledons (seed leaves) their embryo has, and seeds also differ in where the food is kept when mature. Maize and broad bean show the two patterns.
Monocotyledons have one cotyledon; dicotyledons have two. This difference is where the names come from.

Endospermic seeds keep the endosperm as the food store when mature. Non-endospermic seeds have absorbed the endosperm into the cotyledons as the seed developed, so the cotyledons hold the food instead.
Maize (a monocot): one cotyledon; a large endosperm is the food store; the cotyledon passes food from the endosperm to the embryo.
The maize grain is strictly a fruit, because its thin fruit wall is fused to the testa. This is why the fruit wall and testa are labelled together on a maize diagram.
Broad bean (a dicot): two large cotyledons store the food, and there is no endosperm in the mature seed.
Diagram: a broad bean seed opened, with one cotyledon removed, labelled testa, micropyle, hilum, cotyledon, plumule and radicle.
Diagram: a vertical section of a maize grain, labelled fruit wall and testa (fused), endosperm, cotyledon, plumule and radicle.
A fruit does not grow on its own: it is the developing seeds inside that tell the flower to swell into a fruit. They do this with chemical messengers called growth regulators.

A growth regulator (plant hormone) is a chemical made in small amounts in one part of a plant that controls growth or development elsewhere. Developing seeds make growth regulators, mainly auxins (e.g. indoleacetic acid, IAA) and gibberellins.

After fertilisation the developing seeds release these growth regulators into the surrounding tissues. They stimulate the cells of the ovary wall (or, in some fruits, the receptacle, the swollen top of the flower stalk) to divide and enlarge, so the fruit grows.
Without fertilised seeds, most flowers simply wither and fall without forming a fruit, because no growth regulators are released to start fruit growth.
Evidence from strawberry: the fleshy part of a strawberry is the swollen receptacle, and the pips on its surface are tiny dry fruits (achenes), each with one seed.

In experiments by J. P. Nitsch (published 1950), removing the pips stopped the receptacle growing, and applying auxin to the de-seeded receptacle restored its growth. Removing pips from only one strip gave a strawberry that grew only where seeds remained.

The number and spread of seeds affect the size and shape of the fruit. Fruits with few or unevenly spread fertilised seeds are small or misshapen, e.g. poorly pollinated strawberries and apples, which is one reason good pollination matters to growers.

Technology link: seedless fruits (parthenocarpy, fruit formation without fertilisation). Growers spray unpollinated flowers with auxins (e.g. tomatoes) or gibberellins so that the fruit grows without seeds. Gibberellins are sprayed on seedless grape varieties to make the grapes larger.
Some plants form fruit naturally without seeds, e.g. cultivated bananas, which are sterile (triploid, having three sets of chromosomes) plants.
Pulling the block together: a seed is how a flowering plant makes new individuals, protects them, feeds them, spreads them and gets them through hard times.

A seed carries the next generation. The embryo is a new individual formed by sexual reproduction, with half its genes from each parent, so seeds give genetic variation within the species. There is more on this in Mitosis and meiosis.
The testa protects the embryo, and the food store supplies it until the seedling can photosynthesise (make its own food using light).
Seeds, within fruits, allow the plant to spread to new places, away from the parent. This reduces competition between parent and offspring for light, water and nutrients.
Dry seeds with a tough testa can survive conditions that would kill the parent plant, such as winter or drought, so they carry the species through to a new growing season.
Developing seeds make the growth regulators that cause the fruit to form, and the fruit in turn protects and disperses the seeds.

Dispersal is the carrying of fruits and seeds away from the parent plant. Plants cannot move, so dispersal is how they spread their offspring, and it gives the young plants a much better chance of surviving.

Dispersal reduces competition between the young plants and the parent, and among the young plants themselves, for light, water, minerals and space, because seeds spread out are not all drawing on the same patch of soil.
Dispersal lets the species colonise new areas and new habitats, so it can grow beyond the place where the parent happens to live.
Dispersal spreads the population out, so a local disaster, such as disease, fire or flooding, is less likely to destroy all of it.
Seeds that fall directly under the parent are usually shaded and short of water and minerals, so few survive. Plants produce many seeds because most are lost during dispersal or eaten.

Sustainability link: the ability of some plants to spread their seeds widely makes them invasive (they take over) when introduced to new countries, e.g. Himalayan balsam, an invasive plant along Irish rivers with exploding seed pods.
Dispersal works through fruits, so it helps to know what a fruit is. The type of fruit a plant makes decides which dispersal method suits it.

A fruit is a mature ovary (the part of the flower that holds the ovules) containing seeds; its wall is the pericarp. It protects the seeds and is adapted to disperse them. Botanically, many foods called vegetables are fruits, e.g. tomatoes, cucumbers and pea pods.
Fleshy (succulent) fruits have a soft, juicy pericarp, often brightly coloured and sweet when ripe, e.g. blackberry, tomato and cherry; they are mostly dispersed by animals that eat them.
Dry fruits have a hard or papery pericarp, e.g. pea pod, hazelnut and sycamore; they are dispersed by wind, water, animals carrying them, or by splitting open.
A false fruit is one in which other parts of the flower, not only the ovary, form the fruit, e.g. strawberry, where the fleshy part is the receptacle (the swollen top of the flower stalk).
Wind carries a fruit or seed further the more slowly it falls. Wind-dispersed plants therefore make fruits or seeds that are light and have a large surface area compared with their mass.
Adaptations: fruits or seeds are small and light, or have wings or parachutes that increase their surface area, so they fall slowly and are carried further by the wind.
Parachutes: dandelion and thistle fruits each carry a parachute of fine hairs that lets them float long distances.
Wings: sycamore has paired winged fruits and ash has single winged fruits. The wing makes the fruit spin like a helicopter blade as it falls, slowing it so the wind carries it away from the parent.

Censer (pepper-pot) mechanism: the poppy's dry fruit, a capsule, has a ring of pores near the top. When the wind sways the stalk, the tiny seeds are shaken out a few at a time, like pepper from a shaker.
Dust-like seeds: orchid seeds are so tiny and light that they are blown like dust.
Plants growing beside or on water use it to carry their offspring. The key adaptation is the ability to float, so the fruit is carried rather than sinking.
Adaptations: fruits or seeds that float, because they contain air spaces or have a light, waterproof covering, so they can be carried by streams, rivers or the sea.
Coconut: the fruit has a thick, fibrous, air-filled husk and a waterproof outer layer, so it floats for long periods and is carried by ocean currents to other shores and islands.
Alder: a tree of riverbanks whose small fruits contain air and float, and are carried downstream to settle on new banks.
Some plants use animals as couriers by offering them food. The animal eats the fruit, and the seeds travel inside it before being left somewhere new.
Fleshy fruits are eaten by birds and mammals. The animal digests the fleshy pericarp, but the seeds have a tough testa (the hard seed coat) or a hard stone that resists digestion.
The seeds pass out in the faeces, often far from the parent, and the droppings act as a supply of minerals.
Adaptations: bright colours (often red, black or purple) when ripe, attracting birds; sweet, juicy, nutritious flesh as a reward for the animal.
Unripe fruit is green and sour while the seeds are unripe, so the fruit isn't eaten too early, before the seeds can survive and grow.
Examples: blackberry, holly berries and rowan berries (eaten by birds), and tomato.
Animal caching: squirrels and jays bury acorns and hazelnuts as winter stores and fail to recover some, which then grow into new trees.
Other plants do not offer food. Instead their fruits hitch a ride on the outside of an animal.
Fruits have hooks or sticky surfaces that catch on the fur or feathers of passing animals (or on human clothing). They fall or are brushed off later, away from the parent.
Examples: burdock has hooked burs; goosegrass (cleavers) has small fruits covered in hooked hairs.
Technology link: the hooked burs of burdock inspired Velcro, invented by the Swiss engineer George de Mestral after he found burs stuck to his dog's coat.
A few plants need no outside carrier. The fruit itself throws the seeds out.
Some dry fruits split open forcefully as they dry, flinging the seeds out: gorse and pea pods twist and burst in dry weather, and Himalayan balsam pods explode when touched.
Each method of dispersal goes with a matching set of adaptations and named examples. Learn them as method, adaptation and example together.
Wind: wings, parachutes and light seeds (sycamore, ash, dandelion, poppy).
Animal, internal: fleshy, coloured, edible fruits with indigestible seeds (blackberry, holly).

Diagram: labelled drawings of one fruit for each method: sycamore (wing and seed), dandelion (parachute of hairs and the fruit containing a seed), burdock bur (hooks) and blackberry (fleshy fruit and seeds). A coconut in section (fibrous, air-filled husk and seed) is optional.

Every cell has to take in what it needs and get rid of what it doesn't, and the cell membrane is the gatekeeper that controls this. Understanding what the membrane lets through, and how, explains the three transport processes in this subsection.

Every cell is surrounded by a cell membrane: a phospholipid bilayer (a double layer of fat-based molecules) with proteins scattered through it, known as the fluid mosaic model. The membranes around organelles (the small working parts inside a cell) are built the same way.

Materials constantly cross the membrane: cells take in oxygen (O₂), glucose, water and ions (charged particles), and release carbon dioxide (CO₂) and wastes such as urea. This is the transport and transfer of materials across membranes.

The membrane is selectively permeable: it lets some substances through and not others. Small, non-polar molecules (ones with no electrical charge difference across them) such as oxygen and carbon dioxide pass straight through the bilayer.

Water passes through slowly between the phospholipids and quickly through protein water channels (aquaporins). Ions and large polar molecules such as glucose cross only through specific channel or carrier proteins, and large molecules such as proteins and starch cannot cross at all.

Three terms for barriers are easy to mix up. Fully permeable lets water and all solutes through, e.g. the plant cell wall. Semi-permeable (partially permeable) lets water and small molecules through but not larger ones, by the size of its pores, e.g. Visking (dialysis) tubing.
Selectively permeable describes a living membrane, which controls what crosses using its proteins and, unlike the other two, can move substances actively (using energy).

A solution is a solute (e.g. sugar or salt) dissolved in a solvent (water). A concentrated solution has much solute and so a lower concentration of water; a dilute solution has little solute and so a higher concentration of water.
Diffusion is the simplest way for substances to move in and out of cells, and it needs no energy from the cell. It is the baseline against which osmosis and active transport are compared.

Diffusion is the net movement of molecules or ions from a region of their higher concentration to a region of their lower concentration, until they are evenly spread. The difference in concentration between two regions is the concentration gradient, and diffusion is movement down the gradient.
Diffusion is passive: it needs no energy from the cell (no ATP, the cell's energy-carrying molecule), because it results from the random movement of particles, which have kinetic (movement) energy.

Individual particles move in all directions, but more move from the crowded region than into it, which gives the net movement. It happens in gases and liquids, in living and non-living systems, with or without a membrane.

Examples in living things: oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli (the air sacs of the lungs) into the blood while carbon dioxide diffuses the other way. There is more on this in Gas exchange and the breathing mechanism.

Carbon dioxide diffuses into a leaf through the stomata (pores) while oxygen diffuses out, and digested food molecules diffuse from the small intestine into the blood. A non-living example is the scent of perfume spreading through a room.

Facilitated diffusion is passive diffusion of ions and polar molecules, such as glucose, down their concentration gradient through specific channel or carrier proteins. They need the proteins because they cannot cross the bilayer directly; it still needs no ATP, e.g. glucose enters red blood cells this way.

Factors that increase the rate of diffusion are a steeper concentration gradient, higher temperature (particles move faster), a larger surface area, a shorter distance (a thinner barrier) and smaller particles.

Exchange surfaces such as alveoli and villi (finger-like folds of the small intestine wall) have a large surface area, a thin wall and a steep gradient kept up by blood flow, so diffusion is fast. Osmosis depends on the same factors.
Water crosses membranes by its own process, because it is a small molecule that moves in and out of cells all the time. Osmosis is diffusion of water, and it explains why cells swell and shrink.

Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water concentration (a dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (a more concentrated solution) across a semi-permeable (selectively permeable) membrane.
Osmosis is a special case of diffusion: it is the diffusion of water only, and it happens only across a membrane that lets water through but holds back the solute. It is passive and needs no ATP.

Why water moves: solute molecules attract water molecules around them, so fewer water molecules are free to move in a concentrated solution. More free water molecules cross the membrane from the dilute side than from the concentrated side.

This gives a net flow of water into the concentrated solution, until the concentrations are equal or a pressure, such as that of a cell wall, stops it. Water still crosses in both directions; the flow is only greater one way.

Diagram: a U-tube (or beaker) divided by a semi-permeable membrane, dilute solution one side, concentrated sucrose solution the other; larger arrow of water towards the concentrated side, liquid level rising there. Label: semi-permeable membrane, water molecule, sucrose molecule (too large to cross), net movement of water.
Cells sit in watery surroundings, so osmosis decides whether they gain or lose water. Animal cells and plant cells react differently because plant cells have a cell wall.

Three terms describe the solution outside a cell compared with the cell's contents. Hypotonic means more dilute than the cell, so water enters the cell; hypertonic means more concentrated than the cell, so water leaves it; isotonic means the same concentration, so there is no net movement.
Animal cells in a hypotonic solution (e.g. pure water) gain water, swell and may burst, because they have no cell wall to hold them in. Red blood cells bursting is called haemolysis.

In a hypertonic solution animal cells lose water and shrink, and red blood cells become shrivelled and spiky (crenated). This is why body fluids must be kept isotonic with cells (osmoregulation). There is more on this in Water.

Plant cells in a hypotonic solution take water into the vacuole (the large water-filled sac in the cell). The cytoplasm is pushed against the cell wall, which resists further swelling, so the cell becomes turgid (firm) and doesn't burst. The pressure of the contents against the wall is turgor pressure.
Plant cells in a hypertonic solution lose water from the vacuole. The cell becomes flaccid (soft), then the cytoplasm and cell membrane shrink away from the cell wall, which is called plasmolysis.

The gap between wall and membrane fills with the outside solution, because the cell wall is fully permeable. Plasmolysis can be reversed (deplasmolysis) if the cell is put back into water before it is damaged.

Diagram: a plant cell in water (turgid, large vacuole, cytoplasm pressed against wall), in isotonic solution (flaccid) and in concentrated solution (plasmolysed, membrane and cytoplasm pulled from wall). Label: cell wall, cell membrane, vacuole, cytoplasm. Also red blood cells in water (swollen, bursting), isotonic (normal disc) and concentrated solution (crenated).
Diffusion and osmosis only move things down a gradient, but cells often need to collect substances that are already scarcer outside than inside. Active transport does this by spending energy.

Active transport is the movement of molecules or ions across a membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration, against the concentration gradient, using energy from ATP.

Because it needs ATP, active transport happens only in living cells and depends on respiration (the process that makes ATP). It stops or slows if respiration is stopped, e.g. by lack of oxygen, low temperature or a respiratory poison such as cyanide.
Cells that carry out much active transport have many mitochondria (the organelles that make ATP), e.g. root hair cells, cells lining the kidney tubules and cells of the small intestine.
Root hair cells take up mineral ions, e.g. nitrate, from soil water in which they are more dilute than in the cell. There is more on this in Transport in Plants.
Glucose and amino acids are absorbed from the small intestine into the blood, and reabsorbed from the kidney tubules (the tiny tubes that filter blood) into the blood, by active transport.
Active transport is carried out by carrier proteins in the membrane, which act as pumps. Each pump works in the same four steps.
1. The substance binds to a specific carrier protein (a pump) in the membrane, so each pump moves only the substance it fits.
2. ATP made in respiration releases energy, which changes the shape of the carrier protein.
3. The change in shape moves the substance across the membrane and releases it on the other side.
4. The carrier returns to its original shape, ready to pick up another molecule.

Diagram: a carrier protein in a phospholipid bilayer, a molecule binding on the low-concentration side, ATP → ADP + Pi releasing energy, carrier changing shape, molecule released on the high-concentration side. Label: carrier protein, phospholipid bilayer, ATP, direction of movement against the gradient.
This carrier pump moves two ions in opposite directions at once. It is found in animal cells and is essential for nerves.

The sodium–potassium pump is a carrier protein in the membranes of animal cells, including nerve cells. It uses one ATP to pump three sodium ions (Na⁺) out of the cell and two potassium ions (K⁺) into it, both against their concentration gradients.
It keeps Na⁺ high outside the cell and K⁺ high inside, which nerve cells need in order to carry impulses, and it helps control cell volume.
The three processes are easy to confuse, so exams ask you to compare them. Compare them on the same five points each time: energy, direction, what moves, membrane and proteins, and where they happen.
Energy: diffusion and osmosis are passive, so they need no ATP; active transport needs ATP from respiration.

Direction: diffusion and osmosis go down a concentration gradient (high to low concentration of the substance moving; for osmosis, the water concentration), whereas active transport goes against it, from low to high.
What moves: diffusion moves any particle, gases and solutes alike; osmosis moves only water; active transport moves particular solutes, mainly ions and small molecules such as glucose, but not water.

Membrane and proteins: diffusion can happen with or without a membrane and needs no proteins for small non-polar molecules; osmosis needs a semi-permeable membrane; active transport needs specific carrier proteins in a living membrane.
Where: diffusion and osmosis happen in living and non-living systems, e.g. Visking tubing, but active transport happens only in living cells, because it depends on respiration.
Food goes off because microorganisms feed on it, and microorganisms need water to live. Adding a lot of salt or sugar turns osmosis against them: it pulls water out of their cells.

Food spoils mainly because bacteria and fungi (moulds and yeasts) grow on it, digesting it and making it unsafe or unpleasant to eat. Like all cells, they need water for their enzymes to work and to grow and reproduce.
Mechanism, step 1: a high concentration of salt or sugar is added to the food.
2. The food's water is now a concentrated (hypertonic) solution compared with the cytoplasm (the watery contents) of any microorganism on it.
3. Water leaves the microbial cells by osmosis, moving from the more dilute cytoplasm to the more concentrated solution outside.

4. The cells are dehydrated and plasmolysed (the cell membrane shrinks away from the cell wall; bacteria and fungi have cell walls), so their enzymes can't work and they can't grow or reproduce; many die.
The salt or sugar also binds water in the food, so less free water is available to any microbe.
Preserving by drying (e.g. dried fruit and dried fish) works by removing water directly, which has the same effect on microbes. It is related to osmosis but is not osmosis itself.
Three traditional methods preserve food with salt, sugar or acid. Salt and sugar work by osmosis, but acid works in a different way, by its low pH.

Salting: meat and fish are rubbed with dry salt or soaked in strong brine (salt solution), e.g. bacon, ham and salted fish. Salt also draws water out of the food itself by osmosis, drying it further, so even less water is left for microbes.
Sugaring: fruit is preserved in a high concentration of sugar, e.g. jam, marmalade and candied fruit; fruit is also stored in heavy syrup.
Honey keeps for a very long time because its sugar concentration is so high that microbes lose water to it instead of growing.
Pickling: vegetables kept in vinegar are preserved mainly by the low pH of the acid (ethanoic acid), which stops enzymes and microbes working, not by osmosis.
Brine pickles (salt solutions) combine osmosis with acid made by fermentation (microbes breaking down sugars in the vegetable), so both effects protect the food.
Osmotic preservation is useful but not perfect. To evaluate it, weigh what it does well against where it fails and what it does to our health.
Advantages: it is cheap, simple and traditional; it needs no refrigeration, so it was used for long journeys and winter stores; and it works against both bacteria and fungi.
Limits: some microorganisms tolerate high salt or sugar concentrations, especially moulds and yeasts, so jam can still grow mould on its surface once opened and should be refrigerated.

Preservation fails if the salt or sugar concentration is too low, because there is then not enough of a concentration difference to draw water out of microbes. For example, reduced-sugar jams spoil faster.
Osmotic preservation slows microbial growth but doesn't sterilise the food (kill all microbes). It is usually combined with other methods, such as cooking, sealing, refrigeration, smoking and acids.
Health link: salted foods add much salt to the diet, and high salt intake is linked to high blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart disease and stroke.
Sugary preserves add sugar, which is linked to tooth decay and obesity. So salting and sugaring are used less today, and refrigeration and freezing more. There is more on this in Diet.
Osmosis also affects food preparation: salting sliced vegetables, e.g. cucumber and aubergine, draws water out of them.
Limp vegetables, e.g. celery and lettuce, become crisp again when placed in cold water, because their cells take in water by osmosis and become turgid (swollen and firm with water).
Plant cells stay firm because they are filled with water taken in by osmosis, and this water pressure does several jobs for the plant.
Healthy plants keep their cells turgid (full of water and pushing outwards) by taking in water by osmosis into the vacuole (the large sap-filled space) of each cell.
The turgor pressure of cells pressing against their walls supports non-woody plants, leaves and flowers, holding them upright and spreading leaves to the light for photosynthesis.
Turgor pressure drives cell enlargement: young cells expand as water enters their vacuoles, so plant growth depends on water uptake by osmosis.

Guard cells (the pair of cells around each stoma, the tiny pore in a leaf) open the stomata when they become turgid and close them when they become flaccid (soft and limp from losing water), controlling gas exchange and water loss. There is more on this in Transport in Plants.
Wilting: when water is lost from the leaves by transpiration (evaporation from the leaf) faster than the roots take it up, the cells lose water, become flaccid, and the plant wilts.
Wilting closes the stomata, so less carbon dioxide gets in and it reduces photosynthesis and growth. It is reversed if water is supplied soon enough; prolonged wilting kills the plant.
Roots rely on the soil water being more dilute than their own cells. If that balance flips, osmosis runs the wrong way and the plant loses water even though the soil is wet.
Roots take in water by osmosis because the soil water is normally more dilute than the cell sap (the solution in the vacuole) of the root cells. There is more on this in Transport in Plants.

If the soil water becomes more concentrated than the contents of the root cells, water stops entering the roots and can leave them by osmosis. The root cells become plasmolysed, the plant cannot take up enough water, and it wilts and may die, even in moist soil.
Causes of salty soil water: flooding of coastal land by seawater (e.g. storm surges), and salt spread on roads in icy weather, which damages roadside trees and hedges.
Irrigation (watering crops artificially) in hot, dry regions is another cause: water evaporates and leaves salts behind in the soil (salinisation), lowering crop yields.

Fertiliser burn: applying too much fertiliser, especially concentrated fertiliser close to roots or on dry soil, makes the soil solution too concentrated, so water leaves the roots and the leaves turn brown and scorched.
Advice to avoid fertiliser burn: apply the recommended amount, spread it evenly and water it in. Salt was used in the past as a weedkiller for the same reason.
Some plants of salty habitats, such as salt marshes and seashores, survive because their root cells hold a higher solute concentration than the salty soil water, so water still enters by osmosis.

Sustainability link: soil salinisation from irrigation, and seawater flooding linked to rising sea levels and stronger storms, reduce the land available for crops. Careful irrigation and drainage reduce salinisation.
This investigation tests three factors that could change how fast osmosis happens, and the key problem is choosing something you can actually measure.
Aim: to investigate how temperature, the concentration gradient (the difference in concentration across the membrane) and surface area affect the rate of osmosis across a semi-permeable membrane.
Water entering a bag of sucrose solution increases the bag's mass, so the rate of osmosis is the change in mass per unit time (g per minute), or the percentage change in mass in a fixed time.
For potato tissue the percentage change in mass in a fixed time is used, because the pieces start at slightly different masses and a percentage makes them comparable.

An alternative for Visking bags (bags made from Visking tubing, a thin tubing with tiny pores) is the rise of liquid up a capillary tube attached to the bag, called an osmometer. The rate is then measured in mm per minute.
Every version of the investigation uses the same core kit and a range of sucrose solutions, and each value of the factor is repeated so that a stray result does not mislead you.

Equipment and materials: Visking tubing; thread or tubing clips; sucrose solutions and distilled water; syringes or measuring cylinders; beakers or boiling tubes; paper towels; stopwatch; scissors; labels; safety glasses.
For temperature and measuring: thermostatically controlled water baths (or beakers of water heated and topped up, with ice for low temperatures) and thermometers; a top-pan balance reading to 0.01 g.
For potato: a fresh potato, a white tile, a scalpel, a ruler and a cork borer (a metal tube that cuts cylinders of tissue).
Sucrose solutions: a 1.0 M (mol per litre) solution contains 342 g of sucrose made up to 1 litre with distilled water. This works because 342 is the mass of one mole of sucrose.

A range, such as 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 M, is made by diluting the 1.0 M solution with distilled water. For example, 2 cm³ of 1.0 M plus 8 cm³ of water gives 0.2 M. There is more on dilution in Investigation: reducing sugars, quantitatively.
Replicates (repeats): set up three bags, or three sets of potato pieces, for each value of the factor and calculate the mean, so that one odd result has less effect.
Repeat the whole investigation to check repeatability, which means getting similar results when the experiment is done again.
Two of the three investigations use a Visking tubing bag as a model cell. The bag has to be made the same way every time, or differences in the bags will hide the effect you are testing.
1. Cut pieces of Visking tubing of the same length, e.g. 15 cm, and soak them in water for a few minutes until soft, so the tubing can be opened without tearing.
2. Rub one end between finger and thumb to open the tube.
3. Tie one end tightly with thread, or knot the tubing itself, so that nothing can leak out.
4. Using a syringe, add the same volume, e.g. 10 cm³, of sucrose solution to each bag, so that the bags can be compared fairly.
5. Squeeze out the air and tie the other end tightly, leaving the bag slightly slack so it can swell as water enters.
6. Rinse the outside with distilled water to remove any sucrose, blot it dry with paper towel in the same way every time, and weigh it. Surface liquid would otherwise add to the mass.
7. Record this starting mass, which you need in order to work out the change in mass.
Visking tubing is used because it behaves like a simple version of a cell membrane. Knowing what it lets through explains why the bag gains mass.
Visking tubing is semi-permeable: its tiny pores let water molecules through easily but hold back larger molecules.
Sucrose molecules pass only very slowly, so over a short experiment the bag behaves as a membrane permeable to water but not to sucrose, as cell membranes do. Starch is held back completely.
Visking tubing is semi-permeable (partially permeable), not selectively permeable in the way a living membrane is, because it only sorts molecules by size.

Diagram: a tied Visking bag of sucrose solution in a beaker of distilled water, arrow showing water entering; and an osmometer (bag tied to an upright, clamped capillary tube, ruler beside it). Label: Visking tubing, sucrose solution, distilled water, thread, capillary tube, scale.
The first factor is the concentration gradient. Here the bag holds sucrose solution and the beaker holds distilled water, so the gradient is set by how concentrated the solution inside the bag is.

Hypothesis: the greater the concentration gradient between the solution inside the bag and the water outside, the faster the rate of osmosis, because the difference in water concentration across the membrane is greater, so the net movement of water is faster.

Independent variable (the one you change): the concentration of sucrose inside the bag (0.2 to 1.0 M), with distilled water outside. The gradient therefore increases with concentration. Dependent variable (the one you measure): the rate of mass gain (g per minute).

Controlled variables (kept the same): temperature (all at room temperature, or in one water bath, e.g. 25 °C), length and width of tubing (surface area), volume of solution in the bag, volume of distilled water outside, time intervals and blotting method.

Control: a bag containing distilled water, placed in distilled water, so there is no concentration gradient. Its mass should not change, which shows that any change in the other bags is due to osmosis and not to handling, leaking or water left on the surface.
This is the main method. You weigh the bags at regular intervals to follow how fast each one gains mass.
1. Make one bag for each concentration (three of each), plus the control, using the steps for making a Visking tubing bag.
3. Place each bag in its own labelled beaker of distilled water, enough to cover it, and start the stopwatch.
4. Every 10 minutes, for 40 to 60 minutes, remove each bag, blot it dry in the same way, weigh it, and return it to the water.
5. Calculate the mean change in mass for each concentration and the rate in g per minute.

Living tissue can be used instead of a bag. A potato is made of cells whose membranes act as semi-permeable membranes, and the sap inside the cells is the solution. The egg is an optional demonstration.
Second method, potato tissue. 1. Use a cork borer to cut cylinders from one potato, remove the skin, and cut them all to the same length, e.g. 3 cm, on a tile.

3. Place three cylinders in each of a range of sucrose solutions (0.0 M, i.e. distilled water, and 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 M) of the same volume, for the same time (e.g. at least 30 minutes; often left overnight) at the same temperature.
4. Remove them, blot in the same way, reweigh, and calculate the percentage change in mass, which allows for the different starting masses.
5. Plot percentage change in mass against sucrose concentration.

Third method (optional demonstration): an egg whose shell has been dissolved in vinegar over a day or two is held in by its membrane, which is semi-permeable. Placed in distilled water it gains mass, and in concentrated sugar syrup it loses mass.
The egg shows the direction of osmosis clearly, but it is slow and gives only one result per egg.
The second factor is temperature. Visking bags are used here, with the same sucrose concentration in every bag, so that temperature is the only thing that changes.
Hypothesis: the higher the temperature, the faster the rate of osmosis, because water molecules have more kinetic energy (movement energy) and move faster, so more cross the membrane each second.
Independent variable: the temperature, e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C. Dependent variable: the rate of mass gain (g per minute) of the Visking bags.
Controlled variables: sucrose concentration (e.g. 0.5 M in every bag), volume of solution, length and width of tubing, volume of distilled water, time intervals and blotting method.
Control: at each temperature, a bag of distilled water in distilled water, which should show no mass change.

Visking tubing is used rather than potato for temperature, because high temperatures damage the cell membranes of living tissue, making them fully permeable, so the cells would no longer show osmosis.
The bags and the water must both reach the bath's temperature before the timing starts, or the bag will not be at the temperature you think it is.
1. Set water baths to each temperature (use iced water for 10 °C) and check each with a thermometer.
2. Place beakers of distilled water, and boiling tubes of the 0.5 M sucrose solution, in each bath until they reach its temperature.
3. Make the bags with the warmed or cooled solution, using the steps for making a Visking tubing bag, and weigh them.
4. Place three bags in the beaker of distilled water in each bath.
5. Every 10 minutes for 40 minutes, remove, blot, weigh and return each bag, checking the bath temperature each time.
6. Calculate the mean rate (g per minute) at each temperature.

The third factor is surface area. Cutting the same amount of potato into more pieces gives more membrane in contact with the solution while the volume stays the same, so only the surface area changes.
Hypothesis: the larger the surface area of membrane in contact with the solution, the faster the rate of osmosis, because more water molecules can cross the membranes at the same time.
Independent variable: the surface area of potato tissue, changed by cutting the same volume into more pieces. Dependent variable: the percentage change in total mass in a fixed time.

Controlled variables: the total volume (and starting mass) of potato, from the same potato with no skin; the concentration and volume of the solution (e.g. 0.8 M sucrose, or distilled water); temperature, time and blotting method.
Cut 2 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm cubes, each of volume 8 cm³. Leave one cube whole, with surface area 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cm².
Cut one cube in half to give two 2 × 2 × 1 cm slabs, with surface area 2 × 16 = 32 cm².
Cut one cube into four 2 × 1 × 1 cm bars, with surface area 4 × 10 = 40 cm². Cut one cube into eight 1 cm cubes, with surface area 8 × 6 = 48 cm².
The total volume is 8 cm³ in every case, so only the surface area differs, which makes it a fair test.
No separate control is needed, because the treatments are compared with each other; the whole 2 cm cube is the reference. The surface area to volume idea links to Levels of organisation.
Each set of pieces is weighed as a group, so the result is the percentage change in the total mass of the set.
1. Cut the pieces from one potato on a tile, as above, with three sets of each.
2. Blot each set and weigh all its pieces together.
3. Place each set in its own beaker containing the same volume of the same solution, at the same temperature.
4. After a fixed time, e.g. 30 minutes, remove them, blot each piece in the same way, and reweigh the set.
5. Calculate the percentage change in mass for each set, and the mean for each surface area.
Raw masses are only useful once they are turned into a rate or a percentage change. These are the formulas and two worked examples for you to copy the method from.
Change in mass = final mass minus initial mass. Rate = change in mass divided by time.
Percentage change in mass = (final mass minus initial mass) divided by initial mass, multiplied by 100. A gain is positive; a loss is negative.
Worked example, Visking bag: initial mass 12.40 g, mass after 30 minutes 13.30 g. Change = +0.90 g. Rate = 0.90 ÷ 30 = 0.03 g per minute. Percentage change = 0.90 ÷ 12.40 × 100 = 7.3%.
Worked example, potato: a cylinder of 2.50 g has a mass of 2.20 g after 30 minutes in 1.0 M sucrose. Change = −0.30 g, and percentage change = −0.30 ÷ 2.50 × 100 = −12%.
A cylinder of 2.00 g that becomes 2.30 g in distilled water has a change of +0.30 g, so percentage change = +0.30 ÷ 2.00 × 100 = +15%.
Graphs: plot the factor (independent variable) on the x-axis and the rate or percentage change in mass (dependent variable) on the y-axis, using the mean of the replicates.
Alternatively plot mass against time for each value, where a steeper line shows a faster rate, because mass is changing more quickly.
This investigation uses sharp tools, hot water and sugar solution, so each hazard needs a simple precaution.
Cut potato on a white tile, cutting away from the body and fingers; carry scalpels and cork borers safely.
Hot water baths: use a test-tube holder or tongs to handle beakers and bags in water above about 40 °C, and keep baths at or below 50 °C to avoid scalds.
Glass capillary tubes break easily and are sharp; handle and clamp them carefully, and wear safety glasses.
Mop up spilt sugar solution at once, as it makes floors slippery; keep water away from electrical sockets and water-bath controls.
Don't eat any food materials used. If using eggs, wash hands after handling raw egg.
Each factor gives a typical pattern. A good conclusion states the pattern, uses your own data and says whether it supports the hypothesis.

Concentration gradient (Visking): the bags gain mass, faster with higher sucrose concentration, and the control bag stays the same. Conclusion: the rate of osmosis increases as the concentration gradient increases.
In every bag the mass gain slows over time, because the entering water dilutes the solution inside, reducing the gradient, and the bag becomes tight.

Concentration (potato): cylinders gain mass and feel firm (turgid) in distilled water and dilute solutions, because water enters the cells. They lose mass and feel soft and bendy (flaccid) in concentrated solutions, because water leaves the cells.

The larger the difference between the solution and the cell sap, the larger the change. Where the graph line crosses zero change, the solution has the same water concentration as the cell sap (isotonic), so there is no net osmosis.
Temperature: the rate of mass gain increases steadily as temperature increases. Conclusion: the rate of osmosis increases with temperature.
There is no optimum and no sharp fall at high temperature, because no enzyme is involved and Visking tubing isn't denatured (it keeps its shape and does not stop working when hot).

Surface area: the percentage change in mass in the same time is greatest for the eight 1 cm cubes (48 cm²) and least for the whole cube (24 cm²). Conclusion: the rate of osmosis increases with surface area.
Each conclusion should quote the primary data (your own measured results), e.g. the mean rates, and say whether they support the hypothesis.
No school experiment is perfect. Knowing what can go wrong, and how to reduce it, lets you explain unexpected results and suggest improvements.

Blotting: leaving more or less surface water on bags or potato pieces changes the mass, so blot in exactly the same way each time. Potato cut into more pieces holds more surface liquid, which can exaggerate the surface-area effect.
Leaks: badly tied bags leak, so check the knots and discard any leaking bag. Some sucrose diffuses slowly out of Visking tubing, reducing the gradient over time.
Bags or pieces that differ in size, volume of solution or trapped air are not fair comparisons; measure volumes with a syringe and cut potato accurately.
Water-bath temperatures drift, and bags cool while being weighed; check the temperature at each reading and weigh quickly.
A balance reading only to 0.1 g or 1 g can't detect small changes; use one reading to 0.01 g.

Potato tissue varies, between different potatoes or between the centre and edge of one potato; cut all pieces from one potato and use replicates. Cut surfaces are damaged cells that don't behave normally.
Results from Visking tubing model a membrane, but they don't show what living, selectively permeable membranes do, such as moving substances actively.

Every cell produces waste as it carries out its chemical reactions, and some of that waste is harmful if it stays in the body. The kidneys are the main organs that clear it away, and they do a second job at the same time: keeping the body's fluids balanced.

Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism (the chemical reactions in cells). Faeces are not excreted: they are undigested food that was never absorbed, so passing them out is egestion.
The kidneys excrete urea, excess water, excess salts and excess hydrogen ions in urine. Other organs help: the lungs excrete carbon dioxide, and sweat removes some water, salts and a little urea.

Urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids (the units of proteins) by deamination, the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of an amino acid. It is carried dissolved in the blood plasma to the kidneys.
Urea is toxic if it builds up, so it must be removed continuously rather than in occasional bursts.

Transport between environments: blood (the internal environment) carries wastes to the kidneys, the kidneys transfer them from the blood into urine, and urine is passed out of the body (the external environment).
At the same time the kidneys return useful substances (glucose, amino acids, most of the water and most of the salts) to the blood, so nutrients are not lost in the urine.
The kidneys have two roles: excretion (removing urea and other wastes), and osmoregulation and homeostasis, which regulate the volume, water content, salt concentration and pH of the body fluids.
Both roles use the same two processes: filtration of the blood (squeezing small molecules out of it), then reabsorption (taking back what the body needs). What is not reabsorbed is urine.
The kidneys sit well protected at the back of the body and are supplied directly by a large artery. That position and supply let them filter a large volume of blood at high pressure.
The kidneys are a pair of bean-shaped organs at the back of the abdomen, one on each side of the vertebral column (backbone), just below the diaphragm. The lowest ribs partly protect them.
The right kidney is slightly lower than the left because the liver lies above it and takes up space.
Each kidney is embedded in a layer of fat that cushions it against physical damage and helps hold it in place, and is covered by a tough outer membrane, the renal capsule.
The adrenal glands (small hormone-producing glands) sit on top of the kidneys.
Each kidney receives blood from a renal artery, a short wide branch of the aorta (the body's main artery), so blood arrives at high pressure and in large volume, which suits filtration.
Filtered blood leaves by the renal vein, which joins the vena cava (the large vein returning blood to the heart).

Blood in the renal vein has less urea, less oxygen and less glucose than blood in the renal artery, and more carbon dioxide because the kidney cells respire. It is the blood vessel with the lowest urea concentration in the body.

Diagram: front view of the urinary system. Label two kidneys, renal arteries from the aorta, renal veins to the vena cava, ureters, bladder, sphincter muscles and urethra. The adrenal glands on top of the kidneys may be shown.
Once urine has formed it must be carried away, stored and released at a suitable moment. Three structures do this in turn: the ureters carry it, the bladder stores it and the urethra lets it out.
There are two ureters: narrow muscular tubes, one from the renal pelvis (the funnel-shaped collecting space inside each kidney) down to the bladder.
The ureter walls contain smooth muscle that moves urine by peristalsis (waves of contraction), so urine reaches the bladder whatever the body position, not just by gravity.
The urinary bladder is a hollow muscular bag in the lower abdomen (pelvis) that stores urine.
The bladder wall is elastic and folded, so it can stretch to hold a large volume and contract to empty.

Two rings of sphincter muscle (muscle that closes an opening) at the bladder outlet keep it closed: an inner one that works automatically (involuntary), and an outer one under conscious (voluntary) control, which young children learn to control.
The urethra is the single tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body.
In males the urethra is longer, runs through the penis and also carries semen. In females it is short and opens just in front of the vagina.
Cut a kidney lengthways and you can see that it is not uniform inside. The three regions each have a different role in making and collecting urine.
A kidney cut lengthways shows three regions: cortex, medulla and renal pelvis.
Cortex: the dark outer layer, under the renal capsule.
Medulla: the paler inner layer, divided into cone-shaped renal pyramids.

Renal pelvis: a funnel-shaped space on the inner (concave) side that collects urine and leads into the ureter. No filtration happens in the pelvis and urine is not changed there, so it is only a collecting space.
The real work of the kidney is done by microscopic tubes called nephrons. Each one first filters the blood, then takes back what the body needs, and the leftover liquid becomes urine.

Each kidney contains about one million nephrons, microscopic tubules that are the kidney's filtering units, so together they give a huge filtering surface. Each runs from the cortex down into the medulla and back.
The nephron tubules drain into collecting ducts that run through the pyramids and open into the renal pelvis.
Filtration takes place in the cortex: blood is forced at high pressure through knots of capillaries (glomeruli) into the cup-shaped tops of the nephrons (Bowman's capsules).

Small molecules (water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea) are filtered out of the blood. Blood cells and plasma proteins are too large, so they stay in the blood. The filtered liquid is called the filtrate.
Reabsorption (taking useful substances back into the blood) takes place in the cortex, in the coiled tubules, and in the medulla, in the loops of Henle and the collecting ducts.
All the glucose and amino acids, most of the salts and most of the water are taken back into the blood. The remaining liquid, carrying urea and excess salts and water, is urine.

Diagram: longitudinal section of a kidney. Label renal capsule, cortex, medulla, renal pyramid, renal pelvis, ureter, renal artery and renal vein. Draw one nephron from cortex into medulla to show where filtration and reabsorption happen.

Urine is what is left of the filtrate once the body has taken back what it needs. Its volume and concentration change from hour to hour, which is how the kidneys keep the water content of the blood steady.
Urine is mostly water, with urea, salts (mainly sodium chloride) and other wastes dissolved in it.
Healthy urine contains no protein and no glucose, because protein is not filtered out of the blood and all the glucose is reabsorbed.
After drinking a lot of water, the kidneys produce a large volume of dilute (pale) urine, which gets rid of the extra water.
When water is short (little drinking, heavy sweating in exercise or hot weather, or diarrhoea), a small volume of concentrated (dark yellow) urine is produced, so the body saves water.
The control is by the hormone ADH. There is more on this in ADH and osmoregulation; here you only need the effect on urine.
Water is not the only thing the kidneys balance. They also adjust salts and acidity, and together this keeps the body's internal conditions steady.
Salt balance: after a salty meal the kidneys excrete more salt, and when salt is short they reabsorb more.
Keeping the salt and water concentration of the blood steady stops body cells from gaining or losing water by osmosis (the movement of water across a membrane towards the more concentrated solution).
pH: the kidneys remove excess hydrogen ions from the blood in urine, helping to keep blood pH at about 7.4. There is more on this in Minerals.

This is homeostasis: the kidneys keep the internal environment constant whatever is eaten or drunk, much as a thermostat holds a room at one temperature. This works by negative feedback, which is taught in Homeostasis as a stimulus-response model.
Urine is made all the time, but it is passed out only now and then. This sequence shows how it travels and why release can be delayed.
1. Urine forms continuously in the nephrons and drains from the collecting ducts into the renal pelvis.
2. Peristalsis in the ureter carries it to the bladder in small spurts.
3. The bladder fills and its wall stretches. Stretch receptors in the wall send nerve impulses that give the urge to urinate.
4. To urinate, the bladder's muscular wall contracts and the sphincters relax. The outer sphincter relaxes under voluntary control, which is learned after early childhood.
5. Urine leaves the body through the urethra.
Each part of the urinary system has features that suit its job. Examiners ask you to link structure to function, so learn these as pairs.
Fat layer around each kidney: protects it from physical damage.
Renal artery branching directly from the aorta: delivers high-pressure blood for filtration.
About one million nephrons: a huge filtering surface.
Cortex full of capillary knots: the site of filtration.
Long tubules and loops in the medulla: the site of reabsorption.
Muscular ureters: move urine to the bladder by peristalsis.
Elastic bladder with sphincters: stores urine and allows controlled release. The urethra is the exit for urine from the body.
Because healthy urine contains no glucose or protein, finding either one in a urine sample tells a doctor that something is wrong.
Glucose in urine is a sign of diabetes, because blood glucose is so high that not all of it can be reabsorbed.
Protein in urine is a sign of damage to the kidney's filters, because healthy filters do not let protein through.
Urine tests are also used to detect drugs, for example in sport.
If the kidneys stop working, the body can no longer clear its wastes or balance its fluids. There are two treatments: a machine that does the kidney's job, or a replacement kidney.
If the kidneys stop working, urea, salts and water build up in the blood and the person will die without treatment.
Treatment is by dialysis or by a kidney transplant.
A transplant gives a working kidney, but the patient must take drugs to stop the immune system rejecting it, because the body treats the new kidney as foreign. There is more on this in Immunity.
A dialysis machine copies the kidney's filtering. It uses diffusion across a membrane to clean the blood.
The patient's blood is pumped through a machine where it flows past a selectively permeable membrane (one that lets only some substances through), with dialysis fluid on the other side.
Urea and excess salts diffuse out of the blood into the fluid, because their concentration is higher in the blood.
The fluid contains glucose and salts at normal blood concentrations, so these are not lost from the blood. Blood cells and proteins are too large to cross the membrane.
Dialysis must be repeated several times a week, because it does not work continuously the way healthy kidneys do.

Urine is made by tiny tubes called nephrons, so you need to know the parts of one in the order the fluid flows through them. Each part has its own job, and its position in the kidney is part of the answer.

A nephron is one of the about one million microscopic tubules in each kidney. It is the kidney's functional unit (the smallest part that does the kidney's job), where blood is filtered and urine is formed. Its wall is one cell thick throughout.

Bowman's capsule is the cup-shaped, double-walled closed end of the nephron, in the cortex (the outer layer of the kidney), wrapped around the glomerulus (a capillary knot). Its inner wall is made of special cells with gaps between them, so filtered fluid passes easily into the capsule's inner space.
The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) is the first, long, coiled (convoluted) section after the capsule, in the cortex. Proximal means nearer the capsule.
The loop of Henle is a long U-shaped loop that dips down into the medulla (the inner part of the kidney), with a descending limb going down and an ascending limb coming back up to the cortex.
The distal convoluted tubule (DCT) is the second coiled section, back in the cortex. Distal means further from the capsule. It empties into a collecting duct.
The collecting duct is a tube shared by many nephrons that runs down through the medulla, through a pyramid, and opens into the renal pelvis (the funnel that collects urine).
The syllabus does not list the collecting duct, but it is needed to explain water reabsorption and ADH. Some textbooks do not count it as part of the nephron.

A nephron works because blood is brought right up against it. The blood vessels are arranged so that pressure builds up for filtering, and so that the tubule is wrapped in a second set of capillaries (the smallest blood vessels) to take back what it reabsorbs.

A branch of the renal artery (the artery that brings blood to the kidney) divides into arterioles (small arteries). The afferent arteriole (afferent means carrying towards) brings blood to each nephron and divides into the glomerulus, a knot of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule.

The capillaries of the glomerulus rejoin to form the efferent arteriole (efferent means carrying away), which is narrower than the afferent arteriole. The afferent is the wider one, so do not say the efferent is wider.

Because blood enters the glomerulus through a wider vessel than it leaves by, pressure builds up inside the glomerulus, like water backing up behind a narrowed nozzle. This high pressure drives filtration.
The glomerulus is unusual because it is a capillary network lying between two arterioles, not between an arteriole and a venule (a small vein) as capillaries normally do.

The efferent arteriole then branches into a second capillary network that surrounds the PCT, loop of Henle and DCT closely. Substances reabsorbed from the tubule pass into these capillaries, so they must be close to the tubule.
These capillaries also supply the tubule cells with oxygen and glucose for respiration, because the cells need ATP for active transport, and they carry away the cells' carbon dioxide.
The capillaries join into venules, then into a branch of the renal vein, which carries the filtered blood back to the circulation.

Diagram: one nephron with its blood supply, labelled afferent arteriole, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, descending limb, loop of Henle, ascending limb, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct, capillary network around the tubules, branch of renal artery and branch of renal vein; draw a line marking the boundary between cortex and medulla, with the capsule, PCT and DCT above it and the loop and most of the collecting duct below; mark arrows for filtration (glomerulus into capsule) and reabsorption (tubule into capillaries).
The first step in making urine is filtration. It happens in the glomerulus and capsule, where pressure forces fluid out of the blood without checking whether the body needs it.

Filtration, also called ultrafiltration or filtration under pressure, is the forcing of small molecules out of the blood by the high pressure in the glomerulus. They pass through the pores in the capillary walls and the inner wall of Bowman's capsule, into the capsule.

Substances that pass into the filtrate (the fluid that enters the capsule) are water, glucose, amino acids, salts (e.g. sodium and chloride ions), urea (the waste made from breaking down amino acids), vitamins and some hormones.
Substances that are not filtered and stay in the blood are red and white blood cells, platelets and plasma proteins, because they are too large to pass through.

Filtration is not selective: it sorts molecules by size only, so useful substances such as glucose and amino acids are filtered out with the waste. The glomerular filtrate therefore has the same composition as blood plasma minus the proteins.

Scale: the kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid a day but produce only about 1.5 litres of urine, so about 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed (taken back into the blood); this is why reabsorption is essential.

Structure suits filtration: the wide afferent and narrow efferent arteriole raise the pressure, and the capillary wall and the capsule's inner wall are thin and porous, so fluid passes through easily.
The many capillaries in each glomerulus, with about a million glomeruli in the kidney, give a large filtering surface, so a large volume of fluid can be filtered every day.
Filtration lets everything small through, so the body has to take back what it wants. Most of this reabsorption happens in the PCT, whose structure is built for the job.
Reabsorption is the return of useful substances from the filtrate into the blood in the capillaries around the tubule. It is selective: the body keeps what it needs.
The PCT is the main site of reabsorption: all the glucose and all the amino acids, most of the salts (about two-thirds of the sodium) and most of the water (about two-thirds) are reabsorbed here.

Glucose, amino acids and sodium ions are taken up by active transport, which uses ATP (the cell's energy currency) to move them into the cells. Water follows by osmosis, and some urea diffuses back into the blood.
Water is always reabsorbed passively by osmosis; it is never actively pumped. Only salts, glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed actively in the PCT.

The PCT is long and coiled, which gives time and surface area for reabsorption. Its cells have microvilli (tiny finger-like projections) on the side facing the filtrate, greatly increasing the surface area.
The PCT cells have many mitochondria to supply ATP for active transport. The tubule is closely surrounded by capillaries, and its wall is one cell thick, so the distance to the blood is short.

The carriers in the PCT can reabsorb glucose only up to a limit. In untreated diabetes the blood glucose is so high that more glucose is filtered than the PCT can reabsorb, so glucose appears in the urine.
After the PCT, the rest of the nephron fine-tunes the filtrate. The loop of Henle makes the medulla salty, and this lets the collecting duct take back more water.

The ascending limb of the loop of Henle pumps salts (sodium and chloride ions) out into the tissue fluid of the medulla, and its wall does not let water through. This makes the medulla very salty, with the highest solute concentration deep in the medulla.

The descending limb lets water through, so water leaves it by osmosis into the salty medulla and is reabsorbed into the blood. The main job of the loop is to create this salty medulla, which lets the collecting duct reabsorb water later.
In the DCT more salts and water are reabsorbed, with the amounts adjusted to the body's needs.

The DCT also secretes some substances from the blood into the filtrate, such as hydrogen ions (to control blood pH), potassium ions and some drugs. Secretion is the opposite direction to reabsorption.

In the collecting duct, as it passes down through the salty medulla, water leaves by osmosis and is reabsorbed into the blood, so the urine becomes more concentrated. How much water is reabsorbed is controlled by ADH, a hormone. There is more on this in ADH and osmoregulation.
What remains in the collecting duct is urine: water, urea, excess salts and other wastes. Urine then drains into the renal pelvis.
Comparing the composition of blood plasma, glomerular filtrate and urine shows what each part of the nephron has done. Each difference between them has one explanation.
Protein is present in plasma but absent from the filtrate and urine, because it is too large to be filtered.

Glucose and amino acids are present in plasma and filtrate at the same concentration, because filtration lets them through freely. They are absent from urine, because all of them are reabsorbed in the PCT.
Urea is at the same concentration in plasma and filtrate, because it is freely filtered. It is much more concentrated in urine, because most of the water is reabsorbed but most of the urea is not.
Salts are similar in plasma and filtrate. In urine the amount varies with intake, because salt reabsorption is adjusted.

Skill: given a data table of plasma, filtrate and urine, explain each difference. Absent from the filtrate means not filtered (too large); absent from the urine means reabsorbed; more concentrated in the urine means water was reabsorbed and the substance was not.
