Following the fluid from the glomerulus to the renal pelvis, each part of the nephron does one main job.
Glomerulus and Bowman's capsule: filtration under pressure.
Proximal convoluted tubule: reabsorption of all glucose and amino acids, most salts and most water.
Loop of Henle: makes the medulla salty; water is reabsorbed from the descending limb.
Distal convoluted tubule: adjusts salts and water, and secretes hydrogen ions, potassium ions and some drugs.
Collecting duct: water is reabsorbed under ADH control.
Renal pelvis: receives the urine that is left.

The water content of the body is never constant on its own: we take water in and lose it all day. Osmoregulation (keeping the water and solute balance of the body fluids steady) stops these swings from harming our cells.

Osmoregulation in humans is mainly done by the kidneys, which change how much water is reabsorbed (taken back into the blood) from the collecting ducts, the final tubes that carry urine out of the kidney. The variable being controlled is the concentration of the blood plasma.

Water is gained from drink, food and respiration, and lost in urine, sweat, breath (as water vapour) and faeces. Gains and losses change from hour to hour, so the kidney must adjust the urine to match.

If the blood becomes too concentrated, body cells lose water by osmosis (the movement of water from a dilute region to a more concentrated one) and shrink. If it becomes too dilute, cells gain water and swell. Either upsets cell function, especially in the brain.
The kidney needs a message telling it how much water to save. That message is a hormone, ADH, which changes how leaky the collecting duct wall is to water.
ADH stands for antidiuretic hormone. Diuresis is the production of a large volume of dilute urine, so ADH works against it and reduces urine volume. ADH is released from the pituitary gland.
The target cells (the cells that respond to the hormone) line the collecting ducts and the last part of the distal convoluted tubule.
ADH binds to receptors on these cells, which causes water channel proteins, called aquaporins, to be inserted into their membranes. This makes the duct wall more permeable to water.

The collecting duct passes through the salty medulla (the inner region of the kidney), so water moves out of the more permeable duct by osmosis into the medulla and is carried away in the blood capillaries.
More ADH means more water reabsorbed, less water left in the duct, and a small volume of concentrated urine.
Less ADH means fewer water channels, so the duct wall is less permeable and less water is reabsorbed. A large volume of dilute urine is the result.

ADH changes water reabsorption only. It does not change the amount of salt or urea (the waste made from the breakdown of proteins) excreted. There is more on channel proteins in Metabolic roles and nutritional sources.
When the blood becomes too concentrated, the body responds in a fixed sequence that saves water and brings the concentration back to normal. Follow the steps in order.
1. Stimulus: the water concentration of the blood falls (its solute concentration rises), for example after heavy sweating, not drinking enough, eating salty food, or diarrhoea.
2. Receptors: osmoreceptors, special cells in the hypothalamus of the brain that detect the concentration of the blood, notice the change.
3. The hypothalamus causes the pituitary gland to release more ADH into the blood.
4. ADH travels in the blood to the kidneys.
5. The collecting ducts become more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood.
6. A small volume of concentrated, dark-yellow urine is produced.
7. The water concentration of the blood rises back towards normal, and ADH release falls again. This is negative feedback, because the response reverses the original change.
At the same time the hypothalamus triggers thirst, so the person drinks more. Drinking is the only way to replace lost water, because the kidneys can only reduce further loss.
The same system works in reverse when the blood becomes too dilute. The kidney then lets more water go, so the concentration returns to normal.
1. Stimulus: after drinking a large volume of water, the water concentration of the blood rises (it becomes more dilute).
4. The collecting ducts become less permeable to water, because fewer water channels are present in their walls.
5. Less water is reabsorbed, so more stays in the duct.
6. A large volume of dilute, pale urine is produced.
7. The blood's water concentration falls back to normal and ADH release returns to its usual level.
Everyday situations change the concentration of the blood, and ADH release changes with them. Each example below follows the same chain from blood concentration to urine volume.
On a hot day or during exercise, much water is lost in sweat, so more ADH is released and the urine is small in volume and dark.

A high salt intake raises the solute concentration of the blood, so more ADH is released, more water is reabsorbed and a smaller volume of urine is produced. The extra salt is excreted in this smaller volume, and the person also feels thirsty.

Alcohol reduces the release of ADH, so the collecting ducts reabsorb less water and a large volume of dilute urine is produced. This causes dehydration (loss of body water), which contributes to the headache and thirst of a hangover.
The two feedback responses can be drawn as one negative-feedback loop around the normal blood water concentration. Drawing it shows that every change is pushed back towards normal.

Diagram: a negative-feedback loop for water balance, with normal blood water concentration at the centre. One branch shows the water concentration falling, the hypothalamus detecting it, the pituitary releasing more ADH, the collecting ducts becoming more permeable, more water being reabsorbed, a small volume of concentrated urine being produced, and the concentration returning to normal. The other branch shows the water concentration rising, less ADH, less permeable collecting ducts, less water reabsorbed, a large volume of dilute urine, and a return to normal. Optionally add a small sketch of a collecting duct passing through the salty medulla with arrows for water leaving by osmosis.

Humans can't make their own food, so every meal has to be taken in, broken down and moved into the body before cells can use it. This happens in four stages: ingestion, digestion, absorption and egestion.
Humans are heterotrophs, meaning they obtain food from other organisms rather than making it. They are also omnivores: they eat both plant and animal material.
Ingestion is taking food into the body through the mouth, which is where every meal enters the gut.

Digestion is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed. It is both mechanical (physical breakdown into smaller pieces) and chemical (hydrolysis, the splitting of large molecules by enzymes).

Digestion is necessary because large molecules such as starch, proteins and fats cannot pass through the wall of the gut or through cell membranes. It converts them to small soluble molecules (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol) that can be absorbed into the blood.

Cells then use the absorbed molecules to build the body's own molecules or for respiration. This use of absorbed molecules is called assimilation: for example, amino acids are built into proteins and glucose is respired to release energy.

Absorption is the passage of the small soluble products of digestion, together with water, vitamins and minerals, through the wall of the gut into the blood or lymph. It happens mainly in the small intestine.
Egestion is the removal of undigested and unabsorbed material, mainly dietary fibre, as faeces through the anus. This material is left over because the body cannot digest or absorb it.
Egestion is not excretion. Faeces were never part of the body's metabolism (the chemical reactions inside cells), except for bile pigments, whereas excretion removes metabolic waste made by cells.
The alimentary canal, or gut, is the pathway food follows through the body. Its muscular wall and lining are built to move food along and to protect the gut itself.

The alimentary canal, or gut, is a continuous muscular tube from the mouth to the anus. Food passes in order through the mouth, pharynx (throat), oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus.
The gut wall contains two layers of smooth muscle, circular and longitudinal, which move food along by peristalsis (waves of muscle contraction that push food onwards).
The inner lining of the gut makes mucus. Mucus lubricates the food so it slides along, and protects the lining from digestive enzymes and acid, which would otherwise damage the gut's own cells.
Sphincters are rings of muscle that control movement between parts of the gut, for example at the entrance and exit of the stomach (the exit one is the pyloric sphincter) and at the anus.

The first three organs prepare food and carry it onwards. The mouth breaks it up and starts starch digestion, the oesophagus transports it, and the stomach stores and churns it while starting protein digestion.

The mouth is where food is ingested and chewed by the teeth, then mixed with saliva from three pairs of salivary glands. The tongue shapes it into a ball, the bolus, and pushes it back for swallowing. Starch digestion begins here.

The oesophagus, or gullet, is a muscular tube that carries food by peristalsis from the pharynx, down through the chest behind the trachea (windpipe) and through the diaphragm (the sheet of muscle below the lungs), to the stomach. No digestion or absorption happens in it.
During swallowing the epiglottis (a flap) covers the entrance to the trachea, so food goes down the oesophagus and not into the lungs.

The stomach is a J-shaped muscular bag in the upper left of the abdomen, just below the diaphragm. It stores food for a few hours, which means a meal can be eaten quickly and released to the intestine gradually.

The stomach churns food with gastric juice (acid and a protease, an enzyme that digests protein) into a thick liquid called chyme. The acid kills most bacteria in food, and protein digestion begins here.
The pyloric sphincter at the stomach's exit releases chyme a little at a time into the small intestine.

After the stomach, chyme enters the small intestine, where digestion is finished and most absorption happens. What is left passes to the large intestine, which recovers water and stores the waste until it leaves the body.

The small intestine is the longest part of the gut, coiled in the abdomen. Its first part, the duodenum, receives bile from the liver and pancreatic juice from the pancreas, and most chemical digestion happens there.

The later parts, the jejunum and the ileum, complete digestion and absorb most digested food and water through millions of villi (tiny finger-like projections of the lining that give a large surface for absorption).
The large intestine is wider but shorter than the small intestine; "large" refers to its width, not its length. Its parts are the caecum, with the appendix attached, the colon and the rectum.
The appendix is a small dead-end tube with no digestive role in humans, so food is not digested in it.
The colon absorbs water and some minerals from the remaining material, and is home to many bacteria. It is not an excretory organ, because what leaves is egested, not excreted.
The rectum is the last part of the large intestine, which stores faeces until egestion, so waste does not have to leave the body continuously.
The anus is the opening at the end of the gut, closed by sphincter muscles. The outer sphincter is under voluntary control, so egestion can be delayed until it is convenient.
Some organs help digestion without food ever entering them. They make secretions that reach the gut through ducts (narrow tubes), so they are called associated organs.
The salivary glands are three pairs, around the mouth and below the jaw, releasing saliva into the mouth through ducts. Saliva contains water, mucus and the enzyme salivary amylase.
The liver is the largest internal organ, in the upper right of the abdomen just below the diaphragm. Its digestive role is to make bile.

The liver also receives the absorbed products of digestion through the hepatic portal vein (the vein carrying blood from the gut to the liver), stores glycogen and deaminates amino acids (removes their nitrogen-containing part).
The gallbladder is a small sac under the liver that stores and concentrates bile. It squeezes bile through the bile duct into the duodenum when fatty food arrives there. It makes no bile itself.

The pancreas is a soft, pinkish gland behind the stomach, lying in the curve of the duodenum. It makes pancreatic juice, which contains enzymes for starch, protein and fat and sodium hydrogencarbonate, and this flows through the pancreatic duct into the duodenum.
The pancreas is also an endocrine gland (a ductless gland that releases hormones into the blood) making insulin, so it has both ducted (exocrine) and ductless (endocrine) roles.
The liver, gallbladder and pancreas are associated organs: food never passes through them, and their secretions reach the gut through ducts. Food does pass through the mouth, stomach and intestines.
A labelled diagram shows how the gut and its associated organs sit in relation to each other. Getting the positions right matters as much as the labels.

Diagram: alimentary canal and associated glands, front view, as one continuous tube. Labels: mouth, salivary glands, tongue, oesophagus, diaphragm, liver (above stomach, body's right), gallbladder (under liver), bile duct, stomach, pyloric sphincter, pancreas (in duodenum's loop), pancreatic duct, duodenum, ileum, caecum, appendix, colon, rectum, anus.
Following one mouthful from start to finish pulls the stages of nutrition together. Each part of the gut has its own main job.
Mouth: ingestion; mechanical and chemical digestion begin.
Oesophagus: transport of food to the stomach, because the mouth and stomach are too far apart for food to move unaided.
Stomach: storage and churning; protein digestion begins.
Duodenum: most chemical digestion, with bile and pancreatic juice.
Ileum: digestion is completed and absorption takes place.
Colon: absorption of water, so the remaining waste becomes more solid.
Anus: egestion, the removal of faeces from the body.

Before food can be absorbed it has to be broken down in two ways. Mechanical breakdown makes the pieces smaller; chemical breakdown then splits the molecules themselves. This subsection is about the first kind.

Mechanical (physical) digestion breaks food into smaller pieces, or fat into smaller droplets, without changing the molecules: no chemical bonds are broken and no new substances are formed. Chemical digestion, done by enzymes (biological catalysts that speed up reactions), does break bonds. There is more on this in Chemical breakdown.
Smaller pieces have a much larger total surface area, so enzymes can act on more of the food at once and digestion is faster. Think of how sugar dissolves faster as powder than as a lump.
Mechanical breakdown also makes food soft and moist enough to swallow, and mixes it with digestive juices (the watery secretions that contain enzymes), so the enzymes reach all of the food.
The four mechanisms are chewing by the teeth (mouth), peristalsis (the whole gut), churning (stomach), and emulsification of fats by bile salts (duodenum, the first part of the small intestine).
Digestion starts in the mouth, where the teeth cut and crush food into small pieces. Each type of tooth has a shape that suits its job.

Chewing (mastication) breaks food into small pieces and mixes it with saliva. The tongue rolls the moistened food into a bolus (a soft ball of food) for swallowing, and mucus in saliva lubricates the bolus so it slides down easily.
Incisors are at the front of the mouth. They are chisel-shaped with sharp, flat edges, which suits them for biting and cutting food.
Canines, one on each side of the incisors in each jaw, are pointed, so they grip and tear food. Human canines are small compared with those of carnivores (meat-eating animals).
Premolars and molars at the back are broad with ridged surfaces (cusps), for crushing and grinding food. Premolars have two cusps; molars are larger with more cusps.
The jaw moves sideways as well as up and down, so the broad surfaces of the molars can grind food rather than only crush it.

Diagram: (a) the four types of teeth side by side, labelled incisor, canine, premolar and molar, with their roles; (b) a vertical section of a molar labelled crown, root, enamel, dentine, pulp cavity, nerves and blood vessels, gum, cement and jawbone.
The teeth in your mouth can be summarised in a short code called the dental formula. Knowing how a tooth is built also shows why it is hard-wearing yet sensitive.
The dental formula gives the number of each type of tooth in one half of the upper jaw over one half of the lower jaw, in the order incisors, canines, premolars, molars.
The adult human dental formula is 2.1.2.3 over 2.1.2.3, so there are 16 teeth on each side of the mouth (8 in each quarter) and 32 teeth in total.
Child's milk (deciduous) teeth have the formula 2.1.0.2 over 2.1.0.2, giving 20 teeth in total. They have no premolars and only two molars in each quarter, so the adult set has 12 more teeth.
The third molars are the wisdom teeth. They appear last, often in the late teens or later, or not at all.
A tooth has a crown above the gum and a root fixed in the jawbone. Enamel, the hardest substance in the body, covers the crown, so it can withstand biting and chewing.
Dentine, a bone-like layer, lies beneath the enamel. The pulp cavity in the centre contains nerves and blood vessels, which is why a damaged tooth hurts. Cement holds the root in its socket.
Enamel is very hard, but acid can still dissolve it. Tooth decay is the result of bacteria turning the sugar in the mouth into acid.
Bacteria in plaque (a sticky film on the teeth) feed on sugars and release acid. The acid dissolves enamel and then dentine, forming a cavity.
Eating and drinking sugary food less often gives the bacteria less to feed on, so less acid is made.

Brushing with fluoride toothpaste removes plaque and hardens enamel. Drinking fluoridated water (water with fluoride added) also hardens enamel, so it resists the acid. There is more on fluoride in Minerals.
Regular dental check-ups let decay be found and treated early, before the cavity reaches the pulp cavity.
Food has to travel the whole length of the gut, even though the gut has no hands or pump. Peristalsis does this with waves of muscle, and it also helps break the food up.

Peristalsis is a wave of muscular contraction that passes along the wall of the gut, pushing food along. It happens from the oesophagus (the food pipe) to the rectum, and also in the ureters (the tubes from the kidneys to the bladder).
The gut wall has an inner layer of circular muscle and an outer layer of longitudinal muscle. Both are smooth, involuntary muscle, which means they work without conscious control.
1. The circular muscle just behind the bolus contracts, narrowing the gut and squeezing the food forwards.
2. The circular muscle just in front of the bolus relaxes, widening the gut to receive it. The wave then moves along, carrying the food with it.
Peristalsis is automatic (involuntary) once food is swallowed, and it works against gravity: a person can swallow while lying down or upside down, and the food still reaches the stomach.
Peristalsis also mixes food with digestive juices and breaks it up, so it is part of mechanical breakdown. In the small intestine it keeps moving the contents past the absorbing surface.
Dietary fibre adds bulk that the muscles can grip and push against, so a high-fibre diet keeps peristalsis effective and prevents constipation. There is more on this in Diet.

Diagram: a section of the gut showing a bolus with contracted circular muscle (narrow) behind it and relaxed muscle (wide) in front, with an arrow for the direction of movement; label circular muscle, longitudinal muscle, bolus, contraction and relaxation.
The stomach is a muscular bag that holds food for a few hours. Its walls churn the food, which is the third mechanical process after chewing and peristalsis.

The stomach wall has three layers of smooth muscle: longitudinal, circular and an oblique (diagonal) layer. Having muscle running in three directions means their contractions churn the food, breaking it up and mixing it thoroughly with gastric juice (the stomach's digestive secretion).

After a few hours of churning, food becomes chyme, a thick, creamy liquid. The sphincters (rings of muscle that close an opening) at the entrance and exit stay closed during churning, so food is held in the stomach.

The pyloric sphincter, at the exit of the stomach, relaxes now and then to let small amounts of chyme into the duodenum. This means the small intestine is never overloaded and has time to digest and neutralise each portion.
The stomach also has a chemical role, using acid and pepsin. There is more on this in Chemical breakdown.

Fat does not mix with water, so it forms large droplets in the watery gut. Bile salts solve this by breaking fat into tiny droplets, a mechanical step that gives the fat-digesting enzyme far more surface to work on.
Fats and oils do not mix with the watery contents of the gut, so they form large droplets. Lipase (the fat-digesting enzyme, which works in water) can therefore reach only the droplet surfaces.
Bile salts are made by the liver and enter the duodenum in bile. Each bile-salt molecule has one end that attracts water (hydrophilic) and one end that attracts fat (hydrophobic).

The bile salts gather on the surface of fat droplets with the fat-loving end inwards. With the churning of the gut they break the large droplets into many tiny droplets and stop them joining together again.
This is emulsification, and the mixture of tiny droplets in water is an emulsion.
Emulsification is mechanical: the fat molecules are unchanged and no bonds are broken. It greatly increases the surface area of fat exposed to lipase, so fat is digested much faster.
Bile contains no enzymes. Its other roles, neutralising stomach acid and excreting bile pigments (waste products), are in Chemical breakdown.
Washing-up liquid emulsifies grease in the same way, which is why bile salts are often compared to a detergent.
Diagram: one large fat droplet, then, after bile salts, many small droplets each coated with bile-salt molecules, labelled large surface area for lipase.
Food is made of large molecules that are too big to pass into the blood. Chemical digestion cuts them into small units using enzymes (biological catalysts made by the body).
Chemical digestion is the hydrolysis of large food molecules into their small, soluble units by digestive enzymes: each bond is broken by adding a molecule of water, which is what hydrolysis means.
Carbohydrates become simple sugars, proteins become amino acids, and fats become fatty acids and glycerol. These small units are soluble and small enough to be absorbed.
Each digestive enzyme is specific to one type of substrate (the molecule it acts on) and works best at its optimum pH, the pH of the part of the gut where it acts.
The gut changes pH along its length: neutral in the mouth, acid in the stomach and alkaline in the small intestine. This suits the different enzymes working in each place.
Most digestive enzymes are released from glands into the gut cavity, so digestion there is extracellular, meaning it happens outside cells.
Digestion begins in the mouth, where food is mixed with saliva. Saliva moistens the food and also starts the digestion of starch.
Saliva is produced by the three pairs of salivary glands and released into the mouth.
The pH in the mouth is about 7 (neutral to slightly alkaline), which is the optimum for salivary amylase, the enzyme in saliva.
Salivary amylase digests starch to maltose (a sugar made of two glucose units). The product of an amylase is maltose.
Food is in the mouth only briefly, so only a little starch is digested there. Stomach acid denatures (destroys the shape of) the amylase soon after it reaches the stomach.
Saliva also contains water, which dissolves food so that it can be tasted and moistens it, and mucus, which lubricates swallowing.
Saliva also contains lysozyme, an enzyme that kills some bacteria.
In the stomach, food meets a strongly acidic fluid called gastric juice. It begins protein digestion and also protects the body from bacteria that arrive in food.
Gastric juice is produced by gastric glands in the stomach lining and released into the stomach. It contains hydrochloric acid, pepsin (released as inactive pepsinogen) and mucus.
The pH in the stomach is about 2 (strongly acidic), which is the optimum for pepsin.
Hydrochloric acid kills most bacteria in food, which is a defence against infection. It also provides the acid pH that pepsin needs.
Hydrochloric acid converts inactive pepsinogen to active pepsin, and it stops salivary amylase, which cannot work at this pH.
Pepsin is a protease (a protein-digesting enzyme): it hydrolyses peptide bonds inside protein chains, breaking proteins into shorter chains called polypeptides.
The product of a protease is polypeptides. Complete protein digestion needs further enzymes in the small intestine to give amino acids.
Pepsin is made in the inactive form pepsinogen so that it does not digest the gastric gland cells that make it. It becomes active only in the stomach cavity.
A thick layer of mucus protects the stomach lining from the acid and pepsin. If the mucus barrier fails, the lining is damaged, causing a stomach ulcer.
Fat digestion needs help before enzymes can act, and the acid from the stomach has to be dealt with. Bile does both jobs when food enters the duodenum (the first part of the small intestine).

Bile is produced by the liver, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, and released through the bile duct into the duodenum when chyme (the partly digested, acidic food mixture leaving the stomach), especially fatty chyme, arrives.
Bile contains water, bile salts, bile pigments and sodium hydrogencarbonate. It contains no enzymes.
Bile salts emulsify fats, which means they break large fat droplets into tiny droplets. This is a physical change, not a chemical one. There is more on this in Mechanical breakdown.
Sodium hydrogencarbonate is alkaline and neutralises the acid chyme from the stomach. This raises the pH to suit the pancreatic and intestinal enzymes and stops the action of pepsin.
Bile pigments are excretory wastes from the breakdown of haemoglobin from old red blood cells in the liver. They give faeces their brown colour.
The pancreas adds a second fluid to the duodenum, one that carries most of the enzymes needed to digest starch, protein and fat. Because the duodenum is alkaline, these enzymes work best there.

Pancreatic juice is produced by the pancreas and released through the pancreatic duct into the duodenum. It contains sodium hydrogencarbonate, which neutralises acid, and three enzymes: pancreatic amylase, trypsin and lipase.
Pancreatic amylase digests the remaining starch (the starch not digested in the mouth) to maltose.
Trypsin is a protease, released in an inactive form and activated in the duodenum. It digests proteins and polypeptides into shorter peptides.
Lipase digests fats and oils (triglycerides) into fatty acids and glycerol. The product of a lipase is fatty acids and glycerol, not fatty acids alone.
Lipase acts on the tiny droplets made by emulsification, because they give it a much larger surface to work on.
The pH in the duodenum and small intestine is about 8 (slightly alkaline), because of the sodium hydrogencarbonate in bile and pancreatic juice. This suits pancreatic amylase, trypsin and lipase.
The last stage of digestion is done by enzymes made by the cells lining the small intestine. They finish breaking down the sugars and peptides that earlier enzymes produced.
The cells lining the villi (the tiny finger-like projections of the small intestine) make enzymes that complete digestion.
Many of these enzymes are held in the membranes of the lining cells, so the last step of digestion happens right at the absorbing surface.
Maltase digests maltose to two glucose molecules. Sucrase digests sucrose to glucose and fructose. Lactase digests lactose to glucose and galactose.
Peptidases digest peptides to amino acids.
These enzymes work at a pH of about 8, the same alkaline conditions as the duodenum.

Lactose intolerance: people who stop making lactase after childhood cannot digest lactose, so bacteria in the large intestine ferment it, causing bloating, wind and diarrhoea. There is more on this in Variation and Diet.
This table pulls together where each enzyme is made, where it acts, its pH and its products. Each line has the same pattern so you can compare them quickly.
Salivary amylase – made in salivary glands – acts in mouth – pH about 7 – starch → maltose.
Pepsin (protease) – made in gastric glands of stomach wall – acts in stomach – pH about 2 – protein → polypeptides.
Pancreatic amylase – made in pancreas – acts in duodenum – pH about 8 – starch → maltose.
Trypsin (protease) – made in pancreas – acts in duodenum – pH about 8 – proteins and polypeptides → peptides.
Lipase – made in pancreas – acts in duodenum – pH about 8 – fats → fatty acids and glycerol.
Maltase – made in the wall of the small intestine – acts there – pH about 8 – maltose → glucose.
Peptidases – made in the wall of the small intestine – act there – pH about 8 – peptides → amino acids.
Bile salts (not an enzyme) – made in liver, stored in gallbladder – act in duodenum – emulsify fats.
Putting the enzymes in order shows how each nutrient is broken down step by step along the gut. You can then use these flow models to predict what goes wrong when part of the system fails.

Carbohydrate model: starch is digested by salivary amylase in the mouth (pH 7) to maltose. The remaining starch is digested by pancreatic amylase in the duodenum (pH 8) to maltose. Maltose is digested by maltase in the small intestine wall to glucose.
Sucrose and lactose are digested by sucrase and lactase in the small intestine wall. Cellulose is not digested, because humans make no enzyme for it, so it passes on as fibre.
Protein model: protein → (pepsin, stomach, pH 2) → polypeptides → (trypsin, duodenum, pH 8) → shorter peptides → (peptidases, small intestine wall) → amino acids.
Fat model: large fat droplets → (bile salts, duodenum: emulsification, a physical change) → tiny droplets → (lipase from the pancreas, duodenum, pH 8) → fatty acids and glycerol.
Fat is digested only in the small intestine, after emulsification.
Using the models to predict: if the bile duct is blocked, for example by gallstones, fats are poorly emulsified and digested, and undigested fat appears in the faeces.
If the pancreas releases too little juice, as in cystic fibrosis, digestion of all three nutrients is reduced, which is why patients take enzyme capsules. There is more on this in Industrial enzymes.

Diagram: a flow chart with three rows (carbohydrate, protein, fat), each running left to right through mouth, stomach, duodenum and small intestine wall, showing enzyme or bile salts, pH and product at each step; or an alimentary canal (whole gut) outline with enzymes and pH at each site.
Visking tubing is a simple physical model of the small intestine. It shows why food must be digested into small molecules before it can pass into the blood.

Visking (dialysis) tubing is a selectively permeable membrane: it lets small molecules (water, glucose and maltose) through but not large ones (starch). It models the wall of the small intestine, and the water around it models the blood.
Method, step 1: tie one end of two lengths of Visking tubing, after soaking them in water.

Method, step 2: fill tube A with starch solution plus amylase solution. Fill tube B, the control (the comparison with no enzyme), with the same volume of starch solution plus water (or boiled amylase).
Method, step 3: tie the open ends, rinse the outsides, and place each tube in a separate boiling tube of distilled water in a water bath at 37 °C.

Method, step 4: at the start, and again after about 30 minutes, test samples of the water outside each tube with iodine solution (for starch) and with Benedict's solution in a hot water bath (for reducing sugar), using the food tests.
Expected results: the water outside both tubes stays yellow-brown with iodine, so no starch passes out.

After 30 minutes the water outside tube A turns brick red with Benedict's solution, showing reducing sugar, while the water outside tube B stays blue. Inside tube A, a test would show less starch and much reducing sugar.

Conclusion: starch molecules are too large to pass through the membrane. Amylase digests starch to maltose, which is small enough to pass through. This models why food must be digested before it can be absorbed into the blood. There is more on this in Absorption, transport and storage.
Safety: wear safety glasses; Benedict's solution is an irritant; take care with hot water; heat the tubes in a water bath, never directly.
A model is useful only if you know where it differs from the real gut. The tubing copies the barrier but little else.
The tubing has no villi or microvilli, so its surface area is far smaller than the gut's.
No blood flows past to carry products away and keep the concentration gradient (the difference in concentration that drives diffusion).
The real gut absorbs some products by active transport (using energy to move molecules), which tubing cannot do.
Only one enzyme and one nutrient are modelled, at a constant pH, whereas the gut uses a sequence of enzymes and pH values.
The tubing does not move food by peristalsis (the waves of muscle contraction that push food along the gut).

Diagram: a boiling tube of distilled water in a water bath at 37 °C, with a knotted length of Visking tubing containing starch and amylase hanging in it; label Visking tubing, starch and amylase, distilled water, water bath at 37 °C; show the control tube beside it.

Digestion only breaks food into small molecules; those molecules still have to get from the gut into the blood. The small intestine is where this absorption happens, and its structure is built to make it fast.
Most absorption of digested food, and most of the water, takes place in the small intestine, mainly in the ileum (the last section of the small intestine).
The surface area is huge, so many molecules can cross at once. The intestine is very long and its inner wall is folded.

The folds are covered in millions of villi (singular villus), which are tiny finger-like projections. The cells covering each villus have microvilli, microscopic projections of their cell membranes, which increase the area further.
The diffusion distance is short, so substances cross quickly: the lining of each villus (the epithelium) is only one cell thick, and the capillaries (the smallest blood vessels) lie just beneath it.

A steep concentration gradient (a big difference between the gut and the blood) is kept up, because diffusion only works while the gut side has more. A dense network of blood capillaries in each villus constantly carries absorbed products away.
Peristalsis, the waves of muscle contraction along the gut, also helps keep the gradient steep because it keeps moving fresh digested food past the surface.
Each villus contains more than capillaries. It also has a vessel for fats and lining cells equipped to do the work of absorbing, and you need to be able to draw and label all of it.
Each villus has a lacteal, a lymph vessel in its centre, which absorbs fats. Lymph is the clear fluid carried in the lymphatic system, a network of vessels separate from the blood.
The lining cells have many mitochondria to supply ATP (the cell's usable energy) for active transport, which is the movement of substances using energy.
Goblet cells in the lining secrete mucus, which protects and lubricates the gut wall.

Diagram: a longitudinal section of a villus labelled epithelium (one cell thick), microvilli, goblet cell, blood capillary network, arteriole (bringing blood in), venule (leading to the hepatic portal vein), lacteal, and an arrow for the direction of absorption.
Different digestion products take different routes into the body. The route depends on the molecule: water-soluble products go into the blood, while fats go into the lymph.

Glucose and amino acids enter the lining cells of the villus by diffusion and by active transport (using ATP), so they are absorbed even when their concentration in the gut is lower than in the blood. They then pass into the blood capillaries.

Fatty acids and glycerol diffuse into the lining cells, because they pass easily through the lipid membrane (the fatty outer layer of the cell), and are recombined there into fats. The fats are coated with protein and pass into the lacteal, not the blood capillaries.

Lymph carries the fats through the lymphatic system, which drains into the blood in a large vein near the heart. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) are absorbed with them, because they dissolve in fat.

Water is absorbed by osmosis (movement of water across a membrane towards the higher concentration of solutes), following the absorbed solutes. Most water is absorbed in the small intestine; the large intestine absorbs most of what is left.
Minerals and water-soluble vitamins are absorbed into the blood capillaries by diffusion and active transport. Vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium. There is more on this in Vitamins.
Blood from the gut does not go straight back to the heart. First it is sent to the liver, which checks and processes everything that has just been absorbed.

The blood capillaries of the villi join to form veins that unite as the hepatic portal vein, which carries blood from the small intestine, and the rest of the gut, directly to the liver, not to the heart.
A portal vein carries blood between two capillary networks: it begins in capillaries (in the villi) and ends in capillaries (in the liver). The hepatic portal vein is the example to give.

After a meal its blood is rich in absorbed glucose, amino acids, water-soluble vitamins and minerals; the amounts vary greatly with what has been eaten. It is low in oxygen because it has already passed through the gut wall.
The products go to the liver first because the liver processes and stores them and adjusts what is released to the rest of the body, keeping blood glucose and amino-acid levels steady.

Blood leaves the liver in the hepatic vein, which joins the vena cava (the large vein returning blood to the heart). The liver also receives oxygen-rich blood in the hepatic artery. There is more on the full route in Circulation.
Fats do not travel in the hepatic portal vein at first: they reach the blood through the lymph.
Blood glucose rises after a meal and falls between meals. The liver acts as a store, taking glucose in when there is plenty and releasing it when there is not.

After a meal, blood glucose rises. Insulin, a hormone released by the pancreas, causes liver cells to take up glucose and convert it into glycogen, an insoluble storage polysaccharide (a large carbohydrate made of many glucose units). Muscle cells also store glycogen.

Between meals, or during exercise, when blood glucose falls, the liver breaks glycogen back down into glucose and releases it into the blood, so the brain and other cells have a steady supply. There is more on this feedback loop in Homeostasis as a stimulus-response model.
The liver can store only a limited amount of glycogen. Glucose beyond this is converted into fat and stored in adipose tissue (fatty tissue).
The liver also stores iron and vitamins A, D and B12.
Amino acids are needed for building proteins, but the body has no store of them. Whatever is surplus is broken down in the liver, and the nitrogen it contains has to be got rid of safely.
Absorbed amino acids are carried to all body cells and used to make proteins for growth and repair, enzymes, hormones and antibodies; this is assimilation (absorbed food becoming part of the body).
Excess amino acids cannot be stored. Step 1: in the liver, the amino group (–NH₂) is removed from each excess amino acid; this is deamination.
Step 2: the amino group forms ammonia, which is very toxic.
Step 3: liver cells immediately convert the ammonia into urea, which is much less toxic, so it can be carried in the blood safely.
Step 4: urea passes into the blood, is carried to the kidneys, and is excreted in urine. There is more on this in The urinary system.
The rest of the amino acid, the part without nitrogen, is not wasted: it is respired to release energy, or converted into glucose, glycogen or fat.
A very high-protein diet means more deamination and more urea for the kidneys to excrete.
Besides storing glycogen and deaminating amino acids, the liver has several other jobs that you should be able to name.
The liver makes bile, breaks down old red blood cells (forming bile pigments), and breaks down alcohol and many drugs, a process called detoxification because it removes harmful substances.
What the small intestine cannot digest or absorb moves on into the large intestine. Its main jobs are to reclaim water and to form and eliminate the waste.

Material entering the large intestine is watery and contains what could not be digested or absorbed: mainly dietary fibre (cellulose), with dead cells shed from the gut lining, bile pigments, mucus and bacteria.

The colon (the main part of the large intestine) absorbs most of the remaining water, by osmosis, and some mineral ions into the blood, so the contents become semi-solid faeces. This saves water for the body.

Bacteria in the colon (the gut microbiota) feed on undigested material, including some fibre, and make vitamin K and some B vitamins, which are absorbed. There is more on their wider role in health in The microbiome.

Faeces are moved by peristalsis to the rectum (the final section of the gut) and stored there. When the rectum fills, stretch receptors give the urge to egest; the anal sphincters (rings of muscle) relax and the faeces are pushed out through the anus. This removal of undigested waste is called egestion, or elimination.
If faeces move too slowly, too much water is absorbed and they become hard and difficult to pass (constipation); fibre and water prevent this.
If faeces move too fast, as in a gut infection, too little water is absorbed and diarrhoea results, which can cause dangerous dehydration, especially in young children.
Food has to supply energy and raw materials for growth and repair. A balanced diet does this without leaving the body short of anything or overloaded with anything.

A balanced diet contains all the nutrients (carbohydrate, protein, lipid, vitamins and minerals), together with water and dietary fibre, in the right amounts and proportions to meet a person's needs, with enough energy but not too much.
Balanced means right proportions, not equal amounts from each food group. A person needs far more starchy food and vegetables than fats, for example.

Malnutrition is any diet that does not meet the body's needs. Undernutrition is too little energy or too little of a nutrient, e.g. iron-deficiency anaemia or rickets (a bone disease caused by too little vitamin D).
Overnutrition is too much energy or too much of a nutrient, e.g. obesity (a body mass well above the healthy range, from long-term excess energy) or too much salt.
Energy balance: if the energy taken in from food equals the energy used in metabolism (the body's chemical reactions) and activity, body mass stays the same.

Excess energy is stored as fat, causing weight gain. Too little energy means the body uses its glycogen (the short-term carbohydrate store), then fat, and eventually muscle protein, so weight is lost.
The Food Pyramid turns the idea of a balanced diet into a picture of how much of each food group to eat. The wider the shelf, the more servings you should have from it.
Ireland's Food Pyramid (Department of Health, 2016) is a guide to a balanced diet, in which most servings come from the lower shelves.
The lower shelves are vegetables, salad and fruit (5 to 7 servings a day), and wholemeal cereals, breads, potatoes, pasta and rice.

Milk, yoghurt and cheese (3 servings a day, or 5 for ages 9 to 18, because teenagers are growing fast and need more calcium) and meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans and nuts (2 servings) are in the middle.
Fats, spreads and oils are for very small amounts, and the top shelf, foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt, is not for every day.
Body mass index (BMI) gives a quick number for whether a person's mass is suitable for their height. It is a screening tool and you may be asked to calculate and interpret it.
Body mass index (BMI) is mass in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres.
For adults, the World Health Organization classes 18.5 to 24.9 as a healthy weight, 25 to 29.9 as overweight and 30 or more as obese; below 18.5 is underweight.
BMI does not distinguish fat from muscle, so a muscular athlete can have a high BMI even with little body fat. It also does not show where fat is stored.
Children and teenagers are still growing, so they are assessed with growth charts for their age and sex instead of the adult categories.
Worked example: 70 kg ÷ (1.75 m × 1.75 m) = 70 ÷ 3.06 = 22.9, a healthy weight.
A balanced diet is not the same for everyone. What a person needs depends on their health, their age, their gender and how active they are, and each factor has a biological reason.

Health: illnesses change needs. People with coeliac disease (an immune reaction to gluten, a protein in wheat) must avoid gluten, and people with type 1 diabetes match carbohydrate intake to their insulin. There is more on coeliac disease in Emerging diseases and society.

People with high blood pressure are advised to eat less salt, and people with anaemia need more iron to make haemoglobin; people recovering from injury or surgery need more protein for repair, and people with lactose intolerance avoid or limit lactose (milk sugar) and need other calcium sources.

Age, children and teenagers: growing children need more protein, calcium and vitamin D for bones, and more energy per kilogram of body mass than adults. Babies' needs are met by breast milk or formula.
The teenage growth spurt raises energy, protein, calcium and iron needs, which is why the Food Pyramid gives 5 dairy servings for ages 9 to 18.

Age, older people: metabolic rate and activity usually fall, so less energy is needed. Protein (to limit muscle loss), calcium and vitamin D (to limit bone loss and osteoporosis, brittle bones), fibre (constipation is more common) and water (the sense of thirst weakens with age) remain important.

Gender: on average males have more muscle and a larger body, so they need more energy and protein. Females who menstruate lose iron in blood each month, so they need more iron. Pregnancy and breastfeeding raise the need for energy, protein, calcium and iron.
Folic acid (a B vitamin) is advised before and in early pregnancy, and pregnant women should avoid alcohol and liver, which is high in vitamin A.

Activity: active people use more energy, so they need more starchy carbohydrate (builds glycogen stores), protein for muscle repair, and water and salt to replace sweat; inactive (sedentary) people use less energy, so they need less, and eating as though active leads to weight gain.
Eating from every food group is not enough on its own. Eating a range of different foods is what makes sure nothing is missed.

No single food contains every nutrient in the right proportions, so a varied diet from all the food groups is the most reliable way to get all the vitamins, minerals, essential amino acids and essential fatty acids (the ones the body cannot make for itself).

Variety within groups also matters because different fruits and vegetables supply different vitamins, minerals and fibre types, e.g. citrus fruit for vitamin C, green leafy vegetables for iron, calcium and vitamin K, and carrots for beta-carotene.

Combining plant proteins, e.g. beans with cereal, supplies all the essential amino acids, because each food makes up for what the other lacks. There is more on this in Metabolic roles and nutritional sources.
Water makes up most of the body and is constantly being lost, so a diet is only balanced if it also replaces water.

Water is lost every day in urine, sweat, breath and faeces, and must be replaced from drinks and food. Needs rise in hot weather, during exercise, with fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, and when breastfeeding. There is more on the roles of water in Water.

Signs of dehydration (too little water in the body) are thirst, dark-yellow urine in small volumes, headache, tiredness and poor concentration. The urine is dark and scant because the hormone ADH makes the kidneys hold on to water at Higher Level.
Severe dehydration is dangerous, especially in babies and older people.
Water is the best drink. Sugar-sweetened drinks supply water but also free sugars (sugars added to foods and drinks, explained under high-sugar diets below).
Fibre is the part of plant food that passes through you without being digested, yet it is essential for a healthy gut. It supplies almost no energy and is not absorbed.
Dietary fibre, or roughage, is plant material that human enzymes cannot digest, mainly cellulose from plant cell walls. There is more on cellulose in Structures of biomolecules.

Sources of fibre are wholegrain cereals and wholemeal bread, brown rice, vegetables, fruit (especially with skins), beans, peas and lentils, and nuts and seeds. There is no fibre in meat, fish, eggs or dairy produce.

Fibre adds bulk and absorbs water, so faeces are soft and large. This gives the gut muscles something to push against, keeps peristalsis (the waves of muscle contraction that move food along the gut) effective and prevents constipation.
Fibre makes food more filling and slows the absorption of sugar, which helps control body mass and blood glucose.
High-fibre diets are linked to a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and bowel cancer.
Bacteria in the colon ferment some fibre, which supports a healthy gut microbiome (the community of microorganisms living in the gut).
Raising fibre intake suddenly can cause wind and bloating, and fibre needs extra water to work. Very large amounts of bran can reduce the absorption of some minerals such as iron and calcium.
Newspapers and adverts make many claims about food. Researching a claim in steps lets you judge whether the evidence is reliable before you accept it.
1. Pose a specific, testable question, e.g. 'Does a vegan diet supply enough iron for teenage girls?'

2. Find several reliable sources, such as public health bodies, peer-reviewed reviews (checked by other scientists before publication) and textbooks. There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
3. Check who funded and wrote each source, and whether it sells a product, because money can bias what is reported.

4. Judge the type of evidence. Most diet evidence comes from observational studies of large populations, which show links (correlations) but not cause, because people who choose a diet often differ in other ways; vegetarians, for example, on average smoke less and exercise more.
Controlled trials, where researchers assign the diets, give stronger evidence of cause but are usually short and small.
5. Explain the biological mechanism behind each claim, naming the nutrient and the body process.
6. Reach a balanced, justified conclusion for a particular group of people.

Example of funding bias: a 1967 review of diet and heart disease, by Harvard scientists in the New England Journal of Medicine, played down sugar and blamed dietary fat. In 2016 it emerged that the Sugar Research Foundation, the sugar industry's trade group, had paid for it without disclosure.
Some people leave animal foods out of their diet. The different types are defined by exactly which foods they exclude, and each has benefits and risks.

A vegetarian diet excludes meat and fish; most vegetarians eat eggs and dairy produce (lacto-ovo vegetarians). A vegan diet excludes all animal products, including eggs, dairy produce and honey. Pescatarians eat fish but not meat.

Vegetarian and vegan diets are usually higher in fibre, fruit and vegetables and lower in saturated fat, so on average blood cholesterol and BMI are lower. Observational studies link them to a lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.
They avoid processed and red meat, which are linked to bowel cancer.

Producing plant food generally uses less land and water and releases less greenhouse gas than producing meat, which makes these diets more sustainable. There is more on this in Metabolic roles and nutritional sources.
Leaving out animal foods removes some useful nutrients. These risks call for planning, not avoidance, because each can be replaced by other foods or supplements.
Vitamin B12 occurs naturally only in animal foods, so vegans need fortified foods (with nutrients added) or supplements to prevent anaemia and nerve damage. There is more on this in Vitamins.

Iron from plants is less easily absorbed than iron from meat, so vegans should eat iron-rich plants (beans, lentils, green leafy vegetables and fortified cereals) with vitamin C, which helps absorption.
Vegans must get calcium from fortified plant milks, tofu and green vegetables instead of dairy produce.
Iodine comes mainly from milk and seafood, so vegans may be short of it.
The long-chain omega-3 fatty acids are found mainly in oily fish, so vegans and vegetarians who avoid fish get little of them.
Plant proteins must be combined to supply all the essential amino acids, though this is easily done, e.g. beans with cereal.
Teenagers, pregnant women and young children have the highest needs, so a vegan diet for them needs careful planning.
Evidence about these diets mostly comes from large observational studies. Reading the results carefully means knowing what they can and cannot show.

A large UK study of people's diets and health over many years, EPIC-Oxford, found that vegetarians had a lower rate of heart disease but a slightly higher rate of stroke than meat eaters, and that vegans had more bone fractures.
Observational findings like these show links that may have other causes, because people who choose these diets also differ in other ways.
Judgement: a well-planned vegetarian or vegan diet can meet all needs, but it must replace the nutrients that meat, fish and dairy produce supply.
Not all sugar in food is the same. The recommendation applies only to free sugars, so you need to know exactly which sugars count.
Free sugars are sugars added to food and drink, plus the sugars in honey, syrups and fruit juice. The sugar inside whole fruit, vegetables and milk is not counted as free sugar.
The World Health Organization (2015) recommends that free sugars make up less than 10% of daily energy intake, and ideally less than 5%.
Eating a lot of free sugar harms health in several ways, but a fair evaluation also gives the case for sugar. The amount and the frequency are what matter.
Tooth decay: plaque bacteria on teeth ferment sugar to acid, which damages tooth enamel. There is more on this in Mechanical breakdown.

Excess energy from sugar is stored as fat, causing weight gain and obesity, which raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure and some cancers. Obesity is the main link between sugar and type 2 diabetes.
Sugary foods often supply energy with few other nutrients ('empty' energy) and replace more nutritious foods, and sugary drinks add energy without making a person feel full.
Sugar triggers dopamine release (a brain chemical linked to reward), which can drive overeating. There is more on this in Dopamine and endorphins.

Counter-arguments: glucose is the brain's main fuel, and sugar is a quick energy source, useful for example during long endurance exercise or for a person with diabetes whose blood glucose is too low.
Sugar in whole fruit comes with fibre and vitamins and is not the problem; the risk comes from the amount and how often it is eaten.
Policy link: Ireland introduced a tax on sugar-sweetened drinks in 2018.
Judgement: small amounts of free sugar are harmless; frequent, large amounts harm teeth and raise the risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes.
Fat is a necessary nutrient, but the type and the amount matter. Too much saturated fat is the main concern.

Saturated fats, found in butter, lard, fatty meat and cheese, raise the type of blood cholesterol (LDL) that is deposited in artery walls, narrowing them (atherosclerosis) and raising the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Artificial trans fats, once common in processed foods, are worse than saturated fats.
Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated oils (olive oil, nuts and oily fish) lowers this risk.

Counter-argument: fat is needed for energy, insulation, cell membranes, essential fatty acids and the absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K, so a very low-fat diet can cause deficiencies. There is more on this in Vitamins.
Fat has about twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate, so fatty food makes weight gain easy.
People such as body-builders eat extra protein hoping to build muscle. The body does not simply store extra protein as muscle.

Extra protein beyond needs is not stored as muscle. Excess amino acids are deaminated (the nitrogen part is removed) and the urea is excreted, and the rest is used for energy or stored as fat. There is more on this in Absorption, transport and storage.
Muscle growth depends on training, with enough protein and energy.
High-protein diets based on processed and red meat bring more saturated fat, and they are often low in fibre.
Processed foods have been changed by manufacture, such as being cooked, refined or packaged. Many fast and processed foods have a poor nutrient profile.
Many processed and fast foods are high in fat, sugar and salt and low in fibre, vitamins and minerals.
Implications include constipation, a higher risk of bowel cancer, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and obesity, and high salt intake linked to high blood pressure. There is more on salt in Minerals.
Counter-point: some processed foods are useful and nutritious, e.g. frozen vegetables, tinned beans and fortified cereals, so the label, not the word processed, is what matters.
Some people cut out dairy produce or gluten. For some this is medically necessary, but for others it is a choice that has costs.
Dairy-free and gluten-free diets are necessary for people with milk allergy, lactose intolerance (where lactose-free milk is another option) or coeliac disease.

For other people they bring no proven benefit and need care, since dairy produce is the main calcium and iodine source in many Irish diets, and gluten-free products are often lower in fibre and more expensive.
Some people try to lose weight fast by skipping meals or by eating very little (crash diets). This has several biological drawbacks.
Skipping meals and very low-energy (crash) diets run down glycogen stores, leading to tiredness and poor concentration.
The body breaks down muscle protein as well as fat, nutrients are likely to be missed, and weight lost quickly is often regained.
Every living cell needs a steady supply of oxygen and must get rid of the carbon dioxide it makes. The breathing system is the body's way of swapping these gases with the air.
Every cell respires aerobically (releases energy from food using oxygen), so every cell uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide. There is more on this in Respiration as a catabolic process.

The breathing system exchanges gases between the external environment (the air) and the internal environment (the blood and tissue fluid, the fluid that bathes the cells): oxygen is taken into the blood, and carbon dioxide and some water vapour are removed.
Breathing, or ventilation, is the movement of air into and out of the lungs. It is not respiration, which is the chemical release of energy inside cells, and gas exchange is not respiration either.
A large animal such as a human cannot get enough oxygen by diffusion through its skin, because its surface area is too small for its volume and the distances to its inner cells are too great.
So it needs a specialised exchange surface, the alveoli (tiny air sacs in the lungs), and a transport system, the blood, to carry gases to and from every cell.
The breathing tract is the pathway air follows from outside to the lungs. The first parts clean, warm and moisten the air and keep food out of the airway.

Nose (nasal cavity): hairs and sticky mucus trap dust and microorganisms. The lining has a rich blood supply that warms the air, and the mucus moistens it, so the delicate alveoli do not dry out or chill.
Breathing through the mouth skips this filtering, warming and moistening, which is why nose breathing is better for the lungs.
Pharynx (throat): the passage behind the nose and mouth that is shared by air and food.

Epiglottis: a flap of cartilage (firm, flexible tissue) that closes over the entrance to the larynx and trachea during swallowing, so food and drink pass into the oesophagus (the food tube) instead of the airway.
Choking happens when food enters the trachea instead.
Larynx (voice box): at the top of the trachea. It contains the vocal cords, which vibrate as air passes over them, producing sound.
Below the larynx the airway divides again and again, like an upside-down tree, until it reaches the alveoli where gases actually cross into the blood.
Trachea (windpipe): a tube held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage, so it does not collapse when the pressure inside falls during inhalation.
The rings are incomplete at the back, where the trachea lies against the oesophagus, so the oesophagus can expand as food is swallowed.
Lining of the trachea and bronchi: ciliated epithelium (a surface layer of cells carrying tiny hair-like cilia) with mucus-secreting goblet cells. Mucus traps dust and microorganisms.
The cilia beat in waves that sweep the mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed or coughed out. This is part of the body's first line of defence against infection.
Bronchi: the trachea divides into two bronchi (singular bronchus), one to each lung. They are also supported by cartilage.

Bronchioles: each bronchus branches repeatedly into thousands of narrower bronchioles. They have no cartilage; their walls contain smooth muscle, which can narrow or widen them and so change air flow.

The finest bronchioles end in clusters of alveoli (air sacs): tiny thin-walled sacs, each surrounded by a network of capillaries (the smallest blood vessels). The alveoli are the site of gas exchange.
The lungs have no muscle of their own, so they depend on the chest wall and on the muscles around it. The pleural membranes are what link the lungs to the chest wall.
The two lungs are spongy, elastic organs in the thorax (chest cavity), protected by the rib cage (ribs, sternum and vertebrae) and separated from the abdomen by the diaphragm.
Each lung is enclosed by two pleural membranes with a thin layer of pleural fluid between them. The fluid reduces friction as the lungs move.
The fluid also makes the lungs cling to the chest wall, so they expand when the thorax expands.
Diaphragm: a dome-shaped sheet of muscle and tendon forming the floor of the thorax.
Intercostal muscles: two sets, external and internal, lying between the ribs, which move the rib cage.

Diagram: the breathing system in a front view of the chest. Label the nasal cavity, pharynx, epiglottis, larynx, trachea with cartilage rings, two bronchi, bronchioles, lungs, pleural membranes, ribs, intercostal muscles, diaphragm and an outline of the heart. Add an enlarged inset of alveoli wrapped in capillaries.
Breathing in works by changing pressure. The muscles enlarge the thorax, the pressure in the lungs drops below the pressure outside, and air flows in.

Air always moves from a region of higher pressure to one of lower pressure. When the thorax volume increases, the pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure (the pressure of the air outside) and air flows in.
When the thorax volume decreases, the pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and air flows out. The lungs follow the chest wall because they have no muscle of their own.
Inhalation (inspiration) is an active process, which means it uses energy. 1. The brain sends nerve impulses to the breathing muscles.
2. The diaphragm contracts and flattens, moving downwards.
3. The external intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribs and sternum upwards and outwards.
4. The volume of the thorax increases.
5. The lungs expand with it, so the pressure inside them falls below atmospheric pressure.
6. Air rushes in through the nose and trachea until the pressures are equal. Muscle contraction uses ATP (the cell's energy currency), so inhalation is active.
Breathing out at rest needs no muscle contraction at all: the body simply springs back. During exercise, however, extra muscles make exhalation active.
Exhalation (expiration) at rest is a passive process, which means it uses no energy. 1. The impulses stop and the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles relax.
2. The diaphragm returns to its dome shape, pushed up by the abdominal organs, and the ribs move down and in under their own weight.
3. The stretched, elastic lung tissue recoils, like a stretched elastic band springing back.
4. The volume of the thorax decreases and the pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure.
5. Air is forced out. No muscle contracts, so no energy is used.

Forced exhalation, as in exercise, coughing, blowing or speaking loudly: the internal intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribs down and in, and the abdominal muscles contract, pushing the diaphragm up.
This expels air faster and more completely, and because muscles contract, forced exhalation is active.
Putting the two halves of the breathing cycle side by side shows that every change in one is reversed in the other.
Diaphragm: it contracts and flattens in inhalation, but relaxes and domes upwards in exhalation at rest.
External intercostal muscles: they contract in inhalation but relax in exhalation. The ribs move up and out in inhalation, and down and in in exhalation.
Thorax volume increases in inhalation and decreases in exhalation. Lung pressure falls below atmospheric pressure in inhalation and rises above it in exhalation, so air moves in, then out.
Inhalation is active, whereas exhalation at rest is passive.
The bell-jar model shows the volume and pressure principle: pulling the rubber sheet (the diaphragm) down inflates the balloons (the lungs). There is more on this in Models.

Diagram: two side-view sketches of the thorax, one at inhalation and one at exhalation, showing the diaphragm (flat or domed) and the ribs (raised or lowered), with arrows for rib movement and air flow. Label the diaphragm, ribs, intercostal muscles, lungs and trachea.
Breathing continues while you sleep because the brain controls it automatically. The signal that adjusts it is the level of carbon dioxide in the blood.

Breathing is controlled automatically by the breathing (respiratory) centre in the medulla oblongata, at the base of the brain. It sends rhythmic nerve impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, so breathing continues without thought, even during sleep.

We can change breathing voluntarily for a short time, using the cerebrum (the thinking part of the brain), for example by holding our breath, speaking or singing. The automatic control takes over again afterwards.

The main factor that sets the rate and depth of breathing is the level of carbon dioxide in the blood. When CO₂ rises, as during exercise when muscles respire faster, the breathing centre increases the rate and depth of breathing.
This removes more CO₂ and takes in more oxygen. When CO₂ falls, breathing slows. There is more on this in CO₂ as a controlling factor in breathing.
An adult at rest breathes about 12 to 20 times per minute, moving about 500 cm³ (half a litre) of air in each breath, the tidal volume.
During hard exercise both the rate and the depth (the volume of air per breath) increase greatly.
Gas exchange is a simple physical process: oxygen and carbon dioxide each move down their own concentration gradient between the air in the alveolus and the blood in the capillary beside it.

Gases cross between the air in an alveolus and the blood in its capillaries by diffusion, from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated. No energy is used, so it is not active transport.
Oxygen: the air in the alveoli has a higher oxygen concentration than the deoxygenated blood arriving from the body in the pulmonary artery.

Oxygen dissolves in the moisture lining the alveolus, diffuses through the alveolus wall and the capillary wall into the plasma (the liquid part of the blood), and enters the red blood cells, where it combines with haemoglobin to form oxyhaemoglobin.

Carbon dioxide: the blood arriving at the lungs has a higher CO₂ concentration than the air in the alveoli. CO₂, carried mostly in the plasma, diffuses out of the blood into the alveolus and is breathed out.
The oxygenated blood leaves the lungs in the pulmonary veins and returns to the heart. There is more on this in Circulation.
The concentration gradients are kept steep in two ways: breathing constantly brings in fresh air with a high oxygen and low CO₂ content and removes stale air.
Blood flow also keeps the gradients steep, because it constantly carries oxygenated blood away and brings new deoxygenated blood.
The alveoli are built so that diffusion is as fast as possible. Each feature either gives gases more room to cross, a shorter distance to travel, or a steeper gradient.
Very large total surface area: about 300 million alveoli in the two lungs give an exchange surface of roughly 70 m², so a large amount of gas can diffuse at once.
Very thin walls: the alveolus wall and the capillary wall are each one cell thick and pressed close together, so the diffusion distance is very short.
Moist lining: gases dissolve in the moisture before they diffuse across the wall.
Dense capillary network: every alveolus is surrounded by capillaries with a continuous blood flow, which keeps the concentration gradient steep.
Narrow capillaries: they are just wide enough for red blood cells to pass in single file, pressed against the wall. This shortens the distance further and slows the blood, giving time for exchange.
Elastic fibres around the alveoli let them stretch on inhalation and recoil on exhalation, which helps push air out.

Diagram: a single alveolus with a capillary wrapped around it. Label alveolus wall (one cell thick), capillary wall (one cell thick), moist lining, red blood cell and plasma. Add arrows: O₂ into the blood, CO₂ into the alveolus, and blood flow from pulmonary artery (deoxygenated) to pulmonary vein (oxygenated).
The air we breathe out differs from the air we breathe in, because the body takes oxygen from it and adds carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Inhaled air contains about 21% oxygen, about 0.04% carbon dioxide and 78% nitrogen, with a variable amount of water vapour.
Exhaled air contains about 16% oxygen, about 4% carbon dioxide and 78% nitrogen. It is saturated with water vapour and is warmer than inhaled air.
Nitrogen is not used by the body, so its proportion is the same in both.
Exhaled air still contains much oxygen, which is why rescue breaths work in CPR (the emergency procedure that keeps a casualty's blood supplied with oxygen).
Lime water turns milky faster with exhaled air, showing that exhaled air contains more CO₂.
Damage to the breathing system shows why its structures matter: when cilia, alveoli or bronchioles stop working properly, gas exchange suffers.

Smoking: tar and other chemicals in cigarette smoke paralyse and destroy the cilia and increase mucus production, so mucus and trapped microorganisms build up in the airways, causing coughing (smoker's cough) and frequent chest infections.

Emphysema, mainly caused by smoking: if alveolus walls break down and merge into larger air spaces, the surface area for gas exchange falls and the lungs lose their elasticity, so the person becomes breathless. This shows why the large surface area of the alveoli matters.
Carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke combines with haemoglobin, reducing the amount of oxygen the blood can carry. There is more on this in Blood.

Asthma: the smooth muscle in the bronchiole walls contracts, and the lining swells and produces extra mucus, narrowing the airways so that less air reaches the alveoli. Inhalers deliver drugs that relax the smooth muscle.
Every living cell respires, so every cell keeps adding carbon dioxide to the blood. The body has to match its breathing to that supply, and it does so by monitoring CO₂ rather than oxygen.

Carbon dioxide is produced by every respiring cell. If it is not removed, it accumulates in the blood, where it reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ (carbonic acid, hydrogen ions and hydrogencarbonate ions).
The reaction is speeded up by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells. A rise in CO₂ therefore makes the blood more acidic, lowering its pH, because more hydrogen ions are released.

Blood pH is normally kept within a narrow range around 7.4, slightly alkaline. A fall in pH alters the shape of enzymes and other proteins and disturbs cell function, so the CO₂ level must be controlled. Breathing is the body's fastest way of adjusting it.
In a healthy person at sea level, the CO₂ level, not the oxygen level, is the main stimulus for breathing. The body is far more sensitive to a small rise in CO₂ than to a fall in O₂.

Oxygen receptors only strongly increase breathing when the oxygen level falls a lot, for example at high altitude. This is why the urge to breathe when you hold your breath comes from rising CO₂, not falling O₂.
A change in blood CO₂ has to be detected before breathing can respond. Special receptors in two sets of locations do this and report to the breathing centre in the brain.
A chemoreceptor is a receptor that detects the concentration of a chemical, here CO₂ and the hydrogen ions it produces.

Central chemoreceptors lie in the medulla oblongata (the lowest part of the brain, joining the spinal cord), close to the breathing centre. They are responsible for most of the response to a rise in CO₂.

CO₂ diffuses from the blood into the cerebrospinal fluid (the fluid surrounding the brain), where it forms carbonic acid and lowers the pH. The central receptors respond to this rise in hydrogen ions, so they detect CO₂ through its effect on pH.

Peripheral chemoreceptors lie in the carotid bodies, small structures in the wall of each carotid artery in the neck (the arteries that carry blood to the brain), and in the aortic bodies, in the wall of the arch of the aorta.
Peripheral chemoreceptors detect a rise in CO₂ (and H⁺) and also a large fall in O₂ in the arterial blood. They send impulses along sensory nerves to the breathing centre.

Diagram: outline of the head, neck and chest. Label the medulla oblongata (breathing centre and central chemoreceptors), carotid bodies on the carotid arteries, aortic bodies on the aortic arch, nerves to the breathing centre, and nerves from the breathing centre to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles.
Detection is only the start. The signal then passes through a chain from stimulus to response, which brings the CO₂ level back to normal.
1. Stimulus: CO₂ in the blood rises, for example when muscles respire faster during exercise.
2. Receptors: the central and peripheral chemoreceptors detect the rise in CO₂, through the fall in pH.
3. Control centre: impulses reach the breathing centre in the medulla oblongata, which coordinates the response.

4. Effectors (the muscles that carry out the response): the breathing centre sends impulses more often along motor nerves to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, and in heavy breathing to the abdominal muscles.
5. Response: the muscles contract more strongly and more often, so breathing becomes deeper and faster.
6. Return to normal: more CO₂ is exhaled from the alveoli (the air sacs of the lungs) and more oxygen is taken in, so the CO₂ level in the blood falls back towards normal and the pH rises.
7. Reset: the receptors detect the return to normal, the breathing centre sends fewer impulses, and breathing returns to the resting rate.

The loop above is an example of negative feedback, the pattern the body uses to keep conditions steady. The same CO₂ signal also speeds up the heart so that the extra air is matched by faster blood flow.
This is negative feedback: the response, removing CO₂, cancels the change that caused it (the rise in CO₂), keeping the blood CO₂ level and pH near a set point.
It works in both directions: if CO₂ falls below normal, the breathing centre reduces the rate and depth of breathing, so CO₂ builds up again.

The cardiac centre in the medulla (the part of the brain that controls heart rate) responds to the same signals. A rise in CO₂ also increases the heart rate, so blood carries CO₂ to the lungs and oxygen to the muscles faster. There is more on this in Heartbeat.

Diagram: a feedback loop flow chart. CO₂ rises, then chemoreceptors, breathing centre in the medulla, diaphragm and intercostal muscles, faster and deeper breathing, CO₂ falls, back to normal, with a loop arrow returning to the start. Draw a matching loop for CO₂ falling.
The same loop explains several everyday and exam situations. In each case, follow what happens to blood CO₂ and the signal it sends.
Exercise: muscles respire faster and release more CO₂ into the blood. The rise is detected and breathing rate and depth increase within seconds, removing CO₂ and supplying the extra oxygen.

Breathing stays fast for a time after exercise stops, while the extra CO₂ is removed and the oxygen debt from anaerobic respiration (lactic acid) is repaid. There is more on this in Respiration as a catabolic process.

Holding the breath: CO₂ builds up in the blood and the signal from the chemoreceptors to the breathing centre becomes stronger and stronger. Eventually the automatic control overrides the voluntary control by the cerebrum, forcing a breath.
This is why a person cannot hold their breath until they lose consciousness at rest. The urge to breathe comes from rising CO₂, not from falling O₂.
Hyperventilation (deliberate fast, deep breathing) removes extra CO₂, so the CO₂ level falls below normal and the urge to breathe is reduced; the person may feel dizzy.

Before swimming underwater, hyperventilation is dangerous: the urge to breathe comes too late, so the oxygen level can fall far enough to cause blacking out before the swimmer feels the need to surface.
Breathing air with a raised CO₂ content, for example in a poorly ventilated, crowded room or when rebreathing air from a bag, makes breathing faster and deeper through the same loop.
