It keeps the leaf cells supplied with water, so they stay turgid and the leaves stay firm and spread out to the light. Evaporation also cools the leaves in strong sunlight, because evaporating water carries heat away.
Transpiration is unavoidable. The stomata must be open to let CO₂ in for photosynthesis, and water vapour escapes through the same pores.

If water is lost faster than the roots can take it in, the cells lose turgor (they go limp) and the plant wilts. Prolonged wilting stops photosynthesis and can kill the plant, so the plant balances gas exchange against water loss.

Conditions that increase transpiration are bright light, high temperature, wind, low humidity, a large leaf area and a thin cuticle. Each is explained and investigated in Investigation: rate of transpiration.
A stoma is a pore that lets CO₂ in and water vapour out, and the plant can open or close it. The guard cells on either side of the pore do this by changing how much water they hold.

Each stoma is a pore between two guard cells. The wall of a guard cell next to the pore, the inner wall, is thicker and less stretchy than the outer wall, and this difference is what makes the cell bend when it swells.

Opening: in the light, guard cells actively take in potassium ions (K⁺) from neighbouring epidermal cells (the ordinary cells of the leaf surface), using ATP. This raises the solute concentration in the guard cells, so water enters them by osmosis from the surrounding cells.
The guard cells swell and become turgid. Because the thick inner wall stretches less than the thin outer wall, the cells bend outwards and curve apart, and the pore opens.
Closing: potassium ions leave the guard cells, water follows by osmosis, the guard cells become flaccid (limp) and straighten, and the pore closes.

Diagram: a pair of guard cells drawn twice, once open (turgid, curved apart, pore open) and once closed (flaccid, straight, pore closed); label guard cell, thick inner wall, thin outer wall, chloroplast, nucleus and stoma (pore); add arrows for K⁺ and water entering when the stoma opens.
The plant does not open its stomata at random. It opens them when CO₂ is needed and closes them when water must be saved, and it places them where least water is lost.

Stomata are usually open in daylight, when CO₂ is needed for photosynthesis, and when the concentration of CO₂ inside the leaf is low. There is more on this in CO₂ as a controlling factor in plant stomata.
Stomata close at night, when there is no photosynthesis and so no need for CO₂, and in very hot, dry conditions. They also close when CO₂ concentration inside the leaf is high.
When water is short and the plant begins to wilt, a chemical signal from the roots closes the stomata, saving water even though photosynthesis slows.

Stomata are mostly on the lower surface of a broad leaf, where it is shaded and cooler, so less water evaporates from them. Leaves floating on water, such as the water lily, have them on the upper surface instead, because the lower surface touches the water.
Because transpiration cannot be stopped, plants survive by limiting it. Their leaves and habits are adapted to lose less water, most of all in dry, windy or cold places.

Leaf features that reduce water loss include a waxy, waterproof cuticle, thicker on the leaves of plants in dry or windy places; most stomata on the lower, shaded surface; and stomata that close at night and in drought.
Deciduous trees (trees that drop their leaves each year) shed their leaves in autumn, so they do not lose water in winter, when cold soil water is hard to absorb.
Evergreen conifers have needle-shaped leaves with a small surface area and a thick cuticle, which means little water evaporates even though the leaves stay on all year.

Plants of dry habitats (xerophytes) have extra adaptations. Marram grass of sand dunes rolls its leaves into a tube, with the stomata on the inside surface, trapping humid air. Cacti have leaves reduced to spines and store water in a swollen green stem.
Water is not the only thing roots take in. They also absorb dissolved minerals from the soil, but minerals enter by a different process from water, and that process costs the plant energy.

Plants need minerals such as nitrate, phosphate, potassium, magnesium and calcium. They are taken up from the soil water as dissolved ions, for example nitrate (NO₃⁻), potassium (K⁺) and magnesium (Mg²⁺).

Mineral ions are usually more concentrated inside the root hair cells than in the soil water, so they must be pumped in against their concentration gradient by carrier proteins in the cell membrane, using ATP from respiration. This is active transport.
Where the soil concentration is higher than in the cell, some ions also enter by diffusion.

Because active transport needs ATP, roots need oxygen for aerobic respiration. In waterlogged soil the air spaces fill with water, the roots get too little oxygen, mineral uptake falls and the plant grows poorly.
This is one reason soil must be well drained, and why roots have air spaces in the cortex.

The ions move across the cortex to the xylem and are carried up, dissolved in the water of the transpiration stream, to the leaves, growing tips and other parts, where they are taken into cells. The faster the transpiration, the faster minerals reach the leaves.
Pumping mineral ions into the root also makes the root cells more concentrated than the soil water, which keeps water entering by osmosis.
Transpiration pulls water up from above, but roots can also push it up from below. This push is called root pressure, and it is an active process that needs living root cells.
Root pressure is a pressure in the root xylem that pushes water a short distance up the stem from below.

Living root cells actively pump mineral ions into the xylem, using ATP. This makes the xylem sap more concentrated than the surrounding cells, so water passes into the xylem by osmosis, building up a pressure that pushes the water upwards.
Evidence: when a stem is cut off near ground level, sap oozes from the cut stump for some time, pushed out by the roots. Grapevines pruned in spring bleed sap in this way.

Guttation: on cool, humid nights or early mornings, when transpiration is very slow, drops of water are forced out through special pores at the tips and edges of leaves, for example on grass and strawberry leaves.
Guttation drops are not dew, because they appear at the leaf edges, not all over the surface.
Root pressure needs living, respiring root cells. It stops if the roots are killed, cooled or deprived of oxygen.
That it stops in these conditions shows that root pressure is an active process.
Root pressure is most significant at night and in spring, before the leaves have opened and when transpiration is low, and it can refill xylem columns that contain air bubbles.
Root pressure is far too weak to raise water to the top of a tall tree, and some plants show little or none, so it is not the main mechanism.

Root pressure is too weak to lift water to the top of a tall tree, so something else must do it. The cohesion–tension model explains how a pulling force from the leaves, and water's tendency to stick together, raises an unbroken column of water.

The cohesion–tension model explains how water rises to the tops of the tallest trees. It was proposed in 1894 by two Irish scientists at Trinity College Dublin, the botanist Henry Dixon and the physicist John Joly.
1. Transpiration: water evaporates from the walls of the mesophyll cells and diffuses out through the stomata.
2. The mesophyll cells replace the lost water by osmosis from the cells deeper in the leaf, and these take water from the xylem in the veins.

3. Tension: removing water from the top of the xylem puts the column of water in the xylem under tension, a pulling force or negative pressure, which is passed all the way down the stem to the roots. This is the transpiration pull.

4. Cohesion: water molecules are attracted to each other by hydrogen bonds, so they stick together and the column does not break. Each molecule pulled up drags the one behind it, so the whole unbroken column moves up as one.
5. Adhesion: water molecules are also attracted to the walls of the narrow xylem vessels. This helps hold the column up against gravity and stops it pulling away from the walls.
6. At the bottom, water is drawn into the root xylem from the cortex, and into the root hairs from the soil, to replace it.
The process is passive, so the plant spends no ATP on it. The lignified (stiffened with lignin) walls of the xylem stop the vessels collapsing inwards under the tension.
A model is only convincing if observations support it. Two observations show that the water in the xylem really is under tension, and one other factor is too weak to matter.
The trunk of a tree becomes very slightly narrower during the day, when transpiration is fastest, as the tension pulls the xylem walls inwards.
When a xylem vessel under tension is cut, air is drawn in rather than water leaking out. If air enters the xylem the column breaks and water flow in that vessel stops.
This is why the stems of cut flowers should be cut again under water before being placed in a vase.
Capillarity, the rise of water up narrow tubes by adhesion, raises water only a short way and is a minor factor.
The two mechanisms work together to move water, but they differ in direction, energy source, strength and timing. Comparing them in pairs is the clearest way to keep them apart.
Root pressure pushes water from below; cohesion–tension pulls it from above.
Root pressure is active, using ATP in the root cells; cohesion–tension is passive, powered by the sun's energy, which evaporates the water.
Root pressure raises water only a short distance; cohesion–tension is the main mechanism and can lift water to the top of the tallest trees.
Root pressure is most important at night and in spring, when transpiration is low; cohesion–tension works when the stomata are open and transpiration is fast, mainly by day.

Photosynthesis needs a steady supply of carbon dioxide (CO₂), the raw material the plant builds sugar from. A leaf cell has two places to get it from: the air around the plant and its own respiring cells.
A photosynthesising leaf gets CO₂ from two sources: the air outside, entering through the stomata (the tiny pores in the leaf surface), and the plant's own respiring cells.
The air contains only about 0.04% CO₂, so a leaf must exchange large volumes of air to get enough. This is why it has many stomata and a large internal surface.
Every living plant cell respires all the time, day and night, releasing CO₂ from its mitochondria (the organelles where respiration takes place). Plants do not respire only at night.

In the light, the CO₂ released by a mesophyll cell's own mitochondria, and by neighbouring cells, can be used directly by its chloroplasts without ever leaving the leaf. Mesophyll cells are the photosynthesising cells inside the leaf.
Aquatic plants take in CO₂ dissolved in the water around them.

CO₂ has to get from the outside air into the chloroplasts (the green organelles where photosynthesis happens), and it does so in a series of steps with no pump involved. The steps where it moves (2, 3 and 5) are diffusion down a concentration gradient, meaning from where there is more CO₂ to where there is less, and step 4 is the CO₂ dissolving in water.
1. Photosynthesis uses CO₂ in the chloroplasts, so the CO₂ concentration inside the leaf falls below that of the outside air, setting up a concentration gradient.
2. CO₂ diffuses in through the open stomata, from the higher concentration outside to the lower concentration inside.
3. It diffuses through the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll (the loosely packed layer of cells in the lower leaf) to the mesophyll cells.
4. It dissolves in the thin film of water on the moist cell walls, because gases can only enter cells in solution.

5. It diffuses across the cell wall, cell membrane and cytoplasm into the chloroplasts, where it is used in the light-independent stage (the part of photosynthesis that builds sugar from CO₂). The gradient is kept up because CO₂ is used as fast as it arrives.

Diagram: a transverse section of part of a leaf, with arrows for CO₂ diffusing in through a stoma, through the air spaces and into a palisade cell's chloroplast, and for oxygen and water vapour diffusing out; plus a short arrow from a mitochondrion to a chloroplast, labelled CO₂ from respiration.
Because CO₂ moves only by diffusion, a leaf is built to make that diffusion fast and short. Stomata also act as the gates that decide when CO₂ can enter.

CO₂ moves through the plant by diffusion only, through the air spaces and across moist cell surfaces. It is not carried in the xylem or phloem (the plant's water and food-carrying tubes), and no energy is used to move it.

A thin leaf (so the distance to travel is short), a large surface area, many stomata, a network of air spaces and moist mesophyll cell walls with a large total surface all speed up the diffusion of CO₂.

Stomata control the entry of CO₂: they open in the light, when CO₂ is needed. At Higher Level, the CO₂ concentration inside the leaf also helps control whether they open or close. There is more on this in CO₂ as a controlling factor in plant stomata.

Photosynthesis and respiration both happen in a leaf, and they swap the same gases in opposite directions. Which one wins depends on how much light there is, so the net gas exchange changes through the day.
In bright light, photosynthesis is faster than respiration. The leaf uses more CO₂ than its cells produce, so there is a net uptake of CO₂ through the stomata and a net release of oxygen.

In darkness there is no photosynthesis, only respiration. The plant takes in oxygen and gives out CO₂, through stomata that are mostly closed, through the cuticle (the waxy surface layer) in small amounts, and through lenticels (small pores in woody stems).

At dawn and dusk, in dim light, the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration, a point called the compensation point. All the CO₂ produced by respiration is used in photosynthesis, so there is no net exchange of CO₂ or oxygen with the air.

Non-green parts, such as roots, woody stems and the inside of fruits and tubers, only respire because they do not photosynthesise. They take in oxygen and release CO₂ by diffusion: roots to the air spaces in the soil, and woody stems through lenticels.
The oxygen made in photosynthesis is a photosynthetic product too. It is used in the plant's own respiration, and the excess diffuses out through the stomata.

The sugar made in a leaf is needed all over the plant, in places that cannot photosynthesise. Translocation is how it gets there, carried in the phloem by a flow that goes from where the sugar is made to where it is used.

Translocation is the transport of dissolved food made in photosynthesis, mainly sucrose and also amino acids, through the phloem sieve tubes (the living tubes of the phloem) from one part of the plant to another.
Sucrose is the form in which sugar is carried, not glucose. Starch is never transported; it is stored, and must be converted to sucrose before it can move.

Amino acids (the building blocks of proteins) are made in the leaves from sugars and the nitrates brought up in the xylem. They are carried in the phloem to growing regions, where they are used to make proteins.
A source is a part of the plant where sucrose is made or released into the phloem. This is mainly the photosynthesising leaves, and also storage organs when their stores are being used.

A sink is a part where sucrose is used or stored. Sinks include growing shoot and root tips, which use it in respiration and to make cellulose for new cell walls, and developing flowers, fruits and seeds.
Other sinks are the roots and storage organs, where sucrose is converted to starch, as in potato tubers in summer.

Because sources and sinks are in different places and can swap roles, phloem flow is not fixed in one direction. It is also driven by a living, energy-using process, which sets it apart from water movement in the xylem.
Because sinks can be above or below the leaves, phloem transport goes both up and down the plant, at different times in different sieve tubes.

A part can change role. A potato tuber is a sink while it fills with starch in summer, and a source the next spring, when its starch is converted back to sucrose and carried to the growing new shoots.

Translocation needs energy: at the source, companion cells (the cells beside the sieve tubes) use ATP to load sucrose actively into the sieve tubes. So it happens only in living phloem and stops if the phloem is killed, for example by heat.
There is more on this in Plant structures for transport.

Once sucrose is in the sieve tubes, something must push the sap along. The pressure-flow model explains this as a pressure difference between the source and the sink, set up by moving sucrose in and out and by water following it by osmosis (water moving into a more concentrated solution).
1. Loading sucrose at the source makes the sap in the sieve tubes there very concentrated.
2. Water enters the sieve tubes from the nearby xylem by osmosis, because the concentrated sap draws it in, raising the pressure.
3. At the sink, sucrose is removed from the sieve tubes into the cells that use or store it, so water leaves and the pressure there is lower.

4. The sap flows along the sieve tubes, through the sieve plates (the perforated walls between sieve tube cells), from the high-pressure source to the low-pressure sink, carrying the dissolved sucrose and amino acids with it.

Diagram: a plant outline with a leaf labelled source, and a root tip, a fruit and a storage organ labelled sink, with phloem arrows for sucrose moving up and down. Beside it, a sieve tube between source and sink cells: sucrose loaded, water entering by osmosis, flow, sucrose unloaded.

We can't watch sucrose moving inside a sieve tube, so the idea that the phloem carries food rests on experiments and observations. Three pieces of evidence all point to the phloem rather than the xylem.
Ringing, or girdling: removing a complete ring of bark from a woody stem removes the phloem, which lies just inside the bark, but leaves the xylem, the wood, intact.
The bark just above the ring swells as sugars build up there, and the tissues below the ring, including the roots, are starved of food. If the roots run out of food, the whole tree dies.
The leaves above the ring do not wilt at first, because the xylem still carries water up.
Animals that strip a ring of bark from trees, such as deer, rabbits and grey squirrels, can kill them in this way. Foresters protect young trees with tree guards.
Aphids are small insects that feed by pushing their needle-like mouthparts into a single sieve tube. The sap that flows into them is rich in sucrose and amino acids.
If an aphid's body is cut away, the sap keeps oozing out of its mouthparts, which shows that the sap is under pressure in the sieve tube.

Radioactive tracers: if a leaf is given CO₂ containing radioactive carbon (¹⁴CO₂), the radioactive carbon soon appears in sucrose, first in the phloem of the leaf, then in the phloem of the stem and in the sinks, and not in the xylem.
Plants move three different kinds of material by three different mechanisms. Comparing them side by side shows where students most often mix them up.
What moves: water and minerals move in the xylem; sucrose and amino acids move in the phloem; CO₂ and oxygen move by diffusion through air spaces, in neither tissue.
Direction: xylem moves water upwards only; phloem moves food up or down, from source to sink; CO₂ moves down its concentration gradient, into the leaf by day and out of it at night.

Driving force: for water, evaporation from the leaves (the transpiration pull), helped at Higher Level by root pressure; for sucrose, active loading at the source and the pressure difference between source and sink; for CO₂, diffusion down a concentration gradient.
Energy used by the plant: none to lift water, which is driven by the sun's energy; ATP for loading sucrose and for absorbing minerals; none for CO₂ diffusion.

Stomata are the tiny pores in a leaf's surface through which CO₂ enters and water vapour escapes. Their width is not fixed: the plant adjusts it in response to several signals, and the concentration of CO₂ inside the leaf is one of them.
The concentration of CO₂ in the air spaces inside the leaf (the gaps between the cells) is one of the factors that controls the width of the stomatal pores, along with light and water supply.
A low concentration of CO₂ inside the leaf causes the stomata to open, or to open wider, so that more CO₂ can diffuse in.
A high concentration of CO₂ inside the leaf causes the stomata to close, or partly close, so less gas passes through the pore.
Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells, which change shape to open or close the pore. Guard cells respond to the CO₂ concentration around them, so the response is local to each stoma.
Low CO₂ leads to potassium ions (K⁺) being taken into the guard cells, water entering by osmosis and the guard cells becoming turgid (swollen and firm), so the pore opens.
High CO₂ leads to K⁺ leaving the guard cells, water following by osmosis and the guard cells becoming flaccid (limp), so the pore closes.

The response is to the concentration inside the leaf, which depends on the balance between photosynthesis, which uses CO₂, and respiration, which releases it. It is not simply the concentration in the outside air.
The CO₂ response is useful because the CO₂ level inside a leaf changes with the balance between photosynthesis and respiration, so the stomata open when CO₂ is needed and close when it is not.

In the light, photosynthesis uses CO₂ faster than respiration produces it, so the CO₂ concentration in the air spaces falls. The low CO₂ opens the stomata, letting in more CO₂ for photosynthesis exactly when it is needed.
In darkness there is no photosynthesis, but respiration continues, so CO₂ builds up in the air spaces. The high CO₂ closes the stomata.
The plant does not need CO₂ in the dark, so closing the stomata saves water that would otherwise be lost by transpiration (evaporation of water vapour through the open stomata).

This is a negative feedback loop (a change sets off a response that reverses the change). When internal CO₂ is low, the stomata open and CO₂ enters, so its concentration rises; as it rises, the stomata begin to close.

CO₂ concentration therefore helps match the opening of the stomata to the leaf's demand for CO₂, keeping the balance between taking in CO₂ and losing water. There is more on negative feedback in Homeostasis as a stimulus-response model.
The CO₂ response works together with the other controls. Light opens the stomata directly as well as by lowering CO₂ through photosynthesis.

Shortage of water closes the stomata even when CO₂ is low, because preventing wilting takes priority over photosynthesis. So on a hot, dry afternoon the stomata may close although the leaf needs CO₂, and photosynthesis slows.

Experimental evidence: if a leaf in the light is given air with extra CO₂, its stomata close partly. If a leaf in the dark is given CO₂-free air, its stomata open partly. This shows that CO₂ acts on the stomata on its own, separately from light.

Stomata are the main route by which a leaf loses water, so anything that changes their width also changes the rate of transpiration. This links CO₂ to water loss, and to wider questions about farming and climate.

Because CO₂ controls the width of the stomata, it affects transpiration. Raising the CO₂ concentration around a leaf closes the stomata partly and reduces the rate of transpiration; lowering it opens them and increases the rate.
This is why CO₂ concentration is one of the factors in Investigation: rate of transpiration.

Sustainability link: the CO₂ concentration of the atmosphere is rising, mainly from burning fossil fuels. Plants grown in raised CO₂ tend to open their stomata less, so they lose less water per unit of sugar made.
Leaves of the same species collected over the last two centuries and kept in herbarium collections (preserved plant specimens) show fewer stomata per unit area as CO₂ has risen.
Technology link: glasshouse growers add CO₂ to raise photosynthesis. The extra CO₂ also partly closes the stomata, so the plants lose less water.
Plants and humans both use CO₂ concentration to control gas exchange, but they respond in opposite ways. Comparing them shows that the difference comes from what CO₂ means to each organism.
What is detected, in plants: the CO₂ concentration inside the leaf, detected by the guard cells themselves. Plants have no nerves, so the response is local, in each stoma.

What is detected, in humans: the CO₂ concentration of the blood, through its effect on blood pH. Chemoreceptors (cells that detect chemical change) in the medulla oblongata and in the carotid and aortic bodies detect it and signal the breathing centre in the medulla.
Response to high CO₂: in plants the stomata close, reducing gas exchange. In humans the rate and depth of breathing increase, increasing gas exchange.
Response to low CO₂: in plants the stomata open. In humans breathing slows.

Why the responses are opposite, in plants: for a plant in the light, CO₂ is a raw material for photosynthesis, so low internal CO₂ signals that more is needed, and high internal CO₂ signals that none is being used, so water should be saved.
Why the responses are opposite, in humans: CO₂ is a waste product of respiration that makes the blood more acidic, so high CO₂ signals that more must be removed.
What is similar: in both, CO₂ concentration is the main controlling signal for gas exchange, and the control works by negative feedback, returning the CO₂ level towards normal.

In both, the controlled structures adjust how much gas passes across the exchange surface: the stomata in plants, and the diaphragm and intercostal muscles that ventilate the alveoli in humans. There is more on this in CO₂ as a controlling factor in breathing.

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant, mostly through its leaves. The rate of transpiration is the volume, or mass, of water lost by a plant per unit time. It depends on how steep the water vapour concentration gradient is between the air spaces of the leaf, which are saturated with water vapour, and the outside air; how fast water evaporates; and how wide the stomata (the pores in the leaf surface) are open.

Air movement: wind blows away the layer of humid air that builds up around the leaf, keeping the outside air dry and the gradient steep, so the rate increases. In still air the humid layer builds up, the gradient flattens and the rate falls.

Temperature: warmer water molecules have more kinetic energy (movement energy), so they evaporate from the mesophyll cell walls (the moist walls of the cells inside the leaf) and diffuse out faster. Warm air can also hold more water vapour, so the gradient is steeper. The rate increases with temperature.
At very high temperatures the plant may begin to wilt and close its stomata, which stops water vapour escaping, and then the rate falls.
Surface area: more leaves, or larger leaves, mean more stomata and more evaporating surface, so the rate increases roughly in proportion to the leaf area.

Cuticle (the waxy covering of the leaf) is waterproof, so only a little water is lost through it; most is lost through the stomata. A thick cuticle means less loss than a thin one. A surface coated with an artificial waterproof layer, such as petroleum jelly, loses almost none.

Light intensity: stomata open in the light and close in darkness, so the rate increases with light intensity, until the stomata are fully open, and is very low in darkness. A lamp also warms the leaf, which raises the rate further unless the temperature is controlled.

CO₂ concentration: a high concentration of CO₂ around the leaf partly closes the stomata, so the rate falls; a low concentration opens them wider, so the rate rises. The Higher Level explanation is in CO₂ as a controlling factor in plant stomata.

Humidity, not named by the specification but controlled when the other factors are tested: humid air reduces the gradient, so the rate falls. This matters whenever a shoot is enclosed in a plastic bag, as in the CO₂ method, because the air in the bag becomes humid.
A good investigation changes one factor at a time, so that any change in the result can be blamed on that one factor. Planning starts with an aim and a hypothesis (a testable prediction).

Aim: to investigate the effect of one factor (air movement, temperature, surface area, cuticle, light intensity or CO₂ concentration) on the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot. Change one factor per investigation.

Example hypotheses, each resting on the theory above: “Increasing air movement increases the rate of transpiration”; “The rate of transpiration increases as temperature increases”; “The rate increases as leaf area increases”.

More example hypotheses: “Covering the lower surface of a leaf reduces water loss more than covering the upper surface”; “The rate increases as light intensity increases”; “Increasing the CO₂ concentration around a shoot reduces its rate of transpiration”.
The potometer (the apparatus used to measure uptake) measures water uptake, not water loss. The two are almost equal, because nearly all the water a shoot takes up is lost by transpiration.
Only a tiny amount of the water taken up is used in photosynthesis or to keep the cells turgid (firm and full of water). The mass-loss method measures water loss directly.
Once the aim is set, name what you change, what you measure and what you keep the same, and say what each comparison is checked against.

Independent variable (the one factor you change), using light intensity as the example: the lamp distance, or the light meter reading in lux. For the other factors, the independent variable is swapped and everything else is kept constant.
Dependent variable (the one you measure), using light intensity as the example: the rate of water uptake, which is the distance moved by the air bubble per minute, converted to a volume per minute.

Controlled variables (kept the same so the test is fair), using light intensity as the example: the same shoot (same species, same number and size of leaves), temperature (a thermometer by the shoot and a heat shield), air movement (no fans, windows closed).
More controlled variables: humidity (the same room), CO₂ (the same room air), the time allowed to adjust, and the length of each timing.

Controls: a baseline reading for the same shoot in normal room conditions, still air, room temperature and normal light, to compare each change against. A leafless stem in the potometer, with all leaves removed and the cut surfaces sealed, shows that almost all the water is lost through the leaves.

Two more controls: for the cuticle investigation the control is an untreated leaf, and for the CO₂ investigation it is an identical bag with no CO₂ added or removed, so that any effect of the bag itself is allowed for.
The same basic kit serves every factor, with a few extra items added for particular methods. Know what each item is for, because exams ask you to name the apparatus and describe the set-up.
Bubble potometer: a capillary tube (a very narrow tube) with a scale, a reservoir or syringe with a tap for resetting the bubble, and rubber tubing or a bung to hold the shoot.
Other apparatus: clamp stand; a leafy shoot of a woody shrub with a stiff stem, e.g. laurel or privet; sharp knife or scalpel; a basin or sink of water; petroleum jelly (Vaseline); paper towels.

Measuring and fair-test apparatus: stopwatch; ruler; thermometer; bench lamp (LED preferred) and metre stick; light meter (optional); electric fan; heat shield, such as a flat-sided tank or beaker of water.

For the CO₂ method: a clear plastic bag with string or tape; soda lime, to absorb CO₂; and a CO₂ source, either a flask of marble chips with dilute hydrochloric acid connected by tubing, or a CO₂ cylinder.
For the cuticle and surface-area methods: graph paper, for measuring leaf area; and, for the alternative methods, an electronic balance, cobalt chloride paper, forceps and clear tape.
The first stage is to build a potometer that is full of water, airtight and free of air bubbles. If the water column is broken or the joints leak, the readings are meaningless.
1. Cut a leafy shoot from the plant, then immediately recut the stem at a slant under water, a few centimetres further up, so that no air enters the xylem (the vessels that carry water up the stem).
An air bubble in the xylem would break the water columns, so the shoot could not draw water up. There is more on this in Transport of water and minerals.
2. Submerge the potometer in the basin of water so that it fills completely, with no air bubbles.
3. Fit the shoot into the rubber tubing or bung under water, so that the joint is airtight.
4. Take the assembled potometer out of the water and clamp it upright, with the capillary tube horizontal.
5. Seal all joints with petroleum jelly to prevent leaks.
6. Gently dry the leaves with a paper towel, since water on their surface would evaporate and add to the loss.
Once the apparatus is ready, you introduce a single air bubble and use its movement along the scale to measure how fast the shoot takes up water.
7. Introduce one air bubble into the capillary tube by lifting its open end out of the water for a moment, then return it to a beaker of water.
8. Leave the shoot for about 5 minutes to adjust to the conditions, so that the readings reflect the present conditions and not the previous ones.

9. Record the starting position of the bubble on the scale, start the stopwatch, and record the distance the bubble moves towards the shoot in a set time, e.g. 5 minutes. The bubble moves towards the shoot because the shoot is drawing water out of the tube.
10. Return the bubble to the start of the scale by opening the reservoir tap, or by pushing water in from the syringe.
11. Repeat at least three times under the same conditions, and calculate the mean, so that one odd reading does not distort the result.

Diagram: a bubble potometer clamped on a stand. Label the leafy shoot sealed in with petroleum jelly, water-filled tube, reservoir with tap, horizontal capillary tube with scale, air bubble, beaker of water at the open end; draw an arrow for the bubble's direction.
Bubble movement is only a distance, so it has to be turned into a rate, and sometimes into a volume. These worked examples show each calculation step by step.

Rate of water uptake = distance moved by the bubble ÷ time, e.g. in mm per minute. Use this when all the readings use the same potometer, because then the capillary tube is the same and distances can be compared directly.
To give a volume, use the volume of a cylinder (the water in the capillary tube forms a cylinder): volume = πr² × distance moved, where r is the radius of the capillary tube.
Worked example: radius 0.5 mm, bubble moves 30 mm in 5 minutes. Volume = 3.14 × 0.5² × 30 = 3.14 × 0.25 × 30 = 23.6 mm³ in 5 minutes, so the rate is 23.6 ÷ 5 = 4.7 mm³ per minute.

To compare shoots of different sizes, divide by the leaf area, because a bigger shoot loses more water simply by having more leaf. Draw round each leaf on 1 cm² graph paper, count the squares that are at least half covered, and add up the total for all the leaves.
Worked example: 4.7 mm³ per minute ÷ 50 cm² = 0.094 mm³ per minute per cm².
Mass-loss method: rate = mass lost ÷ time, e.g. in g per hour. Percentage mass loss = (mass lost ÷ starting mass) × 100, which allows leaves of different sizes to be compared.
Worked example: a leaf of 2.0 g that weighs 1.5 g after 24 hours has lost 0.5 g, which is 25%.
Here the independent variable is how much air moves past the shoot, set with an electric fan. The idea is to test whether moving air keeps the concentration gradient steep.
1. Take the baseline reading in still air, as in the potometer setup.
2. Place an electric fan at a fixed distance, e.g. 1 m, from the shoot on its lowest setting. Wait 5 minutes and take three readings.
3. Repeat on the medium and highest settings, or with the fan at decreasing distances.
4. Check that the fan does not change the temperature by reading the thermometer near the shoot, because a change in temperature would also change the rate.
Expected: the rate increases as air movement increases, because moving air carries away the humid layer around the leaf.
Temperature is changed by carrying out the readings in places that are at different, steady temperatures. The main difficulty is warming the shoot without also moving the air or changing the light.

1. Take readings with the potometer in places at different, steady temperatures, e.g. a cool room, the laboratory and a warm room, measuring the air temperature beside the shoot with a thermometer each time.
2. Allow the shoot about 10 minutes to reach each temperature before taking three readings.
3. Do not use a fan heater blowing on the shoot, because it changes air movement as well as temperature. If a heater is used, place it at a distance, behind a heat shield.
4. Keep the light intensity the same in each place, with the same lamp and no direct sunlight, because light also affects the rate.
Expected: the rate increases with temperature.

Here the independent variable is the total leaf area of the shoot, which is reduced stage by stage by removing leaves. Because each leaf carries stomata, less leaf means less surface to lose water from.
1. Take readings with all the leaves on the shoot.
2. Remove one or two leaves by cutting them off at the base of the leaf stalk, seal the cut surfaces with petroleum jelly so that no water escapes there, and take new readings.

4. Measure the area of each removed leaf on graph paper, as in the calculation method, so that the total leaf area left at each stage is known. Alternatively, compare shoots with different total leaf areas.
Expected: the rate falls as the leaf area falls, roughly in proportion, and the leafless stem gives almost no movement of the bubble. Plot the rate against the leaf area.
This investigation compares leaves with and without a waterproof coating. Petroleum jelly acts as an artificial, thicker cuticle, so coating different surfaces shows where water is really lost.
1. Pick four similar leaves of the same size from the same plant.

2. Leave leaf A untreated, as the control. Coat the upper surface of leaf B with a thin layer of petroleum jelly, coat the lower surface of leaf C, and coat both surfaces of leaf D. The petroleum jelly acts as an artificial, thicker waterproof cuticle.
3. Seal the cut end of each leaf stalk with petroleum jelly.
4. Weigh each leaf on an electronic balance.
5. Hang the leaves on a string across the room, in the same conditions.
6. Reweigh each leaf every day for several days, and calculate the percentage mass loss. The loss in mass is the water lost.

Expected results: A loses the most mass. B loses nearly as much as A, because its upper surface has a thick cuticle and few stomata. C loses much less, because the stomata on its lower surface are blocked. D loses almost none.
Conclusion: the cuticle greatly reduces water loss, and most water is lost through the stomata on the lower surface.
The cuticle comparison can also be run on a potometer shoot instead of on separate hanging leaves, which gives a rate of water uptake rather than a mass loss.
Variation using the potometer: coat the upper surfaces, then the lower surfaces, of all the leaves on the potometer shoot, and take readings after each, compared with the untreated reading.
Alternative: compare shoots of plants with a thick, shiny waxy cuticle, such as laurel, and plants with thin, soft leaves of similar area.
Cobalt chloride paper is a quick way to show that water vapour leaves a leaf, and from which surface. It supports the main methods rather than replacing them.
Dry cobalt chloride paper is blue, and it turns pink when it absorbs water.

Using forceps, place a small square on the upper surface and one on the lower surface of a leaf still on the plant, and cover each with clear tape so that the paper only picks up water vapour from the leaf.
Time how long each square takes to turn pink.
Expected: the paper on the lower surface turns pink first, showing that more water vapour leaves through the lower surface, where most of the stomata are.

Light intensity is varied by moving a lamp to different distances from the shoot, with a heat shield so that the lamp changes only the light. Light matters because it controls whether the stomata are open.
1. Work in a darkened room, so that room light does not add to the lamp.
2. Place a lamp at a set distance from the shoot, e.g. 10 cm, with a heat shield between them. Wait 5 minutes and take three readings.

3. Repeat at 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm, measuring the distance from bulb to shoot with a metre stick. Alternatively, use a light meter, since intensity does not fall in simple proportion to distance. There is more on this in Investigation: rate of photosynthesis.
4. Take a final set of readings in darkness, with the lamp off and the shoot covered with a black bag or box.
5. Check the thermometer beside the shoot at each distance, because the lamp can warm the shoot.
Expected: the rate is highest with the lamp closest, and very low in darkness, when the stomata close.

CO₂ is varied by enclosing the shoot in a clear plastic bag and either adding CO₂ or absorbing it. The bag causes its own problem, because the air inside becomes humid, so the method needs a control bag.
1. Take readings with the shoot in a clear plastic bag sealed loosely around the stem, with nothing added. This is the control for the effect of the bag and its humidity.
2. Raised CO₂: pass CO₂ into the bag through a tube from a flask of marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid, or from a CO₂ cylinder. Tie the bag, wait 10 minutes and take three readings.
3. Lowered CO₂: place a small open dish of soda lime, which absorbs CO₂, inside the bag, not touching the leaves. Tie the bag, wait 10 minutes and take three readings.
4. Keep the shoot in bright light throughout, at a constant temperature, and keep each run short, because humidity builds up inside the bag.

Expected: raised CO₂ lowers the rate, and lowered CO₂ raises it slightly. The effect is smaller and harder to detect than the effects of light or air movement, so careful repeats and comparison with secondary data are needed.
This investigation combines sharp blades, glass, electricity near water and some hazardous chemicals. Each hazard has a simple precaution.
Cut away from the body on a tile, and take care with the knife or scalpel. Glass capillary tubes break easily, so handle them gently and report breakages.

Keep the lamp, the fan and their cables away from the basin and the potometer, and dry your hands before touching switches, because water and electricity are a dangerous mixture. Keep fingers clear of the fan blades.
Lamp bulbs, except LEDs, get very hot, so let them cool before moving them.
Cobalt chloride paper is toxic and can cause cancer. Handle it only with forceps, wear gloves, and wash your hands afterwards.
Soda lime is corrosive, because it contains sodium hydroxide. Wear safety glasses and gloves, and do not touch it. Dilute hydrochloric acid is an irritant, so wear safety glasses.
Wash hands after handling plants, since some, such as laurel, are poisonous if eaten, and after handling petroleum jelly.
Primary data are the results you collect yourself. They only become evidence when they are tabulated, graphed and explained using the theory of how each factor works.

Record the primary data in a table: the independent variable (e.g. lamp distance in cm, fan setting, temperature in °C or leaf area in cm²), the three readings of distance moved in the set time, the mean, and the rate in mm per minute or mm³ per minute.
For the cuticle investigation, record the starting mass, each day's mass and the percentage mass loss for each leaf.

Plot the mean rate on the y-axis against the independent variable on the x-axis, with units. Use a bar chart for categories, such as fan settings, treatments A to D, or still and moving air, and a line graph for continuous variables, such as temperature, leaf area or light intensity.
Expected patterns: the rate rises with air movement, temperature, leaf area and light intensity. It falls with a thick or artificial cuticle, especially on the lower surface, and with raised CO₂.
At high light intensity the rate levels off once the stomata are fully open, because they cannot open any wider.

Conclusion: state the relationship shown by the primary data, explain it using the theory of how each factor works (gradient, evaporation and stomatal opening), and say whether it supports the hypothesis. Use the mean of the repeats, and compare with other groups' results.

Diagram: four leaves hanging on a string, labelled A untreated, B upper surface coated, C lower surface coated and D both surfaces coated, with a bar chart of the expected percentage mass loss, with A highest, B slightly lower, C much lower and D lowest.

Secondary data are results collected by someone else. They let you test your conclusions against a larger body of evidence, and they are especially useful where a school laboratory cannot show an effect clearly.

Secondary data are results collected by others, such as other groups' class results, published graphs and tables, weather data (temperature, humidity and wind speed from a weather station or Met Éireann, Ireland's national weather service), or results from electronic sensors and data loggers measuring humidity or mass loss.
Pooling class results increases the sample size and checks reproducibility (whether other people get the same results).

Interpreting a graph of transpiration over 24 hours: the rate is very low at night, when the stomata are closed, and the air is often cooler and still. It rises after dawn as the stomata open, light increases and the air warms.
It peaks around the early afternoon, when light and temperature are highest and the air is driest, and it falls in the evening.
On a hot, dry afternoon the graph may dip if the plant begins to wilt and closes its stomata.

Because the effect of CO₂ is small in a school laboratory, published results from controlled-atmosphere experiments can be used for the CO₂ factor. These are plants grown at different CO₂ concentrations, with all other conditions fixed, and they support the conclusion that higher CO₂ reduces stomatal opening and transpiration.

Compare primary and secondary data by checking whether your results show the same trend as the published data. If they differ, look for an uncontrolled variable or a source of error, and evaluate the sources for reliability. There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
Every method has weaknesses that can make results unreliable. For each one, know both the problem and the fix.
The potometer measures water uptake, not water loss, and a small amount of the water taken up is used by the plant, so uptake is slightly higher than the true loss.
Air leaks at the joints, or air entering the cut stem, stop or slow the bubble and give a falsely low rate. Cut the stem under water and seal the joints with petroleum jelly.

Changing one factor often changes another: a lamp heats the shoot, a fan or heater moves air, and a plastic bag raises humidity. Use a heat shield, keep heaters away, use a control bag and check the thermometer.
Room conditions, such as temperature, humidity, sunlight through windows and people moving about, change during a lesson. Take readings close together in time, and repeat them.
Too little time to adjust after each change gives a rate that still reflects the previous condition. Wait about 5 to 10 minutes.
A cut shoot behaves differently from a whole plant and may wilt during a long investigation. Use a healthy shoot and a short investigation, or a fresh shoot for each run, and measure its leaf area.
Reading the bubble position by eye on a scale is imprecise. Read at eye level and repeat at least three times, calculating a mean.
Ecology looks at how living things fit into the world around them. To talk about it clearly, ecologists sort life into levels, each one bigger than the last, and each has its own precise name.

Ecology is the study of the interactions between living organisms, and between organisms and their non-living environment. The word comes from the Greek oikos, meaning house or home, because it is about the place where organisms live and how they get on there.

A population is all the members of one species living in a particular area at the same time, e.g. all the daisies in a field, or all the red squirrels in a woodland. Members can interbreed because they are one species.

A community is all the populations of all the different species living and interacting in an area at the same time, e.g. all the plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms of a woodland. It is the living (biotic) part of an ecosystem only, with no soil, water or air.

The ecological levels, smallest to largest, are: organism, population, community, ecosystem, biosphere. Each level includes the one before it, and from the ecosystem upward the non-living environment is included too.

These levels continue the levels of organisation inside a body (cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism): the organism is where the two sets of levels meet, and ecology then builds upward from it.

Diagram: nested boxes or a stepped sequence. Show one rabbit (organism), a group of rabbits (population), rabbits with grass, foxes and other species (community), the community with soil, water, air and light (ecosystem), and the Earth's living layer (biosphere). Label each level.
The biosphere is the largest ecological level: the whole of the Earth's life taken together. Its limits and the way matter and energy move through it explain why life depends on the Sun.
The biosphere is the part of the Earth where life exists: the lower atmosphere, the land surface and soil, and the water (fresh water and oceans). It is the sum of all the Earth's ecosystems.
The biosphere is a thin layer compared with the size of the Earth. Life is found from the deep ocean floor to a few kilometres up in the air, in birds, spores and bacteria carried on the wind.
Most life is concentrated in a narrow zone near the surface, because that is where light, liquid water and suitable temperatures are all present.

The biosphere is a single, closed system for matter, because atoms are recycled and not added. It is an open system for energy, because energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat. There is more on this in Energy and nutrient transfer, The carbon cycle and The nitrogen cycle.
An ecosystem is a community together with the non-living world it lives in. The living and non-living parts affect each other, which is why you have to study both.

An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with each other and with their non-living (abiotic) environment in a particular area. It has living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts that affect each other.

Biotic factors are the living parts of the environment and the effects organisms have on each other: food supply, predation (one animal hunting and eating another), competition, disease, parasites, pollinators and decomposers.

Abiotic factors are the non-living physical and chemical conditions of the environment: light, temperature, water, oxygen, soil type and pH, minerals, wind, slope and aspect (the direction a slope faces). There is more on this in Abiotic factors within Investigating an Ecosystem, and in Carrying capacity and limiting factors.

Ecosystems have no fixed size: a rock pool, a hedgerow, a lake, a raised bog or an ocean can each be treated as an ecosystem. Their boundaries are often gradual, e.g. a woodland edge merging into grassland.

Every ecosystem needs a continual input of energy, almost always sunlight captured by producers (such as plants) in photosynthesis. Its matter is recycled by decomposers (such as fungi and bacteria), so the ecosystem keeps running.

Producers, consumers and decomposers each have a different role in an ecosystem. Consumers are the animals that get their energy by eating other organisms. The roles of all three are taught in Energy and nutrient transfer.

Irish land ecosystems include grassland, the most widespread land cover in Ireland, mostly farmed pasture and meadow. Woodland includes the native oak woodlands of Killarney National Park. Peatlands have raised bogs in the midlands and blanket bogs in the uplands and the west.

Irish water and coastal ecosystems include freshwater, such as lakes like Lough Derg, a lake on the River Shannon, and rivers. Coastal and marine ecosystems include rocky shores, sandy shores and sand dunes, salt marshes and the open sea.
An ecosystem is too big to describe where one particular animal lives. Ecologists therefore talk about habitats, and smaller microhabitats, to say exactly where an organism is found.

A habitat is the place where an organism lives, which provides the food, shelter and conditions it needs. A woodlouse's habitat is damp leaf litter, a limpet's is the rocky shore, and a frog's is a pond and the damp vegetation around it.

A microhabitat is a small area within a habitat with its own conditions, e.g. the underside of a stone on a rocky shore, a rock pool, a rotting log, or the bark of a tree. Shade, moisture and temperature there can differ greatly from the surroundings.

One ecosystem contains many habitats: a woodland contains the canopy, the trunk, the leaf litter and the soil, each with different species. A habitat is the organism's 'address'; its role there is its niche, which is dealt with in The niche.
Biodiversity is more than a count of species. It describes how much variety there is in life, and it can be measured at three different levels, from genes up to whole habitats.

Biodiversity (biological diversity) is the variety of life in an area, or on Earth, at all its levels. It is usually described at three levels: genetic diversity, species diversity and ecosystem (habitat) diversity.

Genetic diversity is the variety of alleles (different versions of a gene) within a species or population, e.g. the different breeds of cattle, or the variation in disease resistance among wild ash trees. It allows a population to adapt by natural selection when conditions change.
Low genetic diversity left the Irish potato crop of the 1840s vulnerable, because it was largely one variety, so when blight (a disease) arrived it destroyed it.

Species diversity is the variety of species in an area. It has two parts: species richness, the number of different species present, and species evenness, how evenly the individuals are spread among those species.

Two areas with the same species can differ in diversity if one is dominated by a single species. The Simpson's Diversity Index, which combines richness and evenness into one number, is Higher Level only. There is more on this in Simpson's Diversity Index.

Ecosystem (habitat) diversity is the variety of different ecosystems and habitats in a region, e.g. Ireland's bogs, woodlands, grasslands, lakes, rivers and coasts. A region with many habitats supports more species, because each habitat suits different organisms.
Life is not spread evenly across the Earth. Some places hold far more species than others, and Ireland is a good local example of a place with fewer.
Biodiversity is generally higher in warm, wet, stable environments and lower in cold or extreme ones. Tropical rainforests and coral reefs are the most species-rich ecosystems.
Ireland has fewer species than Britain or mainland Europe, partly because it became an island after the last ice age, before many species had recolonised it from the south.

In brief, biodiversity provides food, medicines and materials, supports processes such as pollination and nutrient cycling, and makes ecosystems more stable. There is more on this, and on its loss and conservation, in Biodiversity loss and conservation.
Biodiversity (the variety of living things in an ecosystem) is not just nice to have. It supplies services people depend on, keeps ecosystems stable, and many people argue it has a value of its own.
Ecosystem services are the benefits people get from ecosystems. Provisioning services are the products we take: food (crops, fish and game), timber, fibre, clean water and medicines.

Many medicines come from organisms, for example penicillin from the mould Penicillium, and aspirin's forerunner from willow bark (salicin). Losing a species can mean losing a drug nobody has found yet.
Regulating services control natural processes: pollination of crops by insects, purification of water by wetlands and soil, and pest control by predators. Bogs, forests and the sea also store carbon.
Wetlands and bogs also give flood control, because they soak up rain and release it slowly instead of letting it rush into rivers.

Supporting services keep the system running, such as soil formation and nutrient cycling by decomposers (organisms that break down dead matter). Cultural services include recreation, tourism, education, heritage and wellbeing.

Resilience (ability to withstand change) is higher in an ecosystem with many species and much genetic diversity. If one species declines, others with similar roles can take its place, and some individuals are likely to survive a new disease or a change in climate.
Low-diversity systems, such as a single crop variety, can collapse from one disease, because every plant is equally vulnerable.

The ethical argument: many people argue that species have a right to exist regardless of their usefulness, and that this generation has a duty to pass on a living world to future generations. Extinction is permanent, so the loss can never be undone.
Species are lost mainly because of human activity. There are seven main causes, and each one has Irish examples worth knowing.

Habitat loss and fragmentation is the biggest cause. Land is drained, built on, cut, or converted to intensive farming or plantation forestry. Irish examples: drainage and cutting of raised bogs, drainage of wet grassland, and removal of hedgerows.
Fragmentation (breaking habitat into pieces) leaves small, isolated patches that support only small populations, which are more easily wiped out by predators, disease or chance.

Agricultural intensification means earlier and more frequent mowing for silage (grass cut and stored as animal feed), reseeding with a few grass species, and more fertiliser. These reduce the variety of wild plants and destroy the nests of ground-nesting birds such as the curlew and the corncrake.

Pollution: excess nitrogen and phosphorus from fertiliser, slurry and sewage cause eutrophication (nutrient overload) of rivers and lakes. Silt from drainage, forestry and land works smothers river beds, and pesticides harm insects and their predators.

Invasive species are non-native species introduced by people that spread and harm native species and ecosystems, often because they have no natural predators or diseases in their new home. Irish examples: grey squirrel, zebra mussel and Rhododendron ponticum.
Overexploitation is harvesting faster than a population can replace itself, for example overfishing, peat extraction and over-collection.
Climate change forces species to shift their range or the timing of their life cycles. Cold-adapted species, and those in fragmented habitats, cannot always move far enough.
Disease: new pathogens (disease-causing organisms) spread by trade. Ash dieback, a fungal disease recorded in Ireland in 2012, is killing ash trees in hedgerows and woodland.
Raised bogs are one of Ireland's most distinctive habitats and one of its most damaged. They show clearly how one habitat can matter environmentally, economically, socially and culturally.
Raised bogs are dome-shaped peatlands, mainly in the Irish midlands, formed over thousands of years as Sphagnum moss grew over waterlogged ground. They are wet, acidic and low in nutrients.

Because conditions are so harsh, raised bogs support specialised species: Sphagnum mosses, sundews (insect-eating plants), bog cotton and heather, and animals such as the curlew, the red grouse and the Irish hare.
Loss came from centuries of hand turf cutting, then large-scale industrial peat extraction for fuel and horticulture in the twentieth century, plus drainage for farming and forestry.
As a result, less than about 1% of the original raised bog area is still active raised bog, meaning bog that is still forming peat.
Environmental impacts: loss of a rare habitat and its specialised species; drained peat releases stored carbon; and loss of flood control and water purification.
Economic impacts: peat fuelled power stations and supported jobs in the midlands, so ending extraction cost jobs, while restoration can bring tourism and “green” jobs.

Social and cultural impacts: turf cutting for home fuel is a centuries-old rural tradition, and many families hold turbary (turf-cutting) rights. Bogs also preserve archaeology and are part of Irish heritage and literature.
Once the scale of bog loss was clear, the law and public bodies stepped in. The result protects species but affects people who rely on the bog, so it is a good example of a conservation trade-off.

Many raised bogs are protected as Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) under the EU Habitats Directive. Turf cutting on them is banned, and compensation is offered to turf cutters, which has been controversial.
Bord na Móna ended industrial peat harvesting in 2021. Drained bogs are being rewetted by blocking drains to raise the water table, so that Sphagnum can regrow.
For restoration: it protects species and stores carbon.
Against restoration: it removes a traditional right and a cheap fuel, so it needs compensation and local support to succeed.
The curlew shows how several pressures acting together can push a once-common bird towards disappearing from Ireland. It also shows how targeted conservation work tries to reverse that.
The curlew is a large wading bird with a long, down-curved bill that breeds on bogs and wet grassland. It is now one of Ireland's most threatened breeding birds.
A national survey in 2015–2017 found only 138 breeding pairs in the Republic of Ireland, a decline of at least 96% since the 1980s. A 2021 survey found about 105 pairs, so the fall has continued.
Causes of the decline: loss and drainage of bogs and wet grassland; plantation forestry on breeding sites; intensive farming with early mowing; and predation of eggs and chicks by foxes and crows.
Predation is worse because small breeding areas are surrounded by forest and farmland that support many predators.

Conservation: the Curlew Conservation Programme, run by the National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) since 2017, employs local nest-finders and works with farmers to protect nests, manage habitat and control predators. Electric fencing against foxes is one example.
The corncrake is a second bird lost mainly to changes in how farmland is managed. Its story shows how timing and direction of mowing can decide whether chicks survive.
The corncrake is a secretive grassland bird with a rasping call that was once heard across rural Ireland in summer. Its population has fallen by more than 96% since the 1970s.
It now breeds mainly in Co. Donegal (including offshore islands) and on the western coast of Mayo and Galway. It has not disappeared from Ireland.
Main cause: mechanised mowing of hay and silage during the nesting season destroys nests. Mowing from the edge of a field inwards traps the chicks in the centre, because they have nowhere to escape.
Conservation: farmers are paid to delay mowing until the chicks can fly, to mow from the centre of the field outwards so chicks can escape to the edges, and to leave tall vegetation as cover.
The Corncrake LIFE project, EU-funded and launched in 2022, uses payments based on results, so farmers are rewarded for the outcome for the birds.

Cultural impact of both birds: the sounds of the curlew and the corncrake are part of rural Irish life, folklore, music and place names, so their loss is felt as a cultural loss as well as an ecological one.

An invasive species is one that, once introduced, spreads and harms native species. The grey squirrel is Ireland's best-known example, and the pine marten shows how a native predator can help reverse the damage.

The grey squirrel was introduced from North America. The Irish population began with a few animals released in 1911 at Castle Forbes, Co. Longford. It spread across the eastern half of the island, and red squirrels declined where it arrived.
The grey squirrel is larger and competes with the red squirrel for food, because their niches (their roles and resource needs) overlap.
It carries squirrelpox virus, which does not harm grey squirrels but is usually fatal to red squirrels. It also damages trees by stripping their bark.

The native pine marten, protected under the Wildlife Act 1976, has recovered. Where pine martens are common, for example in the Irish midlands, grey squirrels have declined or disappeared and red squirrels have returned.
The heavier grey squirrel is more easily caught by the pine marten.
This shows how restoring a native predator can help a native species.
Invasive species are not only land animals. In Irish lakes and rivers the zebra mussel removes the phytoplankton that other life depends on, and it has itself now been displaced by a newer invader.

The zebra mussel is a small freshwater mussel native to the Ponto-Caspian region, around the Black and Caspian Seas. It was first recorded in Ireland in Lough Derg on the Shannon in 1997, probably brought on boats.
It spreads attached to boat hulls and in bilge water (the water that collects in the bottom of a boat), which is how it moves between lakes.

The zebra mussel filters huge volumes of water, removing phytoplankton (microscopic algae), the base of the food chain. The water becomes clearer, but food for zooplankton (tiny animals) and young fish falls.
The zebra mussel smothers native mussels and blocks water-intake pipes, an economic cost.
The zebra mussel has itself been displaced in Lough Derg by a related invader, the quagga mussel, first recognised there in 2021. The quagga mussel is a separate species.
A plant can be invasive too. Rhododendron ponticum was brought in as a garden shrub, but in Killarney it now threatens the native woodland.
Rhododendron ponticum is a shrub introduced to Killarney for ornamental planting in the nineteenth century. It forms dense thickets in the native oak woodlands of Killarney National Park.
Its evergreen leaves let very little light reach the woodland floor, so oak seedlings and ground plants cannot grow and the wood cannot regenerate (replace its old trees).
Clearing it by cutting and treating regrowth is slow and costly, and the work must be repeated.
Ireland has other invasive species too, and because removal is so costly, the best approach is to stop them spreading in the first place.
Elodea canadensis (Canadian pondweed) is an invasive plant in fresh water.
Japanese knotweed spreads from small root fragments, which makes it hard to remove, and damages buildings and riverbanks.
Prevention is through biosecurity (measures that stop species being moved). An example is the “check, clean, dry” routine for boats and angling gear moved between waters.
Never release aquarium plants or pets into the wild, because they may establish and spread where they have no natural predators.
Clean water is vital to freshwater life. Two cases show what happens when silt and excess nutrients get into Irish rivers and lakes.

The freshwater pearl mussel is a long-lived mussel of clean, fast-flowing rivers. Its larvae (glochidia) must attach to the gills of young native salmon or trout to develop, and the juveniles need clean, well-oxygenated gravel.
Silt and nutrient enrichment from drainage, forestry and farming clog the gravel. In many Irish rivers few or no young mussels survive, and populations consist only of old adults.
Its decline is also linked to the decline of salmon and trout, its hosts, because without them the larvae cannot develop.
Lough Neagh, in Northern Ireland and the largest lake on the island of Ireland, had a massive bloom of blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) in summer 2023.
The bloom was linked mainly to excess phosphorus from agriculture and wastewater built up over decades, along with warm, still weather and zebra mussels.
Impacts of the Lough Neagh bloom: toxic water unsafe for people, pets and livestock; harm to fish and birds; damage to the eel fishery and to tourism; and anger in local communities.
Biodiversity loss damages ecosystems and costs money. Each point below is paired with an example from the Irish case studies.

Environmental: food webs are disrupted when a species is lost, affecting its predators and prey. Ecosystem services such as pollination, water purification and flood control are lost, ecosystems become less resilient, and extinction is irreversible.

Environmental example: about one third of Ireland's wild bee species are threatened with extinction, mainly through loss of flowers and nesting sites. This threatens the pollination of wild plants and crops.
Economic: farming depends on pollinators and healthy soil, and fisheries and angling depend on clean rivers and lakes.
Tourism, for example at Killarney National Park, the Burren and the bogs, depends on landscapes and wildlife.
Invasive species cost money to control, for example clearing rhododendron or unblocking pipes fouled by zebra mussels. Polluted water also costs more to treat.
Conservation also has costs, including compensation to farmers and turf cutters and lost income from land use.
Biodiversity loss also affects people's health, communities and identity. It can cause conflict, because both loss and the rules to prevent it can hit livelihoods.
Social: health and wellbeing benefit from access to nature. Polluted water threatens drinking supplies and recreation, for example on Lough Neagh.
Social conflict: communities that depend on fishing, farming or peat can lose their livelihoods either from biodiversity loss or from conservation rules, which causes conflict.
Cultural: species and landscapes are part of identity, heritage, folklore, music, literature and place names, for example the curlew, the corncrake and the bogs.
Traditional practices such as turf cutting are themselves cultural heritage, which is why some conservation measures are resisted.
Conservation means acting to protect nature. There are two broad approaches, depending on whether the species is protected where it lives or somewhere else.
Conservation is the protection, management and restoration of the natural environment to maintain biodiversity and prevent extinction, while allowing sustainable use.
In situ conservation (in the natural habitat) uses protected areas such as national parks. Killarney National Park was Ireland's first, in 1932.
Natura 2000 sites across the EU include Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) under the EU Habitats Directive (1992) and Special Protection Areas (SPAs) for birds under the EU Birds Directive (1979).
Species protection under the Wildlife Act 1976 made it illegal to kill or disturb protected species.
Habitat management and restoration: rewetting bogs; planting native trees and hedgerows; and controlling invasive species.
Farming for nature uses agri-environment schemes that pay farmers for results, such as species-rich meadows, for example in the Burren.
Species recovery programmes include the Curlew Conservation Programme and the Corncrake LIFE project.
Ex situ conservation (outside the natural habitat) uses seed banks, captive breeding and reintroduction, for example captive rearing of freshwater pearl mussels to release young mussels into rivers.
Laws and national plans set the direction for conservation, but individuals and communities also take part.
The All-Ireland Pollinator Plan, launched in 2015, asks councils, farmers, schools and gardeners to provide flowers and nesting sites for bees, for example by mowing road verges less often.
In May 2019 the Dáil declared a climate and biodiversity emergency, making Ireland the second country to do so.
The Citizens' Assembly on Biodiversity Loss reported in April 2023 with 159 recommendations.
Ireland's fourth National Biodiversity Action Plan covers 2023–2030.
The EU Nature Restoration Law, adopted in 2024, requires member states to restore damaged ecosystems.

Individuals can record species for citizen-science surveys (research that members of the public contribute to), for example through the National Biodiversity Data Centre. They can also garden for pollinators and avoid spreading invasive species.
A discuss question wants both sides: where conservation has worked, and where it has fallen short. A balanced answer then reaches a conclusion.
Arguments for its effectiveness: protection has brought recoveries, for example the pine marten after 1976, with the return of red squirrels that followed.
Rewetting can restore bog habitat, and targeted payments have raised the breeding success of curlew and corncrake in some areas.
Protected areas keep the last strongholds of rare species.
Limits: declines continue, as curlew numbers fell further between 2015–17 and 2021. Designating a site is not enough without enforcement and management.
Schemes cost money and can conflict with the incomes and traditions of farmers, turf cutters and landowners.
Small, isolated populations may still be lost to predators, disease or chance. Restoration is slow: bogs take centuries to re-form.
Conclusion to model: conservation limits biodiversity loss when it has funding, enforcement and the support of the local people who manage the land.
The syllabus asks you to link what you learn to real, current stories about local ecosystems. Follow these steps to analyse a story.

1. Find a current local story about a local ecosystem or species. Sources include local newspapers and radio, national news, the websites of the NPWS and the EPA (water quality), BirdWatch Ireland, the National Biodiversity Data Centre, and the county council's heritage or biodiversity officer.
2. Identify the ecosystem, the species affected, the cause, and the evidence, such as survey data, photographs or expert opinion.
3. Evaluate the source: who wrote it, whether it is based on data, whether it shows bias (for example from a campaign group or an industry body), and whether other sources agree.
4. Describe the impacts under the four headings: environmental, economic, social and cultural.
5. Assess what conservation is being done and whether it is likely to work.
6. Where possible, visit or survey the ecosystem to gather primary data (data you collect yourself).

This outcome asks you to judge data about how people change the number and mix of species in a habitat. First you need to know which human activities matter, what primary and secondary data are, and how diversity is measured.

Human activities that affect species diversity include trampling, grazing and mowing, ploughing and reseeding, fertiliser and pesticide use, pollution of water and air, drainage, building, forestry, and the introduction of invasive species (non-native species that spread and out-compete native ones).
Most of these reduce diversity, either by removing habitat or by favouring a few tolerant species that out-survive the rest.
Some activities can keep diversity high. Light grazing, or cutting a meadow once a year late in summer, stops a few vigorous species taking over, so weaker species still get light and space.

Primary data are collected by the student in the field. Secondary data come from someone else, such as EPA water-quality reports or a published bird survey. There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
To evaluate data means to judge what the data show, how reliable and valid they are, and what conclusions they can and cannot support.
Species richness is the number of species in a sample. Abundance is the number of individuals of each species, or the percentage cover for plants (the percentage of the ground each species covers).

At Higher Level you also use the Simpson's Diversity Index, which combines richness and evenness (how equally the individuals are shared between the species). There is more on this in Simpson's Diversity Index.
Walking on grass damages it, and a worn path is an easy place to test whether human activity lowers plant diversity. A good plan states a clear aim and hypothesis, and identifies every variable.
Aim: to investigate the effect of trampling on the species diversity of plants in a grassland.
Hypothesis: grassland on a heavily trampled path has fewer plant species than nearby untrampled grassland. The null hypothesis (the statement to be tested against) is that there is no difference.
The independent variable (the one you change or compare) is the amount of trampling, either on the path compared with away from it, or the distance from the centre of the path.
The dependent variables (the ones you measure) are the number of plant species per quadrat, and the percentage cover or number of each species.

Controlled variables are kept the same so they cannot affect the result: the quadrat size (e.g. 0.5 m × 0.5 m), the number of quadrats in each area, the same field (so the same soil type, aspect, slope and management), the same day and observer, and the same identification key.

Control: the untrampled grassland beside the path serves as the comparison area, showing the diversity without trampling. The two areas must be alike except for trampling, otherwise any difference could have another cause.

Equipment: a quadrat (a square frame, e.g. 0.5 m × 0.5 m, often divided into 100 small squares to estimate percentage cover), two measuring tapes, a random-number table or app, an identification key or chart for grassland plants, a recording sheet and a pencil.
Optional equipment: a soil-compaction measure, e.g. how far a metal rod or pencil pushes into the soil under the same force, and a soil thermometer.
The method has to give an unbiased, repeatable sample from both areas. Follow the steps in order.
1. Choose a grassland with a well-used path and similar untrampled grass beside it, so the only major difference is trampling.

2. In each area, lay two tapes at right angles as axes, and use random numbers as coordinates to place each quadrat, so that the sample is not biased by choosing interesting spots. Random sampling is detailed in Surveys.
3. Place at least 10 quadrats in each area. A larger sample makes the means more reliable.
4. In each quadrat, identify every plant species with the key and record the number of species. Estimate the percentage cover of each species, or count individuals, e.g. daisy and plantain rosettes.
5. Optionally, measure soil compaction at each quadrat.
6. Calculate the mean number of species per quadrat for each area, and the mean percentage cover of each species.
7. Repeat on another day, or combine class results, to check repeatability.
