Alternative design: a line or belt transect (a line or strip sampled at set intervals) running at right angles across the path, sampling a quadrat every metre, shows how diversity changes with distance from the path centre.
Fieldwork has risks for you and for the habitat, so a plan must deal with both.
Safety: wash hands after fieldwork; wear suitable clothing and footwear; watch for traffic, livestock, electric fences and stinging nettles; get the landowner's permission; and work in pairs.
Ethics: do not uproot plants (identify them in place), and leave the site as you found it, so your study does not itself damage the diversity you are measuring.
Once the quadrats are counted, the results are summarised as means and ranges. The sample results below show a clear drop in diversity on the path.
Sample data (invented for practice, not real results): number of plant species in each of 10 quadrats. Untrampled grassland: 7, 8, 6, 9, 7, 6, 8, 7, 8, 6 (total 72, mean 7.2, range 6–9).
Sample data for the path (invented for practice): number of plant species in each of 10 quadrats. Path: 3, 2, 2, 4, 3, 1, 3, 2, 3, 2 (total 25, mean 2.5, range 1–4).

Present the results as a bar chart of the mean species per quadrat for the two areas. The independent variable is categoric (it falls into groups, path or untrampled), so a bar chart is used. There is more on this in Producing and analysing data.
Diagram: bar chart of mean species per quadrat, path vs untrampled, with labelled axes.
The data show fewer species on the path. Explaining why, and what the data can prove, is what earns the marks.
Expected pattern: fewer species on the path. The path is dominated by a few trampling-tolerant plants, and bare soil is more common on it.

Greater plantain and daisy form low, flat rosettes of leaves pressed to the ground, so they are not crushed or broken. Perennial ryegrass has tough, flexible leaves and grows from the base. Taller, more delicate plants are found only away from the path.
Explanation: trampling crushes and breaks shoots and kills seedlings. It also compacts the soil, squeezing out air spaces, so roots get less oxygen and water drains poorly or runs off.
Only species adapted to these conditions survive, so richness and evenness fall.

Conclusion: the results support the hypothesis. The mean number of species was much lower on the path (2.5) than in untrampled grassland (7.2), and the ranges do not overlap, so the difference is unlikely to be due to chance.
The link between trampling and lower diversity is likely to be causal, because the areas were otherwise alike.
Sewage and farm runoff add organic matter to rivers, and the animals living on the river bed show the effect. Here you compare a site above the pollution with one below it.
Aim: to compare the diversity of freshwater invertebrates (animals without backbones) upstream and downstream of a source of organic pollution, e.g. a sewage-treatment outfall or a farm drain.
The independent variable is the site (upstream or downstream). The dependent variables are the number of invertebrate groups, and the presence and number of indicator species.

Controlled variables: the same stream, similar depth, flow rate and stony bed at both sites, the same sampling time (e.g. 1 minute of kick-sampling), the same net, and the same day. This means pollution is the main thing that differs.
Kick-sampling collects the animals living among the stones of a river bed. The order of the steps matters, and so does staying safe near water.
1. Sample upstream first, so that you do not carry disturbed material downstream.

2. At each site, hold a net on the river bed facing upstream and kick the stones for a fixed time, so that dislodged animals flow into the net. Kick-sampling is detailed in Collection and identification.
3. Empty the net into a white tray of river water, so the animals show up clearly and stay alive.
4. Identify and count the animals with a key.
5. Measure dissolved oxygen and water temperature at each site.
6. Repeat three times at each site.
7. Return the animals to the river.

Safety: never work alone; wear waders or wellingtons and stay in shallow water; avoid fast or deep water; cover cuts and wash hands, because of the risk of infections such as Weil's disease, which is spread in rat urine; and do no fieldwork in flood.
Some animals can only live in clean water and others cope with pollution, so the animals present tell you the condition of the water. This lets you judge pollution from a living sample.
Indicator species are organisms whose presence, absence or abundance shows the condition of the environment.
Clean, well-oxygenated water: stonefly nymphs and many mayfly nymphs, which are pollution-sensitive.
Moderately polluted water: freshwater shrimps, caddis fly larvae and water lice (water hoglouse).
Badly polluted, low-oxygen water: bloodworms (red midge larvae), sludge worms (Tubifex) and rat-tailed maggots, which are pollution-tolerant.

Expected results: upstream, many groups are present, including stonefly and mayfly nymphs. Downstream there are fewer groups, dominated by large numbers of tolerant species such as sludge worms and bloodworms.
Explanation: decomposing organic matter is broken down by bacteria, whose aerobic respiration (respiration using oxygen) uses up dissolved oxygen. Sensitive species die or leave.
Tolerant species, with less competition and plenty of food, become very numerous. Diversity falls even though the total number of animals may rise.
Your own sampling is primary data. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) publishes secondary data on the same rivers, which you can use to check your results.
The EPA rates Irish rivers with a biotic index (a score based on the living things present) called the Q-value, from Q5 (high quality, unpolluted) to Q1 (bad quality, seriously polluted).
The Q-value is based mainly on the proportions of pollution-sensitive and pollution-tolerant invertebrates, so it uses the same indicator species you counted.
Students can compare their primary data with the EPA Q-values published for the same river.
To evaluate a field study, ask two questions. Can you trust the numbers (reliability), and do they really measure the effect you claim (validity)?

Reliability: was the sample large enough (number of quadrats or kick samples)? Were the results repeatable on repeated sampling? Do class results agree (reproducibility)? A wide range or an anomalous quadrat (one that does not fit the pattern) reduces confidence. There is more on this in Objectivity and data quality.
Validity: was only the independent variable different between the sites? Confounding variables (other differences that could explain the result) could explain the difference instead.

The path might also be drier, more shaded or on a slope, and the downstream site might also be deeper or slower, or have a different bed. Measuring abiotic factors (non-living conditions) at each site helps to rule these out.
Sampling: random placement avoids bias; the quadrat size must suit the plants; and sampling at one time of year misses seasonal species.

Identification errors: similar species, such as grasses or young invertebrates, may be misidentified, so richness may be under- or over-counted. Percentage cover estimates are subjective, because different observers judge them differently.
A field comparison can show that two things go together, but showing that one causes the other needs more. Secondary data also need checking before you trust them.

Correlation and causation: a field comparison shows an association. It supports a cause only if the sites are otherwise alike and a mechanism explains it, e.g. soil compaction or oxygen depletion. There is more on this in Producing and analysing data.

Secondary data, e.g. bird surveys, EPA reports or news articles: check who collected them and why, the sample size and methods, whether the same method was used every year so that trends are comparable, whether raw data are available, and whether the source might be biased.
Improvements: more quadrats or samples, and several paths or streams, so the result is not just one place.
Improvements: measure abiotic factors at each sample point, and sample in different seasons.
Improvements: use the Simpson's Diversity Index to include evenness (Higher Level).
Interpreting counts means looking at both the number of groups and the number of animals. The sample data below show why more animals does not mean more diversity.
Worked example (sample data, invented for practice, not real results): kick samples from an upstream and a downstream site.
Upstream: stonefly nymphs 6, mayfly nymphs 14, caddis fly larvae 5, freshwater shrimps 9, sludge worms 0. This gives 4 groups present and 34 animals.
Downstream: stonefly nymphs 0, mayfly nymphs 0, caddis fly larvae 1, freshwater shrimps 2, sludge worms 41. This gives 3 groups present and 44 animals.
Interpretation: downstream has more animals but fewer groups, and it is dominated by one tolerant group, so diversity is lower. The loss of stonefly and mayfly nymphs indicates low oxygen.
Calculate percentages to compare the samples: sludge worms are 41/44 = 93% of the downstream sample.

Counting how many species live in a habitat doesn't tell you the whole story, because a habitat can contain many species yet be almost entirely one of them. Simpson's Diversity Index is a calculation that captures both how many species there are and how evenly they share the individuals.

A diversity index is a single number that measures the species diversity of a sample, taking into account both the number of species (richness) and how evenly the individuals are spread among them (evenness). Simpson's Diversity Index is the one in the specification.
The equation is Ds = 1 − Σn(n − 1) / N(N − 1). Here n is the total number of organisms of a particular species, and N is the total number of organisms of all species in the sample.

Σ is the Greek capital letter sigma and means “the sum of”, so n(n − 1) is worked out for each species and the results are added. In words, the sum Σn(n − 1) is divided by N(N − 1), and the answer is subtracted from 1.

What it means: Ds is the probability that two individuals picked at random from the sample (the first not put back) belong to different species. Σn(n − 1) / N(N − 1) is the probability that both belong to the same species, and Ds is 1 minus this.

It is better than species richness alone because it gives less weight to rare species and shows when a habitat is dominated by one or two species. Two samples with the same species list can therefore have very different Ds values.
A Ds value is only useful if you know what a high or low answer means. The value is always a probability, so it sits on a fixed scale from 0 to 1.
Ds lies between 0 and 1. Ds = 0 when only one species is present, meaning there is no diversity. The closer Ds is to 1, the higher the diversity.
For a given number of species, Ds is highest when all the species have equal numbers, because then any two individuals picked are most likely to be from different species.
A species represented by one individual contributes 1 × 0 = 0 to the sum, so a species with a single individual adds nothing to Σn(n − 1).
A high Ds generally indicates a stable, healthy ecosystem that is more resilient to change (better able to cope with disturbance).
A low Ds indicates domination by a few species, often after disturbance or pollution.
Calculating Ds is a fixed routine, and the safest way to get it right is to lay the working out in a table and follow the same steps every time.
1. Draw a table with columns for species, n, n − 1 and n(n − 1). 2. Fill in n for each species from the sample.
3. Calculate n − 1, then n(n − 1), for each species, for example 5 individuals gives 5 × 4 = 20.
4. Add the n column to get N, the total number of organisms. 5. Add the n(n − 1) column to get Σn(n − 1).
6. Calculate N(N − 1). This is done once, for the whole sample. 7. Divide Σn(n − 1) by N(N − 1).
8. Subtract the answer from 1 to get Ds.
9. Give Ds to two decimal places and interpret it, by comparing it with another sample or by saying whether it is near 0 or near 1.
Common errors: using n² instead of n(n − 1); forgetting to subtract from 1; and working out N(N − 1) for each species instead of once for the whole sample.
Another common error is rounding too early, which shifts the final answer. Keep four decimal places until the last step.
Here the method is applied to a meadow where no one walks, so the four plant species are fairly evenly spread. The numbers are invented sample data for practice.
Sample data: daisy 10, dandelion 5, white clover 3, buttercup 2. N = 10 + 5 + 3 + 2 = 20.
n(n − 1): daisy 10 × 9 = 90; dandelion 5 × 4 = 20; clover 3 × 2 = 6; buttercup 2 × 1 = 2. Σn(n − 1) = 90 + 20 + 6 + 2 = 118.
N(N − 1) = 20 × 19 = 380. Σn(n − 1) / N(N − 1) = 118 / 380 = 0.31 (0.3105). Ds = 1 − 0.3105 = 0.69, which is fairly high, as expected for a meadow with no single dominant species.
Now the same method is applied to a trampled path in the same field, to show how Ds picks up a difference that a species count would miss. The numbers are invented sample data.
Sample data: daisy 16, dandelion 2, white clover 1, buttercup 1. N = 20. These are the same four species (the same richness) as example 1.
n(n − 1): daisy 16 × 15 = 240; dandelion 2 × 1 = 2; clover 1 × 0 = 0; buttercup 1 × 0 = 0. Σn(n − 1) = 242.
Interpretation: both samples have four species and 20 plants, but the path is dominated by one trampling-tolerant species (daisy), so its evenness and its diversity are lower (0.36 against 0.69).
Species richness alone would have shown no difference between the two samples, which is why Ds is the better measure. There is more on this in Investigation: human activity and species diversity.
These four short samples show the limits of the scale and what happens when richness changes. All the numbers are invented sample data.

Perfectly even sample: four species with 5 individuals each. N = 20. n(n − 1) = 5 × 4 = 20 for each, so Σn(n − 1) = 80. 80 / 380 = 0.2105. Ds = 0.79, the highest possible for four species and 20 individuals.
One species only: 20 individuals of one species. Σn(n − 1) = 20 × 19 = 380; 380 / 380 = 1; Ds = 1 − 1 = 0, which means no diversity.
A richer sample, e.g. a rocky-shore quadrat (a square frame used to sample an area): barnacles 12, limpets 8, dog whelks 6, periwinkles 3, beadlet anemone 1. N = 30.
Ds is used to turn a sample into a number that can be compared between sites or over time. It is also a simplified measure, so you need to know what it leaves out.
Uses: comparing the diversity of two habitats or sites, e.g. trampled and untrampled grassland, upstream and downstream of a pollution source, or a native woodland and a conifer plantation.
Uses: monitoring the same site over time to see whether diversity is falling or recovering, e.g. after bog rewetting or a change in farming, and judging the effect of conservation or human activity.
Limitations: the index depends on accurate identification and counting. Samples must be large, taken at random and taken by the same method for a fair comparison.
Limitations: it is hard to count individual plants that grow in clumps, e.g. grasses, so percentage cover is sometimes used instead, which this equation does not take into account.
Limitations: it treats all species as equally important, so it does not show whether the species are native, rare or invasive, and a sample is a snapshot at one time of year.
Other versions of Simpson's index exist in textbooks and websites, e.g. D = Σn(n − 1) / N(N − 1) without subtracting from 1 (where a low value means high diversity), or its reciprocal.
The specification uses Ds = 1 − Σn(n − 1) / N(N − 1), and this form should always be used, so that a high value always means high diversity.

A population is all the individuals of one species living in one area. Its size rises and falls, and in every habitat there is an upper limit that the environment can support. That limit is the carrying capacity.
A population's size changes through four processes. Births (natality) and immigration (individuals arriving) increase it; deaths (mortality) and emigration (individuals leaving) decrease it.
A population grows when births plus immigration exceed deaths plus emigration. If the two sides are equal, the size stays steady.

Every population could grow very fast if nothing stopped it, because organisms produce more offspring than are needed to replace themselves. In reality, resources run short, so growth slows and stops.

The carrying capacity of an environment is the maximum population size of a species that it can support indefinitely, given the food, water, space and other resources available. It is often given the symbol K.

A limiting factor is any factor that restricts the size, growth or distribution of a population. The factor in shortest supply relative to need sets the limit, even if all the others are plentiful, which is the same principle as limiting factors in photosynthesis.
Carrying capacity is set by the limiting factors acting together, not by any one of them alone.

Carrying capacity is not fixed. It changes when conditions change, such as in a wet or dry year, after a new predator or disease arrives, or with habitat loss or restoration. It also differs between species in the same habitat.
If a population rises above carrying capacity, it damages its resources, for example by overgrazing (eating plants faster than they regrow), and then its numbers fall.
Abiotic factors are the non-living parts of the environment. Each of them can cap the number of plants and animals a habitat supports, and the Irish examples below show how.
Water: all organisms need water. On the dry, free-draining sand of coastal sand dunes, water shortage limits which plants can grow and how many.

Marram grass grows on sand dunes because its rolled leaves and deep roots reduce water loss and reach water, so it survives where most plants cannot. In a dry summer, grass growth slows and fewer grazing animals can be supported.

Oxygen: aquatic animals depend on oxygen dissolved in water, which is scarce compared with air. Salmon, trout and stonefly nymphs need well-oxygenated, cool, fast-flowing water, so oxygen limits their numbers in slow, warm or polluted rivers.

Decomposing organic pollution uses up oxygen in a river, which is why polluted water supports fewer oxygen-demanding animals. In waterlogged bog soil, low oxygen limits roots and decomposers, so few plant species can grow there.

Space: organisms need space to attach, shelter, nest or hold a territory (an area an animal defends). On a rocky shore, bare rock is limited, so barnacles, mussels and seaweeds compete for space to attach.
Seabirds nest only on cliffs and islands with suitable ledges. Many songbirds, such as robins, defend territories, so the number of territories in a woodland limits the breeding population.

Temperature affects enzyme activity, growth and survival. Cold winters kill many small birds such as wrens, and low temperatures in the uplands shorten the growing season, limiting plant growth. Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, so temperature also limits fish.

Soil type, pH, minerals, water content and air content limit plants, and so the animals that feed on them. Acidic, nitrogen-poor bog peat supports only specialised plants such as Sphagnum, heather and sundews.

Soil is one of the factors that limit which plants can grow in a place, and plants are the food base for animals. Light is not on the specification's list of abiotic factors, but it is a key limiting factor for plants.
The thin limestone soils of the Burren, Co. Clare, support lime-loving plants, because only plants suited to thin, lime-rich soil can grow there.
Fertile, well-drained lowland soils support productive grassland, because they are fertile and drain well.
Under a closed woodland canopy (the roof of leaves formed by the treetops) in summer, little light reaches the floor, so few plants grow there.
Woodland plants such as bluebells grow and flower in spring, before the leaves of the trees open, which means they get the light they need while the canopy is still open.

Biotic factors are the living parts of the environment: other organisms and the diseases they carry. Food, disease, competition and predation all limit populations, and some of them also limit one another.
Food: the supply of food usually sets the carrying capacity for animals. For grazers it is the amount of grass or browse (leaves and shoots of shrubs and trees).
Seed-eaters such as squirrels and wood mice do better in years when trees produce large seed crops. Birds of prey such as barn owls are limited by the number of small mammals they can catch.
Disease: disease spreads faster in dense populations, so it limits large populations most. Squirrelpox virus, carried by grey squirrels, kills red squirrels.
Myxomatosis, a viral disease, killed most of Ireland's rabbits after it arrived in the 1950s. Ash dieback is killing ash trees.

Competition: organisms competing for the same limited resource, such as food, light, water, space or mates, reduce each other's share, so fewer survive or breed. Competition between members of the same species (intraspecific) and between different species (interspecific) both limit populations.
Grey squirrels outcompete red squirrels for food in broadleaf woods, and on a woodland floor taller plants shade out shorter ones. There is more on this in Biotic factors and relationships.
Predation: predators kill and eat prey, keeping prey numbers below what the food supply alone would allow. Foxes take rabbits and the eggs and chicks of ground-nesting birds such as the curlew.
Pine martens prey on grey squirrels, reducing their numbers where martens are common. Predator numbers are in turn limited by the number of prey, so the two populations affect each other.
Predation normally keeps herbivore numbers down. Where a predator is missing, food becomes the main limit, and the habitat can pay the price.
Ireland's deer, the native red deer and the sika deer introduced to Powerscourt, Co. Wicklow, in 1860, have had no natural predator since wolves died out in Ireland more than two centuries ago.
Their numbers are limited mainly by food, so in parts of Co. Wicklow they have risen high enough to browse away tree seedlings and stop woodland regenerating.
Culling (killing selected animals) by people is used to keep deer below the level that damages habitats, so people take over the role the predator once had.

Limiting factors fall into two groups, depending on whether their effect changes with how crowded the population is. This explains why some factors steady a population while others crash it without warning.
Density-dependent factors have a greater effect as the population becomes more crowded. They are food shortage, competition, disease and predation, and are mostly biotic.
They slow growth as a population approaches carrying capacity, so they regulate population size, pulling it back towards K.
Density-independent factors affect a population regardless of its size, for example a severe frost, a flood, a storm, a drought or a fire, and are mostly abiotic.
Density-independent factors can cause sudden crashes at any population size, because a frost kills the same fraction whether the population is small or large.
Human activity changes carrying capacity. Draining wet grassland and bogs removes curlew breeding habitat, lowering its carrying capacity.
Rewetting a bog or planting hedgerows raises carrying capacity for the species that depend on them, and garden feeders increase the food available for some birds.
A grassland field shows how several limiting factors act on one species at once. For rabbits, the field's carrying capacity is the result of all of them together.
Food: grass is the main density-dependent limit. As rabbit numbers rise, the grass is grazed shorter and competition increases.
Predation by foxes, stoats and birds of prey removes many young rabbits.
Disease: myxomatosis causes crashes when the population is dense, because the virus spreads fastest between crowded animals.
Space: burrows need well-drained soil, for example on banks and slopes, which limits where warrens (burrow systems) can be dug.
Wet winters, an abiotic and density-independent factor, can flood burrows and kill young rabbits.
The carrying capacity of the field for rabbits is the population that these factors together allow it to support over time.

Diagram: a simple graph of a population rising and levelling off at a horizontal dashed line labelled “carrying capacity (K)”, with arrows labelled “limiting factors (environmental resistance)” pressing down on the curve.

Ecologists track how many individuals of a species live in an area over time, and a graph is the simplest way to show the pattern. Two terms, biotic potential and environmental resistance, explain why population curves take the shapes they do.

A population curve is a graph of population size (number of individuals, on the y-axis) against time (on the x-axis). It is a model of how a population changes, used to explain and predict the effects of limiting factors (things that restrict growth). More in Models.
Biotic potential is the maximum rate at which a population could grow with unlimited resources and no limiting factors. It is the growth a species would achieve if nothing held it back.

Environmental resistance is the combined effect of all the limiting factors, such as food shortage, predation, disease, competition, lack of space and harsh conditions. Together they stop a population reaching its biotic potential.
When a species meets conditions with nothing holding it back, its numbers do not rise steadily. They take off, and the graph takes a J shape. The catch is that this cannot last.

A J-shaped curve shows exponential growth. When resources are unlimited and there is little environmental resistance, the population grows at an ever-increasing rate, because each new generation adds more breeders, e.g. 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
The curve starts slowly, with few breeders, and then rises ever more steeply. It never levels off: a curve that does level off is an S-curve.

Conditions for J-shaped growth are a new habitat with plenty of food and space, few competitors, and no predators or diseases. This often happens when a species arrives in a new area, or after a sudden large supply of nutrients.

J-shaped growth cannot continue. Resources eventually run out, or the population damages its environment, so the population usually crashes suddenly in a boom and bust. It often falls below the carrying capacity (the population the habitat can support) because the habitat has been damaged.

Algal bloom: in a lake enriched with phosphate and nitrate, algae grow explosively in warm, still weather and then die back, the decomposing algae using up oxygen. The blue-green algal bloom on Lough Neagh in 2023 is an example.
The nutrient enrichment behind a bloom is called eutrophication. There is more in Ethics and sustainability of nutrient cycling.
Zebra mussel: its rapid spread through Lough Derg after it arrived in the 1990s is an example, because it met no native predators or competitors adapted to it.
Rabbits introduced to Australia in 1859 are another example. With abundant food and few predators, they grew into plague numbers.
Diagram: a J-shaped curve of population size against time, rising slowly and then steeply, with a sudden vertical crash at the end; labelled “exponential growth”, “resources unlimited” and “crash”.
Real environments have limited resources, so growth cannot stay exponential. The result is an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve, which passes through four phases as environmental resistance builds up.
An S-shaped (sigmoid) curve shows the growth of a population in an environment with limited resources. It has four phases.
Lag phase: slow growth at first, because there are few individuals to breed, they may still be settling in or reaching breeding age, and they are spread out.
Exponential (log) phase: rapid growth, because resources are plentiful and there are now many breeders, so births greatly exceed deaths.

Deceleration (transitional) phase: growth slows as resources begin to run short and density-dependent factors (factors that act more strongly as the population gets more crowded) increase. These are competition for food and space, predation, disease and the build-up of waste. The death rate rises and the birth rate falls.
Stationary (plateau) phase: the population levels off at the carrying capacity (K), where births plus immigration equal deaths plus emigration. Births do not stop; they are balanced by deaths.

In nature the population fluctuates up and down around K rather than staying exactly level, because there is a time lag between a change in numbers and its effect on resources. For example, a large population overgrazes, then falls, and then the food recovers.

An S-curve is the pattern for a population in an environment with limited resources, because the limited supply eventually holds it back. Three examples show this, from a lab flask to a woodland to a rock shore.
Yeast cells growing in a flask of sugar solution follow an S-curve, because the sugar is a fixed supply that eventually limits them.
A population colonising a new habitat follows an S-curve, e.g. grey squirrels spreading into a woodland. They rise rapidly and then level off when food (seeds and nuts) limits them.

Barnacles settling on a newly cleared rock fill the space and then stop increasing, because space is the limiting factor. There is more on microbial growth curves in culture, with their decline and survival phases, and their use in industry, in Microorganisms in industry.

Diagram: an S-shaped curve with the four phases labelled (lag, exponential, deceleration, stationary), a horizontal dashed line labelled “carrying capacity (K)”, small oscillations about K, and the gap between the J-curve and the S-curve labelled “environmental resistance”.
The two curves differ in how much environmental resistance acts on the population, and that depends on how limited the resources are. Each row of the table compares one consequence.
Resources: unlimited for the J-curve; limited for the S-curve.
Environmental resistance: little until the crash for the J-curve; increasing as the population grows for the S-curve.
Growth: ever faster until a crash for the J-curve; fast at first, then slowing to zero for the S-curve.
End point: a crash, often below K, for the J-curve; a stable population around K for the S-curve.
Typical of: invasive species, pests and blooms for the J-curve; established populations in balance with their environment for the S-curve.
Carrying capacity (K) is not a fixed number. When a limiting factor changes, K moves, and the population follows it to a new plateau on its S-curve.
When a limiting factor improves, K rises and the curve rises to a new, higher plateau. Rewetting a drained bog restores breeding habitat for bog species.
A large crop of beech nuts or acorns, a mast year, raises the number of squirrels and wood mice that a woodland can support the following year, because food is the limiting factor.

When a limiting factor worsens, K falls and the population declines to a lower plateau, or to extinction if K falls to zero. Drainage of wet grassland and bogs has lowered K for breeding curlew so far that the population has collapsed. There is more in Biodiversity loss and conservation.
The arrival of grey squirrels and squirrelpox has lowered K for red squirrels in eastern Ireland.

A new predator, or the recovery of a predator, lowers K for its prey. The recovery of the pine marten has reduced grey squirrel populations in the midlands, which in turn has allowed red squirrel numbers to rise towards a higher K.

Removing a predator can let prey overshoot K. Without wolves, deer in Co. Wicklow increase until they overbrowse (damage vegetation by eating too much). The damaged vegetation then lowers the K of the habitat for deer and for other species, and culling holds them below this level.

Density-independent events (acting whatever the density) cause sudden falls at any population size, after which the population climbs back along an S-shaped curve. For example, a severe winter kills many wrens and other small birds, whose numbers then recover over following years.
Predators and their prey limit each other, so their numbers move together in repeating cycles rather than settling at one level.

Predator and prey populations rise and fall in linked cycles, with the predator peak following the prey peak. More prey gives more food for predators, so predators increase; then the prey decrease, the predators starve and decrease, and the prey recover.
Classic example: the snowshoe hare and the lynx in Canada, from fur-trade records (Hudson's Bay Company) kept over many decades. An Irish link is fox and rabbit numbers.

Diagram: (a) a curve that plateaus at K1 and, after a habitat change, falls to a lower plateau K2, labelled “habitat loss lowers carrying capacity”; (b) linked predator and prey curves, with the predator curve lower and lagging behind the prey curve.
Humans are subject to the same rules as other species. Our numbers show how raising carrying capacity can drive J-shaped growth, and how a failing resource can cause a crash.

The world's human population has shown J-shaped growth over the last few centuries, because farming, medicine, sanitation and technology have repeatedly raised the carrying capacity of the Earth for humans, though growth is now slowing in many countries.
Whether it will level off along an S-curve depends on birth rates and on resources such as food, water and energy.

Ireland illustrates a crash when a key resource fails. The population of Ireland reached about 8.2 million in the 1841 census, with many people depending on the potato. Potato blight from 1845 caused the Great Famine, and death and emigration reduced the population sharply. There is more in Variation.
Every ecosystem sorts its organisms by how they get energy and nutrients. Producers bring energy in, consumers pass it along, and decomposers return the nutrients to the soil or water.

Producers are autotrophs: organisms that make their own food from simple inorganic substances, mostly by photosynthesis, using light energy. They include green plants, algae, phytoplankton (microscopic floating algae) and photosynthetic bacteria.

Producers are the entry point of energy and matter into every food chain, because no other group can turn light energy and inorganic substances into organic food. There is more on this in Photosynthesis as an anabolic process.

Consumers are heterotrophs, meaning they cannot make their own food and obtain energy and nutrients by eating other organisms. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers, e.g. rabbits, slugs, caterpillars and limpets.
Secondary consumers eat primary consumers, e.g. thrushes, frogs and crabs. Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers, e.g. sparrowhawks, foxes and herons.
A top (apex) consumer is at the end of a chain and is not normally eaten. Carnivores eat animals; omnivores eat plants and animals, e.g. badgers, foxes and humans.

Decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, feed on dead organisms and waste. They secrete enzymes onto the dead matter and absorb the products (saprophytic nutrition), and so release minerals and CO₂ for producers to reuse.

Detritivores are animals that eat dead organic matter (detritus), e.g. earthworms and woodlice. They break it into smaller pieces, which gives decomposers a larger surface to act on, so decomposition is faster. There is more on this in Bacteria and fungi.
A food chain shows who eats whom, and each step is a trophic (feeding) level. Following the chain shows how energy and nutrients are passed on from one organism to the next.

A trophic (feeding) level is the position an organism occupies in a food chain, according to how it obtains its energy. Producers are trophic level 1, primary consumers level 2, secondary consumers level 3 and tertiary consumers level 4.
A food chain is a sequence of organisms in which each is eaten by the next, showing the transfer of energy and nutrients from one trophic level to the next.
Arrows point from the organism that is eaten towards the organism that eats it, which is the direction of energy flow ("is eaten by").
Irish examples, one per ecosystem. Grassland: grass → rabbit → fox. Hedgerow or woodland: oak leaves → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk. Rocky shore: seaweed → periwinkle → crab → herring gull.
Two more Irish examples. Freshwater: phytoplankton → water flea → minnow → heron (or pike). Sea: phytoplankton → zooplankton → herring → seal.

Grazing food chains start with living producers. Detritus (decomposer) food chains start with dead organic matter, e.g. dead leaves → earthworm → blackbird. Much of the energy in a woodland passes through detritus chains.
Food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels, because so much energy is lost at each level that too little is left to support a further level.
Real organisms rarely eat just one thing or get eaten by just one thing. A food web joins the separate food chains of an ecosystem into one network, which is why it is a more realistic picture.
A food web is a set of interlinked food chains in an ecosystem. It is more realistic than a single chain because most organisms eat more than one type of food and are eaten by more than one predator.
An organism may also feed at more than one trophic level, as an omnivore does, or as a fox does when it eats rabbits and also beetles.

Example grassland and hedgerow web to draw: grass → rabbit, grass → slug and grass → caterpillar; grass seeds → wood mouse; slug → thrush and caterpillar → thrush; rabbit → fox; wood mouse → fox and wood mouse → barn owl; thrush → sparrowhawk.
Decomposers (bacteria, fungi and earthworms) feed on dead material from every level of this web, because every organism eventually dies or produces waste.

Food webs show interdependence: a change in one population affects many others, directly through feeding and indirectly through competition for the same food. For example, the fox and the barn owl both eat wood mice, so they compete.
Diagram: the food web drawn with arrows pointing towards the consumer, organisms placed in rows by trophic level, and decomposers shown at the side receiving arrows from all levels.

Energy enters an ecosystem once, as sunlight, and then dwindles as it is passed along a food chain. Most of it is lost at every step, and this explains both the shape of food chains and how we should feed people.

Energy enters ecosystems as light. Producers capture only a small fraction of the light that reaches them, around 1–2%, and store it as chemical energy in organic molecules. The rest is reflected, passes through leaves, or is lost as heat.
On average only about 10% of the energy in one trophic level is passed on to, and stored in, the next. The figure varies, roughly from 5% to 20%, so about 90% is lost at each transfer.

Respiration releases energy for movement, growth, active transport and keeping warm, and this ends up as heat lost to the surroundings. Birds and mammals lose the most, because they keep a constant body temperature.

Roots, bark, wood, bones and fur are left uneaten. Undigested food is egested as faeces, e.g. cellulose eaten by herbivores, and some energy is lost in excretory products such as urea. The energy in uneaten parts, faeces and dead bodies passes to decomposers, not to the next level.
Energy flows in one direction through an ecosystem and is not recycled: it enters as light and leaves as heat, so an ecosystem needs a continuous input of energy from the Sun.

Worked example (illustrative, using the 10% figure, not measured data): grass in a field stores 10 000 kJ, the rabbits that eat it store about 1 000 kJ, and the foxes about 100 kJ. A fourth level would store about 10 kJ, too little to support a population.
So there are fewer top predators, they often need large territories, and they are especially vulnerable to habitat loss.

Consequence for food production: eating plants directly, a shorter chain, uses the energy captured by crops more efficiently than feeding crops to animals and then eating the animals. A given area of land can therefore feed more people on plant-based food.

Matter, unlike energy, passes along a food chain in the form of the food organisms eat. Some is lost at each level, but the ecosystem as a whole does not lose it, because decomposers send it back to producers.

Nutrients (matter) pass between trophic levels when one organism eats another. The carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids of the food are digested, absorbed and built into the consumer's own body (assimilated).

The elements involved are carbon, hydrogen and oxygen (in all biomolecules), nitrogen (in proteins and nucleic acids), phosphorus (in DNA, ATP and phospholipids), and minerals such as calcium and iron.

The amount of matter passed on also decreases at each level. Much of the food eaten is respired (carbon leaves as CO₂, hydrogen as water), egested in faeces, or excreted (nitrogen as urea or ammonia). So biomass (the mass of living material) also decreases up a food chain.

Unlike energy, matter is not lost from the ecosystem. Decomposers break down dead bodies, faeces and urine, releasing CO₂ and minerals such as nitrate, phosphate and ammonium that producers absorb and reuse, so nutrients cycle.
Contrast: energy flows one way through the ecosystem and is lost as heat, whereas nutrients cycle and are reused again and again.

Persistent substances that are not broken down or excreted, such as the insecticide DDT and mercury, pass up the food chain with the food and build up in the bodies of organisms at each level. They reach the highest concentrations in top consumers, which is called biomagnification.
Biomagnification is how DDT thinned the eggshells of birds of prey, which sit at the top of food chains and so carry the highest doses.

Diagram: a flow diagram of one food chain, with energy arrows getting narrower at each level, heat-loss arrows from every level, and a separate loop of nutrient arrows from all levels to decomposers and back to producers.
A food chain or web is a model: a simplified picture that lets you work out what happens when one population goes up or down. Following a set method keeps the prediction logical.
The method has five steps. 1. Find the organisms that eat the changed species (its predators).
2. Find what the changed species eats (its food).
3. Find its competitors, the species that share its food.
4. Predict the direction of each change, giving reasons.
5. Note other effects, e.g. on plants and habitat.

Worked prediction using the food web above, if a disease such as myxomatosis (a viral disease of rabbits) kills most of the rabbits: (a) grass is grazed less and grows taller, providing more food and cover for slugs, caterpillars and wood mice.

Continued: (b) foxes lose their main prey, so they eat more wood mice and the eggs and chicks of ground-nesting birds, and fox numbers may fall. (c) Wood mice decline from the extra fox predation, so barn owls, which compete with foxes for wood mice, have less food.
Real outcomes depend on how flexible each predator's diet is, because a predator that can switch to other food will be affected less.
Changes spread through a web both when a species is removed and when one is added. Because the model is simplified, its predictions have limits.

Removing a top predator can cause a trophic cascade, a chain of effects passing down the food web. In Ireland, with no wolves, deer numbers increase, they browse young trees, and the woodland cannot regenerate, which affects every species that depends on the woodland.

Adding a species also spreads through a web. An invasive filter-feeder such as the zebra mussel removes phytoplankton at the base of a lake food web, reducing food for zooplankton and for the fish that eat them. There is more on this in Biodiversity loss and conservation.
Food chains and webs simplify real feeding, because many links are left out and diets change with the season and with age.
They usually show no numbers or amounts of energy, which pyramids do, and decomposers are often left out. There is more on models in general in Models.
A food chain tells you who eats whom, but not how many of each organism there are. A pyramid of numbers adds the counts, giving a quick picture of how an ecosystem is built level by level.

A pyramid of numbers is a diagram showing the number of organisms at each trophic level (feeding level) of a food chain or food web in an area at one time. Each level is drawn as a horizontal bar whose width is proportional to the number of organisms.

The producers (organisms that make their own food, such as plants) form the bottom bar. The primary, secondary and tertiary consumers (the animals that eat the level below) are drawn above them in order.

In most ecosystems the pyramid is upright: there are many producers, fewer primary consumers, fewer still secondary consumers, and very few top consumers. For example, many grass plants → fewer grasshoppers → fewer frogs → one heron; or grass → rabbits → foxes.
Numbers usually decrease up the pyramid because about 90% of energy is lost at each trophic level, so each level can support fewer organisms than the one below.
A second reason is size: predators are usually larger than their prey, so each predator needs to eat many prey, which means the prey must be more numerous.

Pyramids, like food chains, are usually restricted to three or four levels. So little energy reaches the top level that it cannot support a further level of consumers. There is more on this in Energy and nutrient transfer.
Ecologists use pyramids of numbers because they turn a food chain into something they can measure, compare and use to make predictions. Drawing one is a short, step-by-step skill.
Feeding relationships: a pyramid shows a food chain quantitatively, that is, how many of each organism there are. It also shows how many prey each predator depends on.
Comparison: it lets two ecosystems, or one ecosystem at different times, be compared, because the bars for each level can be set side by side.

Prediction: it helps to predict the effect of a change in one level on the others. For example, if a disease reduces the primary consumers, the secondary consumers will decline because they have less food.
It also shows why top predators are few and vulnerable: there are only a few of them, so a small loss in their food supply or numbers has a large effect.
How the numbers are found: by sampling the area, for example counting plants in quadrats (square frames laid on the ground) and animals caught in traps or nets, then scaling up to the whole area.
Each organism is then assigned to a trophic level. There is more on sampling methods in Investigating an Ecosystem.

To draw one, step 1: write out the food chain and count, or take from the data, the organisms at each level. Step 2: draw a horizontal bar for each level, with the producers at the bottom, all centred on a vertical line.

Step 3: make each bar's width proportional to the number. Alternatively use a scale, or a logarithmic scale (one that handles very large numbers), or draw it “not to scale” and say so. Step 4: label each bar with the trophic level, the organism and the number.

Diagram: upright pyramid of numbers for grass → grasshopper → frog → heron, with these labels: producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, tertiary consumer, organism name on each bar, number (illustrative) on each bar.
Pyramids of numbers are not always the same shape. The shape depends on how big the producers are and whether the top level is made of parasites, so you need to recognise three cases.
Upright pyramid: the usual shape, wide at the base and narrowing to the top. It occurs when the producers are small and numerous and each consumer is larger than its prey.

Inverted pyramid (narrow base): when one large producer supports many small herbivores, the base is narrower than the level above. For example, one oak tree supports thousands of caterpillars, which support a few blue tits, which support one sparrowhawk, so the second bar is wider than the first.
Another narrow-base example: one rose bush supports many caterpillars or aphids, which support a few blackbirds, which support one hawk. One big plant provides enough food for many small animals.
Because the upper levels still narrow, the narrow-base pyramid is spindle- or diamond-shaped rather than a full upside-down triangle.
Inverted at the top: when the top level is made of parasites (organisms that live on or in a host), which are smaller and more numerous than their host, the top bar is wider than the one below.
Examples of the parasite shape: grass → rabbits → fleas, or one tree → birds → many lice and fleas on each bird.

Diagram: three pyramids side by side. Upright: grass → grasshopper → frog → heron, narrow-base: oak tree → caterpillars → blue tits → sparrowhawk, top-heavy with parasites: grass → rabbits → fleas. Label each level (illustrative numbers).
Counting organisms is a simple idea but it gives a limited picture of an ecosystem. Each of the following weaknesses is a possible exam answer.
They take no account of the size of organisms: one oak tree counts the same as one blade of grass. The shape can therefore be inverted and misleading about how much food each level provides.
The numbers at different levels can differ so much, for example millions of grass plants and one fox, that the pyramid cannot be drawn to scale.
It is hard to decide what counts as an individual for some organisms, for example grass and clover plants that spread by runners (stems growing along the ground), or a clump of moss.
Organisms that feed at more than one trophic level are hard to place. Examples are omnivores, which eat both plants and animals, such as a fox eating rabbits and beetles, or a badger.
Counting is difficult and usually based on samples. Small, hidden, nocturnal or very mobile animals are hard to count accurately, so the numbers are estimates.
It shows the numbers at one moment only, so it changes with the seasons, for example there are many more caterpillars in early summer.

It does not show the amount of biomass (the mass of living material) or the energy at each level, and it usually leaves out decomposers (organisms such as fungi and bacteria that break down dead matter).
The fix for the size problem is a pyramid of biomass, which takes the mass of organisms into account. There is more on this in Pyramids of biomass.

Counting organisms ignores how big they are. A pyramid of biomass fixes this by measuring how much living material there is at each trophic level (feeding level) of a food chain. There is more on how energy and nutrients pass between levels in Energy and nutrient transfer.

Biomass is the total mass of living material, usually measured as dry mass (the mass after all water is removed), in a given area or volume at a given time. It is measured in grams per square metre (g/m²) for land, or grams per cubic metre (g/m³) for water.
A pyramid of biomass shows the total dry mass of the organisms at each trophic level of a food chain or web, at one time, per unit area.
Each level is a horizontal bar whose width is proportional to its biomass, with the producers (organisms that make their own food) at the base.

Dry mass is used because the water content of organisms varies greatly, e.g. lettuce leaves are mostly water and wood much less, and it changes from hour to hour. Fresh (wet) mass would therefore be misleading.

Pyramids of biomass are almost always upright, because biomass decreases at each trophic level. Only part of the food eaten becomes the consumer's body; the rest is respired (lost as CO₂ and water), egested (passed out as undigested faeces) or excreted (waste made by the body's own chemistry).
Biomass cannot be read off an organism directly, because most of its fresh mass is water. It is measured by drying a sample until only the organic material is left.
1. Sample the organisms at each trophic level in a measured area, e.g. a quadrat (a square frame of known size laid on the ground).
2. Dry them in an oven at about 80–100 °C, which is below the temperature at which organic matter burns, so the water is driven off but the organisms' tissue is not destroyed.
3. Weigh them, return them to the oven and reweigh until the mass stays constant, which means all the water has gone.
4. Scale up to the whole area, because the sample covers only a small part of it.
Drying kills the organisms, so only small samples are taken, and the biomass of large organisms such as trees is estimated from their measurements.

Putting a pyramid of numbers beside a pyramid of biomass for the same food chain shows why the two can look so different. A pyramid of numbers counts individuals; a pyramid of biomass counts the mass of material.
In the chain oak tree → caterpillars → blue tits → sparrowhawk, the oak is a single organism, so the numbers pyramid has a narrow base.
That one tree holds far more material than all the animals it supports, so the biomass pyramid is upright with the widest bar for the tree.

Diagram: a pyramid of numbers beside a pyramid of biomass for oak tree → caterpillars → blue tits → sparrowhawk. The numbers pyramid has a narrow base for the one tree; the biomass pyramid is upright, with the widest bar for the tree.
Pyramids of biomass are almost always upright, but not always. In some aquatic ecosystems the base can be narrower than the level above it, which is called an inverted pyramid.

In some aquatic ecosystems, at certain times, the biomass of the producers (phytoplankton, tiny floating photosynthetic organisms) is smaller than that of the primary consumers (zooplankton, tiny floating animals) that eat them, so the pyramid is inverted at the base.

Reason: phytoplankton are tiny, reproduce very rapidly and are eaten almost as fast as they are produced. At any one moment the standing crop, the biomass present, is therefore small, even though over a year they produce far more biomass than the zooplankton.
In other words, the pyramid measures the biomass present at one moment, not the rate at which it is produced. A small, fast-turning-over base can still support a larger mass of consumers.
Diagram: an inverted pyramid of biomass for phytoplankton → zooplankton, with the producer bar narrower than the primary consumer bar, labelled.
Both pyramids are tools for studying how a food chain is built, so they share many features. They differ in what they count, and that decides which gives the truer picture.

Similarities: both show the trophic levels of a food chain or web as stacked bars with the producers at the base. Both are usually upright, both are measured at one time and change with the seasons, and both rely on sampling.
Similarities: both are models that show why there are fewer, or less mass of, top consumers, and both usually leave out decomposers (organisms that break down dead material).
What is measured: the number of individuals for pyramids of numbers, against the total dry mass per unit area for pyramids of biomass.

Size of organisms: pyramids of numbers ignore it, so one tree counts as one. Pyramids of biomass take it into account, so a large tree counts for its full mass. A biomass pyramid therefore gives a truer picture of how much food is available at each level.

Shape: pyramids of numbers are often inverted or spindle-shaped where one large producer feeds many herbivores or where parasites are involved. Pyramids of biomass are almost always upright on land, including for tree-based chains and parasite chains, and are inverted only in some aquatic ecosystems at some times.
Neither pyramid is perfect. The practical difficulties, and the things neither shows, decide which one is more useful for a given study of an ecosystem.

Ease of collecting data: counting is quicker and does not harm the organisms, for pyramids of numbers. Drying and weighing is slow and destructive, so it needs small samples, and large organisms must be estimated, for pyramids of biomass.

Drawing to scale: very large differences in numbers, e.g. millions of grass plants and one fox, make pyramids of numbers hard to draw to scale. Biomass values are usually less extreme, so pyramids of biomass are easier to draw to scale.
What neither shows well is the rate of production over time. Biomass shows only the standing crop, so short-lived, fast-reproducing organisms are under-represented.
What neither shows well is the energy content. A gram of fat contains about twice the energy of a gram of carbohydrate or protein, so equal biomass does not mean equal energy.

Judgement: pyramids of numbers are useful for a quick, non-destructive survey of feeding relationships, especially where the organisms are similar in size. Pyramids of biomass better show the amount of material passing up a food chain and the effect of energy loss, so they are more useful for comparing ecosystems.
A pyramid of energy, which shows the energy flowing through each level over a period of time and is never inverted, overcomes the limitations of both.
Working through numbers shows how the same food chain gives two different pyramids. The data below are invented for practice, with three trophic levels in one area.

Sample data (invented for practice) for a woodland food chain in one area: oak trees 1 (total dry biomass 2 000 kg); caterpillars 5 000 (total dry biomass 0.5 kg); blue tits 4 (total dry biomass 0.02 kg).
Pyramid of numbers: narrow base (1), very wide caterpillar bar (5 000), narrow top (4), so the pyramid is spindle-shaped, wide in the middle and narrow at both ends.
Pyramid of biomass: upright, decreasing from 2 000 kg to 0.5 kg to 0.02 kg (not to scale, because the values differ too much to draw accurately).
Interpretation: the tree is one organism but contains far more material than all the caterpillars, so the pyramid of biomass shows the food available at each level correctly.
Every species does a particular job in its ecosystem (a community of living things together with their non-living surroundings). That job, and the way of life that goes with it, is called its niche.
The niche of a species is its role, or functional position, in its ecosystem. It includes what it feeds on and what feeds on it, where in the habitat it lives and feeds, and when it is active.

The niche also includes the range of abiotic conditions (non-living factors such as temperature, moisture, light and pH) the species can tolerate, its interactions with other species, and its effects on its environment.
Habitat and niche differ. The habitat is where an organism lives, its address; the niche is how it lives there, its profession. Many species share one habitat, but each has its own niche.

Example: in an oak woodland, caterpillars feed on the leaves, woodlice and earthworms feed on dead leaves on the floor, blue tits eat caterpillars in the canopy, and fungi decompose fallen wood. One habitat, five different niches.

A species' niche is the result of its adaptations. Its structural, behavioural and physiological features (its body structure, its behaviour and the way its body works) suit it to a particular way of life, and they also limit it to that way of life.
Because a niche is a set of resources and conditions, two species that want the same ones are in direct competition. Whether they can live side by side depends on how much their niches overlap.

Competitive exclusion: two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche in the same place for long. They compete for the same resources, and the better-adapted species wins while the other declines or is excluded locally.

Example: the grey squirrel and the red squirrel have similar niches in Irish woodland, as tree-living seed and nut eaters. In broadleaf woodland the grey squirrel is larger and can feed efficiently on acorns that red squirrels digest poorly, so it outcompetes the red squirrel.
The red squirrel survives better in conifer woodland, where the grey squirrel's advantage with acorns counts for less.

Niche differentiation: similar species can live together if their niches differ, for example by feeding on different foods, at different heights or at different times of day. This reduces competition between them.

Example: in the same grassland, the kestrel hunts small mammals by day and the barn owl hunts them at night. Both occur in Ireland, and sharing the same prey does not put them in competition because they hunt at different times.
Niches vary in width. A narrow niche can make a species very efficient but fragile, while a broad niche makes a species flexible.
A specialist has a narrow niche, depending on one food or one habitat. This makes it efficient at using that resource but vulnerable to change, because it has nothing to fall back on.
Example: the caterpillars of the marsh fritillary butterfly feed mainly on one plant, devil's-bit scabious, so the butterfly depends on the wet grasslands and bogs where that plant grows.
A generalist has a broad niche. The red fox eats rabbits, mice, birds, insects, earthworms, fruit and scraps, and lives in countryside and towns, so it copes well with change.
An invasive species (one that spreads and thrives after arriving in a new area) is often one that finds a niche unfilled, or fills an existing niche better than the native species, in its new home.
The grey squirrel is an example of an invasive species. There is more on this in Biodiversity loss and conservation.
Questions often ask you to describe the niche of a named organism. A niche is built from several parts, so cover each of them rather than only the food.
State the organism's ecosystem and habitat, then its trophic level (its feeding position in the food chain) and what it eats.
Say what eats it, and when and where it is active, so that its place in the food web and its daily pattern are both clear.
State the conditions it tolerates, then give two or three adaptations, each matched to the part of its niche it suits.

Bog peat is waterlogged, acidic and very short of nitrogen, which plants need to build proteins. The sundew solves this by photosynthesising like other plants but also catching insects to get the nitrogen it lacks.
Niche: a producer that photosynthesises in waterlogged, acidic bog where the peat is very poor in nitrogen, and that supplements its nitrogen by catching and digesting insects.
Adaptation: leaves bearing red hairs (tentacles), each tipped with a drop of sticky fluid that glistens, attracts small insects and traps them.
Adaptation: the tentacles bend over the trapped insect, holding it against the leaf.
Adaptation: glands secrete enzymes that digest the insect, and the leaf absorbs the products, including nitrogen compounds. This makes up for the nitrogen-poor peat.
Adaptation: a small rosette of leaves close to the ground, in an open, sunny habitat, which suits its photosynthesis and the insects that land on it.
Diagram: a sundew leaf with sticky tentacles curved over a trapped insect. Labels: leaf, tentacle, sticky drop, trapped insect.
On a rocky shore, the tide brings waves, predators and drying out in turn. The limpet is a grazer built to hold on, to avoid drying out and to scrape up its food.
Niche: a primary consumer (grazer) that scrapes the thin film of algae off rocks between the tides. It is eaten by birds such as oystercatchers and by crabs.
Adaptation: a low, conical shell that waves flow over without dislodging it.
Adaptation: a strong muscular foot that clamps the limpet to the rock against waves and predators.
Adaptation (behavioural): at low tide it clamps down onto its own home scar, a groove ground into the rock to match its shell. This seals in water and prevents drying out.
Adaptation: a rough, tongue-like radula that rasps algae from the rock.
Adaptation (behavioural): it feeds when covered by the tide and returns to its home scar, so it is always back in its sealed position when the tide goes out.
The barn owl hunts in the dark, so it relies on silence, hearing and night vision more than on sight in daylight. Its adaptations suit each part of that hunting niche.
Niche: a nocturnal predator (secondary or tertiary consumer) of small mammals such as mice, rats and shrews, nesting in old buildings and hollow trees.
Adaptation: soft feathers with fringed, comb-like edges on the flight feathers make its flight almost silent, so prey does not hear it coming.
Adaptation: a heart-shaped facial disc of feathers funnels sound to the ears.
Adaptation: ears at slightly different heights on each side of the head, so it can locate prey by sound alone in darkness.
Adaptation: large, forward-facing eyes give binocular vision (both eyes view the same scene, which helps judge distance) in dim light.
Adaptation: sharp, curved talons and a hooked beak grip and tear prey.
Bees feed on flowers and in doing so carry pollen between them, so their niche is tied to flowering plants. Their body structure and behaviour suit collecting food and moving pollen.

Niche: a primary consumer that feeds on nectar (energy) and pollen (protein), and a pollinator of flowering plants, transferring pollen from flower to flower. There is more on this in Flower structure and pollination.
Adaptation: a long, tube-like tongue (proboscis) to reach nectar inside flowers.
Adaptation: a hairy body to which pollen sticks, which is how pollen is carried from flower to flower.
Adaptation: pollen baskets, stiff hairs on the hind legs, carry pollen back to the nest.
Adaptation: eyes that see the ultraviolet patterns on petals, which guide the bee to nectar.
Adaptation (behavioural): honeybees communicate the location of flowers to others by a dance.
The earthworm lives in the soil, eating dead plant material, so it recycles nutrients. Its body is built for burrowing and for breathing through its skin in damp ground.
Niche: a detritivore (an animal that eats dead leaves and other dead organic matter) feeding on dead leaves and soil organic matter, recycling nutrients.
Its burrows aerate and drain the soil and it mixes the soil layers. It is also food for blackbirds, thrushes, badgers and foxes.
Adaptation: a long, thin, segmented body without legs for burrowing.
Adaptation: tiny bristles (chaetae) on each segment grip the burrow wall.
Adaptation: mucus lubricates movement and binds the burrow walls.
Adaptation: a thin, moist skin exchanges gases, so the earthworm lives in damp soil and comes to the surface mainly at night or in wet weather.
Adaptation (behavioural): it pulls leaves into its burrow, so it feeds below ground, away from predators.
Sand dunes are dry, salty and shifting, so few plants can live there. Marram grass is a pioneer, the first plant to colonise bare ground, and its adaptations suit it to these harsh conditions.
Niche: a pioneer producer that colonises loose, dry, salty sand and binds it into dunes, allowing other plants to settle later. There is more on plant water loss in Transport in Plants.

Adaptation: leaves roll into a tube in dry conditions, with stomata (the pores in the leaf) on the inner surface in grooves lined with hairs. This traps moist air and reduces water loss by transpiration.
Adaptation: long roots reach water deep in the sand.
Adaptation: underground stems (rhizomes) spread and bind the sand.
Adaptation: it grows upward when it is buried by blowing sand, so it is not smothered.

An ecological investigation studies living things in their natural surroundings, and here the surroundings are a grassland habitat. The first job is to find out which organisms live there, because every later measurement is built on that list.

The aim is to find out which organisms live in a chosen grassland habitat (the place where a community of organisms lives), to collect and identify them, and so to build a species list. The surveys, abiotic measurements and feeding-relationship work are all based on that list.
Data gathered first-hand in the field, by your own counting, measuring and observing, are called primary data. Secondary data would come from books or other people’s work.
1. A preliminary visit to choose and map the study area (the mapping is done in the Surveys note).
2. Observe, collect and identify the organisms, which is the stage covered here.
3. A qualitative survey (which species are present, giving a species list) and a quantitative survey (how many of each) are carried out in the Surveys note.
4. Measure abiotic factors (non-living factors such as light and temperature) and relate them to the distribution and abundance of a species, as in the Abiotic factors note.
5. Work out feeding and symbiotic relationships (close partnerships between different species), as in the Biotic factors and relationships note.
6. Present the results and draw conclusions.
Before collecting anything you visit the site once to plan, because what you can find depends on the place, the time of year and the gear you bring.

On the preliminary visit, walk over the site and note its boundaries and main features: hedges, trees, paths, wet patches, slope and gate. These features create different microhabitats (small areas with their own conditions) that you will need to sample.
Get permission from the landowner, check access and hazards, and choose suitable dates, so that the work is legal and safe before anyone arrives with equipment.

Organisms change with the season, so collect over several visits if possible, for example late spring to early autumn, when most plants flower and most invertebrates (animals without backbones) are active.

Collecting equipment: pitfall traps (jars, trowel, flat stones or lids), pooter, sweep net, beating tray and stick, Tullgren funnel, collecting jars and labelled specimen tubes, and white trays on which small animals show up clearly.
Identification and recording equipment: hand lens, identification keys and field guides, camera or phone, notebook and pencil, and labels.
Protection and measuring equipment: gloves, tape measures, and quadrats (square frames used in the Surveys note).
When you compare two areas or two times, the comparison is only fair if the collecting effort is the same each time. That means deciding what you change, what you measure and what you keep constant.
The independent variable (the one you choose to change) is the area or time sampled.
The dependent variable (the one you measure) is the kinds and numbers of organisms caught.
The controlled variables (kept the same) are the type and number of traps, the trapping time, the number of sweeps, the time of day and the weather, so that the collections are a fair comparison.
No true control is possible in a field study, because the conditions in the field can’t be held constant. This is why you control as many variables as you can and repeat the collection.
Not every organism can or should be caught. Large, fast or delicate organisms are studied by looking, and animals that hide are detected from the traces they leave.

Direct observation (looking at the organism itself) is used for organisms that are large, fast or that should not be caught, such as birds, rabbits, foxes and butterflies, and for all plants, which are identified where they grow and not dug up.
Use binoculars for birds and mammals at a distance, and a hand lens (about ×10) for small features such as the hairs or veins of a leaf.
Indirect signs show animals that are rarely seen: droppings, tracks in mud, burrows, nests, feathers, molehills and wormcasts.
Feeding signs are indirect signs too: nibbled leaves, holes in leaves made by slugs or caterpillars, and broken snail shells beside a stone used by a song thrush.

Record each observation at once, so nothing is forgotten: the organism (or ‘unknown species A’ with a sketch or photograph until it is identified) and where it was found (its microhabitat, for example under a stone or on a dandelion leaf).
Also record the time, the weather and what the organism was doing, such as feeding on what.
Photographs record organisms without removing them and can be checked later against keys, so record the location and date with each image.
Many grassland invertebrates (animals without backbones) walk over the soil surface and are hard to spot. A pitfall trap catches them as they travel, with no effort from the collector.

A pitfall trap is a jar or plastic cup sunk into a hole in the ground so that its rim is exactly level with the soil surface. Animals walking across the ground fall in and can’t climb the smooth sides.
A flat stone or lid raised on small stones covers the trap, which keeps out rain and stops birds and other predators taking the catch. Bait, such as a small piece of meat or fruit, can be added.
Pitfall traps catch ground-dwelling (crawling) invertebrates: ground beetles, spiders, woodlice, slugs, ants and millipedes.
Check traps at least every 24 hours, ideally early morning, because predators such as ground beetles and spiders will eat the other animals in the trap.
Remove all traps at the end of the study so that no animal is trapped later.
Diagram: a pitfall trap in section: jar in the soil with rim level with the surface, raised flat stone cover on small supports, bait, and animals inside. Label soil surface, jar, cover, bait.
Tiny animals living in soil and leaf litter (the layer of dead leaves on the ground) are too small to pick out by hand. A Tullgren funnel gets them to leave the sample by themselves.
A Tullgren funnel extracts small animals from a sample of soil or leaf litter.
The sample sits on a wire mesh (gauze) in a funnel under a lamp, a light bulb about 10–20 cm above it.

The heat and light dry the sample from the top, so the animals move down away from the heat, light and dryness, through the mesh and into a collecting beaker below. The lamp drives the animals away; it does not attract them.
The beaker holds damp tissue paper to keep the animals alive, or ethanol if they are to be preserved for identification. Leave the funnel for several hours to a day.
A Tullgren funnel catches mites, springtails, small beetles and their larvae, and small worms.
The mesh must be fine enough to hold back the soil, and too hot a lamp kills the animals before they leave.

Diagram: a Tullgren funnel: lamp, soil or leaf-litter sample, wire gauze, funnel, collecting beaker with damp tissue (or ethanol), and an arrow showing animals moving down away from the heat and light.
Earthworms and mammals need their own methods, because earthworms burrow too deeply for pitfall traps and mammals need careful, humane handling.

Earthworms are collected by digging a measured block of soil and sorting it by hand on a white tray, or by watering a marked area with a mustard-powder solution, which irritates them so that they come to the surface.
Rinse earthworms in clean water at once.
A small-mammal trap is a baited box with dry bedding and food inside. The door closes behind the animal, which is unharmed.
Small-mammal traps are used only under teacher supervision. Check them at least every few hours and release the animal where it was caught.
Some mammal species are protected by law, so trapping may need a licence. Mammals in grassland are more often recorded by observation and signs, because trapping them is restricted.
Many invertebrates live on stems and leaves rather than on the ground. Two methods knock them off the plants so they can be counted.

A sweep net is a strong net with a fine cloth bag on a stout frame and handle. Sweep it quickly through long grass and low plants in a series of side-to-side arcs while walking slowly, so that animals on the plants are knocked into the bag.
After sweeping, fold the bag over to close it, then empty it onto a white tray or into a jar.
A sweep net catches grasshoppers, aphids, flies, beetles, spiders, caterpillars and leafhoppers.
Use a fixed number of sweeps (for example ten) in each area so that catches can be compared.
A sweep net doesn’t work in wet grass, which soaks the bag and damages the animals.
A beating tray is a white sheet or tray (or an upturned umbrella) held under a branch of a hedge, shrub or tree at the grassland edge. The branch is struck sharply with a stick a set number of times.

Animals living on the branch fall onto the tray, where they are easy to see against the white. A beating tray catches caterpillars, beetles, spiders, ladybirds and shield bugs, which are then collected with a pooter.
Small, fast animals are hard to pick up without crushing them. A pooter lets you suck them gently into a container.
A pooter is a clear container (jar or tube) closed by a stopper through which two tubes pass.
The user places the end of the long inlet tube next to a small animal and sucks on the mouthpiece tube. The animal is drawn up the inlet tube into the container.
A piece of fine gauze (muslin) over the inner end of the mouthpiece tube stops the animal or debris being sucked into the user’s mouth.
A pooter is used for small, fast-moving animals (small insects, spiders, springtails) from a beating tray, sweep net, the ground or bark.
Empty it often, because animals inside can harm each other.
Diagram: a pooter: container, stopper, inlet tube, mouthpiece tube, gauze over the inner end of the mouthpiece tube, arrows for the air flow and the animal entering.
Flying insects escape from ground traps and sweep nets, so they need methods of their own. One works by day with a net and one by night with a lamp.

A butterfly net, a light, fine-meshed net on a long handle, catches flying insects such as butterflies and bees. Hold the net closed with a twist of the bag and release the insect after identification.
Bees and wasps can sting, so many are identified by observation instead of being caught.
A light trap (moth trap) is a bright lamp, often ultraviolet, above a box with egg trays inside, left on overnight.

Night-flying insects, mainly moths, are attracted to the light, fall into the box and settle in the trays. They are identified and released next morning, away from birds, which would otherwise eat them.
Once animals are caught, they must be kept alive, named and recorded quickly, because the record is the data the whole investigation depends on.
Place animals in labelled jars or specimen tubes with a little vegetation, keep them cool and shaded, and identify them as soon as possible on a white tray with a hand lens.
Record for each catch the name (or ‘species A’), the number caught, the method and place of capture, and the date and time. These are the raw primary data used in the Surveys note.
Return every animal to the place where it was caught, after identification.
Collect plants only when they are common and can’t be identified where they grow, taking a single leaf or flower rather than the whole plant.
Once you have an organism, you need its name. An identification key gets you there by asking a short series of questions about what you can see.
An identification key is a tool for naming an unknown organism by working through a series of questions or statements about its visible features.
A dichotomous key (‘dichotomous’ means dividing in two) gives a pair of contrasting statements at each step, called a couplet.
The user chooses the statement that fits the organism, and follows the number or name it leads to, until a name is reached.
