Good keys use features that are easy to see and don’t vary between individuals or with age or season: number of legs, number of body parts, wings present or absent, shell present or absent, leaf shape and arrangement, flower colour and number of petals.
Good keys avoid size, which varies with age, and vague words such as ‘large’, because two users might judge them differently.
Here is a key to five grassland invertebrates, written as numbered couplets. Work through it with an animal in mind, then see how such a key is built.
1. Legs present: go to 2. No legs: go to 4.
2. Three pairs of legs (6 legs) and body in three parts (head, thorax, abdomen): insect (for example a ground beetle). More than 6 legs: go to 3.
3. Four pairs of legs (8 legs) and body in two parts: spider. Seven pairs of legs (14 legs) and body flattened and covered with overlapping plates: woodlouse.
4. Body made of many ring-like segments: earthworm. Body not segmented, soft and slimy: go to 5.
5. Shell present: snail. No shell: slug. Using the key: an animal with 14 legs goes 1, then 2, then 3, then woodlouse.
To make a key, list the organisms, then choose a feature that splits them into two groups.
Keep splitting each group with a new feature until each organism stands alone, then check the key by keying out each organism in turn to see that it reaches the right name.
A tree diagram (branching chart) of the same splits is another way to show a key.
Keys are not the only help. Several other aids check or speed up an identification, and you still need a plan for organisms you can’t name.

Illustrated field guides and identification charts (for example of wild flowers, grasses, insects and birds) show pictures to compare with your specimen. You can also compare it with labelled specimens or photographs, or ask an expert such as a teacher or naturalist.
Image-recognition apps on a phone are an aid, but their suggestions must be checked against a key or guide, because they are often wrong for small invertebrates.
A hand lens or a stereo (dissecting) microscope shows small features that decide between similar species.

Identify each organism to species if possible. Where that isn’t possible, name the group (for example ‘a ground beetle’) and give it a code (species A, B …) used consistently throughout the study, so that it can still be counted in the surveys.
Knowing what to expect makes identification quicker. These are the plants and animals typically found in an Irish grassland.
Typical plants: grasses (for example perennial ryegrass in pasture), daisy, dandelion, creeping buttercup, white clover, ribwort plantain and, in damp patches, rushes.
Daisy and dandelion grow as flat rosettes of leaves close to the ground, which helps them survive mowing and grazing.

Typical invertebrates: earthworms, slugs, snails, ground beetles, spiders, woodlice (in damp places under stones or logs), ants, aphids, grasshoppers, ladybirds, caterpillars, butterflies and bumblebees.
Typical vertebrates (animals with backbones): rabbits, the Irish hare, foxes, badgers, hedgehogs, wood mice, pygmy shrews, and birds such as the song thrush, blackbird and kestrel.
The methods above suit grassland. In other habitats the organisms and conditions differ, so you choose different methods to match.

Woodland: beating trays under branches and pitfall traps in the leaf litter are the main methods. Leaf-litter samples go in a Tullgren funnel, trees are identified by leaf, bark and fruit, and the layers (canopy, shrub, herb and ground layers) are recorded separately.

Rocky shore: animals are mostly collected by hand from under seaweed, in rock pools and under stones (turned back the right way up), or simply counted where they are, as many are attached (barnacles, limpets, mussels). Seaweeds are identified with a key.
Rocky shore work is done at low tide, ideally a spring low tide. Check tide tables first, and start at the lowest point as the tide goes out.
Freshwater (stream or pond): a pond net is swept through the water and vegetation.
In a stream, kick sampling is used: the net is held on the bed just downstream while the stones upstream are disturbed with the feet for a fixed time, so that animals are washed into the net.
The catch from kick sampling is emptied into a white tray of water and identified, for example mayfly, stonefly and caddis fly larvae, freshwater shrimps, snails and leeches.
A plankton net (very fine mesh) is towed slowly through the water to collect microscopic organisms.
Freshwater animals are kept in water from the same habitat and returned quickly.
Fieldwork takes you away from the classroom, so you must plan for risks on land and near water.
Work in groups, never alone, and tell someone where you are going. Wear suitable clothes and footwear for the weather.
Take care near livestock, electric fences, nettles and brambles. Wear gloves when handling soil, leaf litter and traps, cover cuts, and wash hands before eating.
Check for ticks after working in long grass, because ticks can carry the bacterium that causes Lyme disease.
Be aware of anyone with an allergy to bee or wasp stings.
Near water, never work alone, and check the depth and the current before entering a stream.
At the shore, know the tide times, watch for incoming tides and take care on wet, slippery rocks covered with seaweed.
Cover cuts and wash hands after contact with fresh water, which can carry the bacteria that cause leptospirosis (Weil’s disease), spread in the urine of rats.
Collecting can damage the habitat you are studying. A code of conduct protects the habitat and its organisms.
Get permission from the landowner, close gates, and keep disturbance and trampling to a minimum.
Replace stones and logs the way they were found, because animals beneath them depend on the damp, dark conditions.
Handle animals gently and return them to where they were caught.
Don’t pick or uproot plants unnecessarily, and never collect protected or rare species.
Remove all traps and litter at the end of the study.
A species list from one afternoon is never complete. Each method, and each visit, has built-in limits that you should recognise and reduce.

Each collection method catches only some kinds of organism: pitfall traps catch only animals that walk on the ground, and sweep nets only animals on tall plants. Several methods must be used to build a complete species list.
Catches depend on the weather, the time of day and the season. Many animals are nocturnal or are active only in warm, dry or damp conditions, so one visit misses many species.
Repeat collections on several days and at different times, under similar conditions when comparing areas.
Animals in traps may escape or be eaten by others before they are counted, so check traps often. Birds may take the catch from uncovered traps.
Misidentification, especially of small invertebrates and of grasses that are not in flower, is a source of error. Check identifications with a second key or guide, or with the teacher.
Disturbance by the collectors (trampling, noise) changes animals’ behaviour and damages the habitat.
A survey is a planned way of finding out what lives in a habitat (the place where a community of organisms lives). There are two kinds: one asks 'which species?' and the other asks 'how many?'.
A qualitative survey records which species are present in the habitat (a species list), without measuring how many of each, so it gives the 'what' but not the 'how much'.
A qualitative survey is built from all the observations and collections made during the fieldwork. There is more on this in Collection and identification.
A qualitative survey can add a subjective estimate of abundance (how many there are) using a scale such as DAFOR: Dominant, Abundant, Frequent, Occasional, Rare, judged by eye for each species.
The DAFOR scale is quick, but different observers give different grades, so it isn't objective (it depends on the person's opinion, not on a measurement).
A quantitative survey measures how many of each species there are, as numbers, percentages or densities: percentage frequency, percentage cover, density per m², or an estimate of population size.

Quantitative data can be compared between areas and analysed mathematically, so it can be used, for example, to calculate a diversity index (a single number describing how varied a community is), such as Simpson's Diversity Index.
Distribution means where in the habitat a species is found; abundance means how many there are. Surveys measure both.

Counting every organism in a habitat is almost never possible, so samples (small parts of the habitat) are taken and the results used to estimate the whole. How the samples are chosen decides whether the estimate can be trusted.
A sample must be representative, meaning it reflects the whole habitat: it must be large enough and chosen without bias (without favouring particular spots).
Random sampling is used when the habitat looks uniform (the same all over), so that every point has an equal chance of being chosen.
1. Lay two long tape measures at right angles along two edges of the study area to form the axes of a grid.
2. Generate pairs of random numbers (with a calculator, a phone app or random-number tables) as coordinates, for example (7, 23) means 7 m along one tape and 23 m along the other.
3. Walk to each coordinate and place the quadrat (the square sampling frame) there, with its corner on the point.
Throwing a quadrat over the shoulder is not truly random and is unsafe, so don't use it.

Random sampling suits an even habitat, but conditions often change from one side of a habitat to the other. Then samples are placed in an orderly way, and enough of them must be taken to give a reliable result.

Systematic sampling places samples at regular intervals, for example a quadrat every 2 m along a line. It is used where conditions change across the habitat (a gradient, for example from a hedge into open field), to show how species change along it; this is a transect.
The more samples, the more reliable the estimate, because chance differences between individual spots average out.
Take quadrats one at a time and keep a running mean (or a running total of species found).
When adding more quadrats no longer changes the mean (or adds new species), enough have been taken. In a grassland this is usually at least 10 to 20 quadrats.
A quadrat is the basic tool for sampling plants. Different designs suit different measurements, and a few rules keep the counting fair.

A quadrat is a square frame of known area used to sample plants and slow-moving or attached animals (ones that can't escape or move while you count). School grassland quadrats are usually 0.5 m × 0.5 m (0.25 m²) or 1 m × 1 m (1 m²).
A gridded quadrat is divided by strings or wires into 100 equal small squares (10 × 10), each 1% of the area, which makes percentages easy to read off.

A point quadrat (point frame) is a frame on legs holding a row of usually 10 long pins (needles) that can be lowered vertically through the vegetation. Each pin that touches a species counts as one 'hit' for that species.
Rule 1: lay the quadrat flat on the ground at the chosen point without moving it towards or away from any plant, so you don't choose which plants fall inside.
Rule 2: use the same size of quadrat throughout, so counts from different quadrats can be compared.

Rule 3: decide in advance how to count plants on the edge (for example count a plant only if more than half of it is inside, or count only those on the top and left edges), and apply the rule every time so no plant is counted twice or missed.

Diagram: a gridded quadrat (100 squares) placed at a random coordinate on a grid laid out with two tape measures at right angles; and a point quadrat with 10 pins, with one pin touching a leaf (a hit).
Percentage frequency tells you how widespread a species is across the samples. It asks only 'is it there or not?' in each quadrat.
Percentage frequency is the percentage of all the quadrats sampled in which a species is present: percentage frequency = (number of quadrats containing the species ÷ total number of quadrats) × 100.
Only presence or absence is recorded in each quadrat, so it is quick and objective, and works for any plant (or attached animal).
It doesn't show how many there are: one daisy or a hundred in a quadrat both count as 'present'.
It depends on quadrat size, because a larger quadrat is more likely to contain the species.
Worked example (sample data): 20 quadrats were placed at random. Daisy was present in 12, dandelion in 5 and white clover in 16.
Results are shown in a table and as a bar chart with one bar per species, with percentage frequency on the y-axis.
Percentage cover is the percentage of the ground area of a quadrat covered by a species, viewed from directly above. It measures how much space a species takes up, not how many individuals there are.
Percentage cover is used for plants that are hard to count as individuals, such as grasses, clover and mosses, which spread to form mats.
Gridded-quadrat method: count the small squares in which the species covers more than half the square; each square is 1%. Repeat in each quadrat and find the mean percentage cover.
Worked example (sample data): in five quadrats white clover covered 30, 45, 25, 40 and 35 squares; total = 175; mean percentage cover = 175 ÷ 5 = 35%.
Point-quadrat method: lower each pin and record every species it touches. Percentage cover = (number of hits on the species ÷ total number of pins lowered) × 100.
Worked example (sample data): the 10-pin frame was placed at 10 random points, so 100 pins were lowered; grass was touched by 72 pins and white clover by 23.
The total cover of all species in a quadrat can be more than 100%, because plants overlap in layers (for example clover leaves above grass).
Percentage cover estimated by eye is subjective. The grid and point methods are more objective, and the point method is the most objective because a pin either touches or doesn't.
Density is the number of individuals per unit area, usually per m². Once you know the density, you can scale up to estimate how many plants live in the whole habitat.
Count the individuals of a species that can be counted separately (for example daisy or dandelion rosettes) in each quadrat. Density = total number counted ÷ total area sampled.
Estimated population = density × total area of the habitat.
The area of the habitat is found by measuring its length and width with tape measures or a trundle wheel (a measuring wheel you roll along the ground).
Worked example (sample data): five quadrats of 0.25 m² contained 4, 7, 3, 6 and 5 daisies. Total = 25 daisies in 5 × 0.25 = 1.25 m².
Density = 25 ÷ 1.25 = 20 daisies per m² (or: mean per quadrat 5 ÷ 0.25 m² = 20 per m²).
The field is 50 m × 40 m = 2000 m², so the estimated population = 20 × 2000 = 40 000 daisies.
Counting individuals is the most informative measure but is slow, and impossible for grasses and other spreading plants, which need percentage cover instead.
A transect is a line across a habitat along which samples are taken at regular intervals. It is the tool for showing how species change when conditions change gradually.

Transects are used where there is a gradient in conditions, to show how the distribution of species changes along it: for example from under a hedge or tree into open grassland, across a trampled path, from a wet hollow to drier ground, or up a rocky shore.
Line transect, step 1: stretch a rope or tape measure tightly across the area at ground level.
Line transect, step 2: at regular intervals (for example every 1 m), record every species touching the line (or directly below it).
Line transect, step 3: record the distance for each species.
A line transect shows where each species occurs (distribution) but not how many, because it only records presence at each point.
A transect is a systematic, not random, sample: it is chosen to cross the gradient.
Several parallel transects give more reliable results, because one line might happen to cross an unusual patch.
A line transect only tells you where species are. A belt transect adds quadrats along the line, so it also tells you how abundant each species is.
Belt transect: quadrats are placed along the line, either side by side all the way (continuous belt transect) or at regular intervals (interrupted belt transect, for example a quadrat every 2 m).
In each quadrat of a belt transect, percentage cover, frequency or numbers are recorded, so a belt transect shows abundance as well as distribution.
Abiotic factors (non-living conditions such as light or soil moisture) are measured at each quadrat to relate them to the species. There is more on this in Abiotic factors.
Diagram: a belt transect from a hedge into open grassland: tape measure from the hedge, quadrats at 2 m intervals, with distances labelled.
Mobile animals move out of a quadrat before you can count them. Instead you catch, mark and release some, then use the proportion of marked animals in a second catch to work out the total population.
Mobile animals can't be counted in quadrats, so their population is estimated by capture–mark–recapture.
1. Catch a sample with a suitable method (for example pitfall traps, sunken containers, for ground beetles or woodlice).
2. Count them (M) and mark each harmlessly, for example with a small dot of non-toxic, quick-drying, waterproof paint on the underside of a woodlouse or the wing case of a beetle.
3. Release them where they were caught and leave enough time (for example 24 hours) for them to mix back into the population.
4. Catch a second sample in the same way and place; count the total caught (C) and the number that are marked (R).

Estimated population size: N = (M × C) ÷ R. This works because the fraction of the second sample that is marked (R ÷ C) is assumed to equal the fraction of the whole population that is marked (M ÷ N).
Worked example (sample data): 30 woodlice were caught, marked and released. Next day 40 were caught, 8 of them marked. N = (30 × 40) ÷ 8 = 1200 ÷ 8 = 150 woodlice.
Second example (sample data): M = 48, C = 50, R = 12; N = 2400 ÷ 12 = 200.
The capture–recapture formula only gives a good estimate if certain conditions hold, and it is easy to mix up the letters. When an exact population isn't needed, a simpler count can be enough.
N must be larger than both M and C, because the population includes every marked animal and every animal caught in the second sample. If it isn't, you have made an error.
R is the number of marked animals in the second sample, not the number marked in the first sample.
Assumption: there are no births, deaths, immigration (animals arriving) or emigration (animals leaving) between the two samples, so the population stays the same size.
Assumption: marked animals mix fully and randomly with the rest, and marked and unmarked animals are equally likely to be caught.
Assumption: the mark doesn't harm the animal, make it easier for predators to see, or wash or rub off.
If marks are lost, R is too small and N is overestimated, because fewer marked animals are recognised in the second sample. The assumptions are rarely fully met in practice.

For comparisons only, a relative count is often enough: for example the number of grasshoppers caught per ten sweeps of a sweep net, or the number of beetles per pitfall trap per day, compared between two areas using the same method.

In ecology a model is a simplified representation of a habitat that describes it and can be used to explain or predict. Here the model is a labelled map with data, built from the primary data (results you collected yourself).
Size: measure the length and width (or the sides of an irregular area) with long tape measures or a trundle wheel, and calculate the area, for example 50 m × 40 m = 2000 m².

Map: draw a sketch map to scale, with a north arrow, showing the boundary, hedges, trees, paths, gates, wet and dry areas, any slope (and which way it faces), the positions of the quadrats, transects and traps, and where the main species were found.
Species: the species list from the qualitative survey, with the quantitative results (percentage frequency, cover, density, population estimates) for the main species.

Abiotic factors: the mean values measured across the habitat (for example light intensity, soil pH, soil water content, air and soil temperature, aspect and slope), with differences between areas marked on the map.
Biotic factors (the effects of living things): the feeding and symbiotic relationships observed, shown as food chains or a food web drawn from the species found.
Biotic factors also include grazing, trampling and human management such as mowing or fertilising.

Using the model: it can explain why species are where they are (for example rushes only in the wet hollow) and predict the effect of a change (for example if mowing stopped, taller grasses would shade out daisies).
Limits of the model: it is a snapshot of one season and of the parts sampled, so it may not hold at other times of year or in unsampled areas.
Raw counts are hard to interpret. Tables and graphs show patterns in species abundance and distribution at a glance.
Record results in tables with headings and units: quadrat number or distance along the transect, species, and the measure used.
Bar charts compare species, for example the percentage frequency of each.
For a transect, plot each species' abundance against distance, or draw a kite diagram.

In a kite diagram, for each species a band is centred on a horizontal line; its width at each point along the transect is proportional to the species' abundance there, so the bands show at a glance where each species is common.
Diagram: a kite diagram for two species along a 10 m transect from a hedge, with distance on the x-axis.
A survey can be set up as a fair test, with an aim, a hypothesis (a testable prediction), and variables. Field studies differ from lab experiments because conditions can't be fully controlled.
Aim: to estimate the abundance and distribution of named species (for example daisy, white clover, grass and woodlice) in a grassland.
Hypothesis (example): 'Daisies are more abundant in the short-mown part of the field than in the long-grass part.'
Independent variable (the one you change or compare) when two areas are compared: the area (for example mown vs unmown).
Dependent variable (the one you measure): the abundance of the species (density, percentage cover or frequency).
Controlled variables (kept the same): the quadrat size and type, the number of quadrats, the method of placing them (random coordinates), the counting rule, the observer, the date and the weather.
There is no true control in a field study, because the two areas can't be made identical in every other way.
Conclusion: state the measured abundance of each species and compare the areas using the means.
Say whether the results support the hypothesis. A difference shows correlation with the area, not proof of the cause.
No survey is perfect. Knowing where errors come from lets you say how reliable your results are and how to improve them.
Too few samples, or samples not placed at random (choosing 'typical' spots), give an unrepresentative estimate; use random coordinates and enough quadrats.
Misidentification of species, especially grasses and small invertebrates, is a source of error.
Estimates of percentage cover by eye are subjective, and inconsistent edge rules change counts.
Results vary with the season and the time of day (plants flower and animals are active at different times), so a single survey is a snapshot.
The assumptions of capture–recapture are rarely fully met.
Trampling during the survey damages the plants being sampled; avoid trampling the quadrat sites before they are sampled.
Reliability improves by repeating the survey (more quadrats, more transects, several dates) and calculating means, because repeats reduce the effect of chance.

Abiotic factors are the non-living features of an environment, such as light, temperature and soil. To explain why a species lives where it does, you must measure them reliably, and a few rules apply whichever factor you measure. There is more on abiotic factors as limiting factors in Carrying capacity and limiting factors.

The specification groups abiotic factors as air (climatic) factors, ground (topographic) factors, aquatic (water) factors and edaphic (soil) factors. “Topographic” means the shape of the land, such as slope and aspect, and “edaphic” means to do with the soil.
The specification names water, oxygen, space, temperature, soil, aspect, wind speed and slope, so you need an instrument and a method for each of these.

Measure abiotic factors at the same places as the quadrats (square frames that mark out a sample area) or transect points (sampling points along a line), and at the same time as the survey, so that each measurement can be linked to the species found there.

Many factors (light, temperature, wind, humidity) change during the day and with the weather. Take all readings within a short period under similar conditions, and record the time and weather, so that readings from different places can be compared fairly.
Repeat each reading (e.g. three times) and use the mean, which reduces the effect of one odd reading.

Electronic probes connected to a data logger (a device that stores readings automatically) can record factors such as temperature, light intensity, humidity, pH and dissolved oxygen continuously over hours or days, and at several points at once. This removes reading errors and shows changes over time.
Calibrate meters before use, which means checking them against a known standard, e.g. a pH meter with buffer solutions of known pH, so that its readings are accurate.
Air factors describe the climate around the organisms. Light and temperature both affect plant growth and animal activity, and each has its own instrument.
Light intensity is the energy for photosynthesis (how plants make food), so it affects plant growth and which plants can grow in shade; it also affects animal activity.
Light intensity is measured with a light meter (lux meter), in lux.

Hold the light sensor horizontally, facing up, at the same height each time (e.g. at ground level or at the top of the vegetation), keep your shadow off it, and take readings quickly, as light changes with cloud cover.

Air temperature controls the rate of enzyme reactions (the chemical reactions in cells), so it affects the activity and growth of plants and of cold-blooded animals, whose body temperature follows their surroundings.

Air temperature is measured with a thermometer or temperature probe, in °C, held in the shade at a set height above the ground (e.g. 1 m) so that direct sunlight doesn’t heat it and give a false high reading.
A maximum–minimum thermometer left on site records the highest and lowest temperatures over a period, e.g. 24 hours, so you do not have to be there at the hottest and coldest moments.
Moving air, water vapour and rain all change how quickly organisms lose or gain water. Each is measured with a different instrument.
Wind speed increases water loss by evaporation and transpiration (loss of water vapour from leaves), cools organisms, can damage tall plants, and makes flying difficult for insects.
Wind speed is measured with an anemometer (a cup anemometer or a hand-held digital one), in metres per second (m/s) or km/h, held at a set height facing into the wind.
Take the mean of several readings, as wind gusts. Wind direction is found with a wind vane or a compass.
Humidity (water in the air) affects water loss from plants and from animals with moist skins; slugs and woodlice need humid places because they dry out quickly.
Humidity is measured with a hygrometer or humidity probe, as relative humidity (%).
Rainfall (water supply) is measured with a rain gauge: a funnel draining into a measuring cylinder, set in an open place so that nothing shelters it, in mm, read at the same time each day.

The shape of the land decides how much water drains away and how much sunlight a place gets. Space decides how many organisms can fit in a habitat. Slope, aspect and space are all measured directly in the field.
Slope affects drainage: water runs off steep slopes, so they are drier and soils are thinner, while hollows at the bottom collect water. Slope also affects the amount of sunlight received.

Slope is measured with a clinometer (an instrument for measuring angles), in degrees. Two people of the same eye height (or two poles marked at the same height) stand up and down the slope a set distance apart.
One person sights the other’s eye level (or the mark) through the clinometer and reads the angle.
Aspect is the compass direction a slope faces, measured with a compass, because direction decides how much sun the slope gets.
In Ireland (northern hemisphere) a south-facing slope receives more direct sunlight than a north-facing one, so it is warmer and drier and plants there start growing earlier in spring.
Space is the room available for organisms to live, grow, find shelter, nest or attach.

Measure the area of the habitat (length × width with tapes or a trundle wheel), and the percentage of bare ground in each quadrat (squares of a gridded quadrat with no plants), which shows the space available for new seedlings.
Density (individuals per m², from surveys) shows how crowded a species is. Shortage of space is a cause of competition. There is more on this in Biotic factors and relationships.
Soil factors are called edaphic. Soil temperature and pH both help decide which plants and soil organisms can live in a place, and each is measured on a small soil sample or with a probe.
Soil temperature affects root growth, germination and the activity of soil organisms and decomposers (organisms that break down dead material).
Push a soil thermometer or temperature probe into the soil to a set depth (e.g. 10 cm), leave it for a minute or two to settle, and read it in °C.
Soil pH affects which plants grow (by changing which minerals are available) and which soil organisms live there; earthworms are scarce in acid soils.
Soil pH method, step 1: take a small soil sample from a set depth.

Soil pH method, step 2: put about 1 cm depth of soil in a test tube, add about the same amount of barium sulfate (which makes the clay particles settle, so that the liquid clears), then distilled water and a few drops of universal indicator.
Soil pH method, step 3: stopper and shake, then leave to settle.
Soil pH method, step 4: compare the colour of the liquid with the universal indicator colour chart to read the pH.

Alternatively, mix the soil with distilled water and use a calibrated pH meter, rinsing the probe in distilled water between samples. Use distilled water, as tap water has its own pH and would change the result.
Soil water decides which plants and soil animals can live in a place. It is measured by drying a soil sample and finding how much mass it loses.
Soil water content affects which plants grow (rushes grow in wet soil) and soil animals (earthworms need moist soil); waterlogged soil lacks air.
Soil water content method, step 1: weigh an empty evaporating dish.
Soil water content method, step 2: add a soil sample and weigh again, to find the fresh mass of soil by subtraction.
Soil water content method, step 3: heat in an oven at about 100–105 °C (hot enough to evaporate water, not to burn humus) for 24 hours.
Soil water content method, step 4: cool in a desiccator (so the soil doesn’t reabsorb water from the air) and reweigh.
Soil water content method, step 5: repeat the heating, cooling and weighing until the mass stays the same (constant mass), showing that all the water has gone.
The water lost on drying is the water the soil held, so the calculation compares the mass before and after heating.
Percentage water = (fresh mass − dry mass) ÷ fresh mass × 100. It is worked out from the fresh mass, which is the mass before drying.
Worked example: fresh soil 50.0 g; dry soil 38.0 g at constant mass. Water = 12.0 g. Percentage water = 12.0 ÷ 50.0 × 100 = 24%.
A soil-moisture probe (meter) gives a quick reading in the field, but less accurately than drying the soil.
Soil is a mixture of solid particles and air spaces. Measuring the air content tells you how well roots and soil animals can breathe.
Soil air content matters because roots and soil animals need oxygen for respiration. Air spaces are larger in sandy soils and smaller in clay and waterlogged soils.
Soil air content method, step 1: find the volume of an empty can by filling it with water from a graduated cylinder.
Soil air content method, step 2: push the can, open end down, into the soil until it is full, dig it out and level the soil with the rim.
Soil air content method, step 3: put a volume of water equal to the can’s volume in a large graduated cylinder.
Soil air content method, step 4: add the soil, and stir with a rod to release the trapped air.
Soil air content method, step 5: read the new level.
Volume of air = (volume of water + volume of soil) − final reading. Percentage air = volume of air ÷ volume of soil × 100.
Worked example: can volume 100 cm³; 100 cm³ water; reading after adding soil and stirring 185 cm³. Air = 200 − 185 = 15 cm³; percentage air = 15 ÷ 100 × 100 = 15%.
Humus is the organic part of soil. Because it burns away when heated strongly and the mineral part does not, the loss in mass measures how much humus there was.
Humus is the dark, partly decomposed remains of dead organisms in soil. It holds water and minerals and feeds decomposers.
Humus method, step 1: weigh a crucible (a small heat-proof pot).
Humus method, step 2: add dry soil from the water-content method and weigh it.
Humus method, step 3: heat it strongly over a Bunsen burner (lid partly on) until the humus burns away (about 15 minutes).
Humus method, step 4: cool in a desiccator and reweigh.
Humus method, step 5: repeat until constant mass, so that you know all the humus has burned away.
Percentage humus = loss in mass ÷ mass of dry soil × 100, so it uses the dry mass because the water has already been removed.
Worked example: dry soil 38.0 g; after burning, 34.2 g. Loss = 3.8 g; percentage humus = 3.8 ÷ 38.0 × 100 = 10% of the dry soil.
Soil texture describes the sizes of the particles in the soil. A simple settling test separates them into layers.
Soil texture method: shake soil with water in a graduated cylinder and leave it to settle.
The particles settle in layers, largest at the bottom: stones and gravel, then sand, silt and clay, with humus floating on top.
The proportions of the layers show the soil type, such as sandy or clay soil.
In water, temperature, dissolved oxygen and pH are measured. Temperature matters for oxygen because cold water holds more of it.
Water temperature is measured with a thermometer or probe in °C, at a set depth. It affects how much oxygen water holds (cold water holds more) and the activity of aquatic organisms.
Dissolved oxygen is measured with an oxygen meter (probe), in mg per litre, or with a chemical test kit.
Animals such as stonefly larvae need high oxygen. Low oxygen is a sign of organic pollution, because decomposers use up the oxygen as they break down the waste.
Water pH is measured with a pH meter or universal indicator paper, as for soil.
Moving water, cloudy water and salty water each create different conditions for organisms. Rate of flow is measured with a simple timed float.
Rate of flow (current speed): mark two points a set distance apart along a straight stretch of stream (e.g. 10 m); time a float (e.g. an orange or a dog biscuit) from one point to the other.
Repeat the timing three times and take the mean time; speed = distance ÷ time.
Worked example: mean time 25 s over 10 m: 10 ÷ 25 = 0.4 m/s.
Fast flow carries away animals that can’t cling on and keeps the water well oxygenated.
Turbidity (cloudiness) is measured with a Secchi disc, a black-and-white disc on a marked rope, which is lowered until it is no longer visible; the depth is recorded.
Cloudy water lets less light reach water plants, so they photosynthesise less.
Salinity (saltiness, in seawater, rock pools and estuaries) is measured with a conductivity or salinity meter. Rock pools become saltier as water evaporates in sunshine.

You must be able to investigate quantitatively (using numbers) how an abiotic factor affects the distribution (where) and abundance (how many) of a species. The standard example is light and daisies on a belt transect (a strip across a habitat, sampled with quadrats at set intervals).
Aim: to investigate quantitatively how light intensity affects the distribution and abundance of the daisy in a grassland, along a belt transect from under a hedge or tree into the open field.
Hypothesis (a testable prediction): “The number of daisies per quadrat increases as light intensity increases.”
Reason for the hypothesis: the daisy is a low-growing rosette plant that needs plenty of light for photosynthesis, and is shaded out where light is low.
Independent variable: light intensity. It varies naturally along the transect, so it is measured, not set by the student.
Dependent variable: the abundance of daisies (number per quadrat, or percentage cover).

Controlled variables: quadrat size, the interval between quadrats, the counting rule, the height and direction of the light sensor, the time of day (all readings within a short period) and the weather.
A field study cannot hold everything else constant. This limits what the results can prove, so it is worth knowing before you plan the method.

No true control is possible: other factors also change along the transect, such as soil water content, leaf litter, trampling, and competition from taller plants near the hedge. Measure these too where possible, so that their effect can be considered.
This is why a field investigation shows a correlation (two things changing together), not proof of cause.
Equipment: two long tape measures (one for the transect), a gridded quadrat, a light meter, pegs, a recording sheet, and a soil-moisture probe or soil-sampling equipment for the second factor.

Other suitable pairs of factor and species: soil water content and rushes (more in wet ground); trampling or soil compaction across a path and plantain or grass cover; soil pH and a named plant; height above low tide on a rocky shore and the cover of each seaweed.
The method lays quadrats at regular intervals along the transect, then counts daisies and measures light at each one.
Step 1: stretch a tape measure from the base of the hedge (0 m) straight out into the open field, e.g. for 10 m.
Step 2: place a gridded quadrat at 0 m and then at every 2 m along the tape (an interrupted belt transect, because it samples at intervals rather than along the whole line).
Step 3: in each quadrat, count the daisy rosettes (or the squares in which daisy covers more than half, for percentage cover).
Step 4: at each quadrat, hold the light meter at ground level, facing up, and take three readings in quick succession; record the mean in lux.
Do all the light readings within a few minutes, ideally under even cloud, because light changes quickly when clouds move.
Repeating the transect and recording results in a table make the data reliable and ready to graph. Fieldwork also carries small risks to manage.
Step 5: measure the second factor (e.g. soil water content) at each quadrat, so that its effect can be compared with that of light.
Step 6: repeat the whole transect at least twice more, parallel to the first and a few metres away, and calculate the mean count at each distance.
Step 7: record the results in a table, and plot a scatter graph of the number of daisies (y-axis) against light intensity (x-axis), or plot both against distance from the hedge.
Safety: take care at hedges with thorns, nettles and brambles; wear gloves when handling soil; wash hands afterwards; avoid trampling the quadrat sites before they are sampled.

Diagram: a belt transect running from a hedge into open grassland with quadrats every 2 m and a light meter at one quadrat. Label the hedge, 0 m, the tape, the quadrats, the light meter and the distances.
Plotting the data shows whether daisy numbers rise with light. The sample data below are illustrative, an example of what results might look like, not real measurements.
Sample data: distance 0 m: light 800 lux, 0 daisies; 2 m: 2500 lux, 1 daisy; 4 m: 6000 lux, 4 daisies; 6 m: 9500 lux, 9 daisies; 8 m: 12 000 lux, 12 daisies; 10 m: 12 500 lux, 11 daisies.
Expected result: daisies are absent or few in deep shade close to the hedge, and become more abundant as light intensity increases into the open field.
Daisies level off once light no longer limits them; other factors, such as space or competition with grass, then limit them.
The scatter graph shows a positive correlation: as light intensity rises, so does the number of daisies.
A conclusion must say whether the data support the hypothesis and how far they can be trusted. Naming the sources of error shows you understand the limits of fieldwork.
Conclusion: the results support the hypothesis that daisy abundance increases with light intensity along this transect.
Because soil water and leaf litter also changed, the result shows a correlation, not proof that light alone is the cause.
A laboratory experiment growing daisies at different light intensities, with other factors controlled, could test the cause.
Sources of error: light intensity changes rapidly with cloud cover, so readings at different quadrats may not be comparable (take readings quickly, or use data loggers at several points at once).

Other sources of error: a single transect may not be representative (use several); counting errors and inconsistent edge rules; misidentification of small daisy rosettes; other factors varying along the transect; the survey is a snapshot of one day and season.
Primary data are the student’s own counts and measurements. They can be compared with secondary data (e.g. published descriptions of where daisies grow) when drawing conclusions.
Each habitat has its own key abiotic factors. A rocky shore, a woodland and a freshwater stream show how different factors dominate.
Rocky shore: the main factor is the time spent out of water at low tide (exposure), which rises with height up the shore and brings drying, temperature change and, in rock pools, salinity change.

This produces zonation, bands of species at different heights. Brown seaweeds (wracks) on Irish shores are zoned from the top down: channelled wrack (highest, survives longest out of water), spiral wrack, bladder wrack and knotted wrack (middle shore), serrated wrack (lower shore), and kelps (at and below the low-tide mark).
Zonation on a rocky shore is measured with a belt transect from low to high water, with height measured using a ranging pole and level.
Woodland: light intensity under the canopy (lowest in summer when trees are in leaf), humidity, leaf-litter depth, soil humus and pH are the key factors.
Many woodland floor plants (e.g. bluebells) grow and flower in spring before the canopy closes, while enough light still reaches the ground.
Freshwater: dissolved oxygen, temperature, rate of flow and pH are the key factors.
Fast, cold streams are rich in oxygen and support stonefly and mayfly larvae; still or polluted water low in oxygen supports fewer species.

Biotic factors are the effects that living organisms have on each other. In a grassland they include food supply, predation, grazing, competition, parasites and disease, pollination and decomposition, and human activities such as grazing livestock, mowing and fertilising. Grazing and mowing show how one biotic factor shapes which plants can live in a habitat.

Grazing by rabbits, cattle or sheep and mowing keep grass short. This lets low rosette plants (plants whose leaves lie flat close to the ground) such as daisy, dandelion and plantain get light, and stops shrubs and trees from invading.
If grazing or mowing stops, taller grasses shade out the rosette plants because they grow above them and take the light. In time scrub (a tangle of woody shrubs, e.g. brambles, hawthorn) invades.
Other living things work in the grassland soil and on its flowers. Some recycle dead material back into the ground, and others carry pollen between flowers.

Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) and detritivores (animals that eat dead organic matter, e.g. earthworms, woodlice, and slugs in part) break down dead plants, dung and dead animals, returning minerals to the soil so that plants can take them up again.
Decomposition recycles carbon and nitrogen, and there is more on this in The carbon cycle, The nitrogen cycle and Bacteria and fungi.
Earthworms also drag leaves underground, mix and aerate the soil (let air into it), and improve drainage.

Pollinators such as bumblebees, hoverflies and butterflies feed on the nectar and pollen of clover, dandelion and buttercup flowers, and carry pollen between them, which is how these plants are pollinated.
To work out who eats whom in a grassland, you gather primary data, meaning information you collect yourself in the field. You then check it against what other people have already recorded.
Direct observation of animals feeding shows a feeding relationship at the moment it happens.
Feeding signs are evidence left behind: nibbled grass, holes in leaves, and broken snail shells at a thrush’s stone.
Droppings and pellets show what an animal ate, e.g. undigested fur and bones in the pellets of birds of prey.
The habitat where each animal was caught is a clue, e.g. aphids found on the stems they feed on.
Your findings are then checked against secondary sources (information collected by others), such as field guides, for what each species eats.
Every feeding relationship starts with a green plant that makes food. Animals then feed on the plants, and on each other, in layers called trophic levels (feeding levels).
Producers in the grassland are grasses, clover, daisy, dandelion, buttercup and other green plants, which make food by photosynthesis.

Primary consumers (herbivores, which eat plants) in the grassland: rabbits and hares graze grass and clover; slugs and snails eat leaves; grasshoppers and caterpillars chew leaves; aphids suck sap from stems; bumblebees take nectar and pollen.

Secondary and higher consumers (carnivores, which eat animals, and omnivores, which eat both): ladybirds eat aphids; spiders catch flies, grasshoppers and other insects; ground beetles eat slugs and other invertebrates.
Song thrushes eat snails (smashing their shells on a stone) and earthworms; blackbirds eat earthworms and insects; hedgehogs eat slugs, beetles and earthworms.
Badgers eat mainly earthworms; foxes eat rabbits, mice and birds; kestrels eat wood mice, pygmy shrews and large insects.
Pygmy shrews eat small invertebrates such as beetles, spiders and woodlice.
A food chain follows one line of feeding, with arrows pointing from the food to the feeder. Because most animals eat more than one thing, the chains join up into a food web.

Worked example of grassland food chains: grass → rabbit → fox; clover leaves → slug → song thrush; plant sap → aphid → ladybird → (insect-eating bird); grass seeds and invertebrates → wood mouse → kestrel.
These chains connect into a food web. For example, the fox eats rabbits, wood mice and birds, so it is on several chains.
The earthworm feeds on dead leaves and is eaten by thrushes, blackbirds, badgers and hedgehogs, so it links the dead material in the soil to several animals above it.
Diagram: a grassland food web of 8–12 of the species listed above, with arrows pointing from the food to the feeder.
A food web shows that organisms depend on each other, so a change in one population spreads through the whole community.
The web shows interdependence: a change in one population affects others.
For example, if disease kills many rabbits, foxes eat more wood mice and birds, so those populations fall, and the grass grows taller because fewer rabbits graze it, shading out daisies.

An omnivore or a predator with several prey is less affected than one with a single food source, because it can switch to another food when one becomes scarce. There is more on predicting changes from webs in Energy and nutrient transfer.
Predation is the best-known feeding relationship between animals. Predators have features that help them find, catch and kill their prey.
Predation is a feeding relationship in which one animal, the predator, kills and eats another, the prey.
Grassland examples of predation: fox (predator) and rabbit (prey); kestrel and wood mouse; ladybird and aphid; song thrush and snail.
The fox has acute hearing and smell to find prey, forward-facing eyes for judging distance, speed and sharp teeth, and hunts mostly at night, when rabbits feed.
The kestrel hovers into the wind while scanning the ground with very keen eyesight, then drops onto its prey, gripping it with sharp talons and tearing it with a hooked beak.
Spiders build webs to trap flying insects.
Prey animals need to spot danger early, escape, or avoid being noticed or eaten in the first place.
Rabbits have eyes on the sides of the head, giving an almost all-round field of view, and large mobile ears, so they can detect a predator coming from any direction.
Rabbits feed in groups so that some can watch for danger, thump the ground with a hind foot and flash the white underside of the tail as a warning, run in zigzags, and shelter in burrows.
Snails withdraw into their shells for protection.
Ladybirds have bright warning colours and a bad taste, so predators learn to avoid them.
Many caterpillars and grasshoppers are green, camouflaged against the grass, so predators find them hard to see.
Predator and prey numbers rise and fall together in a repeating cycle, because each population depends on the other.
1. When prey are plentiful, more predators survive and breed, so predator numbers rise.
2. More predators eat more prey, so prey numbers fall.
3. With less food, predators starve or breed less, so predator numbers fall.
4. With fewer predators, prey numbers recover, and the cycle repeats.
Predator numbers peak after prey numbers, because predators need time to breed once food is plentiful. There are usually fewer predators than prey.
The classic data are the fur-trading records of the snowshoe hare and the lynx in Canada, which rose and fell in cycles of about ten years.
Diagram: a graph of predator and prey numbers against time: two out-of-step waves, the predator curve lower and peaking after the prey curve.
Predators do more than eat prey. They also help to set how many prey a habitat holds.
Predators usually take the old, sick, young or weak prey, which are the easiest to catch.

The effect of predation increases as prey become more numerous, because prey are easier to find. This helps keep the prey population near the habitat’s carrying capacity (the largest population the habitat can support). There is more on this in Carrying capacity and limiting factors.
Removing a predator can let its prey increase until it overgrazes its food.
Organisms compete when they need the same resource and there is not enough for all. Competition can be sorted by who is competing and by how the resource is shared out.

Competition is the struggle between organisms for a resource that is in short supply. Plants compete for light, water, minerals and space; animals compete for food, water, space or territory, shelter and mates.
If the resource is plentiful, there is no competition.

Intraspecific competition is between members of the same species. It is the most intense kind, because they have exactly the same needs, e.g. daisy rosettes crowding each other for space and light, or male blackbirds or robins defending territories that contain food and nest sites.
Interspecific competition is between different species that need the same resource, e.g. grasses and daisies competing for light, or rabbits and sheep grazing the same grass.
Contest competition: there is an active physical contest for the resource and the winner takes it, e.g. birds fighting over territory, or stags fighting over mates.

Scramble competition: each competitor gets as much as it can of a shared resource, so when it is scarce all get too little, e.g. seedlings crowded together all grow weak and thin, or aphids crowded on a stem.
Competition has a cost for the organisms that lose, and this affects the whole population. Organisms also have features that help them win.
Competition reduces the growth, survival and breeding of the losers, and so limits population size. Its effect grows as the population becomes more crowded.

Between species, one may exclude the other from the habitat, or each may survive by using the resources in a slightly different way (different niches, meaning different roles or ways of living in the habitat). There is more on this in The niche.

Adaptations that help organisms compete: fast growth, and tall stems or climbing (e.g. ivy, brambles) in plants competing for light; deep roots for water; rapid breeding; aggressive defence of territory in animals.
Two examples show interspecific competition at work: one in the grassland and one from Ireland.
In short, grazed or mown grass, daisies and other rosette plants get enough light. Where grass is left long, it outgrows and shades them, and they disappear (interspecific competition for light).
Irish example: grey squirrels, introduced to Ireland at Castle Forbes, Co. Longford, in 1911, compete with the native red squirrel for food, especially seeds and nuts.

Grey squirrels are larger, can digest acorns (which red squirrels digest poorly), eat hazelnuts before they ripen, and carry squirrelpox virus, which kills red squirrels but rarely harms grey squirrels. Red squirrels have disappeared from much of the area greys occupy.
Where pine marten numbers have recovered in Ireland, grey squirrels have declined and red squirrels have returned.
Some organisms do not just compete or eat each other but live together. This close partnership is called symbiosis, and it is sorted into three types by who benefits.
Symbiosis is a close, long-term relationship in which two organisms of different species live together.
There are three types, named by who benefits: mutualism (both benefit, +/+), commensalism (one benefits and the other is unaffected, +/0) and parasitism (one benefits and the other is harmed, +/−).

Pollinators and flowers benefit each other (food for the insect, pollination for the plant), so the relationship is mutualistic, but the two don’t live together, so many biologists don’t call it symbiosis.
In mutualism both partners gain. The first example is a bacterium that gives clover a supply of nitrogen, which is why clover can enrich grassland.

Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) live in root nodules (small swellings) of clover and other legumes. The bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonium, which the plant uses to make amino acids and proteins.
The plant gives the bacteria carbohydrates (from photosynthesis) and a protected home.
Active nodules are pink inside, from a pigment (leghaemoglobin) that controls oxygen levels for the bacteria.
This is why clover grows well in soils poor in nitrogen and enriches grassland. There is more on this in The nitrogen cycle.
To observe: dig up a clover plant, wash the roots and examine the nodules with a hand lens; cut one to see the pink colour.
Mutualism is common wherever one partner can do something the other cannot. Here are three more examples, and in each the partners swap food or shelter for something they lack.

Cellulose-digesting microorganisms (bacteria, protists and fungi) live in the rumen (first stomach) of cattle and sheep, and in the caecum (a pouch of the gut) of rabbits. They digest the cellulose of grass, which the animal has no enzyme to digest.

The microorganisms get a warm, food-rich home, and the animal gets the products (fatty acids) as food. Rabbits also eat some of their own soft droppings to absorb nutrients released by these microorganisms.

Mycorrhizal fungi grow around and into the roots of most grassland plants and trees. The fungal hyphae (thread-like filaments) spread far through the soil, absorbing water and minerals (especially phosphate) and passing them to the plant; the plant supplies the fungus with sugars.

Lichens (e.g. on walls, rocks and tree bark around the grassland) are a fungus and an alga (or cyanobacterium) living together. The alga photosynthesises and supplies sugars; the fungus gives shelter, holds water and absorbs minerals.
Bacteria in the human gut are another example of mutualism. There is more on this in The microbiome.
In commensalism one partner gains and the other is neither helped nor harmed. It is easy to confuse with mutualism, so check whether the second partner really gets nothing.
Commensalism: one partner benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.
Mosses and lichens growing on the bark of trees get a place in the light without harming the tree.
Many bacteria living on human skin feed on dead skin cells and sweat without harming the host. There is more on this in The microbiome.

Seeds with hooks (e.g. burdock) are carried in an animal’s fur, and robins follow a gardener or grazing cattle to catch the invertebrates they disturb; both are commensal relationships, since the animal or gardener is unaffected.
A parasite lives on or in another organism, the host, and feeds on it. Unlike a predator, it usually keeps its host alive.
Parasitism: the parasite lives in or on the host and feeds on it, harming it. A parasite usually weakens its host without killing it quickly, since it depends on the host.

Grassland ectoparasites (parasites living on the outside of the host): fleas on rabbits and hedgehogs; ticks on sheep, deer and humans. Ticks are also vectors of Lyme disease, meaning they carry it from host to host.
The rabbit flea carries the myxoma virus that causes myxomatosis, which has killed very large numbers of rabbits.

Grassland endoparasites (parasites living inside the host): liver fluke in sheep and cattle on wet pasture; roundworms and tapeworms in the gut of grazing animals. There is more on liver fluke and tapeworms in Pathogens.
Plant parasites: rust fungi on grasses and cereals.

Yellow rattle, a meadow plant, is a partial parasite: it photosynthesises but taps the roots of grasses for water and minerals, weakening the grasses so that other wild flowers can grow. For this reason it is sown when restoring wildflower meadows.
Ivy is not a parasite: it climbs trees but makes its own food and takes nothing from them.
A parasite usually weakens its host rather than killing it quickly, but parasites and disease can still change how many hosts there are, because weakened hosts breed less and are caught more easily.
Parasites and disease weaken hosts, making them easier prey and less able to breed.
Parasites spread fastest when hosts are crowded, so their effect increases with population density, like predation.
The signs show the effect on each partner: + for benefits, − for harmed, and 0 for unaffected. Use them to compare the five relationships.
Predation (+/−): a predator kills and eats its prey, e.g. fox and rabbit.
Competition (−/−): both organisms lose some of a scarce resource, e.g. grass and daisy for light, or grey and red squirrel.
Mutualism (+/+): both benefit, e.g. nitrogen-fixing bacteria in clover root nodules.
Commensalism (+/0): one benefits and the other is unaffected, e.g. mosses on tree bark.
Parasitism (+/−): the host is harmed but usually not killed quickly, e.g. a flea on a rabbit.
Predation and parasitism are both +/−. The difference is that a predator kills its prey at once and eats it, while a parasite lives on a living host over a long time.

Microorganisms are living things so small that you need a microscope to see them. Bacteria and fungi matter most for nutrient cycling, because they return the nutrients locked in dead matter to the soil.
Microorganisms are organisms too small to be seen without a microscope, e.g. bacteria, many fungi (such as yeasts and moulds), protists and viruses.
Most microorganisms are harmless or useful; only some are pathogens (organisms that cause disease). There is more on this in Pathogens.

Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers: they feed on dead organisms, dead leaves, dung and other wastes, breaking down complex organic compounds (carbon-containing molecules made by living things).
Decomposers release carbon dioxide (by respiration) and minerals such as ammonium and phosphate into the soil, where plants reuse them.
Without decomposers, nutrients would stay locked in dead matter and plants would run out of the minerals they need to grow.

Other bacteria carry out particular steps of the nitrogen cycle. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas from the air into a usable form; they live free in soil or in the root nodules (small swellings) of legumes.
Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate, a form of nitrogen that plants can take up through their roots.
Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate back to nitrogen gas, returning nitrogen to the air.
Bacteria are the simplest cells you need to know. Their outer layers shape and protect the cell, and each layer has a different job.
Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes, which means they have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles (compartments inside the cell, each wrapped in its own membrane).
Most bacteria are about 1–10 µm long, so they appear as tiny dots or rods under the light microscope, and seeing their parts needs the electron microscope.
Cell wall: a rigid layer outside the membrane, made of peptidoglycan, a polymer of sugars and amino acids.
The cell wall gives the cell its shape and stops it bursting when water enters by osmosis (water moving into the cell because it is more concentrated inside).
Penicillin works by stopping bacteria building their cell wall, so the weakened cells burst. There is more on this in Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment.
Capsule (slime layer): a sticky layer of polysaccharide (a large sugar molecule) outside the wall, present in some bacteria.

The capsule protects the cell from drying out and from being engulfed (taken in and destroyed) by white blood cells, and helps it stick to surfaces such as teeth. Bacteria with capsules are often more harmful.
Inside the wall, a bacterium has the same basic machinery as any cell, but it is not packaged in organelles. Everything floats in the cytoplasm, or sits on the membrane.
Cell membrane: controls what enters and leaves the cell. The enzymes of respiration are on it, because bacteria have no mitochondria.
Cytoplasm: the jelly-like contents where most reactions take place. It contains food stores such as granules of glycogen or lipid.
Nucleoid: one circular chromosome of DNA lies free in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid. Bacteria have DNA but no nucleus.

The nucleoid is not enclosed by a membrane and the DNA is not wound around histones (proteins that DNA coils around in eukaryotes). The chromosome carries the genes for all the cell's essential functions.
Plasmids: small extra rings of DNA, separate from the chromosome, which copy themselves independently.

Plasmids carry a few genes that are useful in some conditions, e.g. antibiotic resistance, and can be passed from one bacterium to another, even of a different species. Plasmids are used as vectors (carriers of new genes) in genetic engineering.
Ribosomes: small (70S) ribosomes, free in the cytoplasm, where proteins are made.
Bacterial 70S ribosomes are smaller than the 80S ribosomes in eukaryotic cytoplasm, which is why some antibiotics can block them without harming human cells.
Some bacteria also have threads on their surface. They let the cell swim, stick to things, or swap DNA with another bacterium.
Flagellum (plural flagella): a long, whip-like thread, present in some bacteria, that rotates like a propeller to move the cell, e.g. towards food.
Pili (fimbriae): short, hair-like threads on the surface of some bacteria that attach them to surfaces and host cells (the living organisms a bacterium infects).
A longer sex pilus links two bacteria so that a copy of a plasmid can pass between them.

Diagram: draw a large rod-shaped bacterium. Label capsule, cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleoid with circular chromosome, plasmids, ribosomes, flagellum, pili and a food-storage granule, with a function written beside each label.
Bacteria are classified partly by shape, which you can recognise under the microscope. There are four shapes to know, each with a named example.
Cocci (singular coccus) are spherical: Streptococcus forms chains and Staphylococcus forms clusters.
Bacilli (singular bacillus) are rod-shaped, e.g. Escherichia coli.
Vibrios are comma-shaped, e.g. Vibrio cholerae, which causes cholera.
Diagram: the shapes, each labelled: a chain of cocci, a cluster of cocci, a rod (bacillus), a spiral (spirillum) and a comma (vibrio).
Bacteria multiply by simple splitting, which is quick and makes identical copies. When conditions turn hostile, some of them form a tough resting structure that lets them survive.
Bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission: the circular chromosome is copied, the cell grows and the two copies move apart.
The cell then divides in two as a new wall forms across the middle, giving two genetically identical cells.
In ideal conditions binary fission can happen as often as every 20 minutes, so populations grow very fast. There is more on this in Microorganisms in industry.
Variation in bacteria comes only from mutations (changes in DNA) and from genes passed on plasmids, because binary fission produces identical cells.
Some bacteria, e.g. Clostridium and Bacillus, form an endospore when conditions become unfavourable, such as a lack of nutrients or water.
In an endospore the chromosome and a little cytoplasm are enclosed in a tough, thick wall inside the cell, and the rest of the cell breaks down.
Endospores survive boiling, drying, freezing and many disinfectants for years; when conditions improve, each grows into one new active bacterium.
Endospores are why equipment is sterilised in an autoclave at 121 °C rather than by boiling, and why tetanus can be caught from soil.
Bacteria feed in many ways. Autotrophs, the first group, make their own food from simple inorganic substances, using either light or chemical energy.
Autotrophic bacteria make their own food from simple inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide and water.
Photosynthetic bacteria use light energy, e.g. cyanobacteria, which contain chlorophyll and release oxygen.
Some other photosynthetic bacteria, such as purple and green sulfur bacteria, use hydrogen sulfide in place of water and release no oxygen.
Chemosynthetic bacteria get energy by oxidising inorganic chemicals (adding oxygen to them, which releases energy) instead of from light, e.g. nitrifying bacteria in soil.
Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrite and nitrite to nitrate, and use the energy released to make food from carbon dioxide.
Most bacteria are heterotrophs: they cannot make food, so they take in food made by other organisms. They also differ in whether they can live with oxygen.
Heterotrophic bacteria take in food made by other organisms, and most bacteria are heterotrophic.
Saprophytic bacteria feed on dead organic matter. A saprophyte (saprotroph) secretes digestive enzymes out of its cell onto the food, which is extracellular digestion.
A saprophyte then absorbs the small soluble products, e.g. sugars and amino acids, through its wall and membrane. Saprophytic bacteria are decomposers, and they also cause food to rot.
Parasitic bacteria feed on a living host and harm it, causing disease, e.g. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which causes tuberculosis.
Mutualistic bacteria live with a host to the benefit of both, e.g. nitrogen-fixing bacteria in clover root nodules and bacteria in the gut.
Obligate aerobes need oxygen to respire.
Obligate anaerobes are killed by oxygen, e.g. Clostridium, which is why tetanus grows in deep wounds where oxygen cannot reach.
Facultative anaerobes respire aerobically when oxygen is present and anaerobically when it is not, e.g. E. coli.
Fungi are eukaryotes that look plant-like but are not plants. Most are built from thread-like hyphae, and they spread by spores.
Fungi are eukaryotes: each cell, or each section of hypha, has nuclei with a nuclear membrane, mitochondria and 80S ribosomes.
Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, not cellulose.
Fungi have no chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise; they store carbohydrate as glycogen and lipid, not starch.
Most fungi, such as moulds and mushrooms, are made of hyphae (singular hypha): long, branching, thread-like tubes with a wall around cytoplasm containing many nuclei. A mass of hyphae is a mycelium.
Some fungi have cross-walls (septa) dividing the hyphae into cells; Rhizopus has none.
Mushrooms are the reproductive structures of a mycelium that grows mostly hidden in soil or wood.

Fungi reproduce by spores, tiny reproductive cells released in great numbers and carried by air, water or animals. Each spore can grow into a new mycelium on a suitable food; fungi also reproduce sexually.
Yeasts are the exception among fungi, because they are not made of hyphae. Each yeast is a single cell.
Yeasts are single-celled fungi, e.g. Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's and brewer's yeast), which are oval cells.
Yeasts reproduce asexually by budding: a small outgrowth grows from the parent cell, the nucleus divides by mitosis (copying itself to give two identical nuclei), and the bud separates as a new cell.
Yeast can respire aerobically or ferment sugar to ethanol and CO₂, which is why it is used in baking and brewing.
Rhizopus is a mould you can see growing on stale bread. Its body is made of different kinds of hypha, each with a job.
Rhizopus stolonifer (black bread mould) is a common mould that grows on bread, fruit and other moist, starchy or sugary food.
Its spores are everywhere in the air, which is why bread left moist and warm goes mouldy within days.
Hyphae: the mycelium is made of branched hyphae with no cross-walls, so each hypha is a continuous tube of cytoplasm with many nuclei. The walls of the hyphae contain chitin.
Stolons are hyphae that grow horizontally over the surface of the food, spreading the mould to new areas; the name stolonifer means “bearing stolons”.
Rhizoids are short, branched, root-like hyphae that grow down into the food where a stolon touches it.
Rhizoids are hyphae, not roots: they anchor the mould, secrete digestive enzymes into the food and absorb the products, not water from soil.
Sporangiophores are upright hyphae that grow up from the stolons, above the rhizoids, each carrying a sporangium at its tip.
The upright hyphae carry the spore cases. Spores are how Rhizopus spreads, and the food it grows on is also its only source of nutrients.
A sporangium (plural sporangia) is a round spore case at the tip of a sporangiophore, white at first and black when ripe, which gives the mould its black, fuzzy look.
Inside the sporangium, many spores form around a dome-shaped swelling at the top of the sporangiophore, the columella, which supports the sporangium.
When the sporangium is ripe, its wall breaks and the spores are released and carried by air currents.
Each spore that lands on moist food grows into a new hypha and mycelium; this is asexual reproduction, so the offspring are genetically identical.
Rhizopus is a saprophyte, feeding on dead organic matter. Being heterotrophic, it cannot make food, so it must grow on its food.
Diagram: draw Rhizopus on bread. Label mycelium, hyphae, stolon, rhizoids penetrating the bread, sporangiophores, a sporangium cut open (spores, columella) and spores being released.
Fungi cannot make their own food, so every fungus feeds on organic matter made by other organisms. They differ in whether that food is dead, living or shared.
All fungi are heterotrophic; none is autotrophic, because fungi have no chlorophyll.
Most fungi are saprophytes, feeding on dead organic matter by extracellular digestion (digesting food outside the cell).
Rhizopus secretes enzymes from its rhizoids and hyphae into bread: amylase digests starch to maltose and glucose, and proteases digest proteins to amino acids.
The soluble products diffuse back and are absorbed, then used for respiration and growth.
Mushrooms and other wood- and leaf-rotting fungi are the main decomposers of the cellulose and woody material of dead plants, which most bacteria cannot break down.
Parasitic fungi feed on living hosts and harm them, e.g. athlete's foot in humans and ash dieback in ash trees.
Mutualistic fungi live in partnership with other organisms to the benefit of both: mycorrhizal fungi with plant roots, and the fungus in a lichen.
Bacteria and fungi both decompose dead matter, but their cells are built very differently. These contrasts are the first set to learn, as a pair for each feature.
Cellular nature: bacteria are prokaryotic, with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles; fungi are eukaryotic, with nuclei, mitochondria and other membrane-bound organelles.
DNA: bacteria have one circular chromosome, not wound around histones, plus plasmids; fungi have several linear chromosomes of DNA wound around histones, inside a nucleus.
Ribosomes: bacteria have 70S ribosomes; fungi have 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
Cell wall: bacteria have peptidoglycan walls; fungi have chitin walls.
Organisation and size: bacteria are single cells about 1–10 µm long, which grow in colonies but each cell lives independently.
Most fungi are multicellular, with hyphae that form a mycelium visible to the naked eye, although yeasts are single cells, larger than most bacteria.
Food stores: bacteria store glycogen or lipid granules; fungi store glycogen and lipid, and neither stores starch.
The other differences are in how they feed, reproduce and respond to drugs. The groups also share some features, so a full comparison includes both.

Nutrition: bacteria can be autotrophic (photosynthetic or chemosynthetic) or heterotrophic (saprophytic, parasitic or mutualistic); fungi are always heterotrophic (saprophytic, parasitic or mutualistic).
Reproduction: bacteria reproduce by binary fission, and some form endospores for survival; fungi reproduce by spores (moulds) or budding (yeasts), and also sexually.
Treatment of infections: antibiotics act on bacteria, targeting the peptidoglycan wall or 70S ribosomes, and not on fungi; fungal infections need antifungal drugs.
Similarities: both can be decomposers that digest food outside their cells and absorb it; both have cell walls, a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.
Both groups include pathogens and many useful species. There is more on this in Microorganisms in industry.

Before testing what helps or harms microorganisms, you need to know what counts as growth and how to put a number on it. Most investigations in this subsection measure growth in one of the ways below; the antibacterial test measures the width of a clear zone instead.

Growth of a microbial population means an increase in the number of cells (bacteria and yeasts dividing) or in the size of the mycelium (the mass of thread-like filaments that makes up a mould), not the growth of one cell.

A colony is a visible mass of cells on a solid medium (a jelly-like surface the cells grow on), grown by repeated division from a single cell or spore. Counting colonies therefore estimates how many living cells were on the plate.
Bacterial colonies are usually small, round, shiny or matt spots; mould colonies are fuzzy and spread outwards. This difference in appearance helps you tell which organism has grown.
On plates, count the colonies on each plate if they are separate, or measure the diameter of a mould colony with a ruler under the base of the plate.
Alternatively, estimate the percentage of the plate's surface covered, using a grid of squares drawn on the base. This works when colonies have merged and cannot be counted.
In liquid broth cultures, measure the cloudiness (turbidity) with a colorimeter, an instrument that measures how much light passes through. Cloudier broth has more cells and absorbs more light.
For yeast, count cells with a microscope and a counting chamber (a slide marked with a grid of known volume), or measure the CO₂ produced.
Microorganisms need a source of nutrients (for energy and raw materials), water, a suitable temperature and pH and, for most, oxygen. Each of these is one factor tested later in this subsection.
Harmful chemicals and high external solute concentrations (a lot of dissolved salt or sugar outside the cells) inhibit growth, so these are tested too.
Microorganisms are everywhere: in the air, on skin and on benches. Aseptic technique is how you grow only the organism you chose, without letting it or any contaminant spread.
Aseptic technique is the set of procedures that keep unwanted microorganisms out of cultures, so that only the intended organism grows and results are valid.
Aseptic technique also keeps the cultured microorganisms from escaping onto people and surfaces, for safety.
Any culture may contain or become contaminated with harmful microorganisms, so every culture is treated as a possible pathogen (a microorganism that causes disease).

Before starting: tie back long hair, cover cuts with a waterproof plaster, wash hands with soap and water, and wipe the bench with disinfectant. Each step reduces the microorganisms that could get into the culture or onto you.
Do not eat, drink or touch the face during the practical, because this could carry cultured microorganisms into your mouth or eyes.

Sterilise all equipment and media before use: nutrient agar, broths and glassware are heated in an autoclave (or pressure cooker) at 121 °C for 15 minutes, which kills all microorganisms, including bacterial endospores (tough resting cells that survive ordinary heat).
Plastic Petri dishes (the shallow lidded dishes that hold the agar) are bought pre-sterilised and sealed, because plastic would melt in an autoclave.
Once equipment is sterile, the risk is airborne microorganisms and anything that touches the culture. These bench habits deal with both.
Inoculating loop (a wire loop used to transfer microorganisms): heat it in the hottest part of a Bunsen flame until it glows red-hot, before and after every use, to kill any microorganisms on it.
Let the loop cool for a few seconds, without putting it down, before touching the culture, so that the heat does not kill the microorganisms being transferred.
Work close to a lit Bunsen burner: the rising hot air carries airborne microorganisms upwards and away from the open plates and bottles.
When opening a culture bottle or tube, hold the cap in the little finger and never put it down on the bench, because the bench could contaminate the inside of the cap.
Pass the neck of the bottle briefly through the flame after opening and before closing it, to kill microorganisms at the mouth and create an upward air current.
Open a Petri dish lid only slightly, tilted up like a clam shell, and for as short a time as possible, so that airborne microorganisms do not land on the agar.

After inoculating (putting the microorganism onto the plate), the plate must be closed, labelled, incubated (kept warm to let growth happen) and finally disposed of safely. Each rule here has a reason.
