After inoculating, secure the lid to the base with two or four short strips of sticky tape, not sealed all the way round, so that oxygen can still enter. Sealing the lid fully would make conditions anaerobic (without oxygen), which would favour the growth of harmful anaerobic bacteria.
Label the base, not the lid (which could be swapped), around the edge with name, date and treatment.
Incubate plates upside down, lid at the bottom, so that condensation forming on the lid does not drip onto the agar and spread the colonies, and the agar does not dry out.
Incubate school cultures at about 25 °C, never at 37 °C, because body temperature favours the growth of microorganisms that are pathogenic to humans.

Never open plates after incubation: examine and count colonies through the closed lid. Never culture samples from the human body, toilets or animal waste, because these are likely to contain pathogens.

Disposal: put used plates and cultures into an autoclave bag and autoclave them (121 °C, 15 minutes) before putting them in the bin, or soak them in strong disinfectant. Disinfect the bench again and wash hands thoroughly at the end.
Spills: cover with paper towels soaked in disinfectant, leave for the time stated on the disinfectant, then clear up wearing gloves, and tell the teacher.

Ethanol, used to sterilise a glass spreader, is highly flammable: keep the beaker of ethanol away from the Bunsen flame. Pass the spreader through the flame only briefly, to burn off the ethanol, holding it pointing down.
A culture medium is the food and water the microorganisms grow on or in. Choosing the right one, and a safe organism, is the first step of every investigation.

A culture medium supplies microorganisms with nutrients and water. Nutrient agar contains agar, a jelly extracted from seaweed, which sets solid and which most microorganisms cannot digest, so the surface stays firm while they grow.
Nutrient agar also contains nutrients such as meat or yeast extract and peptone (partly digested protein), giving amino acids, sugars, vitamins and minerals.
Nutrient broth is the same as nutrient agar without the agar, so it is liquid.
Fungi such as yeasts and moulds grow better on malt agar or potato dextrose agar, which are sugar-rich and slightly acidic.
Suitable microorganisms are baker's yeast suspended in sterile water or sugar solution, moulds such as Rhizopus from bread, or non-pathogenic bacterial cultures supplied for schools.
The source of the microorganism must be known, so the risk is low.
A poured plate is a layer of sterile agar in a Petri dish. How you then put the microorganisms on it depends on what you want to see: separate colonies or an even covering.
Pouring a plate, step 1: melt the sterile agar in its bottle in a boiling water bath.
Step 2: cool the agar to about 50 °C, which is still liquid and cool enough not to kill an organism added to it (agar sets as it cools below about 40 °C).
Step 3: flame the neck of the bottle, to kill microorganisms at the mouth.
Step 4: lift the Petri dish lid slightly and pour in enough agar to cover the base (about 15–20 cm³).
Step 5: replace the lid, swirl gently and leave on a level surface to set.
Streaking: draw the flamed, cooled loop, dipped in the culture, across the agar in a zigzag. This thins the cells out along the line, so they form separate colonies.

Spreading: spread a set volume (e.g. 0.1 cm³) of a culture or diluted suspension evenly with a sterile glass spreader to make a lawn (growth covering the whole plate). A lawn is needed for the antibacterial test. There is more on this in the antibacterial and antifungal investigation below.

Diagram: a Petri dish after inoculation, shown upside down in the incubator. Labels: base labelled with name, date and treatment, lid held with two short strips of tape. Beside it, a flamed inoculating loop held in a Bunsen flame.
All six factor investigations below follow one plan: change one thing, keep everything else the same, and compare against controls. Learn this plan once and you can design any of them.

Aim: to investigate how a named factor affects the growth of a named microorganism. Each investigation changes one factor, the independent variable, and measures growth after a fixed time; the dependent variable is colony count, colony diameter, percentage cover or turbidity.

Controlled variables (kept the same so the test is fair): the same microorganism, culture and volume of inoculum (the amount of culture added) on every plate; the same medium and volume of agar; and the same incubation time.
Also controlled, except when it is the factor tested: the same temperature, pH, nutrient level and water availability, and the same method of measuring.

Uninoculated control: an uninoculated plate (sterile medium only) is incubated with the others. No growth on it shows that the medium and technique were sterile, so any growth on the test plates came from the inoculum.
A reference plate with normal conditions (e.g. normal pH, no added salt, or a water disc in the antibacterial test) is compared with the tested conditions, so you can tell what the factor changed.

Replicates: set up at least three plates for each value of the factor and calculate the mean, so that one contaminated or unusual plate does not mislead. Worked example: colony counts of 42, 38 and 46 at 25 °C give a mean of 126 ÷ 3 = 42 colonies.
Record results in a table: value of the factor, growth on each replicate, and the mean. Plot a bar chart for categories or a line graph for a continuous factor, with mean growth on the y-axis.
Conclusion: describe the trend in the mean results and say whether they support the hypothesis. Explain the results using the biology given for each factor, and compare them with secondary data.
Temperature changes how fast the chemical reactions inside cells run. This investigation compares growth at several temperatures, and tests high temperatures by heating the culture before plating.
Hypothesis: “Growth increases with temperature up to an optimum, then decreases.” The optimum is the temperature at which growth is fastest.
Independent variable: temperature, i.e. about 4 °C, 15 °C, 20 °C and 25 °C, plus 40 °C, 60 °C and 80 °C for the heated cultures.
Step 1: inoculate identical plates with the same volume of the same culture, e.g. yeast.
Step 2: incubate sets of three at about 4 °C (refrigerator), 15 °C, 20 °C (room) and 25 °C (incubator) for the same time, e.g. 2–3 days.
Step 3: count the colonies or measure colony diameter.

Step 4: to test high temperatures safely, heat tubes of the culture in water baths at 40 °C, 60 °C and 80 °C (or boil one) for 10 minutes before plating them. Heating the culture first avoids incubating dangerously warm plates.
Step 5: incubate all the plates at 25 °C, so that the only difference between them is the heat treatment.
The results fit a pattern: slow growth when cold, faster when warmer, and death when too hot. The explanation comes from enzymes, the proteins that control the reactions in cells.
Expected result: little or no growth at 4 °C. Growth increases with temperature over the range tested. Cultures heated to about 60 °C or more grow poorly or not at all.
Explanation: growth depends on enzyme-controlled reactions, and at low temperatures molecules move slowly, so reactions and growth are slow.
Cold does not kill the cells: growth resumes when they are warmed, which is why refrigerated food still goes off slowly and frozen food starts to go off when thawed.
Above the optimum, enzymes and other proteins are denatured (their shape is permanently changed so they stop working), so cells die. There is more on this in Investigation: rate of enzyme activity.
Bacterial endospores survive higher temperatures than active cells, so heating that kills the active cells may leave endospores alive.
pH measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is (7 is neutral). This investigation grows bacteria on agar made up at different pH values to find the range they prefer.
Hypothesis: “Bacteria grow best at about neutral pH and poorly in strongly acidic or alkaline conditions.”
Independent variable: the pH of the agar or broth, e.g. 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11.

Step 1: make nutrient agar (or broth) at different pH values, e.g. 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11, by adding buffer solutions (which hold the pH steady) or dilute acid or alkali, checked with a pH meter, before pouring.
Step 2: inoculate each with the same volume of culture.
Step 3: incubate all at the same temperature for the same time.
Bacteria and fungi prefer different pH ranges, and the reason lies in the proteins that run the cell. The same effect is used to preserve food.
Expected result: most bacteria grow best near neutral pH (about pH 6–8) and little in strongly acidic conditions.
Fungi such as yeasts and moulds tolerate, and often grow best in, slightly acidic conditions (about pH 5–6). Repeating the investigation with a fungus and a bacterium shows this difference.
Explanation: pH outside the optimum changes the charges on enzymes and other proteins, so their shape changes and they work slowly or are denatured.
Acid conditions are used to preserve food, e.g. pickling in vinegar, because few microorganisms grow well at low pH.
Yogurt keeps longer because the lactic acid made by its bacteria lowers the pH.
Nutrients are the food a microorganism uses for energy and to build new cells. This investigation compares media with and without nutrients, or with increasing amounts of sugar.
Hypothesis: “Microorganisms grow more when more nutrients are available, until another factor limits growth.”
Independent variable: the nutrient content of the medium, e.g. plain agar compared with nutrient agar, or glucose at 0%, 1%, 2% and 5% for yeast.
Step 1: compare plain agar (agar and water only, no nutrients) with nutrient agar; or use broths (or agar) with increasing concentrations of glucose, e.g. 0%, 1%, 2%, 5%, for yeast.
Step 2: inoculate each with the same volume of yeast culture.
Step 3: incubate all the plates together at the same temperature.
Step 4: measure growth by colony count or percentage cover.
More food means more growth, but only up to a point. The results also show a link forward to the solute investigation, because very high sugar is harmful.
Expected result: little or no growth on plain agar, because there is nothing for the cells to use.
Growth increases with nutrient concentration and then levels off, as another factor, such as space or the build-up of wastes, becomes limiting (the one that stops growth rising further).
At very high sugar concentrations, growth falls again. There is more on this in Investigation: effect of external solute concentration.
Explanation: nutrients supply the energy, released by respiration of sugars, and the raw materials for new cells, i.e. sugars, amino acids, minerals such as nitrate and phosphate, and vitamins.
Variation: starch agar shows that only microorganisms that secrete amylase (the enzyme that digests starch) can use starch.
Flooding the plate with iodine after incubation leaves a clear zone around such colonies, where the starch has been digested. The rest of the plate turns dark because iodine stains starch.
This investigation uses bread and mould instead of agar plates. It tests whether mould needs moisture by comparing dried bread with moistened bread.
Hypothesis: “Moulds grow only on food that is moist.”
Independent variable: the water content of the bread, dried compared with moistened.
Step 1: take slices of the same bread (without preservatives, which would inhibit growth); dry some fully in an oven at a low temperature and moisten others with the same volume of sterile water.
Step 2: expose each slice to the air of the same room for the same time, e.g. 30 minutes, so that mould spores land on it.
Step 3: seal each in a clear plastic bag or sealed dish and label it.
Step 4: keep all in the same warm, dark place, about 25 °C, for 5–7 days.
Step 5: estimate the percentage cover of mould on each, using a transparent grid of squares held over the bag, e.g. 37 of 100 squares covered = 37%.
Do not open the bags, because the spores released could be breathed in.
Water is essential for life, and microorganisms are no exception. The result explains why drying is an old way of keeping food.
Expected result: mould grows on the moist bread and not, or very little, on the dried bread.

Explanation: microorganisms need water because their enzymes work only in solution, nutrients are absorbed in solution after extracellular digestion (digestion outside the cell), and water is needed for cells to grow and divide.
Dried foods, e.g. dried fruit, pasta, powdered milk and cereals, keep for a long time for this reason.
Safety: mould spores can trigger allergies and asthma, so keep the bags sealed throughout and dispose of them unopened.
A solute is something dissolved in water, such as salt or sugar. This investigation adds increasing amounts of solute to the agar to see what happens to growth.
Hypothesis: “Growth decreases as the concentration of salt (or sugar) outside the cells increases.”
Independent variable: the concentration of sodium chloride (salt), e.g. 0%, 2%, 5%, 10% or 20%, or of sucrose (sugar).
Step 1: make nutrient agar containing increasing concentrations of sodium chloride (e.g. 0%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%) or of sucrose.
Step 2: inoculate each with the same volume of bacterial culture.
Step 3: incubate all the plates together for the same time.
Step 4: measure growth by colony count or colony diameter.
Salt and sugar slow growth because of what they do to water movement across the cell surface. This is the basis of salting and sugaring food.
Expected result: growth decreases as the solute concentration rises, with little or no growth at the highest concentrations.

Explanation: when the solution outside a cell has a higher solute concentration, and so lower water concentration, than the cytoplasm, water leaves the cell by osmosis (the movement of water across a membrane towards the more concentrated solution).
The cell then loses water, its enzymes cannot work, and it stops growing or dies.
In a very dilute solution water enters the cell, but the bacterial or fungal cell wall stops the cell bursting.
This is the basis of preserving food with salt (salted fish and bacon) and sugar (jam). There is more on this in Osmosis in food preservation and plant health.
Some chemicals stop microorganisms growing. Knowing which type acts on which group, and what the investigation sets out to show, comes before the method.

Antibacterial chemicals kill bacteria or stop them growing: antibiotics (e.g. penicillin, streptomycin), antiseptics (used on living tissue, e.g. on skin) and disinfectants (used on surfaces and objects).
Antifungal chemicals, e.g. the antifungal creams used for athlete's foot, or fungicides, act on fungi.
Antibiotics do not affect fungi, and antifungals generally do not affect bacteria, because the two groups have different structures. There is more on this in Bacteria and fungi.
Hypothesis: “Different antiseptics (or antibiotics) inhibit the growth of a bacterium to different extents.”
Independent variable: the antibacterial or antifungal chemical on each disc; dependent variable: the diameter of the clear zone around the disc.
In the disc diffusion method, paper discs soaked in chemicals are placed on a lawn of bacteria. Wherever the chemical stops growth, a clear zone appears around the disc.
Step 1: spread a set volume of the culture evenly over a nutrient agar plate with a sterile spreader, to make a lawn.

Step 2: using sterile forceps (flamed and cooled), dip paper discs of the same size (e.g. 6 mm, cut with a hole punch and sterilised) in each chemical for the same time, drain them, and place them on the lawn, well spaced.
Step 3: include a control disc dipped in sterile distilled water. Ready-made antibiotic discs, or a multi-disc with several antibiotics on one ring, can be used instead.
Step 4: tape and label the plate.
Step 5: incubate upside down at about 25 °C for 2–3 days.
Step 6: measure the diameter of the clear zone around each disc with a ruler on the base of the plate.

For an antifungal chemical, make a lawn of yeast on malt agar and use discs of the antifungal, with a water control and, to show the difference in antibacterial and antifungal action, an antibiotic disc.
Diagram: a lawn plate with four discs. Labels: each disc's chemical, clear zones of inhibition of different sizes, and no zone around the water control.
The clear zones are the result. Their size tells you how well each chemical works, and the way they form explains why.
Expected result: a clear zone, the zone of inhibition, forms around discs whose chemical stops the bacterium growing.
There is no clear zone around the water control, which shows that the disc and the water alone do not stop growth.
The larger the zone, the more effective the chemical is against that organism at that concentration. In other words, the bacterium is more sensitive to it.
On the yeast lawn, the antifungal gives a clear zone and the antibiotic gives none.
The chemical diffuses outwards from the disc into the agar, so its concentration falls with distance; bacteria cannot grow where the concentration is high enough to kill or inhibit them.
A zone's size also depends on how fast the chemical diffuses, so it is a guide to strength, not an exact measure.
A bacterium that grows right up to an antibiotic disc is resistant to that antibiotic.
In hospitals the same test is used to find which antibiotic will work against the bacterium from a patient. There is more on this in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.
Comparing zone areas, not just diameters, is fairer. Here is the calculation for a clear zone of diameter 18 mm around a 6 mm disc.
Radius = 9 mm; area of the zone = π r² = 3.14 × 9 × 9 ≈ 254 mm².
Subtracting the disc (radius 3 mm, area ≈ 28 mm²) gives a clear area of about 226 mm², which is the area where bacteria were actually stopped from growing.
Areas let zones be compared fairly, because doubling the diameter quadruples the area.
Your own results are primary data. A good conclusion also checks them against data collected by other people.
Secondary data are results collected by others, e.g. other class groups, textbooks, published research or food-safety guidance.
Conclusions must be supported by both primary and secondary data: compare your own results with the class's pooled results and with published findings.
Published findings include that most human pathogens grow best near body temperature and neutral pH, and that most bacteria grow little below refrigerator temperature.
Each factor you investigated is used to keep food safe. Preserving food means stopping microorganisms growing, either by killing them or by making conditions unsuitable.
Temperature: refrigeration and freezing slow or stop growth but do not kill microorganisms.
Heat: pasteurisation, heating milk briefly to a temperature below boiling and then cooling it quickly, kills most microorganisms.
Sterilisation: canning and ultra-heat treatment (UHT) heat food enough to sterilise it, and sealing keeps microorganisms out.
Water: drying removes water, which microorganisms need for their enzymes to work.
Solute: salting and sugaring use high solute concentration, which draws water out of microbial cells.
The remaining factors give further preservation methods and wider uses in hygiene and in industry.
Oxygen: vacuum packing removes oxygen, slowing aerobic microorganisms (those that need oxygen to grow).
Health and hygiene: antiseptics on wounds and skin, disinfectants on surfaces, and aseptic technique in surgery. There is more on this in Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment.
Industry: bioreactors (vessels in which microorganisms are grown on a large scale) are kept at the optimum conditions found by such investigations to maximise growth.
Every fault below can make results unreliable. Each has a simple fix, so learn each error together with its fix.
Contamination by airborne or skin microorganisms gives colonies of a different appearance; check with the uninoculated control, and repeat with better aseptic technique.
Unequal inoculum, i.e. different volumes or numbers of cells, on different plates; use a measured volume from a well-mixed culture.
Colonies that grow together cannot be counted; dilute the culture so that colonies are separate, or measure percentage cover instead.
Agar or broth that is not at the intended pH or concentration; check with a pH meter and measure accurately.
Temperature not constant, e.g. the “room temperature” plates are near a radiator.
Discs not equally soaked, or chemicals not of known concentration; soak all discs for the same time.
Too few replicates; use at least three and calculate means.

Industry needs living things that work fast, cheaply and in a controlled space. Microorganisms (bacteria, yeasts and other fungi, and microscopic organisms such as protists) fit that need, for the reasons below.
Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their parts, such as cells and enzymes, to make useful products or provide services.
Microorganisms are the most used organisms in biotechnology, for the six reasons that follow.
They reproduce very rapidly: some bacteria divide every 20 minutes in ideal conditions, so large amounts of product are made quickly.
They can be grown on cheap nutrients, including waste materials from other industries, such as whey from cheese-making and molasses (the dark syrup left over) from sugar refining.
They can be grown in any climate or season, in a controlled vessel that takes little space, so production does not depend on the weather or on farmland.
They carry out a huge range of chemical reactions at low temperatures and normal pressure, which saves energy compared with chemical manufacture.
They are easy to modify genetically, so they can be made to produce human proteins. There is more on this in Genetic engineering.
Many secrete their products into the medium (the liquid they grow in), which makes the products easier to collect.
What a company gets out of a microorganism falls into three groups. Being able to say which group an example belongs to makes it easy to give a named example in an answer.
The cells themselves are the product, for example yeast for baking and mycoprotein (protein from a fungus) for food.
Substances the cells make are the product, for example ethanol, antibiotics, enzymes and insulin.
Changes the cells make to a material are the product, for example milk turned to yogurt, slurry (animal waste) turned to biogas, and sewage treatment.

To get useful amounts of product, microorganisms are grown in a purpose-built vessel where every condition can be controlled. The first half of the design is the vessel itself and how food, oxygen and mixing reach the cells.

A bioreactor, or fermenter, is a vessel in which microorganisms, cells or enzymes are grown or used on a large scale under carefully controlled conditions to make a product. There is more on enzyme bioreactors in Industrial enzymes.
The vessel is made of stainless steel because it is strong, does not corrode, and is easy to sterilise with steam.
Inlets allow sterile nutrient medium and the inoculum, a pure starter culture of the microorganism, to enter the vessel.

A sterile air supply is bubbled in at the bottom through a sparger (a device that breaks the air into fine bubbles), giving oxygen to aerobic microorganisms. The air is filtered so that no contaminating microorganisms enter.
A motor-driven stirrer (impeller) keeps the cells, nutrients and oxygen evenly mixed, so no cell is starved, and it spreads heat evenly.

A water jacket, or cooling coils, with cold water flowing through it removes the heat released by the microorganisms' respiration, keeping the temperature at the optimum (the best temperature for growth).

The second half of the design keeps conditions steady while the culture grows and lets the product out. A computer watches the sensors, so the conditions stay at the optimum without constant manual checking.
Probes monitor temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen and foam level, and are linked to a computer.
Inlets for acid or alkali correct the pH when the probes show it drifting from the optimum.
A gas outlet releases CO₂ (made by the cells' respiration) and excess air.
An outlet at the base, the harvest tap, removes the culture and product.

Diagram: a labelled bioreactor showing the vessel, nutrient and inoculum inlets, sterile air inlet and sparger, stirrer and motor, water jacket with cold water in and warm water out, temperature, pH and oxygen probes, acid/alkali inlet, gas outlet and harvest outlet.
A bioreactor must contain only the chosen microorganism, and once the product is made it still has to be separated and purified before it can be used.
Before use, the vessel, pipes and medium are sterilised with steam, so that no contaminating microorganisms compete with the culture, use up nutrients or spoil the product.
This is aseptic technique (working so that unwanted microorganisms are kept out) on an industrial scale.

Downstream processing is everything done after the product is made: it is separated from the cells and medium by filtering or centrifuging (spinning at high speed), then purified, concentrated and packaged.
If the product is inside the cells, the cells are first broken open so that it can be released.
The pharmaceutical industry makes medicines, and microorganisms are the source of many of them. Antibiotics are the first example to learn.
Antibiotics are chemicals made by microorganisms that kill or inhibit bacteria. They do not work on viruses.
Penicillin is made by the fungus Penicillium, not a bacterium. Alexander Fleming discovered its effect in 1928, and Howard Florey and Ernst Chain purified it and showed it cured infections from 1940.
Penicillium is now grown in bioreactors, using strains selected and mutated to give far more penicillin than the original, which makes large-scale production possible.
Streptomycin, tetracycline and many other antibiotics are made by soil bacteria of the genus Streptomyces.
Genetic engineering lets bacteria and yeast make human medicines that once had to be taken from other sources. Vaccines also depend on microorganisms grown in culture.
The gene for human insulin is inserted into bacteria (E. coli) or yeast, which are grown in bioreactors. The insulin is then extracted and purified.
Human insulin was the first genetically engineered medicine approved for use, in 1982.
Before that, people with diabetes injected insulin extracted from the pancreases of pigs and cattle, which was in shorter supply and caused allergic reactions in some people.
Human growth hormone, for children who make too little, is made by genetically modified bacteria.
The hepatitis B vaccine is made by genetically modified yeast, which produces a hepatitis B virus surface protein (the antigen, the part the immune system learns to recognise) without the virus.
Other vaccines contain killed or weakened microorganisms grown in culture. There is more on this in Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment.
In hospitals and clinics, microorganisms and the enzymes and toxins they make are used to diagnose disease and to treat it.
Diagnosis: the enzyme glucose oxidase, made by the fungus Aspergillus niger, is used in the test strips with which people with diabetes measure their blood glucose.

Diagnosis: Taq polymerase, a heat-stable enzyme from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus, which lives in hot springs, is used in PCR (a method that copies DNA) because it is not destroyed by the high temperatures PCR needs.
PCR detects pathogens, for example in COVID-19 tests, and is used in DNA profiling.

Treatment: faecal microbiota transplant, in which gut microorganisms from a healthy donor are placed in a patient's gut, is used to treat repeated infections with the bacterium Clostridioides difficile that antibiotics have failed to clear.
Treatment: probiotics, live microorganisms taken as food or supplements, are used to try to restore gut microorganisms after antibiotics; the evidence is mixed.
Treatment: the toxin of the bacterium Clostridium botulinum, in tiny purified doses (botulinum toxin, Botox), relaxes overactive muscles and is used to treat some muscle spasms and other conditions.
Medicines and vaccines are made in the pharmaceutical industry, so the medical uses here are those in diagnosis and treatment in hospitals and clinics. The two headings overlap.
Soil microorganisms can feed crops, protect them from insects and even carry new genes into them. Each use cuts the need for chemicals or improves the crop.

Nitrogen fixation (turning nitrogen gas from the air into a form plants can use): seeds of legumes such as clover, peas and beans can be coated with nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) before sowing.
The crop then forms root nodules and needs less nitrogen fertiliser. This is mutualism, a partnership in which both organisms benefit.

Biological pest control: the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) makes a protein that is toxic to the larvae of certain insects, for example caterpillars, but harmless to humans and most other animals.
Bt is sprayed on crops as a biopesticide (a pesticide made from a living organism).
The Bt toxin gene has been put into some genetically modified crops, for example Bt maize, which then make their own insecticide.
Genetic modification of plants: the soil bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens naturally transfers part of a plasmid (a small ring of DNA) into plant cells.
Biotechnologists use Agrobacterium as a vector (a carrier) to insert useful genes into crop plants.
Farms produce large amounts of plant and animal waste. Microorganisms turn these into winter feed, energy and soil improver.
Silage: grass stored airtight, in a pit covered with plastic or in wrapped bales, is fermented by lactic acid bacteria, which convert its sugars to lactic acid.
The low pH stops other microorganisms rotting the silage, so it keeps as winter feed for cattle and sheep. Silage-making is widespread on Irish farms.
Anaerobic digestion: animal slurry, food waste and crop waste are broken down by microorganisms in sealed tanks without oxygen.

Methane-producing microorganisms (archaea, a group of single-celled organisms) produce biogas, which is mainly methane and is burned for heat or electricity. The remaining digestate is spread as fertiliser.
Composting: aerobic decomposition (breakdown using oxygen) of plant waste by bacteria and fungi produces compost, which returns humus and minerals to soil.
Yeast is a fungus that ferments sugar, which means it breaks it down without oxygen to make ethanol and CO₂. Bakers and brewers use the two products for different purposes.
Bread: baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) ferments sugars in dough, producing CO₂, which makes the dough rise.
The ethanol made in the dough evaporates during baking.
Beer and wine: yeast ferments the sugars in malted barley (beer) or grape juice (wine) to ethanol and CO₂, under anaerobic conditions (without oxygen).
Lactic acid bacteria ferment the sugar in milk to lactic acid. The acid changes the milk's texture and taste, and it also helps to keep the food from spoiling.
Yogurt: milk is pasteurised (heated to kill unwanted microorganisms), cooled and inoculated with lactic acid bacteria, for example Lactobacillus and Streptococcus species.
The inoculated milk is incubated warm, at about 40–45 °C, for several hours, which is the temperature range that suits these bacteria.
The bacteria ferment lactose (the sugar in milk) to lactic acid, which lowers the pH, making the milk proteins thicken and giving the sour taste.
The low pH also preserves the yogurt, because few spoilage microorganisms grow in acid.
Cheese: lactic acid bacteria sour the milk, and rennet clots it into curds (the solid part of milk). Rennet, or chymosin, is now mostly made by genetically modified microorganisms.
Bacteria and moulds ripen the cheese and develop its flavour; the blue veins of blue cheeses are the mould Penicillium roqueforti.
Microorganisms are grown as food themselves, and they also make flavourings and preservatives.
Mycoprotein: the fungus Fusarium venenatum is grown in large continuous fermenters (vessels fed continuously) on glucose and mineral salts.
Its hyphae (the thread-like cells of a fungus) are harvested, heated and pressed to make mycoprotein, sold as Quorn, a high-protein, high-fibre, low-fat meat substitute.
Vinegar is made when bacteria (Acetobacter) oxidise the ethanol in wine, cider or beer to acetic (ethanoic) acid.
Soy sauce is made by fermenting soya beans and wheat with the mould Aspergillus oryzae.
Citric acid, a flavouring and preservative in soft drinks, is made by the mould Aspergillus niger.
Microorganisms are also used outside medicine and food, wherever waste has to be broken down or a fuel made.

Sewage treatment: in the secondary stage, aerobic bacteria and protists in aerated tanks (activated sludge) feed on the organic matter in sewage, so the water can be returned to rivers without causing oxygen depletion. The sludge can be anaerobically digested to biogas.
Bioremediation (using living organisms to clean up pollution): microorganisms that break down pollutants, for example bacteria that digest oil, are used to clean up oil spills and contaminated land.
Biofuels: yeast ferments sugars from crops, for example sugar cane or maize, to ethanol, which is blended with petrol. There is more on this in Climate change and biological strategies.
When you are asked to discuss importance, give benefits and limits side by side. In health, microorganisms have transformed treatment, but they have also created a serious problem.
For: antibiotics have made most bacterial infections curable and have made surgery much safer.
For: insulin, vaccines and other medicines from microorganisms are cheap, pure and available in large amounts.
For: human insulin from microorganisms avoids reliance on animal pancreases and the reactions some people had to animal insulin.

Against: overuse of antibiotics in medicine and in farm animals has selected for resistant bacteria, so some antibiotics no longer work. There is more on this in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.
Against: new antibiotics are expensive and slow to develop, so resistant bacteria cannot easily be replaced with new treatments.
Microorganisms help farmers and food producers, but the genetic technology involved raises concerns for some people.
For: fermentation preserves food and creates many foods.
For: mycoprotein and other microbial protein need far less land and water than livestock.
For: biopesticides and Rhizobium inoculants reduce the use of chemical pesticides and fertilisers, and silage gives winter feed.
Against: genetically modified microorganisms and crops raise concerns about safety, the environment and who controls the technology. There is more on this in Ethics of genetic technologies.
Against: insects can evolve resistance to the Bt toxin, and some people object to GM (genetically modified) ingredients.
Microorganisms can reduce pollution and energy use, but running them at industrial scale has costs of its own.
For: microorganisms turn wastes, such as whey, slurry, sewage and food waste, into useful products, reducing pollution.
For: biogas and bioethanol are renewable energy, and biological processes run at low temperatures, using less energy than chemical manufacture.
For: biotechnology and pharmaceutical manufacturing are major employers and exporters in Ireland.
Against: bioreactors need sterile conditions, energy for stirring and cooling, and careful disposal of waste culture.
Against: contamination of a batch can waste the whole product, and growing crops for biofuel uses land that could grow food.
A good discussion ends with a judgement. It weighs the benefits against the limits and gives a conclusion that depends on a stated condition.

On balance, microorganisms are essential to modern medicine, food production and waste treatment, and their importance is growing as biotechnology replaces fossil-fuel-based chemical processes. There is more on this in The cross-cutting themes, on health, sustainability and technology.
This judgement holds provided that antibiotic use and genetic modification are regulated, because the main limits are antibiotic resistance and the concerns about GM organisms.

When microorganisms are put into fresh medium, their numbers do not rise steadily. A growth curve records what actually happens over time, and the shape of the curve is the key to getting the best yield of a product.

A growth curve shows how the number of living cells in a population of microorganisms changes over time when they are grown in a closed system: a fixed volume of medium, with no nutrients added and no wastes removed (batch culture).

The number of cells is usually plotted as a logarithm, log₁₀ of the number of cells, because numbers rise from thousands to billions; on a log scale the exponential phase (the steep rise) is a straight line.
Diagram: a growth curve with log number of living cells on the y-axis and time on the x-axis, with the five phases labelled in order: lag, log (exponential), stationary, decline (death) and survival.
The curve begins with a pause and then a rapid rise. These two phases show what the cells need to get started and how fast they can grow when conditions are ideal.
Lag phase: little or no increase in cell number.
During the lag phase the cells adjust to the new medium: they take in water and nutrients, switch on genes, make the enzymes needed to use the nutrients present, and grow in size before dividing.
The lag phase is longer if the new conditions differ greatly from those the cells came from.
Log (exponential) phase: the cells divide at their maximum rate, as nutrients are plentiful and wastes are low.
The number doubles in each generation time (the time for a population to double), for example every 20–30 minutes, so the population grows exponentially.
This is when the cells grow fastest and make most of the products linked to growth, the primary metabolites. Primary metabolites include ethanol made by yeast and the cells themselves as mycoprotein.
Growth cannot go on for ever in a closed system. As nutrients run out and waste builds up, the curve levels off, falls, and then flattens at a low level.
Stationary phase: the rate of cell division equals the rate of cell death, so the number of living cells stays constant. Cells are still dividing and dying; the population has not simply stopped.
The stationary phase is caused by nutrients running out, toxic waste products such as acids and ethanol building up, oxygen possibly running short, and changes in pH.
Many microorganisms make secondary metabolites, such as antibiotics, in this phase; some bacteria form endospores (tough resting cells that resist harsh conditions).
Decline (death) phase: the death rate is greater than the rate of division, so the number of living cells falls, because nutrients are exhausted and wastes are at toxic levels.
Dead cells may break open in the decline phase.
Survival phase: a small number of cells survive for a long time, with the number falling only slowly or levelling off.
Cells survive the survival phase by forming endospores (in some bacteria), by becoming inactive, or by using nutrients released from dead cells that have broken open.
Because the log phase is exponential, the number of cells can be worked out from the number of generations. The same idea works backwards to find the generation time.
Number of cells after n generations of the log phase = starting number × 2ⁿ.
Worked example: one bacterium dividing every 20 minutes, for 2 hours: n = 120 ÷ 20 = 6 generations; number = 1 × 2⁶ = 64 cells.
Worked example: with 1000 starting cells and a generation time of 30 minutes, after 3 hours: n = 6, number = 1000 × 64 = 64 000.
Working out generation time from a graph or table: in the log phase the number rose from 1 × 10⁴ to 8 × 10⁴ cells in 90 minutes.
8 = 2³, so there were 3 generations in 90 minutes; generation time = 90 ÷ 3 = 30 minutes.
Reading a log-scale graph: each step of 1 on a log₁₀ axis is a tenfold increase, for example from log 4 = 10 000 cells to log 5 = 100 000 cells.
Industry can run a bioreactor in two ways. In batch culture the culture goes through every phase of the growth curve and is then harvested all at once.
Batch culture: the bioreactor is filled with a fixed amount of sterile medium, inoculated, and left to grow for a set time, with temperature, pH and oxygen controlled.
In batch culture nothing is added except air, acid or alkali, and nothing is removed until the end, when the whole contents are harvested.
The vessel is then emptied, cleaned and sterilised for the next batch, and the population passes through the lag, log and stationary phases.
Advantages: it is simpler to set up and control, and if a batch is contaminated only that batch is lost; it is best for products made in the stationary phase.
Disadvantages: the vessel is idle while being emptied, cleaned and refilled, and for much of each run the cells are not in the log phase, so output per vessel is lower.
Metabolites are the substances cells make. Which phase of the growth curve gives the most product depends on the kind of metabolite wanted.
Primary metabolites are substances the cells make as part of normal growth, mostly in the log phase, for example ethanol by yeast, amino acids, enzymes, and the cells themselves as mycoprotein.
Secondary metabolites are not needed for growth and are made mainly in the stationary phase, for example the antibiotic penicillin.
Continuous culture avoids the stop-and-start of batch culture by feeding the vessel and draining it at the same time. This holds the cells at their fastest-growing stage.
Continuous culture: fresh sterile nutrient medium is added continuously, and culture (cells, medium and product) is removed at the same rate, so the volume stays constant.
Nutrients never run out and wastes do not build up, so the population is held in the log phase for weeks. In continuous culture the population does not reach the stationary phase.
Advantages: high output from a smaller vessel, no idle time between batches, and a steady, uniform product.
Disadvantages: it is harder to control; if contamination enters, a long run is lost; mutations can arise over many generations; and it suits only products made during growth, for example mycoprotein.
Knowing the phases of the growth curve lets a producer take steps to get more product from each run. Each step matches one phase of the curve.

Shorten the lag phase by inoculating with a large volume of actively growing cells taken from the log phase of a culture grown in the same medium and at the same temperature, so the cells do not need to adjust.

Keep the log phase going as long as possible by holding temperature, pH and oxygen at the optimum with the probes, and by supplying fresh nutrients and removing wastes (continuous culture, for primary metabolites).

Harvest at the right phase: primary metabolites at the end of the log phase or continuously, and secondary metabolites, for example penicillin, in batch culture during the stationary phase, before the decline phase reduces yield.
Delay the stationary and decline phases by removing toxic products, for example ethanol, or by adding nutrients gradually (fed-batch culture, a batch to which nutrients are added during the run).
Your body, and every patch of soil, is home to huge numbers of tiny organisms that live together rather than alone. Biologists treat that whole community as one thing, called a microbiome.

A microbiome is the whole community of microorganisms (bacteria, archaea, fungi, protists and viruses) living together in a particular environment, such as the human gut, the skin or the soil. It is a community of many kinds, not a single species and not just bacteria.
A microbiome also includes the genes of these microorganisms and the products they make.
The organisms themselves are often called the microbiota; many people use the two words for the same thing, so don't be thrown if a question uses either.
A microbiome is an ecological community (different species living and interacting in one place): its members compete, feed on each other's products and interact with their host or surroundings.
The make-up of a microbiome changes with conditions such as food, pH, oxygen, temperature and water, because each species thrives only in certain conditions.
A diverse microbiome, with many species, is generally more stable and recovers better after a disturbance, because if one species is lost others can often do its job.

Most microorganisms are not pathogens (disease-causing): the majority in a healthy microbiome are harmless (commensals, which gain without harming the host) or beneficial (mutualists, where both sides gain). There is more on this in Biotic factors and relationships.
A microbiome is hard to study because you can't simply grow its members in a dish. Scientists read the DNA of the whole community at once instead.
Most of these microorganisms cannot be grown on agar (the jelly used to culture microbes in the laboratory), so culturing would miss most of the community.
Microbiomes are therefore studied mainly by extracting all the DNA from a sample, e.g. faeces or soil.
The extracted DNA is sequenced to identify which organisms and genes are present, so the community can be described without growing any of it. There is more on this in DNA sequencing.
Humans are not microbe-free. Several parts of the body carry their own microbiomes, and the biggest by far is in the gut.
Humans carry microbiomes in the gut, mouth, nose, skin and vagina.

The largest is in the gut, and most of the gut's microorganisms live in the large intestine (colon), where food moves slowly and there is almost no oxygen, so most are anaerobic bacteria (bacteria that live without oxygen).
A 2016 estimate found that the body contains about as many bacterial cells (about 38 trillion) as human cells (about 30 trillion), a ratio of roughly 1 : 1.
The older, often-quoted figure of ten bacteria for every human cell is now thought to be an overestimate.
The gut contains hundreds of species, and each person's combination is different.
A baby starts life with almost no microbiome and builds one from its first contacts. How it is born and fed shapes which microorganisms arrive first.
A baby's gut is colonised (first settled by microorganisms) at birth and soon after.
Babies born vaginally pick up microorganisms from the mother's vagina and gut.
Babies born by caesarean section are first colonised mostly by skin and hospital microorganisms, so their early gut microbiome is different.
Breast milk contains sugars (oligosaccharides) that the baby cannot digest but that feed beneficial gut bacteria such as Bifidobacterium.
The microbiome changes with diet, weaning (the switch from milk to solid food), antibiotics, environment (e.g. pets, farm animals, siblings) and age, becoming more stable in childhood.
The host provides a warm, moist, food-rich, stable home, and the microorganisms provide digestion, vitamins and protection.
This mutualism (a relationship in which both partners benefit) is an example of how organisms depend on each other.
Humans can't digest everything they eat, but gut bacteria can. They turn part of our undigested food into useful products.
Human enzymes cannot digest dietary fibre, e.g. cellulose and other plant cell-wall polysaccharides, and resistant starch, so it reaches the large intestine undigested.
There, gut bacteria ferment the fibre anaerobically (break it down without oxygen), using their own enzymes.
The main products of fermentation are short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): acetate, propionate and butyrate.
The colon absorbs the SCFAs: butyrate is the main energy source of the cells lining the colon, which keeps the lining healthy.
The other SCFAs are carried to the liver and body cells and used for energy.
Gases, namely CO₂, hydrogen and, in some people, methane made by archaea, are by-products of fermentation.
Fermentation is not the only service gut bacteria provide. They also make vitamins and handle substances our own enzymes can't.
Gut bacteria make vitamin K, needed for blood clotting, and some B vitamins, part of which the body absorbs.
Gut bacteria also break down some substances that human enzymes cannot, e.g. some plant chemicals and some drugs.
Gut bacteria convert bile salts (made by the liver to help digest fats), which affects how fats are absorbed.
Herbivores depend even more on their microbiome: cattle, sheep and rabbits rely on microorganisms to digest cellulose, which their own enzymes cannot do.
The large intestine, where most of this happens, also absorbs water from the remaining food. There is more on this in The Digestive System.
A gut full of harmless bacteria leaves little room for invaders. This crowding-out effect protects the host and is called colonisation resistance.
Protection against pathogens is called colonisation resistance: the normal gut microbiota occupy the space and attachment sites on the gut lining and use up the nutrients that pathogens would need.
Some gut microorganisms make acids that lower the pH, and some make antibacterial proteins (bacteriocins) that kill competing bacteria.
The skin and vaginal microbiota protect in the same way.
In the vagina, Lactobacillus bacteria make lactic acid, keeping the pH low, which stops many pathogens growing. There is more on this in Innate and adaptive immunity.
Colonisation resistance only works while the normal bacteria are present. If they are wiped out, harmful microorganisms can move in.
When antibiotics kill many normal gut bacteria, pathogens can take over: e.g. the bacterium Clostridioides difficile can multiply and cause severe diarrhoea.
The yeast Candida can also overgrow when the normal microbiota are reduced, causing thrush. There is more on this in Pathogens.
Repeated C. difficile infection can be treated by faecal microbiota transplant, which restores a healthy microbiome from a donor.
The gut microbiome also talks to the immune system. Chemical signals from the microorganisms help the body learn what to attack and what to ignore.
The gut wall contains a large part of the body's immune tissue, so the microorganisms are in constant contact with immune cells.
Molecules from gut microorganisms, e.g. parts of their cell walls and SCFAs such as butyrate, are detected by immune cells in the gut lining, which then send signals.
In early life these signals 'train' the immune system to tolerate harmless microorganisms and food while still responding to pathogens.
E.g. butyrate promotes suppressor T cells (also called regulatory T cells), which damp down inflammation. There is more on this in White blood cells.
The microbiome also helps keep the gut wall intact. Evidence for its role in immunity is real, but much of it shows links rather than proof of cause.
The microbiome helps maintain the gut barrier: it stimulates the lining to make mucus and keeps its cells tightly joined.
This stops bacteria and their products leaking into the blood and triggering inflammation.
Germ-free mice, raised completely free of microorganisms, have poorly developed gut immune tissue, which suggests the microbiome is needed for normal immune development.

A less diverse or altered gut microbiome has been linked to inflammatory bowel disease, allergies, asthma and some autoimmune diseases (where the immune system attacks the body's own cells), which fits the hygiene hypothesis. There is more on this in Emerging diseases and society.
These links are mostly correlations: it is often not known whether the altered microbiome causes the disease or results from it.
Metabolic health is about how the body handles energy. The gut microbiome influences it in three main ways.
Metabolic health means healthy body mass, blood glucose, blood fats and blood pressure, without obesity or type 2 diabetes.
First, it affects how much energy is extracted from food: more efficient fermentation of fibre releases more energy as SCFAs.
Second, signals from SCFAs affect appetite hormones and how the body stores fat and controls blood glucose.

Third, inflammation from a leaky gut barrier (one that lets bacteria and their products into the blood) is linked to insulin resistance, where cells respond poorly to insulin and blood glucose stays high.
Animal experiments suggest the microbiome can affect body fat, but human evidence is weaker. Diet is a major factor in shaping the microbiome itself.
In a 2006 study, germ-free mice given gut microorganisms from obese mice gained more body fat than germ-free mice given microorganisms from lean mice, on the same diet.
This shows the microbiome can affect fat storage, at least in mice, because diet was the same in both groups.
In humans, people with obesity or type 2 diabetes often have a less diverse gut microbiome, but this is a correlation, partly explained by differences in diet.
A diet high in varied fibre from vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains feeds fibre-fermenting bacteria and is linked to a more diverse microbiome and more SCFAs.
A diet high in sugar, fat and processed food and low in fibre is linked to lower diversity.
A healthy microbiome is balanced, and that balance can be lost. Some everyday habits protect it.
Dysbiosis is an imbalance in the microbiome, e.g. a loss of diversity or of beneficial species, or overgrowth of harmful ones.
Causes of dysbiosis include antibiotics, which kill beneficial as well as harmful bacteria, a low-fibre diet, infection, stress and some medicines.
Eat plenty of varied fibre to promote a healthy gut microbiome, because fibre feeds the fermenting bacteria.
Eat fermented foods containing live microorganisms, e.g. live yogurt or kefir.
Take antibiotics only when needed and complete the course as prescribed; this also reduces antibiotic resistance. There is more on this in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.
Two similar-sounding words describe two different ways of supporting gut bacteria: adding live microorganisms, or feeding the ones already there.
Probiotics are live microorganisms taken in food or supplements, e.g. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species, to benefit health.
Prebiotics are food components that humans cannot digest but that feed beneficial gut bacteria, e.g. some fibres in onions, garlic, leeks, bananas and oats.
Evidence that probiotics help is good for some conditions, e.g. reducing diarrhoea caused by antibiotics, but weak or mixed for many claims.
Most probiotics do not permanently change the microbiome.
A gram of fertile soil holds hundreds of millions to billions of bacteria, so its microorganisms cycle many nutrients, and carbon is the first example.
A single gram of fertile soil can contain hundreds of millions to billions of bacteria, many metres of fungal hyphae (thread-like fungal filaments) and thousands of species.
Together these microorganisms cycle many nutrients, not just one.
Carbon: bacteria and fungi decompose dead plants, animals and dung, respiring the organic carbon and releasing CO₂.
Part of the dead matter is turned into stable humus, which stores carbon in the soil for many years. There is more on this in The carbon cycle.
Fungi are the main decomposers of wood and of the tough lignin and cellulose of dead plants.
Plants need nitrogen in a form they can absorb, and soil microorganisms supply it at several steps.
Decomposers release ammonium from proteins in dead matter.
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, both free-living and in legume root nodules, add nitrogen from the air.
Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate, the main form plants absorb.
Denitrifying bacteria in waterlogged soils convert nitrate back to nitrogen gas, and some nitrous oxide, N₂O, is released. There is more on this in The nitrogen cycle.
Soil microorganisms also free up phosphorus and sulfur for plants, and they control whether soil gives off or takes up methane.
Phosphorus: some soil bacteria and fungi release phosphate from organic matter and from insoluble minerals.
Mycorrhizal fungi (fungi living in partnership with plant roots) carry phosphate and water to plant roots in exchange for sugars. There is more on this in Biotic factors and relationships.
Sulfur: decomposers release sulfur from proteins as sulfate, which plants absorb.
Methane: in waterlogged soils and bogs, where there is no oxygen, methane-producing archaea release methane.
In drier, aerated soils other bacteria oxidise methane, so soils can be a source or a sink of methane.
Beyond cycling nutrients, soil microorganisms shape the soil itself and affect how well plants grow. Farming methods can help or harm them.
Soil structure: fungal hyphae bind soil particles together, and bacteria make sticky polysaccharides, forming crumbs, called aggregates, with air spaces between them.
This structure improves drainage and aeration and reduces erosion.
A healthy, diverse soil microbiome suppresses some plant diseases, by competition and by antibiotic production.
Some bacteria and fungi promote plant growth, e.g. nitrogen fixers and mycorrhizae.
Intensive farming, with heavy use of artificial fertiliser and pesticides, frequent ploughing and compaction, can reduce soil microbial diversity.

Practices such as adding manure or compost, growing clover, reduced ploughing and crop rotation support soil microbial diversity. There is more on this in Ethics and sustainability of nutrient cycling.
Soil microorganisms respire faster when it is warmer. Because soils hold so much carbon, this can feed back into climate warming.

A rise in temperature speeds up the enzyme-controlled respiration of soil microorganisms, up to their optimum (the temperature at which their enzymes work best), so they decompose soil organic matter faster and release more CO₂.
Long-term field experiments have measured extra loss of soil carbon as CO₂ from warmed plots: forest soil plots are warmed by buried heating cables and compared with unheated plots.
Soils store more carbon than the atmosphere and all plants together, so even a small proportional loss matters.
Extra CO₂ released by warming adds to the greenhouse effect, which causes more warming, which speeds decomposition further.
This positive feedback (a change that drives more of the same change) is a major uncertainty in climate predictions.
Two kinds of waterlogged or frozen ground hold carbon that microorganisms can't normally break down. Warming can release it.
In the Arctic, frozen soils, called permafrost, store huge amounts of undecomposed organic matter.
As permafrost thaws, microorganisms decompose this matter, releasing CO₂ and, in waterlogged thawed soil, methane, a more powerful greenhouse gas.
Irish bogs store carbon as peat, because waterlogging stops decomposition.
Warmer, drier summers, and draining, lower the water table and let air in, so aerobic microorganisms decompose the peat and release CO₂.
Warmer waterlogged peat also releases more methane. There is more on this in Climate change and biological strategies.
Warming and drought also change nutrient cycling and which microorganisms dominate. How big the long-term effect will be is still being researched.
Warming can speed up the release of ammonium and nitrate, giving plants more nutrients in the short term but causing more leaching (washing out by water) of nitrate.
Warming can also increase the nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas, released by nitrifying and denitrifying bacteria.
Drought reduces microbial activity, and rewetting dry soil causes a sudden burst of CO₂ release.
Warming and drought change which species dominate, e.g. the balance of bacteria and fungi, which can change how fast nutrients are cycled.
In some long-term experiments the extra CO₂ release declined after some years, because the easily decomposed carbon was used up or the microbial community adjusted (acclimatised).
How large the long-term feedback will be is still being researched.
Aim: to show that soil microorganisms release CO₂ by respiration, and that they do so faster when warmer.

Independent variable: temperature, e.g. 5 °C, 15 °C and 25 °C. The dependent variable is the time the indicator takes to change colour. Equal masses of the same fresh soil keep other variables constant.
1. Put equal masses, e.g. 20 g, of the same fresh soil into sealed containers, each with a small open tube of hydrogencarbonate indicator (or limewater) suspended above the soil, not touching it.
2. Set up a control with the same mass of soil that has been sterilised by heating in an oven, so its microorganisms are dead.
3. Keep sets at different temperatures, e.g. 5 °C, 15 °C and 25 °C, in the dark.
4. Record the time for the indicator to change from red to yellow (more CO₂), or for the limewater to turn milky.
Expected result: the colour changes fastest at the highest temperature, and not, or very little, in the sterilised control. The control shows the CO₂ comes from living microorganisms.
Keep the apparatus in the dark, so that no photosynthesis by algae or seedlings removes CO₂.
Safety: wash hands after handling soil.
Two skills matter for microbiome questions: reading the CO₂ indicator, and judging published studies.
Hydrogencarbonate indicator colours: red (orange-red) at normal air CO₂ levels, yellow when CO₂ rises, and purple when CO₂ falls.

Secondary data to explore include published results of microbiome sequencing studies, e.g. comparisons of the gut microbiomes of people on different diets, or of babies born vaginally and by caesarean section.
Long-term soil-warming experiments and soil carbon measurements are also secondary data to explore.
When evaluating these data, check the sample size, whether the study was in humans or animals, and whether it shows correlation or cause. There is more on this in Evaluating evidence.
Matter is not created or destroyed, so the elements living things are built from have to be reused. Carbon is the clearest example: it moves round and round between organisms and their surroundings.
A biogeochemical cycle, or nutrient cycle, is the continuous movement of a chemical element between living things (bio) and the non-living environment (geo): the air, water, rocks and soil.

Matter is not created or destroyed, so the same atoms are used again and again. Energy, by contrast, flows through an ecosystem once and is lost as heat. There is more on this in Energy and nutrient transfer.

Carbon is the element at the centre of every biomolecule (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids; see Biomolecules and metabolism), so every organism needs a constant supply. Producers (organisms that make their own food, such as plants) take it in as CO₂; consumers get it already built into food.

A store (reservoir) is a place where carbon is held: the atmosphere (as CO₂, and a little methane, CH₄); living organisms (biomass, the mass of living material); dead organic matter in soil; the oceans (dissolved CO₂, hydrogencarbonate and carbonate); rocks such as limestone and chalk (calcium carbonate); and fossil fuels.
A process, or flux, is whatever moves carbon from one store to another. Stores are the boxes of the cycle and processes are the arrows between them.
CO₂ makes up only about 0.04% of the air (over 420 parts per million), yet it is the source of carbon for almost all life on Earth, because photosynthesis starts from it.
Carbon dioxide leaves the air in only a few ways. By far the most important is photosynthesis, but dissolving in water and shell building also lock carbon away.

Photosynthesis by plants, algae and phytoplankton (tiny floating algae) fixes CO₂ into glucose and then into the rest of their biomass, so they act as carbon sinks (stores that take in more carbon than they release).
Photosynthesis is the only major route by which carbon enters living things, so nearly all the carbon in a food chain started as CO₂ taken in by a producer.
Dissolving: CO₂ dissolves in the surface of the oceans, lakes and rivers, and aquatic producers take it up for photosynthesis.
Shell and skeleton building: many marine organisms (e.g. corals, molluscs and some phytoplankton) combine dissolved carbonate with calcium to make calcium carbonate shells and skeletons.

When these organisms die, their shells and skeletons settle on the sea floor and, over millions of years, form limestone and chalk. These rocks are very long-term stores because the carbon stays locked in them for so long.
Once carbon is in a producer it does not stay there. It passes along the food chain and into the dead matter that every organism leaves behind.

Feeding: carbon in the producer's biomass passes to herbivores and then carnivores when they eat and digest it. At each step most of it is respired away (broken down to release energy, giving off CO₂) rather than built into the consumer's body.
Each step in a food chain is a trophic level (a feeding level). There is more on this in Energy and nutrient transfer.

Egestion and excretion: carbon leaves animals in faeces and in wastes such as urea, and enters the dead organic matter store, as do shed leaves and dead organisms. This store is the food supply for decomposers.
Carbon dioxide is put back into the air by respiration, by decomposers, by burning and by geological release. If it were not returned, producers would run out of CO₂.
Respiration by plants, animals and microorganisms breaks down glucose and releases CO₂. Details are in Respiration as a catabolic process.

Plants respire all the time, day and night, so the respiration arrow must start from plants as well as animals. Over a growing season photosynthesis exceeds respiration, so the plant as a whole gains carbon.
Combustion: burning biomass (wood, peat, forest fires) or fossil fuels combines the carbon with oxygen and releases it as CO₂ very quickly.
Natural geological release: volcanoes release CO₂ from rocks, and the weathering of limestone releases some. This is small compared with the biological fluxes and with fossil-fuel burning.
Dead organisms, faeces and fallen leaves contain a lot of carbon. Decomposers are the living things that break this matter down and return its carbon to the air, so the cycle can keep turning.

Decomposers are bacteria and fungi. They feed saprophytically (on dead organic matter): they secrete enzymes that digest the matter outside their cells, absorb the products, and respire them, releasing CO₂ and minerals.
Say that decomposers digest the matter and then respire the products. The CO₂ comes from their respiration, not from the matter breaking down into CO₂ directly.

Without decomposers, carbon would stay locked in dead matter and the CO₂ supply for photosynthesis would run out. There is more on this in Bacteria and fungi, and soil microbiomes are covered in The microbiome.
Decomposers work fastest when it is warm, moist and well aerated, because they respire aerobically (using oxygen).
In cold, waterlogged, acidic or oxygen-poor places decomposition is very slow, so dead matter builds up, e.g. as peat in bogs.

Anaerobic decomposition: where there is no oxygen (waterlogged soils, bogs, rice paddies, landfill, slurry tanks and the stomachs of cattle and sheep), some microorganisms break organic matter down to methane (CH₄) instead of CO₂.
The methane-producing microorganisms are archaea, a separate group of single-celled organisms from bacteria (see Domains of life). Methane in the air is slowly converted to CO₂.
Fossil fuels are a store of carbon that the natural cycle leaves almost untouched. People now burn them, which is why they matter so much to the carbon cycle.
Fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas) are the remains of organisms that lived millions of years ago and were buried before they could decompose fully.

Coal formed mainly from land plants in ancient swamps. Oil and natural gas formed mainly from tiny marine organisms (plankton) buried in sea-floor mud. Heat and pressure over millions of years changed them into fuels.

The carbon in fossil fuels was fixed by photosynthesis long ago, so they store ancient solar energy and carbon. Peat is an early stage of the same process, which is why it is sometimes counted with them.
In the natural cycle almost no carbon leaves this store.

Burning fossil fuels since the Industrial Revolution moves carbon locked away for millions of years into the atmosphere in a few centuries, far faster than photosynthesis and the oceans can take it back, so atmospheric CO₂ rises. Consequences are in Climate change and biological strategies.

Whether a store helps to lower or raise atmospheric CO₂ depends on whether carbon is flowing in or out. Photosynthesis shows how plants act as sinks; here the sink and source distinction is applied to every store and to the overall balance of the cycle.
A store acts as a sink when its inputs exceed its outputs, so it gains carbon, and as a source when its outputs exceed its inputs, so it releases carbon.

The same store can switch between the two: a growing forest is a sink; a mature forest roughly balances; a burning or felled forest is a source. A healthy wet bog is a sink; a drained or burning bog is a source.

The main natural sinks on a carbon-cycle diagram are land plants (forests and grassland, with the soil carbon under them); algae and phytoplankton in the oceans (with dissolving CO₂ and shells sinking to the sea floor); bogs and other wetlands; and limestone and fossil fuels as very long-term stores.
These sinks are compared, and the strategies that use them are described, in Climate change and biological strategies.

Before large-scale fossil-fuel burning, the CO₂ taken up by photosynthesis and the oceans each year was roughly balanced by the CO₂ released by respiration, decomposition and natural fires. Atmospheric CO₂ therefore stayed nearly constant, at about 280 parts per million before the Industrial Revolution.
Deforestation and fossil-fuel burning have tipped this balance, so more CO₂ is now added than removed.

Seasonal pattern: atmospheric CO₂ falls each northern summer, when photosynthesis exceeds respiration over the large land area of the northern hemisphere, and rises each winter, when respiration and decomposition exceed photosynthesis. This happens on top of the long-term rise.
A model represents the cycle in a diagram and in words, and is used to explain and predict. It is only as good as its limits allow.
Diagram: draw boxes for the stores: carbon dioxide in the air; green plants and algae; animals; dead organisms and wastes; decomposers (bacteria and fungi); fossil fuels; oceans.

Diagram arrows, each labelled with its process: photosynthesis (air → plants); feeding (plants → animals); death and excretion (plants and animals → dead matter); decomposition (dead matter → decomposers); respiration (plants, animals and decomposers → air).
Diagram arrows, continued: fossilisation (dead matter → fossil fuels, over millions of years); combustion (fossil fuels and wood → air); dissolving (air ↔ oceans).
Prediction (a): cutting down and burning a forest removes photosynthesis and adds combustion and the decomposition of the remains, so atmospheric CO₂ rises.
Prediction (b): draining a bog lets air in, so aerobic decomposers break down the peat and release CO₂.

Prediction (c): if decomposers were killed (e.g. by soil made very acidic or polluted), dead matter would accumulate, minerals would not be returned to the soil, and plant growth would eventually fall.

Limitation: a diagram shows the processes but not how much carbon moves or how fast. It also treats each store as one box, although the oceans, soils and forests each hold carbon for very different lengths of time.
Limitation: it simplifies feedbacks, e.g. warming speeds up decomposition, which releases more CO₂. It is also a snapshot that hides seasonal and long-term change. There is more on this in Models.

Every living thing needs nitrogen, yet the huge store in the air is out of reach for almost all of them. Nitrogen therefore has to be converted into usable forms and then recycled, or life would run out of it.

Living things need nitrogen to make amino acids and proteins, nucleic acids (DNA and RNA), ATP (the cell's energy carrier) and chlorophyll (the green pigment in plants). Minerals goes into why plants need it and the signs of deficiency.
About 78% of the air is nitrogen gas (N₂), but plants and animals cannot use it. The two atoms are held together by a very strong triple bond that few organisms can break.

Plants can absorb nitrogen only as ions dissolved in soil water, mainly nitrate (NO₃⁻) and also ammonium (NH₄⁺). So nitrogen must be converted, or fixed, before it enters food chains, and recycled from dead matter.

The forms to recognise are nitrogen gas (N₂); ammonia (NH₃) and ammonium (NH₄⁺); nitrite (NO₂⁻); nitrate (NO₃⁻); and organic nitrogen, which is nitrogen built into proteins, nucleic acids and urea (the waste molecule in mammals' urine).

Nitrogen fixation converts nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds that living things can use, such as ammonium, ammonia or nitrate. The biological route is carried out by bacteria, either living freely or in partnership with plants.
Free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soil and in water convert N₂ to ammonium, which they use to make their own proteins. When they die, decomposition releases the nitrogen to the soil.
Other nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in root nodules (small swellings on the roots) of legumes, the pea family, for example clover, peas and beans. They fix nitrogen for the plant.

The bacteria give the plant ammonium, which it uses to make amino acids. The plant gives the bacteria carbohydrates from photosynthesis and a protected, low-oxygen home. Both benefit, so this is mutualism.

Fixation takes a lot of energy, supplied as ATP from the bacteria's respiration, and uses an enzyme that oxygen damages. This is why nodules keep oxygen levels low: they contain a red pigment that binds oxygen, so active nodules are pink inside.
Legumes grow well in nitrogen-poor soil because their bacteria supply the nitrogen. When they die or are ploughed in, the nitrogen in their tissues enriches the soil.
Clover grown with grass, and legumes in crop rotation (growing different crops in turn on the same field), reduce the need for nitrogen fertiliser. This is why farmers grow clover.
Bacteria are not the only route from nitrogen gas to usable nitrogen. Lightning does a little of it naturally, and humans do a great deal of it in factories.

Atmospheric fixation by lightning: the energy of lightning makes nitrogen react with oxygen to form nitrogen oxides, which dissolve in rain and reach the soil as nitrate. This is a small contribution compared with biological fixation.
Industrial fixation by the Haber process: nitrogen from the air combines with hydrogen (made mainly from natural gas) at high temperature and pressure to make ammonia.
The ammonia is turned into nitrogen fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate and urea, which farmers spread to give crops usable nitrogen.
Human activity, mainly the Haber process, now fixes at least as much nitrogen each year as all natural processes on land. There is more on this in Ethics and sustainability of nutrient cycling.
Once nitrogen is in the soil as nitrate or ammonium, it moves into living things and along food chains. Assimilation means the plant builds absorbed nitrogen into its own molecules.

Uptake: plant roots absorb nitrate and ammonium from soil water. Nitrate is taken in by active transport, against its concentration gradient, using ATP, and travels to the leaves in the xylem (the tubes that carry water up the plant).
Assimilation: the plant uses the nitrogen, together with sugars from photosynthesis, to make amino acids, then proteins, and also nucleic acids and chlorophyll.
Feeding: animals get nitrogen only by eating plants or other animals. They digest the proteins into amino acids and build their own proteins from them.
Excretion and death: animals excrete excess nitrogen (in mammals, as urea in urine). Faeces, urine, dead plants and dead animals return organic nitrogen to the soil.
Dead matter and wastes are full of organic nitrogen that plants cannot use directly. Decomposition is the step that turns it back into a usable form.

Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) feed on dead organisms, faeces and urine. They digest the proteins and other nitrogen compounds and release the nitrogen as ammonia, which dissolves in soil water as ammonium (NH₄⁺). This step is often called ammonification (putrefaction).
Without decomposition, the nitrogen in dead matter would be locked up and the soil would run out of usable nitrogen.
Decomposition is fastest in warm, moist, aerated soil (soil with air spaces), because these conditions suit the decomposers. There is more on this in The carbon cycle.
Ammonium is the starting point for nitrification. Some ammonium is also taken up directly by plants.
Ammonium from decomposition is not the form plants take up most. Nitrifying bacteria in the soil convert it to nitrate in two steps.

Nitrification is the conversion of ammonium into nitrate by nitrifying bacteria in the soil, in two steps. First, one group of nitrifying bacteria oxidises ammonium (NH₄⁺) to nitrite (NO₂⁻). Second, a second group oxidises nitrite to nitrate (NO₃⁻).

Nitrifying bacteria are aerobic: they need oxygen. Nitrification is therefore fastest in well-drained, well-aerated soil. Ploughing and draining help it, while waterlogging (soil with all its air spaces filled with water) stops it.
Nitrifying bacteria are autotrophic (they make their own food): they get energy from these chemical reactions (chemosynthesis) rather than from light or from eating other organisms.

Nitrate is the form plants absorb most. It is also very soluble and is not held by soil particles, so heavy rain easily washes it out of the soil (leaching) into ground water, rivers and lakes. There is more on this in Ethics and sustainability of nutrient cycling.
Nitrification builds up nitrate in the soil. Denitrification is the opposite journey, returning nitrogen to the air and completing the cycle.
Denitrification is the conversion of nitrate in the soil back into nitrogen gas (N₂) by denitrifying bacteria. This returns nitrogen to the atmosphere and completes the cycle.

Denitrifying bacteria work in anaerobic conditions (no oxygen), such as waterlogged, compacted or poorly drained soils and the mud of lakes and marshes. They use nitrate in place of oxygen in respiration.
Denitrification removes usable nitrogen from the soil, lowering fertility, so farmers drain wet land to stop it.
It also gives off some nitrous oxide (N₂O), a greenhouse gas (one that traps heat in the atmosphere). There is more on this in Climate change and biological strategies.
In wetlands and water treatment, denitrification is useful because it removes excess nitrate before it reaches rivers.
Fixation, decomposition, nitrification and denitrification are the four named processes of the cycle. Comparing them side by side shows what each converts, who does it, and what it needs.
Fixation: N₂ becomes ammonium. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (free-living or in nodules) do it. It is anaerobic inside a nodule, and it adds usable nitrogen.
Decomposition: organic nitrogen becomes ammonium. Bacteria and fungi do it. It is aerobic or anaerobic, and it recycles nitrogen.
Nitrification: ammonium becomes nitrite and then nitrate. Nitrifying bacteria do it. It needs oxygen, and it makes the form plants use most.
