The protein affected in cystic fibrosis is CFTR, a channel that moves chloride ions across cell membranes.
Huntington's disease: gene HTT (huntingtin), chromosome 4 (4p16.3); autosomal dominant.

The Huntington's allele has too many repeats of the three bases CAG near the start of the gene: 40 or more repeats cause the disease, 36 to 39 may or may not, and unaffected people usually have 26 or fewer.
Each CAG codes for the amino acid glutamine, so the huntingtin protein carries an abnormally long chain of glutamines, which damages nerve cells in the brain.
Third example (optional, may be given as a row in the table): sickle-cell anaemia; gene HBB (beta-globin), chromosome 11 (11p15.4); autosomal recessive.
The sickle-cell allele is one base substitution changing glutamic acid to valine in beta-globin (haemoglobin S).
OMIM is one source. NCBI and Ensembl let you look up the same gene again, which is how you check a result.
NCBI: choose the Gene database, search the gene name with "human" (for example "CFTR human"), and open the human gene record.
The NCBI gene record gives the official name, the chromosome location, a summary of what the gene does, and links to OMIM and ClinVar.
In ClinVar, a search for the gene lists the variants reported in patients, each with a classification: pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance, likely benign or benign.
A disease-causing allele is one classified as pathogenic, which is why not every variant in the database counts as one.
Ensembl: choose the human genome, search for the gene name, and open the gene page.
The Ensembl gene page shows the gene's position on the chromosome, its coding and non-coding sections, and a table of known variants with their consequences.
The same gene can be viewed in other species to see how similar it is.
The results show what databases do well. They also show why a database result is only part of the picture.
Each disease is caused by alleles of a single gene at a known chromosome location.
Cystic fibrosis is recessive, so a person needs two disease-causing alleles, while Huntington's disease is dominant, so one is enough.
Databases record many different disease-causing alleles of the same gene.
Many variants are of "uncertain significance", meaning it is not yet known whether they cause disease.
Most common diseases, such as heart disease and type 2 diabetes, involve many genes and the environment, so no single allele "causes" them.
Databases contain far more data from people of European ancestry than from other populations, so variants in other groups are less well understood.
Databases are for research and professionals, so a result should be interpreted with a doctor or genetic counsellor. There is more on the privacy of genetic data in Ethics of genetic technologies.
A DNA profile is a pattern of bands on a gel (a jelly-like slab), one set of bands for each person. This investigation uses those patterns to answer two questions about who a piece of DNA came from.
Aim: to compare DNA profiles in order to (a) find whether a suspect’s DNA matches DNA from a crime scene and (b) find which of several men could be the biological father of a child.
The data may be primary, which means you collect it yourself: a gel the student runs with DNA samples supplied in a school kit, already copied or cut and ready to load.
Or the data may be secondary, which means someone else collected it: profiles given as diagrams, tables of band sizes or repeat numbers, or from a published case or simulation.

Hypotheses to write, for example: “The crime-scene DNA came from suspect B”; “Man X is the biological father of the child”. The null outcome (the result if the hypothesis is wrong) is an exclusion, meaning the person is ruled out.
A fair test changes one thing and keeps everything else the same. Here the only thing that should differ between lanes is whose DNA is loaded, and controls let you trust the bands you see.
Independent variable (the thing you change): the source of each DNA sample, that is, each person.
Dependent variable (the thing you measure): the position of each band, measured as the distance it travels from the well (the slot the sample is loaded into) in mm, or its size read from the ladder.
Controlled variables (kept the same): the gel, with all samples on the same gel and the same agarose and buffer, the volume of each sample loaded, the voltage and running time, and the staining time.
Control: a DNA ladder (size marker, a mixture of fragments of known sizes) in one lane, so band sizes can be read and different gels compared.
Negative control: a lane loaded with loading dye and buffer but no DNA should show no bands, so any band there shows contamination.
In a real case, a reference sample of known origin (positive control) is run beside the unknowns, so you can see that the method works and what a known person’s profile looks like.
The equipment makes a gel, passes an electric current through it and makes the invisible DNA visible. Knowing what each item is for helps you recall the list.

Making the gel: gel casting tray and comb (the comb makes the wells), agarose powder and running buffer as the kit instructions give, a conical flask, and a microwave (or hot plate) to melt the agarose, with a heat-resistant glove.
Running the gel: electrophoresis tank with lid and electrodes, and a power pack to supply the current.
Loading: micropipette and tips (or fine plastic droppers), DNA samples with loading dye (crime scene and suspects; or mother, child and possible fathers), and a DNA ladder.

Staining and recording: a DNA stain safe for schools (for example methylene blue, which is viewed in white light) and a staining tray, a white light box, a ruler, and a camera or phone to record the gel.
Electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size in an electric field. First you make the agarose gel with wells in it, then load each person’s sample into its own well.
1. Mix agarose powder with running buffer in a conical flask and heat it, swirling, until it dissolves and the liquid is clear.

2. Let it cool until the flask can be held (about 55–60 °C), then pour it into the casting tray with the comb in place at one end. Leave it to set (it becomes firm and cloudy). Remove the comb gently, leaving a row of wells.

3. Place the gel in the tank with the wells at the negative (black) electrode end, and pour in running buffer until the gel is just covered. DNA is negatively charged, so it will move away from the wells towards the positive end.

4. Using a fresh micropipette tip for each sample, so that samples don’t mix, load the same volume of each sample into its own well. Hold the tip just inside the well without piercing the bottom of the gel, and push the plunger slowly.
Load the ladder in the first well and the no-DNA control in another. Record which sample is in which lane, because the lanes cannot be told apart once the gel is stained.
Once the samples are loaded, the current moves the DNA through the gel. The bands then have to be stained before you can see and measure them.

5. Put the lid on and connect the leads, black to black (negative) and red to red (positive): DNA “runs to red”. Switch on at the voltage the kit instructions give. Bubbles rising from the electrodes show that current is flowing.

6. Run until the coloured loading dye has moved about three-quarters of the length of the gel, without letting it run off the end, because the DNA would be lost with it. Switch off the power pack before removing the lid.

7. Wearing gloves, move the gel to a staining tray, cover it with stain for the time the kit gives, then pour off the stain and rinse (destain) with water until the bands show clearly against a pale background.
8. View the gel on a white light box, photograph it beside a ruler, and measure the distance from the well to each band.
9. Repeat with a second gel, or compare with other groups’ gels, to check that the pattern is repeatable.

Option where no DNA kit is available: food dyes loaded on an agarose gel separate into bands as they move in the electric field. This models the method (loading, running, band patterns), but the dyes separate by their charge and size, not as DNA fragments.
This practical combines electricity, water, hot liquid and chemical stains, so each stage has its own hazard and its own precaution.

Electricity and water: switch the power pack off before connecting or disconnecting leads or opening the lid; keep the lid on while running; don’t touch the buffer while the current is on; keep hands and bench dry; use only low-voltage equipment designed for schools.
Hot agarose can boil over suddenly in a microwave and cause burns: heat in short bursts, swirl with a heat-resistant glove, point the flask away from people, and wear safety glasses.
Stains mark skin and clothing, and some are harmful, so wear gloves and glasses. Don’t use ethidium bromide or UV light in school.
Handle micropipettes carefully, dispose of gels and tips as the teacher directs, and wash hands after the practical.

In a forensic case you compare DNA left at a crime scene with DNA from each suspect. This is an invented teaching example, not a real case. Each number is the number of repeats of an allele (a version of the gene region); each allele is one band, and more repeats means a longer fragment, nearer the wells.
Method: 1. Compare the crime-scene lane with each suspect’s lane, one locus (a fixed position on a chromosome, shown as a band or pair of bands) at a time.
2. A suspect matches only if every band is in the same position as a crime-scene band and there are no extra or missing bands.
3. One mismatched band at any locus excludes the suspect, because the DNA cannot have come from someone with a different pattern.
4. A single band at a locus means the person has two alleles with the same number of repeats, so both alleles run at the same position.
Crime scene: locus 1, 12 and 15; locus 2, 8 only; locus 3, 10 and 13. Suspect A: 12 and 15; 8 and 9; 10 and 13. Suspect B: 12 and 15; 8 only; 10 and 13. Suspect C: 11 and 15; 8 only; 10 and 13.
Analysis: suspect A has an extra band (9) at locus 2, so is excluded; suspect C has 11 instead of 12 at locus 1, so is excluded; suspect B matches at all three loci.
Conclusion: suspect B cannot be excluded and is very likely the source of the crime-scene DNA; A and C did not leave it.
A real profile tests more than ten loci, which makes a chance match between unrelated people extremely unlikely. There is more on this in DNA profiling.

A child inherits one allele at each locus from the mother and one from the father. To test a possible father, first remove the mother’s contribution, then see which man has the bands that are left. This is an invented teaching example, not a real case.
Method: 1. At each locus, find which of the child’s bands it shares with the mother (the maternal band).
2. The child’s other band must have come from the father (the paternal band).
3. A man who lacks the paternal band at any locus is excluded as the father. 4. A man who has every paternal band cannot be excluded; he is very likely to be the father.
Mother: locus 1, 10 and 14; locus 2, 7 and 9; locus 3, 11 and 12. Child: locus 1, 10 and 16; locus 2, 9 only (two alleles of 9); locus 3, 12 and 15.
Man X: 13 and 16; 6 and 9; 15 only. Man Y: 16 and 17; 7 and 8; 11 and 15. Man Z: 12 and 16; 9 and 10; 13 and 14.
Analysis: the child’s maternal bands are 10 (locus 1), 9 (locus 2) and 12 (locus 3), all present in the mother. So the paternal bands must be 16, 9 and 15.
Man X has 16, 9 and 15, so he cannot be excluded. Man Y has no 9 at locus 2, so he is excluded. Man Z has no 15 at locus 3, so he is excluded. Conclusion: man X is very likely the biological father.

Diagram: a gel for the paternity case, lanes for ladder, mother, child, X, Y and Z; join each of the child’s bands by a line to the matching band in the mother or man X. Labels: wells, ladder, maternal band, paternal band.
The forensic case can be drawn the same way.
Results need to be recorded in a form someone else can check. The conclusion then says who matches or is excluded, which band decides it, and whether the hypothesis is supported.

Record primary data as a labelled drawing or photograph of the gel, and a table of each lane’s bands (distance from the well in mm, or size read from the ladder). Bands at the same distance on the same gel are the same size.

Reading sizes: compare each band with the ladder; for a more exact size, plot a graph of the ladder’s known fragment sizes (on a logarithmic scale) against distance travelled, and read the unknown bands’ sizes from it.
Conclusion: state whether each person matches or is excluded, giving the locus or band that decides it, and say whether the results support the hypothesis.

A match supports, but does not prove, that the DNA came from that person, because unrelated people could share a pattern by chance; an exclusion is definite if the results are reliable. There is more on this in DNA profiling.
Identical twins give identical profiles, because they come from one fertilised egg and so have the same DNA.
Brothers and sisters share some but not all bands, because each inherits a random one of each parent’s two alleles at each locus.
Every band of a child is found in at least one parent, because the child receives one allele at each locus from each parent.
A gel can go wrong at every stage, from loading to staining, and the faults show up in particular ways. Knowing the cause of each fault lets you name an error and say how it affects the bands.
Contamination: DNA from the student or a reused tip gives extra bands, shown by bands in the no-DNA control lane.
Loading errors: piercing the well bottom loses sample; air bubbles or overfilling cause sample to spill into the next well, mixing lanes; unequal volumes give bands of different strength.
Running errors: wells at the positive end send the DNA off the gel into the buffer; too short a run leaves bands too close together to separate; too long a run sends small fragments off the end.
Smeared or faint bands come from too much or degraded DNA, or from too short a staining time.
Measuring band distances by eye and ruler has limited precision; repeat measurements or have a second person check them.
Secondary data: check the source and whether profiles were run on the same gel; bands on different gels can be compared only through the ladder.

Genetic technologies raise questions that experiments cannot answer, so exam answers need a method for reasoning about them. Follow the same five steps every time and you will always cover both sides and reach a conclusion.
1. Say what the technology does and what is new about it, so that the reader knows exactly what is being judged.
2. Identify who is affected: the person tested or treated, relatives, future children, society, other species, and the environment.

3. Give arguments for and against, linking each to a principle: autonomy and consent (people decide for themselves, with full information), doing good (beneficence), avoiding harm (non-maleficence), justice and fairness, privacy, and the precautionary principle.
The precautionary principle means taking care when the risks are unknown. There is more on these principles in “Science, scientists and society”.
4. Say what rules or safeguards exist or could be added, such as laws, consent procedures or ethics committees.
5. Reach a justified conclusion, which means a decision that follows from the arguments you have given.

Ethics is decided by reasoning about values informed by evidence: science says what can be done and with what risks, not whether it should be done. This is why two people can agree on the science and still disagree on the ethics.
Genetic data is the information in a person’s DNA, for example a genome sequence or a test result. It raises ethical problems that ordinary personal data does not, for three reasons.
Genetic data is permanent: it cannot be changed like a password, so once it is leaked the damage cannot be undone.
It identifies a person, and it predicts some future health risks, so it is both highly personal and potentially harmful if misused.
It is shared with relatives, so one person’s test reveals information about family members who did not consent.
Under the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, applying since 2018), genetic data is a special category of personal data with extra protection.

Researchers can learn far more about disease when they can study many people’s genomes alongside their health records. This benefit has to be set against the risks to the people who donate their data.

For: large databases of genomes and health records (biobanks) speed research into the causes and treatments of disease, and allow faster diagnosis of rare diseases. There is more on this in “Bioinformatics: genome databases”.
Against: there is a risk of data leaks, or of re-identification of people from “anonymous” data, because a genome is so distinctive that removing a name does not always hide who it belongs to.
Against: people must give informed consent and know how their data will be used and shared, otherwise their autonomy is not respected.
Against: questions arise about who profits from discoveries made with donated data, because the people who donated it may not share in the benefit.
Insurers and employers would like to know about a person’s health risks. Genetic data could give them that knowledge, which is why laws now limit its use.

Risk: insurers or employers could charge more or refuse people with a high genetic risk. This would be unjust, because people don’t choose their genes, and fear of it could stop people having useful tests.
In Ireland the Disability Act 2005 prohibits the use of genetic test results in insurance, pensions, mortgages and employment.
In the USA the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (2008) protects against discrimination in health insurance and employment.
Argument on the other side: insurers say that if customers know their risk and insurers don’t, pricing becomes unfair, because people at high risk could buy cover cheaply.

Police can store DNA profiles (the pattern of a person’s DNA used to identify them) from crime scenes and from people they arrest. This helps solve crimes but puts a great deal of personal information in state hands.
For: national DNA databases solve crimes, including old cases, and clear innocent people.
Ireland’s database was set up under the Criminal Justice (Forensic Evidence and DNA Database System) Act 2014.
Against: privacy, especially when profiles are kept of people who were arrested but never convicted.
In S and Marper v United Kingdom (2008), the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the UK’s keeping of the DNA of people not convicted of any crime breached their right to privacy.
Against: groups that are policed more heavily are over-represented on databases, so they are more likely to be matched or wrongly suspected.
Against: a match can be given too much weight in court. There is more on this in “DNA profiling”.
People send DNA to companies to learn about their ancestry. That data can be used for purposes the customer never intended, and it also exposes their relatives.
People send DNA to companies for ancestry tests, and may upload it to public genealogy websites so that they can find relatives.
In 2018 police in California identified the “Golden State Killer”, Joseph James DeAngelo, by matching crime-scene DNA with distant relatives who had uploaded their DNA to such a website.
For: serious crimes were solved. Against: the relatives never consented to police use of their DNA, which shows how one person’s upload can expose others.
Company data can be hacked or sold: in 2023 a data breach at the testing company 23andMe exposed the ancestry information of millions of customers.

Developing genetic tests and treatments is expensive, and companies protect their investment with patents (legal rights to be the only seller of an invention). The question is whether a part of the human body can be owned.
For: companies invest in genetic tests and treatments and need patents to recover the cost.
Against: patenting human genes lets one company control testing and set high prices.

In 2013 the US Supreme Court ruled, in the case against Myriad Genetics, which held patents on the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes (genes linked to breast cancer risk), that naturally occurring human DNA cannot be patented.
After this ruling, other laboratories began offering BRCA tests, so patent control had been keeping testing limited. There is more on BRCA genes in “Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer”.
Justice: benefits from the genetic resources of poorer countries (e.g. crop varieties, local plants) should be shared with them, rather than all the profit going to the companies that develop them.
Genetic data is also collected on crops and farm animals, and the same questions of access and ownership arise.
For: genetic data on crops and livestock speeds the breeding of higher-yielding, disease-resistant varieties, because breeders can pick out useful alleles quickly.
Against: control of seed varieties and their genetic data by a few large companies, and loss of traditional varieties, which could leave farmers dependent and food supplies less varied.
A GM (genetically modified) crop has had a gene from another organism added to its DNA. Supporters see this as a way to grow more food with less damage to the environment.
Higher yields and less crop loss, because the crop resists pests or disease or tolerates harsh conditions.
Bt crops (which make a natural insecticide, the Bt toxin) need less insecticide spraying, which protects farm workers and other insects. There is more on this in “Genetic engineering”.
Crops can be modified for drought or salt tolerance, or for added nutrition, such as Golden Rice, which is designed to help tackle vitamin A deficiency.
GM crops could help feed a growing population on less land.
Major scientific bodies have found approved GM foods to be as safe to eat as their conventional equivalents.
Opponents of GM crops raise concerns about the environment, farmers’ independence, people’s right to choose, and whether it is right to modify living things.
Genes can spread in pollen to wild relatives or to non-GM and organic crops nearby, a process called gene flow.

Weeds have evolved resistance to the herbicide glyphosate where herbicide-tolerant crops are sprayed repeatedly, and some insect pests have evolved resistance to Bt toxins. This is natural selection: resistant individuals survive and pass on their alleles. There is more on this in “The theory of evolution by natural selection”.
Large areas of a single crop reduce biodiversity, because fewer kinds of plant and animal can live there.
Patented seed must be bought each year, making farmers dependent on companies.
Consumers have a right to choose, so the EU requires food containing more than 0.9% GM material to be labelled.
Some people object that GM is unnatural (“playing God”).
Golden Rice is an example of a GM crop designed to improve health, and it shows both sides of the debate clearly.
Supporters say opposition has delayed a way to save children’s sight and lives, because vitamin A deficiency can cause blindness and death.
Opponents say vitamin A deficiency is better tackled by a more varied diet and supplements.
Its approval in the Philippines has been challenged in court.
Animals can also be genetically modified, either to produce more food or to help medical research. Animals feel pain and can escape, so the issues differ from those for crops.
For: faster-growing food animals such as AquAdvantage salmon need less feed per kilogram of food. There is more on this in “Genetic engineering”.
For: GM animals model human diseases in medical research, so treatments can be studied before they are tried in people.
Against: animal welfare, judged using the 3Rs (replace, reduce, refine animal use). There is more on this in “Science, scientists and society”.
Against: risk to wild populations if GM fish escape and breed, because their modified genes could spread.
Against: public unease about eating GM animals.

Gene therapy and gene editing change the DNA of a person’s own body cells (somatic cells, those that are not eggs or sperm) to treat disease. Because the change is not inherited, the ethical issues are fewer than for germline editing.
For: these can treat or cure serious genetic diseases, e.g. the CRISPR treatment for sickle-cell disease approved in the UK in 2023. There is more on this in “Genetic engineering”.
For: the changes are in the patient’s body cells only, so only a consenting patient is affected and nothing is passed on to children.
Against: long-term risks are not yet known, including edits at the wrong place in the genome.
Against: treatments are extremely expensive, so access is unequal (justice).

Germline editing changes eggs, sperm or embryos (the germline). Every cell of the resulting person carries the change, and so do their descendants, which makes it far more controversial than somatic therapy.
Changes to eggs, sperm or embryos would be passed to all future generations, who cannot consent.
In November 2018 the scientist He Jiankui announced in China the birth of twin girls whose embryos he had edited with CRISPR to try to make them resistant to HIV.
It was condemned worldwide as unsafe, unnecessary and done without proper consent, and he was sentenced to three years in prison in 2019.
For: it could in future remove a serious disease allele from a family permanently.
Against: unknown risks to future generations.
Against: it could lead to “designer babies” chosen for traits such as height or intelligence rather than to prevent disease, and could increase inequality.
Germline editing is not allowed in most countries.

Some serious diseases are caused by faulty mitochondrial DNA, which a child inherits from the mother’s egg. Mitochondrial donation replaces the faulty mitochondria with a donor’s healthy ones; the UK permitted it by law in 2015. There is more on the technique in “Nuclear and non-nuclear inheritance”.
For: it lets a woman with a mitochondrial disease have a genetically related child free of that disease.
For: the donor contributes only the mitochondrial DNA (37 genes), not the nuclear DNA that determines the child’s characteristics.
Against: it is a germline change, passed on by daughters to their children.
Against: long-term safety is still being studied.
Against: questions arise about the donor’s relationship to the child (the “three-parent baby”).
Against: some fear it is a step towards other germline changes.

DNA testing looks for disease alleles in a person’s DNA, unlike DNA profiling, which identifies people. The ethics depend on what the test is for, so each kind is taken in turn, starting with the most straightforward.
For: diagnostic testing confirms a diagnosis so that treatment can start.

For: carrier testing (finding out whether a healthy person carries one copy of a recessive disease allele, e.g. for cystic fibrosis, common in Ireland) informs people’s choices before having children. There is more on this in “Benefits and limitations of Mendelian genetics”.
Against: a positive result may reveal that relatives are also carriers, raising questions about whether and how to tell them.
Predictive testing finds out whether a healthy person will develop a disease later in life. It is most controversial when the disease has no cure.
Huntington’s disease is an example of a late-onset disease (one that appears in adulthood) with no cure. It is dominant, so a child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 risk.
For: predictive testing gives certainty, and the chance to plan life, career and family.
Against: a positive result may cause great distress, and many people at risk choose not to be tested.
Against: the right not to know (autonomy) must be respected.
Testing children is usually delayed until they can decide for themselves, because they cannot give informed consent and cannot be helped by knowing early.
Genetic counselling before and after testing is essential, so that people understand the choices and are supported with the result.
Some alleles only raise the chance of disease rather than guaranteeing it, and tests can also be done on embryos. Both create hard choices.

Testing for risk alleles (e.g. BRCA1 and BRCA2): a positive result gives a raised risk, not certainty, so people face hard decisions about preventive surgery. There is more on this in “Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer”.
A negative result may give false reassurance, because the person can still develop the disease for other reasons.

Preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) tests embryos made by IVF (in vitro fertilisation, fertilising eggs outside the body) so that only embryos without a serious disease allele are implanted. Prenatal tests on the foetus and newborn screening belong to “Prenatal and postnatal care”.
For: parents avoid passing on a serious disease.
Against: unused embryos are destroyed, which some people believe is wrong because an embryo has the moral status of a person.
Against: there is worry about choosing embryos for non-medical traits (sex, appearance).
Against: concern that it devalues the lives of people living with the condition.
Some companies sell genetic tests straight to the public, online, without a doctor’s involvement.
For: tests bought online are cheap and convenient, and respect autonomy because people choose to find out for themselves.
Against: results given without counselling may be misunderstood, and accuracy varies.
Against: they may reveal unexpected family relationships, e.g. that a parent is not the biological parent.
Against: data privacy, because the company holds the customer’s permanent genetic data. The ancestry tests and police access block above gives an example.
Stem cells are the body’s raw material for growing and repairing tissue. Their ethics depend on where they come from, so first learn the types and what each can become.

A stem cell is an unspecialised cell that can divide by mitosis to make more stem cells, and can differentiate (become specialised) into specialised cell types. There is more on this in “Levels of organisation”.
Embryonic stem cells, from the inner cell mass of an embryo about five days old (a blastocyst), are pluripotent: they can become any type of body cell.
Adult (tissue) stem cells, e.g. in bone marrow, skin and the lining of the gut, are multipotent: they can become only a few related cell types. Bone-marrow stem cells give rise to the blood cells.
Induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells are adult body cells (e.g. skin cells) reprogrammed in the laboratory, by switching on a few genes, to behave like embryonic stem cells.
Shinya Yamanaka first made iPS cells (in mice) in 2006, and shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with John Gurdon.
iPS cells avoid the use of embryos and, made from a patient’s own cells, would not be rejected by the immune system, because the cells are recognised as the patient’s own.
Because stem cells can replace lost or damaged cells, they are used or being tested as treatments for many conditions.
Bone-marrow (stem-cell) transplants already treat leukaemia and some other blood disorders. There is more on this in “Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer”.
Skin grown from stem cells treats severe burns.
Stem-cell treatments are being tested in clinical trials for conditions where cells are lost, e.g. Parkinson’s disease, type 1 diabetes, spinal cord injury, heart damage and some forms of blindness.
Stem cells grown into tissues are used to test new drugs and to study diseases.
A clone is a genetically identical copy. The same laboratory method can be used for two very different purposes, depending on whether the embryo is allowed to grow into an animal.
A clone is a genetically identical copy.

Reproductive cloning makes a whole organism by somatic cell nuclear transfer: the nucleus of a body cell is put into an egg cell whose own nucleus has been removed, the egg is stimulated to divide into an embryo, and the embryo is placed in a surrogate mother.
Dolly the sheep was born on 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh, Scotland. She was the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell (a cell from the udder), not an embryo cell.
Dolly was one success from 277 attempts, and died in 2003 aged six.
Therapeutic cloning uses the same method to make an early embryo only to obtain embryonic stem cells that match the patient; the embryo is not implanted, so no baby is produced.

Diagram: somatic cell nuclear transfer as a flow diagram: body cell from adult A → nucleus removed; egg from female B → its nucleus removed; nucleus of A inserted into the empty egg → embryo; then two arrows: implanted in surrogate mother → clone of A (reproductive cloning), or grown in the laboratory → embryonic stem cells → specialised cells for the patient (therapeutic cloning).
Embryonic stem cells can become any type of body cell, but getting them means destroying an embryo. This is why they are ethically controversial.
For: they have the potential to treat many serious diseases and relieve great suffering (beneficence).
For: the embryos used are often spare embryos from IVF that would otherwise be discarded.
Against: obtaining the cells destroys an embryo, which those who believe life begins at fertilisation regard as killing a human being.
Against: there is concern about creating embryos for research.
Adult stem cells and iPS cells largely avoid the embryo issue, but they have their own concerns.
iPS cells may carry a risk of tumours.
Unproven “stem-cell clinics” sell untested, expensive and sometimes harmful treatments to desperate patients.
Consent is needed from donors of cells and tissues.
Reproductive cloning produces a living animal or, in principle, a person. The arguments differ a great deal between animals and humans.
In animals, for: copying valuable farm animals or conserving endangered species.
In animals, against: low success rates, many failed pregnancies and animal suffering, and clones’ health problems (animal welfare).
Reproductive cloning in humans is almost universally rejected, because of the risk of serious abnormality, the clone’s identity and individuality, and the use of people as means to an end.
It is prohibited by the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union.
Research fraud has also damaged trust in this field (the Hwang Woo-suk case). There is more on this in “Science as a global enterprise”.
Therapeutic cloning aims to make stem cells genetically matched to a patient, but it raises the embryo issue again and adds a new problem about eggs.
For: it produces stem cells that exactly match the patient, so there is no rejection.
Against: embryos are created to be destroyed.
Against: it needs many donated eggs, and egg donation carries health risks and could exploit poor women if they are paid.
Against: it may make reproductive cloning easier.
The separate issues above keep returning to the same few principles, which is why they make a good checklist for any new genetic technology.

Common threads in all these issues: consent (including that of relatives and future generations, who cannot consent); privacy of permanent, shared genetic information; and fair access to expensive technologies (justice).
Two more threads: the precautionary principle where long-term effects are unknown, and the need for laws and independent ethics committees to keep up with fast-changing technology.
